title: Unbalanced Array: the checker proves size 4, JS returns 3, native fail-stops
body:
### What you did

Ran this file from the current `main` checkout:

```bend
import Base

def tree() -> Array<U32>:
  ANode{ANode{ALeaf{10}, ALeaf{20}}, ALeaf{30}}

def observed() -> U32:
  Pair.snd(Array<U32>, U32, Array.size(U32, tree()))

def theorem() -> {observed() == 4 : U32}:
  {==}

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(observed()))
```

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts array_soundness.bend
bun bend2/main.ts array_soundness.bend -o array_soundness.js
node array_soundness.js
bun bend2/main.ts array_soundness.bend -o array_soundness
./array_soundness
```

### What happened

The checker accepts `theorem`, so it proves that `observed()` is `4`.

The JS lane and emitted JS both print:

```text
3
```

The native binary exits with code 1:

```text
bend: runtime fail-stop
```

`Array<T>` is an unrestricted `ALeaf | ANode(Array<T>, Array<T>)`, so the unbalanced tree above is well-typed. The source `Array.size` follows the left child and doubles its size, which gives `4`.

The JS representation flattens `ANode` with `$0.concat($1)`, reconstructs children by splitting at `$0.length >> 1`, and implements `Array.size` as `$0.length`. It loses the original boundary and returns the number of leaves, `3`. The native representation fail-stops on the same value.

The runtime paper calls `Array<T>` a perfect binary tree, but neither the type nor the checker enforces that. Its constructors are public, while the backends assume both children have equal depth. This uses no `@unsafe`, FFI, open law, or `?TODO`.

This is different from #804. That issue is about the allocation cost of split/join on regular arrays. Here a checked equation becomes false at runtime.

### Bend version

```text
bend 2.0.5
main @ 0b7e2b11
```

### Operating system

```text
Darwin arm64
```

### C compiler version

```text
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: C and JS lanes decode invalid UTF-8 differently: io_str accepts overlong, surrogate and out-of-range sequences (File.read, get_env, TCP.recv, UDP.recv)
body:
### What you did

```
bend u.bend          # JS lane
bend u.bend -o u && ./u   # C lane
```

### What happened

Every effect that turns OS bytes into a `String` uses a different UTF-8 decoder on
each lane, so the same program on the same input produces two different `String`s.

The C kit decodes with `io_str` (`bend2/comp.ts:5357`), a hand-rolled backward
scanner with no validation. The JS kit decodes with `io_text` (`bend2/comp.ts:6114`),
i.e. `TextDecoder`, which is WHATWG-strict and substitutes `U+FFFD`.

`io_str` is shared by `File.read`, `IO.get_env`, `TCP.recv`, `UDP.recv_from` and
`UDP.poll` — every untrusted-input seam, including the network ones.

Reading these 23 bytes

```
41 7c 80 7c c0 80 7c ed a0 80 7c f7 bf bf bf 7c ff 7c e6 97 7c c3 a9
```

and printing `Char.to_u32` of each char:

```
JS: 65 124 65533 124 65533 65533 124 65533 65533 65533 124 65533 65533 65533 65533 124 65533 124 65533 124 233
C:  65 124 128   124 0           124 55296            124 2097151              124 255   124 230 151   124 233
```

| input bytes | what it is | C lane | JS lane |
|---|---|---|---|
| `80` | stray continuation byte | `Chr{128}` (read as Latin-1) | `Chr{65533}` |
| `c0 80` | **overlong NUL** | `Chr{0}` | `Chr{65533}` ×2 |
| `ed a0 80` | **surrogate U+D800** | `Chr{55296}` | `Chr{65533}` ×3 |
| `f7 bf bf bf` | **U+1FFFFF, above U+10FFFF** | `Chr{2097151}` | `Chr{65533}` ×4 |
| `ff` | invalid | `Chr{255}` | `Chr{65533}` |
| `e6 97` | truncated 3-byte | `Chr{230} Chr{151}` | `Chr{65533}` |

`String.length` of the same file is **16** in C and **21** in JS. Neither lane
reports an error; both exit 0.

`IO.get_env` shows it too, so it is not specific to `File.read`. With
`BADUTF` set to `41 ed a0 80 c0 80`:

```
JS: 65 65533 65533 65533 65533 65533
C:  65 55296 0
```

Three consequences beyond the divergence itself:

**1. The C lane breaks its own UTF-8 law on output.** `tests/io/text_utf8.bend` and
`tests/io/print_utf8_law.bend` pin that "a String reaches the OS as UTF-8, one
sequence per Char, in every lane". But `io_utf8` (`bend2/comp.ts:5308`) does not
validate either, so reading the file above and writing it straight back gives:

```
in:      41 7c 80 7c c0 80 7c ed a0 80 7c f7 bf bf bf 7c ff 7c e6 97 7c c3 a9
C out:   41 7c c2 80 7c 00 7c ed a0 80 7c f7 bf bf bf 7c c3 bf 7c c3 a6 c2 97 7c c3 a9
JS out:  41 7c ef bf bd 7c ef bf bd ef bf bd 7c ef bf bd ef bf bd ef bf bd 7c ...
```

`ed a0 80` and `f7 bf bf bf` come back out verbatim, so the C lane's own output is
not valid UTF-8. The overlong `c0 80` also becomes a raw `00` byte in the output
stream. The bytes that *are* decoded as Latin-1 come back re-encoded
(`80` → `c2 80`, `ff` → `c3 bf`, `e6 97` → `c3 a6 c2 97`), which is exactly the
mojibake the `text_utf8` comment says was fixed in the other direction.

**2. The C lane can build a `Char` the JS lane refuses to construct.** `char_new`
(`bend2/comp.ts:567`) throws on surrogates and on anything above `0x10FFFF`:

```js
if (code > 0x10FFFF || (code >= 0xD800 && code <= 0xDFFF)) {
  throw "bend: " + code + " is not a Unicode scalar value";
}
```

Those are precisely the values `io_str` hands back. So a `String` a C-lane program
can hold is not representable in the JS lane at all.

**3. Overlong encodings are accepted.** `c0 80` → `Chr{0}` means a NUL char can be
introduced into a `String` from file or socket input. `tests/io/nul_bytes.bend`
takes care that "a NUL byte never crosses a char* OS seam"; the `io_nul` guard
still catches it at the path/mode/host seams, but the char itself is created
silently and the two lanes disagree on whether it exists.

### The file

```python
import Base

def codes(s: String) -> String:
  match s:
    case SNil{}:
      ""
    case SCon{c, t}:
      U32.show(Char.to_u32(c)) ++ " " ++ codes(t)

def read_go(m: File & Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String), String>) -> IO(Unit):
  (f, r) = m
  do IO<Unit>:
    data : String <- IO.pass(String, r)
    p : Unit <- IO.print(codes(data))
    File.close(f)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    f : File <- IO.try(File, File.open("./bad.bin", "r"))
    m : File & Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String), String> <- File.read(f, 64)
    read_go(m)
```

Make the input with:

```
printf 'A|\200|\300\200|\355\240\200|\367\277\277\277|\377|\346\227|\303\251' > bad.bin
```

title: A + on a field binder in a braced pattern, then a nested pattern in the same column: 'an annotated term (cannot infer)' on a valid program
body:
### What you did

Ran this file from the current `main` checkout:

```bend
import Base
def f(ys: List<&2, U32>) -> U32:
  match ys:
    case Con{h, +z}:
      1
    case [c, d]:
      (c + d : U32)
    case _:
      0
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(f([3, 4])))
```

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts plus_field_nested.bend
```

### What happened

The checker rejects the file:

```text
Error:
- expected : an annotated term (cannot infer)
- observed : [d]
Context:
- h : U32
- d : U32
Location: f
3 |   match ys:
4>|     case Con{h, +z}:
5 |       1
```

The same file with `Con{h, z}` in the first row, no `+`, checks and prints `1`. So does the file with a flat `Con{c, r}` in the second row instead of `[c, d]`. It needs both: a `+` on a field binder in a braced pattern, and a later row of the same column whose pattern nests a constructor under that field. The number of columns and what the other columns hold do not matter; a `[h, +z]` list pattern in the first row passes.

The observed term `[d]` is `Con{d, Nil{}}`, the tail of the second row's pattern, shown as a list.

### Why

A `+` on a field binder is parsed as a rebinding let around the row's body, `+z' = z` (`parse_bind` pushes it to `p.plus`, `body_plus` wraps it as a `Local` of quantity Many), the same mechanism as `+x => e` on a lambda. The let's value is a variable and infers.

`match_flatten` splits a column on the first constructor row it finds. For column `z` that is the second row, `Con{d, Nil{}}`, so the reconstruction term for the column is `Con{d, Nil{}}`, and `body_sub` rewrites every `z` in the earlier rows' bodies to it, because inside that arm only the fields exist. Every other occurrence of `z` sits in a checked position and takes the substitution. The one inside the let becomes `+z' = Con{d, Nil{}}`, and the let rule infers its value: a constructor has no inference rule, since its fields do not fix the datatype's parameters (`d : U32` fixes the element, nothing fixes the list's quantity, and a bare `Nil{}` fixes nothing), so the checker stops there.

The reconstruction is the right term; it is what makes the aliasing between `z` and its fields visible to the use counts. The problem is only that its type exists in one place, the Mat rule, which builds the same `Ctr(k, fields)` inside the motive when it checks the arm, and never hands it to the term.

A `+` on a lambda binder cannot hit this, because a lambda's variable is never substituted. Only a pattern column can be split by a later row.

```text
main @ 438bf744
```

```text

```

```text
Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.4.2)
```

title: Add a native library target for pure definitions
body:
## Use case

A Rust or C host needs to call a pure Bend definition many times in one process:

```text
step(current_state, event) -> decision
```

Bend owns the transition and its laws. The host owns process control, persistence, and any effects represented by the returned value.

Bend 2.0.5 provides this shape for JavaScript. The [documented loader](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7/bend2/main.ts#L1-L9) lets JavaScript preload `bend2/main.ts`, import a `.bend` module, and call its non-IO definitions. Native hosts have no documented equivalent.

## Current native behavior

This file provides a minimal probe:

```python
import Base

def add(a: U32, b: U32) -> U32:
  (a + b : U32)

def main() -> U32:
  add(20, 22)
```

Commands:

```console
$ bend probe.bend -o probe.c
$ bend probe.bend -o probe
$ rg --no-line-number '^int main' probe.c
int main(int argc, char** argv) {
$ nm -g --defined-only probe | awk '$2 ~ /^[TW]$/ {print $3}'
_fini
_init
_start
data_start
main
$ ./probe
42
$ ./probe input
bend: unknown option input
```

The [native CLI path](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7/bend2/main.ts#L196-L211) asks `compile_book` for a whole C program. The result has a public `main`, but no supported callable ABI for `add` or another chosen pure definition. This observes the public artifact surface; it does not assume that every Bend definition should lower to a standalone C symbol. Supplying application values requires foreign IO, source generation plus recompilation, a JavaScript sidecar and IPC schema, or patches against private compiler/runtime representations.

The generated runtime also keeps [process-global state](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7/bend2/comp.ts#L3442-L3455) and handles runtime errors with [`_exit(1)`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7/bend2/comp.ts#L3604-L3612). A library target therefore needs explicit lifecycle and failure contracts alongside exported symbols.

## Requested contract

Please add a documented native library target for chosen pure Bend definitions:

- build a native library once and call each exported definition many times with different values;
- choose exports through a public compiler or source mechanism;
- document the supported signatures for exports and reject unsupported signatures at build time with a clear diagnostic;
- emit a C header or a machine-readable ABI description from which tools can generate Rust bindings;
- define whether setup or teardown is required, whether runtime state is process-wide or instance-owned, and whether calls may overlap or reenter;
- document value ownership, allocation, release, and malformed-value behavior;
- return recoverable boundary, setup, and call errors to the host, and document any runtime failures that remain process-fatal;
- state that Bend proofs cover source terms rather than the generated library, runtime, or ABI;
- version each generated declaration/library pair, make mismatches fail deterministically, and document compatibility across Bend releases; a stable cross-release ABI is not required for the first slice;
- require no foreign IO in an exported definition or its reachable dependencies.

Maintainers should choose the representation. Opaque handles with generated encode/call/decode functions are sufficient if hosts do not need to reproduce Bend's private value layout or constructor schema. The first slice may be CPU-only on one documented native platform.

## Acceptance slice

A small checked-in example can keep the first implementation narrow:

1. Define `step(U32, Bool) -> Decision`, where `Decision` is a two-constructor `Data` type with `U32` fields, and check at least one law about it.
2. Build the module once as a native library and generated declaration.
3. Compile a C host against that declaration.
4. Call `step` twice with different values and inspect both constructor results.
5. Exercise each lifecycle operation the generated API exposes, handle the result under its documented ownership rules, and verify that one recoverable boundary error returns control to the host.
6. Reject one unsupported export signature with a compiler diagnostic.
7. Confirm that a deliberately mismatched generated declaration/library pair is rejected before the exported definition runs.

The test covers scalar input, algebraic output, repeated calls, lifecycle ownership, host-safe boundary errors, the unsupported-signature boundary, and ABI mismatches. Later changes can add types or platforms.

## Probe environment

```text
bend 2.0.5 (38ad3382d8b611fa83bba769c15fa3612cce9fc7)
Linux x86_64
Bun 1.3.13
Ubuntu clang 18.1.3
```

title: JS loader: document ownership transfer and aliasing for Array arguments
body:
## Summary

When JS calls an exported Bend def, what are the **ownership rules for Array arguments**? The guide documents that within Bend, Array updates (`Array.set`) are in-place and return the same array without copying — fine inside Bend's one-owner discipline. But at the JS boundary the caller keeps its own reference to the same object, so a Bend def can mutate caller-owned JS data, and nothing in the docs tells the caller whether an argument was borrowed, transferred, or copied.

This is not a claim that Bend's in-place Array semantics are wrong — it is a request to document what a *JS caller* must do to preserve Bend's ownership assumptions, and what the caller may assume about arrays it hands over.

## Environment

bend 2.0.5 (`main` @ e6676b0), Linux x86_64, node v24.19.0.

## Minimal repro (executed)

`ffi.bend`:

```bend
import Base

def set0(a: Array<U32>, v: U32) -> Array<U32>:
  Array.set(U32, a, 0, v)
```

`ffi.mjs` (run with `node --import bend2/main.ts ffi.mjs`):

```js
import B from "./ffi.bend";

const a = [10, 20, 30, 40];   // valid power-of-two array
const r = B.set0(a, 99);
console.log(a === r, a);      // true [ 99, 20, 30, 40 ]
```

Observed: the returned value **is** the caller's own array object, mutated — after the call, JS-side `a` reads `[99, 20, 30, 40]`.

## Questions the docs should answer

1. Is an Array argument borrowed, transferred, or copied? May the caller keep using its own reference afterwards as an independent value?
2. If zero-copy is intentional: a prominent "the boundary is unchecked and zero-copy; validate and copy on the JS side" note where the JS interop is documented (`guide/GUIDE.md` ~L377).
3. Adjacent facts worth one line each in the same section: Nat arguments must be BigInt; erased (`-`) parameters are absent from the JS-callable signature; runtime traps surface as plain thrown strings, not `Error` instances.

(Related but distinct: #808 covers soundness of *unbalanced* Arrays constructed inside Bend; this issue is about the caller-side ownership contract for valid arrays crossing the boundary.)

## Acceptance criteria

- The intended ownership/aliasing contract for JS↔Bend calls is documented — no behavior change required if zero-copy is the design.

title: Frontend: computed-value destructuring reports an inapplicable match-order error
body:
## Summary

Destructuring a computed value in place is rejected — by design, since only parameters may be matched — but the diagnostic reports an internal pattern-flattening constraint ("reorder the match") in a program that contains no `match`, and its advice is unusable at source level.

## Environment

bend 2.0.5 (`main` @ e6676b0), Linux x86_64.

## Failing case (executed)

```bend
import Base

def pair() -> U32 & U32:
  (1, 2)

def main() -> U32:
  (a, b) = pair()
  a
```

```
Error:
- message  : match scrutinees in binder order (this variable is unbound, consumed, or out of order: reorder the match)
7>|   (a, b) = pair()
```

## Working counterpart (executed — prints `1`)

```bend
import Base

def pair() -> U32 & U32:
  (1, 2)

def first(p: U32 & U32) -> U32:
  (a, b) = p
  a

def main() -> U32:
  first(pair())
```

## Suggested diagnostic

> cannot destructure a computed value here; pass it to a helper and destructure the helper's parameter

(Note: suggesting "bind it to a local variable" would be wrong — let-bound scrutinees are prohibited too; the helper parameter is the correct workaround.)

## Acceptance criteria

- The message names the actual source-level rule and points at the helper-parameter workaround.

title: The checker never visits the argument of an applied lambda whose binder is unused
body:
### What you did

`bend tests/check/usage_counts_source.bend`
`bend repro/undefined_name.bend`

### What happened

`term_infer`'s `App` case reduces a literal lambda on the spot and infers the body
(`bend.ts:3352-3354`), so `tm.x` reaches the checker only where the substitution puts
it back. When the lambda's binder is UNUSED, the argument is dropped before anything
inspects it -- and the runtime drops it too. An unbound name and a type that names
nothing both pass:

    # (y => x)(nonsense_undefined_name), x : Nat
    $ bend undefined_name.bend
    5n

    # (y => x)({5 : NoSuchType}), x : U32
    $ bend unknown_type.bend
    1

### The file

    import Base

    def drop2(x: Nat) -> Nat:
      (y => x)(nonsense_undefined_name)

    def main() -> Nat:
      drop2(5n)

Two controls, both of which behave correctly:

    # the same name under a binder the body USES -> rejected
    def f() -> U32:
      (y => y)(nonsense_undefined_name)
    # Error: - expected : a defined name

    # an unused binder whose BODY cannot be inferred fails on the body first
    def f() -> U32:
      (y => 5)(nonsense_undefined_name)
    # Error: - expected : an annotated term (cannot infer)
    #        - observed : 5

So the condition is: binder unused AND body inferable.

### Is this intended?

I genuinely cannot tell, and it may be deliberate: the argument of an unused binder is
dead at runtime, and the header says dead code may diverge and inhabit `Empty`. Two
things make me unsure rather than confident it is a bug:

- The header lists exactly what checks dead -- "a type position, an erased (`-`)
  argument, an equality endpoint or a motive". An unused plain binder is none of
  those; `y` is not spelled `-y`.
- `tests/check/usage_counts_source.bend` shows the argument of this redex is source
  the checker is meant to *count*: its comment says "the checker counts unevaluated
  source syntax ... or `consume(t)`'s occurrence of `t` vanishes". It is visited there
  only because its binder `z` is used.

Both observed defects are resolution failures, not typing failures -- the class the
language reports as "a defined name", which is not demand-dependent anywhere else.

### A candidate fix that does NOT work

Adding `term_infer(book, lhs, tm.x, None(), ctx, d, [])` before the short-circuit
closes both cases above but breaks two shipped files, because a bare constructor can
be checked but never inferred and the short-circuit runs in inference mode:

    demos/pure_hvm5_mini/PROOF.bend         exit 0 -> exit 1 ("cannot infer", observed main.Names{m, n})
    tests/check/usage_counts_source.bend    the pinned usage-count error becomes "cannot infer"
    demos/pure_hvm5_mini/LAWS.bend          "8 TODOs found" becomes "cannot infer"

Measured by differential over all 1,332 test and demo files: 3 change, one stops
checking. Recorded so nobody walks that dead end twice.

A narrower option, if this is judged a defect: walk the dropped argument for names
that resolve to nothing, without typing it. I have not implemented it.

title: Metal: U32 remainder returns 4294967295 for 4294967294 % 3
The guide does not document the native C side of custom effects
body:
## What I did

The guide says that each effect may import a `.c` and `.js` implementation and that users can add effects the same way as Base. I used that path for a native program whose custom effects own resources and park on file descriptors.

The native effect path works on Bend 2.0.7 after I reused Base handle types, but I had to derive the C interface from `comp.ts`, the Base effect sources, and the IO tests. The guide specifies the generated host-function name and stops there.

## Missing native documentation

A native custom effect must answer questions that the guide does not cover:

- Which C function signature and registration call should an imported effect use?
- Which result constructors may it return, including `io_fail` with custom text?
- Which `IoWork` fields may it own across `io_work` or `io_wait_on`, and who releases their memory after success or failure?
- Can a package rely on `io_eff`, `io_hand`, `io_hand_v`, `io_work`, and `io_wait_on`, or are those helpers private compiler details?
- Does Bend support a nominal opaque handle type for a custom resource?
- What compatibility, if any, does Bend promise for imported C across releases?

The handle question has no documented answer. This declaration follows the guide's affine-handle description and compiles:

```python
import Base

type Handle is Type:

def Handle.open() -> IO(Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Handle>):
  import "./handle.c"

def Handle.close(handle: Handle) -> IO(Unit):
  import "./handle.c"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    handle : Handle <- IO.try(Handle, Handle.open())
    Handle.close(handle)
```

`handle.c`:

```c
static Term handle_open_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  return io_done(e, io_hand(42));
}

static Term handle_close_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  fprintf(stderr, "handle=%llu\n", (unsigned long long)io_hand_v(f[0]));
  return term_pak(CID_UNIT, 0);
}

static void __attribute__((constructor)) handle_effects_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID_HANDLE_OPEN, handle_open_run, 0);
  io_eff(CID_HANDLE_CLOSE, handle_close_run, 0);
}
```

```console
$ bend main.bend -o main && ./main
handle=0
```

`Handle.close` receives a zero word rather than `42`. An unfilled `law Handle: Type` fails with `1 TODO found`. The working fallback I found defines `Handle` as `File`, `Socket`, or `Listener`, which loses nominal separation between unrelated resources.

This probe does not assume that an empty datatype should carry a foreign word. It shows that the guide does not name a supported custom-handle mechanism or state that none exists.

## Requested documentation

Please document the native C side of custom effects, or state that packages must treat it as unsupported compiler internals. A small checked-in example or a guide link to an existing test would be enough. It should cover:

1. one synchronous effect and its registration;
2. the supported value and error representations;
3. the supported pattern, if any, for an opaque affine resource handle;
4. one worker or file-descriptor park/resume path and its memory ownership;
5. the compatibility policy for imported C across Bend releases.

This request does not require a stable C ABI. Documentation may state that a custom effect must track its exact Bend compiler version.

## References

- The current guide claim: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/b4929c2d0d9d1e9598954aa37758954bab4d8a77/guide/GUIDE.md#L371-L375
- Existing foreign-value test: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/b4929c2d0d9d1e9598954aa37758954bab4d8a77/tests/io/foreign_types.c
- Existing worker-effect test: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/b4929c2d0d9d1e9598954aa37758954bab4d8a77/tests/io/help_flood.c
- A built-in parked effect: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/b4929c2d0d9d1e9598954aa37758954bab4d8a77/bend2/effs/tcp_recv.c

## Environment

```text
bend 2.0.7 (b4929c2d0d9d1e9598954aa37758954bab4d8a77)
Linux x86_64
Bun 1.3.13
Ubuntu clang 18.1.3
```

title: Guide says `--gpu 4GB` "enables the GPU", but the GPU is on by default; `--gpu off` is the CPU baseline and is undocumented there
body:
## Summary

`GUIDE.md:498` documents the runtime flag as:

```
./file --gpu 4GB          # enables the GPU, with max 4GB memory
```

The GPU is on by default, so "enables" is misleading. The compiled binary's own
`--help` has it right:

```
--gpu on|off|4GB  run ! calls on the GPU, over this much of its memory
                  (default: on if present, over 2GB on Metal)
```

A reader who takes the guide at face value concludes that a run *without* the
flag is a CPU run, and uses it as a CPU baseline. It is not one: a binary
containing `!` loads its `.gpu` program and runs on the device either way. Every
"GPU vs CPU" A/B built that way has the GPU on both sides and reports a tie.

That is not hypothetical — I published a benchmark report built on exactly that
mistake, with five "refuted" hypotheses that were all GPU-against-GPU. `--gpu
off` is the control I needed and I did not know it existed, because I read the
guide and never ran `./binary --help`.

## Reproduction

```python
import Base
def pow2(+n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n: 1
    case 1n+p:
      a b = pow2(p) pow2(p)
      (a + b : U32)
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(pow2!(31n)))
```

Hiding the `.gpu` file makes the binary recompile it *whether or not* `--gpu` is
passed, which is the direct evidence that the flag is not the switch.

## Results

Mandelbrot, 512² × 200 iterations, `IO.now()` inside the process, median of 5:

| invocation | ms/frame |
|---|---|
| `--gpu off --threads 1` | 213 |
| `--gpu off --threads 10` | 31 |
| no flag | 8 |
| `--gpu 2GB` | 7 |

Rows 2 and 3 are the ones that matter: omitting the flag is not row 2.

## Suggested fix

Change the guide line to something like:

```
./file --gpu off          # keep ! calls on the CPU
./file --gpu 4GB          # cap the GPU heap at 4GB (the GPU is on by default)
```

and mention `--gpu off` as the way to get a CPU baseline. Listing the flag in
`bend --help` as well would help, since that is where people look first.

## Environment

Bend 2.0.6, macOS 26.6.2, Apple M5 (10 CPU / 8 GPU cores), Metal.

title: Base: the O(n) and O(value) functions hold the obvious names, while the O(1) primitives are `law` and invisible to `grep '^def'`
body:
## Summary

In Base, the O(n) and O(value) functions hold the obvious names, while the O(1)
primitives that do the same jobs are declared `law` and so do not appear when
you grep the output of `bend base` for `^def`.

```
$ bend base U32.shln
def U32.shln(a: U32, n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n: a
    case 1n+p: U32.shl(U32.shln(a, p))      # one shl per unit of n

$ bend base U32.from_nat
def U32.from_nat(n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n: 0
    case 1n+p: U32.inc(U32.from_nat(p))     # one inc per unit of the VALUE

$ bend base F32.to_u32
law F32.to_u32:
  for a: F32
  U32                                        # O(1), but not a `def`
```

## Why this bites

`grep '^def F32'` is the natural way to ask "what does Base give me for floats",
and it answers "no trigonometry, no float/int conversion". Both are there, as
`law`. I hit this twice in one session on the same day: I started hand-writing a
Taylor series for `F32.sin` before finding it, and I used the `Nat` round-trip
for a float floor in an inner loop before finding `F32.to_u32` / `U32.to_f32`.

To be accurate about the cost: when I later swapped the `Nat` round-trip for the
primitives, it measured **no speedup** in either of my programs. So this is a
discoverability problem, not a performance one — what it cost me was time and a
wrong hypothesis, not milliseconds. `U32.shln` being O(n) is the one that is a
genuine trap, since a shift by a variable amount inside a loop is a normal thing
to write.

## Suggested fix

Any one of these would have saved me:

- have `bend base --types` (or `bend base <name>`) list `law` declarations
  alongside `def`s, so one listing shows everything;
- note in the guide that O(1) primitives are `law` and will not show up as
  `def`s;
- or mark the O(n) / O(value) definitions as such in a comment where they are
  defined, since their names give no hint.

## Environment

Bend 2.0.6, macOS 26.6.2, Apple M5.

title: Fork depth for a `!` call changes GPU frame time by up to 8x, and the same sweep is flat on the CPU
body:
## Summary

For a GPU (`!`) call, how deep the parallel fork goes before switching to
straight-line work changes the frame time by up to 8x. The same sweep on the CPU
is flat, so the variable is invisible unless you happen to test on the device.
Nothing in the guide mentions tuning it, and the one piece of guidance I found —
the `Cell.fork` comment in `demos/app_slash_boss_3d/bend3d.bend`, *"a fork per
pixel drowns in scheduling, a fork per cell leaves lanes idle"* — steered me to
the coarse end, which is the wrong end for a raycaster.

## Measurements

A voxel raycaster at 512². The benchmark sums every pixel colour and prints the
checksum, so the rows are verified to render the same image. 40 frames per run,
median of 5, `IO.now()` inside the process.

| fork depth | leaf | `--gpu 2GB` | `--gpu off`, 10 threads |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 levels | 8×8 tile | 14 (14–16) | 19 (18–19) |
| 7 levels | 4×4 tile | **6 (6–8)** | 20 (19–20) |
| 8 levels | 2×2 tile | 8 (8–9) | 20 (20–21) |
| 9 levels | 1 pixel | 7 (7–8) | 21 (20–21) |

An interactive voxel world at 128², which also reads a shared `Data` quadtree
per DDA step. Checksum `747218888` on every row:

| fork depth | leaf | `--gpu 2GB` |
|---|---|---|
| 4 levels | 8×8 tile | 234 (232–236) |
| 5 levels | 4×4 tile | 87 (87) |
| 6 levels | 2×2 tile | **28 (28–34)** |

`--gpu off` on 10 threads: 178 ms. So at the coarse granularity that program was
**slower on the GPU than on the CPU**, and 8.4x slower than the same program
forked two levels deeper.

## What is surprising

- The CPU column is flat, so a CPU-side experiment reports "granularity does not
  matter" and is wrong about the device. I drew exactly that conclusion and
  shipped it.
- The optimum is not universal: the raycaster wants a 4×4 leaf, the voxel world
  wants 2×2. It has to be swept per program.
- Granularity is necessary but not sufficient. A third program forks per pixel
  and still does not win (48 with `!` vs 43 on 10 threads) because it lacks a
  ray/box clip, so cheap rays never get cut.

## Suggested fix

A paragraph in the guide saying that fork depth for `!` is a tuning parameter,
that the CPU will not reveal it, and that the useful range is a leaf of a few
pixels rather than a tile. If `bend3d.bend` is the reference people are pointed
to, the `Cell.fork` comment could note that binning per tile pays when the tile
shares work (its triangle list), and not when every leaf is independent.

I am not reporting this as a bug — the scheduler behaving this way is
reasonable. It is that the one number that mattered most for my GPU performance
is undocumented and invisible from the CPU.

## Environment

Bend 2.0.6, macOS 26.6.2, Apple M5 (10 CPU / 8 GPU cores), Metal.
Full sources: https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending

title: After a parallel let whose calls apply a closure, later forks in the same IO step run on one core
body:
*Posted by Claude (Claude Code, an AI assistant) on behalf of @o1lo01ol1o, who asked me to file it. The programs and timings below were run in that session; the companion issue about fork-free closure code is #832.*

### What you did

`bend a.bend -o a && bend b.bend -o b`, then `/usr/bin/time -p ./a --threads 1` and `--threads 12` for each binary (best of 3).

### What happened

```text
a  --threads 1   real 0.78  user 0.76
a  --threads 12  real 0.77  user 0.76    <- one core
b  --threads 1   real 0.78  user 0.76
b  --threads 12  real 0.40  user 0.77
```

Both print `1954641925`. The two files differ in one line: the first parallel let in `a.bend` applies two closures (`a b = f(1) g(2)`), and in `b.bend` it calls the def directly (`a b = inc(1) inc(2)`). The second parallel let, which does all the work, is identical, and so are the closures (`f = g = inc`).

Variations, same harness, 12 threads:

| first fork | result |
| --- | --- |
| applies caller-built lambdas instead of `inc` | one core (0.78) |
| calls a def that applies the closure inside (`call(f, 1) call(g, 2)`) | one core (0.78) |
| no fork: `a = f(1)` and `b = g(2)` in sequence | parallel (0.40) |
| calls defs that themselves fork, with no closure anywhere | parallel (0.40) |
| none; the heavy fork alone, over closures (`c d = f(2) g(3)`, `f = g = work`) | parallel (0.40) |
| as in `a.bend`, with an IO effect between the two forks | parallel (0.40) |

So the trigger looks like a forked task that applies a closure: after it, later forks in the same IO step run sequentially, including forks in other defs reached afterwards. An IO step boundary resets it. It came up stepping two independent state machines in lockstep, where each step is a closure: only the first round used more than one core.

A possible lead, not traced to the line: `comp.ts` seeds `FID_CLO_APPLY` as always forky (`const forky = new Set(["FID_CLO_APPLY", ...])`), so a task that applies a closure is never fork-free, and `monk_step` treats fork-free and forky tasks differently while a lane grows.

### The file

`a.bend` (`b.bend` replaces `a b = f(1) g(2)` with `a b = inc(1) inc(2)`):

```python
import Base

def spin(n: Nat, x: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      x
    case 1n+p:
      spin(p, (x * 1664525 + 1013904223 : U32))

def work(x: U32) -> U32:
  spin(U32.to_nat(400000000), x)

def inc(x: U32) -> U32:
  (x + 1 : U32)

def both(f: U32 -> U32, g: U32 -> U32) -> U32:
  a b = f(1) g(2)
  c d = work(a) work(b)
  (c + d : U32)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(both(inc, inc)))
```

### bend --version

bend 2.0.9 (main @ 0da46e8); the same numbers on bend 2.0.3 (b9d1352)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64 (Apple M2 Max, 12 cores)

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 21.1.8

title: Fork-free code that applies closures runs 2x slower with --threads > 1: each such call saves its continuation as a heap task
body:
*Posted by Claude (Claude Code, an AI assistant) on behalf of @o1lo01ol1o, who asked me to file it. The programs and timings below were run in that session; the companion issue about forks after a closure-applying fork is #831.*

### What you did

`bend s1.bend -o s1 && bend s2.bend -o s2`, then `/usr/bin/time -p ./s1 --threads N` for N in 1, 2, 4, 12, and the same for `s2` (best of 3).

### What happened

```text
s1  --threads 1   real 0.73  user 0.71
s1  --threads 2   real 1.50  user 1.48
s1  --threads 4   real 1.50  user 1.48
s1  --threads 12  real 1.51  user 1.48
s2  --threads 1   real 0.19  user 0.18
s2  --threads 12  real 0.19  user 0.18
```

Neither program has a parallel let. Both print `877972487`. `s1.bend` builds and applies one closure per loop iteration, and it runs twice as slow with any `--threads` above 1; `s2.bend` is the same loop with a def call in place of the closure, and thread count does not affect it. Since `--threads` defaults to the CPU count, sequential code that uses closures pays this by default.

The emitted C shows why. In `FID_LOOP`, the call `call(f, x)` is compiled as a cut: with `seq` it pushes a stack frame, without it every iteration allocates a task node for the continuation:

```c
      if (seq) {
        WL_ROOM(2);
        STK(0) = p_0;
        STK(1) = FID_LOOP_K6;
        WL_PUSHN(2);
      } else {
        u64 t_0 = task_node(e, FID_LOOP_K6, WL_CONT, WL_IDX, 1);
        e.mem[t_0 + 0] = p_0;
        WL_CONT = term_tsk(FID_LOOP_K6, t_0);
        WL_IDX = 1;
      }
```

With more than one thread `seq` is false, because `main` can reach a fork: `comp.ts` seeds `FID_CLO_APPLY` into the forky set unconditionally (`const forky = new Set(["FID_CLO_APPLY", ...])`). So any call that may apply a closure is treated as a potential fork, whatever the closure's body does. `s2.bend` has no such path, and its loop pushes frames.

### The file

`s1.bend`:

```python
import Base

def call(f: U32 -> U32, x: U32) -> U32:
  f(x)

def loop(n: Nat, x: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      x
    case 1n+p:
      loop(p, call((y => (y * 3 + 1 : U32)), x))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(loop(U32.to_nat(200000000), 7)))
```

`s2.bend`:

```python
import Base

def step(y: U32) -> U32:
  (y * 3 + 1 : U32)

def loop(n: Nat, x: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      x
    case 1n+p:
      loop(p, step(x))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(loop(U32.to_nat(200000000), 7)))
```

bend 2.0.9 (main @ 0da46e8); the same numbers on bend 2.0.3 (b9d1352)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64 (Apple M2 Max, 12 cores)

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 21.1.8

title: term_show cache collisions cause wrong template results and SHOW_DESC layouts
body:
### What you did

```text
bend repro.bend
bend repro.bend -o repro && ./repro
bend repro.bend -o repro.js && bun repro.js
```

### What happened

Expected:

```text
Out{True{}, False{}, Box{(8, 9)}, Box{7}}
```

`bend repro.bend`:

```text
Out{True{}, True{}, Box{(8, 9)}, Box{7}}
```

`./repro`:

```text
Out{True{}, True{}, Box{(8, 9)}, Box{(7, 51412992)}}
```

`bun repro.js`:

```text
bend: runtime fail-stop
```

The two `Array` terms have the same leaves but different tree shapes. `term_show` prints both as `[1, 2, 3]`. That string is used as an identity key in two places:

1. The template cache reuses the first `baked` instance for the second call, so the second field is `True{}` instead of `False{}`.
2. `show_main` reuses the descriptor for the `Box` whose field is `U32 & U32` for the `Box` whose field is `U32`. The generated C main returns `WL_RETN(5)`, but the reused descriptor reads the final `Box` at absolute word offsets 4 and 5. Word 5 does not belong to main's result; `51412992` is the adjacent heap word observed in this run. The JS lane fail-stops on the same descriptor mismatch.

This seems separate from WONTFIX #808. Neither `Array` is executed at runtime: the `baked` arguments are compile-time values, and the `Box` arguments are erased type indices. The generated main returns only the two booleans and the three `U32` words.

Tested on current main at `0da46e82e6e964e1e998f20be378be61f571fb01`.

### The file

```bend
import Base

def left_is_leaf(xs: Array<U32>) -> Bool:
  match xs:
    case ALeaf{x}:
      False{}
    case ANode{ALeaf{x}, r}:
      True{}
    case ANode{ANode{a, b}, r}:
      False{}

def baked(~xs: Array<U32>) -> Bool:
  left_is_leaf(xs)

def LowType(xs: Array<U32>) -> Type:
  match xs:
    case ALeaf{x}:
      U32
    case ANode{ALeaf{x}, r}:
      U32 & U32
    case ANode{ANode{a, b}, r}:
      U32

type Box<-xs: Array<U32>> is Type:
  Box{value: LowType(xs)}

type Out is Type:
  Out{
    first: Bool,
    second: Bool,
    wide: Box<ANode{ALeaf{1}, ANode{ALeaf{2}, ALeaf{3}}}>,
    narrow: Box<ANode{ANode{ALeaf{1}, ALeaf{2}}, ALeaf{3}}>
  }

def main() -> Out:
  Out{
    baked(~ANode{ALeaf{1}, ANode{ALeaf{2}, ALeaf{3}}}),
    baked(~ANode{ANode{ALeaf{1}, ALeaf{2}}, ALeaf{3}}),
    Box{(8, 9)},
    Box{7}
  }
```

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.9
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: Guide: what a shared +Data costs inside a parallel call is only documented in a demo's comments
body:
## Summary

The guide says that `+` values carry a reference count. It does not say what
that count costs inside a parallel call: one atomic operation per node touched
per use, on a counter that every other lane is touching too. That fact decided
the performance of everything I built in two days of Bend renderers, and the
only place it is written down is in comments inside
`demos/app_slash_boss_3d/bend3d.bend`:

```
# All scalars: the record rides in registers through every
# call and fork; a boxed record shared by every vertex is an atomic
# count per use.
```
```
# One list per cell, not per pixel: a list shared by
# pixels is contended atomics.
```

The guide's Parallelism section lists the two promises a parallel call makes:
the calls are independent, and they run in roughly the same time. In practice
a third thing decides the speed — what the lanes *share* — and the guide is
silent on it. Worse, a reader of the guide alone is steered toward the wrong
design: `Array` is `Type` and cannot be read by both sides of a parallel call,
so the natural next move for a world every pixel reads is a shared `+Data`
tree, which is exactly what those comments warn against.

## Measurements

Voxel raycaster, 32×32 columns, each column a `U32` of heights. Every row of
each table renders the same image: the harness sums all pixel colours and the
checksum is identical across rows. Bend 2.0.9, Apple M5, median of 5.

Reading the world once per column crossing, 512²:

| the world is | ms/frame |
|---|---|
| a pure function of `(x, z)`, nothing shared | 23 |
| a shared `+Data` quadtree of all 1024 columns | 220 |

Attempts to make the tree read cheaper, checksum identical each time: a
`Bool.pick` chain instead of a 4-way `match` helper, 1.2x; packing four
columns per leaf, 1.00x; hoisting the frame-constant camera basis out of the
per-pixel loop, 1.00x; caching the ray's region node, 1.00x; unrolling the
recursive walk, 1.00x; the last two together, 1.2x. The cost is touching the
shared top-level nodes, not depth or arithmetic.

Storing only the player's edits (a `WNone{}` constructor means "nothing edited
below"; the world starts as one) and computing the rest, 256², N edited
columns scattered over the world. Only the tree's shape changes, and the
checksum is identical on every row:

| edited columns | ms/frame |
|---|---|
| 0 | 7 |
| 16 | 35 |
| 64 | 38 |
| 256 | 44 |
| all 1024 | 41 |

Played interactively with `tick` instrumented, the first edit doubles the
frame and it plateaus at about 4x the untouched world. Sixteen edits anywhere
turn the root into a node every ray must touch.

## What I am asking for

A paragraph in the Parallelism section, next to the two promises, saying
roughly:

> A `+` value shared across the lanes of a parallel call is reference-counted,
> and every node a lane touches is an atomic operation on a count that every
> other lane is also touching. Keep per-lane state in scalars: they ride in
> registers through every call and fork. Read a shared structure once per
> group of lanes, not once per lane, and never in the innermost loop.
> `bend3d.bend` bins its scene per screen cell for exactly this reason.

That is the content of the two comments above, in the place people look
first. I would have designed the world differently on day one with that
paragraph, and #828 (fork depth) is the other half of the same lesson. When I
brought this up on Discord the answer was that this needs to be covered at
the guide level, so this issue is just the tracking item for that.

## A design question, asked as a question

Is a *borrowed* read of a `+Data` inside a `!` region, one that does not touch
the count because the compiler can see the value is only read and never
dropped inside the fork, something the runtime model could support? It is the
capability that would make the shared-tree design viable as written. If it
cannot fit, that is just as useful to state in the guide: "a shared tree read
per lane is not something the runtime will make cheap."

## Environment

Bend 2.0.9, macOS 26.6.2, Apple M5 (10 CPU / 8 GPU cores), Metal.
Every number above, with the harnesses and checksums, is in the README
section "Onde isto para": https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending

title: macOS: window_pump drains the queue without running the run loop, so input reaches the app frames late (title-bar drag lags ~70 ms)
body:
### What you did

```
bend drag.bend -o drag && ./drag
```

Then grabbed the window's title bar and dragged it around.

### What happened

The window lags well behind the pointer, and the app's own frames stutter while
the drag starts. Every input event reaches the app several frames after the
window server sent it.

`window_pump` in `bend2/effs/window_frame.c` pumps once per frame with

```objc
NSEvent* ev = [NSApp nextEventMatchingMask:NSEventMaskAny
  untilDate:NSDate.distantPast inMode:NSDefaultRunLoopMode dequeue:YES];
```

`untilDate:distantPast` returns without running the run loop, so AppKit only
hands over what already sits in the app's queue. Events the window server sent
in the meantime are picked up a frame or more later, and the delay compounds
while a drag is in flight.

I measured it by printing `CACurrentMediaTime() - ev.timestamp` for each event
the pump dequeues (the age of the event when the app finally handles it), plus
the durations of `window_pump`, `[layer nextDrawable]` and `[cb
waitUntilCompleted]`.

Bend 2.0.5, macOS, app that draws a solid color and nothing else:

| | drag events (type 6) | mean age | max age |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| as shipped | 13 | 68.6 ms | 98.8 ms |

Frame pacing was fine throughout (no gap over 25 ms), and `[NSApp sendEvent:]`
itself took 0-7 ms, so the time is spent waiting for events to show up, not
handling them.

Giving the pump a small deadline fixes it. The deadline is taken once, at the
pump's start, so a dense event stream still ends the loop and the frame gets
drawn:

```diff
 static void window_pump(void) {
   @autoreleasepool {
+    NSDate* due = [NSDate dateWithTimeIntervalSinceNow:0.002];
     for (;;) {
       NSEvent* ev = [NSApp nextEventMatchingMask:NSEventMaskAny
-        untilDate:NSDate.distantPast inMode:NSDefaultRunLoopMode dequeue:YES];
+        untilDate:due inMode:NSDefaultRunLoopMode dequeue:YES];
       if (ev == nil) {
         break;
       }
       [NSApp sendEvent:ev];
```

With that patch, my real app (an ERD editor, a few hundred rectangles and glyphs
per frame) shows a mean age of 13.3 ms over 543 drag events, with 1787 frames at
a mean spacing of 11.1 ms. The two rows are not measured on the same program, so
they do not compare directly; I did not measure the shipped runtime on the
editor. The improvement is obvious to the eye either way.

Costs nothing that I can see: the frame waits for the display's next tick
anyway, and the call returns immediately whenever an event is already there.

Things I tried that made it worse, in case they come up:

| change | mean frame spacing | frames over 25 ms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the 2 ms deadline above | 11.1 ms | 1% |
| 8 ms deadline | 18.0 ms | 24% |
| `maximumDrawableCount = 3` | 14.0 ms | 10% |
| `displaySyncEnabled = NO` | 22.9 ms | 41% |

One thing the patch does not address: the mouse-down that starts a title-bar
drag arrives with a mean age of ~40 ms, while the matching mouse-up arrives at
5.6 ms. Raising the deadline to 8 ms only moved that to 38 ms, so the pump
window is not the lever there. I have not worked out why the two differ.

`bend2/effs/window_frame.c` and `window_open.c` are byte-identical between
2.0.5 and 2.0.13, so this is still current.

### The file

```python
import Base

def tick(events: List<Event>, s: U32) -> IO(Maybe<U32>):
  match events:
    case Nil{}:
      IO.pure(Maybe<U32>, Some{s})
    case Con{Close{}, rest}:
      IO.pure(Maybe<U32>, None{})
    case Con{e, rest}:
      tick(rest, s)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  App.run(~U32, ~App{+s => (s, Pix{s}), tick}, "drag me", 800, 600, 2105376)
```

Darwin arm64

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

title: C backend: nested product type uses K^depth memory (974-byte file, 19.3 GB RSS)
Would bend have built-in std libs for Http/Tls/Crypto?
body:
### What Bend should do

```python
// this is a demo from https://github.com/H4ad/bend-stdlib/blob/master/demo/api.bend

import Base
import ./vendor/json.bend as JSON
import ./vendor/http/http.bend as HTTP
import ./vendor/http/router.bend as Router
import ./vendor/http/server.bend as Server

def hello(ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  Router.text(200, "bend-stdlib http api")

def health(ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  Router.json(200, JSON.Obj{[JSON.Member{"status", JSON.Str{"ok"}}]})

def greet(ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  Router.text(200, "hello, " ++ Router.param("name", "world", ctx))

def u32_or.read(mb: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> U32:
  match mb:
    case Some{+n}:
      n
    case None{}:
      0

def u32_or(s: String) -> U32:
  u32_or.read(U32.read(s))

def sum(ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  +ps = Router.query(ctx)
  a = u32_or(Router.param.list("a", "0", ps))
  b = u32_or(Router.param.list("b", "0", ps))
  Router.json(200, JSON.Obj{[JSON.Member{"sum", JSON.Num{U32.show(U32.add(a, b))}}]})

def echo(j: JSON.Json, ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  Router.json(200, j)

def powered(resp: HTTP.Response) -> HTTP.Response:
  Router.header("X-Powered-By", "bend-stdlib", resp)

def routes(ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  Router.dispatch([
    Router.GET("/", hello),
    Router.GET("/health", health),
    Router.GET("/hello/:name", greet),
    Router.GET("/sum", sum),
    Router.POST_JSON("/echo", echo)
  ], ctx)

def app(ctx: Router.Ctx) -> IO(HTTP.Response):
  Router.map(~powered, routes)(ctx)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  Server.listen(~app, 8080)
```

### Why

I'm doing a experiment to create a HTTP Framework for bend, and I'm missing few features in the standard lib:

| patch | effect it adds | used by | why Bend cannot |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tcp: add recv_bytes and send_bytes effects` | `TCP.recv_bytes`, `TCP.send_bytes` | `http`, `pg` | `TCP.recv` and `TCP.send` speak `String`, a sequence of code points. A byte over 127 or an invalid UTF-8 sequence does not survive the round trip, and a read that splits a multi-byte character corrupts it. HTTP framing is byte counts and the pg wire is byte frames. |
| `tcp: resolve host names in TCP.connect` | `TCP.connect` by name | `http`, `pg` | connects to a numeric quad only; a host name fails with EINVAL. |
| `crypto: add random_bytes effect` | `Crypto.random_bytes` | `crypto`, `pg` | has one `IO.random_u32`; SCRAM needs N bytes of entropy. |
| `crypto: add native pbkdf2 effect` | `Crypto.pbkdf2.native` | `crypto`, `pg` | has no KDF. This is OpenSSL PKCS5_PBKDF2_HMAC, the SCRAM key derivation. The patch also links `-lssl -lcrypto` for any program whose C includes OpenSSL. |
| `tls: add OpenSSL effects` | `TLS.wrap`, `TLS.accept`, `TLS.self_signed`, `TLS.send`, `TLS.recv`, `TLS.close` | `tls`, `pg` | Bend has no TLS surface. Its own `tests/io/tls_connect_close.bend` pins that `TLS.connect` is undefined. |

You can find these commits/patches at https://github.com/h4ad-forks/bend/commits/main/

Out of the current patches, the most blocking ones are TCP not accepting/working with bytes and no way to use OpenSSL in C code to be able to have TLS/Crypto

I wonder if this is something you want to bring to the language or you explicitly want to keep out of the language because it's not what it was suppose to do.

title: A proof cannot reuse a hypothesis, so theorems over abstract structures (Mathlib-style libraries) are out of reach
body:
*Posted by Claude (Claude Code, an AI assistant) on behalf of @o1lo01ol1o, who asked me to file it. Every program below was run on Bend 2.0.16 (main at 15ae0c8) and gives the same verdict on 2.0.3.*

### What Bend should do

A proof should be able to use a hypothesis about an abstract structure as many times as the proof needs, while runtime values stay affine. The smallest case is a theorem about every semigroup on `Nat`, whose proof applies the associativity hypothesis twice:

```python
import Base

law reassoc4:
  for op: Nat -> Nat -> Nat
  for assoc: @x: Nat -> @y: Nat -> @z: Nat -> {op(op(x, y), z) == op(x, op(y, z)) : Nat}
  for +a: Nat
  for +b: Nat
  for +c: Nat
  for +d: Nat
  {op(op(op(a, b), c), d) == op(a, op(b, op(c, d))) : Nat}

def reassoc4(op, assoc, a, b, c, d):
  %assoc(a, b, op(c, d)) : {op(op(op(a, b), c), d) == _ : Nat}
  %Equal.sym(Nat, op(op(op(a, b), c), d), op(op(a, b), op(c, d)), assoc(op(a, b), c, d)) : {_ == op(op(a, b), op(c, d)) : Nat}
  {==}

def main() -> Nat:
  0n
```

```text
Error:
- expected : assoc
- observed : assoc (consumed more than once)
Context:
- op : @_:Nat -> @_:Nat -> Nat
Location: reassoc4
16>| def reassoc4(op, assoc, a, b, c, d):
```

The same should hold when the law is used once per step of an induction, as in any lemma about folds, logs or batches, and when the operation and its law are packaged as a record.

### Why

#### The goal: Mathlib-style libraries

Mathlib, the algebra hierarchy of the Agda standard library, and agda-categories are built from one move repeated thousands of times. A theorem is stated once over an abstract structure such as a semigroup, monoid, category or functor. It is proved once, using the structure's laws as often as the proof needs. Then it is applied at every instance.

We are not asking for implicit arguments or instance search. Explicit dictionaries are fine. The blocker is that the move itself is unavailable.

#### What fails today

1. **A law hypothesis is affine.** A law about an abstract operation is a function-typed hypothesis. No function type is `Data`, so the hypothesis cannot be marked `+`, and the example above fails at its second use. An inductive proof needs the law once per step, so no lemma about a fold can be proved parametrically.
2. **Packaging does not help.** A record holding the operation and its law is `Type`-kinded. A fold that passes it to its own recursive call fails before any proof is written, with `s (consumed more than once)`. Marking it `+s` gives `expected : Data, observed : Type`. The full file is in the first collapsible section below.
3. **Laws cannot take template parameters.** Writing `for ~op` in a `law` is a parse error: `expected : a name, observed : '~'`.
4. **Templates are not theorems.** #784 establishes that `~` arguments are compile-time by design, so a template never reaches a structure chosen at run time. For closed structures, a template body is not checked until it is instantiated, so this definition checks although its proof cannot be right:
   ```python
   def reassoc4(~op: Nat -> Nat -> Nat, ~assoc: @x: Nat -> @y: Nat -> @z: Nat -> {op(op(x, y), z) == op(x, op(y, z)) : Nat}, +a: Nat, +b: Nat, +c: Nat, +d: Nat) -> {op(op(op(a, b), c), d) == op(a, op(b, op(c, d))) : Nat}:
     {==}
   ```
   Since 2.0.16, every template instance also counts as an unsafe annotation. Our port admits no unsafe definitions, so templates, the one route to reuse that worked, are closed to it.
5. **Erased binders trade one gap for another.** When the points of a law are `Type`-kinded, as morphisms are, a generic proof needs them erased so that it can mention one morphism in two applications. An instance whose law is proved by induction then cannot match its erased argument. The two versions of associativity of `Nat.add` below differ only in erasure. The live one checks, and the erased one fails with `a live scrutinee (a - scrutinee matches only in a dead region)`. Erased record fields do not help either. They are checked in the dead fragment, where Curry's paradox inhabits `{0n == 1n : Nat}`, so an erased law field is not an obligation. The second and third collapsible sections have the code. In our port of polynomial lenses, one family of proofs had to stay in such a field, type-checked but not certified.

All five symptoms have one cause. BendTT's consistency rests on the affinity of live code, because `Type : Type` and negative datatypes make the dead fragment inconsistent. Contraction in proofs is exactly what that argument cannot allow. The single universe also prevents a faithful port of level-polymorphic structures such as agda-categories' `Category o ℓ e`.

<details><summary>The packaged semigroup: a fold over a record fails before any proof</summary>

```python
import Base

type Semigroup is Type:
  MkSemigroup{
    A: Data,
    op: A -> A -> A,
    assoc: @x: A -> @y: A -> @z: A -> {op(op(x, y), z) == op(x, op(y, z)) : A}
  }

def Semigroup.A(s: Semigroup) -> Data:
  match s:
    case MkSemigroup{A, _, _}:
      A

def Semigroup.op(s: Semigroup) -> (Semigroup.A(s) -> Semigroup.A(s) -> Semigroup.A(s)):
  match s:
    case MkSemigroup{_, op, _}:
      op

def Semigroup.fold(s: Semigroup, xs: List<Semigroup.A(s)>, acc: Semigroup.A(s)) -> Semigroup.A(s):
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      acc
    case h <> t:
      Semigroup.fold(s, t, Semigroup.op(s)(acc, h))

def main() -> Nat:
  0n
```

```text
Error:
- expected : s
- observed : s (consumed more than once)
Location: Semigroup.fold
```

With `+s: Semigroup` instead: `expected : Data, observed : Type`.
</details>

<details><summary>Induction on an erased argument is rejected; the live version checks</summary>

```python
import Base

# Checks.
def add_assoc(x: Nat, +y: Nat, +z: Nat) -> {Nat.add(Nat.add(x, y), z) == Nat.add(x, Nat.add(y, z)) : Nat}:
  match x:
    case 0n:
      {==}
    case 1n+p:
      %add_assoc(p, y, z) : {1n+Nat.add(Nat.add(p, y), z) == 1n+_ : Nat}
      {==}

def main() -> Nat:
  0n
```

```python
# The same with -x, -y, -z fails:
# - message  : a live scrutinee (a - scrutinee matches only in a dead region)
def add_assoc(-x: Nat, -y: Nat, -z: Nat) -> {Nat.add(Nat.add(x, y), z) == Nat.add(x, Nat.add(y, z)) : Nat}:
  ...
```
</details>

<details><summary>An erased proof field accepts a proof of 0n == 1n</summary>

```python
import Base

type Bad is Type:
  MkBad{ apply: Bad -> Empty }

def Bad.apply(b: Bad) -> (Bad -> Empty):
  match b:
    case MkBad{f}:
      f

def absurd(e: Empty) -> {0n == 1n : Nat}:
  match e:

type Claim is Type:
  MkClaim{ -pf: {0n == 1n : Nat} }

# The field is checked dead, where contracting b is free.
def claim() -> Claim:
  MkClaim{absurd((b => Bad.apply(b)(MkBad{Bad.apply(b)}))(MkBad{(b => Bad.apply(b)(MkBad{Bad.apply(b)}))}))}

def main() -> Nat:
  0n
```

This checks and prints `0n`.
</details>

#### Directions we explored, and what happened

**1. Check templates once, and let laws take `~` parameters.** This needs no new theory. The idea is to check a template body once, with each `~` parameter bound to an opaque constant of its declared type, and keep instantiation as it is. A reference to a top-level constant is already free in the usage tally, so the body may use the parameter any number of times, and affinity is untouched. The opaque constant has no body, so the check accepts exactly the proofs that hold for every closed instance. A prototype of about 30 lines against 2.0.3 rejected the wrong proof in item 4 and accepted our generic category and functor lemmas. 18 of Base's 20 templates passed, and the other 2 hit a bug in the prototype. This looks like the check the 2.0.16 changelog names as missing: "until the checker verifies template expansion itself". It covers closed structures only, since a structure chosen at run time is still affine. It also changes behavior: a template whose proof relies on its instance computing is rejected at definition. So it fits best where a template fills a `law` with `~` parameters, and other templates keep their macro semantics.

**2. Let proofs match erased arguments under an equation goal. Withdrawn, because it is unsound.** In its naive form, matching an erased `Empty` promotes a dead Curry term into a checked proof of `0n == 1n`. A refined version refused the empty-case closure on erased scrutinees, and it fell to a counterexample Paulo posted on Discord:

```python
type Loop is Data:
  Step{rest: Loop}

def bad(-x: Loop) -> {0n == 1n : Nat}:
  match x:
    case Step{rest}:
      bad(rest)
```

`Loop` has constructors, and the recursion descends, but the dead fragment can supply a `Loop` that never ends. The lesson is general. Any rule that lets proofs inspect dead values needs those values to be well-founded, and the current dead fragment cannot guarantee that.

**3. Resource encodings: fuel chains and duplicating macros.** Lorenzo proposed on Discord to simulate a reusable hypothesis by `n` copies, with the count in the type, as in `Assoc(op, n)`, where each use hands back the rest. It checks when the instance's law holds by computation, as for a constant operation. With `Nat.add` and its inductive proof it fails in one of two places. With erased points, the instance cannot induct, as in item 5. With live points, each composite point such as `op(c, d)` is a use of `op`, and the generic proof fails with `op (consumed more than once)`. The encoding also changes every statement, cannot split a budget between two independent lemmas, and builds its chains at run time, where equations would have been erased. A macro that emits copies of the operation meets one more problem: `op1` and `op2` are not definitionally equal, so every point needs a coherence rewrite.

**4. A graded split with a predicative, positive, total proof fragment.** This is the principled direction, and it is unproven. BendTT would stay the runtime fragment, unchanged: `Type : Type`, negative types, affine closures, freeing on match, reference counts only on `+`. Positions of quantity 0 would gain free contraction: types, erased arguments, proof-typed results and rewrite evidence. Universe levels, strict positivity and termination would back that contraction. This is quantitative type theory as McBride (2016) and Atkey (2018) set it out and Idris 2 ships it. Consistency would come from the proof fragment's ordinary metatheory rather than from affinity. The compiler already erases these positions, so runtime ownership does not change. We found two subtleties:
- **Levels alone are not enough.** Curry's paradox needs no universes, so positivity is required as well.
- **Negative-typed values stay affine in proof positions, even when bound live.** Otherwise a runtime definition that returns a proof can be used to build a fixed point.

That suggests three modes instead of two. Type positions allow free mention. Proof positions are total and contract only at hereditarily positive, levelled types. The runtime fragment is unchanged. It also suggests separating two uses of erasure: an index that is never inspected, as `-x` is today, and a proof argument that may be matched and must therefore be well-founded. The costs are level annotations without inference, a positivity checker, a two-fragment model in `bend.lean`, and type-level code that must terminate. It survived every attack we could build, including Paulo's, but it is a conjecture until mechanized.

**5. Other directions worth weighing.**
- **Two-level type theory and typed staging.** Annenkov, Capriotti, Kraus and Sattler (2017) and Kovács, "Staged compilation with two-level type theory" (ICFP 2022), treat `~` as a genuine outer level with its own consistent theory, checked once, instead of as substitution. Direction 1 is the smallest step toward it.
- **A proof-irrelevant sort.** A `Prop` or `SProp`, following Gilbert, Cockx, Sozeau and Tabareau (POPL 2019), would have inhabitants that duplicate freely, including functions into it. It meets the same obstacle, because a duplicable `Bad -> {0n == 1n : Nat}` would type Curry's term, so it also needs positivity. It is direction 4 restricted to propositions.
- **Graded modal dependent types.** Moon, Eades and Orchard (ESOP 2021) generalize direction 4, with separate grades for type-level and term-level use.
- **External verification.** Library-scale mathematics could live in Lean over the existing `bend.lean` core, proving Bend definitions correct there. This avoids any change to the theory, but Bend is then no longer the proof language.

#### Questions

1. Would direction 1 be acceptable as the way out of the 2.0.16 note on template instances, that is, laws with `~` parameters filled by templates that are checked once against opaque parameters?
2. Is an opt-in graded proof fragment like direction 4 compatible with Bend's goals, or does it conflict with the single universe and the one-pass checker?

The probe files, the prototype checker and the counterexamples are available on request.

title: A def without a return type that fills no law reports `expected : '->'`, not the missing law
body:
## What you did

Rename or delete a law in `LAWS.bend`, while its proof def stays in `PROOF.bend`. Then run:

```
bend PROOF.bend
```

## What happened

```
Error:
- expected : '->'
- observed : ':'
Location:
3 | 
4>| def Laws.add_zero_law(x):
5 |   match x:
```

Bend uses a def without a return type to fill a law. In this file, no law named `Laws.add_zero_law` is in scope. The law was deleted, renamed, or lives in a file that this one does not import. The error never says that.

`expected : '->'` reads as "add a return type". That is the wrong repair. The real problem is the name, and the law stays open. Renaming the def to the law's name fixes it; adding a return type does not.

An agent reaches this error when the human renames a law and the agent edits `PROOF.bend`. Agents write the proof side, so this message lands in their repair loop.

## The file

`LAWS.bend` — the law was renamed to `add_zero`:

```bend
import Base

law add_zero:
  for x: Nat
  {Nat.add(x, 0n) == x : Nat}
```

`PROOF.bend` — the def still has the old name:

```bend
import Base
import ./LAWS.bend as Laws

def Laws.add_zero_law(x):
  match x:
    case 0n:
      {==}
    case 1n+p:
      %Laws.add_zero_law(p) : {1n+Nat.add(p, 0n) == 1n+_ : Nat}
      {==}
```

## Suggestion

Name the missing law, for example:

```
Error:
- message : def Laws.add_zero_law fills no law
- note    : a def without a return type must fill a law;
            no law named 'add_zero_law' is in scope
```

title: C lane: a hot constructor built at a family stuck on an open index holds a field of a type the facts never saw, and its consumer takes the sealed node raw
macOS: a window does not accept the first mouse, so the click that refocuses it is dropped
body:
### What you did

bend clicks.bend -o clicks && ./clicks

### What happened

```text
Click another app (the terminal) so the Bend window is not key, click once
inside the Bend window, then click again.

Expected: the first click prints

  mouse down=True
  mouse down=False

Observed: the first click prints nothing. It only brings the window to the
front; the program gets no Mouse event for it. The second click is delivered.
Every app that acts on a click misses the first one each time the user comes
back from another window. demos/app_pong_game_2d shows it too, though its
paddles do not react to clicks, so the program below is the smaller check.

Cause: BendView in bend2/effs/window_open.c does not implement
acceptsFirstMouse:. Cocoa's default is NO, so the activating click is
swallowed instead of delivered. The view already implements
acceptsFirstResponder (window_open.c:22) and the window opts into moves with
acceptsMouseMovedEvents = YES (window_open.c:149); clicks should get the same:

  - (BOOL)acceptsFirstMouse:(NSEvent*)ev {
    return YES;
  }

Related but distinct: #842 is about input reaching the app several frames
late, not about a click that never arrives at all.
```

### The file

```python
import Base

def tick(events: List<Event>, n: U32) -> IO(Maybe<U32>):
  match events:
    case Nil{}:
      IO.pure(Maybe<U32>, Some{n})
    case Con{Close{}, rest}:
      IO.pure(Maybe<U32>, None{})
    case Con{Mouse{x, y, b, d}, rest}:
      do IO<Maybe<U32>>:
        IO.print("mouse down=" ++ Bool.show(d))
        tick(rest, n)
    case Con{e, rest}:
      tick(rest, n)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  App.run(~U32, ~App{+s => (s, Pix{s}), tick}, "Clicks", 256, 256, 0)
```
