title: A TCP receive with a deadline, as UDP.poll: today a Bend server cannot drop an idle connection
body:
### What Bend should do

A TCP receive that gives up after `ms` milliseconds, shaped like `UDP.poll`, which Base already has (a receive that answers `None{}` when nothing is there):

```python
# as UDP.poll(sock, max): Done{None{}} when nothing arrived within ms;
# ms = 0 answers at once, as UDP.poll does today.
def TCP.poll(sock: Socket, max: U32, ms: U32) ->
  IO(Socket & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Maybe<&1, String>>)
```

What a server writes with it — a keep-alive connection that reads the next request or drops the peer after ten seconds of silence:

```python
def conn_talk(s: Socket) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    got : Socket & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Maybe<&1, String>> <- TCP.poll(s, 8192, 10000)
    conn_reply(got)   # Done{None{}}: the peer sent nothing in 10 s, close it
```

The C side is `udp_poll.c` with `recv` in place of `recvfrom`, and, for `ms > 0`, the parked wait of `tcp_recv.c` (`io_wait_on(w, fd, POLLIN, ..)`) given a deadline; the JS side is the same over `io_park_on`. I can send that as a PR if the shape is right.

### Why

`TCP.recv(sock, max)` parks until the socket is readable, with no deadline, and the one way to end a parked receive from outside — a watchdog that closes the socket — cannot be written: `Socket` is a handle law of kind `Type`, so a second reference to it is refused (design, WONTFIX #825; this is not a request to change that):

```
def watchdog(+s: Socket, ms: U32) -> IO(Unit):
Error:
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
```

So a Bend server cannot drop an idle connection. A peer that connects and sends nothing (or sends a request header and never its last `\r\n`) holds its handler parked forever — the slowloris shape — and a proof-checked server that any client can pin down is not a server one can expose. Today the timeout has to live outside Bend, in a reverse proxy, and people are writing HTTP servers in Bend (#846).

The workaround that exists: a user effect can take a Base `Socket` handle (guide, Effects), so a program can ship its own `tcp_poll.c` and `tcp_poll.js`. It works, and it means every server re-implements in two languages a primitive the UDP side of Base already has.

bend 2.0.16, Linux x86_64.

title: Maybe<_, _> in return position fails to elaborate ('non-inferrable term')
body:
bend 2.0.16.

A function returning `Maybe` fails to check, regardless of payload:

```python
import Base

def t(b: Bool) -> Maybe{&2, Bool}:
  match b:
    case True{}:
      Some{False{}}
    case False{}:
      None{}
```

```
Error:
- expected : Type
- observed : non-inferrable term 'Maybe{&2, Bool}'
```

Same result with `Nat` and user-type payloads, `&1` or `&2`, and either
branch order. (Side note: an identical snippet checked twice earlier the
same day before failing consistently ever since — mentioning it in case
some stale state is involved; glad to provide any cache info if useful.)

Workaround used: a local option type with the same shape elaborates fine:

```python
type Opt2 is Data:
  nenhum{}
  algum{lado: Lado2}
```

So this looks like an elaborator gap for `Maybe` in return position
specifically, not a fundamental restriction.

title: A page target: -o file.html builds the runtime as WebAssembly, a worker a core, and a Window on its canvas
body:
**Live:** <https://adrielsantana.github.io/bendcraft/> (a first-person voxel game, this target on ten workers) and <https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/> (Mandelbrot, Pong, the triangle, a raycaster, `demos/app_ray_tracer_3d`), served with `coi-serviceworker` for the headers.

## What

`bend file.bend -o file.html` builds the program's C, unchanged, with Emscripten into `file.html`, `file.js` and `file.wasm`: the same runtime as WebAssembly, a Web Worker per core, `!` on the cores. A `Window` draws on the page's canvas and reads its keyboard and mouse; frames are paced by the display (`requestAnimationFrame`), as the Mac's display sync.

The JavaScript target runs on one core, and so does the playground in #859 (it runs the JS target in a Worker). The C runtime already compiles as C11 with pthreads and 32-bit atomics, so the browser gap was the target, not the language: with `-pthread -mtail-call` the segment machine's `musttail` calls become wasm tail calls, the pool's mutex/condvar/atomics become `SharedArrayBuffer` + `Atomics`, and `preserve_none` is ignored (wasm has no callee-saved registers).

## Measured

Apple M5 (10 cores), Chrome 153, Emscripten 6.0.9, Node 24. A windowless 512×512 Mandelbrot, 50 iterations, quadtree built with parallel calls, summed to a checksum; `IO.now()` around the computation only, five frames with varying input, median. Every cell has the same checksum.

| ms per frame | 1 thread | 4 threads | 10 threads |
|---|---|---|---|
| JS target (bun) | 530 | – | – |
| WebAssembly in Chrome | 26 | 7–8 | 4–5 |
| WebAssembly in Node | 26 | 7–8 | 5 |
| native binary (clang) | 22 | 6 | 6 |

With a window, frames drawn in 5 s (300 display ticks), headless Chrome; 288 is the 60 Hz ceiling:

| page | 1 thread | 2 threads | 4 threads | 10 threads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mandelbrot 512², recomputed every frame | 143 | 288 | 288 | 288 |
| `demos/app_pong_game_2d` | – | – | – | 283 |

The live pages, ten workers, frames per second the page counts, with the same program's native frame on Metal where it was measured (Bend 2.0.23):

| page | fps in Chrome | the frame on Metal |
|---|---|---|
| Mandelbrot 512², Pong, the triangle | 60 | |
| Bendcraft, 512² (a voxel world edited through the array fork, a ray a pixel) | 31 | 3 ms |
| Bendcraft, 512×288 rays in a 1024×576 canvas | 53 | |
| `demos/app_ray_tracer_3d`, 1024×768 | 19 (4 on one core) | |

Bendcraft's frames are its native build's: the bench's 30 checksums are the same from this tree and from the shipped 2.0.23. The first frame costs ~70 ms extra while the Workers start.

## Try it

```sh
brew install emscripten            # or emsdk; 3.1.35+ for tail calls
bun bend2/main.ts demos/app_pong_game_2d/main.bend -o pong/pong.html
```

Threads need cross-origin isolation, so the page must be served with two headers (`file://` cannot work):

```sh
cd pong && python3 -c '
import http.server as h
class H(h.SimpleHTTPRequestHandler):
    def end_headers(s):
        s.send_header("Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy", "same-origin")
        s.send_header("Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy", "require-corp")
        super().end_headers()
h.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 8000), H).serve_forever()'
```

Then open `http://127.0.0.1:8000/pong.html` (the selector under the canvas, or `?threads=1`, to compare). On GitHub Pages, which sets no headers, the `coi-serviceworker` trick works.

## Changes

- `bend2/main.ts`: `cli_build_web` (the `emcc` line) and `PAGE`, the page it writes: the canvas, a thread-count selector (it reloads with `?threads=N`, clamped to the cores, since the runtime sizes its pool at start), the frames per second the program delivered, a line per print; help text. 8085 ttok of 10000.
- `bend2/comp.ts`: a segment takes the `Env`'s two words instead of the struct, on every host (`WL_SIG`/`WL_ALL`, `WL_OPEN` rebuilds `e`): wasm passes a struct by a pointer into the caller's frame, and a `return_call` pops that frame, so from `-O2` up a segment read a stale `Env` (`heap_alloc_miss` trapped on an unaligned atomic with `e.mem` = garbage; `-O1` only worked by luck). On arm64 and x86-64 a two-pointer struct already travels in two registers, and the benchmark's compute segments compile to the same instructions either way, so the signature is one for all rather than a wasm `#ifdef`. Also the runtime's sizes for wasm32 (`STACK_LEN`, `CORPUS_LEN`, `CORPUS_MIN`: wasm commits what it maps, the Loc space is 4 GiB, and the corpus, which grows in place on the cores, is one `memalign`'d block of 1 GiB there, asked for no place and never grown); `pool_try` as `memalign` on wasm, since Emscripten's `mmap` is `memalign` plus a `memset` of memory that is zero already (140–230 ms per page load for the 1 GiB corpus, measured). 64972 ttok of 65000.
- `bend2/effs/window_{open,frame,close,set_title}.c`: an `#elif defined(__EMSCRIPTEN__)` branch each, between the Linux one and the stub, with `BendWin` under the X11's `#ifndef BendWin` guard. The page's side is two `EM_JS` functions in `window_open.c` (the canvas and its listeners; a frame's blit and event drain on the next animation frame, or a 16 ms timer while the tab is hidden), called on the main thread through `MAIN_THREAD_EM_ASM`; the program's thread waits on a futex the page signals. Key codes, buttons and the five-word events are the Mac's, as on Linux; `mouseup` is heard on the window, so a button released off the canvas still comes up, and a button past the middle one is dropped. `window_k` (the quadtree's depth) and `window_host` (the pixel walk) live in `window_open.c` and the Mac, Linux and wasm frames share them; the window's size check is in `window_open_run`, out of the three platforms. 3620 / 3981 / 378 / 419 ttok of 4000.
- `guide/GUIDE.md`, `README.md`: the target, the headers, the Emscripten need.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS 46 / 46 on 2.0.23. No new files; nothing outside the allow list.

## Since it was written

The PR was written against 2.0.16 and rebased through 2.0.22 and 2.0.23 (one commit, squashed). What the runtime's own moves changed here: 2.0.22's corpus grows in place on the cores, which wasm32 cannot do, so there the corpus is one block asked for no place and never grown; `window_k` and `window_host` moved from `comp.ts` into `window_open.c`, which every window effect follows, to keep `comp.ts` under its cap; the two-word `Env` held. What did not change: the page, the workers, the canvas `Window`, the numbers.

## What a next step keeps

- The host: the page, its Workers, the `coi-serviceworker` on a static host, the canvas `Window` with the Mac's key codes. A WGSL lane (#920) would keep all of it and add a device path the way the Mac has one: the page dispatches the `!`'s frontier on WebGPU instead of the pool. The reasons a port of the Metal runtime cannot be that lane, and a runtime built for WebGPU with its measurements (0.3 ms for the Mandelbrot frame, 1.8 for the raycaster's), are in #920.
- `window_host` could fork, as the Linux frame could.
- A stack guard on the host under `__EMSCRIPTEN__`.

## Limits, stated

- Memory is 2 GiB, fixed (`-sINITIAL_MEMORY`), no growth, so the `HEAP*` views the page's JS reads stay valid; corpus 1 GiB, halved down to 256 MiB if the allocation fails; 16 MiB stack per thread (native reserves 2 GiB lazily; wasm cannot). iOS Safari gives a page far less than 2 GiB; untested there.
- No stack guard: `sigaltstack`/`SIGSEGV` are stubs, so a host recursion past 16 MiB corrupts memory instead of failing. A `WL_ROOM`-style check on the host under `__EMSCRIPTEN__` is the follow-up.
- `window_host` walks the quadtree on the program's thread, single-threaded (~3 ms at 512²), as Linux without CUDA; the Mac does it on Metal. It could fork.
- One window per page (the canvas is `#bend`); the page keeps at most 1024 events for a frame that has not come.
- Audio, files and sockets have no browser branch: audio compiles to the stub (`ENOTSUP`), files hit Emscripten's in-memory FS (Bendcraft's save lasts until the tab closes), sockets are untested. AudioWorklet, OPFS and WebSocket are the paths.
- Safari caps `navigator.hardwareConcurrency` at 8; Firefox and Safari 18.2+ have the needed wasm features (threads, tail calls) but only Chrome was measured.
- `!` runs on the cores; the GPU in the browser is #920.

## How this was made

Written by Claude (Anthropic) with Adriel Santana driving, as this repo's runtime was; every number above was measured on his M5. The diff had a review pass (bugs, reuse, simplification, efficiency, depth of each change) before the squash.

title: match on U32 literal patterns emits a 32-bit decomposition tree, not a lookup table (256 arms: 3.5 GiB, 1.46 MB C; the same table on Nat: 0.24 GiB, 87 KB)
body:
### What you did

```
bend tbl_u32.bend -o tbl_u32.c
bend tbl_nat.bend -o tbl_nat.c
```

### What happened

A `match` on `U32` literal patterns lowers to a nested test over all 32 bits of the scrutinee. The same table written with contiguous `Nat` patterns lowers to a native lookup table. Both give the same answers, but the `U32` form costs emitter memory, emission time and output size that grow with the arm count, while the `Nat` form stays flat.

Measured on main at 15ae0c86 (bend 2.0.16); max RSS from `/usr/bin/time -l`, size is the emitted `.c`.

| arms | U32 `-o .c` | Nat `-o .c` |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 0.26 GiB, 133 KB | 0.11 GiB, 86 KB |
| 32 | 0.64 GiB, 267 KB | 0.12 GiB, 86 KB |
| 64 | 1.02 GiB, 442 KB | 0.12 GiB, 86 KB |
| 128 | 1.91 GiB, 786 KB | 0.18 GiB, 86 KB |
| 256 | 3.5 GiB, 1.46 MB (5 s) | 0.24 GiB, 87 KB (under 1 s) |
| 512 | 6.84 GiB, 2.77 MB (8 s) | 0.39 GiB, 89 KB (1 s) |

The JS lane shares the lowering: at 256 arms, `-o .js` is 1.40 GiB and 2.67 MB against 0.22 GiB and 15 KB.

At 256 arms the `U32` version emits one 26,148-line function:

```c
FAR Term spin_5(Env e, THR Term* o, u32 r0) {
  ...
  u32 s_0 = ((x_6 >> 0) & 1);
  u32 s_1 = ((x_6 >> 1) & 1);
  ...
  u32 s_31 = ((x_6 >> 31) & 1);
  if (s_0 == 0) {
    if (s_1 == 0) {
      if (s_2 == 0) {
        ...
```

All 32 bits are decomposed although no arm is above 255, and the `if` tree that follows is the whole body. The `Nat` version emits, for the same table:

```c
CONSTV u64 TAB_0[] = { 11ull, 48ull, 85ull, 122ull, ... };
#define TAB_AT(T, S, I) T[S < I ? S : I]
...
v_9 = TAB_AT(TAB_0, x_6, 256);
```

The two sit next to each other in `emit_match`: `comp.ts:2632` sets `word` for `U32`/`F32` and `comp.ts:2634` builds the scrutinee as 32 one-bit words (`U32{data: Word(32n)}` in `base.bend` really is a `Word.Con` chain, so the match is over that ADT and the emitter is lowering it faithfully), while `comp.ts:2641` gates the table on `adt.k === "Nat"`:

```ts
const ls = adt.k === "Nat" ? emit_nat(x) : null;
const id = emit_tab(fl, ls, all.B(DUMMY));
```

The JS emitter has the same gate at `comp.ts:3046`. A `U32` match whose arms are dense literals returning constants seems to be the same shape `emit_tab` already handles for `Nat`.

Correctness is not affected: 1,500 random draws through each binary, every observed index returned `(i * 37 + 11) % 251` on both lanes (the `U32` run happened to miss 1 of the 256 indices, the `Nat` run hit all 256).

### The file

Both files are generated; this shell writes the 256-arm pair.

```bash
for M in u32 nat; do
  { echo "import Base"; echo
    if [ $M = u32 ]; then echo "def tbl(x: U32) -> U32:"; else echo "def tbl(x: Nat) -> U32:"; fi
    echo "  match x:"
    for i in $(seq 0 255); do
      if [ $M = u32 ]; then echo "    case $i:"; else echo "    case ${i}n:"; fi
      echo "      $(( (i * 37 + 11) % 251 ))"
    done
    echo "    case _:"; echo "      0"; echo
    echo "law main:"; echo "  IO(Unit)"; echo
    echo "def main():"; echo "  do IO<Unit>:"
    echo "    r : U32 <- IO.try(U32, IO.random_u32())"
    if [ $M = u32 ]; then
      echo "    IO.print(U32.show(tbl((r % 256 : U32))))"
    else
      echo "    IO.print(U32.show(tbl(U32.to_nat((r % 256 : U32)))))"
    fi
  } > tbl_$M.bend
done
```

It came up as a 256-entry byte table in a codec; rewriting the scrutinee as a `Nat` was the workaround, at the cost of a conversion on every lookup.

### bend --version

bend 2.0.16

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)

title: JS emitter treats dots in field names as property paths and silently reads a different field
body:
### What you did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts dotted_field.bend
bun bend2/main.ts dotted_field.bend -o dotted_field && ./dotted_field
bun bend2/main.ts dotted_field.bend -o dotted_field.js && bun dotted_field.js
```

### What happened

The evaluator and the C binary print:

```text
9
```

The emitted JS prints:

```text
5
```

The checker also accepts `second_is_nine`, so the source semantics reduce the second field to `9`.

A dot is legal in a Bend name; the guide says that dots inside a name are just characters. The JS emitter creates the constructor with the right property names:

```js
{$: "Outer", ["a"]: {$: "Inner", ["b"]: 5}, ["a.b"]: 9}
```

but a match reads a field by concatenating `.` with its name (`keys.map((n) => s + "." + n)` in `comp.ts`). The generated binding for the second field is therefore:

```js
const q_0 = x_0.a.b;
```

That reads the `b` field inside `a` and returns `5`, instead of reading the distinct property `x_0["a.b"]`, whose value is `9`.

This is silent JS wrong-code from a checked program. It uses no `@unsafe`, FFI, open law, runtime limit or native numeric edge case.

Tested on current main at `15ae0c86`.

### The file

```bend
import Base

type Inner is Data:
  Inner{b: U32}

type Outer is Data:
  Outer{a: Inner, a.b: U32}

def second(x: Outer) -> U32:
  match x:
    case Outer{p, q}:
      q

law second_is_nine:
  {second(Outer{Inner{5}, 9}) == 9 : U32}

def second_is_nine():
  {==}

def main() -> U32:
  second(Outer{Inner{5}, 9})
```

### bend --version

```text
bend 2.0.16
```

### uname -sm

```text
Darwin arm64
```

### clang --version (the first line)

```text
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: Integrate Why3 for short automatic proofs
body:
Bend currently makes checking proofs very fast at the cost of requiring significant work to construct and maintain proofs. Very routine and simple proof steps can account for significant amounts of code.

I propose integrating Why3 into proof elaboration. Let ATPs discharge simple obligations with a short timeout and then make the results available as theorems in larger manual proofs. By doing so, the ability to quickly check proofs is maintained while massively reducing the amount of manual proof code that needs to be written.

This also opens up the possibility of faster iteration times during development. During iteration, Why3 can be used to do most of the work and then before release a manual proof can be performed if it's determined that the extra performance is required.

I have used a LLM to create a small proof-of-concept which can be found here: https://github.com/liampwll/bend

Even in this early proof-of-concept, the results are promising, as shown in the below table, and I believe there's a lot of room for improvement:

| Demo | Original lines | Why3 lines | Reduction | ATP goals | Before check (s) | After check (s) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| app_pong_game_2d | 52 | 5 | 90.4% | 1 | 0.198 | 0.468 |
| app_ray_tracer_3d | 15 | 10 | 33.3% | 1 | 0.233 | 0.553 |
| app_slash_boss_3d | 86 | 77 | 10.5% | 1 | 7.909 | 10.805 |
| app_triangle_2d | 12 | 12 | 0.0% | 0 | 0.188 | 0.186 |
| app_win_is_bug_2d | 391 | 29 | 92.6% | 4 | 0.803 | 1.335 |
| io_hello_world | 5 | 5 | 0.0% | 0 | 0.169 | 0.171 |
| io_http_fetch | 26 | 26 | 0.0% | 1 | 0.206 | 0.837 |
| io_http_server | 17 | 5 | 70.6% | 1 | 0.197 | 0.543 |

| **Total** | **1109** | **502** | **54.7%** | **42** | **11.435** | **23.573** |

Here's proof_3200, I kept it in it's own table to avoid dominating all the other results:

Obviously there is a time cost here; however, I believe that in many situations this is a worthwhile tradeoff, so the option should be available when the developers decides that it's worth it.

title: JS loader treats a user-defined Nat as Base.Nat, producing wrong code and duplicating an affine capture
JS channels confuse a null payload with a parked receiver, causing a false deadlock
body:
### What you did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts chan_null_proof.bend
bun bend2/main.ts chan_null_proof.bend -o chan_null_proof.js
bun chan_null_proof.js
bun bend2/main.ts chan_null_proof.bend -o chan_null_proof
./chan_null_proof
```

### What happened

The default/JS lane reports a deadlock and exits 1:

```text
bend: deadlock: every computation waits on a channel
```

The native binary prints `ok` and exits 0. The JS result is stable (20/20 runs here).

The program sends an equality proof through a rendezvous channel. A second rendezvous channel is only a handshake: it makes sure the producer reaches and parks at the proof send before the consumer tries to receive it.

### The file

```bend
import Base

def producer(
  +data: Chan({0 == 0 : U32}),
  +ready: Chan(Unit)
) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    Bool <- Chan.send(Unit, ready, Unit{})
    Bool <- Chan.send({0 == 0 : U32}, data, {==})
    IO.pure(Unit, Unit{})

def run(data: Chan({0 == 0 : U32}), ready: Chan(Unit)) -> IO(Unit):
  +d = data
  +r = ready
  do IO<Unit>:
    Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, producer(d, r))
    signal : Maybe<&1, Unit> <- Chan.recv(Unit, r)
    proof : Maybe<&1, {0 == 0 : U32}> <- Chan.recv({0 == 0 : U32}, d)
    Unit <- Chan.close(Unit, r)
    Unit <- Chan.close({0 == 0 : U32}, d)
    IO.print("ok")

def with_data(data: Chan({0 == 0 : U32})) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    ready : Chan(Unit) <- Chan.new(Unit, 0)
    run(data, ready)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    data : Chan({0 == 0 : U32}) <- Chan.new({0 == 0 : U32}, 0)
    with_data(data)
```

### Why it happens

The emitted JS passes the proof to `Chan.send` as `null`:

```js
$Chan$send$(data_0, null, x_4)
```

But the JS channel queue also uses `item: null` to mean that the queued entry is a receiver. `chan_send.js` parks a full/rendezvous send as:

```js
row.wait.push({ cont: k, item: value });
```

and `chan_recv.js` recognizes a parked sender only with:

```js
row.wait.length > 0 && row.wait[0].item !== null
```

So a parked sender carrying a proof is read as another parked receiver. The real receiver parks behind it and the scheduler reports a deadlock.

The C lane has a separate `TERM_HOLE` sentinel for receivers, so the proof value does not collide and the rendezvous completes. A tagged queue entry on JS would make the distinction explicit too.

This is a clean program: no `@unsafe`, templates or custom FFI. Live `Type` values also compile to `null`, so the collision is not limited to equality proofs. A full buffered channel can hit the same path when a `null` payload sender has to park.

### Environment

- bend 2.0.16, main at `15ae0c86`
- Darwin arm64
- Apple clang 21.0.0

title: JS F32 sNaN mismatch can duplicate an affine Chan through a dependent Quant
body:
### What I did

I used the known sNaN round-trip difference from #797 as the tag of a dependent `Quant`:

```text
bun bend2/main.ts f32_duplicate_chan.bend
bun bend2/main.ts f32_duplicate_chan.bend -o out.js && bun out.js
bun bend2/main.ts f32_duplicate_chan.bend -o out && ./out
```

```bend
import Base

def as_f32(u: U32) -> F32:
  U32{w} = u
  F32{w}

def bits(f: F32) -> U32:
  F32{w} = f
  U32{w}

def runtime_tag() -> Bool:
  U32.is_eq(bits(as_f32(2139095041)), 2139095041)

def static_tag() -> {runtime_tag() == True{} : Bool}:
  {==}

def payload_grade(tag: Bool) -> Quant:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      &2
    case True{}:
      &1

def Payload(tag: Bool) -> Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      U32
    case True{}:
      Chan(U32)

type Copies<tag: Bool> is Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  CopiesValue{fst: Payload(tag), snd: Payload(tag)}

def forge(tag: Bool, a: Payload(tag), b: Payload(tag)) -> Copies<tag>:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      +copy = a
      CopiesValue{copy, copy}
    case True{}:
      CopiesValue{a, b}

def use(copies: Copies<True{}>) -> IO(Unit):
  CopiesValue{fst, snd} = copies
  do IO<Unit>:
    Unit <- Chan.close(U32, fst)
    sent : Bool <- Chan.send(U32, snd, 7)
    IO.print(Bool.show(sent))

def with_first(first: Chan(U32)) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    second : Chan(U32) <- Chan.new(U32, 1)
    use(forge(runtime_tag(), first, second))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    first : Chan(U32) <- Chan.new(U32, 1)
    with_first(first)
```

### What happened

The C binary prints `True`. It closes the first channel and sends on the separate second channel.

The default JS lane and emitted JS print `False`.

The checker accepts `static_tag`, so it reduces `runtime_tag()` to `True`. The caller therefore passes two affine `Chan(U32)` values to `forge` and gets a `Copies<True{}>` back.

At runtime JS quiets the signaling NaN and gets `False`. That selects the arm where `Payload(False{})` is `U32`, so `+copy` is legal. The value in `a` is actually the first channel, and the emitted code puts the same object in both fields:

```js
if (!tag_0) {
  const copy_0 = a_0;
  return {$: "CopiesValue", fst: copy_0, snd: copy_0};
}
```

`use` closes `fst`, then the send through `snd` sees that same channel as closed. The real second channel was dropped.

The new part compared with #797 is where the known F32 difference ends up. It reaches a dependent kind and lets the JS backend contract an opaque affine handle in a branch checked as `Data`.

A full bit-exact F32 representation is not the only possible fix. The JS lane could fail-stop when `F32{w}` cannot round-trip through its native-number representation (including the constant-folded constructor path). Native F32 arithmetic could stay as it is.

No `@unsafe`, custom FFI or open user law is involved.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.16
commit 15ae0c86
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: IO foreign defs are trusted invisibly: a forged Rfl silently transports Unit{} into F32 arithmetic — the verdict should count foreign defs like it counts ~ instances
body:
### What you did

Two files: ffi_forge_rwt.bend + its JS twin ffi_forge_rwt.js (below; also at Cypoe/bend-probe). bun bend2/main.ts ffi_forge_rwt.bend

### What happened

```text
> nan
> exit 0
```
The checker demands the {Unit == F32 : Type} evidence live (Rwt checks it) but erases it in codegen ([t.f]), so the forged Rfl is never inspected — Unit{} flows into F32.add unchecked. `All terms check.` is printed with no indication the book's consistency rests on a foreign promise.

Sibling repro (ffi-empty-trap): a foreign def forge() -> IO(Empty) checks clean (ffi_forge_verdict.bend → All terms check.) and fail-stops the runtime when run — IO(Empty) is a payload no honest foreign impl can ever deliver, since Empty has zero constructors.

The ask: #841 already counts ~ instances as unsafe annotations (t.u === true || k.includes("~")). Foreign defs (tld.i set) are the bigger trust boundary and invisible to the same verdict — All terms check, with N foreign defs is the same disclosure applied to FFI. Optionally, IO(E) for ctorless E is statically refusable. (Neither demo is a kernel inconsistency — every lie arrives IO-headed.)

`bend.ts`'s header claims "no closed live inhabitant of `Empty`" and carves out
only `@unsafe`. Foreign books aren't carved out, so the stated invariant is
falsified as written. `IO(Empty)` is also the one foreign payload no honest
implementation can ever deliver to a continuation — provably a lie, not merely
unverified. 

JS emitter path only; C build fails earlier at emit-time layout check.
comp.ts:1737 (val_word) — the C emitter tracks value layouts and catches Unit{} (0 words) being read as F32 (1 word) at compile time. Plus the C backend requires a .c twin per foreign def (comp.ts:2733), which this repro doesn't ship — it would die on that too.


### The file

```python
function forge_eql(kont) {
  return { $: "Rfl" };
}


import Base
 
def forge_eql() -> IO({Unit == F32 : Type}):
  import "./ffi_forge_rwt.js"
 
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    p : {Unit == F32 : Type} <- forge_eql()
    x : F32 = %r@p : _; Unit{}
    IO.print(F32.show(F32.add(x, 2.5)))
```

### bend --version

bend 2.0.16

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 18.1.8 (Target: x86_64-pc-windows-msvc)

title: User-defined Clo.apply collides with the compiler closure sentinel and duplicates a linear File
body:
### What I did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts clo_apply_duplicate_file.bend
bun bend2/main.ts clo_apply_duplicate_file.bend -o out.js
bun out.js
bun bend2/main.ts clo_apply_duplicate_file.bend -o out
./out
```

The source defines an ordinary function named `Clo.apply`. Its body always returns `False{}`, and the checker accepts a proof of that result:

```bend
def static_tag() -> {runtime_tag() == False{} : Bool}:
  {==}
```

`False{}` selects the linear `File` payload and keeps two distinct files. The program closes the first file and writes to the second, so its source result is `True`.

### What happened

The default IO lane and emitted JS print:

```text
False
```

The native binary aborts with:

```text
bend: an alien request
```

Changing only `Clo.apply` to `User.apply` makes the default lane, emitted JS, and native binary all print:

```text
True
```

The compiler uses the source-level string `"Clo.apply"` as its synthetic closure-application sentinel:

```ts
const CLO_APPLY = "Clo.apply";
```

The JS emitter therefore compiles the direct user call `Clo.apply(return_true, 0)` as a dynamic call of `return_true`. The emitted user function exists but is never called:

```js
function $runtime_tag$() {
  return run_tail(run_clo((x_0) => {
    return run_jump($return_true$, [x_0]);
  }), 0);
}

function $Clo$apply$(f_0, x_0) {
  return false;
}
```

That changes the dependent tag from the checker's `False{}` to runtime `True{}`. The `True{}` branch was checked with a `Data` payload, so it duplicates `a`. At runtime, `a` is the first `File` from the statically selected linear branch. Both result fields therefore contain the same file handle. The program closes `fst`; writing through `snd` then fails because it is the same closed handle, while the distinct second file is dropped.

This is observable wrong-code, dependent subject-reduction failure, and contraction of an opaque linear runtime handle. `File` is declared as an opaque `Type` law specifically so programs cannot forge, copy, or reuse it. The reproducer uses no `@unsafe`, user FFI, open user law, template, malformed pattern, or custom built-in datatype. It has the same dependent-grade consequence as #872, but a different cause: a legal source definition collides with a compiler-internal call sentinel.

A smaller pure reproducer isolates the same collision: the evaluator returns `12`, emitted JS returns `22`, and native C returns `0`.

### The file

```bend
import Base

def Clo.apply(f: U32 -> Bool, x: U32) -> Bool:
  False{}

def return_true(x: U32) -> Bool:
  True{}

def runtime_tag() -> Bool:
  Clo.apply(return_true, 0)

def static_tag() -> {runtime_tag() == False{} : Bool}:
  {==}

def payload_grade(tag: Bool) -> Quant:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      &1
    case True{}:
      &2

def Payload(tag: Bool) -> Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      File
    case True{}:
      U32

type Copies<tag: Bool> is Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  CopiesValue{fst: Payload(tag), snd: Payload(tag)}

def forge(tag: Bool, a: Payload(tag), b: Payload(tag)) -> Copies<tag>:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      CopiesValue{a, b}
    case True{}:
      +copy = a
      CopiesValue{copy, copy}

def status_bool(status: Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Unit>) -> Bool:
  match status:
    case Done{value}:
      True{}
    case Fail{error}:
      False{}

def after_write(result: File & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Unit>) -> IO(Bool):
  (file, status) = result
  do IO<Bool>:
    Unit <- File.close(file)
    return status_bool(status)

def use(copies: Copies<False{}>) -> IO(Bool):
  CopiesValue{fst, snd} = copies
  do IO<Bool>:
    Unit <- File.close(fst)
    result : File & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Unit> <- File.write(snd, "x")
    after_write(result)

def with_first(first: File) -> IO(Bool):
  do IO<Bool>:
    second : File <- IO.try(File, File.open("/tmp/bend_clo_apply_second", "w"))
    use(forge(runtime_tag(), first, second))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    first : File <- IO.try(File, File.open("/tmp/bend_clo_apply_first", "w"))
    result : Bool <- with_first(first)
    IO.print(Bool.show(result))
```

### Likely fix

Do not represent synthetic closure application with a source-level `Name`. An internal tagged call kind would make it impossible for a user definition to compare equal to the sentinel. Rejecting `Clo.apply` as a source name in both the frontend and module loader would be a narrow guard.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.16
commit 15ae0c86
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: Android/Termux: build Bend locally with Bun instead of downloading Linux binary
body:
### What Bend should do

The current installer downloads the Linux ARM64 release binary on "aarch64" systems. This does not work natively on Android/Termux because the downloaded binary expects the Linux dynamic linker ("/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1").

On Android/Termux, the installer could use an installed Bun to produce a native Android executable instead of downloading the Linux release binary.

Proposed installer logic:

1. Detect Android/Termux.
2. Check whether "bun" is available.
3. If "bun" is available, build Bend locally with Bun, e.g. using "bun build --compile" on "bend2/main.ts", and install the resulting executable as "~/.bend/bin/bend".
4. If "bun" is not available, ask the user whether they want to install/provide Bun; otherwise report that Bun is required for the Android local-build path and exit without installing the incompatible Linux binary.
5. Keep the existing prebuilt-release path unchanged for Linux/macOS/etc.

Alternatively, you could arrange for the Termux repository to package `bend` themselves, if you don't want to manage the process. However, you would then need to specify this in the installation instructions.

### Why

This would make the installer produce an Android-native Bend binary and would also allow the user to use their locally built Bun rather than a prebuilt Bun/JSC runtime.

title: A fully shadowed `match` arm is dropped unchecked: case order silently changes the result, and the dead arm may call undefined names or be ill-typed while the file prints "All terms check."
body:
### What you did

    bend main.bend

### What happened

`bend main.bend` prints `1` (the interpreter), and the same program compiled with `bend main.bend -o main.js` / `bend main.bend -o main` prints `1` on the JS and C lanes too. The file is accepted with the clean verdict, yet the author clearly intended `sign(0n)` to be `0n`: the `case 0n:` arm is fully shadowed by the `case k:` catch-all above it, and nothing reports that.

The dropped arm is not just unused, it is never checked at all. This variant also prints `All terms check.` although the second arm calls a name that is declared nowhere and contains a non-decreasing self-call (`f(1n+p)` passes the matched value back unchanged):

```python
import Base

def f(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:
    case k:
      0n
    case 1n+p:
      nosuchname(True{}, p, f(1n+p))
```

So does an arm whose body has the wrong type (`case 0n: True{}` under a `Nat` goal), a duplicated constructor row (`case True{}` twice, the second with garbage), a nested duplicate (`case Con{0n, t}` after `case Con{h, t}`), and a multi-scrutinee row (`case 0n 0n:` after `case x y:`). A `?TODO` inside a dead arm is still counted (the counter is parse-time), which is the only signal that survives.

Mechanism (bend2/bend.ts, 2.0.16): `match_flatten` compiles the rows into the `\{K: h; m}` chain and, when a column runs out (`m.e.length === 0 && m.r.length > 0`, around line 2706), `body_flatten(m.r[0].f, ...)` keeps the first remaining row and discards the others. The discarded rows are never passed to `term_higher`, so their names are never resolved, and never reach `term_check`, so their types and self-calls are never checked. The checked term is the executed term (first arm wins on every lane), so this is not a soundness problem; it is a program the checker accepted without reading part of it.

Overlapping arms are a documented feature (the guide's `case Con{Close{}, rest}` followed by `case Con{e, rest}` relies on first-arm-wins), and this report is not about overlap. It is about an arm that can never be selected. Note that a row can be redundant on one path and needed on another: with `case Con{h, Nil{}}`, `case Con{0n, t}`, `case Con{h, t}`, the third row is live for `Con{1n, Con{..}}` and its body is checked (an undefined name there is reported). So the right condition is "a source row that wins no leaf", not "more than one row left at some leaf".

Suggested fix: have `match_flatten` record which source rows reach a leaf as the first row, and refuse the def when a row reaches none, with an "unreachable case" error pointing at that arm, in the spirit of the existing "a constructor of X (missing, or already matched)" that the raw `\{K: h; m}` form already gives for a duplicated constructor. WONTFIX #820 says the unused argument of an applied lambda is dead code the checker need not visit; an unreachable arm differs in that the author wrote it to handle a case, and its being dead changes what the program computes.

This report was prepared with AI assistance while stress-testing the checker. Each repro above was re-run against 2.0.16 (commit 15ae0c86) before filing.

### The file

```python
import Base

# The author means 0n to be special, but the catch-all comes first.
def sign(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:
    case k:
      1n
    case 0n:
      0n

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(Nat.show(sign(0n)))
```

    bend 2.0.16

    Darwin arm64

    Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)

Reduce the default CPU arena reservation to 128 GiB for faster startup
body:
Reduce the default CPU-only arena reservation from **8 TiB to 128 GiB** to improve startup performance for small native Bend programs. Keep an explicit opt-in, such as `--big-heap`, for programs that need the previous 8 TiB reservation.

On an Apple M4, this saves approximately **4.8 ms per process launch** in both a minimal print program and the Koru suite's wordfreq benchmark. That is a substantial part of the execution time of a small CLI tool: the minimal program drops from **5.819 ms to 1.043 ms** (82% lower), and wordfreq from **6.003 ms to 1.220 ms** (80% lower).

For a CLI launched repeatedly by a shell script, build tool, editor, or subprocess loop, this startup cost is paid on every invocation. At the observed saving, 1,000 sequential launches would spend roughly 4.8 seconds less on this overhead; that is an extrapolation, not a separate benchmark. Long-running compute jobs should see a much smaller relative benefit.

### Proposed behavior

- Reserve **128 GiB by default for CPU-only execution**.
- Offer `--big-heap` (or an equivalent explicit size option) to request the previous **8 TiB** span.
- Keep the current capacity checks and mapping-failure fallback, and make an exhausted default heap's error point to the override.
- Keep GPU-active execution controlled by the existing `--gpu` memory option.

The current runtime uses `mmap` with `MAP_NORESERVE`, so this is **virtual address space**, not 8 TiB of physical RAM allocated at startup. The proposed change targets the measured process startup overhead associated with the larger reservation. These measurements do not isolate individual kernel operations or claim an equivalent reduction in resident memory.

128 GiB retains substantial headroom while capturing nearly all the startup saving. In this sweep, shrinking further to 8 GiB saves only about **0.08 ms** for the minimal program and **0.07 ms** for wordfreq. The arena also contains runtime metadata, so its reservation size is not all usable program heap.

### Full Hyperfine sweep: 1 GiB through 8 TiB

All times are **milliseconds**. Each configuration has **100 measured runs**, after **10 excluded warmups**. The ± values are **sample standard deviations**, not confidence intervals.

title: evaluation resources
body:
### What you did

bend memover.bend

### What happened

Pure evaluation can consume ~740 MiB and grow until the host kills the process

Environment

- Bend: "2.0.16"
- Platform: Android 10 / Termux / "aarch64"
- Bun: "1.4.2"
- Bend was built locally from the "v2.0.16" sources using the local Bun installation.
- The official Linux ARM64 Bend binary is not used.

Reproducer

```
import Base

def tri(+n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      1
    case 1n+p:
      a b c = tri(p) tri(p) tri(p)
      ((a + b : U32) + c : U32)

def main() -> U32:
  tri(10n)
```

Running it directly:

$ bend --version
bend 2.0.16

$ BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 time bend memover.bend
59049

real    1m7.207s
user    2m13.736s
sys     0m5.524s

Peak resident memory was measured by polling "/proc/<pid>/status" during the same run:

exit: 0
peak VmRSS: 757052 kB
output:
59049

So the evaluator reaches approximately 740 MiB RSS for a computation whose result is simply:

59049

Comparison with compilation

The same source passes through the non-evaluating paths very quickly:

$ time bend --checkup memover.bend

real    0m1.370s
user    0m3.336s
sys     0m0.320s

Generating C:

$ time bend memover.bend -o ./memover.c

real    0m1.218s
user    0m3.396s
sys     0m0.180s

$ ls -lh ./memover.c
-rw------- ... 78K ... memover.c

The generated C produces exactly the same result:

$ clang -std=c11 -O3 ./memover.c -lpthread -lm -o ./memover_native

$ time ./memover_native
59049

real    0m0.050s
user    0m0.028s
sys     0m0.032s

Thus the approximately 67-second / 740-MiB cost is specific to the direct pure-evaluation path, not to the algorithm itself or to C code generation.

Question

What is the intended resource-limit behavior of direct evaluation of a pure "main"?

In this case memory usage keeps growing during normalization/evaluation. With deeper variants of the same recursive computation, the process can eventually be terminated by the JavaScript runtime or by the host rather than Bend reporting a controlled resource-limit failure.

Is there an intentional Bend-level memory/resource limit for this evaluation path?

If there is no such limit, what is the intended behavior when normalization requires more memory than is available? For example, should a pure computation be allowed to continue allocating until Bun/JSC or the Android system kills the process?

The concern is not simply that the evaluator is slower than generated native code. The concern is that resource consumption appears to be bounded only by the host environment, with no graceful failure mode visible at the Bend level.

The reproducer terminates successfully at ~740 MiB for this input, but increasing the recursion depth can make the same evaluation grow until the runtime/host terminates it.

The generated native version, by comparison, computes the same result in about 50 ms.


### bend --version

2.0.16

### uname -sm

Android 10 / Termux / "aarch64"

title: bend run-cu silently returns `Result: <Invalid>` ("Reached Root") on GPU node-arena exhaustion instead of reporting out-of-memory
Deque in Base
body:
### What Bend should do

```python
import Base

def main() -> List<&2, U32>:
  d = Deque.new(&2, U32)
  d = Deque.push_back(&2, U32, 1, d)
  d = Deque.push_back(&2, U32, 2, d)
  d = Deque.push_front(&2, U32, 0, d)
  Deque.to_list(&2, U32, d)  # [0, 1, 2]

# Deque.pop_front and Deque.pop_back answer Maybe<&1, A & Deque<a, A>>:
# the element next to the deque that is left, or None when it is empty.
```

### Why

tests/base/heap_queue_deque.bend pins Heap, Queue and Deque as absent, and gives "Map and Set are its containers" as the reason. I would like to know whether that line still stands before writing any code for the repo.

I wrote a Deque while learning the language: two lists, a front and a reversed back, with the back reversed into the front when the front runs out. Each element moves at most once, so pushing and popping on either end is amortized O(1). It is around 60 lines in the Base style with its helpers, and a Queue is the same type using two of the four operations.

What makes it worth having in Base instead of in every project is the proof. Taking to_list as the reading of a deque, the laws are short enough to be free: to_list(push_front(x, d)) == x <> to_list(d) and to_list(new()) == Nil{} both hold by computation, which I have checked. Anyone writing their own deque has to state and prove that again.

If it belongs in Base, I will send a PR with the defs, a tests/base/deque_ops.bend in the #| format, the laws as a tests/proof file, and heap_queue_deque.bend narrowed to Heap and Queue. If it does not belong there, that is a fine answer too.

title: A bang cannot borrow an `Array`: the editable voxel world reads its tree at 13 → 26 ms, the same frame reads a flat buffer at 1.3 → 1.4
body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #836, after the Ownership section (thanks: that one owned use was the whole cost). The borrowed tree read took the edited world from 100–110 ms to 26 ms at 512², but the read still doubles the frame once the world has edits (13 → 26 ms), and the same frame drawn from a flat buffer costs 1.3 ms edited or not. An `Array` is that flat buffer, and the runtime's `get` opens no half, but a bang cannot borrow one: `w` is "consumed more than once" on the two sides of a parallel let, `+w` is "expected Data, observed Type", and the guide says so ("An `Array` has one owner, so it cannot go down a fork tree: build lists"). The question is whether a read-only borrow of an `Array` by a bang — host-owned, borrowed by the bang and returned, as the scene is — fits the runtime, or is ruled out by something I do not see.

## What I did

The program is `gfx/05_craft.bend` in [AdrielSantana/metal-bending](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending): a 32×32×32 editable voxel world, `fork!(7n)` over 4×4 tiles at 512², the world a terrain function plus a quadtree of edits, read by one recursive `wget` that matches and recurses into one field (the guide's rule; in the emitted C the read is `term_peek` only). Windowless bench: five frames, the camera turning 0.01 rad a frame, a `total(9n)` checksum per frame, the ten checksums identical across every row below; "built" is 300 blocks placed in one corner. Apple M5; Bend 2.0.16 and 2.0.17 give the same numbers.

| 512², Metal | untouched | 300 blocks placed |
|---|---|---|
| the read that returned the chosen node (`Bool.pick`), before #836's answer | 15 ms | 100–110 ms |
| borrowed recursive walk (`term_peek` only) | 13 ms | 25–29 ms |

What remains in the edited world is the walk itself: five dependent reads per column crossing (five levels for 32×32 columns), where an untouched world is one `WNone` match plus the terrain function.

To see what a flat read is worth, I ran the same pixel function on WebGPU (the leaf translated by hand into WGSL, on the runtime shape described in the "WebGPU, measured" section of #866), with the world as a 1024-word buffer, one word of 32 height bits per column, 0xFFFFFFFF for "not edited, compute the terrain". The frame's checksum, computed as `total(9n)` does (a collapsed 2×2 tile counts once), equals the Bend program's on both worlds — 751552256 untouched, 351470114 built — so it is the same picture:

| 512², WebGPU, flat buffer | untouched | 300 blocks placed |
|---|---|---|
| the same pixel function | 1.34 ms | 1.40 ms |

So in the Bend build the tree read is most of the frame and all of the edit cost; a flat indexed read makes edits free, as in a conventional voxel engine.

## What the checker says

```bend
import Base

def at(+i: U32, wv: Array<U32> & U32) -> U32:
  (w2, v) = wv
  v

def sum4(+k: Nat, w: Array<U32>, +i: U32) -> U32:
  match k:
    case 0n:
      at(i, Array.get(U32, w, i))
    case 1n+j:
      a b = sum4(j, w, (i * 2 : U32)) sum4(j, w, (i * 2 + 1 : U32))
      (a + b : U32)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    +w : Array<U32> = Array.new(U32, 10n, 3)
    IO.print(U32.show(sum4!(4n, w, 0)))
```

```
- expected : w
- observed : w (consumed more than once)
```

With `+w: Array<U32>`:

```
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
```

Both are right by the guide's rules (`at` drops `w2`, which is what a read-only use would want anyway).

## The question

The Ownership section says the compiler borrows a boxed parameter "(not an `Array`)" that a def only matches or passes on, and the emitter's own note says `get`, `set`, `swap`, `size` and `new` open no half, so an array is a flat block that lanes could index. Is a read-only borrow of an `Array` inside a bang — the bang takes the block's address, every lane reads `Array.get` in place with no count and no split, nothing writes it until the bang returns it to the host, the way `bend3d`'s scene is host-owned, borrowed and returned — something the runtime could support, or is there a reason it cannot (the block classes, the CUDA fault-per-page case, the checker's `Type`/`Data` split)? If it cannot, is the guide's per-tile list the intended shape for a DDA too, where a ray crosses a few dozen columns and the list would be walked per crossing? A sentence in the guide either way settles where an editable voxel world stops in Bend today; the numbers above are the case.

Written by Claude (Anthropic) with Adriel Santana driving; the numbers are from his M5.

title: A literal Nat fuel unrolls the recursion on the device: the voxel DDA at 60n is 13,913 lines, 944 keeps and 2x the frame of U32.to_nat(60)
body:
## Summary

A recursive def called with a literal `Nat` fuel is unrolled by the compiler: `dda(60n, ...)`, the DDA step of an editable voxel world, becomes one device function of 13,913 lines with 60 copies of the step and 944 `term_keep` calls, and no loop. The same def called with `U32.to_nat(60)` stays a loop (7,053 lines of C for the whole program against 20,459; 6 keeps against 950) and the frame costs half: 13 → 6 ms untouched, 26 → 17 ms with 300 edits, at 512², same checksums. `def fuel() -> Nat: 60n` is inlined and unrolled too. Neither guide mentions it, and the GUIDE recommends the `Nat` fuel as the way to write a bounded loop, so the natural spelling is the slow one on the device.

## What I did

`gfx/05_craft.bend` in [AdrielSantana/metal-bending](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending) (the program of #885): `fork!(7n)` over 4×4 tiles at 512², a DDA of 60 steps per ray written as the guide says:

```bend
def dda(fuel: Nat, +w: World, ...) -> U32:
  match fuel:
    case 0n:
      col
    case 1n+f:
      ...
      dda(f, w, nvx, nvy, nvz, ...)

def run_dda(...) -> U32:
  ...
  +c = dda(60n, w, vx, vy, vz, ...)
```

Bench: windowless, five frames with the camera turning 0.01 rad a frame, a `total(9n)` checksum per frame, "built" = 300 blocks placed in one corner; three alternating runs each, the ten checksums identical across every row. Apple M5, Bend 2.0.17.

| 512², Metal | untouched | 300 blocks placed | C lines | `term_keep` in the C |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `dda(60n, ...)` | 13–14 ms | 25–28 ms | 20,459 | 950 |
| `dda(U32.to_nat(60), ...)` | **6 ms** | **17–18 ms** | 7,053 | 6 |
| `dda(fuel(), ...)` with `def fuel() -> Nat: 60n` | as the literal | as the literal | 20,459 | 950 |

In the emitted C of the literal version, `run_dda` is `spin_25`: `FAR`, 13,913 lines, no `WL_AGAIN`, 1,521 calls to the small spins (787 to the generic `Bool.pick`, which `term_sink`s the branch it drops), and 944 `term_keep`, four per unrolled step on the values the step passes on. In the `U32.to_nat` version the same def is a `WL_SPIN` loop with the step once.

For scale: the same pixel function written by hand in WGSL, the step as a `for` loop of 60, draws the identical frame (same checksums) in 1.34 ms on the same GPU through Chrome. The numbers in #885 are the literal's; with the loop they are 6 / 17 ms, and that question stands.

## The question

Is the unroll of a literal fuel intended, and should the device keep the loop instead, or should the guide say that a fuel must be a runtime value on the device? Today the spelling the GUIDE teaches for a bounded loop is the one that unrolls.

Written by Claude (Anthropic) with Adriel Santana driving; the numbers are from his M5.

title: The Metal lane forces precise:: trigonometry and MTLMathModeSafe: a third of the voxel frame, same checksums with fast::; an opt-in?
body:
## Summary

The Metal lane compiles the program with `MTLMathModeSafe` and `#define sin precise::sin` (cos, sqrt, exp, log, tan, pow, fmod likewise). On the voxel program of #885 and #886 the precise trigonometry is a third of the untouched frame: the emitted C rebuilt by hand with `fast::sin`, `fast::cos` and `fast::sqrt` renders the same ten checksums in 4 ms instead of 6 (15 instead of 17 with 300 edits). The math mode alone changes nothing in time and flips one frame's checksum. Is an opt-in for the fast functions something you would take, a flag on the binary or a pragma in the program, or is precise the line for CPU/GPU parity?

## What I did

`gfx/05_craft.bend` in [AdrielSantana/metal-bending](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending), after #886's fix: the terrain is `12.0 + 5.0 * F32.sin(x * 0.26) + 4.0 * F32.cos(z * 0.19)`, computed once per column crossing of the DDA, and the camera basis is four trigonometric calls per pixel. Bench as in #886 (five frames, `total(9n)` checksum, "built" = 300 blocks), the timer around the `!` only, three alternating runs. `bend x.bend -o x.c`, then the C edited and built as `bend` does (`clang -x objective-c -fobjc-arc -fmodules -std=c11 -O3 -DBEND_METAL=1 x.c -lpthread -lm -o x && ./x --gpu-build`). Apple M5, Bend 2.0.17.

| 512², Metal | untouched | 300 blocks placed | checksums |
|---|---|---|---|
| as emitted (`MTLMathModeSafe`, `precise::`) | 6 ms | 17 ms | reference |
| `fast::sin`, `fast::cos`, `fast::sqrt` | **4 ms** | **15 ms** | all ten identical |
| `MTLMathModeFast`, `precise::` kept | 6 ms | 17 ms | one frame differs |
| both | 3–4 ms | 14–16 ms | all ten identical |

The inputs are small (the sine's argument is at most 32 × 0.26), which is where `fast::sin` is exact enough; a program with large arguments would see a difference, so this is not a case for changing the default.

For scale, the same pixel function written by hand in WGSL runs in 1.34 ms on the same GPU through Chrome, which compiles Metal shaders with `fastMathEnabled` unless strict math is requested, so that number had the fast functions. With them the compiled leaf is at 3x of the hand shader; the remaining part I could not attribute from the outside (the fork skeleton alone, every pixel the sky, is 1–2 ms against 0.2 in the WGSL runtime; the ray about 2.5 against 1.1).

Written by Claude (Anthropic) with Adriel Santana driving; the numbers are from his M5.

title: Enforce proof verification before execution: refuse to run or build when accompanying proofs fail
body:
### What Bend should do

When running or building a Bend program (e.g. `bend main.bend` or `bend main.bend -o <out>`), Bend should verify accompanying proofs (`PROOF.bend` / `LAWS.bend` in the same module directory or project) before allowing execution or binary compilation. If proofs fail or contain open `TODO`s / holes, execution should be aborted immediately.

Users should have a unified workflow rather than having to manually remember to run two separate, disconnected commands:
```bash
# Current workflow:
bend PROOF.bend  # Can fail with TODOs
bend main.bend   # Runs anyway despite failing proofs!

# Desired workflow:
bend main.bend   # Automatically checks PROOF.bend (if present); halts if proofs fail, runs only if valid
```

Whether enabled by default when `PROOF.bend` is present beside `main.bend` or via an option (e.g. `bend run --verify`), verification and execution should be seamlessly linked.

### Why

Currently, running `bend main.bend` does not check `PROOF.bend`. It is possible for an application's formal proofs and laws to be completely broken or incomplete, yet the code compiles and runs without any warning.

In a language featuring dependent types and machine-checked proofs, allowing programs to run when their declared specifications/laws are actively failing undermines the safety guarantees. Unifying proof verification and execution ensures that runtime execution always respects proven invariants.

title: GPU out-of-heap: failing lanes share one free-list chain, so the error takes seconds to minutes to report
`!` on AMD GPUs: an experimental HIP/ROCm lane works
body:
### What Bend should do

I built a third GPU lane on top of commit 8008146, for AMD cards through HIP and HIPRTC. It runs. The patch is 545 lines (`comp.ts` +376 −11, `main.ts` +9 −3).

Tested on one card only: Radeon RX 7800 XT (gfx1101, 16 GB), ROCm 7.2.1, WSL2.

## The port

HIPRTC compiles the CUDA lane's device code as written: `__global__`, `__shared__` (including the `extern __shared__ hold[]` sized at launch), `__syncthreads()`, `__threadfence()`, `__clz`, `atomicAdd/Sub/CAS`. I checked the barrier, shared memory and CAS on the card with 128 × 128 lanes. Two differences:

- HIPRTC defines `__HIPCC_RTC__`, not `__CUDACC_RTC__`. One `BEND_RTC` macro replaces the six tests.
- HIPRTC ignores `-default-device`, so plain functions compile as host functions. `#pragma clang force_cuda_host_device begin` fixes it.

The host side is a `BEND_HIP` block beside `BEND_CUDA`, nearly one-to-one, with the same hash-keyed `.gpu` cache. AMD's clang 22 has `#embed`, and `cc_find` accepts its version string.

## The memory model

Consumer Radeons report `concurrentManagedAccess = 0`: managed memory is pinned host RAM read over PCIe, and nothing migrates. `gpu_probe` would refuse the card. Relaxing the probe works but is unusable: lanes keep their stacks, rings and free lists in that block, so queens takes 47 s and tree-bitonic 41 s.

The corpus is index-based, though: every `Loc` is a word index, and lanes derive their pointers from `H + offset` at kernel entry. So the device can hold it at another address. My second mode keeps a twin of the corpus in VRAM. Each `!` copies in the header, the live ring planes, the static image, the heap under the bump and the live bank entries; runs every round on the device, exchanging only the header; then copies back. CPU and GPU never run together, so this is legal. queens drops from 47 s to 1.4 s of device time.

## Numbers

`bench/runtime/`, perf.ts protocol and spans, 16 CPU threads against the HIP lane with the VRAM twin. Wall seconds, single runs on a desktop, so ±10%. Every row prints the pinned checksum on both lanes.

| bench | 16 threads | HIP wall | HIP device passes |
| - | - | - | - |
| gameoflife | 1.50 | **0.27** | 0.02 |
| nbody | 0.65 | **0.26** | 0.01 |
| raytrace | 0.87 | **0.34** | 0.09 |
| kmeans | 0.93 | **0.42** | 0.15 |
| mandelbrot | 0.54 | **0.28** | 0.02 |
| merkle | 0.63 | **0.39** | 0.02 |
| tree-bitonic | 2.29 | **1.87** | 1.48 |
| bfs | 0.45 | 0.65 | 0.26 |
| tree-matmul | 0.56 | 0.80 | 0.22 |
| symreg | 0.55 | 0.92 | 0.67 |
| terrain | 0.41 | 0.96 | 0.55 |
| editdist | 0.36 | 1.00 | 0.66 |
| hashmap | 0.48 | 1.13 | 0.45 |
| lexer | 0.41 | 1.24 | 0.94 |
| tree-radix | 0.87 | 1.38 | 0.28 |
| queens | 1.17 | 1.63 | 1.39 |

Bimodal, as in the paper. On the divergent programs all device time is inside one work kernel; growth, barriers and packing are about 0 ms. 128 groups was best or near-best on 7 of 10 programs swept; editdist and terrain ran 2 to 3 times faster at 32.

The 11 runnable `!` tests print the same bytes as the CPU lane in both memory modes. I cannot run `gates/test.ts`; a local copy of its rules gives 1299 / 1302 with the patch and 1300 / 1302 without. The difference is a TCP test with no `!` that is flaky here on the unpatched tree too.

## Weak points

- One card, one OS. No native Linux, no second AMD part, no medians.
- You have no AMD hardware in the gate, so you could not test this lane.
- The memory mode is an environment variable. It should be decided in the probe, with the span from free VRAM.
- The whole heap under the bump is copied both ways on every `!`; tree-radix moves 3.7 GB over three turns.
- Under WSL, ROCm spends 0.5 s at first use searching Windows directories on `$PATH`. I trim `PATH` around the first transfer, which is a hack.
- `effs/window_frame.c` still has only its CUDA device path.
- The patch carries a debug counter and two tuning variables. I have not checked `gates/repo.ts`'s size cap.

## The question

Would you want an AMD lane in the tree, given you cannot gate it? If yes, I would fix the points above before sending anything. If not, one finding stands without AMD: the corpus is position-independent, so a VRAM-twin mode is open to any card without migrating managed memory.

### Why

I don’t have an NVIDIA GPU 🥴

title: Three string-literal match arms exceed 512 MiB during C generation on 2.0.19
body:
### What you did

I hit compiler memory pressure while building an OpenAI SDK for Bend. I reduced one part of it to three string-literal cases on Bend 2.0.19. This looks related to #867, but uses string patterns rather than the dense U32 tables fixed there.

Compile the file below to C. On Linux I ran the reproduction in a memory-limited scope so it could not take down the desktop:

```sh
systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=512M -p MemorySwapMax=0 \
  timeout 30s bend literal.bend -o literal.c
```

### What happened

The compiler exceeded the 512 MiB cgroup limit and was killed before emitting C. The kernel recorded a memory-cgroup OOM with 521956 KiB anonymous RSS. This is a bounded reproduction, not a measurement of how much memory an unrestricted run would eventually need.

Replacing the string patterns with `String.eq` and a match on three Bools compiled successfully under the same limit: 1.06 s, 136048 KiB maximum RSS, approximately 97 KiB of C.

In the larger SDK I also observed multi-gigabyte compiler processes and a host OOM while two builds overlapped. I have stopped overlapping builds and now use memory limits. The SDK workaround is to use enums/comparisons for protocol dispatch. I am not claiming the three-case example alone caused the host OOM.

Is there a small emitter-side optimization for these literal string matches, or should this remain a documented limitation? I avoided touching the language/checker.

### The file

```bend
import Base

def classify(s: String) -> U32:
  match s:
    case "response.completed": 1
    case "response.failed": 2
    case "response.incomplete": 3
    case _: 0

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    s : String <- IO.try(String, IO.get_env("BEND_REPRO_INPUT"))
    IO.print(U32.show(classify(s)))
```

Comparison version:

```bend
import Base

def classify_flags(a: Bool, b: Bool, c: Bool) -> U32:
  match a b c:
    case True{} _ _: 1
    case _ True{} _: 2
    case _ _ True{}: 3
    case _ _ _: 0

def classify(+s: String) -> U32:
  classify_flags(String.eq(s, "response.completed"), String.eq(s, "response.failed"), String.eq(s, "response.incomplete"))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    s : String <- IO.try(String, IO.get_env("BEND_REPRO_INPUT"))
    IO.print(U32.show(classify(s)))
```

Bend 2.0.19 (official Linux x64 release)

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 21.1.8 (Fedora 21.1.8-6.fc43)

The failing command only emits C, so Clang is not invoked.

title: C backend takes the ANode arm for an ALeaf; the flipped tag can duplicate an affine closure
body:
### What I did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts generic_array.bend
bun bend2/main.ts generic_array.bend -o out.js
bun out.js
bun bend2/main.ts generic_array.bend -o out
./out --threads 1
./out --threads 8
```

```bend
import Base

type Duo is Data:
  DuoV{a: U32, b: U32}

type Boxed<-A: Data> is Data:
  BoxedV{item: A}

def node_tag(value: Bool) -> Bool:
  match value:
    case False{}:
      True{}
    case True{}:
      True{}

def tag(-A: Data, array: Array<Boxed<A>>) -> Bool:
  match array:
    case ALeaf{item}:
      False{}
    case ANode{left, right}:
      node_tag(tag(A, left))

def runtime_tag() -> Bool:
  tag(Duo, ALeaf{BoxedV{DuoV{10, 20}}})

def static_tag() -> {runtime_tag() == False{} : Bool}:
  {==}

def main() -> Bool:
  runtime_tag()
```

### What happened

The evaluator and emitted JS print:

```text
False{}
```

The native binary prints this at both thread counts:

```text
True{}
```

The input is an `ALeaf`, and the checker accepts a proof that the result is `False`. The only way this program can return `True` is by taking the `ANode` arm once and recursing into a fabricated half.

### What the emitted C shows

The generic body treats `Boxed<A>` as one boxed word and uses block class 0 as the leaf class:

```c
if (blk_cls(array_0) == 0) {
  // ALeaf
} else {
  Term h_0 = blk_half(e, array_0, 0);
  // ANode
}
```

The call instantiates `A` with the flat two-word `Duo`, so main creates the single leaf with element width 2 and block class 1:

```c
Term fv_0[2];
fv_0[0] = 10ull;
fv_0[1] = 20ull;
r0 = blk_new(e, 0, 0, 1, 2, fv_0);
```

`Array<A>` is rejected as having an open element type, but `Array<Boxed<A>>` passes because the outer element type is an ADT. Its physical layout is still open: `Boxed<A>` is one box in the generic body and two `w32` words at this call. The array handle crosses that boundary without a representation conversion, so the generic match interprets element width as tree depth.

This is not the unbalanced-array runtime limit from #808. There is no source `ANode` in the value at all, and every backend accepts the program. It is C wrong-code on a balanced array and a legal erased specialization.

### Affine consequence

I then used `False` for an affine `U32 -> U32` payload and `True` for a reusable `U32` payload. The `True` arm contains the otherwise legal `+copy = a; CopiesValue{copy, copy}`. Each affine function captures a different `Array<U32>`.

The evaluator and JS return `32`: the statically selected `False` arm keeps the two closures distinct. C returns `22` on 1 and 8 threads: its wrong `True` tag enters the reusable arm, copies the first closure, drops the second and invokes the first closure twice. The full reproducer replaces `main` above and appends:

```bend
def payload_grade(tag: Bool) -> Quant:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      &1
    case True{}:
      &2

def Payload(tag: Bool) -> Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      U32 -> U32
    case True{}:
      U32

type Copies<tag: Bool> is Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  CopiesValue{fst: Payload(tag), snd: Payload(tag)}

def forge(tag: Bool, a: Payload(tag), b: Payload(tag)) -> Copies<tag>:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      CopiesValue{a, b}
    case True{}:
      +copy = a
      CopiesValue{copy, copy}

def array_sum(array: Array<U32>) -> U32:
  match array:
    case ALeaf{value}:
      value
    case ANode{left, right}:
      (array_sum(left) + array_sum(right) : U32)

def capture(array: Array<U32>) -> (U32 -> U32):
  n => (array_sum(array) + n : U32)

def invoke(copies: Copies<False{}>) -> U32:
  match copies:
    case CopiesValue{fst, snd}:
      (fst(1) + snd(1) : U32)

def main() -> U32:
  invoke(forge(runtime_tag(),
    capture(ALeaf{10}), capture(ALeaf{20})))
```

### Expected behavior

The compiled lanes should both return `False`. A layout-polymorphic type nested inside an array element needs either consistent specialization or the same open-element rejection as a bare `Array<A>`.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.20
commit 75616561
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: A failing law over a Nat literal from about 12200n crashes the error renderer with RangeError instead of printing expected/observed
body:
When a law does not check and its residual term carries a `Nat` literal of about 12,200 or more, the checker dies with an unhandled host `RangeError` from its own error renderer instead of printing the expected/observed mismatch. The same law at 12,000n prints the diagnostic. Checking is not the problem here: the crash is in `err_show` -> `expr_show` -> `term_snf` (`bend2/bend.ts:1483`), which strongly normalizes the residual term for display and expands the literal into its Succ chain.

This is a different path from #779, which was the check path (`term_check` / `tele_check`) and was fixed in 2.0.7 by the compact `U32.to_nat` literal.

## Version

```
bend 2.0.16   (pinned checkout, git 981899d6)
bun 1.3.14
Darwin arm64  (macOS)
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)
```

Also reproduced on `main` at `7561656` ("The flake names 2.0.20"), `VERSION = "2.0.20"`, same bun and host.

## File

`nat_literal_stack.bend`:

```bend
import Base

law window_fits:
  for +now: Nat
  {Nat.is_le(Nat.sub(20000n, Nat.add(20000n, now)), 20000n) == True{} : Bool}

def window_fits(now):
  {==}
```

The law is false: `Nat.sub` cannot case-split on the variable, so the residual is `Cmp.is_le(Nat.cmp(Nat.sub(0n, now), 20000n))`. Reporting that residual is what crashes.

## Command

```
bun bend2/main.ts nat_literal_stack.bend
```

## Observed

Exit 1, 10 runs out of 10:

```
763 |     }
764 |     case "Min": {
765 |       return Min(term_higher(tm.a, env), term_higher(tm.b, env), tm.s);
766 |     }
767 |     case "App": {
768 |       return App(term_higher(tm.f, env), term_higher(tm.x, env), tm.s);
                       ^
RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.
      at term_higher (bend2/bend.ts:768:18)
      at map (1:11)
      at term_higher (bend2/bend.ts:774:29)
      at map (1:11)
      at term_higher (bend2/bend.ts:774:29)
      at term_wnf (bend2/bend.ts:2912:19)
      at term_snf (bend2/bend.ts:3070:14)
      at map (1:11)
      at term_snf (bend2/bend.ts:3108:29)
      at map (1:11)
      at async cli (bend2/main.ts:107:11)

Bun v1.3.14 (macOS arm64)
```

## Expected

The diagnostic the identical law prints when the literal is 12000n:

```
Error:
- expected : Cmp.is_le(Nat.cmp(Nat.sub(0n, now), 12000n))
- observed : True{}
Context:
- now : Nat
Location: window_fits
 6 | 
 7>| def window_fits(now):
 8 |   {==}
```

## Threshold

Same file, only the three literals changed, 10 runs each, counting runs that printed `Maximum call stack size exceeded`:

| literal | RangeError |
|---|---|
| 12000n | 0/10 |
| 12100n | 1/10 |
| 12200n | 10/10 |
| 13000n | 10/10 |
| 20000n | 10/10 |

`ulimit -s` does not move it: at 8192 and at 65520, 20000n crashes and 12100n prints the diagnostic.

## Note on a second regime

A law that *holds* at 20000n checks 10/10 as a standalone file that imports only `Base`. Inside a 137-law book it checks 2/10, the other 8 runs printing `Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)`. That one is nondeterministic and sensitive to how much stack the rest of the book has already spent; it is reported here only to separate it from the deterministic renderer crash above, which does not depend on book size.
