title: C emitter evaluates F32 lookup tables through JS; sNaN bits flip a dependent tag and duplicate an affine closure
body:
### What I did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts f32_table_affine.bend
bun bend2/main.ts f32_table_affine.bend -o out.js
bun out.js
bun bend2/main.ts f32_table_affine.bend -o out.c
clang -O2 -pthread out.c -o out
BEND_THREADS=1 ./out
BEND_THREADS=8 ./out
```

### What happened

The evaluator prints:

```text
34
```

Generated JS prints `64`, as expected from the documented JS NaN limitation in #797/#872.

Generated C also prints:

```text
64
64
```

This is not the JS lane merely disagreeing with the C reference. The C artifact already contains JS-canonicalized NaN bits:

```c
CONSTV u64 TAB_0[] = { 2139095041ull, 2139095042ull, 2139095043ull };
CONSTV u64 TAB_1[] = { 2143289344ull, 2143289344ull, 2143289344ull };
```

`TAB_0` is the U32 table used by `expected` and preserves `0x7f800001`, `0x7f800002` and `0x7f800003`. `TAB_1` is the F32 table used by `table`; all three signaling NaNs became the canonical quiet NaN `0x7fc00000` while C was being generated.

The control is changing only `table` so it is too sparse for the lookup-table optimization:

```bend
    case 100:
      as_f32(2139095043)
```

That arm is unreachable in this program. With it present, the evaluator and generated C both print `34`, and the F32 `TAB_1` is absent. Direct C construction also preserves the original bits.

### Why

`emit_tab` evaluates constant rows with JavaScript's `Function(...)`, then calls `Bend.f32_to_bits` on the resulting JS Number when producing a C table. Loading a signaling NaN into a JS Number quiets/canonicalizes it, so the C emitter bakes the JS representation loss into native code.

The WONTFIX entry for #797/#872 says the C lane is the reference when JS cannot preserve F32 NaN payload bits. Here the C lane stops being the reference only because the dense-match optimizer ran, so this looks distinct from that limitation.

The changed bits are observable as more than a numeric mismatch. The checker accepts both `static0` and `static1`. At runtime the false tag enters a branch checked for a reusable `U32`, while the actual value is a closure containing an affine `Array<U32>`. The branch copies that closure. The evaluator keeps each closure distinct and returns `34`; C invokes each captured closure twice and returns `64`. Poisoning every freed heap slot still returns `64`, and the allocation ledger ends at zero, so this is semantic affine contraction rather than a stale-slot artifact.

The file uses no `@unsafe`, FFI, open law, custom built-in datatype or malformed Array.

### Reproducer

```bend
import Base

def as_f32(u: U32) -> F32:
  U32{w} = u
  F32{w}

def bits(f: F32) -> U32:
  F32{w} = f
  U32{w}

def table(n: U32) -> F32:
  match n:
    case 0:
      as_f32(2139095041)
    case 1:
      as_f32(2139095042)
    case _:
      as_f32(2139095043)

def expected(n: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0:
      2139095041
    case 1:
      2139095042
    case _:
      2139095043

def runtime_tag(+n: U32) -> Bool:
  U32.is_eq(bits(table(n)), expected(n))

def static0() -> {runtime_tag(0) == True{} : Bool}:
  {==}

def static1() -> {runtime_tag(1) == True{} : Bool}:
  {==}

def payload_grade(tag: Bool) -> Quant:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      &2
    case True{}:
      &1

def Payload(tag: Bool) -> Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      U32
    case True{}:
      U32 -> U32

type Copies<tag: Bool> is Kind(payload_grade(tag)):
  CopiesValue{fst: Payload(tag), snd: Payload(tag)}

def forge(tag: Bool, value: Payload(tag)) -> Copies<tag>:
  match tag:
    case False{}:
      +copy = value
      CopiesValue{copy, copy}
    case True{}:
      CopiesValue{value, x => x}

def use(n: U32, value: Payload(runtime_tag(n))) -> Copies<runtime_tag(n)>:
  forge(runtime_tag(n), value)

def array_sum(a: Array<U32>) -> U32:
  match a:
    case ALeaf{x}:
      x
    case ANode{left, right}:
      (array_sum(left) + array_sum(right) : U32)

def capture(a: Array<U32>) -> (U32 -> U32):
  x => (array_sum(a) + x : U32)

def invoke(copies: Copies<True{}>) -> U32:
  match copies:
    case CopiesValue{fst, snd}:
      (fst(1) + snd(1) : U32)

def main() -> U32:
  a b = invoke(use(0, capture(ALeaf{10}))) invoke(use(1, capture(ALeaf{20})))
  (a + b : U32)
```

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.20
commit 75616561
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: Bend 2 accepts repeated fields; JS overwrites one and duplicates an affine closure
A do-block header is not resolved when the block has exactly one statement, so a wrong header compiles and runs
body:
> [!NOTE]
> This issue was investigated and written by an AI agent, at the repository
> owner's direction, on the owner's machine. All outputs below come from runs
> of the shown commands against the v2.0.20 release. The owner read this text
> before posting.

## Summary

A `do` block with exactly one statement compiles as that statement. The header
is dropped before anyone resolves it. So a header that names a family with no
`.bind` gives no error, and the program runs:

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do List<Unit>:      # List has no .bind
    IO.print("x")
```

This prints `x`. Add a second statement, or a `<-`, and the same header fails
with `expected : a defined name` on `List.bind`.

## The four cases

bend v2.0.20, release tarball. The interpreter and a compiled build agree in
every case.

**Case A — one bare statement.** Compiles and runs, and prints:

```python
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do List<Unit>:
    IO.print("A\n")
```

**Case B — a bind site.** Fails. The error names `List.bind` at the statement:

```python
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do List<Unit>:
    x : U32 <- IO.now()
    return x
```

```
Error:
- expected : a defined name
- observed : List.bind
Location: main
4 |   do List<Unit>:
5>|     x : U32 <- IO.now()
```

**Case C — two bare statements, no `<-`.** Also fails on `List.bind`. The
first statement becomes a bind site when a statement follows it.

**Case D — the same single-statement block with a correct header.** With
`do IO<Unit>:` it compiles and runs. So cases A and D both give no signal:
from the outside, a wrong header and a correct header look the same.

One more boundary: a single `<-` statement with no statement after it is a
parse error (`expected : a term` / `observed : end of input`). So the inert
case is exactly one bare statement and nothing else.

## What we think the rule is

The desugaring of a one-statement block is the statement itself. The header
names a bind/pure pair, but nothing emits a call to them, so nothing resolves
the names. The rule is Haskell-Report-like (`do { e }` is `e`), but Haskell
has no header to drop; its monad comes from the terms. In Bend the header is
a reference that the programmer writes. Here the compiler drops that
reference without reading it.

## Why report it

- A typo in the header (`List` for `IO`, or the wrong type) is invisible in a
  small program.
- The failure appears later, when someone adds a second statement or a `<-`
  to a body that never used the header's family. The error then points at the
  new statement and names `<Family>.bind`. The reader must know the
  desugaring to find the real culprit, which is the header one line above.
- The same header passes or fails depending on code that never mentions it.

## Question

Which rule do you intend?

1. The header always resolves its `.bind`/`.pure` names, even when the block
   never uses them.
2. A one-statement block is intentionally sugar-free, and the header is
   deliberately inert.

If 2, would a warning on the inert header be acceptable? ("This `do`-block
header is never used.") For a comparison: GHC's `QualifiedDo` resolves the
named `bind`/`return` unconditionally and reports the missing name. F#
computation expressions check the named builder's members, per construct
used, and report the missing member on the builder. Both keep the header
honest.

## Reproduce

```sh
# bend v2.0.20, tarball bend-2.0.20-darwin-arm64.tar.gz
# sha256 e8da8e28ea963e4d3956b4ab80f1c1df... (first 32 hex)
bend doheader_a.bend        # prints A
bend doheader_b.bend        # expected : a defined name, on List.bind
bend doheader_c.bend        # expected : a defined name, on List.bind
bend doheader_d.bend        # prints D
bend doheader_e.bend        # expected : a term / observed : end of input
```

Also present in 2.0.16, which our book repository pins. The probe
[`basics/do_list_bind.bend`](https://github.com/nohzafk/bend2-from-zero/blob/main/basics/do_list_bind.bend)
records the same behavior there.

title: A product over an indexed type family dies with a memory fault from depth 2 unless a second recursion over the same types is reachable
body:
### What you did

bend repro.bend -o r && ./r 1 && ./r 2

### What happened

bend 2.0.20 (release binary; 2.0.16 and 2.0.18 behave the same), Darwin
arm64 (Apple M4 Pro), Apple clang 21.0.0, macOS 26.5. The checker
accepts the file and the interpreter prints the right answer at every
depth.

## The file

`Mat(r, c)` is a family of 2^r x 2^c floats: a leaf holds one float, a node is split in two by rows, in two by columns, or in four. `Mat.matmul` is the product over three depths (rows of `a`, the shared side, columns of `b`), eight cases, its operands shared with `+`. `main` reads the depth `d` from the command line and prints the sum of ones times ones at 2^d x 2^d, which is 8^d: 8, 64, 512, 4096 for d = 1, 2, 3, 4.

Full file:

```python
import Base

# Mat(r, c): 2^r rows and 2^c columns of F32, a leaf holding one float,
# a node split in two by rows, in two by columns, or in four
law Mat:
  for r: Nat
  for c: Nat
  Data

type Mat.Leaf is Data:
  MatB{x: F32}

type Mat.Rows<-p: Nat, -c: Nat> is Data:
  MatR{top: Mat(p, c), bot: Mat(p, c)}

type Mat.Cols<-r: Nat, -q: Nat> is Data:
  MatC{left: Mat(r, q), right: Mat(r, q)}

type Mat.Quad<-p: Nat, -q: Nat> is Data:
  MatQ{tl: Mat(p, q), tr: Mat(p, q), bl: Mat(p, q), br: Mat(p, q)}

def Mat(r, c):
  match r c:
    case 0n 0n:
      Mat.Leaf
    case 1n+p 0n:
      Mat.Rows<p, 0n>
    case 0n 1n+q:
      Mat.Cols<0n, q>
    case 1n+p 1n+q:
      Mat.Quad<p, q>

def Mat.full(+r: Nat, +c: Nat, +x: F32) -> Mat(r, c):
  match r c:
    case 0n 0n:
      MatB{x}
    case 1n+p 0n:
      t b = Mat.full(p, 0n, x) Mat.full(p, 0n, x)
      MatR{t, b}
    case 0n 1n+q:
      l r2 = Mat.full(0n, q, x) Mat.full(0n, q, x)
      MatC{l, r2}
    case 1n+p 1n+q:
      a b c2 d = Mat.full(p, q, x) Mat.full(p, q, x) Mat.full(p, q, x) Mat.full(p, q, x)
      MatQ{a, b, c2, d}

def Mat.add(+r: Nat, +c: Nat, m: Mat(r, c), n: Mat(r, c)) -> Mat(r, c):
  match r c:
    case 0n 0n:
      MatB{x} = m
      MatB{y} = n
      MatB{(x + y : F32)}
    case 1n+p 0n:
      MatR{mt, mb} = m
      MatR{nt, nb} = n
      x y = Mat.add(p, 0n, mt, nt) Mat.add(p, 0n, mb, nb)
      MatR{x, y}
    case 0n 1n+q:
      MatC{ml, mr} = m
      MatC{nl, nr} = n
      x y = Mat.add(0n, q, ml, nl) Mat.add(0n, q, mr, nr)
      MatC{x, y}
    case 1n+p 1n+q:
      MatQ{ma, mb, mc, md} = m
      MatQ{na, nb, nc, nd} = n
      w x y z = Mat.add(p, q, ma, na) Mat.add(p, q, mb, nb) Mat.add(p, q, mc, nc) Mat.add(p, q, md, nd)
      MatQ{w, x, y, z}

def Mat.add4(+p: Nat, +q: Nat, a0: Mat(p, q), b0: Mat(p, q), a1: Mat(p, q), b1: Mat(p, q),
             a2: Mat(p, q), b2: Mat(p, q), a3: Mat(p, q), b3: Mat(p, q)) -> Mat(1n+p, 1n+q):
  w x y z = Mat.add(p, q, a0, b0) Mat.add(p, q, a1, b1) Mat.add(p, q, a2, b2) Mat.add(p, q, a3, b3)
  MatQ{w, x, y, z}

def Mat.add2r(+p: Nat, a0: Mat(p, 0n), b0: Mat(p, 0n), a1: Mat(p, 0n), b1: Mat(p, 0n)) -> Mat(1n+p, 0n):
  x y = Mat.add(p, 0n, a0, b0) Mat.add(p, 0n, a1, b1)
  MatR{x, y}

def Mat.add2c(+q: Nat, a0: Mat(0n, q), b0: Mat(0n, q), a1: Mat(0n, q), b1: Mat(0n, q)) -> Mat(0n, 1n+q):
  x y = Mat.add(0n, q, a0, b0) Mat.add(0n, q, a1, b1)
  MatC{x, y}

def Mat.sum(+r: Nat, +c: Nat, m: Mat(r, c)) -> F32:
  match r c:
    case 0n 0n:
      MatB{x} = m
      x
    case 1n+p 0n:
      MatR{t, b} = m
      x y = Mat.sum(p, 0n, t) Mat.sum(p, 0n, b)
      (x + y : F32)
    case 0n 1n+q:
      MatC{l, r2} = m
      x y = Mat.sum(0n, q, l) Mat.sum(0n, q, r2)
      (x + y : F32)
    case 1n+p 1n+q:
      MatQ{a, b, c2, d} = m
      w x y z = Mat.sum(p, q, a) Mat.sum(p, q, b) Mat.sum(p, q, c2) Mat.sum(p, q, d)
      ((w + x) + (y + z) : F32)

# a * b over three depths: r rows of a, k the shared side, c columns of b
def Mat.matmul(+r: Nat, +k: Nat, +c: Nat, +a: Mat(r, k), +b: Mat(k, c)) -> Mat(r, c):
  match r k c:
    case 0n 0n 0n:
      MatB{x} = a
      MatB{y} = b
      MatB{(x * y : F32)}
    case 1n+p 0n 0n:
      MatR{at, ab} = a
      x y = Mat.matmul(p, 0n, 0n, at, b) Mat.matmul(p, 0n, 0n, ab, b)
      MatR{x, y}
    case 0n 0n 1n+s:
      MatC{bl, br} = b
      x y = Mat.matmul(0n, 0n, s, a, bl) Mat.matmul(0n, 0n, s, a, br)
      MatC{x, y}
    case 0n 1n+q 0n:
      MatC{al, ar} = a
      MatR{bt, bb} = b
      x y = Mat.matmul(0n, q, 0n, al, bt) Mat.matmul(0n, q, 0n, ar, bb)
      Mat.add(0n, 0n, x, y)
    case 1n+p 1n+q 0n:
      MatQ{a0, a1, a2, a3} = a
      MatR{bt, bb} = b
      p0 q0 p1 q1 = Mat.matmul(p, q, 0n, a0, bt) Mat.matmul(p, q, 0n, a1, bb) Mat.matmul(p, q, 0n, a2, bt) Mat.matmul(p, q, 0n, a3, bb)
      Mat.add2r(p, p0, q0, p1, q1)
    case 0n 1n+q 1n+s:
      MatC{al, ar} = a
      MatQ{b0, b1, b2, b3} = b
      p0 q0 p1 q1 = Mat.matmul(0n, q, s, al, b0) Mat.matmul(0n, q, s, ar, b2) Mat.matmul(0n, q, s, al, b1) Mat.matmul(0n, q, s, ar, b3)
      Mat.add2c(s, p0, q0, p1, q1)
    case 1n+p 0n 1n+s:
      MatR{at, ab} = a
      MatC{bl, br} = b
      w x y z = Mat.matmul(p, 0n, s, at, bl) Mat.matmul(p, 0n, s, at, br) Mat.matmul(p, 0n, s, ab, bl) Mat.matmul(p, 0n, s, ab, br)
      MatQ{w, x, y, z}
    case 1n+p 1n+q 1n+s:
      MatQ{a0, a1, a2, a3} = a
      MatQ{b0, b1, b2, b3} = b
      p0 q0 p1 q1 p2 q2 p3 q3 = Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a0, b0) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a1, b2) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a0, b1) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a1, b3) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a2, b0) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a3, b2) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a2, b1) Mat.matmul(p, q, s, a3, b3)
      Mat.add4(p, s, p0, q0, p1, q1, p2, q2, p3, q3)

def depth.of(m: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> Nat:
  match m:
    case None{}:
      2n
    case Some{k}:
      U32.to_nat(k)

def depth(args: List<String>) -> Nat:
  match args:
    case []:
      2n
    case a <> rest:
      depth.of(U32.read(a))

# the sum of ones * ones at 2^d x 2^d: 8^d
def run(+d: Nat) -> F32:
  Mat.sum(d, d, Mat.matmul(d, d, d, Mat.full(d, d, 1.0), Mat.full(d, d, 1.0)))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    IO.print(F32.show(run(depth(args))))
```

Output:

$ bend repro.bend -o r
$ ./r 1
8
$ ./r 2
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
$ ./r 3
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
$ ./r 4
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
$ bend repro.bend 3        # the interpreter
512


On 2.0.18 the depth-2 run sometimes printed `nan` or `out of memory`
instead; on 2.0.20 it is the memory fault every time.

## What makes it run

Add a second recursion over the same constructors and call it once.
`withsq.bend` is `repro.bend` with these lines inserted before
`depth.of`:

```python
# the square product over one depth, walking the same nodes
def Mat.matmul.sq(+d: Nat, +a: Mat(d, d), +b: Mat(d, d)) -> Mat(d, d):
  match d:
    case 0n:
      MatB{x} = a
      MatB{y} = b
      MatB{(x * y : F32)}
    case 1n+p:
      MatQ{a0, a1, a2, a3} = a
      MatQ{b0, b1, b2, b3} = b
      p0 q0 p1 q1 p2 q2 p3 q3 = Mat.matmul.sq(p, a0, b0) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a1, b2) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a0, b1) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a1, b3) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a2, b0) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a3, b2) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a2, b1) Mat.matmul.sq(p, a3, b3)
      Mat.add4(p, p, p0, q0, p1, q1, p2, q2, p3, q3)

def run.sq(+d: Nat) -> F32:
  Mat.sum(d, d, Mat.matmul.sq(d, Mat.full(d, d, 1.0), Mat.full(d, d, 1.0)))
```

and this `main` instead of the one above, printing the square product's
sum before the general one's:

```python
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    +d : Nat = depth(args)
    IO.print(F32.show(run.sq(d)))
    IO.print(F32.show(run(d)))
```

Both products are now right at every depth, the general one included:

```
$ bend withsq.bend -o s
$ ./s 1 ; ./s 2 ; ./s 3 ; ./s 4
8
8
64
64
512
512
4096
4096
```

`Mat.matmul.sq` walks the same `MatQ` nodes through the same `Mat.add4`
as the general product's last case. Making a different def reachable
instead (a transpose over the same types) does not help. With a literal
depth in `main` (`run(2n)` in place of `run(depth(args))`) the general
product is right even without the square one, so the failure needs a
depth the compiler cannot see.

## Guess / possible directions

The ownership analysis of `Mat.matmul` (three depths, eight arms, `+`
operands opened by several arms) comes out different when the same
constructors are also opened by another recursive def, and the first
outcome is wrong. In the emitted C the arms open their operands with
`ctr_take` in the failing build and `term_peek` in the working one. Might be related to #853

2.0.20

Darwin arm64

Apple clang 21.0.0

title: A template passed through a ~ parameter bypasses descent and proves False{} == True{}
body:
### What you did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts template_cycle.bend --check-only
```

### What happened

```text
All terms check.
```

The file contains a closed `boom() -> Empty` and derives `False{} == True{}` from it. It does not import Base and uses no `@unsafe`, FFI, law, hole or runtime backend.

The direct self-call control is rejected as expected:

```bend
def direct(~k: Key, u: Unit) -> Empty:
  direct(~k, u)
```

```text
Error:
- expected : a decreasing self-call (arguments are read left to right: each passed unchanged until one shrinks)
- observed : direct
```

The accepted version moves the partial self-reference through a template parameter:

```bend
def bounce(~f: Unit -> Empty, u: Unit) -> Empty:
  f(u)

def loop(~k: Key, u: Unit) -> Empty:
  bounce(~loop(~k), u)
```

During the generic check of `loop`, `loop(~k)` is the erased `~f` argument, so the reference is checked dead and the self-call descent check does not run. Checking the closed call later creates `loop~0`, whose body creates `bounce~0`. The instantiated body of `bounce~0` uses its opaque template argument live and becomes a call back to `loop~0`.

At that point `loop~0` already exists as the in-progress placeholder installed by `def_inst`. Reusing that instance does not recheck that its body is still null, and the current lhs is `bounce~0`, so it is not recognized as a self-call either. The accepted live graph is therefore:

```text
loop~0(u)   = bounce~0(u)
bounce~0(u) = loop~0(u)
```

This is a two-definition cycle with no decreasing argument. It breaks the checker's weak-normalization claim and admits a closed inhabitant of `Empty`.

### The file

```bend
type Empty is Data:

type Unit is Data:
  Unit{}

type Key is Data:
  Key{}

type Bit is Data:
  False{}
  True{}

def bounce(~f: Unit -> Empty, u: Unit) -> Empty:
  f(u)

def loop(~k: Key, u: Unit) -> Empty:
  bounce(~loop(~k), u)

def boom() -> Empty:
  loop(~Key{}, Unit{})

def absurd(-A: Type, e: Empty) -> A:
  match e:

def false_theorem() -> {False{} == True{} : Bit}:
  absurd({False{} == True{} : Bit}, boom())
```

```text
bend 2.0.20
commit 75616561
```



title: JS emitter produces invalid identifiers for imports from hyphenated directories
body:
### What you did

Compiled a small program importing a module from a directory containing a hyphen:

```sh
bend main.bend --check-only
bend main.bend
bend main.bend -o main.js
node main.js
```

Reproduced with the official Linux x64 releases **2.0.20 and 2.0.21**. Node was explicitly in CommonJS mode (`package.json` below).

### What happened

Both Bend versions give the same results:

| Command | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `bend main.bend --check-only` | `All terms check.`, exit 0 |
| `bend main.bend` | `1`, exit 0 |
| `bend main.bend -o main.js` | No diagnostics, exit 0 |
| `node main.js` | Syntax error, exit 1 |

The generated JavaScript contains this invalid identifier:



Expected: emit valid JavaScript preserving the evaluator's result. If such import paths are unsupported, compilation should reject them with a diagnostic instead of successfully emitting unparsable JavaScript.

title: Duplicate template binder names collide during generic checking, forge Data, and admit Empty
body:
### What I did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts duplicate_binder_curry.bend --check-only
```

### What happened

```text
All terms check.
```

The file has a closed `boom() -> Empty` and derives `False{} == True{}` from it. It does not import Base and uses no `@unsafe`, FFI, law, hole, native definition, or runtime backend.

```bend
type Empty is Data:

type Bit is Data:
  False{}
  True{}

def cast(~T: Type, ~x: T, ~T: Type) -> T:
  x

type Bad is Type:
  MkBad{apply: @+x: cast(~Type, ~Bad, ~Data) -> Empty}

def Bad.apply(b: Bad) -> (@+x: cast(~Type, ~Bad, ~Data) -> Empty):
  match b:
    case MkBad{f}:
      f

def step(+b: cast(~Type, ~Bad, ~Data)) -> Empty:
  Bad.apply(b)(MkBad{Bad.apply(b)})

def boom() -> Empty:
  step(MkBad{step})

def absurd(-A: Type, e: Empty) -> A:
  match e:

def false_theorem() -> {False{} == True{} : Bit}:
  absurd({False{} == True{} : Bit}, boom())
```

### Why it happens

`def_check` names each opaque template parameter with `k + "~" + h.k`. The two source binders named `T` therefore both become `cast~T`, and the second declaration overwrites the first one in the generic checking book. That makes this invalid generic cast check as though its source and target types were the same.

Renaming the last binder makes the same definition fail at its body, as expected:

```bend
def cast(~T: Type, ~x: T, ~U: Type) -> U:
  x
```

```text
Error:
- expected : cast~U
- observed : cast~T
Location: cast
```

The exploit uses `cast(~Type, ~Bad, ~Data)` only in type positions. Its declared result type is `Data`, so the checker accepts it as the domain of a `+` binder. Normalization unfolds the raw template body to `Bad`, which is actually `Type`-kinded. This gives the negative `Bad` value a forged contraction license, and the ordinary Curry term in `step` inhabits `Empty`.

This is separate from #902. No live `cast` instance is created here; after checking the file, `book.tmps["cast"]` is still empty. A live use of the same cast does create an instance and is rejected at `cast~0` with `expected Data, observed Type`. The hole is specifically the generic opaque-name collision combined with type-position template reduction.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.21
main commit 8a51f9de
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

```text
through JS.

A second symptom on the same input: --checkup resolves an absolute import
relative to the importing file, so it cannot open it at all. This one does not
need a hyphen:

    2

    --- /tmp/nohyphen/lib.bend ---
    Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, open '/tmp/nohyphen/tmp/nohyphen/lib.bend'

cannot read it. GUIDE.md documents only ./file.bend and 0x<hash>/main.bend, so
if an absolute path is simply not a supported import, a clear error in both
lanes would beat invalid JS and a doubled path.
```

title: Fix/string literal term
body:
# A string literal checks as one node

Pull request for bendlang/bend from `fix/string-literal-term`.

## What changes

A string literal now parses as one term node, `Lit`, that holds its text.
Its type is `String`. It means the same `SCon` chain as before, and the
checker unfolds it one character at a time where a chain is read:

- a match frame in `term_wnf` reads `"ab"` as `SCon{'a', "b"}`;
- `term_compare` compares two literals by text, and unfolds a literal that
  meets a constructor, so `{"ab" == SCon{'a', "b"} : String}` holds by `{==}`;
- `term_descend` unfolds a literal argument against a constructor column;
- a literal pattern (`case "one":`) is its chain's pattern, as before;
- `term_check` accepts a literal at `String` when its head constructor is not
  peeled off the type. For any other type it checks the first unfolding, so
  the error message is the one the constructor gave.

Before this change the parser turned `"text"` into
`SCon{Chr{U32{WCon{...}}}, ...}`, about 70 term nodes per character. The
checker lifted, copied, checked and kept that chain. A literal cost about
40 KB of memory per character, and a literal past about 5000 characters
overflowed the host stack in `term_check`. A Nat literal had the same
problem before 2.0.7 (#779, #791).

The compiler sees no difference. `def_body` in comp.ts expands every literal
back into its chain (`lit_expand`) before the compiler lifts a body. The
emitted C and JS are byte-identical to main for every test in `tests/`. The
C, Metal and CUDA lanes run the same code as before.

A JS string holds Unicode scalar values only. A literal that spells a
surrogate or a code point past U+10FFFF still parses as its chain
(`tests/check/string_literal_surrogates.bend`).

## Numbers

Checker peak memory and wall time with `--check-only`, bun 1.4.2, WSL2 on
x86_64. "before" is main at 6018e28e.

| Program | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| 50 defs of one 1000-character literal each | 2.60 GB, 4.00 s | 74 MB, 0.14 s |
| one 200,000-character literal | stack overflow | 76 MB, 0.17 s |
| a CLDR table module of 185 K literal characters (out of tree) | 11.2 GB, 26 s | 248 MB, 0.9 s |
| a 2466-line check suite over the CLDR plural rules (out of tree) | 10.3 GB, 16 s | 190 MB, 0.5 s |
| bench/checker/proofs_3200 (3 runs) | 2.38 to 2.56 s, 821 to 843 MB | 2.24 to 2.50 s, 831 to 839 MB |
| bench/checker/generics_3200 (3 runs) | 1.12 to 1.28 s, 353 to 369 MB | 1.09 to 1.20 s, 350 to 358 MB |

Emission: `-o x.js` and `-o x.c` of a 4000-character literal overflowed on
main. They work now: 15.5 KB of JS, 255 KB of C. The emitters still walk a
literal as its chain, so one literal past about 8000 characters still
overflows in `-o`. The checker has no limit.

## Files

| file | change |
|---|---|
| bend2/bend.ts | the `Lit` node: type, `Lit`, `lit_of`, `lit_chain`, `lit_step`, `lit_expand`; one case each in `term_higher`, `term_lower`, `term_snf`, `term_show`, `parse_patt`, `match_flatten`; the unfolding in `term_wnf`, `term_compare`, `term_descend`; the `check-lit` rule; the string case of the parser; `chr_show`, shared by the char and string printers |
| bend2/comp.ts | `def_body` expands literals before lifting |
| gates/repo.ts | bend2/bend.ts may reach 43500 ttok (was 42000) |
| tests/check/string_literal_long.bend | a 6000-character literal checks and interprets |
| tests/check/string_literal_surrogates.bend | a surrogate escape keeps its two characters |
| tests/printer/string_literal_tail.bend | a literal prints back; a chain that ends in a literal prints as one string |
| tests/proof/string_literal_unfolds.bend | equalities between literals and chains, `String.length`, `String.append`, `String.eq`, a match on literal patterns |

bend2/bend.ts: 41915 -> 43203 ttok (cl100k, counted with js-tiktoken; the
`ttok` binary was not available here). bend2/comp.ts: 63466 -> 63471.

bend2/bend.lean does not change. The core has no literal forms. Every
literal sugar already lives outside it and means its constructor chain.
`Lit` follows that convention, as a Nat literal above 256n does since 2.0.7.
The core judges the chain. The checker computes the same judgment on the
compact form, and every read of a `Lit` unfolds it.

AGENTS.md says bend2/bend.ts is human-written and not to be edited. This
change is in that file because the cost is in the checker's representation.
No other file can remove it. The diff is 130 lines. Every new function is
named `lit_*` and sits in one section after `u32_to_term`.

## Verified locally

- `tests/`, 1382 files (1378 on main plus the four here): the JS-lane run
  output (stdout, stderr and exit code) of the 1273 tests outside tests/io is
  identical before and after, except `string_literal_long`, which overflows
  on main. This harness does not run tests/io, which waits on the gate's
  harness. The emitted C (601 files) and JS (617 files) of every test are
  byte-identical.
- The four new tests pass. On main, `string_literal_long` overflows the
  stack, and the other three pass with the same output.
- `tsc -p bend2/pack/tsconfig.json` reports the same two pre-existing errors
  and no new one.
- Not run here: gates/test.ts on the mini cluster. The C, Metal and CUDA
  lanes are covered by the byte-identical emission only. Please run the gate.

## Related

- #779 and #791: the Nat literal precedent, fixed in 2.0.7 by parsing a large
  literal as `U32.to_nat(n)`.
- #892: three string-literal match arms exceed 512 MiB during C generation.
  That report has the same root, on the emitter side. This change does not
  touch the emitters. A `Lit` reaches `def_body` intact, so an emitter that
  wants the text has it.
- #873: strings as views over buffers in the runtimes. A `Lit` is a direct
  constant for that representation.

title: Support .cjs output for Node projects with type: module
body:
### What Bend should do

Recognize `.cjs` as a JavaScript output suffix, using the same executable output currently emitted for `.js`:

```sh
bend main.bend -o out.cjs
node out.cjs
```

This should work inside a Node package with `"type": "module"`. The requested change is an additional output suffix for the existing CommonJS code, not a new ESM backend or library target.

### Why

I am evaluating Bend alongside a TypeScript monorepo with ESM packages. Node-based build and verification scripts need to run the generated programs without changing the surrounding package's module type.

On Bend 2.0.21, `.js` output uses `require`, so Node rejects it in that package. Requesting `.cjs` output invokes the native compiler instead. Renaming the generated `.js` to `.cjs` works, so the existing JavaScript output is already sufficient for this example.

Minimal reproduction, run from the Bend checkout root:

`main.bend`:

```python
import Base

def main() -> U32:
  5
```

`package.json`:

```json
{"type":"module"}
```

Commands and observed results:

```sh
BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun bend2/main.ts main.bend --check-only
# All terms check.

BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun bend2/main.ts main.bend -o out.js
node out.js
# ReferenceError: require is not defined in ES module scope
# Exit 1. The generated io_out function calls require("fs").

cp out.js renamed.cjs
node renamed.cjs
# 5
# Exit 0.

BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun bend2/main.ts main.bend -o out.cjs
file out.cjs
# out.cjs: Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64
```

The `.js` output also prints `5` under Bun. The failure depends on Node treating `.js` as ESM, not on the Bend program or an import path.

The current workaround is the copy or rename above. Supporting `.cjs` directly would remove that extra build step and make the artifact's format explicit in the build command. In [`cli_emit`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6018e28ecc67cf1fffc0c20c64b11023474c2df8/bend2/main.ts#L293), only `.js` selects JavaScript output; `.cjs` falls through to the native build branch.

title: Array operations: Array.copy_range
body:
### What Bend should do

Two array primitives are missing from Base. Both are trivial inside the runtime and neither can be expressed in Bend today without a large performance cost.

## 1. `Array.copy_range(dst, src, from, count)` — bulk copy

There is no bulk copy between two arrays. Destructuring the array tree incurs in large performance overhead. The only way is a get/set loop which seems like it doesn't benefit from optimizations like memcpy or SIMD

```python
# Suggestion
def Array.copy_range(-T: Data, dst: Array<T>, src: Array<T>, +from: U32, +count: U32) -> Array<T> & Array<T>
```

`Data` is required here (values are duplicated); `count = 0` should be a no-op. An `Array.fill(a, v, from, count)` would cover the same gap for initialization.

## 2. `Array.swap2(a, i, j)` — swap two slots in-place

The current `Array.swap` allows taking an element out of an `Array<T>` where `T: Type` but it requires an external placeholder ("hole"), to take a value out you already need another value in hand

Two workarounds:

- **Thread a hole through every signature.** Works, O(1) (3 swaps), but the hole infects every type in the call chain: `swap_at(~T: Type, arr: Array<T>, hole: T, i: U32, j: U32) -> Array<T> & T`. It also if `i == j` the hole stays inside so every call site needs a guard.
- **Structural recursion**, descending to both `ALeaf` and rebuilding them swapped. Hole-free and `i == j` is a no-op for free, but it is **O(n)**, because opening a node materializes the subtree

```python
# Suggestion, not possible without a hole as of today
def Array.swap2(-T: Type, a: Array<T>, +i: U32, +j: U32) -> Array<T>
```

### Why

Both come up in any array-heavy program, `swap2` is what Fisher–Yates and any in-place sort need, and `copy_range` is what any "write a slice of this buffer from that one" needs. Measured on bend 2.0.21, Linux x86-64 (i5-1245U), native binaries built with `-o`.

title: An annotated operator corrupts a call to a relatively-imported def: Nat../../demos/python/scanner.pos_col
body:
Context: we keep a public fork (phenomenon0/bend) and build a Python→Bend toolchain on it. We synced to 2.0.17; both sites below are verified byte-identical on main today (2.0.21).

The 2.0.16 rule that a spaced binary operator demands an enclosing `( .. : T)` forced a sweep over our tree. Three call sites could not be repaired into the annotated-operator form and are written as `Nat.add` / `Nat.mul` calls instead (e.g. `demos/python/lexer.bend:74`, `demos/python/lint.bend:50` in our fork), because the repair produced a corrupted reference:

- `parse_term_ns` (`bend2/bend.ts`; the `if (f.k[0] === ".")` branch) prefixes **any** head `Ref` whose key starts with `.` with the annotation's type namespace: `f.k = parse_reso(p, h.k + f.k);`
- Under the suites' relative imports a local call's key is e.g. `../../demos/python/scanner.pos_col` — it starts with `.`, so wrapping it in an annotated operator produced `Nat../../demos/python/scanner.pos_col` and resolution failed.
- The diagnostic nearby already knows the distinction — on main, `bend2/bend.ts:725` tests `tm.k[0] === "." && tm.k[1] !== "."` (a *single* leading dot is a relative qualifier; `..` is a path) — but the namespace walk applies no such guard.

Repro shape: load a module through a `../../`-style path (as our suites do), then wrap a call to another def of that module in an annotated spaced operator:

```bend
# C = import ../../demos/python/scanner.bend as C
def g(lo: Char) -> Nat:
  (C.pos_col(lo) + String.length(raw) : Nat)
```

Observed at 2.0.17: `Nat../../demos/python/scanner.pos_col`. (A minimal same-directory `./` import did not reproduce it for me — the `../../` key depth seems part of the trigger.)

Impact: annotated operators cannot wrap relative-imported calls; the workaround is the explicit `Nat.add(...)` form in three sites of our tree.

title: `+name` misparses as quantified-datatype syntax when a def of the same name exists in the file
body:
Keeping a public fork (phenomenon0/bend), our 2.0.17 sync hit this in situ: in `demos/python/nodes.bend`, the local

```bend
+many = String.eq(get_tag(e), "Tuple") && Bool.not(is_grouped(e))
```

— originally `+bare = …`, where the same file also defines `def bare(+e: S.Expr, tag: String) -> Bool` — parsed as quantified-datatype syntax (`+D<..>`), not a binder. Our fix was a rename; the public commit trail: `c932ae00` in phenomenon0/bend ("nodes.bend's +bare is +many: a local +x whose name is a def in the same file parses as +D<..> now").

Code pointer (main today, unchanged): the term parser's `case "+"` — after `parse_term`, it consults `p.book.tlds[k]`; with a same-file name the binder position falls into the quantified-datatype branch (diagnostic: "a quantified datatype after + (+D<..> sets D's leading quantities to &2)").

Honesty note: I could not reduce it to a minimal isolated file — a plain `+binder: T` parameter and a plain local `+let = v` with a same-named def both check fine for me in isolation — so this is the in-situ observation with the code pointer and the public rename as the evidence. It likely interacts with the 2.0.16 operator-annotation context or our suite load paths; happy to help narrow it further.

title: C facts ignore a concrete type argument of a stuck family, so a checked True becomes False
body:
On current `main` (`6018e28e`, Bend 2.0.21), `facts_fam` does not visit a concrete type argument of a stuck family. The checker proves the result is `True{}`, while native C deterministically returns `False{}`. The file has no templates, `@unsafe`, FFI, holes or open user laws.

```bend
import Base

type RT is Data:
  RT{a: U32, b: U32, c: U32}

law F:
  for n: Nat
  for A: Data
  Data

def F(n, A):
  match n:
    case 0n:
      U32
    case 1n+p:
      A

type Carrier<-n: Nat> is Data:
  Carrier{item: F(n, RT), tail: Maybe<&2, Carrier<n>>}

def hold(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  n

def opaque_one() -> Nat:
  a b = hold(0n) hold(0n)
  1n+a

def make(+n: Nat, +x: U32) -> F(n, RT):
  match n:
    case 0n:
      0
    case 1n+p:
      RT{x, U32.add(x, 1), U32.add(x, 7)}

def pack(+n: Nat, x: F(n, RT)) -> Carrier<n>:
  Carrier{x, None{}}

def first(c: Carrier<0n>) -> U32:
  Carrier{x, tail} = c
  x

def heat(+c: Carrier<0n>) -> U32:
  U32.add(first(c), first(c))

def use(+n: Nat, c: Carrier<n>) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      Carrier{x, tail} = c
      x
    case 1n+p:
      Carrier{x, tail} = c
      RT{a, b, c} = x
      U32.add(a, c)

def result() -> U32:
  +n = opaque_one()
  U32.add(heat(Carrier{U32.from_nat(n), None{}}), use(n, pack(n, make(n, 10))))

def runtime_tag() -> Bool:
  U32.is_eq(result(), 29)

def runtime_tag_ok() -> {runtime_tag() == True{} : Bool}:
  {==}

def main() -> Bool:
  runtime_tag()
```

```text
$ bun bend2/main.ts arg.bend --check-only
All terms check.
$ bun bend2/main.ts arg.bend
True{}
$ bun bend2/main.ts arg.bend -o out.js && bun out.js
True{}
$ bun bend2/main.ts arg.bend -o out && ./out
False{}
```

The C result is deterministic. Returning `result()` directly gives `29` in the evaluator and JS and `2198905222` in C on my machine.

`facts_fam` receives `F(n, RT)` and `term_spine` contains both actual arguments `[n, RT]`, but the body it walks is the generic body:

```text
Zero -> U32
Succ -> A
```

It marks the generic `A` as unknown, caches only `m:F`, and returns from every later `facts_hot(F(...))` without walking the actual `RT` argument. `CID_CARRIER` becomes hot while `CID_RT` remains cold. The hot `Carrier` build emits `rfc_seal(e, x)`, then the `Succ` consumer takes that sealed value as a raw three-word `RT` through `term_loc`, reads the seal cell as the record, and frees it at class 3.

Two controls isolate this path:

- Replacing the type parameter with a monomorphic family whose `Succ` arm returns `RT` makes C print `True{}`.
- In a temporary compiler copy, walking the concrete family arguments before returning from `facts_fam` also makes C print `True{}`.

This is a remaining case related to #853, whose 2.0.17 fix introduced `facts_fam`. It is separate from #901's nested `Mat`: recursively walking `Mat` fixes #901 but leaves this repro at `False{}`, while walking the concrete family arguments fixes this repro but leaves #901 at `False{}`.

title: Add bend init for a minimal law-backed starter
body:
### What Bend should do

```python
bend init hello-bend
cd hello-bend
bend main.bend
bend PROOF.bend

# Creates, without overwriting an existing directory:
# hello-bend/main.bend
# hello-bend/LAWS.bend
# hello-bend/PROOF.bend
# hello-bend/AGENTS.md
# hello-bend/README.md
```

### Why

The current getting-started path explains each piece, but a new user still has to assemble the first project and remember the `LAWS.bend` / `PROOF.bend` convention. A deliberately small `bend init <directory>` would turn the documented happy path into one safe command and make `bend guide`, `bend main.bend`, and `bend PROOF.bend` discoverable inside the generated project.

This should stay tiny: no manifest, dependency manager, template matrix, or hidden framework. One current starter, a useful no-argument help message, and a hard failure when the target already exists would be enough.

I built a minimal external proof of concept to test the workflow: https://github.com/gouveags/bend-init. It is 1 Bend entry point plus a small C/JS `mkdir` effect, creates the five files above, runs on both backends, and is published on Bend Hub as https://hub.bend-lang.com/0x1e0cc3677d46304c29af14dfd5553385. The repo is evidence for the interaction, not a request to adopt that implementation; a first-party command could live directly in the existing CLI.

title: `!` over a right-spine fork of ~1000 levels dies with "memory fault (machine stack overflow?)" on Metal; the CPU pool and a balanced tree of the same leaves are fine
body:
A `!` call whose parallel lets form a long right spine (`a b = f(x) go(rest)`, the natural shape of "one task per element of a list") dies on the Metal lane with `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)` once the spine is roughly 1000 levels deep. `--gpu off` runs the same program fine at any depth, and a balanced fork tree over the same number of leaves runs fine on the GPU.

## Program

```python
import Base

# a right spine of forks under one bang: each leaf builds a short list
def row(n: Nat, +y: U32, acc: List<&2, U32>) -> List<&2, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n++p:
      row(p, y, U32.add(y, U32.from_nat(p)) <> acc)

def spine(n: Nat, +w: U32) -> List<List<&2, U32>>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      Nil{}
    case 1n++p:
      a b = row(U32.to_nat(w), U32.from_nat(p), Nil{}) spine(p, w)
      a <> b

def total(xs: List<List<&2, U32>>, acc: U32) -> U32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      acc
    case x <> rest:
      total(rest, U32.add(acc, U32.from_nat(List.length(&2, U32, x))))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(total(spine!(1000n, 96), 0)))
```

```
bend spine.bend -o spine
./spine --gpu off     # 96000
./spine --gpu on      # bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)   exit 1
```

## What varies it

| spine length | `--gpu off` | `--gpu on` |
|---|---|---|
| 200, 300, 400, 500 | ok | ok |
| 1000 | ok | memory fault |
| 3000, 10000 | ok | memory fault |
| 1000 with `w = 1` (a one-word leaf) | ok | memory fault |

So it is the depth of the spine, not the work per leaf or the size of the result. The same 1000 leaves as a balanced tree are fine on the GPU:

```python
def tree(d: Nat, +y: U32, +w: U32) -> U32:
  match d:
    case 0n:
      U32.from_nat(List.length(&2, U32, row(U32.to_nat(w), y, Nil{})))
    case 1n++p:
      a b = tree(p, y, w) tree(p, U32.add(y, U32.shln(1, p)), w)
      U32.add(a, b)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(tree!(10n, 0, 96)))   # 98304 on both lanes
```

Where I hit it first: a ray tracer whose `!` forks a list of tiles as a spine, each tile forking its rows as a tree; there 300 tiles were enough, presumably because the per-tile trees add their own depth. The upstream guide already recommends balanced trees for lane utilisation, so this may be "as designed" for performance; but the failure mode is a host segfault reported as a stack overflow rather than an error naming the cause, and the CPU pool accepts the same shape, so a program that works with `--gpu off` dies when the GPU is on.

## Environment

bend 2.0.20; macOS 26.7 on an Apple M2 Pro; Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2). Built with `bend file.bend -o file` (the `.gpu` program is written and used; the balanced-tree program proves the lane works).

title: A WGSL lane: `-o x.html` with its `!` on WebGPU
body:
## Summary

A proposal, after the wasm page target (#866) and the array fork of 2.0.22: a WGSL lane, so `bend x.bend -o x.html` runs its `!` on WebGPU.

Metal gets the GPU for free because Apple's compiler takes the emitted C as it is, 64-bit terms included. A browser takes only WGSL: no 64-bit integers, no pointers, no recursion, no tail calls. So the device code has to be emitted in WGSL from the compiled form, the way the JS lane emits JS from it.

## What is measured

A prototype runtime of about 300 lines of JS ([rt.js](https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/rt.js)) runs the fork tree on WebGPU with the dispatch boundary as the only fence: terms as pairs of u32, a task is a node on the heap, one indirect dispatch per fork level, and the leaves work their subtree sequentially on a lane. With the leaves translated by hand it draws the same frames as the Bend program (same checksums) at 0.3 ms for Mandelbrot 512², 1.8 ms for the voxel raycaster 512² and 2.4 ms for `app_ray_tracer_3d` at 1024×768, against 4.5 / 42 / 53 ms on ten wasm threads in the same browser (Chrome 153, Apple M5): [the pages](https://adrielsantana.github.io/metal-bending/). Bendcraft's editable world at 512² was 1.3 ms against 18 in wasm and 4 on Metal, before its hand port was retired for not following the program.

## The shape

The hand-written leaves are the missing piece. The Metal kernel is already a `switch(fid)` inside a loop over the segments; the lane would emit that loop in WGSL, over the same segments, with every term operation on two 32-bit words and the heap as a storage buffer. The host stays the wasm page: it uploads the program, dispatches the fork levels, reads the result back; IO stays on the host, as on Metal.

## The question

Is this something you want in Bend, and if so, how: a lane next to JS, or a device target of the C lane? I would rather build it your way than twice.

title: Window: a way to grab the mouse for a first-person camera
body:
## Summary

`Window` delivers `Move{x, y}` as an absolute position and the cursor leaves the window, so a first-person camera has to be turned by dragging (Bendcraft, `gfx/05_craft.bend` in [AdrielSantana/metal-bending](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/metal-bending)). A game wants pointer lock: the cursor hidden and the window fed with deltas until Esc or a click releases it.

## A shape

On the Mac, hide the cursor and re-centre it each frame (`CGWarpMouseCursorPosition` under `CGAssociateMouseAndMouseCursorPosition(false)`), delivering the delta from the centre; on the page, `canvas.requestPointerLock()` and `movementX` / `movementY`; on X11, `XGrabPointer` and a warp. Either a `Window.grab(w, on: Bool)` effect with `Move` carrying the delta while grabbed, or a new event `Look{dx, dy}`, signed.

Would you take it, and in which shape? I can write the three hosts, on the wasm page's branch (#866) or on main.

title: A local named after a def of its own module fails to parse once the module is imported
body:
## Summary

A def that binds a local with the name of another def of the same file checks on its own, and fails to parse once the file is imported as a module. Parameters with such a name are fine; only `+x = ..` and `x = ..` bindings break.

```python
# m.bend
import Base

def foo(+x: U32) -> U32:
  (x + 1 : U32)

def bar(+y: U32) -> U32:
  +foo = (y * 2 : U32)
  (foo + 1 : U32)
```

```python
# main.bend
import Base
import ./m.bend as M

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(M.bar(3)))
```

`bend m.bend --check-only` prints `All terms check.`; `bend main.bend` prints

```
Error:
- expected : a quantified datatype after + (+D<..> sets D's leading quantities to &2)
- observed : '='
```

With `foo = (y * 2 : U32)` instead of `+foo = ..` the message is `expected : a pattern (a binder or a constructor)`. With `def bar(+foo: U32)` (a parameter named `foo`) both check and run. Bend 2.0.22.

## Where it came up

Splitting a 1000-line game into modules ([AdrielSantana/bendcraft](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/bendcraft)): the single file had `def kind`, `def shade`, `def hit` and locals `+kind`, `+shade`, and a parameter `hit`, and every one of them parsed as one file. After the split, `src/render.bend` checked alone and failed from `main.bend` at the first such local, so I renamed the locals (`kind` → `what`, `shade` → `tone`). It looks like the module's defs get their `M.` prefix before the body is parsed, so a bare `foo` at the head of a statement no longer reads as a fresh binder. If that is the intended rule (a local may not shadow a def of its module), a message that names it would save the next person the bisect; the same program parsing differently alone and imported is the surprising part.

title: Window: a way to go full screen
body:
## Summary

`Window.open(title, w, h)` opens a titled, closable, miniaturizable window of `w` x `h` points with a drawable of the same size, and no way to go full screen: the style mask has no `NSWindowStyleMaskResizable`, so the green button is disabled and `toggleFullScreen:` is not offered. A game wants the whole screen. Would you take one of these, or should I open a PR for one?

1. **A size of 0 means the screen**: `Window.open(title, 0, 0)` opens a borderless window the size of the main screen (`NSScreen.mainScreen.frame`, `NSWindowStyleMaskBorderless`, `level` above the menu bar, or `toggleFullScreen:` on a resizable window), and the events come in that window's coordinates. On the web target the canvas calls `requestFullscreen()`. The program reads the size it got from the first frame's events, or from a new `Window.size(window) -> IO(Window & (U32 & U32))`.
2. **A `Window.fullscreen(window, on: Bool)` effect** that toggles it after the open, keeping the drawable at `w` x `h` and letting the layer scale, which is what the compositor already does for a Retina screen.

The second keeps the render's cost independent of the screen, which matters here: the frame's shader walks the image quadtree from the window's size and stops at the first `Pix`, so a 960 x 540 image fills a 1920 x 1080 drawable by itself, nearest neighbour, and a game can choose its cost.

## Where it came up

[AdrielSantana/bendcraft](https://github.com/AdrielSantana/bendcraft): the game takes `W H S` on the command line and opens a `W` x `H` window with the render `S` times smaller a side (`bendcraft 1920 1080 2` renders 960 x 540 rays in 13 ms on an M5 against 3-7 ms for 512 x 512; every pixel a ray is 50 ms), so "full screen" today is the user typing their screen's size and getting a window with a title bar over the whole desktop. That works, but the window still has its bar, sits under the menu, and needs the size typed in. Related: #921 (grabbing the mouse), the other half of a first-person window.

title: Feature/nat literal term
body:
A nat literal is one Lit node in the checker

A nat literal up to 256 parsed as a Succ chain, and a larger one as
U32.to_nat(n), an application. Two forms meant one literal: the parser, the
pattern reader and the printer each knew both, and a self-call on a literal
past 256 failed the termination check, since the check reads constructors
and saw a function call. A Lit now holds a number as it holds a text, and
the same peel reads it: 0n is Zero{}, n is Succ{n-1}.

What changes

- The checker unfolds a nat literal one Succ at a time where a chain is
  read: a match frame, a comparison, a descent, and the check rule's
  fallback. Against Nat it checks in O(1), with the same guard the string
  rule has: the Nat in scope must declare Succ and Zero.
- Inference steps a literal once, so an undeclared Nat still reports
  "a declared constructor".
- The printer prints a literal as its number, and a Succ chain that ends
  in a literal as one number.
- "1n+0n" parses as 1n, so a template's ~ key agrees with 1n.
- nat_to_term and the App form of a nat pattern are gone. NAT_LITERAL_MAX
  stays for two uses: "n + T" past it is Nat.add(n, T), and the compiler
  emits U32.to_nat(n) past it. U32.to_nat is an intrinsic ($0 in C,
  BigInt($0) in JS), so this costs nothing at run time.
- comp.ts reads a literal through term_lit in term_kids and term_any, so
  the reference to U32.to_nat counts for reachability.

Emitted code and behavior

- The C and JS of every runnable test are byte-identical to the base.
- The checker's output is the same on every non-IO test (1291).
- 2000 defs of 200n: 1.06 s and 366 MB to 0.18 s and 83 MB.
- case 300n: down(299n) now passes the termination check.

Tests

- tests/proof/nat_literal_unfolds.bend: a comparison sees 300n as
  Succ{299n} and 0n as Zero{}, a match reads a literal pattern past 256
  and a literal scrutinee, a self-call on a smaller literal descends, a
  literal at the u32 bound passes through Nat.add unforced.
- tests/check/nat_literal_own_nat.bend: a module's own Nat with other
  constructors rejects 3n with the base's exact error.
- tests/printer/nat_literal_print.bend: a literal prints back as a
  literal, "n+T" past 256 is Nat.add, a chain that ends in a literal
  prints as one number.
- tests/check/nat_literal_pattern_empty.bend spells its pattern 0n. It
  wrote U32.to_nat(0), the form the parser gave a literal, which is no
  pattern anymore. It prints the same error.

Size: bend2/bend.ts 42981 and bend2/comp.ts 64977 ttok (cl100k), under
the caps of 43000 and 65000 with no room to spare. If your ttok reads
higher, the caps need to move.
