title: Expose the effective runtime worker count to Bend programs
body:
### What Bend should do

Expose the effective number of CPU worker threads to a running Bend program. For example:

```python
def IO.thread_count() -> IO(U32):
  ...

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    workers : U32 <- IO.thread_count()
    run_bounded_pipeline(workers * 2)
```

On native builds this should return the runtime's effective worker-pool size: the value selected by `--threads`, or the detected available CPU count when the flag is omitted, after runtime clamping. A generated JavaScript program should return `1`, since that lane is sequential.

The native runtime already computes this as `pool_size`, but it is not exposed to Bend code. `IO.args()` cannot recover it because the runtime consumes `--threads` before invoking the program. A public Base API would avoid relying on a custom effect that reaches into runtime implementation details.

### Why

Programs with bounded parallel pipelines need to choose their amount of in-flight work from the actual runtime concurrency. A fixed queue either leaves workers idle or retains much more input, output, and scratch memory than necessary.

For example, a parallel compressor should usually retain only a small multiple of the active worker count. Today it cannot distinguish `--threads 1`, `--threads 8`, and the default, so it must over-allocate, under-utilize the machine, add its own unrelated configuration flag, or duplicate the runtime's CPU-detection logic in foreign code.

title: TCP.listen_shared lets N processes share a port; TCP.listen keeps owning its own
body:
## What changes

- `TCP.listen_shared(port)`, new in `bend2/base.bend`: a listener with `SO_REUSEPORT` set before the bind, so N processes that all call it share one port. If the option is refused, the call fails (`ENOPROTOOPT` where the platform lacks it) instead of quietly owning the port.
- `TCP.listen` is as it was before this PR: `SO_REUSEADDR` only, so a second listener on its port fails with `EADDRINUSE`.
- Both defs share `bend2/effs/tcp_listen.c` and `.js`; each effect sits under its own `CID_*` guard, as in `file_read.c`.
- `guide/GUIDE.md`: what each call does; on Linux the kernel spreads accepted connections over the sharers, on macOS the bind is permitted but the first listener takes every connection.
- `tests/io/tcp_listen_shared.bend`: probes a port upward from 19947 with `TCP.listen_shared`, shares it twice, and pins that a plain `TCP.listen` on it answers `Address already in use`.

## Why

Bend's IO loop is one per process -- threads only run spawned `!` work -- so the only way a lightweight route uses N cores is N processes on one port. Measured on one 4-core machine, same light route, same client: one Bend process with 4 threads serves 88.3k req/s; a second Bend process on the same port cannot start; Bun with 4 processes on one port (`reusePort: true`) serves 118.9k.

## Why opt-in

The first version of this PR set `SO_REUSEPORT` in `TCP.listen` by default and argued nothing would regress, since no test asserted that a second listen fails. Review showed that was wrong: `tcp_listen_any`, in the TCP tests, finds a free port by a `TCP.listen` that fails, so concurrent copies of those tests shared ports and accepted each other's clients (@nicolas-abril, on macOS). Reproduced on Linux x86-64, four concurrent copies of each test, three rounds, native lane:

| test | base | default-on | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tcp_loopback` | 12/12 | 8/12 | 12/12 |
| `tcp_short_recv` | 12/12 | 11/12 | 12/12 |
| `tcp_spawn` | 12/12 | 8/12 | 12/12 |
| `tcp_poll` | 12/12 | 10/12 | 12/12 |

Beyond the tests, default-on turns a loud mistake into a silent one: on Linux an accidental second instance splits traffic with the first; on macOS it starts and never receives a connection (@nicolas-abril, @paulovitin). Opt-in keeps `EADDRINUSE` as the default on both, and puts the Linux-only benefit behind a name that says what it does -- the shape Bun (`reusePort: true`) and Node 23.1+ (`net.listen({reusePort: true})`) already use.

## Test output

`tests/io/tcp_listen_shared.bend`, in the check, interpreted, JS-built and C-built lanes (this repo's `bend2/main.ts` via `bun`), prints:
```
shared
shared again
Address already in use
```
It also passes with four concurrent copies. Negative check: with `TCP.listen` made shared again, the third line becomes `plain listen shared the port`.

The existing `tcp_loopback`, `tcp_short_recv`, `tcp_spawn`, `tcp_poll` and `tcp_send_slow_peer` pass in the interpreted, JS and native lanes, and the table above was rerun on this PR's head. This PR applies on 2.0.26 and together with #977 and #978 in any order.

Not tested here: macOS (no machine; the guide's macOS sentence rests on the two reviewers' measurements), and the cluster-backed `gates/` harness.

## Duplicate check

`gh issue list` and `gh pr list` on `bendlang/bend` for `reuseport`, `SO_REUSEPORT` and `TCP.listen`: nothing open or closed.

title: --check-only hangs on a four-line self-application during eager beta reduction
body:
## What you did

Run `bun bend2/main.ts omega.bend --check-only` on the file below.

## What happened

The command consumes a CPU core indefinitely and produces no output. I confirmed that it was still running after 20 seconds and had to interrupt it. The same command on ordinary invalid files returns immediately with a diagnostic.

The term is invalid and should be rejected quickly: the lambda parameter is self-applied and used twice. This is therefore a frontend/checker denial of service from a four-line source file, rather than accepted nontermination.

## The file

```python
type Empty is Data:

def boom() -> Empty:
  (x => x(x))(x => x(x))
```

## Cause

`term_higher` eagerly beta-reduces an `App` whenever its elaborated function is a `Lam`: [bend.ts:781-787](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdf/bend2/bend.ts#L781-L787). For Ω, substituting the right lambda into `x(x)` reconstructs the same application, so `term_higher` recurses forever before `term_check` can reject the non-inferrable or affine-invalid lambda.

I have not derived a checked nonterminating term or an inhabitant of `Empty`; the observed issue is nontermination while processing invalid input.

## Version / system

`Bend 2.0.25` (`a49524265bdf`), Bun 1.4.2, Darwin arm64 27.0.

title: feature/js-plains
body:
# The JS lane stops paying for calls: selector intrinsics + plain defs off the trampoline

Three changes to `bend2/comp.ts`; the first two are invisible to the C
emitter, the device and the checker, and the third gives the C lane the same
templates (no base.bend, bend.ts or Lean surface is touched).

## 1. Selector intrinsics (b4ebc8bf)

JS-only `OPERATIONS` entries for `bool_and`, `bool_not`, `bool_pick`,
`u32_min`, `u32_max`, `f32_min`, `f32_max`, `nat_min`, `nat_max`.

Before, `U32.min(a, b)` emitted a trampolined call into `$U32$min$`, which
trampolined again into `$Bool$pick$` — three frames and two `$JMP`
allocations for one compare. Now the ternary emits in place.

Each template mirrors its base.bend body exactly:

- `pick c a b = c ? a : b`, `min = a < b ? a : b`, `max = a < b ? b : a`
- F32 NaN answers keep following `is_lt`, as `Bool.pick` of `F32.is_lt` does
- `Nat.min/max`'s Succ-peeling recursion (O(min(a,b)) BigInt steps) becomes
  one BigInt compare
- `bool_pick` stays JS-only because its `A` is polymorphic; on native lanes
  no single word shape fits

## 2. Plain defs are called directly (8ff7eab8)

A def is *plain* when its emitted JS can never return a `$JMP`: no tail
self-call and no closure applied in tail position. Every other return comes
back through the machine stack, whose depth the def call DAG bounds — Bend
has no mutual recursion and no forward calls.

`js_call` now calls a plain callee directly (tail or not), so the JIT can
inline it. A self tail call keeps `run_jump`; a tail call into a trampolined
callee absorbs its `$JMP`s with `run_loop` in place, costing one bounded
frame. `plain_of` reads the property off the body with `term_any`'s tail
flag; a closure body counts as tail, which only errs toward keeping the
trampoline.

## 3. The C lane gets the same templates (036e0b47)

As @jeromelaurens pointed out, since 2.0.17 (#860, 4033e90c) `Nat.min`/`Nat.max`
peel successors in lockstep, and the C lane ran that recursion as written:
one continuation frame per successor, O(min(a, b)), so
`Nat.min(10^9, 2*10^9)` dies with `bend: memory fault (machine stack
overflow?)`. Clang can't recover the compare because the recursion goes
through the runtime's work loop.

C templates now sit beside the JS ones for `nat_min`, `nat_max`, `u32_min`,
`u32_max`, `f32_min`, `f32_max`, `bool_and` and `bool_not`:

- `nat_min/max`: `($0 < $1 ? $0 : $1)`, the same raw-word compare as
  `nat_sub` and `nat_is_lt`
- `u32_min/max`: compare as `U32.is_lt` does (`(u32)` casts, like
  `U32_BIN`) and return the operand normalized to 32 bits
- `f32_min/max`: compare as `F32.is_lt` does (`f32_unbox`) and return the
  original word, bit-identical to `Bool.pick`, so NaN and ±0 behave as in Base
- `bool_pick` keeps no C template: its untaken side may own a box to drop,
  and a wider `A` isn't one word, so the C lane keeps its match

Only the Nat pair was a real cost; `U32`/`F32` min/max are a `Bool.pick`
over `is_lt` in base.bend, already O(1) on C, and their templates are for
lane parity.

## Measurements (WSL, bun, medians of three, identical outputs and RSS)

| workload (10M iterations)                | before | after  | speedup |
|------------------------------------------|--------|--------|---------|
| Base selector ops (min/max/pick/is_even) | 1.30 s | 0.51 s | ~2.5x   |
| chain of three small user defs per step  | 1.26 s | 0.49 s | ~2.6x   |
| single pure Nat tail loop (control)      | 0.98 s | 0.94 s | ~1.0x   |

The control row is expected: a def that never calls anything gains nothing;
its costs (per-iteration `run_jump` allocation, BigInt Nat arithmetic) are
follow-up work, not this PR.

### C and JS lanes after change 3 (WSL, clang 18 -O3 and bun, medians of three, identical outputs)

Before is `main`; RSS is the median max RSS (`/usr/bin/time`).

| workload (10M iterations)                        | lane | before           | after           | speedup |
|--------------------------------------------------|------|------------------|-----------------|---------|
| `Nat.min(p, 100)` + `Nat.max(p, 50)` per step    | C    | 1.39 s, 2.0 MB   | 6.0 ms, 2.4 MB  | ~230x   |
| `Nat.min(p, 100)` + `Nat.max(p, 50)` per step    | JS   | 81.2 s, 56.4 MB  | 0.59 s, 39.0 MB | ~138x   |
| U32/F32 min/max, `Bool.and`/`not` per step       | C    | 8.6 ms, 2.5 MB   | 7.2 ms, 1.9 MB  | ~1.2x   |
| U32/F32 min/max, `Bool.and`/`not` per step       | JS   | 2.13 s, 44.2 MB  | 0.61 s, 40.8 MB | ~3.5x   |
| the report: `Nat.min(10^9, 2*10^9)`, one call    | C    | memory fault (2.0 GB) | 1000000000, 1.9 MB | fixed |
| the report: `Nat.min(10^9, 2*10^9)`, one call    | JS   | memory fault     | 1000000000      | fixed   |

The C selector row is mostly process startup: clang already compiled the
`Bool.pick` match to the same compare. The report row ran once per side.

## Verification

- A scratch program exercising every intrinsic through constant and
  variable arguments prints the same value interpreted and emitted.
- 73 tests across `tests/base`, `tests/eval` and `tests/io` pass on both
  the run path and the emitted-JS path.
- The C lane (WSL, clang 18): the report's program and every runnable
  `tests/base` test agree across check, C and JS; five tests my local
  harness couldn't build fail the same way on `main`.
- The cluster gates did not run (no ssh access from this machine); the
  perf pins and the device lane still need the usual gate pass.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Shared Array redirect lookup races with atomic reference-count updates
body:
## What you did

On unmodified commit `e52cda47a58967aa65d1eb26efe8f42a0b0407df`, compile this program to C and run the result under ThreadSanitizer with at least two workers:

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts redirect-race.bend -o /tmp/redirect-race.c
clang -x c -std=gnu11 -O1 -g -fsanitize=thread -pthread /tmp/redirect-race.c -o /tmp/redirect-race
TSAN_OPTIONS='halt_on_error=0 exitcode=0' /tmp/redirect-race --threads 2 --gpu off
```

## What happened

ThreadSanitizer reliably reports an 8-byte non-atomic read in `blk_loc` racing with a 4-byte atomic write in `term_keep` / `rfc_bump`:

```text
WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race
  Read of size 8 ... by thread T1:
    #0 WL_FID_FAN
    #1 monk_step
    #2 pool_work

  Previous atomic write of size 4 ... by thread T2:
    #0 WL_FID_FAN
    #1 monk_step
    #2 pool_work

SUMMARY: ThreadSanitizer: data race in WL_FID_FAN
4
ThreadSanitizer: reported 1 warnings
```

The redirect cell is initialized as:

```c
e.mem[r] = ((u64)term_loc(t) << 24) | cnt;
```

`blk_loc` reads the complete cell as a plain `u64`:

```c
return blk_shr(a) ? H[term_loc(a)] >> 24 : term_loc(a);
```

At the same time, `rfc_bump` and `term_drop` perform atomic 32-bit read-modify-write operations on the low half of that same `u64`. Mixing the overlapping non-atomic 64-bit access and atomic 32-bit access is a C data race even though the returned location appears stable in practice.

I could not manifest this as an incorrect or nondeterministic Bend result. The reproducer prints the expected `4`, including when ThreadSanitizer continues after reporting the race. A deeper version with 262,144 concurrent leaves, hundreds of repetitions, worker counts 2/4/8/16, Apple Clang and Homebrew Clang/GCC at several optimization levels including LTO, and arm64 and Rosetta x86-64 all produced the expected result.

There is a runtime invariant that explains that result: valid reference-count changes are confined to the low 24 bits, while `cell >> 24` returns the immutable target location. A live reader owns a reference, so the redirect wrapper cannot be freed and reused during that read. Refcount overflow is rejected with `ERR_RFCS`. Thus this is a confirmed language-level C race and possible portability/miscompilation issue, but there is currently no known Bend program whose unsanitized result it corrupts.

Using the existing atomic reconstruction in `rfc_view` for shared `blk_loc` calls removes the ThreadSanitizer report. A representation with separately addressable location and reference-count fields would also avoid overlapping accesses.

## The file

```bend
import Base

@unsafe
def leaf(a: Array<U32>) -> Array<U32>:
  Array.set.fin(U32, Array.atomic.add(a, 0, 1))

@unsafe
def fan(+d: Nat, +a: Array<U32>) -> Array<U32>:
  match d:
    case 0n:
      leaf(a)
    case 1n+p:
      l r = fan(p, a) fan(p, a)
      Array.join(U32, l, r)

def done(r: Array<U32> & U32) -> IO(Unit):
  (a, x) = r
  IO.print(U32.show(x))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  done(Array.get(U32, fan!(2n, [0 : U32*1n]), 0))

#|4
```

## Environment

- `bend --version`: `bend 2.0.24`
- Commit: `e52cda47a58967aa65d1eb26efe8f42a0b0407df`
- `uname -sm`: `Darwin arm64`
- `clang --version`: `Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.4.2)`

title: fix(compiler): reset probes between compilations
TCP.listen's backlog is 512, not 16: a burst of 10k connections is answered in full
body:
## What changes

`bend2/effs/tcp_listen.c` and `bend2/effs/tcp_listen.js` call
`listen(fd, 512)` instead of `listen(fd, 16)`: the same number in both
lanes, the value Bun uses (Node uses 511). The kernel caps the backlog at
its own limit (`net.core.somaxconn` on Linux, 4096 by default;
`kern.ipc.somaxconn` on macOS, 128), so on every platform the accept queue
is 512 or as deep as the system allows.

(Revised after review: the first version used `SOMAXCONN` in C and the
platform's value in JS; one constant gives the same behaviour in both
lanes.)

A new test, `tests/io/tcp_listen_backlog.bend`, listens and then connects
32 times in a row without ever accepting: with a backlog of 16 the
eighteenth SYN is dropped and that connect stalls on retransmits, so a
regression shows as a hang rather than a wrong line; with 512 all 32
complete at once and the test prints its `#|` line.

## Why

A backlog of 16 is the accept queue's depth. Once 16 handshakes are
waiting for `TCP.accept`, the kernel drops further SYNs and the clients
retransmit after 1 s, then 3 s -- the connection is not refused, it is
silently delayed, and under a burst many of them time out on the client's
side before the server gets to them.

Measured with `demos/io_http_server` built from this tree once with each
backlog, on one 4-core Linux machine: 10,000 connections opened at once,
each sending one `GET /`, 10 s window, one run each:

| backlog | answered | timed out | last answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 9,920 / 10,000 | 80 | 6.51 s |
| `SOMAXCONN` (4096, the first version) | 10,000 / 10,000 | 0 | 3.39 s |
| **512** | **10,000 / 10,000** | **0** | **2.37 s** |

`ss -ltn` shows the listener's `Send-Q` go from 16 to 512.

## Test output

`tests/io/tcp_listen_backlog.bend`, all four lanes on this tree
(`bun bend2/main.ts <file> [--check-only | -o x.js | -o x]`):

```
All terms check.
32 connected, none accepted
```

Negative check: the same test run with the released `bend` 2.0.22, whose
runtime still has `listen(fd, 16)`, hangs (killed by `timeout 25`, no
output) -- the eighteenth connect never completes.

The existing `tests/io/tcp_listen_close`, `tcp_loopback`, `tcp_poll`,
`tcp_spawn`, `tcp_short_recv`, `tcp_send_slow_peer`,
`tcp_connect_black_hole` and `port_bound` print their expected lines on
the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes of this tree. The cluster-backed
`gates/` harness is not available in this environment; the test file
follows the `tests/<ns>/[a-z0-9_]+.bend` rule and is well under the token
ceiling.

## Duplicate check

No open or closed issue or PR in `bendlang/bend` mentions `backlog`,
`SOMAXCONN` or the listen depth; `WONTFIX.txt` does not cover it.

title: TCP gets the byte twins File already has: recv_bytes, send_bytes and poll_bytes
body:
## What changes

TCP gets the byte twins `File` already has, with the same types and the
same shape:

| text | bytes |
|---|---|
| `File.read` | `File.read_bytes` (today) |
| `File.write` | `File.write_bytes` (today) |
| `TCP.recv` | **`TCP.recv_bytes`** |
| `TCP.send` | **`TCP.send_bytes`** |
| `TCP.poll` | **`TCP.poll_bytes`** |

`List<&2, U32>`, exactly as `File.read_bytes` and `File.write_bytes`
already use. No new type and no new concept. The text effects keep their
code unchanged, now under `#ifdef CID(TCP.*)` the way `effs/file_read.c`
already guards its pair, since each pair shares one effect file; the send
loop, the receive step and the poll deadline are shared rather than
copied, and the JS lane mirrors the C lane through the same pack-shaped
parameter.

`TCP.poll_bytes` is in the set because `TCP.poll` is the only receive
with a deadline: without it, a server that drops idle connections cannot
read bytes.

## Why

A socket carries bytes. `TCP.recv` answers a `String`, so `io_str`
decodes each read as UTF-8 and writes U+FFFD over whatever it cannot
decode. Two kinds of payload do not survive that.

**A body that is not text** — an image, a protobuf frame, a gzip
stream — loses every byte that is not valid UTF-8. `FF 00 80` reads back
as three replacement characters, and `TCP.send` cannot spell those bytes
either, since it encodes the String as UTF-8.

**A valid character split across two reads.** This is the one that bites
a correct program. `"café"` is `63 61 66 C3 A9`; the network may deliver
`C3` at the end of one read and `A9` at the start of the next. Each read
decodes on its own, with no state carried over, so both halves become
U+FFFD. Measured against a Bend receiver:

```
sent:  63 61 66 C3 | A9          ("café", split by the network)
got code points: 99 97 102 65533
got code points: 65533
```

Sent whole, the same bytes give `99 97 102 233`. Nothing in that program
is wrong: the split is the network's choice, it depends on load, and the
loss is silent.

`File` already draws this line. `File.read` decodes; `File.read_bytes`
answers, in the words of the comment in `effs/file_read.c`, "the bytes as
they are (0..255), one List cell each; a text reader would decode them as
UTF-8". A socket is the same seam as a file, and today only the file has
both doors.

This is also where #809 leaves things. That issue found the two lanes
decoding invalid UTF-8 differently, and the fix in 2.0.7 made the C
runtime a forward WHATWG decoder, one U+FFFD per maximal subpart, exactly
as `TextDecoder` does. That is the right decode — and it is precisely
why a decoding reader cannot be the only way to read a socket: now that
both lanes agree, they agree on discarding the bytes. The decoder is
correct; what is missing is the door that does not decode.

## Alternatives considered

**Make `TCP.recv` carry decoder state between calls**, so a character
split across two reads is stitched back. Rejected: it would make a
`recv` stateful and still leave no way to read a byte that is not text,
so the binary case stays broken. It would also change what an existing
`TCP.recv` returns.

**Preserve undecodable bytes inside the String** (surrogate escapes, as
Python's `surrogateescape` does). Rejected: a `String` would stop being
a sequence of valid code points, and the split-character case still needs
the program to re-decode by hand — the work of bytes, with a type that
says text.

**Ship only `recv_bytes`/`send_bytes`** and leave `poll_bytes` out.
Rejected: `TCP.poll` is the only receive with a deadline, so a server
that times out idle connections would be forced back to text.

`UDP.recv_from` and `UDP.poll` have the same seam and are not touched
here, to keep this reviewable; happy to follow up with the same pair for
UDP if you want it.

## Test output

`tests/io/tcp_bytes_split.bend` sends a character in two halves and then
three bytes that are not text, reading both back over loopback in one
program:

```
first read: 99 97 102 195
second read: 169
not text: 255 0 128
```

Checked, interpreted, JS-built and C-built on this tree
(`bun bend2/main.ts <file> [--check-only | -o x.js | -o x]`): all four
lanes print those three lines. The same exchange through `TCP.recv`
gives `99 97 102 65533` / `65533` instead, which is the defect.

`tests/io/tcp_bytes_edges.bend`, written in review, covers the edges:
an empty send, a byte past 255 (`EINVAL`, nothing sent), and
`poll_bytes` idle, with data and at EOF, where `recv_bytes` answers
`[]`.

No regressions, on Linux x86-64 with Bun 1.3.11, on main 95317d95:

- The 19 `tcp_*`, `udp_*`, `file_*` and `port_bound` tests, the two
  new ones included, print their expected lines on the check,
  interpreted, JS and C lanes.
- The `tests/io` checkup (119 modules, one process, as `gates/test.ts`
  runs it) is identical to main's but for the two new tests' sections.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes 46 / 46.
- Each pair shares one effect file, and the runtime refuses an effect
  registered twice, so a program that uses both effects of a pair must
  still build: `tcp_bytes_split` mixes `recv` and `recv_bytes`, and a
  scratch program mixing `send`/`send_bytes` and `poll`/`poll_bytes`
  passes all four lanes.

macOS was not re-run here after the rebase onto #1042.

## Duplicate check

No open issue or PR asks for byte-level socket effects. #809 (closed,
fixed in 2.0.7) is the decode-divergence issue this builds on, and #846
asks about bundled HTTP/TLS/crypto libraries, which is a different
question — this adds no library, only the byte door on the effect that
already exists. `WONTFIX.txt` does not cover it.

title: HIP: cut per-turn copy overhead and fill Window.frame on the device
body:
A `!` turn in this probe family cost 8.3--9.4 ms less after these changes. The probe is one coupled grid,
stepped once per turn; these are stats-off medians in milliseconds per step. I measured on an RX 7800 XT
with ROCm 7.2.1 under WSL2. HIP probes used `--gpu 3GB`; CPU comparisons used 16 workers. Each sample estimates
a step as `(wall(N) - wall(1)) / (N - 1)`. HIP entries are medians of nine interleaved samples: 1024² used
N=401, while 4096² and 8192² used N=101. CPU entries are medians of five N=101 samples.

| Life probe | merged `hip` (`2ba2bd1e`) | this branch | CPU-16 |
| ---------- | ------------------------: | ----------: | -----: |
| 1024²      |                    13.023 |       4.765 |  2.156 |
| 4096²      |                    19.149 |       9.859 | 20.522 |
| 8192²      |                    36.418 |      26.983 | 81.284 |

The 8192² base spread is large, but its base and branch samples do not overlap.

These results cover this Life quadtree workload only; I have not measured other many-turn workloads. The
16 `bench/runtime` programs make one to three turns each. No measured median regressed by more than 3%; changes
ranged from +0.76% to -8.79%.

## Turn statistics

`BEND_GPU_STATS` is presence-based: set it to any value to enable it and unset it to disable it. The optional
statistics commit adds no transfers or synchronization. It reports evaluator turns, launch/run/wait time, and
corpus-copy totals on normal exit. Heap totals also include lazy host faults and uploads for `Window.frame`;
the presentation kernel and pixel readback are not timed by these counters. Its stats-off comparisons were
12.527 -> 12.897 ms at 1024², 20.369 -> 19.187 ms at 4096², and 36.557 -> 35.991 ms at 8192², all inside the
corresponding spreads. Cost: 598 `comp.ts` tokens.

## Empty banks

`gpu_sync` no longer calls `gpu_copy` for a bank whose `rd`, `wr`, and `top` cursors all imply an empty span.
For every live bank, the existing `b->off .. b->off + n + 1` range is unchanged. This moved the 1024² probe
from 12.602 to 8.259 ms/step (-4.343 ms, beyond the 2.412 ms larger spread) and the 8192² probe from 36.108
to 31.129 ms/step. Cost: 11 `comp.ts` tokens.

## Smaller lazy chunks

The HIP heap's lazy chunk is 256 KiB instead of 2 MiB. `gpu_heap` and `gpu_fault` still track whole chunks;
the fault lock and alias mapping still fill a protected chunk before exposing it to host threads. The 401-step
1024² comparison moved from 8.048 to 4.515 ms/step (-3.533 ms, beyond the 2.128 ms larger spread), and the
8192² probe moved from 31.206 to 27.138 ms/step.

The trade-off is host reading: a sequential fold of a 4M-leaf device-built tree showed an observed median
increase of 5.7% with 256 KiB chunks. With 64 KiB chunks the observed median increase was 14.8%, for only
another 0.26 ms on the 1024² turn, unresolved within both candidates' spreads. I kept 256 KiB. Cost: no
token-count change.

## Device-side `Window.frame`

On HIP, `window_fill` now calls `gpu_show`: it uploads the static heap prefix and dirty tracked chunks through
`gpu_heap`, launches `window_dev`, and copies only the pixel buffer back. `H_BUMP` is current after
`gpu_leave`, stale protected chunks are skipped, and `Window.frame` runs after `corpus_eval` has rendezvoused
the host pool. The kernel argument struct is checked at 40 bytes, and both pixel-buffer release and allocation
are checked.

At 1024x768, average fill time over the measured frames fell from 54.3 to 2.3 ms/frame. Frames were
byte-identical before and after on both the HIP and CPU-16 lanes. A no-heap-upload negative control differed at
byte 5, so the probe exercises the upload. Cost: 511 tokens: 478 in `comp.ts` and 33 in `window_frame.c`.

## Fly demo

End to end, the stock `app_ray_tracer_3d` main in a 1024x768 window over 300 frames of `App.loop`, `--gpu 3GB`,
stats off, three interleaved rounds each: merged `hip` took 25.80, 25.92 and 26.49 s (11 fps); this branch took
5.72, 5.73 and 5.72 s (52 fps). With statistics on, the branch made 600 turns (the frame build and `Image.drop!`),
7.0 ms/frame of device passes and 5.1 ms/frame of copies (heap 0.55, banks 0.39, rings 0.36, header 0.22);
the 2 KB header copies average 108 us up and 84 us down, so the remaining copy cost is call latency, not bandwidth.

## Tried and not kept

Registration reduced standalone copy latency, but registering the fixed low corpus region did not improve the
runtime median. The comparison was 3.963 -> 3.982 ms/step, and the one-step process median increased by 15 ms.
I removed it. I did not try queued copies: AMD documents synchronous behavior for pageable memory, and
registration had not earned a place in the runtime.

## What is left

Copies still account for about 2.6--3.3 ms per turn: about 20 `hipMemcpy` calls per turn with aggregate
means of 133--160 us/call, including transfer and fault-path costs. Banks are the largest region; five
non-contiguous bank classes were live in this sampled Life workload. Fewer, larger copies are the next step,
but that needs a design and token-budget decision.

## Side finding

`tests/run/gpu_turns.bend` says it makes three device turns; on this lane it makes two, as measured by the new
statistics. Its unbanged `gen(10n, 3)` forks, then the rest of evaluation stays on the cores. A sequential
`gen` makes all four bangs reach the device and still prints `691345207`.

## Checks

- The `turns4`, `gpu_turns`, `gpu_mark`, `gpu_trig`, `lw_d7_n21`, and `lw_d9_n21` correctness probes matched
  with both the HIP and CPU-16 lanes compared.
- `gates/repo.ts` passed 46/46.
- The local gate passed check 1414/1414 and interpreter 929/929. Its C lane passed 622/624; both misses are
  identical on unmodified `hip`: this machine lacks the ALSA development header, and the TCP slow-peer case
  prints both expected lines before its timeout.
- CUDA and Metal are untested because this machine has neither lane. Every edit is inside `#elif BEND_HIP`
  except the six-line `#if BEND_HIP` branch in `bend2/effs/window_frame.c`.
- Token counts are `bend2/comp.ts` 69,115/70,000 and `bend2/effs/window_frame.c` 3,780/4,000.
- Coverage probes, each byte-identical between the HIP and CPU-16 lanes: a 2.02 GiB live heap kept across
  turns; a `Window.frame` image in the static region, with and without a turn before the first frame; live data
  in the eagerly copied tail past the tracked chunks; two windows of different sizes in one process (the pixel
  buffer grows, then is reused); and 1x1, 33x9, 800x600 and 1023x767 frames with a guard word after the pixels.
  With the 2.02 GiB heap alive, a cheap turn took 1.05 ms with 256 KiB chunks against 2.92 ms with 2 MiB chunks
  (2,001 turns, seven interleaved rounds, no overlap), so the larger flag count costs nothing visible; reading
  the whole 2 GiB back on the host was about 11% slower (8.08 s against 7.30 s).
- The probes, harness and results are outside the four commits. Raw samples are kept for the final table; the
  per-commit comparisons above are the medians and spreads recorded when each change was measured.

I can drop the 598-token statistics commit if preferred: omit it, apply the empty-bank guard without its
stats-only context, and remove the `gpu_part = 2` / `gpu_part = 0` assignments around `gpu_heap` in `gpu_show`;
the remaining changes have no other dependency on it.

title: Two errors name the wrong value: a bad + marker reports another parameter, and a double use in a pattern reports another binder
body:
Two checker errors name a value that is not the cause. The rules behind them are clear, and the guide documents both. Only the messages are wrong.

## 1. The `+` marker on a `Type` parameter

A `+` marker makes a value reusable. The guide says that this marker needs a `Data` value, and that functions, arrays and IO handles are `Type`. So the checker refuses `+` on those values. That refusal is correct.

The message does not say this. It reports `expected : Data / observed : Type`. It never mentions the marker, the copy, or the parameter. When the def has more than one parameter, the `Context` block names a different parameter. That parameter is correct.

```bend
import Base

def two(+name: String, +res: Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Unit>) -> Unit:
  Unit{}
```

Output:

```
Error:
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
Context:
- name : String
Location: two
3>| def two(+name: String, +res: Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Unit>) -> Unit:
```

The offender is `res`. The `Context` block names `name`.

With one parameter, the same error gives no `Context` block at all:

```bend
import Base

def hold(+h: File) -> Unit:
  Unit{}
```

```
Error:
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
Location: hold
```

## 2. A double use inside a `1n+f` pattern

This def matches `n`, then uses `n` again in the body. That is two uses of `n`, and `n` is affine. The checker refuses it.

The message names `f` instead. `f` occurs one time, in the recursive call.

```bend
import Base

def count(n: Nat, acc: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+f:
      count(f, (n + acc : Nat))
```

Output:

```
Error:
- expected : f
- observed : f (consumed more than once)
Location: count
7>|     case 1n+f:
8 |       count(f, (n + acc : Nat))
```

The line numbers are correct. The name is not.

## What would help

1. Name the value that breaks the rule. For the `+` case, that is the marked parameter. For the pattern case, that is the value used two times.
2. State the rule in the message. For the `+` case, a sentence such as "`+` needs a Data value; this type is Type" would remove the guesswork.

## Version

```
bend 2.0.25   (installed with `bend update`)
bun 1.3.14, Darwin arm64
```

Related: #957, #964, #965 -- the three bugs this project works around.

---

The reproducers were run by me with an AI assistant.

title: A non-decreasing Nat literal self-call makes descent checking exponential
body:
<!-- Title: A non-decreasing Nat literal self-call makes descent checking exponential -->

## What you did

Run `bun bend2/main.ts repro-descent-literal-exponential.bend --check-only` on the file below.

## What happened

The checker does not return. This self-call increases its argument from `32n` to `33n`, so I expected the ordinary `expected: a decreasing self-call` diagnostic.

The slowdown begins with small literals and approximately doubles for every added `Succ` on my machine: `16n -> 17n` takes 0.23 s, `20n -> 21n` 0.55 s, `21n -> 22n` 0.83 s, `22n -> 23n` 1.47 s, `23n -> 24n` 2.69 s, `24n -> 25n` 5.25 s, and `25n -> 26n` 10.50 s. The `32n -> 33n` file did not finish within 30 seconds.

## The file

```bend
import Base

def down(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:
    case 32n:
      down(33n)
    case _:
      n
```

## Cause

A numeric pattern is expanded into its full `Succ` chain by `lit_full` ([bend.ts:1807](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L1807)). When the recursive argument is larger than that chain, `term_descend` first compares corresponding fields recursively ([bend.ts:912](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L912)); after that comparison returns `GT`, it recursively searches the same argument against each field of the pattern ([bend.ts:920](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L920)). On unary `Succ` chains this recomputes overlapping suffix comparisons and gives the observed exponential growth.

This is a checker denial of service on a small source file. I have not derived an accepted non-decreasing definition or an inhabitant of `Empty` from it.

## Version / system

`bend 2.0.25` (`a49524265bdf`), Bun 1.4.2, Darwin arm64 27.0.0, Apple clang 21.0.0.

title: C backend rejects case-distinct constructors because both names become the same CID macro
body:
## What you did

Run:

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts case-folded-ctor.bend -o /tmp/case-folded-ctor.c
```

The same file evaluates normally and emits working JavaScript:

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts case-folded-ctor.bend
bun bend2/main.ts case-folded-ctor.bend -o /tmp/case-folded-ctor.js
bun /tmp/case-folded-ctor.js
```

## What happened

The evaluator and emitted JavaScript both print:

```text
done{}
```

The C emitter refuses the same checked program:

```text
Error: two names mangle to CID_DONE
```

`Base` declares the constructor `Done`, while this file declares the distinct constructor `done`. Bend accepts both names and the evaluator and JavaScript backend keep them distinct. The C backend builds a constructor macro with `"CID_" + name_clean(k).toUpperCase()`, so both source names become `CID_DONE`. The duplicate check then aborts emission. [`comp.ts:1537-1539`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/comp.ts#L1537-L1539), [`comp.ts:2903-2910`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/comp.ts#L2903-L2910)

This is related to the name-mangling collision class in #790 and #799, but it occurs in the constructor ID table rather than the JavaScript definition table or FFI effect table. The collision is detected, so I have not observed wrong code or a soundness failure; the result is that a valid program supported by the evaluator and JavaScript backend cannot be compiled to C.

## The file

```bend
import Base

type Lower is Data:
  done{}

def main() -> Lower:
  done{}
```

## Expected behavior

Case-distinct Bend constructor names should receive distinct C identifiers, or the frontend should reject the unsupported naming combination before backend selection.

## Environment

- `bend version`: `bend 2.0.25`
- commit: `a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868`
- `uname -sm`: `Darwin arm64`
- `clang --version`: `Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)`

title: The unsafe-code report collects a term's refs with a loop over its fields, not a recursion
body:
## The unsafe-code report collects a term's refs with a loop, not a recursion

`book_promises` decides which of a file's defs rely on unsafe or foreign code. It does so by collecting the names each reachable def refers to, Base's included, from its type, its datatype's and constructors' types, and its elaborated term.

`term_refs` was a recursion over `Object.entries` of every object. That allocated a pair array per field per node, pushed every primitive, and walked shared subterms once per path. It is now a loop with an explicit stack and a visited set, over every object in every field but the span:
- **Not recursive:** a deep term cannot overflow the stack.
- **Bounded:** each object is visited once, so a shared subgraph is walked once and a cyclic graph ends the walk.
- **Does not depend on node shapes:** a new node kind is walked like any other, which a typed switch could only do with a case per tag and a `never` check.
- **Short:** 17 lines.

As before, it reads a checked subterm's type (the value of a `Var`), takes a name only from a `Ref` or `ADT` with a string `k`, and skips spans. It does not enter functions: a binder's body held as a closure inside such a type is not walked, exactly as the old walk did not.

The branch's history: the PR first replaced the walk with a recursion by node kind; review asked to make that one complete by construction, which the second commit does; the third replaces it with the loop; the fourth adds the visited set and the `k` check from a second review. Only the loop is in the final diff.

## Checks

- **Same ref sets:** on every book under `tests/` and `demos/` (1,145 books, 458,215 defs, datatypes and constructors, walked as `book_promises` walks them after #1220), the committed `term_refs` gives the same ref sets as the old walk.
- **Edge cases:**
  - None of those graphs has a cycle (spans aside, which the walk skips).
  - No node has an inherited enumerable key, so `for…in` sees what `Object.entries` did.
  - A term nested 1,000 to 20,000 deep gives the same result on `main` and here: bend2's own checker, not this walk, sets the stack limit (both overflow from about 8,000).
- **Walk time over those books:**

  | walker | total |
  |---|---|
  | old | 12,426 ms |
  | typed recursion | 1,922 ms |
  | `JSON.stringify` with a replacer, as `term_key` does | 17,349 ms (rejected) |
  | this loop, without the visited set | 4,265 ms |
  | this loop | 5,369 ms |

- **`demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend --check-only`**, medians of five interleaved runs:

  | | walk | whole run | peak memory |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `main` | 51–53 ms | 2.80 s | 325 MB |
  | this PR | 33–42 ms | 2.80 s | 293 MB |

  The earlier description's "0.48 s → 0.32 s" and "40% of check time" don't reproduce on current `main`; the memory saving does.
- **Gates:**
  - `gates/_run.ts` gives repo PASS 50 / 50, test PASS 1569 / 1569 (including the tests that expect an unsafe report, #1220's among them), and perf PASS 120 / 124.
  - `gates/safe.ts tests`: per file, identical to `main`'s table (1,010 agree, 74 unsafe).
  - `tsc` reports nothing in `main.ts`.

Rebased on `main` (d052d4f3, which includes #1220).

title: C backend: a constructor with 256 single-word fields still exceeds CID_ARITY_T after #944
body:
### What you did

I generated a datatype with one constructor containing 256 live `U32` fields, then checked and ran it with the interpreter, JS, and native C backends:

```python
from pathlib import Path

n = 256
fields = ", ".join(f"f{i}: U32" for i in range(n))
values = ", ".join("x" for _ in range(n))
binders = ", ".join(f"f{i}" for i in range(n))

Path("repro.bend").write_text(f"""import Base

type R256 is Data:
  MkR256{{{fields}}}

def mk(+x: U32) -> R256:
  MkR256{{{values}}}

def pick(r: R256) -> U32:
  match r:
    case MkR256{{{binders}}}:
      f255

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(pick(mk(42))))
""")
```

```bash
python3 gen.py
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend --check-only
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend -o /tmp/repro.js
bun /tmp/repro.js
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend -o /tmp/repro
```

### What happened

The checker accepts the file, and the interpreter and JS both print `42`. The native build fails before invoking clang:

```text
Error: an arity over 255
```

Changing `n` from 256 to 255 makes the native build succeed and print `42`.

This is a remaining direct-constructor case after #944. `lay_wide` handles a layout past `WIDE` by replacing each multi-word field layout with `BOX`, which fixes a small number of wide nested fields. Here every field is already one word, so the mapping leaves all 256 fields unchanged. `lay_node(...).ks.length` reaches `CID_ARITY_T` as 256, and `compile_tables` rejects it because the table is `u8`.

This is separate from the wide fork-join shape noted in the closing comment on #944: no fork or wide intermediate result is involved.

### Expected

The C backend should represent or box a checker-accepted constructor with 256 single-word fields instead of failing on an internal runtime-table limit. If 255 source fields is intended to be a language limit, the checker should diagnose it consistently rather than leaving the file accepted by the checker, interpreter, and JS backend.

### Environment

```text
bend 2.0.25 (a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868)
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: fix(loader): register in Node worker threads
Equality checking revisits a shared constructor DAG exponentially
body:
<!-- Title: Equality checking revisits a shared constructor DAG exponentially -->

### What I did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts shared_tree_equality.bend --check-only
```

```bend
type N is Data:
  Z{}
  S{p: N}

type T is Data:
  L{}
  B{l: T, r: T}

def d(n: N) -> T:
  match n:
    case Z{}:
      L{}
    case S{p}:
      +x = d(p)
      B{x, x}

def n() -> N:
  S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{S{Z{}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}}

def boom() -> {d(n()) == d(n()) : T}:
  {==}
```

### What happened

The file is accepted, but equality checking takes about 1.9 seconds. Increasing only the number of `S` constructors makes the time grow exponentially even though `d` returns a linearly sized DAG: each `B` shares the same `x` in both fields.

I generated otherwise identical files and measured `parse_book` plus `book_valid` in one Bun process:

| Depth | Check time |
| ---: | ---: |
| 18 | 28 ms |
| 20 | 103 ms |
| 22 | 417 ms |
| 24 | 1.85 s |
| 25 | 4.37 s |
| 26 | 8.84 s |
| 27 | 16.50 s |

The depth-27 source is 314 bytes without formatting whitespace. As a control, changing only `B{x, x}` to `B{x, L{}}` at depth 24 reduces the same check from 1.72 seconds to 8.2 milliseconds.

### Why it happens

Weak-head normalization preserves the let sharing. A demanded value becomes a share cell, and constructor fields are themselves placed in cells when that value is filled ([bend.ts:2892-2901](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L2892-L2901), [bend.ts:3018-3032](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L3018-L3032)). Each side of the equation therefore normalizes to a DAG with one node per level.

`term_compare` only short-circuits when the left and right objects are identical. The two independently written calls `d(n())` produce distinct left and right cells, so that shortcut does not apply ([bend.ts:3194-3201](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L3194-L3201)). The constructor case then compares both fields independently ([bend.ts:3277-3279](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L3277-L3279)). Both fields contain the same already compared pair of share cells, but the comparison has no visited-pair cache, so it walks that sub-DAG twice. The recurrence is approximately `C(n) = 2 C(n - 1)`.

This is distinct from #984: that issue expands duplicated global quantity references while normalizing a definition DAG. Here normalization preserves the local sharing, but structural equality repeatedly traverses the same pair of normalized nodes. It is also separate from #983, which is in `term_descend` and uses literal-pattern suffixes.

### Expected behavior

Equality checking should preserve the linear sharing already present in the normalized terms. Memoizing compared node pairs for one `term_compare` call would make this reproducer linear in the depth of `d(n())`.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.25
commit a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: A constructor name reused by a later definition bypasses #905 and admits Empty
body:
### What I did

Put these three files in one directory and check `main.bend`.

`law.bend`:

```bend
law k:
  for ~B.x: Data
  Data
```

`law.k~B.bend`:

```bend
import ./law.bend as L

type Empty is Data:

type Bit is Data:
  False{}
  True{}

type Marker is Data:
  x{}

def L.k(B.x):
  x

type Bad is Type:
  MkBad{apply: @+b: L.k(~Empty) -> Empty}

def x() -> Type:
  Bad

def Bad.apply(b: Bad) -> (@+x: L.k(~Empty) -> Empty):
  match b:
    case MkBad{f}:
      f

def step(+b: L.k(~Empty)) -> Empty:
  Bad.apply(b)(MkBad{Bad.apply(b)})

def boom() -> Empty:
  step(MkBad{step})

def absurd(-A: Type, e: Empty) -> A:
  match e:

def false_theorem() -> {False{} == True{} : Bit}:
  absurd({False{} == True{} : Bit}, boom())
```

`main.bend`:

```bend
import ./law.k~B.bend as E

def boom() -> E.Empty:
  E.boom()
```

Then run:

```text
bun bend2/main.ts main.bend --check-only
```

### What happened

```text
All terms check.
```

The accepted safe book has no holes, open laws, `@unsafe` definitions, FFI, or Base import. It contains the closed `boom() -> Empty` and derives `False{} == True{}`.

### Why it happens

The imported module's namespace is `law.k~B`. Its constructor `x{}` therefore owns the constructor key `law.k~B.x`. The fill body `x` resolves through that constructor-table entry to `Ref("law.k~B.x")`. Definitions and constructors use separate freshness checks, so the later `def x() -> Type` is also admitted under the TLD key `law.k~B.x`. [`parse_reso`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L1751-L1759) [`parse_fresh`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L2526-L2540)

`book_valid` hides later TLDs and reveals declarations in order. When it checks the earlier fill of `law.k`, the constructor is visible but the later TLD `law.k~B.x` is not. `def_check` constructs exactly that name for the opaque `~B.x` parameter and tests freshness only in the currently visible TLD table. The test therefore passes, the opaque temporarily shadows the constructor key, and the body checks as `Data`. [`def_check`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L3769-L3784) [`book_valid`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868/bend2/bend.ts#L3860-L3879)

Validation then reaches the later `def x() -> Type` and installs it under the same key. From that point, reducing the already checked body of `L.k` resolves its `Ref("law.k~B.x")` to this definition and yields `Bad`, which is `Type`-kinded. The declared result of `L.k` is still `Data`, so `L.k(~Empty)` licenses the `+` binder over the negative `Bad` type. The ordinary Curry term in `step` then inhabits `Empty`.

This is a bypass of the opaque-name freshness guard added for #905. Moving the later `def x` before the law fill makes that guard reject the opaque name as expected; leaving it later keeps it outside the visible TLD table during generic checking.

### Expected behavior

An opaque template parameter should have an identity that cannot be captured by constructor or definition names, including declarations revealed later. At minimum, constructor and TLD keys should not be reusable in this order-sensitive way, and opaque-name freshness should cover the complete namespace rather than only the currently visible TLD table.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.25
commit a49524265bdfa5753a4bf38e25f0574a705dd868
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
```

title: Names on the hub: import name@version, --publish name@version, bend link, bend login

Packages on the hub get names. `import <name>@<version>/x.bend as X` asks the hub once for the hash (`GET /name/<name>@<version>`) and keeps it under `BEND_LIB/names`. `bend <file> --publish <name>@<version>` checks the name and version with the hub before mining, publishes, registers the name if free and links it. `bend link <name>@<version> 0x<hash>` names a package already on the hub. `bend login` is Bender's CLI login; the key lives in `~/.bend/bender.json` (0600).

title: Fix the shared array redirect race
body:
## Problem

`blk_loc` reads a shared Array redirect as a `u64` while other handles atomically change its 32-bit reference count. The previous patch used `rfc_view` for every lookup, adding atomic reads to the array-access path.

## Change

A redirect still occupies one eight-byte slot, but its count and immutable target are separate `u32` fields. Array and buffer handles carry the target's low eight bits in unused aux bits. `blk_loc` reads the other 32 bits from the redirect and reconstructs the location.

The lookup therefore uses one ordinary read from the same slot as before, with no atomic read or fence per array access. The full-word redirect reads in the runtime and Window renderer have also been changed to read the fields separately. Constructor IDs are unchanged.

On the Metal source path, the lookup remains one plain device-memory read, now of the upper 32 bits rather than the full 64-bit slot. The additional shifts and OR use bits already in the handle. Creating a redirect takes two field stores instead of one full-word store.

## Validation

On unmodified main (`6a77e124`), the 256-leaf reproducer reports a race with two workers under ThreadSanitizer. With this change, five runs each at 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers printed `256` without diagnostics. Three other array-fork tests ran cleanly under ThreadSanitizer at 2 and 4 workers.

Nine RFC tests and eight array tests passed in the interpreter and generated JS, and in native CPU runs with 1 and 4 workers. A separate C probe covered 40-bit redirect targets, constructor IDs and the CPU Window lookup. The repository gate passed 46/46.

On WSL x86-64 with Clang `-O3`, a scaled stencil (2^18 cells, 64 leaves, 160 passes) took a median 0.1035 s on main and 0.1058 s with this change at one worker; at four workers the times were 0.0752 s and 0.0754 s. These are CPU measurements. For the shared-array path on Metal, the scaled stencil in #999 is the relevant comparison: all 16 existing runtime benchmarks compile with `BLK_SHR=0` and do not exercise this lookup.

title: A shared array resolves its redirect once: a spin takes each box word's storage
body:
Draft: this needs a decision on `bend2/comp.ts`'s ttok cap before it can land (see **Size** below).

## What this changes

With any Array shared, `BLK_SHR` is on and a handle is a redirect: `blk_loc` reads the handle's cell to find the storage. Clang cannot hoist that load out of a loop, because array cells are written through `u32a`, which is `may_alias`, so a cell store may be the redirect word. It does already merge the reads within one iteration, and it unswitches the rfc test when a handle is unshared at runtime, so what is left is one load per handle per iteration.

A spin now takes, beside each box word, the storage its caller resolved (`q`), and keeps the handle it was entered with (`h`):

```c
INLINE Term spin_7(Env e, THR Term* o, ..., Term r2, Loc q2, Term r3, Loc q3) {
  Term h2 = r2;
  Term h3 = r3;
  ...
      at_0 = a == h2 ? q2 : a == h3 ? q3 : blk_loc(e.mem, a);
```

Once the spins are inlined, a handle a loop carries is visibly the same value as its `h`, so clang folds the test and the loop reads the redirect once instead of per access. A handle that matches none reads it as before, so a loop that swaps its arrays, or hands over one it built itself, stays correct. Segments that are not spins are untouched.

Three details each paid for themselves in a measurement:

- **A handle that is the spin's own word is tested against that word alone.** editdist's DP rows swap every row, so the tests run for real; against every word they cost 2.3%.
- **The word keeps the handle it came with,** rather than the back edge resolving the current one. Recomputing per iteration cost editdist 2.7% and bfs 4.9%, on loops that gain nothing.
- **With no Array shared the words take nothing.** `blk_loc` is then a mask with no load, and the extra values only cost registers: 2.3% on editdist, 0.9% on bfs.

## Measurements

Apple M4, one thread unless noted, `cc -std=c11 -O3`.

A scaled `tests/run/stencil3d.bend` (2^21 cells, 128 leaves, 160 passes: the GPGPU pattern, forked handles to one block, 7 gets and 1 set per cell):

| lane | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| SEQ | 530 ms | 445 ms |
| PAR, 10 threads | 119 ms | 101 ms |
| Metal | 7.18 s | 1.31 s |

The kernel loop keeps its 7 cell reads and no redirect load. I have no account of the Metal factor beyond the loads being global memory there.

Programs that share one array and run their hot loops over unshared ones: editdist 2.139 → 2.139 s, bfs 4.00 → 3.93 s.

Every bench in `bench/runtime` emits the C it emitted before, byte for byte, so the suite is unchanged by construction.

## Tests

- Every test under `tests/` built and run on the C lane locally: 617 pass, the same set as main, and the same 9 `tests/io` and `tests/run/nat_overflow` failures on both.
- The six tests whose programs share an Array (`array_fork`, `array_fork_unshare`, `stencil3d`, `array_atomic_fadd`, `brw_audit2_array_field`, `brw_audit2_array_match`) pass on Metal.
- The cluster gates have not been run.

## Size

`comp.ts` 64941 → 65174 ttok, over the 65000 cap in `gates/repo.ts`, so `bun gates/repo.ts` fails at 45/46. main sits 59 ttok under the cap. Every piece of the change was removed in turn and each one cost time, so the choice is to raise the cap by ~200 or to find that much elsewhere in the file.

## One sharp edge

`q` is trusted when a handle is bitwise equal to `h`. A redirect's storage is written only by `rfc_wrap`, when the redirect is made, so it never moves while a handle holds it. The exception would be a spin that drops the last reference to its entry handle and then shares a new array whose redirect reuses that freed cell with the same bits. Safe Bend never copies an Array, so this needs `@unsafe` and a fork-free def.

title: One `@unsafe` law fill in a file PROOF.bend imports silently proves every law: `bend PROOF.bend` prints a clean "All terms check." (regression from #848)
body:
### What you did

Three files in one directory:

```python
# LAWS.bend
import Base

law false_law:
  {1n == 0n : Nat}
```

```python
# Helper.bend
import ./LAWS.bend as Laws

@unsafe def Laws.false_law():
  Laws.false_law()
```

```python
# PROOF.bend
import ./Helper.bend as H
```

```
bend PROOF.bend; echo exit=$?
```

### What happened

```text
All terms check.
exit=0
```

The verdict is unsound: `LAWS.false_law : {1n == 0n : Nat}` holds only because an `@unsafe` self-call skips the termination check, yet bend reports every term as checked and prints no unsafe note. `LAWS.bend` is imported (through Helper), so the "PROOF.bend must import ./LAWS.bend" check passes, and no law is open, so there is no TODO error.

The false law is then an ordinary hypothesis for every other law. With a second law in LAWS.bend

```python
law succ_is_id:
  for +n: Nat
  {1n+n == n : Nat}
```

and its proof added to Helper.bend, derived from `false_law` with no further `@unsafe`:

```python
def disc(n: Nat) -> Type:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      Empty
    case 1n+p:
      Unit

def boom() -> Empty:
  %Laws.false_law() : disc(_)
  Unit{}

def ex(+n: Nat, e: Empty) -> {1n+n == n : Nat}:
  match e:

def Laws.succ_is_id(n):
  ex(n, boom())
```

`bend PROOF.bend` still prints a clean `All terms check.` (exit 0). One `@unsafe` line in a file PROOF.bend imports closes every law of LAWS.bend without a note.

The report itself works when it starts from the right place. The unsafe fill written in PROOF.bend instead gives

```text
All terms check, but 1 def relies on unsafe or foreign code:
- LAWS.false_law
```

and the derivation written in PROOF.bend (the unsafe fill still in Helper) gives

```text
All terms check, but 2 defs rely on unsafe or foreign code:
- boom
- LAWS.succ_is_id
```

This is a regression. Running the first repro (`false_law` only) across commits:

| commit | verdict |
|---|---|
| `5e565504` (the #776 fix) | `All terms check, with 1 unsafe annotation.` |
| `f1d23d3c~1` | `All terms check, with 1 unsafe annotation.` |
| `f1d23d3c` (the #848 fix) | `All terms check.` |
| `a4952426` (2.0.25) | `All terms check.` |

Since `f1d23d3c`, `cli_report` walks the references of the root file's own entries (`book.order.slice(n0)`), so "an imported `@unsafe` def the file never calls" stays silent. A law fill is not a call, though: it closes a claim of LAWS.bend from whichever file holds it, and the root never refers to it. The fill is pushed to `book.order` inside Helper's range, so the walk never starts there.

WONTFIX says of #776 and #805: "read the note, not the exit code". Here there is no note, so the gate the guide describes ("`bend PROOF.bend` is the gate: it fails while any law is open or false") reports success for a false law with no signal at all.

A possible fix: seed the walk with every law of the book that was filled outside Base (or at least every law of `LAWS.bend` when the root is `PROOF.bend`), not only the root's entries.

### The file

See above (LAWS.bend, Helper.bend, PROOF.bend).

### bend --version

bend 2.0.25 (main @ a4952426)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)

title: Names resolve to keys other files register under the importer's namespace: an app file can rewrite what LAWS.bend says, or make PROOF.bend check different code than `bend main.bend` runs
body:
**Update:** the same rule also splits the proven program from the one that runs, with LAWS.bend and PROOF.bend both canonical. See the comment below.

### What I did

Put three files in one directory.

`LAWS.bend` (the human's file, unchanged throughout):

```bend
import Base

law two_plus_two:
  {Nat.add(2n, 2n) == 5n : Nat}
```

`LAWS.Nat.bend`:

```bend
import Base

def add(a: Nat, b: Nat) -> Nat:
  5n
```

`PROOF.bend`:

```bend
import Base
import ./LAWS.Nat.bend as H
import ./LAWS.bend as Laws

def Laws.two_plus_two():
  {==}
```

Then run:

```text
bun bend2/main.ts PROOF.bend
```

### What happened

```text
All terms check.
```

Exit code 0. There is no `@unsafe`, FFI, hole or open law. Without the `import ./LAWS.Nat.bend as H` line, the same PROOF.bend is rejected with `expected : 4n / observed : 5n` at `LAWS.two_plus_two`, as it should be.

### Why it happens

`parse_reso` resolves a name `k` written in a module with namespace `ns` to `ns + "." + k` whenever that key is already in `book.tlds` or `book.ctrs`, and falls back to the global `k` otherwise ([`parse_reso`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/26659268/bend2/bend.ts#L1751-L1761)). When PROOF.bend imports `./LAWS.bend`, LAWS.bend is parsed with namespace `LAWS`, so its `Nat.add` is first looked up as `LAWS.Nat.add`.

A file named `LAWS.Nat.bend` gets namespace `LAWS.Nat`, and its `def add` is stored under the key `LAWS.Nat.add`. If that file is loaded before LAWS.bend, the lookup succeeds and the law's `Nat.add` becomes a `Ref("LAWS.Nat.add")` to the attacker's definition. The two keys never meet `parse_fresh`: `LAWS.Nat.add` and Base's `Nat.add` are different keys, so nothing is a duplicate.

The same rule applies to every call site of `parse_reso`: references, constructors, `D<..>` families, patterns, operator sugar and dotted field access.
### It does not need PROOF.bend to look suspicious

The injected file can also be imported by application code that the AI owns. In `demos/app_win_is_bug_2d`, add one line to `main.bend` and one file:

```bend
# main.bend, after `import Base`
import ./LAWS.U32.bend as Q
```

```bend
# LAWS.U32.bend
import Base

def is_eq(a: U32, b: U32) -> Bool:
  False{}
```

LAWS.bend is unchanged, and PROOF.bend keeps its canonical `import Base / import ./main.bend as Game / import ./LAWS.bend as Laws` header. Loading main.bend first registers `LAWS.U32.is_eq`, so the `U32.is_eq(code, k)` in LAWS.bend's `ch` now always returns `False{}`, and `never_on_flag` no longer looks at the board the page draws. This proof, which never mentions the map, then replaces the demo's certificate:

```bend
def row_no(s: String, x: Nat) -> {Laws.flag_in_row(s, x) == False{} : Bool}:
  match s:
    case SNil{}:
      {==}
    case SCon{c, rest}:
      match c:
        case Chr{code}:
          match x:
            case 0n:
              {==}
            case 1n+p:
              row_no(rest, p)

def at_no(y: Nat, x: Nat, s: String) -> {Laws.flag_at(y, x, s) == False{} : Bool}:
  match y:
    case 0n:
      row_no(s, x)
    case 1n+q:
      at_no(q, x, Laws.next_row(s))

def g_no(g: Game.Game) -> {Laws.at_flag(g) == False{} : Bool}:
  match g:
    case Game.Game{x, y, won}:
      at_no(y, x, Laws.drawn())

def Laws.never_on_flag(moves):
  g_no(Game.replay(Game.start(), moves))
```

`bun bend2/main.ts PROOF.bend` prints `All terms check.` and exits 0. Without the extra import in main.bend, the same proof fails with `expected : Cmp.is_eq(U32.cmp(code, 70)) / observed : False{}`.

Checking `bend LAWS.bend` on its own does not reveal anything, because as the root file LAWS.bend has namespace `""` and resolves everything to Base.

### Relation to #1001

This is related to #1001 in that a file PROOF.bend imports defeats the gate, but the mechanism is different and a fix for #1001 does not close it. There is no `@unsafe` to disclose here: every definition is safe and every law is filled. The problem is that the law being proven is not the law the human wrote.

### Expected behavior

What a name in LAWS.bend refers to should not depend on which other files were loaded before it. The resolution of a name written in a module should depend only on that module's own declarations, its own imports and Base. A key that a different file registered under the module's namespace prefix should not count. Alternatively, the checker could reject any declaration whose key lands in another file's namespace, like `LAWS.Nat.add` from `LAWS.Nat.bend`, or a file namespace that is a dotted extension of another loaded file's namespace.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.25
commit 26659268
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
```

title: A literal is one node per kind: Lit{k, v} steps through lit_step, and U32 and F32 literals are kinds
body:
Draft: this needs a decision on `bend2/bend.ts`'s ttok cap before it can land (see **Size** below). It is an alternative to #936, which adds U32 and F32 literals by tagging `Lit` with an optional `k`.

## What this changes

Since #907 and #924, a string or nat literal is one `Lit` node that unfolds one constructor at a time where it is read. Its kind was implicit in `typeof v`, and each reader (the step, the full unfolding, check-lit, the printer, `nat_from_term`) spelled out Nat and String by hand. #936 extends that to U32 and F32 with a `k !== undefined` branch at each of those sites.

Here every literal carries its kind, and the kind decides the payload's type:

```ts
export type Lit =
  | { k: "Nat"; v: number }
  | { k: "String"; v: string }
  | { k: "U32"; v: U32 }
  | { k: "F32"; v: U32 };
```

`lit_step` is the only code that knows a kind: one `case` per kind, returning the constructor it unfolds to. Everything else reads a literal through it:

- the termination check, the match frame, `term_compare` (a mixed Lit/Ctr pair steps the literal) and infer-err, as before;
- check-lit takes the head constructor from the step instead of a Zero/Succ/SNil/SCon ternary;
- the printer prints a literal as its first step, so the existing Nat, String, U32 and F32 sugar does the work;
- `lit_full` (patterns, and the compiler's `term_force`) is one worklist that steps any literal it finds in a step's fields;
- two literals are equal when their kind and payload are.

So a new kind is a `Lit` variant, its `case`, and its parse rule. Kinds nest: a string's step holds its character as `Chr{U32 literal}` rather than a 33-word chain, and a char literal `'c'` parses to the same 2-node shape. `Ctr` and `u32_to_term` return the `Ctr` variant, so `lit_step` needs no cast, and narrowing on `k` types `v`, so the readers need none either.

In `comp.ts` only the big-Nat case of `term_force` changes (`s.k === "Nat"`).

## Measurements

Apple M4, min of 5, seconds / peak MB:

| | main | #936 | this |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 defs, each a U32 literal, `--check-only` | 0.28 / 334 | 0.06 / 107 | 0.06 / 120 |
| 2000 defs, each an F32 literal, `--check-only` | 0.28 / 339 | 0.06 / 108 | 0.06 / 119 |
| a 200-case U32 match, `--check-only` | 1.11 / 1167 | 0.19 / 236 | 0.21 / 242 |
| the same, `-o main.c` | 1.82 / 1389 | 0.42 / 358 | 0.43 / 360 |
| demos/app_slash_boss_3d `--check-only` | 0.49 / 526 | 0.17 / 199 | 0.18 / 201 |
| demos/app_slash_boss_3d `-o main.c` | 2.01 / 2238 | 1.44 / 1814 | 1.49 / 1692 |

The extra ~12 MB against #936 on the literal-per-def files is check-lit building a U32's first step (its word) where #936 reads the head from the tag. String-heavy programs (2000 string defs, a 100-case string match) are unchanged from main on all three.

## Tests

- The C, JS and stderr output of every test, bench and demo with a main (2411 files) is byte-identical to main.
- The interpreter lane (`bend t.bend`) over all 1429 tests under `tests/` prints the same as main.
- #936's nine tests (`check/`, `compile/`, `parse/`, `printer/` and `proof/` `*_literal_*`, `parse/nat_plus_u32`) are included and pass; the two compile tests print right on C and JS and emit the same code as main.
- The cluster gates have not been run.

## Size

`bend.ts` 42979 → 43217 ttok, over the 43000 cap in `gates/repo.ts`, so `bun gates/repo.ts` fails. #936 costs about the same and raises the cap to 43200. The choice is to raise the cap to ~43300 or to find that much elsewhere in the file.

The u32/f32 tests are @MattCozendey's, from #936.

title: Feature/general literals
body:
# A literal carries its Base type: one `Lit` for Nat, String, U32, F32 and Char

This PR (#1004) generalizes the compact literal. It is an internal change: no
syntax, no program meaning, no printed output and no emitted code changes.

## Where this comes from

1. #907 made a String literal one `Lit` node that unfolds one character at a
   time where it is read.
2. #924 did the same for Nat literals.
3. #936 extended `Lit` to U32 and F32 with an optional tag `k`. Each reader
   (the step, the full unfolding, check-lit, the printer, `nat_from_term`, the
   compiler) got a `k !== undefined` branch next to its `typeof v` branch.
4. #1003 (Nico Abril) is an alternative to #936: every literal carries its
   kind, and `lit_step` is the one place that knows a kind.

This PR starts from #936 (its commits and its nine tests are included) and
takes the same direction as #1003. It adds the compiler and checker work that
removes the cost of the step, and it deletes the code that the tag makes
unnecessary.

## The design

A literal is one node that holds a closed value of its Base type:

```ts
| { $: "Lit"; k: "Nat" | "U32" | "F32"; v: number }   // 3n, 7, 1.5 (its bits)
| { $: "Lit"; k: "String"; v: string }                // "text"
```

1. The union ties each kind to its payload, so narrowing on `k` types `v`, and
   `Lit("Nat", "x")` does not compile.
2. `lit_step` unfolds one constructor. Its fields can be literals again: a
   String's step and a char literal `'c'` hold the code as `Chr{Lit(U32)}`, one
   node, not a 65-node Word chain. Char needs no kind of its own.
3. Check-lit is one condition: `Lit(k, v)` checks at Base's type `k`. Base
   loads with the empty namespace, and each head constructor of Nat, String,
   U32 and F32 is declared by that type alone, so this accepts exactly the
   terms that the old `ctrs_find` rule accepted, with no step built.
4. The printer prints a literal as its first step, so the existing sugar
   prints every kind (this idea is from #1003).
5. The compiler steps a literal one constructor at a time, as the checker
   does. `lit_full` is gone.
6. `term_const` in the compiler answers "constant" for a literal at once. It
   unfolded each U32 literal into 65 nodes to find every node constant: 75%
   of the compiler's U32 unfolds in `pure_hvm5_mini` came from there.
   `lit_call` is the one place for the exception, a Nat past the cap.
7. A step is a closed tree of `Ctr` and `Lit` nodes, the same in both body
   representations, so the checker and the compiler use it without a
   `term_higher` copy.

Removed: `lit_full`, `u32_to_term`, `lit_chain`, every `typeof v` and
`k === undefined` test, and the per-kind printer branch. The per-kind code is
`lit_step` and the parser.

## Correctness

`bend2/bend.lean` models literals as their constructor trees ("Literals are
base.bend constructors, not calculus"), so the proof holds while these hold:

1. Meaning: each `Lit` means one closed tree of Base constructors, the tree
   that `main` parses.
2. Typing: the fast check accepts `Lit(k, v)` only at Base's type `k`.
3. Equality: two literals are equal only when `k` and `v` are equal.
4. Reading: each reader of a term head unfolds a literal first (`term_compare`,
   `term_descend`, the match frame, `parse_patt`, infer-err, the compiler's
   `term_force`); `u32_from_term` reads a U32 literal's value directly.

Nothing mutates a step's nodes, so sharing a step is safe; `main` shares its
parsed U32 trees the same way.

## Measurements

WSL (Ubuntu 24.04, 20 threads). Each cell is CPU time (user + sys) in seconds
and peak memory in MB, the median of 5 rounds that rotate the three trees.
All three trees emit identical C for every program measured. "Run" is
`bend file.bend` (check and interpreter). The three literal programs are
generated scratch files, not part of the PR.

| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5000 Char literals, check | 2.17 / 418 | 0.50 / 97 | **0.45 / 95** |
| 5000 Char literals, run | 2.53 / 480 | 1.01 / 132 | **0.65 / 122** |
| 5000 Char literals, `-o main.c` | 3.27 / 629 | 2.00 / 240 | **0.97 / 144** |
| 500 Strings + 200 String proofs, check | 0.56 / 92 | 0.27 / 78 | 0.27 / 78 |

| 2500 U32 + 1000 F32 literals, check | 1.74 / 318 | 0.34 / 88 | **0.31 / 84** |
| 2500 U32 + 1000 F32 literals, run | 1.97 / 379 | 0.77 / 129 | **0.51 / 103** |
| 2500 U32 + 1000 F32 literals, `-o main.c` | 2.47 / 490 | 1.42 / 193 | **0.68 / 112** |

   32 bits where a U32 unfolds (`term_compare` against computed values, the
   `Word.*` functions), so a lazy word adds nodes; it also needs a width field,
   a Nat-index test in check-lit and a `Word` case in `u32_from_term`.
2. A per-literal cache of word steps in the checker: measured on top of this
   PR, it gained nothing.
3. User-overloadable literals (`T.literal`): a language feature, not this
   change.
