title: The effects guide gives the JS park its deadline, as it gives the C one, and names select, not poll, in io_sys()
body:
## What changes

Two edits in one paragraph of `guide/EFFECTS.md`, "The JS side":

```diff
 `more()` when `fd` is ready; `more` answers the value, or `undefined` to
-park again. `io_sys()` is `libc` through `bun:ffi`
-(`read`, `recv`, `poll`, `errno`); `tcp_recv.js` shows the full shape.
+park again. Add an absolute `performance.now()` deadline as a fifth
+argument to also wake on time. `io_sys()` is `libc` through `bun:ffi`
+(`read`, `recv`, `select`, `errno`); `tcp_recv.js` shows the full shape.
```

## Why

- The C side says how a park also wakes on time ("Replace `0` with an
  absolute `io_tick()` deadline", since #947). The JS side showed only
  `io_park_on(fd, out, k, more)`. The JS runtime's `io_park_on` has taken
  a fifth argument, `at`, since TCP.poll (#861), and `tcp_poll.js` uses
  it. It is an absolute `performance.now()` time in ms: `io_wait` turns it
  into `select`'s timeout and compares it with `performance.now()`. If you
  leave it out, the park waits on `fd` alone. The argument appears only in
  the runtime source inside `comp.ts`, and no Base signature shows it. So
  someone writing a JS twin of a timed C effect cannot find it.
- `io_sys()` has had no `poll` since the JS loop moved to `select` in
  #932. `io_sys().poll` is `undefined`, and `select` is the call it binds.

## How it was checked

Linux x86-64, Bun 1.3.11, clang 22.1.8. I did not run it on macOS.

- A throwaway effect opens a pipe that nobody writes. It parks on the read
  end with `io_park_on(p[0], false, k, more, performance.now() + 50)`, and
  `more` reports how long the park lasted. Its C twin parks with
  `io_wait_on(w, fd, POLLIN, io_tick() + 50 ms, more)`. Over four runs:

  | lane | empty pipe, 50 ms | one byte, 1 s | no fd, 50 ms |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | `bend main.bend` | 50.6-51.4 ms | 0.0-0.1 ms | 50.2-50.5 ms |
  | `-o x.js && bun x.js` | 50.7-50.8 ms | 0.0 ms | 50.2-50.3 ms |
  | `-o x && ./x` | 50.1 ms | 0.0 ms | 50.1 ms |

  On every lane, the empty-pipe wake comes after the deadline and its read
  finds nothing.
- Without the fifth argument, the same park on the empty pipe does not
  wake within 3 s.
- `typeof io_sys().poll` is `"undefined"` and `typeof io_sys().select` is
  `"function"`, on both JS lanes.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: 46 / 46. The guide is 1592 ttok, under its cap of
  1600.

No test is added because the change is to the guide only.
`tests/io/tcp_poll.bend` already exercises the JS deadline through
`TCP.poll`.

title: Process.run: a grandchild that keeps writing makes C answer Fail where JS answers Done
body:
## Behavior

When the direct child exits but a background grandchild keeps writing to the inherited stdout, the C lane and the JS lane answer different things:

```bend
Process.run("/bin/sh", ["-c", "yes & echo hi"], "", 65536, 1500)
```

| Lane | Result |
| --- | --- |
| native C | `Fail{(27, "File too large")}` (output past `max_output`) |
| JS (Bun) | `Done{(0, ("hi\n", ""))}` |

Observed on macOS arm64 on `main` at 168534fe, right after #1030. Both lanes leave the `yes` running, as the guide documents ("Timeouts do not kill descendants").

## Cause

After #1030's review, the C loop in `bend2/effs/process_run.c` (`process_call`, lines 161–205) reaps the direct child on every pass. Once it has exited, the loop polls with a 0 ms timeout and stops only when a poll returns nothing ready (line 205) or every pipe is closed (line 189). A grandchild that never stops writing keeps the pipe readable, so the loop keeps draining until the output passes `max_output`. The deadline no longer applies at that point either (line 175 checks it only while the child is alive).

A grandchild that writes slowly (`(while :; do echo x; sleep 0.01; done) & echo hi`) does not trigger it: the drain finds an empty poll and stops, and both lanes answer `Done`. They differ only in how many `x` lines they catch, which is a timing race.

It cannot hang, because the output stays capped by `max_output`, but the two lanes should answer the same thing.

## Possible fix

Once the direct child has been reaped, drain in a single pass: read only what is readable at that moment (for example, bounded by `FIONREAD` per pipe, or by one poll and read round), then stop. That matches what the guide promises ("The call waits for the direct child and drains ready output; a descendant holding an inherited pipe open does not extend the wait") and what `Bun.spawnSync` does.

A test in `tests/io/process_run.bend` with the call above and an exact expected result would keep the lanes in step.

title: Due timers wake by deadline, so spawn_sleep and fork_join sleep 1-3 ms
body:
## Problem

Both IO loops (C and JS `io_wait`) woke every due park in the order it was parked. macOS's `select` wakes several ms late; a 5 ms timeout returned after 11 ms. When two timers fell due in the same pass, a 9 ms sleep parked before a 1 ms sleep resumed first. So `IO.sleep` kept deadline order only for deadlines more than about 6 ms apart, and `spawn_sleep` and `fork_join` needed 17 ms of sleeps to pass (5108d040).

## Change

`io_wait` collects the parks due in a pass. It then sorts the pure timers among them by deadline (C: `qsort` on (deadline, slot); JS: a stable sort) and wakes them in the slots the timers held.

- A socket's wake keeps its place.
- Nothing waits longer than before: every due park still wakes in the same pass, so a batch can't be starved or deferred.
- It does not make timers less late; it only fixes their order.

`spawn_sleep` and `fork_join` drop to 1/2/3 ms.

## Verification (local, M-series Mac)

- `spawn_sleep` and `fork_join` at 1/2/3 ms: 30/30 on interpreter, C and JS. Before this change they failed nearly every run at those spans.
- Every other `tests/io` test gives the same result on all three lanes as on `main`.
- `gates/repo.ts`: 46/46.
- `gates/test.ts` **not run**: SSH to the cluster nodes was refused from this machine.

## Performance

This is not a runtime speedup. It is neutral on C and costs a little on JS (hyperfine, 30 runs):

| bench | C before → after | JS before → after |
|---|---|---|
| 20000 timers, all due in one pass (worst case) | 10.9 → 11.1 ms | 53 → 60 ms |
| 2000 computations × 10 sleeps of 1–7 ms | 90.9 → 89.6 ms | 97.4 → 100.2 ms |

On the worst-case JS bench, the 18k-entry sort takes 1.5 ms; the rest comes from resuming the computations in deadline order instead of parking order. The gain for the test gate is about 14 ms less sleeping in each of two tests, on three lanes.

title: JS F32.read double-rounds a finite decimal to infinity while C keeps it finite
body:
### What you did

```text
bend f32_read_rounding.bend -o f32_read_rounding.js && bun f32_read_rounding.js
bend f32_read_rounding.bend -o f32_read_rounding && ./f32_read_rounding
```

### What happened

The JS build prints:

```text
False
2139095040
```

The C build prints:

```text
True
2139095039
```

Both lanes accept the decimal, but `F32.read` returns positive infinity (`0x7f800000`) on JS and the largest finite F32 (`0x7f7fffff`) on C. The difference changes the result of an ordinary `F32.is_lt` branch.

### The file

```bend
import Base

def below_inf(m: Maybe<&2, F32>) -> Bool:
  match m:
    case None{}:
      False{}
    case Some{x}:
      F32.is_lt(x, F32.div(1.0, 0.0))

def bits(m: Maybe<&2, F32>) -> U32:
  match m:
    case None{}:
      0
    case Some{F32{w}}:
      U32{w}

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    Unit <- IO.print(Bool.show(below_inf(F32.read("340282356779733661637539395458142568447"))))
    IO.print(U32.show(bits(F32.read("340282356779733661637539395458142568447"))))
```

### Why it happens

The overflow rounding threshold is `2^128 - 2^103`, or `340282356779733661637539395458142568448`. The input is exactly one below that threshold, so a direct decimal-to-binary32 conversion rounds to the largest finite F32, `0x7f7fffff`.

The C runtime performs that direct conversion with `strtof`. The JS runtime first evaluates `Number(s)`. Binary64 cannot retain the one-unit difference at this magnitude, so it rounds the input up to the exact overflow threshold; `Math.fround` then returns infinity.

The same double rounding also occurs away from overflow. For example, `F32.read("0.9999999701976776")` returns `0x3f800000` (`1.0`) on JS and `0x3f7fffff` (the adjacent finite value below `1.0`) on C.

This is distinct from #801: both lanes accept the same grammar here, but assign different finite values to the accepted input. It also does not involve the documented JS limitation around NaN payload bits.

The lanes could agree either by parsing directly to binary32 on JS, or by making C deliberately follow the same binary64-then-binary32 conversion. The former also preserves the correctly rounded result produced by `strtof`.

### bend --version

```text
bend 2.0.27
```

Tested again at `5108d0406b2a1f6f53bc6440b0872930665ae523`.

### uname -sm

```text
Darwin arm64
```

### clang --version (the first line)

```text
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: Emission does less work: lay_of answers a word type before it builds a key, and term_const takes a nullary constructor as constant without a memo
body:
Jesse Nadeau · [@villain_thropic](https://x.com/villain_thropic) on X

Two changes make C and JS emission do less work, and add no state. Nothing else changes: all 1485 programs under `tests/` and `bench/runtime` give byte-identical C and JS, or the same error. This PR is independent of the U64 and F64 PRs (#1057, #1058, #1059).

## What changes

1. **`lay_of` answers a word type first.** It turned each type into a string key (`term_lower` and `JSON.stringify`) before it looked at `WORDS`, which answers U32, F32 and Nat on its own.
2. **`term_const` answers a nullary constructor without its memo.** A leaf has no subtree for a `CONSTS` hit to skip, and on nbody 34,268 of the memo's 70,797 lookups were leaves. The memo stays for constructors with fields, where each hit skips a subtree: without it `term_const` runs 224k times on nbody instead of 84k, and 272k times on raytrace instead of 76k. This change leaves those counts as they were.

## Verification

- **Output:** each program was compiled on both builds and the outputs diffed. 664 emit C and 683 emit JS, byte-identical; the rest stop at the same load or compile error.
- **Emission, 40 compiles in one process** (median of 11): nbody 43.4 → 38.1 ms, raytrace 43.8 → 39.4.

title: U64: 64-bit unsigned words as two U32 halves, a u64 literal, Word(64n) defs for every op and a native on every lane
body:
Jesse Nadeau · [@villain_thropic](https://x.com/villain_thropic) on X

U64 was on the launch's cut list ("U64 and F64 (just U32 and F32 for now)"). This adds it as a Base type whose ops are defs, with a native on every lane. It is independent of #1056; #1058 and #1059 build on it.

## What changes

1. **Representation: `type U64 is Data: U64{lo: U32, hi: U32}`.** A runtime cell holds 48-bit immediates and reads bit 63 (`RFC_BIT`) and the all-ones word (`TERM_HOLE`) as tags, so a U64 never sits in one cell. Its halves travel as two U32 words, flat in registers and as two fields in a node.
2. **Every op is a Base def over `Word(64n)`** (`U64.word` joins the halves, `U64.of` splits them back):
   - add, sub, mul, div (by 0 is 0), mod (by 0 the dividend), not, and, or, xor;
   - shl, shr, shln and shrn (past 63 is 0), inc, cmp and the six predicates, is_zero, min, max, clz, mul_hi;
   - from_nat, to_nat, to_u32, `U32.to_u64`, `Bool.to_u64`, show and read.

   `U64.add_comm` proves commutativity from `Word.add_comm`, as `U32.add_comm` does. Word gains the generic shln, shrn, cat, take, drop, divmod, div, mod, is_zero and clz those defs need.
3. **Natives:** C and CUDA run each op on one u64 (`mul_hi` as `__int128`, `__umul64hi` under NVRTC, `mulhi` on Metal's ulong); JS runs it on a BigInt. `U64.to_nat` fail-stops past 2^48-1, as `Nat.add` does.
4. **Literal:** `NUMBER "u64"` (a new row in bend.ts's grammar table) is `U64{lo, hi}` of two U32 Lits. The checker therefore reduces U64 arithmetic on literals, and a match reads a wide literal pattern. A literal past 2^64-1, with a fraction or with an `n` suffix is a parse error. `term_show` and both printers spell a U64 as that literal.
5. **Compiler:**
   - a native reads each argument in the layout it takes, so a boxed U64 from a generic def is unboxed first (the same fix as #1038);
   - a two-word argument enters a template as one u64, and a two-word result leaves as its halves (`intr_c`);
   - a spin is keyed by its erased arguments' layouts, so `Bool.pick` at U64 passes the halves flat instead of boxing them.

## Kernel

`bend.ts` changes only where a literal is read and shown: the `u64` suffix in `NUMBER`, `parse_term_num`'s branch for it, `term_show`'s sugar and the grammar table's row. The checker itself is untouched.

## Verification

- **Tests (7):** each expected line was computed from exact integers in Python.
  - `base/u64_ops`: every op at 0, 1, 2^32-1, 2^32, 2^63 and 2^64-1.
  - `base/u64_transport`: 2^63, 2^64-1 and tag-shaped words through a record, a pair, a Maybe, a recursion, a fork, an Array get and swap, a closure, a generic pick and a `!` call.
  - `proof/u64_literal_unfolds`: wrapping, `mul_hi` of (2^64-1)², a literal pattern and `add_comm`, checked by the checker.
  - `printer/u64_print`, `parse/u64_literal_overflow`, `check/u64_literal_own_u64` and `run/u64_nat_overflow`.
- **Gates, run locally:** `gates/test.ts`'s probes 1468 / 1469; `gates/repo.ts` 46 / 46. The failure is `io_process_run`'s inherited-pipe case on the Bun lanes, which fails the same way on upstream here.
- **CUDA:** `base/u64_transport` also passes on an RTX 4070 SUPER (NVRTC 12.9).
- **Op grid:** 7 edge values × 23 ops match exact integers on JS, C, CUDA and the interpreter.
- **Size:** `bend.ts` goes from 43761 to 44058 ttok, so `gates/repo.ts` allows 44500; `comp.ts` is 63916 and `base.bend` 28616.
- **Speed:** a run that imports Base checks 275 more lines, so `bend hello.bend` goes from 77.9 to 81.0 ms on x86.
- **Runtime:** with #1058 and #1059 on top, the 16 runtime benches, built and run as the perf gate runs them, give the same output as upstream and time within noise of it: ratios 0.990 to 1.004 on one thread, 0.966 to 1.014 on all (two noisy benches rerun at 11 samples).

## Not done

- **Metal was not run.** The `!` in `base/u64_transport` will be its first run on the gate's minis.
- The cluster gates (test, perf, GPU) were not run.

title: F64: IEEE 754 binary64 as its bits, an f64 literal, every op a Base def in integer arithmetic, a native where the lane has a double, and the same bits on every lane
body:
Jesse Nadeau · [@villain_thropic](https://x.com/villain_thropic) on X

F64 was cut because Metal has no double. Here every F64 op is a Base def that computes IEEE 754 binary64 in integer arithmetic, so Metal runs the defs while C, CUDA and JS run natives, and every lane gives the same bits.

**Builds on #1057.** Until that merges, this diff shows both commits; review the second (F64).

## What changes

1. **`type F64 is Data: F64{bits: U64}`**, with an F64 literal `(NUMBER | F32's) "f64"` that holds its binary64 bits. A literal that rounds to infinity is a parse error.
2. **Every op is a Base def over U64:** add, sub and mul through fma, a restoring divide, a digit-by-digit square root, the six predicates through an order key, and the conversions to and from U64, U32 and F32. The rules:
   - round to nearest even, no flush to zero, fma rounded once;
   - every NaN a result makes is 0x7FF8000000000000, while neg, abs and a move keep a payload;
   - a comparison with a NaN is false, except is_ne;
   - to_u64, to_u32 and to_f32 answer 0 (to_f32 the quiet NaN) for NaN, negatives and overflow.
3. **Natives (comp.ts's `SOFT` table):** C and CUDA run each op on a double, in place under `#ifndef __METAL_VERSION__`, and Metal calls the def. JS runs them on a Number, with an exact fma (a BigInt product and one rounding).
4. **show and read** are laws with a native each, like F32's. show gives the shortest text that reads back; on C, at a power of two, the digit above is tried too.
5. **No sin, exp or log.** A host libm differs across lanes, the same reason F32's min, max and round were left out (WONTFIX entry).

## Verification

- **Tests (6):** each expected line was computed in Python's binary64.
  - `base/f64_ops`: every op and conversion at subnormals, signed zeros, infinities and NaN payloads.
  - `base/f64_transport`: payload NaNs come back untouched through every path.
  - `base/f64_fork`: a `!` fork of fma sums, which is Metal's soft float on the gate's Macs.
  - `proof/f64_literal_unfolds`: `F64.bits(F64{x}) == x` for every x, neg twice, and `1.0 + 2.0 == 3.0` through the soft float, checked by the checker.
  - `printer/f64_print` and `parse/f64_literal_overflow`.
- **Gates, run locally:** `gates/test.ts`'s probes 1474 / 1475; `gates/repo.ts` 46 / 46. The failure is `io_process_run`'s inherited-pipe case on the Bun lanes, which fails the same way on upstream here.
- **Differential:** 22 op groups × 2^14 generated cases, bit-exact with a numpy/Fraction oracle on JS, C, CUDA, CUDA running the defs (Metal's path), C running the defs, and the interpreter at 2^2. The groups cover sums, fused sums, cancellation, products, quotients, square roots, the predicates, every conversion and the U64 ops.
- **Metal visibility:** evaluating the emitted C's `#if` tree with `__METAL_VERSION__` keeps no double-precision line.
- **Show:** the JS show matches the shortest round-trip rule on 2,003,689 doubles. The C text routine prints all 2^32 F32 bit patterns exactly as upstream's does.
- **Size:** `bend.ts` is 44376 ttok, `comp.ts` 65510 and `base.bend` 33120, so `gates/repo.ts` allows 66000 and 33500. With #1059 as well, `base.bend` is 31939, under the old 32000.
- **Speed:** a run that imports Base loads and checks 281 more lines and collects once more, so `bend hello.bend` goes from 81.0 to 88.6 ms on x86 (upstream 77.9).
- **Runtime:** with #1059 on top, the 16 runtime benches, built and run as the perf gate runs them, give the same output as upstream and time within noise of it: ratios 0.990 to 1.004 on one thread, 0.966 to 1.014 on all (two noisy benches rerun at 11 samples).

- The cluster gates (test, perf, GPU) were not run.

title: JS F32.pow returns NaN for 1.0 ^ infinity while C returns 1.0
body:
### What I did

I raised `1.0` to positive infinity and observed both the comparison result and the raw F32 bits.

```bend
import Base

def main.out() -> String:
  inf = F32.div(1.0, 0.0)
  +x = {F32.pow(1.0, inf) : F32}
  Bool.show(F32.is_eq(x, 1.0)) ++ " " ++ U32.show(F32.bits(x))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(main.out())
```

```text
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend --check-only
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend -o out.js
bun out.js
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend -o out
./out
```

### What happened

The program checks successfully, but the two backends take opposite answers to `F32.is_eq(x, 1.0)`:

```text
$ bun out.js
False 2143289344

$ ./out
True 1065353216
```

`2143289344` is `0x7fc00000`, a quiet NaN. `1065353216` is `0x3f800000`, exactly `1.0`. The same divergence occurs for all four combinations `F32.pow(1.0, ±infinity)` and `F32.pow(-1.0, ±infinity)`.

This changes program control flow, rather than only the spelling or payload of a NaN: a branch on equality with `1.0` selects opposite arms in JS and C.

### Why it happens

The emitter maps the operation directly to the hosts:

```ts
...tpl_ops("f32_", "pow atan2",
  "f32_rewrap((f32)$o(f32_unbox($0), f32_unbox($1)))",
  "Math.fround(Math.$o($0, $1))"),
```

JavaScript's `Math.pow` has a historical special case where a base whose magnitude is exactly 1 and an infinite exponent produces NaN. C `pow` returns 1 for those inputs. `Math.fround` preserves the semantic difference, so Bend inherits two different definitions of the same primitive.

This is also the kind of host special-value discrepancy the runtime already normalizes: the adjacent `atan2_c99` shim changes Metal's NaN at the origin to the libm result. `pow` currently has no equivalent normalization.

I also compared one million random pairs plus the special values across the extracted C and JS implementations. `atan2` and `mod` agreed throughout; `pow` differed on precisely these four special-value combinations.

### Prior work

Closed, unmerged PR #929 contained an exact normalization for this discrepancy in its larger proposed math runtime: it returned `1` for `x === 1`, and also for `x === -1` with an infinite exponent, before calling `Math.pow`. The helper is not present on `main`, and the open F32 PR #1046 only adds `F32.fma`.

### Expected

`F32.pow` should have one backend-independent result for these inputs. If C's result is the intended one, the JS implementation can special-case `abs(base) == 1 && exponent is infinite` before calling `Math.pow`.

### Environment

```text
bend 2.0.27
commit 5108d0406b2a1f6f53bc6440b0872930665ae523
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: The JS lane loops tail cycles and calls every def directly (on top of #1043)
body:
Builds on #1043 by @MattCozendey, which carries #1040 and #974. It contains #1043's six commits unchanged, plus commits on top that keep its tail loops and remove most of the machinery around them. It supersedes #1040.

## What changes relative to #1043

- **No new fields on `Src` or `File`.** A def's tail loop comes from `loop_of(cb, k)`, a Tarjan search over tail callees (self calls included), memoized in a `LOOPS` cache that is declared and cleared with the other per-book caches. `carb_book` no longer records `tails`, and `plain_of`, `Src.plain`, `Src.loop` and `File.loop` are gone.
  - `fl.seg.def` names the def being emitted, as it does in C. A tail call into that def's loop continues it; a closure's segment has no def, so its tail calls never do.
  - A self loop is just a loop of one, so `js_def`'s second walk looking for self tail calls is gone.
- **One loop shape.** A looping def is its own function, `let $pc = <its case>; for (;;) switch ($pc)`, so there are no entry functions and no self-loop special case. Each member of a mutual cycle gets its own copy of the loop; cycles have at most three members.
- **No plainness.** Every tail call into a def is a direct JS call.
  - This is safe because tail cycles run as loops: a direct tail call can only get back to its caller through a closure, and a closure's `run_tail` still bounces on the trampoline.
  - `run_jump` and the plainness fixpoint are gone. A non-tail call still goes through `run_loop`.
- **Only `Nat.min` and `Nat.max` stay as intrinsics, on both lanes,** as one `tpl_ops` row. Base defines them in unary (`1n+Nat.min(ap, bp)`), so as written they recurse min(a, b) deep and overflow the stack on large Nats.
  - The other selectors are now cheap direct calls, and their C side measured nothing, because clang already inlines the Base definitions. They're removed along with `tests/base/selector_intrinsics.bend`.
  - `tests/run/unsafe_law_tail_cycle.bend` repeated `unsafe_tail_cycle.bend`, so it's removed too.

Against current `main` (rebased on `db84f207`), `comp.ts` changes by +62 −11 lines and +627 ttok (62,808 → 63,435, under the 64,000 cap); #1043 added +127 −15 against its base.

## Measurements

JS lane, M-series Mac, hyperfine, 15 runs, in ms:

| workload | #1043 (bun) | this (bun) | #1043 (node) | this (node) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| three-def tail cycle, different arities, 10M steps | 175 | 176 | 86 | 86 |
| two-def mutual tail recursion, 30M steps | 282 | 282 | 131 | 131 |
| a wrapper tail-calling a self loop, 3M calls | 137 | 148 | 75 | 77 |
| fib 32 through a helper | 152 | 157 | 66 | 68 |
| a closure bounce, 3M steps | 263 | **118** | 144 | **93** |
| list build and sum, 3M | 148 | 149 | 112 | 112 |
| `bench/runtime/hashmap` | 5303 | 5296 | | |

`fib` is about 3% slower because its non-tail calls keep `run_loop`, and `wrapper` about 7% slower under bun because each short self loop now sets up `$pc` and a `switch` (node: within about 3%). `bounce` is 1.5–2.2× faster because a tail call into a def that bounces a closure no longer goes through the trampoline.

## Verification

- Every runnable test, demo and runtime bench, built to JS and run under bun: the same output as #1043, apart from the two removed tests.
- Emitted C is byte-identical to `main`'s, except `tests/base/nat_ops` and `tests/base/num_kit`, which call `Nat.min`/`Nat.max`; both pass on C.
- Stress programs at 10⁶ steps (continuation-passing, a def/closure ping-pong, `List.foldl`, a recursive `IO` loop) run on the JS lane.
- `gates/repo.ts`: 46/46. `tsc`: the 4 existing errors, none in `comp.ts`.
- Merges cleanly into current `main`.

Not done: the cluster, perf and GPU gates. SSH to the nodes is refused from this machine.

title: F32.pow(1, y) and F32.pow(±1, ±Infinity) are 1 on JS, as on C
body:
Math.pow returns NaN for `1` raised to NaN and for `±1` raised to `±Infinity`. libm `pow` returns 1, so `F32.is_eq` of that result took opposite branches on the JS and C lanes (#1060). `pow(-1, NaN)` stays NaN on both, and `pow(-1, 3)` stays `-1`.

The JS lane calls `f32_pow`, which returns 1 for those inputs and otherwise `Math.fround(Math.pow(...))`. The C lane is still libm `pow`.

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/reg/f32_pow_one_inf.bend` checks, and the interpreter, the emitted JS, and the C binary print the same line: the four infinities, `pow(1, NaN)`, `pow(-1, 3)`, and `pow(-1, NaN)`
- [x] `tests/run/float_ops.bend` still prints `1.5 -1.25 1024 0.7853982 1.5707964 0 0.7853982 3 7` on the interpreter and the C binary
- [x] `tests/run/float_specials.bend` still prints `12` on the interpreter, JS, and C
- [x] A grid of the other specials (zeros, `±inf`, NaN bases, `pow(2, ±inf)`, `pow(0.5, ±inf)`, `pow(-1, 2)`, `pow(-2, inf)`) is identical on JS and C
- [ ] Cluster gate (`gates/test.ts`)

Closes #1060.

title: Non-inferrable errors drop the term echo; locations underline their span
body:
Five commits:

**1. A non-inferrable term's observed reads "non-inferrable term"** (38cb7dbc)

`typeless_show` goes. The four check sites with no type for the observed slot (a lambda, a match, `{==}`, an undeclared constructor against a goal of the wrong shape) pass the fixed text `non-inferrable term` instead of echoing the term. The "X is a datatype: write its arguments as <>" hint on a Ctr naming a datatype moves to the error's `Note:`. Four golds change.

**2. An error's location underlines its span** (66ecce0a)

The echo was the only thing that pinpointed the subterm, since the location marks a line, not a column. `err_show` now adds a caret line under the marked line, from the span's first column to its end, clipped to that line (one `^` for an empty span; tabs in the prefix are kept so it lines up):

```
Location: t
4 |
5>| def t(b: Bool) -> Maybe{&2, Bool}:
  |                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
6 |   match b:
```

Every gold with a location gains its caret line and nothing else (verified by script: removing the caret lines gives back the old gold). `parse/do_bind_continuation`, whose error points past its own last line, renumbers to its new length.

**3. A constructor that misses its goal throws once** (437c4200)

The Ctr site's two throws become one, and `err_show`'s line-number width is `num`, so it no longer shadows the context's `wid`.

**4. A parse error on a token it has read underlines that token** (74bd10d1)

`parse_fail` marked a zero-width span at the parser's position, which for an error raised after reading a token is the column past it (`law law⟦ ⟧: Type`, `law main⟦:⟧`, `case Zw{}, x, Zw{}:⟦⟧`). It now takes the token's start (and, for a case's patterns, its end), and shows the token as observed:

```
6>| law law : Type
  |     ^^^
```

This covers a keyword used as a name, a duplicate declaration or field, a bad dotted name, a u32 literal past 4294967295, a keyword heading a term, and a case with the wrong number of patterns. 42 golds change only in their observed and caret lines.

**5. `err_show` takes the caret's column from the prefix it already splits** (1bd0d9b3)

The text left of the span on its line is the last piece of the split that counts the line, so `parse_col` and three locals go. Output is byte-identical.

In total, `bend2/bend.ts` grows by 123 ttok (43761 → 43884, cap 44000).

Notes for review:
- A lambda's span is its binder (`Lam(x.k, x.i, f, x.s, x.q)` in the parser), so `x => add_zero(x)` underlines only `x`. Left as is since binder errors rely on it.
- A multi-line span underlines only its first line.
- This touches ~475 golds, so open PRs that add error tests will need their golds regenerated.
- `bend2/bend.ts` is edited, which AGENTS.md reserves for humans; flagging it.

Testing: the 481 error-expecting tests run locally through `bend2/main.ts` pass 478/481 after all four commits, same as main; the other 982 tests still pass `--check-only` (the 3 misses are IO tests whose errors come from the compile lane, which the local runner doesn't run). `tsc` shows the same 4 pre-existing errors as main. The cluster gate hasn't been run.

title: WSL2 NVIDIA: ! build cannot find -lcuda; a present unsupported GPU is reported as missing and fallback is silent
body:
## What you did

From a clean archive of current `main` commit `47bed75adedd6d6dd811721905f06569bf465f85`, on WSL2 with CUDA 13.1/NVRTC installed:

```sh
$HOME/.bun/bin/bun bend2/main.ts smoke.bend -o smoke
```

Then, as a diagnostic workaround only:

```sh
LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/lib/wsl/lib \
  $HOME/.bun/bin/bun bend2/main.ts smoke.bend -o smoke

./smoke --threads 2
./smoke --gpu on --threads 2
./smoke --gpu 512MB --threads 2
./smoke --gpu off --threads 2
```

## What happened

The default build fails:

```text
/usr/bin/x86_64-linux-gnu-ld.bfd: cannot find -lcuda: No such file or directory
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation)
Error: clang failed to build smoke
```

WSL exposes the driver library at `/usr/lib/wsl/lib/libcuda.so`, but `cli_build` only passes the CUDA toolkit's `lib64` and `lib` directories. Supplying `LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/lib/wsl/lib` makes the exact same build succeed.

The linked binary then behaves as follows:

```text
$ ./smoke --threads 2
65536

$ ./smoke --gpu on --threads 2
bend: --gpu on, but this binary found no GPU device

$ ./smoke --gpu 512MB --threads 2
bend: --gpu on, but this binary found no GPU device

$ ./smoke --gpu off --threads 2
65536
```

There is a CUDA device. A Driver API capability probe reports:

```text
name                                      NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090
CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_MANAGED_MEMORY        1
CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_CONCURRENT_MANAGED_ACCESS 0
```

The current `gpu_probe` folds initialization, device discovery, the required managed-memory capability, context setup and success into one Boolean. Refusing this GPU is correct for the current shared-corpus CUDA runtime; reporting that no device exists is not. The default run also silently executes the marked call on CPU, making it difficult to know that requested GPU work never used the GPU.

Requested fixes:

1. On WSL, add `/usr/lib/wsl/lib` to the link search when `libcuda.so` exists (or use the toolkit stub for link-time only).
2. Preserve the probe failure reason and distinguish no driver, no device, no managed memory, no concurrent managed access, and context failure.
3. When a binary with reachable `!` calls falls back because a present GPU lacks a required capability, print a clear one-time note, or provide an explicit status/diagnostic mode.

This is current on `47bed75`; older Bend 1 WSL issues were closed during the Bend 2 repository transition and do not cover this runtime.

## The file

```python
import Base

def pow2(+n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      1
    case 1n+p:
      a b = pow2(p) pow2(p)
      (a + b : U32)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(pow2!(16n)))
```

## bend --version

The current source prints `bend 2.0.27` via `bend version`; commit tested: `47bed75adedd6d6dd811721905f06569bf465f85`.

## uname -sm

`Linux x86_64` — Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL2, kernel `6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2`, RTX 5090, Windows NVIDIA driver 610.62, CUDA toolkit 13.1.

## clang --version (first line)

`Ubuntu clang version 21.1.8 (6ubuntu1)`

title: A parallel host phase makes later ! calls silently run on CPU instead of GPU
body:
## What you did

I ran two semantically identical programs through the CUDA lane. Both contain three marked calls:

```python
t0 = gen!(16n, 1)
t1 = bump(t0)
t2 = flip!(t1)
IO.print(U32.show(sum!(t2)))
```

The only difference is the unmarked host `bump` implementation.

Sequential control:

```python
def bump(t: Tr) -> Tr:
  match t:
    case Lf{v}:
      Lf{U32.inc(v)}
    case Nd{l, r}:
      x = bump(l)
      y = bump(r)
      Nd{x, y}
```

Parallel host phase:

```python
def bump(t: Tr) -> Tr:
  match t:
    case Lf{v}:
      Lf{U32.inc(v)}
    case Nd{l, r}:
      x y = bump(l) bump(r)
      Nd{x, y}
```

The CUDA test backend increments a counter immediately around the existing `corpus_eval` GPU seam; it does not change which calls are dispatched. I ran each binary with `--threads 2 --gpu 512MB` and required the GPU banner plus exact CPU/GPU output.

## What happened

Both CPU programs print the same value:

```text
3841805111
```

The sequential-host control reaches all three marked GPU calls:

```text
bend: gpu twin: 3 turns, 0.039 s in turns, 0.037 s copying 160.7 MB
```

The parallel-host variant reaches only the first marked call:

```text
bend: gpu twin: 1 turns, 0.019 s in turns, 0.018 s copying 32.4 MB
```

It still exits 0 and prints `3841805111`; the later two marked calls silently execute on CPU.

This reproduces on NVIDIA CUDA the observation recorded in #891's HIP work: after the host pool has forked, a later `!` can stay on the CPU; a sequential host phase does not trigger it.

The live CUDA reproduction used upstream commit `b7ebee9217c8813067e200b0c0c9153a3be31c5e` with the corpus-storage twin patch. That patch wraps the existing GPU seam to copy the corpus and count turns; the dispatch decision remains upstream's `io_gpu && fid_bangs(...)` branch.

I also inspected current `main` at `47bed75adedd6d6dd811721905f06569bf465f85`. The surrounding code has evolved, so I am not claiming a live current-main reproduction, but the same mechanism remains: `corpus_eval` recognizes a marked task on the main thread, while `pool_open()` starts persistent workers and `cube_run(H, false)` hands host work to them.

Expected behavior: each reachable `!` call uses the selected GPU lane, independent of whether an earlier unmarked host phase used parallel CPU workers. If a marked call cannot migrate back to the GPU seam, the runtime should at minimum report that it fell back rather than silently changing lanes.

A likely place to investigate is the ownership/routing of tasks produced by `task_deal` after `pool_open`: worker threads drain rings directly, while the GPU-dispatch test lives only in the main-thread `corpus_eval` loop.

## Complete file

```python
import Base

type Tr is Data:
  Lf{v: U32}
  Nd{l: Tr, r: Tr}

def gen(+n: Nat, +x: U32) -> Tr:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      Lf{x}
    case 1n+p:
      l r = gen(p, U32.shl(x)) gen(p, U32.inc(U32.shl(x)))
      Nd{l, r}

def bump(t: Tr) -> Tr:
  match t:
    case Lf{v}:
      Lf{U32.inc(v)}
    case Nd{l, r}:
      x y = bump(l) bump(r)
      Nd{x, y}

def flip(t: Tr) -> Tr:
  match t:
    case Lf{v}:
      Lf{v}
    case Nd{l, r}:
      x y = flip(l) flip(r)
      Nd{y, x}

def sum(t: Tr) -> U32:
  match t:
    case Lf{v}:
      v
    case Nd{l, r}:
      x y = sum(l) sum(r)
      U32.add(U32.xor(U32.mul(x, 2654435761), y), 7)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  t0 = gen!(16n, 1)
  t1 = bump(t0)
  t2 = flip!(t1)
  IO.print(U32.show(sum!(t2)))
```

For the sequential control, replace `x y = bump(l) bump(r)` with the two sequential assignments shown above.

## Environment

- Bend source under test: `b7ebee9217c8813067e200b0c0c9153a3be31c5e`
- Current main inspected: `47bed75adedd6d6dd811721905f06569bf465f85`
- Linux x86_64, Ubuntu 26.04 / WSL2
- RTX 5090, driver 610.62, CUDA 13.1, clang 21.1.8

title: CUDA needs a maintained device-resident corpus path for dynamic CPU/GPU programs on WSL2
body:
## What Bend should do

Add a maintained CUDA memory mode for devices where managed memory exists but `CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_CONCURRENT_MANAGED_ACCESS == 0` notably NVIDIA CUDA under WSL2 that keeps the Bend corpus in VRAM and synchronizes only state the host actually reads or writes.

The goal is not to optimize selected benchmark winners. It is to make long-lived, dynamic Bend programs viable when they repeatedly alternate:

```python
host mutates a device-built graph
-> ! device rewrite/fold
-> host consumes and rebuilds parts
-> ! again
```

A production design should preserve normal Bend semantics across arbitrary repeated CPU/GPU seams and should avoid copying every potentially live word at each `!` boundary. Possible implementations include explicit dirty chunks/pages, generated write barriers, or another upstream-owned ownership protocol. If demand paging is used, CUDA calls should run on a helper thread rather than directly from a SIGSEGV handler.

This request is specifically for the existing NVIDIA CUDA lane. It complements #891: that issue proved the device-corpus and dirty-chunk approach on AMD/HIP, but was declined for `main` because the team lacked AMD hardware. The same architectural limitation and solution have now been independently reproduced on an RTX 5090 through CUDA.

## Why

Stock Bend's CUDA runtime requires concurrent managed access. WSL2 reports:

```text
CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_MANAGED_MEMORY             1
CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_CONCURRENT_MANAGED_ACCESS  0
```

So stock Bend refuses the device and silently runs `!` on CPU unless GPU use is forced, in which case it reports no device. A serialized host-attached managed-memory mode is semantically workable but not useful: on 11 of 16 upstream runtime benchmarks it was 45x to 547x slower than CPU-16 because kernels read host memory over the WSL/PCIe path.

I then implemented a research-only CUDA twin on upstream commit `b7ebee9217c8813067e200b0c0c9153a3be31c5e`:

- keep the normal host corpus;
- allocate an equal corpus in VRAM with `cuMemAlloc`;
- copy the header, live ring slots/counters, static image, heap under the bump and live bank entries up before each `!` turn;
- run every pass against the VRAM pointer;
- copy the same regions down after the turn.

This is an intentionally simple eager implementation, not a proposed production patch. It establishes that WSL can fully execute Bend's CUDA kernels when the corpus is actually in VRAM:

- all 16 `bench/runtime` outputs matched CPU/pinned outputs;
- GPU beat CPU-16 on 9/16 cases;
- strongest measured wins were gameoflife 3.20x, nbody 2.69x and mandelbrot 2.27x;
- geometric mean was still about 10% slower than CPU-16 because eager synchronization dominates dynamic/irregular cases.

The decisive dynamic test was a single process with ten `!` turns. A depth-16 tree alternated between a host-only sequential rebuild (every node replaced, including reused heap slots) and a device mirror (every node rewritten), followed by a marked fold. CPU and GPU both printed:

```text
854543159
```

The CUDA statistics were:

```text
10 turns, 0.092 s in turns, 0.089 s copying 610.3 MB
```

So **96.7% of GPU-turn time was synchronization**, not computation. Whole execution was 0.227 s versus 0.006 s for the already-built CPU binary. This is the real dynamic workload problem: adding more kernels or tuning launch geometry cannot recover time spent copying mutable runtime state at every boundary.

Additional bounded experiments:

- A three-turn merkle run moved 691.3 MB and spent 147 of 155 ms of turn time copying (~95%).
- Fully pinned transfers were much faster, but registering 768 MB cost about 190 ms and `cuMemHostAlloc(768MB)` cost about 318 ms; a short dynamic process cannot amortize either.
- Lazy registration halved copy time but paid ~47 ms registration inside the turns and did not beat the eager best.
- Adjacent host registrations do not merge for a transfer whose first page is pinned under this WSL/DXG driver; boundary-sensitive schemes failed with `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE`.
- Skipping heap download is unsound: host evaluation writes freed/reused words (`TERM_HOLE`, allocator updates) below the old bump.
- Ring data was already contiguous; merging copy ranges did not reduce bytes.
- The `.gpu` module is a cubin/fatbin, so load-time PTX JIT was not the missing cost.

#891's later dirty-chunk HIP result is the important positive evidence: reducing tree-radix from 3.7 GB copied to 17 MB turned several losses into wins and supported repeated host mutation. Its author also identified the production concern: calling HIP copy APIs directly in a SIGSEGV handler is not POSIX-safe; a helper-thread design is the clean version.

What I am asking upstream to own is the abstraction boundary, not this local twin:

1. A device-resident corpus mode in the CUDA lane for non-concurrent managed-memory devices.
2. Correct repeated host/device mutation, including frees/reuse below the bump and multiple `!` turns in one process.
3. Dirty-range synchronization or another mechanism whose cost scales with host-touched state, not the whole live heap.
4. Explicit diagnostics/telemetry for lane selection and transfer volume, so silent CPU fallback and copy-bound execution are visible.
5. Tests with dynamic graph/tree mutation around multiple `!` calls, not only one-shot static kernels.

Without this, WSL users can either get silent CPU execution, catastrophically slow host-backed kernels, or maintain a large out-of-tree copying runtime. The last option is what we tested and are deliberately stopping: it proves the need, but it is too complex and too eager to be the solution.

## Environment and evidence scope

- RTX 5090 (sm_120), NVIDIA driver 610.62
- Ubuntu 26.04 / WSL2, kernel 6.18.33.2-microsoft-standard-WSL2
- CUDA 13.1 / NVRTC 13.1.115, clang 21.1.8
- CUDA twin source base: `b7ebee9217c8813067e200b0c0c9153a3be31c5e`
- Current upstream `main` inspected: `47bed75adedd6d6dd811721905f06569bf465f85`
- Every GPU attempt was serialized, heap-capped, timeout-bounded, and checked against CPU output; VRAM returned to 0 MiB after runs.

title: C emission references an undeclared constructor ID when a pure main exposes a datatype through a generic family field
body:
### What I did

I returned a generic record from a pure `main`. The record's field type is a family that reduces to a user datatype at this instantiation.

```bend
import Base

type Inner is Data:
  Inner{a: U32, b: U32}

def Pick(b: Bool) -> Data:
  match b:
    case False{}:
      U32
    case True{}:
      Inner

type Box<-b: Bool> is Data:
  Box{value: Pick(b)}

def main() -> Box<True{}>:
  Box{Inner{1, 2}}
```

```text
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend -o out.js
bun out.js
bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend -o out.c
clang -std=c11 -O2 out.c -lpthread -lm -o out
```

### What happened

The evaluator and emitted JS both accept the program and print the expected value:

```text
Box{Inner{1, 2}}
```

Emitting C also exits successfully, but the generated source does not compile:

```text
out.c:409:79: error: use of undeclared identifier 'CID_INNER'
  409 | static const u32 SHOW_DESC[] = { ..., CID_INNER, ... };
      |                                       ^
1 error generated.
```

The generated declarations contain `#define CID_BOX 13`, but no definition for `CID_INNER`.

The same failure occurs when `Inner` has multiple constructors: `SHOW_DESC` references every hidden arm's CID, while none of those CID macros are declared.

### Why it happens

`compile_book` computes the compiler reachability set before building the pure-main display descriptor. The generic `Box` field is seen as `Pick(b)` during reachability, so the concrete `Inner` datatype is not included among the constructors whose C IDs are emitted. `show_main` later reduces the concrete result type `Box<True{}>`, discovers `Inner`, and writes `CID_INNER` into `SHOW_DESC` anyway.

A direct `Inner` field makes the failure disappear because that separately roots its constructor ID. The failure therefore comes from disagreement between compilation reachability and the concrete type traversal used by `show_main`, rather than from the value itself.

### Expected

A C file emitted successfully for an accepted program should compile and print the same `Box{Inner{1, 2}}` value as the evaluator and JS backend. Constructors referenced by the pure-main descriptor need to be included in the emitted CID table, including constructors reached only after reducing a family at a generic instantiation.

### Environment

```text
bend 2.0.27
commit 47bed75adedd6d6dd811721905f06569bf465f85
Bun 1.4.2
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: A constructor of any width builds on C: term_drop walks a node past 247 words as an array
body:
Closes #991. Supersedes #1044.

## Why

A record of 256 one-word fields is checked, interpreted and run on JS, but the C build refuses it with `an arity over 255`. The limit comes from `term_drop`, not from the language. It frees a tree without a stack, and for each node it packs the position (40 bits), child index (8), arity (8) and size class (8) into one word. #944's `lay_wide` and #1044 both work around that packing in the compiler.

The same walker already frees arrays of any size. It takes an array's cell count from its size class and keeps the running index in the node's own slot 1, which has already been visited. This PR lets wide constructors use that path.

## What changes (`bend2/comp.ts`, +20 / −16)

- **`CID_ARITY_T` stays `u8`.** A constructor past 247 words stores `240 + log2` of its node size there (8 to 15, so up to 32,768 words). Only `term_drop` and `io_exec` read the table, and effect nodes are small.
- **`term_drop`: one line.** An entry past 247 takes the array walk at that size class.
- **`lay_node`:** a node past 247 words is padded to its size class. Construction already writes `0` to every word of a constructor it doesn't fill, so the tail comes out zero with no extra code.
- **`WIDE` becomes 247,** for flat layouts and segments, so only a constructor's entry can pass it. That keeps the check in `term_drop` a single comparison. A value past `WIDE` words travels boxed (`lay_of`).
- **`lay_wide` is gone.** It boxed a datatype's multi-word fields only to keep its node under 255 words. Its one remaining use, a def's parameters (#944), is inlined in `sig_def`. The emitted C for every `tests/compile` program, the wide-record tests and the benches is byte-identical before and after that inline.

A program without such a node emits the same C as `main`, apart from that one line in `term_drop`, and its tables are identical.

## Tests and docs

- `tests/reg/wide_record_drop` comes from #1044 (thanks @oxura). It drops six unopened 256-field records, then builds six 300-field ones. Its header is updated for this design. #1044's `record_256_fields` isn't included: its literal record folds away, so its C never built a wide node.
- `tests/reg/wide_record_stale` (new): 250-field nodes, padded to 256 words, are built in blocks that still hold `String` pointers from opened 256-field records, then dropped unopened. If the padding isn't written as zero, C prints `77777!/77777!77777!/7` instead of `777777!/7/77`.
- Updated headers: `arity_wall` (a 255-field record now travels boxed), `record_wide_node` (`R2` is now one 512-word node) and `record_deep_boxed` (the 512-word level is one box).
- `guide/SHADERS.md`: a def or continuation now takes at most 247 words.

## Verification (macOS, Apple M4)

- **Wide records:** these agree in the interpreter, JS and C: records of 256, 512 and 520 fields; multi-word fields mixed with a run of 260 one-word fields; a sum type with a 300-field arm; wide records inside `Maybe` and `List`; a pure `main` printing a 258-field record.
- **Local test gate** (`gates/test.ts`'s shard script run in a local bash): 1464 / 1467. The failures are the two `gfx` tests that need a machine without a display, and one timing test whose sleeps 5108d040 shortened (`io_spawn_sleep` in one run, `io_fork_join` in another), which passes 10 / 10 when run alone.
- **`bun gates/repo.ts`:** 46 / 46. `comp.ts` grows by 58 ttok.
- **Runtime benches, 16 × SEQ-CPU / PAR-CPU / PAR-GPU against `main`, alternating runs:** within ±2.5%, with the same outputs.
  - editdist is about 20% faster, from code layout.
  - lexer SEQ-CPU is +2.6% in the default build and identical with `-falign-functions=64 -falign-loops=64`.
  - A program that only builds and frees 2²¹-leaf trees is within 0.995–1.014.
- **Cluster gates:** not run. This machine's key is refused by the minis.

## Limits

- **Segments:** a function or continuation that keeps more than 247 one-word values live across a call still fails to compile. The cap drops from 255 to 247. That limit belongs to the register bank and the C calling convention: raising it made clang crash. That's tracked in #1069.
- **Constructor size:** a single constructor wider than 32,768 words fails to compile.

title: C backend: a segment with more than 247 live one-word values fails to compile
body:
## Behavior

The checker, interpreter and JS accept a program in which a function or continuation keeps more than `WIDE` one-word values live across a call. The C build refuses it with `an arity over 247` (`an arity over 255` before #1068). Example: a record of 300 `String` fields where each field is built with a call.

```bend
import Base

type R is Data:
  Mk{f0: String, f1: String, ..., f299: String}

def mk(+s: String) -> R:
  Mk{(s ++ "0"), (s ++ "1"), ..., (s ++ "299")}
```

Each `++` is a call, so the continuation after the *k*-th field (`mk$k265` to `mk$k300`) carries every field built so far as a parameter, up to 300 words. `FID_ARITY_T` passes `WIDE` and the build stops.

## Why the limit is real

This isn't the node limit fixed in #1068. A segment's parameters live in the register bank and are passed through `preserve_none` / `musttail` calls. With the table check lifted, clang 21 crashes on this program at every optimization level:

```text
fatal error: error in backend: live register clobbered by inserted prologue instructions
```

#944 handles part of this: a def whose parameters span past `WIDE` words takes its multi-word parameters boxed. But one-word live values have nothing to box, the same gap #991 had for constructor fields.

## Possible direction

When a segment's live set is still past `WIDE` words after multi-word values are boxed, spill a run of the one-word values into a boxed tuple, and read them back in the continuation.

Found while reviewing #1044, with the reproducer run on the interpreter (correct), JS (correct) and C (refused).

title: A path with no suffix imports a folder: every .bend file right in it, under one alias
body:
`import ./lib as L` now loads every `.bend` file directly inside `lib/` under the one alias `L`. Subfolders of `lib/` are not loaded.

```python
import Base
import ./folder as F        # folder/sq.bend, folder/dbl.bend; folder/deep/ is not read

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(Nat.show(F.dbl(F.sq(3n))))   # 18
```

## Behavior
- An import path with no suffix names a folder. The folder's `.bend` files load in sorted order, each under its usual namespace (`lib/a`, `lib/b`). A path with any other suffix is still refused before the file system is read. The error message is now `an import of a .bend file, or of a folder`.
- `L.x` resolves to the one file in the folder that declares `x`. If two files declare `x`, it is refused where it is used: `an unambiguous name (L.x is declared by more than one file of the folder L)`. Filling a law as `def L.name(..)` resolves the same way.
- If a folder has no `.bend` file directly in it, the import is refused with `a folder with .bend files in it`.
- `--checkup` checks a folder import one file at a time. Before this change it failed with `EISDIR`.
- Hub paths (`0x<hash>/dir`) go through the same code, and `--publish` needs no change: it already publishes every file the loader read.

## ⚠️ This edits `bend2/bend.ts`
AGENTS.md says `bend.ts` is human-written and should not be edited. The import loader (`book_load`) and alias resolution (`parse_reso`) both live there, so this feature can't be built anywhere else. The edit is small:
- the `Parse.al` alias map changes from `Record<Name, Name>` to `Record<Name, Name[]>`
- the folder branch in `book_load`
- choosing among the folder's namespaces in `parse_reso`

Please review it with that in mind.

## Other changes
- `gates/repo.ts`: test fixtures may now sit two folders deep (`tests/<ns>/<dir>/<dir>/x.bend`). The tests need this to show that a subfolder is not loaded.
- `guide/GUIDE.md`: one paragraph in Modules and one line in the syntax reference.
- New tests: `tests/import/folder_import.bend` (loads the folder; `folder/deep/sq.bend` would fail the check if it were loaded), `folder_clash.bend` and `folder_sub.bend`. Three existing goldens pick up the new wording of the suffix error.

## Testing
- All of `tests/import/*.bend` match their goldens locally.
- Across all 1467 tests, the checker/interpreter results on this branch match `main`. Both have the same set of local failures (lanes this Mac can't run). `io/spawn_sleep` failed once under 8 parallel jobs and passed 3 of 3 alone.
- `folder_import` prints `18` through the interpreter, the C binary and the JS build.
- `tsc`: the same 4 errors as on `main`, none new.
- I haven't run the cluster gates (`gates/test.ts`, `gates/repo.ts`) or measured the ttok caps (`ttok` isn't installed here).

title: Conversion checking normalizes before comparing, so identical large terms overflow the stack
body:
### What happens

The checker cannot confirm that a closed term equals an identical copy of itself when the term is large:

```bend
import Base

def p() -> {U32.to_nat(1073741824) == U32.to_nat(1073741824) : Nat}:
  {==}
```

```text
$ bend p.bend --check-only
Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)
```

The same happens when both sides apply the same function to the same argument:

```bend
import Base

def w(x: Nat) -> Nat:
  Nat.add(x, 0n)

def q() -> {w(U32.to_nat(1073741824)) == Nat.add(U32.to_nat(1073741824), 0n) : Nat}:
  {==}
```

Both files are valid and both fail within a second (bend 2.0.25).

### Why

`term_compare` skips work only when the two sides are the same object. Otherwise it puts both sides in weak head normal form and compares the results. Here that means expanding 2^30 into `Succ` nodes on each side and comparing them one by one, even though the two sides are the same term before any reduction.

### Suggestion

Before normalizing, try the cheap checks that conversion checkers usually try first:

1. If the two sides are syntactically identical (no unfolding), they are equal.
2. If both sides apply the same definition, compare the arguments; if they match, the applications are equal without unfolding the definition.
3. If the heads differ and one of them is a plain wrapper definition (its body is another call), unfold it one step and retry.

Each check only ever answers "equal", and each such answer is a valid conversion step. When a check does not apply, the checker falls back to what it does today. So the set of accepted programs stays the same; only the resource failures above go away. I tried this on a large proof development and it also made checking 2-4x faster overall.

title: Window.grab holds the cursor for a first-person camera, and the mouse's motion comes as Look{dx, dy} (#921)
body:
Closes #921.

A first-person camera needs the mouse's motion, not the cursor's position: today `Move{x, y}` is clipped to the window, so turning stops at its edge.

## The change

- **`Event` gains `Look{dx: F32, dy: F32}`.** It is signed and in `Move`'s units. `Move` keeps meaning a position rather than switching to a delta in a hidden mode, and `U32` could not carry a negative delta anyway.
- **`Window.grab(window, on: Bool) -> IO(Window)`**, the same shape as `Window.set_title`. While a window is grabbed, the cursor is hidden and held, and motion comes as `Look` instead of `Move`.
- **Releasing:** a grab ends on `Window.grab(w, False{})`, on closing the window, or when the window loses focus (Cmd-Tab, alt-tab), so a user is never left without a cursor. Whether Esc releases it is the program's choice. Only a focused window takes the grab.

Per host:
- **Mac:** the view's grab setter moves the cursor to the window's centre, hides it and detaches it from the mouse (`CGAssociateMouseAndMouseCursorPosition(false)`). Each mouse event then pushes a `Look` with its `deltaX`/`deltaY`. The setter is reached by key, the way `window_frame.c` already reads the view's events.
- **X11:** `XGrabPointer`, confined to the window under a blank cursor, so there's no XFixes dependency. The pump keeps the pointer's last position and ends each frame with one `Look` from the centre, then moves the pointer back there. That move's own event lands on the centre, so it counts as zero. `FocusOut` releases the grab.
- **JS:** `Window.open` already fails there, so `window_grab.js` hands the window back. A browser `requestPointerLock` belongs to the browser-target discussion on #866.

Also:
- `tests/gfx/app_play` plays a `Look`.
- `tests/gfx/window` grabs and releases the mouse (only reached on a display).
- The slash boss proof matches `Look`.
- The guide describes `Look` and `Window.grab`.

**Compatibility:** a program that matches every case of `Event` explicitly now needs a `Look` case. It fails to check, which is better than changing meaning silently. In the repo only `demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend` did that.

## What I verified

- `gates/repo.ts`: 46 / 46. `window_frame.c` is at its 4000 ttok cap exactly.
- `tests/gfx/app_play` and `tests/gfx/window` match their golds when interpreted and on JS, and `app_play` also natively. The error tests match 478/481, the same as main (the 3 misses are compile-lane IO tests the local runner can't reproduce). Every other test passes `--check-only`, and every demo and proof checks.
- The Mac (Objective-C) build compiles and links.
- The X11 code type-checks against the real Xlib headers (`clang -fsyntax-only -D__linux__`).

## Not verified yet (why this is a draft)

- **The grab with a real mouse.** A probe that grabs for 5 s ran on an M4, but macOS blocks synthetic mouse events without Accessibility permission, so it saw no motion either way. Someone needs to run it and move the mouse.
- **X11 at runtime.** It has only been type-checked, never run on Linux.

title: The emitted C builds at -O0: segments take preserve_none only when clang optimizes
body:
`bend x.bend -o x.c` emits the C source (the guide's Tooling section), and building it by hand is how one gets a debug build, to step through a foreign effect's own C in a debugger. With clang 19 or later that fails at `-O0` once a program's segments carry more than a few words, and it does on eight of the repo's own IO tests:

```
$ bun bend2/main.ts tests/io/tcp_poll.bend -o tcp_poll.c
$ clang -std=c11 -O0 -g tcp_poll.c -lpthread -lm -o tcp_poll
error: <unknown>:0:0: ran out of registers during register allocation in function 'WL_FID_ENTER'
error: <unknown>:0:0: ran out of registers during register allocation in function 'WL_FID_IO_PASS_C3'
```

The segments are `preserve_none` functions chained by `musttail` (386b7fc1), and clang's `-O0` register allocator cannot place that chain. `-O1` and up are fine, which is why `bend -o`, always `-O3`, never sees it.

### The change

`PRESERVE(A)` applies `preserve_none` and `preserve_most` only when `__OPTIMIZE__` is defined. At `-O0` the segments take the default calling convention, the one clang 14-18 and gcc 15+ already build the runtime with since cd3366a9, and `musttail` still makes every jump a tail call. The note joins the `// Dialect` header's paragraph:

```c
// ... Only clang 19+ has both
// preserve_none and preserve_most, and compiles preserve_most soundly; at
// -O0 its register allocator cannot place a preserve_none segment, so an
// unoptimized build takes neither. ...
#if __has_attribute(preserve_none) && __has_attribute(preserve_most) \
  && defined(__OPTIMIZE__)
```

### Evidence (clang 22.1.8, Linux x86-64)

Every test in `tests/io`, emitted and built with `-O0 -g`, on main and on this branch. 82 of the 123 emit C; the other 41 pin a parse or check refusal.

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| compile at `-O0 -g` | 74 of 82 | 82 of 82 |
| the 8 main cannot build | — | build and print their `#\|` lines |

- The eight: `file_binary`, `process_run`, `tcp_loopback`, `tcp_poll`, `tcp_short_recv`, `udp_poll`, `udp_send_recv`, `udp_truncate`.
- Every other result matches main's test by test. Nine runs fail under my runner on both trees: eight fail the same way at `-O3` (my runner is not `gates/test.ts`), and `tcp_send_slow_peer` only needs more than the 10 s I gave it (16.9 s at `-O0`, against 2.0 s at `-O3`).
- At `-O1`, `-O2` and `-O3` the assembly of `tcp_poll`, `process_run` and `udp_truncate` is byte-identical to main's, so what `bend -o` builds does not change.
- Re-checked on main 675381e7, after merging it in: the eight build at `-O0 -g` and print their `#|` lines, the `-O1`, `-O2` and `-O3` assembly of `tcp_poll`, `process_run` and `udp_truncate` is still byte-identical, and `gates/repo.ts` passes 50 / 50.

There is no test file: the harness builds a test's binary at `-O3`, so a `#|` test cannot pin a compile flag. Glad to add one in whatever shape you prefer.

arm64: @Lorenzobattistela confirmed the `-O1`, `-O2` and `-O3` assembly is byte-identical there too, and `-O0` already built there (24 argument registers), so this makes `-O0` the same on every target. macOS not tested. The device code is untouched: the `#if` sits in the host branch.

title: Conversion checks syntactic identity before normalizing (#1071)
body:
Fixes #1071. **Disclosure:** I wrote this change with Claude Code (an AI coding agent). `AGENTS.md` asks that `bend2/bend.ts` be written by humans, so feel free to close this and write it yourselves. The patch is short, and the tests and measurements below still apply. ### Change Before `term_compare` normalizes both sides, it checks whether they are syntactically identical. The check forces share cells, unfolds nothing, visits heads and first arguments first, and stops after 4096 visits, counting a shared node at every visit. Identical terms are convertible, so the check only ever answers "equal". If it finds a difference or runs out of visits, the comparison runs exactly as before. It only runs when a side is a call (`App` or `Ref`), because values already compare structurally at the same cost. `gates/repo.ts`: the `bend.ts` cap goes from 44000 to 45000 ttok, since the file is 44444 after this change. #996 and 942573f raised it the same way. Lean 4's kernel does the same: `is_def_eq` starts with `quick_is_def_eq`, which first asks `equiv_manager` whether the two terms are structurally equal, before any reduction (`src/kernel/type_checker.cpp`, `src/kernel/equiv_manager.cpp`). ### Budget fix (bdb251f) The first version tested the budget only on pairs of distinct nodes. When visit 4096 was a pointer-identical pair, the counter went past zero and was never tested again, so the walk had no limit. On a term with much sharing, where the tree is exponentially larger than the graph, it did not finish. The loop now stops at the budget, and the answer is "equal" only when the walk completed. `tests/check/conversion_same_before_whnf.bend` has a case that hung before this commit. ### Checker benches (3ddfb03) Two small benches in `bench/checker`, pinned for `apple_m4` at 0.070 s each (best of 5 on an M4): - `hashes_4` (37 lines), the use case: four laws from the generator below. - `shared_4` (27 lines), the regression: `dag(d, z) == wrap(d, z)` at the four depths where the first version's walk did not finish. | bench | main | first version | this PR | |---|---|---|---| | hashes_4 | 6.1 s | 0.21 s | 0.21 s | | shared_4 | 0.21 s | did not finish (killed at 60 s) | 0.21 s | Linux server, one run each, startup included. ### Benchmark: proofs about code that hashes The generator below (in the collapsed block) writes N laws of the shape `{under(root(ws), L) == under(root(ws), L)}`. Here `root` is a 64-round hash over 16 words, and `L` is a list limit between 2^20 and 2^30. That is the shape a proof about hashing code reaches after a rewrite: both sides compute the same root of the same fixed data. `main` evaluates both roots for every law. With this PR, the two sides are recognized as identical and nothing is evaluated. | laws | main | this PR | |---|---|---| | 2 | 1.75 s, 240 MB | 0.06 s, 57 MB | | 5 | 5.00 s, 232 MB | 0.06 s, 59 MB | | 10 | 18.5 s, 230 MB | 0.14 s, 53 MB | | 25 | 31.6 s, 238 MB | 0.11 s, 59 MB | | 50 | 60.7 s, 244 MB | 0.10 s, 64 MB | | 100 | 114 s, 261 MB | 0.09 s, 68 MB | Control: a law equating the roots of two word lists that differ in one word fails on both, with the same error.
gen.py (python3 gen.py N 64 > bench.bend) ```python """Generate a checker bench shaped like proofs about hashing code (SSZ roots). python3 gen.py LAWS ROUNDS > bench.bend Each law states that two expressions with the same closed hash computation are equal: a Merkle-style root of 16 words, as a proof meets it after a rewrite (the goal and the lemma both mention root([..]) and differ only elsewhere), and a large list limit, as SSZ schemas carry (2^20 .. 2^30). """ import random, sys laws, rounds = int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2]) rnd = random.Random(1) out = ['import Base', '', 'def mix(+a: U32, +b: U32) -> U32:', ' U32.add(U32.xor(a, U32.shln(b, 5n)), U32.xor(U32.shrn(a, 3n), b))', '', 'def fold(xs: List<&2, U32>, a: U32) -> U32:', ' match xs:', ' case []: a', ' case x <> rest: fold(rest, mix(a, x))', '', 'def rounds(n: Nat, a: U32, +xs: List<&2, U32>) -> U32:', ' match n:', ' case 0n: a', ' case 1n+p: rounds(p, fold(xs, a), xs)', '', 'def root(+xs: List<&2, U32>) -> U32:', f' rounds({rounds}n, 0, xs)', '', 'def under(h: U32, limit: Nat) -> Bool:', ' Nat.is_le(U32.to_nat(U32.and(h, 1023)), limit)', ''] for i in range(laws): ws = ', '.join(str(rnd.randrange(1 << 32)) for _ in range(16)) lim = 1 << rnd.randrange(20, 31) out += [f'law root_{i}:', f' {{under(root([{ws}]), U32.to_nat({lim})) == under(root([{ws}]), U32.to_nat({lim})) : Bool}}', f'def root_{i}(): {{==}}', ''] out += ['law main:', ' U32', '', 'def main(): 0', ''] print('\n'.join(out)) ```
### Case study: a verified SSZ library SSZ ("Simple Serialize") is how Ethereum encodes its consensus data (blocks, validator records, the chain state) as bytes. It also defines how every such value hashes to a 32-byte "root": the data is split into 32-byte chunks and hashed pairwise with SHA-256 into a Merkle tree. Nodes compare these roots to agree on the state. We wrote an SSZ library in Bend, with proofs that its encoder, decoder and root function match an independent transcription of the specification. It has about 300 proof modules. Many laws say "the root the code computes is the root the spec defines". Proving them means comparing terms that both contain the same hash computations over fixed data, such as the precomputed roots of empty subtrees and the SHA-256 constants. They also contain large protocol limits, for example 2^30 bytes for a transaction. On `main`, each such comparison evaluates the hash, or expands the limit in unary. Some of these checks overflow the stack, and others take minutes and gigabytes. With this PR, the SHA-256 correctness gate of the library (the runtime SHA-256 equals the FIPS 180-4 specification) goes from 7.97 s / 474 MB to 0.85 s / 253 MB.

title: A + binder in a nested tuple let fails with 'an annotated term (cannot infer)' when the goal mentions the pair
body:
### What I did

Bend 2.0.28 on macOS 26 (darwin 25.6.0), arm64. `bend update` reports no newer version.

```python
import Base

def third(r: U32 & Bool & List<&2, U32>) -> List<&2, U32>:
  (a, b, c) = r
  c

def lemma(r: U32 & Bool & List<&2, U32>) -> {third(r) == third(r) : List<&2, U32>}:
  (a, rest) = r
  (b, +c) = rest
  {==}
```

```sh
bend pair.bend
```

### What I expected

`All terms check.` The file checks when `+c` is written as `c`.

### What happened

```text
Error:
- expected : an annotated term (cannot infer)
- observed : _ => List<&2, U32>
Context:
- a : U32
- b : Bool
Location: lemma
127 | def Pair(-A: Type, -B: Type) -> Type:
128>|   Sigma<&1, &1, A, _ => B>
```

It needs all three parts:

- a `+` on a binder in a tuple let,
- a let on a pair that came out of an earlier tuple let (`rest`), and
- a goal that mentions the outer pair `r`, so the checker refines it.

A flat `(a, +c) = r` checks, and so does `(a, b, c) = r` without `+`. This looks like the tuple-let path of #810: that fix moved `+` onto the binder for braced patterns, and the observed term is the `Pair` family lambda, which does not infer.

### Workaround

Bind the components without `+` and pass them to a helper that takes `+` parameters.

title: A `!` runs on the GPU under WSL2: a CUDA device without concurrent managed access gets a twin of the corpus
body:
## Summary

WONTFIX tells Windows users to use WSL, and a user there expects `!` to use
the GPU. Today it does not build (`cannot find -lcuda`), or, with
`LIBRARY_PATH` set, it runs on the cores without a message. This PR makes
the WONTFIX advice true.

## Terms

- **Concurrent managed access:** a CUDA device attribute
  (`CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_CONCURRENT_MANAGED_ACCESS`). With it, the host and
  the device can use one managed allocation at the same time; the CUDA lane
  on main needs it for its corpus. A GPU under WSL2 reports 0, so main's
  probe refuses it.
- **Twin:** this PR's answer for such a device. The corpus stays in host
  memory, and a second copy of it (the twin) lives in VRAM. A `!` turn
  copies what it can touch to the twin before it runs, and back after.
- **Watchdog:** Windows' display driver model (WDDM), which every WSL2 GPU
  runs under, stops any single GPU launch after about 2 s (the TDR).
- **Parking:** a lane that has used its time budget saves its state and
  stops; the next launch resumes it. So no launch reaches the watchdog,
  however long the whole `!` runs.

## Why it is safe, and why it is needed

### 1. Linux: nothing changes for existing users

On native Linux, the CPU build is byte-identical to main's, and a CUDA
device with managed access takes main's path and main's device program.

- The CPU build's assembly (`clang -O3 -S`) is byte-identical to main's for
  the 16 runtime benches and the 19 `!` tests that compile.
- The CUDA host build contains the twin code behind `if (gpu_twin)`. On a
  device with managed access those branches never run.
- Without a twin, NVRTC (NVIDIA's runtime compiler, which builds the device
  program at `--gpu-build`) gets main's options, and the program's text
  differs from main's only where it compiles out or expands to main's
  macros (point 2). Its cubin is byte-identical to main's for the same 35
  programs.

### 2. Metal: no Metal code changed

No Metal code changed; every shared change compiles out or expands to
main's text on Metal. Please confirm on the minis (test and perf gates).

- The emitter's jumps now pass the number of registers they fill, which a
  parking lane saves: `WL_GO(F, K)` expands to `WL_JMP(F)` and
  `WL_AGAIN(F, K)` to `continue`, as before.
- The parking code is under `#if BEND_PARK`, which only the twin's NVRTC
  build sets.
- `gpu_twin` is `#define`d as `false` outside CUDA, so `POOL_ALT` (the
  signal stack's size, larger for a twin) is `SIGSTKSZ`, and `gpu_sync`
  (a twin's copies around a turn) does nothing.
- The new header words `H_PARKED` and `H_BUDGET` (`LINE + 1`, `LINE + 2`)
  are read and written only by the twin and parking code.

### 3. WSL: `!` now builds and runs on the GPU

- The build links `libcuda` against the toolkit's stub, which comes after
  the other `-L` paths; its soname is `libcuda.so.1`, so at run time the
  loader loads the driver's library.
- A device without concurrent managed access gets a twin. The heap is
  synced lazily, in 2 MB chunks: after a turn, the host downloads a chunk
  only when it touches it (a page fault), and the next turn uploads only
  the chunks the host wrote. So data that stays on the device is not
  copied back and forth.
- The 20 `!` tests that compile pass on WSL2 (RTX 4050, CUDA 13.3), by
  default, with `--gpu off` and with `--gpu 512MB`.

### 4. Why parking is needed, despite the comment on #1012

- **A different problem.** #1012 was about a `!` with no parallelism on
  Metal. Here the program is parallel, and Windows' display driver (WDDM,
  which every WSL2 GPU uses) stops any launch after about 2 s. The
  maintainer's fixes do apply, but they give up the GPU:
  - "Use the CPU" would move every long-running `!` on WSL to the cores, so
    WSL users would still not have the GPU for real work (point 5).
  - "Fail cleanly" is in this PR (the watchdog message), but by itself it
    would stop the program instead of finishing it.
  - Parking is the only one of the three that lets a long, parallel `!`
    finish on the GPU under a 2 s limit.
- **No cost for others.** Parking is compiled only for a twin
  (`-DBEND_PARK`). Metal and Linux with managed access run main's device
  program.
- **Simpler than #1012:** no new task tag, no call-graph pass, no fuel
  constant and no build knob. The budget is time, read from `%globaltimer`.
- **Tested on a GPU:** on WSL2, `queens` at size 18 ran about 12 s on the
  GPU with no driver reset. With the budget forced down to 0.2 ms, so that
  lanes parked every few thousand steps, 2,501 rounds of parking and
  resuming gave the same results as the cores (RTX 4050 Laptop, under
  WDDM).

### 5. WONTFIX sends Windows users to WSL

WONTFIX says "Use WSL", and a user there expects `!` to use the GPU. Today
it does not build, or it runs on the cores without a message. This PR
makes the WONTFIX advice true.

## The commits

1. A `!` program links libcuda against the toolkit's stub where the
   driver's is off the linker's path.
2. A `!` runs on a CUDA device without concurrent managed access: the corpus
   gets a twin.
3. A twin's GPU lanes park at a budget, so no launch meets the display
   driver's watchdog.
4. A twin's ring sync copies the slots written since the last sync, so a
   take racing a push no longer reads a dead task (the race found by
   @costamatheus97; twin-only).
5. A twin's copies run pinned: gpu_alias pins each 8 MiB step it carries
   hot.
6. A twin's ring sync mends the slots the other side took, so no busy
   turn's planes cross whole (it replaces commit 4's copy, which cost a
   busy program about 15%, with @costamatheus97's mend; twin-only).
7. A twin's heap splits between the host and the lanes, so a turn leaves the
   host's pages alone.

## Review notes

- **The only shared code this PR modifies is the allocator's (commit 7),
  and every change is behind an `#if`.** `heap_alloc_miss`, `heap_free` and
  `bank_at` change only under `BEND_SPLIT`, which only a twin's NVRTC program
  sets, or `TWIN_SPLIT`, the CUDA host build's. The CPU build's assembly and
  the managed CUDA program's cubin are byte-identical to main's; Metal
  sets neither (`TWIN_SPLIT` is 0 off CUDA; not built here); in the CUDA
  host build a managed device never takes the split's branches.
- **The SIGSEGV handler calls CUDA.** It is safe here because only a host
  touch of a stale chunk causes that fault, on the thread that touched it.
- **CUDA now has two memory models.** The twin runs only when the device
  reports no concurrent managed access; everything else is main's.
- **The twin duplicates the HIP lane's design (#891).** It follows the same
  design on the CUDA driver API; a shared twin layer is possible if HIP
  merges.
- **Parking depends on `gpu_twin`, not on the watchdog attribute.** A Linux
  desktop that shows X on the GPU does not get it yet.
- **One kind of loop cannot park.** The compiler emits some pure sequential
  loops as a plain C loop (`spin_N`, from `emit_native`), which has no point
  where a lane can stop and save its state. One such loop in a `!` must
  still end within 2 s, and the README states this. For that case, a
  warning or a CPU fallback (#942) is the right fix.

## Request

Please run the gates (test and perf) on the minis for Metal, and on a
native Linux CUDA machine if one is available. These were not tested here.

## Evidence

On the branch rebased onto Bend 2.0.29 (`574b6d39`); times are medians of 5
runs, with the range.

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Linux CPU assembly against main (`clang 20 -O3 -S`), 16 runtime benches and 19 `!` tests | 35 of 35 byte-identical |
| CUDA device program without a twin against main (NVRTC 13.3, sm_89), the same 35 | 35 of 35 cubins byte-identical |
| `!` tests on WSL2 (RTX 4050): default, `--gpu off`, `--gpu 512MB` | 20 of 20 tests, 60 of 60 runs |
| `queens` size 18 on WSL2 | Same answer as the cores, no driver reset; 12.3 s (10.5–14.7), the cores 9.3 s |
| `gpu_turns` with a tree of 2^24 leaves, four `!` turns, WSL2 | Same answer as the cores; 1.7 s (1.2–2.5), the cores 0.33 s |
| Parking with the budget forced to 0.2 ms (WDDM): `queens` size 18 (2,501 resume rounds), the 2^24 tree (4), 5 `!` tests | Same results as the cores |
| Ring audit of both sides' lap words after each sync: `gpu_turns`, a 2^20 tree folded 24 times on each side, and Slash Boss's probe | Stale slots before commit 4: 468,960, 22.1M and 209M on the host (and 24.8M on the device in Slash); none after commits 4 and 6 |
| Slash Boss's probe frame (`SLASH_PROBE=300`), WSL2, before and after commit 5 | 42.9 to 35.3 ms (draw 29.1 to 24.0), output unchanged; the other checks hold |
| Slash Boss's probe frame, WSL2: no ring fix, commit 5 and commit 6, interleaved | 29.2, 33.6 and 29.4 ms |
| Commit 7 on WSL2: Slash Boss's probe frame; particles (@costamatheus97's demo) at 16K, 64K, 262K with host binning; the tree of 2^24 leaves and the folded 2^20 tree | 29.9 -> 14.2 ms; 22.9 -> 15.3, 52.9 -> 40.7, 171.8 -> 123.4 ms; 1.07 -> 1.33 s and 0.66 -> 0.76 s (they walk everything the device built) |

Not tested: Metal, native Linux CUDA, the perf gate.
