title: F32 on JS answers as C: pow's specials, printf's even tie in F32.show, strtof's single rounding in F32.read
body:
Closes #1112.

On the JS lane (and so the interpreter), three float operations answer differently from C. This PR changes the JS side only, so it answers as C does. The C and device lanes are untouched.

| | C | JS before | JS after |
|---|---|---|---|
| `F32.pow(1.0, nan)`, `F32.pow(-1.0, ±inf)` | 1 | nan | 1 |
| `F32.show(1.44140625)` | 1.4414062 | 1.4414063 | 1.4414062 |
| `F32.read("1.0000000596046447753906250001")` | 1.0000001 | 1 | 1.0000001 |

## Changes (`bend2/comp.ts`, one commit each)

1. **`F32.pow`.** A small `f32_pow` answers C99's specials: `pow(1, y)` is 1 for any `y`, and `pow(-1, ±inf)` is 1. Everything else goes to `Math.pow`. `atan2` stays on `Math.atan2`, which already agrees with C on all its specials.
2. **`F32.show`.** JS's `toExponential` rounds a last-digit tie up, where `printf` rounds it to even. The two only differ when a float's exact decimal expansion lands on the tie. That needs a short expansion (at most 10 digits), which `x * 2^(10 - E)` being whole tests exactly. In that case `f32_show` reads `x`'s exact digits and cuts the tie to even. Every other float takes the old path.
3. **`F32.read`.** `Number()` then `Math.fround` rounds twice, and that is only wrong when the double is exactly a float midpoint. That's an exact test on doubles, with 2^128 as the float past the largest, so a decimal just under the overflow midpoint still reads as the largest float. In that case `f32_near` compares the decimal's own digits with the midpoint in BigInt and takes the side they lie on, as `strtof` does.

A fourth commit adds `tests/run/float_lane_edges.bend`, which prints all three cases (plus the decimal just under the midpoint) and pins the C answer.

## Evidence

- **The new test:** it prints `1 1 1 1.4414062 1.0000001 1` on C, JS (bun and node) and the interpreter. On main, JS and the interpreter print `nan nan nan 1.4414063 1 1`.
- **Sampling:** the fixes came out of comparing C with JS.
  - **show:** 200k sampled floats, 0.45% of which differed.
  - **read:** 1,500 decimals just above a float midpoint, all of which differed.
  - **pow:** the special cases of C99 Annex F.
- **Cost:** a round trip of `F32.show` then `F32.read`, 2^20 times on bun, goes from 1.87 to 2.03 s (+8%). `pow` and floats that aren't ties take the old path.
- **`bun gates/repo.ts`:** 47/47. `comp.ts` goes from 62,584 to 63,196 ttok, under its 64,000 cap.
- **Full local test gate (no GPU lane):** 1475/1479, the same 8 lane failures as main (the `io_audio_only_*` tests on C and JS, since this machine has no ALSA headers, and `io_process_run` on the interpreter and JS)

## Not verified

- JS engines other than JSC (bun) and V8 (node), e.g. Firefox's.
- The macOS lanes. They share this JS code, but I didn't run them.

title: Deliver signed, fractional Scroll events from native windows (#1020)
body:
Closes #1020.

Add `Scroll{x: U32, y: U32, dx: F32, dy: F32}` to Base’s `Event`. The macOS `BendView` now handles `scrollWheel:` and stores the pointer position and the native AppKit deltas as F32 bits, preserving fractional trackpad input. The Linux X11 pump maps button presses 4/5 to vertical +1/−1 and 6/7 to horizontal −1/+1, with pointer coordinates clamped as for `Mouse`; wheel button releases are not emitted. Both platforms marshal the four payload fields into the normal native `Window.frame` event list. Existing mouse button behavior is unchanged. The guide documents the event and platform delta units, and the exhaustive game proof handles the new constructor.

Native X11 integration exercised on a running display: compiled a Bend program calling `Window.open` / `Window.frame`; sent synthetic X11 presses/releases for buttons 4–7 plus normal button 1; observed exactly `S 17 23 0 1`, `S 17 23 0 -1`, `S 17 23 -1 0`, `S 17 23 1 0`, `M 17 23 0 True`, `M 17 23 0 False` in order. The new permanent viewport test checks independently signed fractional axes, pointer hit-testing and clamping on interpreter, emitted JS and native C (all `1 0.25`). `tests/gfx/app_play.bend` passes on all three lanes; `tests/gfx/window.bend` native display and no-display JS paths pass; the exhaustive `demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend` checks. `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS 47/47. title: The Linux window fills a frame by squares: each node once, not a walk from the root per pixel
body:
Based on 2.0.31 (af569d48). One commit, `bend2/effs/window_frame.c` only.

## Why

On Linux without the CUDA device fill, `window_fill` calls `window_pix` for every pixel. `window_pix` walks the image quadtree from the root, so each pixel costs k node reads (k = 11 at 1920x1200). The walk runs single-threaded on the IO thread. On this machine it takes 19 ms of Slash Boss's 30 ms frame.

## What changes (`bend2/effs/window_frame.c` only; 3758 → 3991 ttok, cap 4000)

`window_sq` walks the tree once, from the root:
- a Qua recurses into those of its four quarters that meet the frame;
- any other node paints its square, clipped to the w x h frame, with the color `window_pix` reads at its corner.

So each node is read once and each pixel is written once. The pixels are the same as before in the edge cases too:
- a leaf above pixel level;
- a subtree below pixel level (`window_pix` takes its first quarter, as before);
- a frame that isn't a power of two.

A node's location comes from `term_peek`, the runtime's read of a shared node. It returns the same value as `window_pix`'s inline `H[term_loc(t)] >> 24`.

The CUDA arm (`window_dev` when `io_gpu`) and its statics are unchanged byte for byte. So is the Mac's Metal shader. No new file and no `comp.ts` change.

## Measurements

The machine is an AMD Ryzen 7 5800XT (16 threads) under WSL2, with no display. clang-16 `-O3`, CPU lane.

**Method.** Each program ran offscreen: a test-only patch of the emitted C opens a window with no display and skips the X11 pump, the 60 Hz pace and `XPutImage`. It also scripts input every frame: a mouse path, clicks, and keys held.

The two builds come from the same emitted C with only the fill block swapped. I ran 5 interleaved rounds, flipping the order each round, and report medians in ms. The frame time is the interval between `Window.frame` calls. The 1-minute load was 12.6 at the start (another job's tail) and 2.4–6 through the runs, from their own workers.

| program | size | fill main | fill this | frame main | frame this |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| app_slash_boss_3d (`Play.run`) | 1920x1200 | 18.98 | 2.99 | 29.77 | 12.91 |
| app_ray_tracer_3d | 1024x768 | 11.98 | 5.90 | 44.12 | 38.22 |
| app_triangle_2d | 512x512 | 0.867 | 0.063 | 2.72 | 1.82 |
| app_pong_game_2d | 512x512 | 0.526 | 0.025 | 2.41 | 1.79 |
| io_rollback_netcode/walkers_demo | 512x512 | 0.394 | 0.034 | 1.49 | 1.02 |
| tests/gfx/window | 64x48 | 0.007 | 0.001 | 0.94 | 0.94 |
| tests/gfx/clicks (one `Pix`) | 256x256 | 0.003 | 0.003 | 0.004 | 0.004 |

- Slash's frame is not equal work: its sim steps from `IO.now` at 60 Hz, so the slower old frames carry about one more sim tick each; the fill columns are the clean comparison.
- The ray tracer's image splits at nearly every pixel, which leaves less to save: 2x on the fill.
- A particles demo at 1024x768 from my fork behaves the same way: 6.5 → 4.0 ms.

## Verification

- **Pixels.** A test build ran both fills on every frame, main's per-pixel loop and this one. Each wrote into its own buffer, pre-filled with `0xFFFFFFFF` (a value no fill can write), and I compared them with `memcmp`.
  - **Programs:** every windowed program above, plus the particles demo and a scratch program that draws a random 14-level quadtree with shared subtrees each frame.
  - **Sizes:** each program's own size, then 1x1, 16384x1, 1x16384, 641x479, 3x2 and 4097x3.
  - **Result:** 63 runs of up to 600 frames, all identical, with no unwritten pixel. The frames really changed: Slash had 240 distinct frames in 240, pong 395 in 600.
  - **Positive control:** swapping the quarter offsets gives a mismatch on every frame.
- **`bun gates/repo.ts`:** 47/47.
- **Local CPU gate** (`ROCM_PATH=/nonexistent`): 1475/1479. The 4 failures are main's: `io_audio_only_{open,write,close}` (no ALSA headers here) and `io_process_run` on interp and JS.
- **CUDA arm:** compiles with `-DBEND_CUDA=1` against CUDA-over-HIP shim headers (ROCm clang 22), with no errors or warnings. This is the same as main.

## Not verified

- **macOS / Metal.** The Mac path is untouched. I didn't build it.
- **NVIDIA / CUDA at run time.** I only compiled it, against a shim. It wasn't linked, and it didn't run on a GPU: no `io_gpu` frame and no `window_dev` launch.
- **A real X display.** Every run was offscreen, with no `XPutImage`, pace or event pump. The fill writes the same buffer with the same bytes, but I haven't looked at a window on screen.
- **Other machines.** All of this ran on one WSL2 host. Timings on the perf gate's hardware may differ.
- **Slash's sound.** It ran silent: I stubbed the ALSA headers only for the test build.

title: `--safe` follows `<file>.bendtt -> /dev/null`, so the proven kernel checks an empty book instead of the elaboration
body:
# `--safe` follows `<file>.bendtt -> /dev/null`, so the proven kernel checks an empty book instead of the elaboration

### What you did

Create `PROOF.bend`:

```python
type Unit is Data:
  Unit{}

def keep(u: Unit) -> Unit:
  u
```

Put a symlink at the implicit output path, then run `--safe`:

```text
ln -s /dev/null PROOF.bendtt
bend PROOF.bend --safe
echo exit=$?
readlink PROOF.bendtt
```

The symlink can be committed to a Git repository: Git records it as a mode `120000` entry, so cloning the repository on macOS or Linux recreates it without running any checkout hook or other code.

This vector does not travel through BendHub packages. `--publish` serializes the files the loader read as a JSON map from paths to text, with no file-mode or symlink representation, and the adjacent `.bendtt` file is not part of that set. The affected inputs are Git checkouts, archives or local directories that can already contain the symlink.

### What happened

```text
All terms check.
BendTT: All terms check.
exit=0
/dev/null
```

The normal Bend checker does run first. The bypass is specifically of the independent BendTT recheck:

1. `safe_book` builds a nonempty BendTT elaboration in memory.
2. `safe_emit` calls `fs.writeFileSync("PROOF.bendtt", got.text)`.
3. The OS follows the symlink and writes the elaboration to `/dev/null`, which discards it.
4. `kernel_check` starts the proven kernel with `PROOF.bendtt` as a path.
5. The kernel opens that path afresh, follows the symlink, reads an empty file, accepts the empty book, and exits 0.

Running the kernel directly on `/dev/null` confirms the last step:

```text
$ bendtt /dev/null
All terms check.
$ echo $?
0
```

No race, helper process or write outside the checkout is needed. The same repository entry controls both opens, while `/dev/null` gives them different effective contents: writes disappear and reads return EOF.

This does not contradict the Lean proof: the kernel correctly establishes its claims for the empty book, but the binding between the checked Bend book and the bytes given to the kernel is broken.

The immediate sample is sound under the normal checker, but the purpose of the second checker is to catch a soundness bug in that first checker. Combining any such Bend-checker bug with the committed symlink makes `--safe` print a clean kernel verdict without the kernel seeing the offending elaboration. In other words, the first checker still has to accept the source, but the advertised independent recheck becomes vacuous.

Unlike an explicit `-o` whose destination the user chooses, `--safe` silently derives the adjacent `.bendtt` path. If that entry is an ordinary symlink to a regular file, the same write also truncates another user-writable file without the user having selected it as output.

### Expected behavior

The kernel should check the exact bytes returned by `safe_book`, independently of any filesystem entry controlled by the project being checked.

For example, `--safe` could create a private temporary directory, write the elaboration to a newly created file in that directory, and give only that path to the kernel. The adjacent `.bendtt` path could remain exclusive to an explicit `-o`; if it is used, it should not follow symlinks. Merely checking with `lstat` before `writeFileSync` would leave a check/write race.

As defense in depth, the kernel could also report how many definitions it parsed and checked, and `safe_check` could compare that with the number actually emitted. The current `n` is not directly that value—it counts in-scope roots rather than every emitted BendTT definition—so the elaborator would need to return the emitted-definition count separately. This would detect other cases where the kernel reads a different book, not only this symlink.

### The file

```python
type Unit is Data:
  Unit{}

def keep(u: Unit) -> Unit:
  u
```

### bend --version

```text
bend 2.0.31
main commit af569d4826913b2ce3557e9829ccad31fcf86f94
```

### uname -sm

```text
Darwin arm64
```

### clang --version (the first line)

```text
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: File.sendfile puts a file's bytes on a socket without passing them through the program
body:
`File.sendfile(sock, file, off, len)` moves `len` bytes of `file`, from `off`, onto `sock`, in the kernel.

- Linux and macOS: one `sendfile(2)`. The bytes go from the page cache to the socket; no byte passes through the program.
- The file's own position does not move: the offset travels by value.
- Non-blocking: a full socket takes EAGAIN, the computation parks until the socket is writable, and the loop resumes — the shape `TCP.send` already has, without a deadline.
- All `len` out is Done. A file that ends first is `ENODATA`. A file the kernel refuses to send is that errno; there is no fallback.

The JS lane has no `sendfile(2)`: it copies one 64 KiB block at a time, and its comment says so.

`tests/io/file_sendfile.bend` builds fixtures in `/tmp`: offsets, the file's position, zero length, an offset past the end; then a 4 MiB send from a fork — larger than the loopback buffers, so the park and the resume really run — drained in 32 KiB reads and compared byte for byte with `cmp`. Interpreted, C and JS lanes: every line green. `gates/repo.ts`: 47/47.

title: Make --safe check private elaboration bytes, not project-controlled paths (#1116)
body:
Closes #1116.

`--safe` previously wrote `<file>.bendtt` through an existing symlink and then had the verified kernel reopen that same project-controlled path. A checked book with `PROOF.bendtt -> /dev/null` therefore presented an empty book to the independent checker. `safe_check` now elaborates once into a new file with mode 0600 inside a `mkdtemp` directory (0700), and gives that private path to the kernel. Its output log is also created exclusively inside that directory; both are removed on every exit path. The adjacent `.bendtt` artifact remains available for users and the existing safe-gate diagnostics, but is published **after** the kernel run by writing a new sibling file with `wx` and atomically renaming it over the destination. Renaming replaces a symlink instead of following it. An explicit `-o <file>.bendtt` keeps its existing, user-selected output behavior. Updated the guide and raised the `safe.ts` token budget by 300 for this boundary.

Failing-before: a byte-sensitive checker invoked through `$BENDTT` received an empty file for a nonempty Bend book when `PROOF.bendtt` pointed to `/dev/null`. After: it received `/tmp/bend-safe-…/book.bendtt` (0600 in a 0700 directory), checked its nonempty contents, returned success, and the symlink was replaced by a nonempty regular `.bendtt`. A symlink to a separate regular file left that target unchanged. Rejection of nonempty elaboration remained a nonzero `--safe` exit with the artifact published for diagnosis; vacuous books still say “nothing to check”; an unavailable kernel produces a nonzero exit. Explicit `-o .bendtt` still emits a nonempty file. `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS 47/47. Project TypeScript checking reports ten existing diagnostics away from the modified lines (six in older portions of `safe.ts`, two in `bend.ts`, two missing canvas typings). Lean v4.34 is unavailable on this Linux host, so the real BendTT binary was not run; the byte-sensitive `$BENDTT` process verifies the file/stdio/exit boundary, not proof semantics. The mini-cluster safe gate was not run.

title: Achados do JevGate: a lei `body_after_blank` afirma menos do que o comentário promete, e o `33n` do Map na Base não tem nome
body:
_English version below._

Oi @VictorTaelin! Sou o @tbytefrontier do X. Como te falei, depois de integrar o Bend 2 no [JevGate](https://github.com/Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate) eu ia abrir issues com o que ele encontrasse aqui no repositório, pra você ver se os achados são bons. O suporte a Bend 2 saiu hoje, na versão 0.22.0, com uma regra feita só pro Bend: ela compara o comentário de cada `law` com o que a lei realmente afirma.

Estes são os achados mais valiosos que encontramos rodando o JevGate no Bend durante a integração. Conferimos cada um no código, e todos continuam valendo no `main` atual (`af569d4`).

### Como aparece no terminal

```text
$ jevgate check demos/io_http_fetch bend2/base.bend
JevGate: consider · gate passed · 4 files · 16 API requests · 27497 input tokens · ~$0.0012

Consider (4):
  bend2/base.bend:2492 [maintainability/hardcoded-values] `Map.diff.fin` likely uses a value whose meaning a reader must guess (0.88). The value is 33n.
    → Give the value a descriptive constant name
  demos/io_http_fetch/LAWS.bend:8 [tests/laws] The comment above law `body_after_blank` promises more than the law states (0.81). A definition could break that promise while every proof passes.
    → State the comment's promise in the law, or narrow the comment to what the law states
  bend2/base.bend:2479 [maintainability/hardcoded-values] `Map.diff.chr` likely uses a value whose meaning a reader must guess (0.89). The value is 33n.
    → Give the value a descriptive constant name
  bend2/base.bend:2457 [maintainability/hardcoded-values] `Map.bit` uses a value whose meaning a reader must guess (0.88). The value is 33n.
    → Give the value a descriptive constant name

35 optional notes on code that reads well as it is; --verbose shows them.
```

### 1. `demos/io_http_fetch`: as leis não fixam o `http_body` numa resposta com cabeçalhos

O `LAWS.bend` diz que as leis fixam "the cut that strips the status line and the headers off a response", e o comentário de `body_after_blank` diz "the text after a blank line is the body, whatever follows it". Mas a lei só cobre textos que *começam* pela linha em branco:

```python
# LAW: the text after a blank line is the body, whatever follows it.
law body_after_blank:
  for b: String
  {Fetch.http_body("\r\n\r\n" ++ b) == b : String}

# LAW: the body is a suffix of the text: some prefix, then the body,
# is the text itself.
law body_suffix:
  for +s: String
  exs p: String
  {p ++ Fetch.http_body(s) == s : String}
```

E `body_suffix` também vale para `http_body(s) = s`. Então um `http_body` que só remove um `\r\n\r\n` do começo e devolve qualquer outro texto sem mudar satisfaz as duas leis, e mesmo assim devolveria a linha de status e os cabeçalhos de toda resposta real. O `http_body.go` atual corta certo uma resposta real; as leis é que não o seguram nisso, e uma mudança futura poderia quebrá-lo com o `PROOF.bend` ainda passando.

Sugestão: fixar o corte numa resposta com cabeçalhos. Por exemplo, uma lei que diga que `http_body(s)` é o texto depois do primeiro `\r\n\r\n`, ou `""` quando não há nenhum, contra uma definição de referência.

Conferindo essa lei, apareceu um detalhe: o `http_body.go` atual só a satisfaz quando todo caractere de `s` está abaixo de 256, como os bytes de uma resposta. Ele junta os quatro últimos caracteres num `U32`, e `ഊ` (U+0D0A) seguido de `\r\n` dá o mesmo número que `\r\n\r\n`, então `http_body("ഊ\r\nhello")` devolve `"hello"` sem haver linha em branco no texto. A lei pode exigir essa condição, ou a janela pode comparar os caracteres um a um.

### 2. `bend2/base.bend`: o `33n` das chaves crit-bit do `Map` não tem nome

`Map.bit` (`Nat.divmod(pos, 33n)`), `Map.diff.chr` (`Nat.sub(33n, Map.msb.u(32n, x))`) e `Map.diff.fin` (`Nat.add(33n, Map.diff(xt, yt))`) escrevem o mesmo `33n` solto. Cada caractere de uma chave ocupa 33 posições de bit: a posição 0 diz que há um caractere, e as posições 1 a 32 guardam o código, do bit mais alto pro mais baixo (é o que o `Map.bit.chr` lê).

Nada no `base.bend` diz isso. Quem lê precisa deduzir do `Map.bit.chr`, e os três `33n`, com o `32n` e o `31n` ao lado, precisam mudar juntos se a codificação mudar. Um def sem argumentos com um comentário sobre o layout (algo como `Map.stride()`) diria isso num lugar só.

### JevGate no CI do Bend

Se você gostar dos achados e quiser rodar o JevGate no CI do Bend, tem uma GitHub Action pronta, a [Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate-action](https://github.com/Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate-action). Eu te passo uma chave de API do Jev e os custos ficam por minha conta.

E se não gostar dos achados, por favor me diz o que ficou ruim. É esse feedback que eu uso pra melhorar as regras.

Valeu!

---

## English

The same findings in English, for anyone on the team who doesn't read Portuguese.

We added Bend 2 support to [JevGate](https://github.com/Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate), a code review CLI. It shipped today in 0.22.0, with a rule made just for Bend: it compares the comment on each `law` with what the law actually states. These are the most valuable findings from running JevGate on this repository during the integration. We checked each against the code, and both still hold on the current `main` (`af569d4`). The terminal output above is how JevGate reports them.

### 1. `demos/io_http_fetch`: the laws don't pin `http_body` on a response with headers

`LAWS.bend` says its laws pin "the cut that strips the status line and the headers off a response", and the comment on `body_after_blank` says "the text after a blank line is the body, whatever follows it". But the law only covers texts that *start* with the blank line:

```python
# LAW: the text after a blank line is the body, whatever follows it.
law body_after_blank:
  for b: String
  {Fetch.http_body("\r\n\r\n" ++ b) == b : String}

# LAW: the body is a suffix of the text: some prefix, then the body,
# is the text itself.
law body_suffix:
  for +s: String
  exs p: String
  {p ++ Fetch.http_body(s) == s : String}
```

`body_suffix` also holds for `http_body(s) = s`. So an `http_body` that only removes a leading `\r\n\r\n` and returns any other text unchanged satisfies both laws, yet would return the status line and headers of every real response. The current `http_body.go` cuts a real response correctly; the laws just don't hold it to that, so a later change could break it while `PROOF.bend` still passes.

Suggestion: pin the cut on a response with headers. For example, a law saying that `http_body(s)` is the text after the first `\r\n\r\n`, or `""` when there is none, against a reference definition.

Checking that law turned up a detail: the current `http_body.go` only satisfies it when every character of `s` is below 256, as the bytes of a response are. It packs the last four characters into a `U32`, and `ഊ` (U+0D0A) followed by `\r\n` gives the same number as `\r\n\r\n`, so `http_body("ഊ\r\nhello")` returns `"hello"` though the text has no blank line. The law can require that condition, or the window can compare the characters one by one.

### 2. `bend2/base.bend`: the `33n` in `Map`'s crit-bit keys has no name

`Map.bit` (`Nat.divmod(pos, 33n)`), `Map.diff.chr` (`Nat.sub(33n, Map.msb.u(32n, x))`) and `Map.diff.fin` (`Nat.add(33n, Map.diff(xt, yt))`) each write the same bare `33n`. Each character of a key takes 33 bit positions: position 0 says a character is there, and positions 1 to 32 hold its code, from the highest bit to the lowest (that's what `Map.bit.chr` reads).

Nothing in `base.bend` says this. A reader has to work it out from `Map.bit.chr`, and the three `33n`, with the `32n` and `31n` next to them, have to change together if the encoding changes. A def with no arguments and a comment on the layout (something like `Map.stride()`) would say it in one place.

### JevGate in Bend's CI

If you like these findings and want to run JevGate in Bend's CI, there's a ready GitHub Action, [Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate-action](https://github.com/Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate-action). I'll provide a Jev API key and cover the costs.

And if you don't like the findings, please tell me what was off. That feedback is what I use to improve the rules.

Thanks!

title: F64: native 64-bit floats in Base
body:
### What Bend should do

A 64-bit float type in Base, `F64`, lowered to native code the same way `F32` is:

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    x = F64.from_u32(2)
    IO.print(F64.show(F64.sqrt(x)))                  # 1.4142135623730951
    IO.print(F64.show((x / F64.from_u32(3) : F64)))  # 0.6666666666666666
```

What we have in mind:

- `type F64 is Data: F64{data: Word(64n)}`, with the same pure Word spec and native lowering as `F32{data: Word(32n)}`: C `double`, JS `number`, and CUDA `double`. Metal has no `double`, so a device segment that reaches F64 would get the existing "the device does not hold this function" refusal.
- The same operations `F32` has: arithmetic, comparisons, `sqrt`, `pow`, the trig and exp/log functions, `floor`/`ceil`/`round`, `min`/`max`, `show`, `read`, and conversions to and from `F32`, `U32`, and `Nat`.
- Bit access (`to_bits`/`from_bits` over `Word(64n)`, or over `U64` once #1027 lands) so that libraries can encode and decode IEEE 754 values.

### Why

Libraries outside Base cannot give pure code an `F64` that is fast. A foreign def returns `IO(...)`, so pure code cannot use it to add two doubles or call `sin`. The only way left is soft-float over `Word(64n)`. Our `Word(64n)` integer ops take about 68 µs each, so a soft-float built on them would be much slower than native code, and it would need its own versions of every transcendental function.

Doubles are the default number type in JSON, JavaScript, SQLite, Postgres, and most scientific and geospatial data. A JSON parser that reads numbers into `F32` loses precision on common values, such as timestamps in milliseconds and latitudes with seven decimal places.

We maintain [bend-kit](https://github.com/paymog/bend-kit) and track this as paymog/bend-kit#37. If you would rather not add F64 to Base, please tell us, and we will build a pure soft-float in the kit.

title: A TCP receive with a max of 0 fails with EINVAL instead of answering "", the peer's close, on a socket that is still open
body:
This is the `max = 0` fix @nicolas-abril suggested sending as its own PR during #978's review.

### What changes

`recv(2)` of 0 bytes answers 0 when data waits, the same 0 it answers when the peer closes. So on a socket whose peer is still open and has sent `"hello"`:

| call | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `TCP.recv(s, 0)` | `Done{""}` | `Fail{(22, "Invalid argument")}` |
| `TCP.recv_bytes(s, 0)` | `Done{[]}` | `Fail{(22, "Invalid argument")}` |
| `TCP.poll(s, 0, ms)` | `Done{Some{""}}` | `Fail{(22, "Invalid argument")}` |
| `TCP.poll(s, 0, 2000)`, idle socket | `Done{None{}}` after 2003 ms | `Fail{(22, "Invalid argument")}` at once |

The first three are the answers a closed peer gets, so a reader that loops until `""` stops early and drops a live connection. The three receives now refuse `max = 0` the way `TCP.send_bytes` refuses a byte past 255: before any `recv`, and in the poll before it parks. `TCP.recv`'s refusal still comes after the loop's park on readability, which runs before the effect, as its `""` did. Three lines in each of `tcp_recv.c`, `tcp_recv.js`, `tcp_poll.c` and `tcp_poll.js`.

Left as they are: `UDP.recv_from` and `UDP.poll` with max 0 answer the sender and `""`, dropping the datagram, which is the truncation `tests/io/udp_truncate` pins; `File.read_at(f, at, 0)` answering `[]` is pinned by `tests/io/file_binary`.

### Test

`tests/io/tcp_recv_max_zero.bend`: the peer sends `"hello"` and stays open; poll, recv and recv_bytes with max 0, then a recv of 64. On main the interpreted, JS and C lanes print `poll: some:`, `recv: done:`, `recv_bytes: done:`, then `hello`. Here each of the three fails with `22 Invalid argument`, and the recv of 64 still reads `hello`, so nothing was taken from the socket.

### Checks (Linux x86-64)

- The 20 `tcp_*`, `udp_*`, `file_*` and `port_bound` tests, the new one included, print their expected lines on the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes 47 / 47.

Not tested on macOS. If you'd rather read 1 byte for a max of 0 than refuse it, that's an easy change, though it answers more than was asked.

title: IO.within's deadline, and every timer, waits while two computations talk over a channel
body:
### What you did

bend within.bend -o within && ./within

### What happened

```text
pipeline done after 209 ms
10 ms timer fired after 209 ms
within(10) answered None after 209 ms
```

Two computations pass 2M values over a channel, a third runs `IO.within(Unit, 10, IO.sleep(5000))`, and a fourth sleeps 10 ms. The deadline and the timer both fire only when the pipeline ends. The JS lane does the same, later: `within(10)` answers after ~1264 ms under bun, and after ~1562 ms interpreted.

As far as I can tell, the loop consults the poller only when no step is runnable (`if (io_runs == NULL) { ... io_wait(e); }` in `io_loop`), and computations that wake each other on a channel keep `io_runs` from ever emptying, so every parked wait, timers included, waits for the whole chain. This is not a long pure computation: every step is short and is an effect. The guide says `IO.within` "answers `None{}` if the deadline wins", and here the deadline cannot win while any two computations exchange messages, which is a common shape for a server built on `IO.fork` and channels.

### What I tried

In the emitted C only, not as a patch: every 64 turns, at most once every 10 ms, the loop takes a glance at the parked waits through one wait that is already due, so `select` does not block, and then goes on.

```c
if ((n & 63) == 0 && io_park != NULL && io_tick() > look) {
  look = io_tick() + 10000000;
  io_wait_on(&io_glance, 0, 0, 1, io_none); // io_none answers IO_PARK
  io_wait(e);
}
```

| C, Linux x86-64 | main | with the glance |
|---|---|---|
| `within(10)` answers, beside the 2M-round pipeline (3 runs each) | 209-210 ms | 10 ms |
| the 2M-round pipeline itself (3 runs each) | 209-210 ms | 213-214 ms |
| a 1M-round pipeline beside 2,000 idle parked sockets, where `io_wait` walks every parked wait (medians of 7 interleaved runs) | 110 ms | 117 ms (+6.4%) |

I know bf745e31 made the loop poll only when no step is runnable, for a good reason: a poll every 64 steps cost 650 ms over 64,000 steps beside 2,000 parked sockets. The glance above is rate-limited to once every 10 ms, which keeps that walk to at most 100 a second and is where the 6.4% comes from; epoll/kqueue, which that commit left open, would change the cost again. So how the loop should look is your call. I'd be glad to turn whichever shape you prefer into a PR for both lanes, with this program as its test.

### The file

```python
# IO.within(10, ..) and a 10 ms timer beside two computations that pass
# 2M values over a channel: when does each answer?
import Base

def produce(+c: Chan(Nat), n: Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  match n:
    case 0n:
      Chan.close(Nat, c)
    case 1n+p:
      +q = p
      do IO<Unit>:
        Bool <- Chan.send(Nat, c, q)
        produce(c, q)

def since(t0: Nat, what: String) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    t1 : Nat <- IO.now()
    IO.print(what ++ " after " ++ Nat.show(Nat.sub(t1, t0)) ++ " ms")

def alive(m: Maybe<&1, Nat>) -> Bool:
  match m:
    case None{}:
      False{}
    case Some{value}:
      True{}

def consume(f: Nat, +c: Chan(Nat), +t0: Nat, live: Bool) -> IO(Unit):
  match f live:
    case 0n _:
      IO.pure(Unit, Unit{})
    case 1n+g False{}:
      since(t0, "pipeline done")
    case 1n+g True{}:
      IO.bind(Maybe<&1, Nat>, Unit, Chan.recv(Nat, c), got => consume(g, c, t0, alive(got)))

def timer(t0: Nat, +ms: U32) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    Unit <- IO.sleep(ms)
    since(t0, U32.show(ms) ++ " ms timer fired")

def within.got(t0: Nat, r: Maybe<&1, Unit>) -> IO(Unit):
  match r:
    case None{}:
      since(t0, "within(10) answered None")
    case Some{u}:
      since(t0, "within(10) answered Some")

def within(t0: Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  IO.bind(Maybe<&1, Unit>, Unit, IO.within(Unit, 10, IO.sleep(5000)), r => within.got(t0, r))

def main.run(+ch: Chan(Nat), +t0: Nat) -> IO(U32):
  do IO<U32>:
    Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, within(t0))
    Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, timer(t0, 10))
    Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, produce(ch, 2000000n))
    Unit <- consume(2000002n, ch, t0, True{})
    return 0

def main.go(ch: Chan(Nat)) -> IO(U32):
  IO.bind(Nat, U32, IO.now(), t0 => main.run(ch, t0))

def main() -> IO(U32):
  IO.bind(Chan(Nat), U32, Chan.new(Nat, 0), main.go)
```

body:
### What you did

```sh

```

### What happened

```text
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : Array<U32>
- observed : non-inferrable term
Context:
- w : Array<U32>
- w : Array<U32>
Location: main
12>|   f = {(\{False: w => Array.set(U32, w, 0, 9); sx => v => v}) : (Bool) -> (Array<U32> -> Array<U32>)}(True{})
```

The parser reads any `Array.set(..)` followed by `;` as the write statement `w = Array.set(..); rest` (the `a[i] <- v` rule), also for an explicit call and inside parentheses. So the inline match's second row becomes the first arm's continuation:

```text

parses as \{False: (w => w = Array.set(U32, w, 0, 9); sx => v => v)}
```

With `U32.add` or `Array.get` in the arm, the rows parse as two rows.

title: BendTT name escaping merges distinct constructor labels across module paths
body:
## Summary

BendTT name escaping is not injective for constructor labels. Two distinct
Bend source constructors can therefore become the same semantic label in the
generated BendTT book.

For example, a literal source substring `_2d_` collides with the encoding of
`-`, and `_2f_` collides with `/`.

Top-level BendTT definition names go through `fresh`, so one colliding
definition receives an underscore suffix. Constructor labels do not go
through `fresh`. In the reproduction below, two nominally distinct source
datatypes consequently receive structurally identical BendTT bodies.

I did not derive a proof of `Empty` from this. I am reporting it as a
translation correctness and hardening issue, not as a bounty claim.

## Version

```text
bend 2.0.32
v2.0.32 commit 573002f01ec6c52416d44489543f69a9625facf8
Linux x86-64 release binary
```

## Reproduction

Create this layout:

```text
name-collision/
  main.bend
  a-b/
    lib.bend
```

`name-collision/a-b/lib.bend`:

```python
type Good is Data:
  K{}
```

`name-collision/main.bend`:

```python
import ./a-b/lib.bend as Far

type a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good is Data:
  a_2d_b_2f_lib.K{}

def imported() -> Far.Good:
  Far.K{}

def local() -> a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good:
  a_2d_b_2f_lib.K{}
```

Run:

```bash
bend name-collision/main.bend --verdict
bend name-collision/main.bend -o /tmp/name-collision.bendtt
```

The verdict is:

```text
ALL PROOFS CHECK
```

The relevant generated BendTT is:

```text
a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good.arms : ∀x0 : <a_2d_b_2f_lib.K> -> *2 =
  λ{.a_2d_b_2f_lib.K: <()>; λ{}}

a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good : *2 =
  Σx0 : <a_2d_b_2f_lib.K> -> (a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good.arms x0)

a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good_.arms : ∀x0 : <a_2d_b_2f_lib.K> -> *2 =
  λ{.a_2d_b_2f_lib.K: <()>; λ{}}

a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good_ : *2 =
  Σx0 : <a_2d_b_2f_lib.K> -> (a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good_.arms x0)

imported : a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good =
  (.a_2d_b_2f_lib.K, ())

local : a_2d_b_2f_lib.Good_ =
  (.a_2d_b_2f_lib.K, ())
```

The two source constructors are:

```text
a-b/lib.K
a_2d_b_2f_lib.K
```

Both become the BendTT label:

```text
a_2d_b_2f_lib.K
```

## Cause

[`name_tt`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L484-L486)
leaves `_` and hexadecimal-looking text unchanged while replacing unsupported
characters with `_hex_`:

```typescript
function name_tt(k: Name): string {
  return k.replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9_.]|^[.0-9]/g, (c) => "_" + (c.codePointAt(0) ?? 0).toString(16) + "_");
}
```

Datatype enum labels and match arms use that value directly. Mutually
recursive group selector labels use the same encoding, so the same collision
class appears possible there.

This seems closely related to the uniqueness work in #1042, but it occurs in
the Bend-to-BendTT proof translation rather than the source name table or
runtime identifiers.

## Expected behavior

Distinct canonical Bend constructor names should produce distinct BendTT
labels, or the translator should reject a collision.

## Suggested fix

Use an injective encoding for semantic labels and apply one canonical mapping
consistently to:

- datatype enum labels;
- constructor tuples;
- match arms;
- mutually recursive group selectors.

One simple encoding is a length-prefixed hexadecimal encoding of every UTF-8
byte, including underscores. A per-book `Map<Name, string>` that allocates
unique labels would also work if every label-emitting path uses it.

The exact two-file example above would make a useful regression test. The
generated constructor labels should differ. Related cases include `_2f_`
versus `/`, hyphenated package namespaces, and group member selectors.

title: The work pass after a grow runs each lane's own ring, up to the put the grow left (#925)
body:
Answers the last question of #925. Two commits on main (`ebd9e904`): Adriel's, which adds the work pass after a grow, and a follow-up that limits it to rounds grown from few roots, after review found it cost tree-matmul 11% on the gate's minis.

## Why

A round of `gpu_run` grows the frontier (one group while f < `CUBE_T`, `CUBE_G` groups while f < `LANES`), then the work pass drains every ring with `rg = ring_flip(me)`. On Metal `CUBE_LOG` is 7, so `CUBE_G` is 128 and work group `row` takes ring position `row` of every grow group: lanes 32s..32s+31 of a SIMD group run one task from each of grow groups 32s..32s+31. After a grow from one root those are 32 unrelated subtrees, and every branch any of them takes is paid by all 32. A raycaster's lanes trace 32 patches of the screen far from each other.

The obvious fix, `rg = me`, is a disaster on trees (2.0.29, wall time: kmeans 0.587 → 11.969 s, tree-bitonic 1.898 → 45.155 s, tree-matmul 0.727 → 3.428 s). `TG_HOLD` holds one group per Apple core, so the work groups run in waves and each reads its rings' `put` when it starts. With `me` a group holds a whole grow group, its joins complete in the first wave, and their forks, dealt through the cursor to `ring_flip(c)`, land under a later group's `put` and run whole on one lane.

## What changes

- **After a grow from under `CUBE_T` roots, the work pass (pass 3) drains each lane's own ring**, only up to the `put` the ring held when the grow ended. A late group leaves deals made during the pass to the next round.
- **Grow passes store each ring's `put` in the upper half of its `put` word** (`ring_held`). `ring_put` is a `u32` view of a 64-bit plane word whose other half was unused, so the layout does not change at any `CUBE_LOG`, and CUDA's memset already zeroes it.
- **Every other round keeps pass 1**: `ring_flip` and the live `put`, as on main.

Why only from few roots: when several lanes of a grow group fork together, the group's cursor puts kid i of lane L at `24i + L`, so neighbouring rings hold the same kid of different parents. From one root those parents are cousins, and a SIMD group of neighbouring rings runs related work. From f >= `CUBE_T` roots dealt through the cursor, deal c sits in grow group `c % CUBE_G` and neighbouring rings hold unrelated deals, while `ring_flip` reads consecutive deals (a fork's kids, which in tree-matmul share their input blocks) in one SIMD group. Pass 3 on every grow measured tree-matmul at 1.11x and tree-bitonic at 1.07x on the M4 minis.

### Why it cannot hang

A pass-3 lane stops when its ring's `get` reaches the stored `put`.
- **The stored `put` is fresh.** Pass 3 runs only when f < `CUBE_T`, so the grow on `CUBE_G` groups ran right before it in the same `gpu_run`; its lanes cover all `LANES` rings and store at their end.
- **It comes after the grow's last push within the group.** A grow lane pushes only within its own group, and the group's lanes leave the loop together after a barrier.
- **`get` never passes it.** It starts at or below the stored `put` and advances only by draining a slot below it, which the grow wrote in an earlier dispatch.

### Limits

- **Some deals made during a grow wait a round.** A continuation can deal through the cursor into a group that already finished growing; the task lands above that ring's stored `put` and runs next round, like a task dealt during pass 3.
- **Fork-free tasks the grow leaves in place run where the cursor dealt them**, as before.

## Measured

Gate minis (Apple M4), `gates/perf.ts` over BEND_HOC, main `ebd9e904` and this branch in turn, 5 rounds, median PAR-GPU time:

| bench | main | this PR | PR / main |
|---|---|---|---|
| raytrace | 0.406 s | 0.326 s | 0.80 |
| tree-matmul | 0.944 s | 0.910 s | 0.96 |
| tree-bitonic | 1.794 s | 1.715 s | 0.96 |
| editdist | 0.509 s | 0.529 s | 1.03 |
| histogram | 1.483 s | 1.503 s | 1.01 |

The other benches are within ±2%; terrain lands at 0.23 or 0.32 s on both sides, run by run. Every output is the same.

On Adriel's M5 (2.0.32, before the follow-up, which leaves single-root rounds unchanged), the Bendcraft raycaster's frame was 1.7x to 2.8x faster by GPU time, and the program in #925 read A 4.6, B 15.6 and C 1.35 ms (5.8, 18.5 and 2.1 before). The first question of #925, a fill that stops at "every lane has a task" whatever the sizes, is untouched.

## Tests

On `ebd9e904`, with this branch and with main:
- `gates/repo.ts` 50 / 50 on both. `comp.ts` is 63,949 ttok against its cap of 64,000 (main 63,838).
- `gates/test.ts` 1576 / 1576 and `gates/ping.ts` 47 / 47 on both.
- `gates/safe.ts tests`: 1017 agree, 74 unsafe, 491 rejects, 1 false reject (`agree_32`), the same on both.
- `gates/perf.ts`: 122 to 124 / 124 on this branch, 119 to 123 / 124 on main; the misses on both are raytrace's compiler time and mandelbrot's sub-100 ms GPU cell.
- `paper/BendRT.pdf` rebuilt with Typst 0.15.1 (`--root bend2/docs`); main's source rebuilds to within one byte of main's PDF.
- Not run: CUDA, which runs the same kernel and `gpu_run`.

After merging, re-pin `apple_m4`'s PAR-GPU column with `--pin`, so a change that undoes raytrace's gain fails the gate.

title: --verdict: the kernel rejects a +-bound Equal.cong over a pair whose endpoint is a call (an unannotated eta-expansion), and the verdict does not say why
body:
### What you did

```sh
bend lemma.bend              # the file below
bend lemma.bend --verdict
bend lemma.bend -o lemma.bendtt && ~/.bend/bendtt/7f6ef51c9f75d7de/bendtt lemma.bendtt
```

### What happened

bend2 accepts the file, and the BendTT kernel rejects the term bend2 accepted:

```
$ bend lemma.bend
ALL PROOFS CHECK
Use --verdict for mathematical validity.

$ bend lemma.bend --verdict
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Sorry - this is a mismatch between the TypeScript implementation, and the formalized BendTT kernel. [...] feel free to open an issue to report this bug.

$ ~/.bend/bendtt/7f6ef51c9f75d7de/bendtt lemma.bendtt
SOME PROOFS FAIL
In lemma:
expected: an annotated term
observed: λx3 => (snd_of x3)
```

The translation eta-expands `snd_of` (the `f` of `Equal.cong`) into a lambda with no annotation, and the kernel cannot infer its type. What it takes, each variant checked with bend2 and with the kernel binary:

| variant | kernel |
|---|---|
| the file below: `+h2 = Equal.cong(U32 & Bool, Bool, snd_of, x, mk(n), h)` | rejects |
| the same without the `+` on the let (`h2 = …`) | accepts |
| the same with a variable endpoint (`y`) instead of the call `mk(n)` | accepts |
| `Equal.cong(…)` returned directly, no let | accepts |
| a non-pair domain (`Box{t: Tag}`), variable endpoints, `+` let | accepts |

So the trigger seems to be a `+`-bound let of an `Equal.cong` whose endpoint is a call and whose domain is a pair. Writing the function as `p => snd_of(p)` at the source gives the same unannotated term. We hit it in a larger proof (a map lemma: `Equal.cong((String & String) & Cmp, Cmp, cmp_of, r, String.cmp(key, k), hr)` bound with `+`), where it was the only def the kernel refused in a ~3,000-line proof file.

A smaller ask, in the same spot: `--verdict`'s FAIL says only "Sorry - this is a mismatch"; the kernel's own line (`In lemma: expected: an annotated term`) is visible only through `-o` and the cached kernel binary. Printing that line under the verdict would say which def and why.

### The file

```python
import Base

def snd_of(p: U32 & Bool) -> Bool:
  (a, b) = p
  b

def mk(n: U32) -> U32 & Bool:
  (n, True{})

def lemma(+n: U32, x: U32 & Bool, +h: {x == mk(n) : U32 & Bool}) -> {snd_of(x) == snd_of(mk(n)) : Bool}:
  +h2 = Equal.cong(U32 & Bool, Bool, snd_of, x, mk(n), h)
  h2
```

title: A match out of binder order is reported as "a consumed binder: give the value its own def"
body:
### What you did

```sh
bend nested.bend
bend joint.bend
```

### What happened

Both files match on `t` after `mv` while the signature binds `t` first. The guide says scrutinees follow binder order, and indeed both check once the signature lists `mv` before `t`. But the error names another cause:

```
$ bend nested.bend
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- message  : a match on a parameter or field (this name is a def or a consumed binder: give the value its own def)
Location:
11 |     case Some{v}:
12>|       match t:
   |             ^

$ bend joint.bend
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- message  : a match on a parameter or field (this name is a def or a consumed binder: give the value its own def)
Location:
7 | def f(t: Ty, mv: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> String:
8>|   match mv t:
   |            ^
```

`t` is neither a def nor consumed, and "give the value its own def" sends the reader to a helper that is not needed: swapping the two parameters (`def f(mv: Maybe<&2, U32>, t: Ty)`, and the call) makes both files check and print `str`. A message naming the rule would have saved us several rounds, e.g. "`t` is bound before `mv`: scrutinees follow binder order".

Not the same as #1125 (another message, a list-literal row) nor #817.

### The file

`nested.bend`:

```python
import Base

type Ty is Data:
  TStr{}
  TU32{}

def f(t: Ty, mv: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> String:
  match mv:
    case None{}:
      "none"
    case Some{v}:
      match t:
        case TStr{}:
          "str"
        case TU32{}:
          "u32"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(f(TStr{}, Some{1}))
```

`joint.bend` is the same with the body `match mv t:` / `case None{} _:` / `case Some{v} TStr{}:` / `case Some{v} TU32{}:`.

title: An application is inferable only when its arguments are, so a + let of Equal.cong over a function name goes to the kernel annotated
body:
Fixes #1133, on the elaborator's side.

### What happens

`inferable(o)` in `safe.ts` says an application infers when its head does, whatever its arguments. But an argument of a function type goes out η-long, a lambda, which the kernel cannot infer; and a `+` let (or a rewrite's evidence) is inferred, not checked. So

```python
+h2 = Equal.cong(U32 & Bool, Bool, snd_of, x, mk(n), h)
```

went out as `!+x3 = (Equal.cong … -λx3 => (snd_of x3) …)`, bend2 accepted the file and the kernel answered `expected: an annotated term / observed: λx3 => (snd_of x3)`. Without the `+` the let is checked against its use and the same term passes, which is why #1133's table turns on the `+`.

### The change

One line: an application is inferable when its head and its arguments are. With that, `let_term` and `rwt_term` do what they already do for any other non-inferable value, annotate it with the type bend2 knows:

```
!+x3 = {(Equal.cong -(Pair -U32 -Bool) -Bool -λx3 => (snd_of x3) -x1 -(mk x0) x2) : {(snd_of x1) == (snd_of (mk x0)) : Bool}}; x3
```

I checked the kernel side too, in case you'd rather fix it there: on the emitted `.bendtt`, the same lambda annotated by hand passes, a bare `-snd_of` passes, and annotating only the lambda's body does not. So the kernel wants the argument inferable, and the elaborator now makes the let so.

### Checks (Linux x86-64, kernel binary 7f6ef51c)

- `tests/proof/cong_lambda_argument.bend` is the issue's lemma with a `main`. On main, `bend f.bend` says `ALL PROOFS CHECK` and `--verdict` says `SOME PROOFS FAIL`; here both say `ALL PROOFS CHECK`, and so does the kernel binary on the emitted `.bendtt`, with the function written as `snd_of` or as `p => snd_of(p)`.
- Over `tests/proof`, `tests/check` and `tests/spec` (338 files), `--verdict` answers the same on main and here, file by file.
- The new test prints `True` on the interpreted, JS and C lanes; `gates/repo.ts` passes 47 / 47.

Not run: `gates/safe.ts` on a cluster, and macOS.

title: A match out of binder order says so: which binder came first, which was matched first, and the order that works
body:
Fixes #1134. I know `bend.ts` is yours to write; this is small and self-contained, so I'm sending it in case it saves you the round trip, and happy to see it rewritten.

### What happens

`match_flatten` closes a pending binder as a lambda when a later binder is matched before it (the order ban of `tests/flatten/order_ban_*`). If that earlier binder is matched afterwards, it is no longer pending, and the error at that point is the one for a name that was never a pending binder:

```
- message  : a match on a parameter or field (this name is a def or a consumed binder: give the value its own def)
```

Neither is the case, and the advice sends the reader to a helper def that is not needed. The `order_ban_000` header calls this the order ban; the message didn't.

### The change

`match_flatten` and `body_flatten` carry `past`, the binders closed ahead of a later scrutinee, as `[closed, matched]` pairs; the branch that closes a binder adds the pair when the scrutinee is a pending binder. At the error, a scrutinee found in `past` gets its own message (when the binder matched first is a field a constructor pattern bound, the message says "a field" rather than its generated name):

```
- message  : a match in binder order (t is bound before mv, which was matched first: match t first, or give the value its own def)
```

Everything else keeps its message: a def, a consumed binder, and a binder hidden by a local statement (`order_ban_002` and `_003` are unchanged). `past` is an optional parameter with a default, so the two exported functions' other callers are untouched.

### Checks (Linux x86-64)

- Four pinned tests print the new message, one line each: `order_ban_000` (top level), `order_ban_001` (nested in a constructor arm), `dead_residue_elision_003` ("out-of-order nested matches", its header says) and `error_window_substituted_scrutinee`. In the last one the source matches `y`, a var-column substitute for `a`, and the message names the binders underneath, `a` and `b`; if you'd rather it name `y`, the span is there to do it. `order_ban_004` is the issue's nested case.
- Over `tests/flatten`, `tests/check` and `tests/parse` (631 files), `bend f.bend`'s output is the same on main and here, file by file, except those four message lines.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes 47 / 47; `bend.ts` is at 43428 of its 48000 ttok.

title: The BendTT kernel rejects what bend2 accepts
body:
<!-- SUPERSEDED (2026-09-28). The same bug is already reported as
     https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/1133 (opened 2026-09-27 18:54 UTC —
     after our duplicate check, but before our report was delivered), with the
     author's elaborator-side fix in PR #1136. Do NOT file this as a new issue:
     post COMMENT_1133.md as a comment on #1133 instead. This file is kept for
     reference; its attachments are reused by the comment. -->

# The BendTT kernel rejects what bend2 accepts: an affine let bound to `Equal.cong` with a λ motive and non-variable arguments fails `--verdict` with "an annotated term"

## What I did

Bend 2.0.32 (Linux x86_64). A proof binds a `cong` step with a λ motive to a duplicable (`+`) let, and the motive is applied to arguments that are not variables — the natural shape for "rewrite under a function" steps (`affine_cong_repro.bend`):

```python
import Base

def mini(+a: Nat) -> {Nat.add(a, Nat.add(a, a)) == Nat.add(a, Nat.add(a, a)) : Nat}:
  +p = Equal.cong(Nat, Nat, (z) => Nat.add(a, z), Nat.add(a, a), Nat.add(a, a), {==})
  p

def main() -> Nat:
  0n
```

```sh
bend affine_cong_repro.bend          # checks the file, runs main
bend affine_cong_repro.bend --verdict
```

## What I expected

`ALL PROOFS CHECK` from both commands: `bend` accepts the file (it prints `0n` and exits 0), so the kernel should agree — that is the point of `--verdict`.

## What happened

```text
$ bend affine_cong_repro.bend
0n

$ bend affine_cong_repro.bend --verdict
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Sorry - this is a mismatch between the TypeScript implementation, and the formalized BendTT kernel. Your proofs may or may not be correct, and we cannot validate them yet. This will be addressed in a future update. Meanwhile, feel free to open an issue to report this bug.
```

Running the kernel directly on the elaboration (`bend affine_cong_repro.bend -o r.bendtt`, then `bendtt r.bendtt`, where `bendtt` is the kernel binary the CLI caches for `--verdict`, or one built from `bend2/bendtt.lean` as shown in Verification) localizes it:

```text
SOME PROOFS FAIL
In mini:
expected: an annotated term
observed: λx1 => ((Nat.add x0) x1)
```

The elaborated def is:

```text
mini : ∀+x0 : Nat -> {(Nat.add x0 (Nat.add x0 x0)) == (Nat.add x0 (Nat.add x0 x0)) : Nat} =
  λ+x0 => !+x1 = (Equal.cong -Nat -Nat -λx2 => (Nat.add x0 x2) -(Nat.add x0 x0) -(Nat.add x0 x0) {==}); x1
```

A standalone kernel-level repro — the elaboration above plus its dependencies, as `bendtt_affine_cong_repro.bendtt`:

```text
Nat : *2 =
  Σx0 : <Zero, Succ> -> (Nat.arms x0)

Nat.arms : ∀x0 : <Zero, Succ> -> *2 =
  λ{.Zero: <()>; λ{.Succ: Σx0 : Nat -> <()>; λ{}}}

Nat.add : ∀x0 : Nat -> ∀x1 : Nat -> Nat =
  λ{(,): λ{.Zero: λ{(): λx0 => x0; λ{}}; λ{.Succ: λ{(,): λx0 => λ{(): λx1 => (.Succ, ((Nat.add x0 x1), ())); λ{}}}; λ{}}}}

Equal.cong : ∀-x0 : *1 -> ∀-x1 : *1 -> ∀-x2 : ∀x2 : x0 -> x1 -> ∀-x3 : x0 -> ∀-x4 : x0 -> ∀x5 : {x3 == x4 : x0} -> {(x2 x3) == (x2 x4) : x1} =
  λ-x0 => λ-x1 => λ-x2 => λ-x3 => λ-x4 => λx5 => %x5 : x6, x7 => {(x2 x3) == (x2 x6) : x1}; {==}

mini : ∀+x0 : Nat -> {(Nat.add x0 (Nat.add x0 x0)) == (Nat.add x0 (Nat.add x0 x0)) : Nat} =
  λ+x0 => !+x1 = (Equal.cong -Nat -Nat -λx2 => (Nat.add x0 x2) -(Nat.add x0 x0) -(Nat.add x0 x0) {==}); x1
```

```sh
bendtt bendtt_affine_cong_repro.bendtt   # SOME PROOFS FAIL (In mini: an annotated term)
```

The control (`bendtt_linear_ok.bendtt`) is the same file with the let's quantity changed from `!+` (duplicable) to `!` (linear):

```text
mini : ∀+x0 : Nat -> {(Nat.add x0 (Nat.add x0 x0)) == (Nat.add x0 (Nat.add x0 x0)) : Nat} =
  λ+x0 => !x1 = (Equal.cong -Nat -Nat -λx2 => (Nat.add x0 x2) -(Nat.add x0 x0) -(Nat.add x0 x0) {==}); x1
```

```sh
bendtt bendtt_linear_ok.bendtt            # ALL PROOFS CHECK
```

It needs all three parts: a `+` on the let (the linear control above checks), a λ motive, and non-variable arguments (hoisting them into their own lets also checks — the elim rule's variable arm applies; see Workaround).

## Where it comes from

Reading `bend2/bendtt.lean` at v2.0.32:

1. `Term.infer`'s `App` rule instantiates the function's codomain with `Term.inst B x`, without β-reducing, so instantiating `cong`'s result type `{(x2 x3) == (x2 x4) : x1}` at a λ motive leaves β-redexes **inside the type** — `(λx2 => …) (Nat.add x0 x0)`. That is fine for `wnf`/`conv`/`fit`, which β-reduce.
2. The `Let` rule rechecks `V : *2` when `q == Q2` (the `+` case), and checking an `Eql` type rechecks its two sides.
3. Checking a redex `App q (λ…) (t…)` falls through to the catch-all `infer`, and `infer` has no rule for a λ-headed application — only `check` mode can type a λ, against an expected type. Hence "an annotated term".
4. The check-mode **elim** rule that would handle it, `App q f (Var i)`, only fires when the argument is syntactically a variable — which is why the variable-argument variant of the same proof passes.

So the TS elaborator produces a term the TS checker accepts, but the kernel's algorithmic rules cannot re-derive its declarative typing, and the verdict reports a mismatch.

A tempting one-line fix — teach `infer` to β-reduce (`infer (App _ (Lam _ g) x) := infer (inst g x)`) — is **unsound against the declarative semantics**: it would accept redexes whose argument is untyped garbage whenever the λ's binder is unused, while the declarative `app` rule types both sides. I tried it; `theorem chk` cannot be proven for it.

## Workaround

Bind the `cong` step once per use (two linear lets instead of one duplicable let), or hoist the non-variable arguments into their own lets so the elim rule's variable arm applies. Both check under `--verdict` today; the attached real-world proof (2.8k lines, 12 laws of an mpn arithmetic library) ships with the split applied.

## Proposed fix

Patch against v2.0.32, `bend2/bendtt.lean` (also attached as `bendtt_elim_patch.diff`). It generalizes the elim rule from variable arguments to any argument:

```diff
--- a/bend2/bendtt.lean
+++ b/bend2/bendtt.lean
@@ -252,6 +252,16 @@
   | Efq       => true
   | _         => false
 
+-- the elim rule's motive: a variable argument abstracts the goal by pick
+-- (the goal may depend on it); any other argument cannot be named by
+-- the goal, which takes it as its constant codomain, lifted
+def Term.elim_P (x : Term) (T : Term) : Term :=
+  match x with
+  | Var i => Term.ren (Ren.pick i) T
+  | Ref _ | Ann _ _ | Let _ _ _ | Typ _ | All _ _ _ | Lam _ _ | App _ _ _
+  | Sig _ _ _ | Tup _ _ _ | Lab _ | Prj _ | Mat _ _ _ | Efq | Eql _ _ _
+  | Enu _ | Rfl | Rwt _ _ _ => Term.ren Nat.succ T
+
 -- a former whose parts may bind a variable
 def Term.binds : Term → Bool
   | All .. | Lam .. | Sig .. | Rwt .. => true
@@ -1025,9 +1035,12 @@
 -- ------------------------------------------------------- rwt
 -- Γ ⊢ %e : x, h => P; f : T
 --
--- Γ ⊢ x : A   Γ ⊢ f : ∀q s:A -> T[x := s]    f's head is a λ or a λ-match
--- -------------------------------------------------------------- elim
+-- Γ ⊢ x : A   Γ ⊢ f : ∀q s:A -> P   f's head is a λ or a λ-match
+-- ------------------------------------------------- elim
 -- Γ ⊢ (f q x) : T
+-- (P is T with x abstracted when x is a variable, so T may depend on
+-- it; any other argument cannot be named by T, so P is T lifted, its
+-- constant codomain)
 --
 -- Γ ⊢ x : U   U ≤ T
 -- ----------------- any
@@ -1106,13 +1119,12 @@
       Ctx.fit ck c (Term.inst (Term.inst P (Term.ren Nat.succ e)) b) T
       Term.check ck n c f (Term.inst (Term.inst P Rfl) a)
     | E => Ctx.fail c "an equation" E
-  | n + 1, c, App q f (Var i), T =>
+  | n + 1, c, App q f x, T =>
     if Term.takes (Term.unspine f []).1 then do
-      let A ← Term.infer ck n c (Var i)
-      let P := Term.ren (Ren.pick i) T
-      Term.check ck n c f (All q A P)
+      let A ← Term.infer ck n c x
+      Term.check ck n c f (All q A (Term.elim_P x T))
     else do
-      let U ← Term.infer ck n c (App q f (Var i))
+      let U ← Term.infer ck n c (App q f x)
       Ctx.fit ck c U T
   | n + 1, c, t, T => do
     let U ← Term.infer ck n c t
@@ -1657,6 +1669,15 @@
     funext j; by_cases h : j = i <;> simp [Ren.pick, Subst.one, h]
   rw [Term.inst, sub_ren, this, sub_var]
 
+-- a lifted type is its own constant codomain: instantiating it with any
+-- argument gives it back, so the elim rule can check a λ-headed redex
+-- (App q f x, x not a variable) against T by checking f against
+-- ∀q _:A -> (lift T), with A the inferred type of x
+theorem lift_inst : Term.inst (Term.ren Nat.succ T) x = T := by
+  have : Subst.one x ∘ Nat.succ = Var := by
+    funext j; cases j <;> rfl
+  rw [Term.inst, sub_ren, this, sub_var]
+
 theorem unspine_spine : Term.unspine (Term.spine t xs) [] = Term.unspine t xs := by
   induction xs generalizing t with
   | nil => rfl
@@ -2206,6 +2227,24 @@
   have ⟨_, h1, h2⟩ := e' ▸ wnf_conv (c := c) (T := D) hcl
   .conv (.conv h (.inl ⟨_, pars_all h2, pars_all h1⟩)) (wnf_fits hcl e).1
 
+-- the elim rule, declaratively: f checked against ∀q _:A -> elim_P x T
+-- and x checked against A type the application (App q f x) with T, be x
+-- a variable (pick, so the goal may depend on it) or any other term (the
+-- goal's lift, its constant codomain)
+theorem elim_sound {bk : Book} {σ : Subst} {Γ : List Term} {q : Quan} {A T f x}
+    (hf : Typed bk Γ (Term.sub σ f)
+      (All q (Term.sub σ A) (Term.sub (Subst.up σ) (Term.elim_P x T))))
+    (hx : Typed bk Γ (Term.sub σ x) (Term.sub σ A)) :
+    Typed bk Γ (Term.sub σ (App q f x)) (Term.sub σ T) := by
+  have e : Term.inst (Term.sub (Subst.up σ) (Term.elim_P x T)) (Term.sub σ x)
+      = Term.sub σ T := by
+    cases x <;> simp only [Term.elim_P] <;> first
+      | (rw [← inst_sub]; exact congrArg (Term.sub σ) pick_inst)
+      | (rw [sub_succ, lift_inst])
+  have h := Typed.app hf hx
+  rw [e] at h
+  exact h
+
 -- each checker rule lands on its Typed rule, through Ctx.drop
 theorem chk (hcl : Sees ck bk) (n : Nat) : ∀ c t T, Ctx.ok bk c →
     (Term.infer ck n c t = .ok T → Chk bk c t T) ∧
@@ -2259,18 +2298,8 @@
     · rename_i e
       obtain ⟨hp, h3, h2⟩ := h
       exact snd_wnf2 hcl e rfl (.lam hp (fun e => C _ _ (h3 e)) (B h2))
-    · rename_i x
-      cases x <;> simp only [Term.check] at h
-      case Var i =>
-        split at h
-        · simp at h
-          obtain ⟨A, h1, h2⟩ := h
-          have e := congrArg (Term.sub (Ctx.drop c)) (pick_inst (T := T) (i := i))
-          rw [inst_sub] at e
-          rw [Chk, ← e]
-          exact .app (C _ _ h2) (I _ _ h1)
-        · exact A h
-      all_goals exact A h
+    · obtain ⟨A, h1, h2⟩ := h
+      exact elim_sound (C _ _ h2) (I _ _ h1)
     · rename_i e
       obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := h
       exact .conv (.sig (C _ _ h1) (B h2)) (wnf_fits hcl e).1
```

- `Term.elim_P x T` — the motive: `Term.ren (Ren.pick i) T` when `x` is `Var i` (unchanged behavior, the goal may depend on it), and the lift `Term.ren Nat.succ T` otherwise — the goal cannot depend on a term it does not name, so the lift is its constant codomain.
- The rule `App q f x` checks `f` against `∀q _:A -> elim_P x T`, with `A` inferred from `x`.
- `lift_inst` (`inst (ren succ T) x = T`) and `elim_sound` carry the soundness argument, and `theorem chk` still compiles — the kernel's own soundness proof accepts the new rule.

The old variable case is byte-for-byte the same rule, so nothing that checked before can change verdict (the `takes`-false arm is also unchanged).

## Verification

| `affine_cong_repro.bend` | ok | **mismatch** | `ALL PROOFS CHECK` |

| real proof, workaround kept; `mpn.bend`, `mpn_par.bend`, `sym.bend` | ok | check | check |
| `demos/proof_numerics` | ok | checks | checks |
| 155 elaborated files from `tests/{check,proof,base}` | — | identical verdicts, 0 differences | identical verdicts, 0 differences |
| `lean` compile of `bendtt.lean` incl. `theorem chk` | — | clean | clean |

Build the patched kernel with the elan toolchain the CLI already uses:

```sh
lean -c bendtt.c bendtt.lean && leanc -O3 -DNDEBUG bendtt.c -o bendtt
BENDTT=./bendtt bend affine_cong_repro.bend --verdict
```

## Attachments

- `bendtt_elim_patch.diff` — the patch above as a standalone file, for `git apply`
- `bendtt_patched.lean` — the full patched `bend2/bendtt.lean`, for building directly
- `PROOF_workaround_reverted.bend` — the real 2,789-line proof with the workaround reverted: the stock kernel fails in `Wb.limb_mul_eq` with the same message, the patched kernel reports `ALL PROOFS CHECK`
- `affine_cong_repro.bend`, `bendtt_affine_cong_repro.bendtt`, `bendtt_linear_ok.bendtt` — the repros, also inline above

## Side note: an environment failure reports the same "mismatch"

While triaging this on a 3 GB machine I first hit a different failure with the same message: `kernel_check` sets `LEAN_STACK_SIZE_KB: "4194304"` unconditionally, the kernel binary then aborts at startup (`lean::exception: failed to create thread: Resource temporarily unavailable`, exit 134), and the CLI reports it as a mismatch between the implementations. A spawn failure or empty kernel output is an environment problem, not a TS/kernel disagreement; distinguishing those (or catching the thread error) would save users a misleading diagnosis. This note is separate from the bug above — with enough memory the repro's mismatch is real and deterministic.

title: 2.0.32 makes each read of a shared Array two atomic loads: frames 3 to 4x slower on Metal
body:
Since 2.0.32 (`573002f0`, the fix of #975), `blk_loc` reads a shared Array's redirect through `term_peek`. That read is `rfc_view`: two relaxed atomic loads of the cell's halves, plus a device fence when the count is one. Every `Array.get` on an Array that a fork shares now pays it.

What the atomic load costs depends on the target:
- On the CPU, a relaxed load is a plain load.
- On CUDA, `a32_load` is a volatile load.
- On Metal, it is a real atomic load, and that is where the time goes.

None of `bench/runtime` shares an Array (`BLK_SHR` is 0 in all 16), so the perf gate cannot see this.

## What you did

`shared_reads.bend`: one `!` over 65,536 leaves, each reading one shared `Array<U32>` 256 times.

```bend
import Base

# Every leaf of a fork reads the one Array the fork shares, 256 times.
def walk(fuel: Nat, +i: U32, +acc: U32, r: Array<U32> & U32) -> Array<U32> & U32:
  match fuel:
    case 0n:
      (a, x) = r
      (a, (acc + x : U32))
    case 1n+f:
      (a, x) = r
      +j = ((i * 1664525 : U32) + 1013904223 : U32)
      walk(f, j, (acc + x : U32), Array.get(U32, a, j))

def add(l: Array<U32> & U32, r: Array<U32> & U32) -> Array<U32> & U32:
  (a, x) = l
  (b, y) = r
  (Array.join(U32, a, b), (x + y : U32))

@unsafe
def fan(+d: Nat, +a: Array<U32>, +k: U32) -> Array<U32> & U32:
  match d:
    case 0n:
      walk(256n, k, 0, Array.get(U32, a, k))
    case 1n+p:
      l r = fan(p, a, (k * 2 : U32)) fan(p, a, ((k * 2 : U32) + 1 : U32))
      add(l, r)

def done(r: Array<U32> & U32) -> IO(Unit):
  (a, x) = r
  IO.print(U32.show(x))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  done(fan!(16n, [1 : U32*4096n], 0))

#|16842752
```

```sh
bend shared_reads.bend -o shared_reads && ./shared_reads
```

## What happened

The output is right on both builds, but the `!` takes 6.6 times as long on 2.0.32. Bendcraft, a voxel ray caster whose every pixel reads one shared `Array<U32>`, draws the same pixels 3 to 4 times slower.

GPU time (each round's command buffer, `GPUEndTime - GPUStartTime`), on an Apple M5 (8 GPU cores):

| | `84a16cf3` (before 2.0.32) | `b2111cf4` (main) | main / before | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `shared_reads.bend`, the `!` | 1.7 ms | 13.2 ms | 6.6x | [5.7, 8.0] |
| Bendcraft, 512 x 512 | 8.0 ms | 28.6 ms | 4.0x | [2.9, 4.3] |
| Bendcraft, 512 x 512, 300 blocks built | 8.1 ms | 26.1 ms | 3.7x | [2.6, 4.2] |
| Bendcraft, 735 x 398 | 18.8 ms | 54.4 ms | 2.9x | [2.2, 3.8] |
| Bendcraft, 960 x 540 | 36.4 ms | 106.4 ms | 2.9x | [2.3, 4.0] |
| Bendcraft, 1470 x 796 | 76.2 ms | 222.3 ms | 2.9x | [2.5, 3.4] |
| Bendcraft, 1920 x 1080 | 152.1 ms | 427.0 ms | 2.9x | [2.4, 3.1] |

How these were measured:
- Runs go in pairs, before then after and after then before in turn: 10 pairs of each program, on a machine in use. A Bendcraft row is the fastest frame of its size.
- The machine's load inflates the fast build most. On a quiet machine, the bench's own readout was 47 ms against 204 at 1470 x 796.

## Which part costs

I rebuilt Bendcraft's 2.0.32 C with other bodies for `blk_loc`. Every variant gives the same checksums. The time is the fastest frame at 1470 x 796.

| `blk_loc` reads the cell as | ms |
|---|---|
| one plain 64-bit load (before 2.0.32) | 48 |
| two volatile plain `u32` halves | 48 |
| a volatile plain high half and a relaxed atomic low half | 188 |
| two relaxed atomic halves, no fence | 203 |
| `term_peek` (2.0.32: atomic halves through a volatile local, a fence at count one) | 207 |
| one plain load, and a fence when the count is one | 69 |

So the atomic load is the cost; neither the volatile local nor the width is. A fence in the read path costs on its own too.

A fix that keeps #975 fixed follows as a PR.

## Environment

- `bend --version`: 2.0.32 (main at `b2111cf4`), before it `84a16cf3`
- macOS 26.6.2, Apple M5 (8 GPU cores)

title: A device peek reads a redirect with one plain load, as before 2.0.32 (#1139)
body:
Fixes #1139 and keeps #975 fixed. On main (`b2111cf4`). One commit: one line of `bend2/comp.ts` and the comment above `rfc_view`, 63,573 → 63,595 ttok.

## Why

2.0.32 reads a redirect cell as two atomic halves, so that no read overlaps the count's atomic adds (#975). `blk_loc` now reads through `term_peek`, so every read of a shared Array costs two atomic loads, plus a fence when the count is one.
- On the CPU, a relaxed load is a plain load.
- On CUDA, `a32_load` is a volatile load.
- On Metal, it is a real atomic load, and a Bendcraft frame went from 47 to 204 ms (#1139).

## What changes

On the device, `term_peek` reads the cell with one plain load, `H[loc] >> 24`. That is how the device reads every other heap word, and how `blk_loc` read before 2.0.32.
- **The read is exact.** The loc cannot change while the peek holds its share.
- **The host is untouched.** It still peeks through `rfc_view`, so its emitted C is main's (checked by diffing it), and ThreadSanitizer sees what it sees on main.
- **`ctr_take` and `rfc_view` are unchanged on every target.** A take still reads the count atomically, and acquires at count one before it frees the redirect.
- **A device peek no longer fences at count one.**
  - That fence only mattered to a write through a handle that was shared, such as `Array.set` after an `@unsafe` fork. The same write races whenever the other handle is still alive, and before 2.0.32 the device did not fence there either.
  - I can put it back in `arr_op`'s write path if you want it.
- **Below Metal 3.2**, `DEV` is plain `device`. The peek is then as coherent as every other plain heap read, as `blk_loc` was before 2.0.32.

## Tried

- **A redirect of two words.** This is #975's other suggestion: the loc in one word, read plainly on every target, and the count in the next, touched only by atomics. It is race-free by construction and made Bendcraft 4.4x faster, but it lost badly on hashmap with threads.
  - A redirect grows from class 0 to class 1.
  - hashmap's redirects per table then pass `KEEP_WORDS` and share their class with its nodes, so blocks move between threads and the counts' atomics fight over cache lines.

  | hashmap, `--gpu off` | main | two words | two words, class 3 |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 1 thread | 2096 ms | 1811 ms | 1982 ms |
  | 2 threads | 1068 ms | 1683 ms | 1053 ms |
  | 8 threads | 456 ms | 1118 ms | 657 ms |

- **A volatile load under `rfc_view` on Metal.** It was as fast as this, but `ctr_take` would then decide to free or share from a count that is not read atomically. It would also be a load form that no M1 has compiled, beside the M1 note on `a32_load`.

## Checked

- **ThreadSanitizer** finds nothing on #975's repro, on `tests/rfc/*`, on #1139's repro, or on a tree that two parallel walks share. The outputs are right.
  - The build: `clang -x c -std=gnu11 -O1 -g -fsanitize=thread`, run with `--threads 2` and `--threads 8`, `--gpu off`.
  - 2.0.29 reports #975's race on the same build.
- **Every test with `#|` lines**, built natively and run on the M5, gives the same results as main. 661 match their `#|` lines on both; 13 differ on both, only because my runner reads stdout alone (no stderr, no exit codes) and has a display.
- **`bun gates/repo.ts`**: 47/47.
- **No bench in `bench/runtime` shares an Array**, which is why the perf gate could not see this. I can add #1139's repro as a bench if you want it gated.

## Measured

The method is #1132's:
- Apple M5 (8 GPU cores), macOS 26.6.2, on a machine in use.
- Each program is emitted by `b2111cf4` and by this branch.
- The time is the GPU's, summed over each round's command buffer (`GPUEndTime - GPUStartTime`).
- Runs go in pairs, before then after and after then before in turn. Each row gives the median ratio of before over after, and a bootstrap 95% interval of it.
- The CPU was not re-timed, since its C is main's.

**Bendcraft** (`test/bench.bend`, the fastest frame of each size, every checksum equal to main's), 10 pairs:

| frame | main | this | main / this | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 512 x 512 | 25.3 ms | 7.0 ms | 3.75 | [3.00, 4.40] |
| 512 x 512, 300 blocks built | 24.9 ms | 6.8 ms | 3.69 | [2.94, 4.27] |
| 735 x 398 | 53.1 ms | 14.6 ms | 3.68 | [3.04, 4.02] |
| 960 x 540 | 103.6 ms | 26.1 ms | 3.97 | [3.33, 4.26] |
| 1470 x 796 | 215.1 ms | 58.5 ms | 3.77 | [3.68, 3.90] |
| 1920 x 1080 | 449.8 ms | 122.9 ms | 3.58 | [3.22, 4.43] |

Against main with only `blk_loc`'s line put back to the plain load of `84a16cf3` (8 pairs), every size read 0.97 to 1.06, and each interval held 1.

**#1139's repro and a shared tree** on the GPU, 12 pairs. The tree is `tests/rfc/share_forked.bend` with 2^22 leaves and its work in a `!`.

**bench/runtime on the GPU**, 10 pairs, with the flags of `gates/perf.ts`. None of these shares an Array, and every output equals main's.
