title: The JS lane lowers String.reverse's loop to a flat reverse
body:
## What

Base's `String.reverse.go` compiles to a loop that prepends one code point at a
time, `acc = h + acc`. In JavaScriptCore every `+` is a rope node, so a reversed
string reaches the host as a chain of one-character nodes, all of them alive while
the string is. A core that builds a value backwards and reverses it at the end
pays for that chain.

`js_reverse` (in `comp.ts`, just above `js_def`) replaces a def of that shape by

```js
return Array.from(s).reverse().join("") + acc;
```

— the same value over code points, computed flat. Every other def is left alone.

The def supplies the precondition: a lone tail loop whose two live parameters are
both `String` (`fun_of`, `ty_adt`, `loop_of`). The def's own emitted lines supply
the names, each one back-referenced, so a def that only looks like this one does
not match. Nothing outside the JS emitter changes — the C lane still emits the
loop, and the C output of every test in the suite that builds a C program is
byte-identical.

## How it was found

The measurements below come from an RFC 4180 CSV parser I have written in Bend
as a proved core, to see what the language is like to build and prove in. It
builds each field backwards and calls `String.reverse` on it, which is exactly
the pattern that makes the rope chain large — that is the whole reason this
change exists. Nothing in the change depends on that parser, and the benchmark is
nothing more than a real core of a few hundred lines, so that the numbers below
come from parsing rather than from a microbenchmark.

## Measured

The core, 10 MB of CSV, under bun on 2.0.32. Peak RSS is the kernel's own
number for the whole process, so it is directly comparable between the two
builds; rows are counted in both to show the answer did not change.

| input | build | peak RSS | rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 MB | as shipped | 108 MiB | 42,254 |
| 1 MB | with this change | 67 MiB | 42,254 |
| 10 MB | as shipped | 1.06 GiB | 422,536 |
| 10 MB | with this change | 0.36 GiB | 422,536 |

A 67% drop at 10 MB, and the per-byte cost falls from about 113 to about 70
bytes. Parse time does not move (975–1196 ms either way; that is the state
machine, not the strings). Both builds emit the same module except for the one
function, and the C output is byte-identical.

## Tests

`js_reverse_lower` pins the value of Base's own def, of a def with the same body
under another name, and of one whose parameters are the other way round —
astral characters included, where a reverse over UTF-16 units would differ.

`js_reverse_keep` pins two defs that only look like `String.reverse.go`: one whose
accumulator takes a `"!"` between the head and the rest, one whose accumulator is
the third parameter. Both must keep their loop. Each of the three ways this
pass can be got wrong was checked by breaking the pass deliberately and watching
the relevant test fail: reversing over UTF-16 units, binding the two roles by
position instead of by use, and accepting any accumulator expression.

## Not run here

`gates/test.ts` (the cluster gate) and `gates/repo.ts` did not run: the first
needs the mini cluster, the second needs `ttok`, which is not installed on this
machine. The JS lane was run locally instead — 681 of 682 tests pass, and
`process_run`'s two descendant cases fail on a pristine compiler too.

title: U32.to_nat widens to u64 in C, so Nat arithmetic on a u32 local no longer wraps at 2^32
body:
**Disclosure:** I wrote this change with Claude Code (an AI coding agent). It touches only `bend2/comp.ts` (one template) and adds one test; `bend2/bend.ts` is untouched.

### Bug

In compiled C, `U32.to_nat` emitted the `u32` unchanged. When the word is kept as an unboxed `u32` local (it is used more than once in the function), `Nat` arithmetic on the converted value runs in 32 bits before `nat_chk` sees it, so it wraps at 2^32:

```bend
import Base

def b(+x: U32) -> String:
  U32.show(x) ++ " " ++ Nat.show(1n+U32.to_nat(x))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(b(4294967295))
```

| | output |
|---|---|
| interpreter | `4294967295 4294967296` |
| JS | `4294967295 4294967296` |
| C, 2.0.28 and 2.0.32 / main `b2111cf` | `4294967295 0` |

`Nat.add(U32.to_nat(x), U32.to_nat(y))` wraps the same way (`4294967294` instead of `8589934590`); `Nat.add(U32.to_nat(x), 1n)`, `Nat.mul`, a single use of `x`, or a `Nat` helper function all compile correctly. We hit it as wrong U64 division results in verified code (the source and its proofs are right; only the compiled binary differed).

### Fix

```diff
   u32_to_nat: {
-    C:  "$0",
+    C:  "((u64)$0)",
```

### Test

`tests/compile/u32_to_nat_widen.bend` prints both shapes at `x = y = 2^32 - 1`; interpreter, JS and C now agree (`4294967296` / `8589934590`). It fails on main's C lane without the fix.

I don't have the mini cluster, so I ran locally (Apple M-series): every test under `tests/` that mentions `to_nat` (102 files) built and run on the C backend with main and with this branch — the only difference is the new test (fails before, passes after).

title: Metal: heap_free's error check is an atomic load of one word on every free, 7-12% of the allocating tree benches
body:
On a device, `heap_free` checks the error flag before it frees:

```c
INLINE void heap_free(Env e, u32 cls, u64 loc) {
  if (err_seen(e.mem)) {
    return;
  }
```

`err_seen` is `a32_load(a32_at(H, H_ERROR_CODE))`, so every free on every lane is an atomic load of the same word. On Metal this costs tree-bitonic about 12% of its GPU time and tree-radix about 7%.

I have not sent a PR, because the cheap forms of this read carry risks that are yours to weigh (below).

## What I measured

These numbers come from the emitted C of `c23aa1f4` (#1140 over main `b2111cf4`), with one site changed at a time.
- The time is the GPU's, summed over each round's command buffer (`GPUEndTime - GPUStartTime`).
- Runs alternate: in pairs, before then after and after then before in turn, or, with more than two builds, in an order that rotates and reverses every round. Each row gives the median ratio of before over after, and a bootstrap 95% interval of it.
- Every output equals the unchanged build's.

There are three per-call checks of `err_seen` on the device. On tree-bitonic (`--gpu 768MB`, 12 rounds), `heap_free`'s is the whole cost:

| tree-bitonic, the check dropped from | as is / changed | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|
| `heap_free` | 1.128 | [1.115, 1.143] |
| `BLK_ALLOC` | 0.998 | [0.985, 1.000] |
| `FID_EXIT` in the work loop | 0.981 | [0.968, 0.995] |
| all three | 1.125 | [1.114, 1.133] |

Across benches (10 rounds), I compared the build with all three dropped, as a ceiling, against a build that keeps `heap_free`'s check but reads the flag with a volatile load, `*(volatile DEV u32*)a32_at(e.mem, H_ERROR_CODE) != 0`:

| bench | all three dropped | 95% interval | volatile read in `heap_free` | 95% interval |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tree-bitonic | 1.127 | [1.119, 1.138] | 1.116 | [1.104, 1.124] |
| tree-radix | 1.073 | [1.068, 1.085] | 1.070 | [1.066, 1.076] |
| tree-matmul | 1.032 | [1.015, 1.038] | 0.977 | [0.953, 1.001] |
| merkle | 1.008 | [0.992, 1.015] | | |
| hashmap | 0.996 | [0.988, 1.008] | | |
| bfs | 0.997 | [0.988, 1.010] | | |

- tree-matmul's own runs varied from 570 to 667 ms between sessions, so I read its rows as noise.
- A Bendcraft frame did not move: its hot loop does not allocate.

The likely cause is that every lane loads one address atomically on each free, and atomics on one address are served one at a time. A volatile load of the same word can be served from the cache.

## Why I have not sent a PR

- **A volatile device load is a new load form.** At MSL 3.2 it compiles to `air.load.device_coherent.volatile`. No M1 pipeline has compiled it here, and `a32_load`'s comment says M1's pipeline build dies on some load forms. If it did on this one, every `!` on an M1 would fail.
- **Below MSL 3.2, the load is not coherent.** There `DEV` is plain `device`. A lane that posts `ERR_HEAP` with `a32_cmpx` can keep reading 0 from its L1 and go on freeing what its failed allocations left at `HEAP_OFF`, which may write out of bounds.
- **Dropping the check** changes what a lane does after an error, so I only took that as a ceiling.

## Options I see

- **Read the flag with a volatile load on MSL 3.2 and later only**, after the pipeline builds on an M1.
- **Poll the flag in `heap_free` every N frees**, as `err_spun` does in the loops. A lane would then free a few blocks after another lane's error. Its own `ERR_HEAP` would need a local test instead, for example on `heap_alloc_miss` returning `HEAP_OFF`.
- **Keep it as it is**, if 7-12% on the allocating trees is not worth either.

## Environment

- `bend --version`: 2.0.32 (main at `b2111cf4`; measured with #1140 applied)
- macOS 26.6.2, Apple M5 (8 GPU cores)

Written by Claude (Anthropic) with Adriel Santana driving; the numbers are from Adriel's M5.

title: bend -o `<out>.mjs`: also write the type declaration
body:
Follow-up to #1029, closed as done. That issue asked for a Bend file built as an
ES module and type declarations beside it. The module landed in 2.0.32; the
declarations did not.

`bend core.bend -o dist/core.mjs` currently writes only the `.mjs`. Emitting
`<out>.d.mts` alongside it allows TypeScript hosts to typecheck calls against
the compiled module.

For example, given this self-contained core (`core.bend`):

```
import Base

type Slot is Data:
  Slot{start: Nat, end: Nat}

def start(s: Slot) -> Nat:
  match s:
    case Slot{st, e}:
      st

def end(s: Slot) -> Nat:
  match s:
    case Slot{st, e}:
      e

def both(a: Bool, b: Bool) -> Bool:
  match a:
    case True{}:
      b
    case False{}:
      False{}

def hits(+a: Slot, +b: Slot) -> Bool:
  both(Nat.is_lt(start(a), end(b)), Nat.is_lt(start(b), end(a)))

def free(a: Slot, ovl: Bool) -> Bool:
  match ovl:
    case True{}:
      False{}
    case False{}:
      True{}

def fits_go(+a: Slot, taken: List<&2, Slot>, +acc: Bool) -> Bool:
  match taken:
    case Nil{}:
      acc
    case b <> t:
      fits_go(a, t, both(acc, free(a, hits(a, b))))

def fits(+a: Slot, +taken: List<&2, Slot>) -> Bool:
  fits_go(a, taken, True{})
```

Build it, and check a host against it:

```sh
bend core.bend -o dist/core.mjs
```

```ts
// host.ts
import core, { type Slot } from "./dist/core.mjs";

const S = (s: bigint, e: bigint): Slot => ({ $: "Slot", start: s, end: e } as any);
const r: boolean = core.fits(S(9n, 10n), null as any);
```

```
$ bunx tsc --noEmit --skipLibCheck --module esnext --target esnext --moduleResolution bundler host.ts
host.ts(2,33): error TS7016: Could not find a declaration file for module './dist/core.mjs'. '/where/you/built/it/dist/core.mjs' implicitly has an 'any' type.
```

With a matching declaration beside the module, the same command passes with
exit 0. On an invalid call, `tsc` catches the error:

```ts
// bad.ts -- the same core, one call wrong
import core from "./dist/core.mjs";
const r: boolean = core.fits(9n, "not a slot");
```

```
bad.ts(2,30): error TS2345: Argument of type 'bigint' is not assignable to parameter of type 'Slot'.
```

**The module itself is not the problem.** It runs, and its values are ordinary
JS: `Nat` is a `bigint`, `String` is a `string`, and a constructor is
`{ $: "Name", ... }`. In 2.0.32 the module has exactly one export statement:
`export default { ... }` with no named exports. If a declaration declares named
exports instead, a host writing `import { fits }` typechecks at compile time
and then fails at runtime with `SyntaxError: Export named 'fits' not found in module`.
The declaration has to describe exactly what the module exports.

### File naming

For a `.mjs` output, TypeScript resolves `<out>.d.mts`; it never looks for
`<out>.d.ts` beside a `.mjs`. Running `tsc --traceResolution` against this core
confirms that TypeScript searches for `core.mts`, then `core.d.mts`, and stops.
For `bend core.bend -o dist/core.mjs`, the declaration must therefore be written
to `dist/core.d.mts`.

### Declaration rules

I suggest three rules for emission, based on what I have running in `bend-emit`:

- **Derived, never hand-written.** The `type ... is Data:` blocks and `def`
  headers in the source are the inputs, mapping Bend types to the runtime's JS
  encoding. An unmapped type is a compile error naming the def, rather than a
  fallback to `any`.
- **Omitted, not approximated.** A def whose signature cannot be written
  faithfully remains in the module and callable; only its declaration is
  omitted. This covers defs returning `IO(...)`, template parameters (`~f`),
  returning `Data` or `Type`, types computed by a def, or erased parameters (`-A`).
- **Exactly named.** The declared names must be exactly the names the compiled
  module exports, or nothing is written.

### Something that already works

I wrote [bend-emit](https://github.com/nohzafk/bend-emit) for this and have been
using it. Over the core above it writes a 27-line declaration: one `export type`
for `Slot` (as `{$: "Slot"; start: bigint; end: bigint}`), five generic shapes
for Base, one `export declare function` per def, nothing in it written by hand.
It writes that as `core.d.mts` beside its `core.mjs`, which makes `host.ts`
above typecheck and `bad.ts` fail with TS2345.

I offer it in case the mapping logic is useful to reference; Bend does not need
to depend on it.

This belongs in the compiler rather than in an external tool. A tool outside the
compiler has to reconstruct signatures from source text, whereas the Bend
checker already holds every def's signature, parameter erasedness, and datatype
constructor fields in memory. The module half is done; the declaration half is
what is left.

title: `--gpu on` on native Linux says "WSL2's lack" concurrent managed access when cuInit itself failed
body:
## What you did

```
bend gpu_probe_message.bend -o gpu && ./gpu --gpu on
```

inside a Docker container (`nvidia/cuda:13.0.0-devel-ubuntu24.04`, `--runtime=nvidia -e NVIDIA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=all`)
on a native Ubuntu 22.04 host (not WSL), started **without** `--device /dev/nvidia-uvm --device /dev/nvidia-uvm-tools`.

## What happened

```text
$ ./gpu --gpu on
bend: --gpu on, but this binary found no usable GPU (a CUDA GPU needs concurrent managed access, which WSL2's lack)
$ echo $?
1
```

The machine is not WSL2, and the GPU has concurrent managed access. The real failure is earlier: in
that container `cuInit(0)` returns `CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN` (999). A 10-line Driver API probe in the same container:

```text
without --device /dev/nvidia-uvm:  cuInit -> 999 CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN
with    --device /dev/nvidia-uvm:  cuInit -> 0 CUDA_SUCCESS, CU_DEVICE_ATTRIBUTE_CONCURRENT_MANAGED_ACCESS = 1
```

With `--device /dev/nvidia-uvm --device /dev/nvidia-uvm-tools` the same binary prints `1048576` under `--gpu on`
(and the build writes `gpu.gpu`, which it does not do in the failing container).

The CUDA error is an environment problem, not a Bend one. The problem is the message. `gpu_probe`
(`bend2/comp.ts`, the `BEND_CUDA` branch) ignores the return codes of `cuInit`, `cuDeviceGet`,
`cuDevicePrimaryCtxRetain` and `cuCtxSetCurrent`, and returns a single bool. `main` then prints a fixed
explanation for every failure, and that explanation names WSL2. Printing the failing call and its `cuGetErrorName` would have
pointed straight at the driver/container setup. #1064 point 2 asked for this ("distinguish no driver, no device, no managed memory, no
concurrent managed access, and context failure"). The fix for #1064 changed the text, but it is still one reason for every
failure.

Default runs (no `--gpu`) fall back to the CPU silently in the failing container. This is documented
("A machine without a GPU runs `!` on the CPU"), so it is not reported here.

## The file

```python
import Base

def pow2(+n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      1
    case 1n+p:
      a b = pow2(p) pow2(p)
      (a + b : U32)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(pow2!(20n)))
```

(saved alongside as `gpu_probe_message.bend`; it is the GUIDE's example)

## bend --version

bend 2.0.32. Reproduced with the release checkout (commit d2066a52) and with main at
b2111cf4 (2026-09-27), which also reports `bend 2.0.32`.

## uname -sm

Linux x86_64. Container: Ubuntu 24.04, CUDA 13.0 (nvcc V13.0.48). Host: Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 6.8.0-138-generic,
2x RTX 4090, driver 580.65.06, Docker 28.3.3 with the NVIDIA runtime.

## clang --version (the first line)

Ubuntu clang version 19.1.1 (1ubuntu1~24.04.2)

---
Internal notes (not for the issue):
- Repro run on nathan-lambda, `~/bend_bugrepro/run.sh` + `probe.c`, image `bend-gpu` (docker/Dockerfile.bendgpu).
- Duplicate search: "no usable GPU", "WSL2", "concurrent managed", "cuInit", "gpu on", "CUDA docker", "nvidia-uvm".
  Closest: #1064 (closed, WSL2, asked for per-reason diagnostics), #1066 (closed, WSL2 capacity). No open issue covers it.
- Severity is low (a diagnostic). The maintainers may consider it covered by #1064. It is still worth filing, because the current text
  is actively misleading on the platform they support best.

Chan.try_send and Chan.try_recv: channel operations that answer at once
body:
### What Bend should do ```python # Answers at once. A full or closed channel hands the value back, since a # value is affine and a failed send must not consume it. def Chan.try_send(-A: Type, chan: Chan(A), value: A) -> IO(Maybe<&1, A>) # Answers at once: a value, Empty{} while none is ready, Closed{} once the # channel is closed and drained. type Chan.Poll is Kind(a): Got{value: A} Empty{} Closed{} def Chan.try_recv(-A: Type, chan: Chan(A)) -> IO(Chan.Poll) # A queue that drops under load instead of blocking its producers: def record(+queue: Chan(Span), span: Span) -> IO(Unit): do IO: back : Maybe<&1, Span> <- Chan.try_send(Span, queue, span) count_dropped(back) ``` ### Why Today a send parks while the channel is full and a receive parks while it is empty. `IO.within` bounds how long the caller waits, but the losing operation is not cancelled (WONTFIX, #1034), so it still acts after the deadline, on both lanes: - **A receive under `IO.within` takes the next value and drops it.** The first program prints `within: timeout`, `send 1: True`, `send 2: True`, `recv: 2`: the timed-out receive took 1 and handed it to `IO.within`'s join channel, which was already closed, so 1 is gone although `Chan.send` answered `True`. - **A send under `IO.within` delivers after the deadline.** The second program prints `within send 2: timeout`, `recv: 1`, `recv: 2`. Until a receiver comes, the parked send keeps the value, so a producer that moves on after a timeout piles up parked sends. So a bounded queue that drops under load cannot be written: the producer either blocks or loses values that were reported as sent. That queue is the core of every logging, metrics and tracing pipeline and of load shedding in a server. OpenTelemetry's batch span processor, for example, must drop spans once its queue (2048 by default) is full rather than block the application, and must not grow memory without bound. With `Chan.try_send` the producer answers at once and counts the drop. With `Chan.try_recv` an exporter drains what is queued without parking, so it needs no deadline race at all; #1122 shows that a deadline cannot be relied on while channels are busy anyway. A library cannot add these. The channel's state lives in Base's `chan` effect, `IO.fork`, `IO.join` and `IO.within` are built on Base's `Chan`, and a library's own channel would need a handle type of its own (#825). Neither operation parks, so neither needs cancellation. Go (`select` with `default`), Rust (`try_send`/`try_recv`), Java (`offer`/`poll`), Kotlin (`trySend`/`tryReceive`) and .NET (`TryWrite`/`TryRead`) all provide them.
The receive: bend main.bend and bend main.bend -o main && ./main print the same ```python import Base def show(got: Maybe<&1, U32>) -> String: match got: case None{}: "none" case Some{n}: U32.show(n) def show_within(got: Maybe<&1, Maybe<&1, U32>>) -> String: match got: case None{}: "timeout" case Some{inner}: show(inner) def producer(+c: Chan(U32)) -> IO(Unit): do IO: u : Unit <- IO.sleep(50) a : Bool <- Chan.send(U32, c, 1) v : Unit <- IO.print("send 1: " ++ Bool.show(a)) b : Bool <- Chan.send(U32, c, 2) IO.print("send 2: " ++ Bool.show(b)) def run(c: Chan(U32)) -> IO(Unit): +ch = c do IO: w : Maybe<&1, Maybe<&1, U32>> <- IO.within(Maybe<&1, U32>, 10, Chan.recv(U32, ch)) u : Unit <- IO.print("within: " ++ show_within(w)) s : Unit <- IO.spawn(Unit, producer(ch)) r : Maybe<&1, U32> <- Chan.recv(U32, ch) IO.print("recv: " ++ show(r)) def main() -> IO(Unit): do IO: c : Chan(U32) <- Chan.new(U32, 0) run(c) ``` ```text within: timeout send 1: True send 2: True recv: 2 ```
The send: both lanes print the same ```python import Base def show(got: Maybe<&1, U32>) -> String: match got: case None{}: "none" case Some{n}: U32.show(n) def show_sent(got: Maybe<&1, Bool>) -> String: match got: case None{}: "timeout" case Some{sent}: Bool.show(sent) def run(c: Chan(U32)) -> IO(Unit): +ch = c do IO: a : Bool <- Chan.send(U32, ch, 1) w : Maybe<&1, Bool> <- IO.within(Bool, 10, Chan.send(U32, ch, 2)) u : Unit <- IO.print("within send 2: " ++ show_sent(w)) r1 : Maybe<&1, U32> <- Chan.recv(U32, ch) v : Unit <- IO.print("recv: " ++ show(r1)) r2 : Maybe<&1, U32> <- Chan.recv(U32, ch) IO.print("recv: " ++ show(r2)) def main() -> IO(Unit): do IO: c : Chan(U32) <- Chan.new(U32, 1) run(c) ``` ```text within send 2: timeout recv: 1 recv: 2 ```

`-o x.mjs`: a Nat leaves through a return type the marshal cannot resolve as a number, not a BigInt
body:
bend 2.0.32, macOS arm64, bun 1.4.2.

GUIDE.md says a `Nat` crossing into JS is a `BigInt`, and the out-marshal does convert
one when the return type is concrete. It does not when the type is one the marshal
cannot resolve (a type family), and by then the value is the runtime's own — a number,
because the in-marshal converted it.

mini.bend

    import Base

    type S is Data:
      SNat{}

    def M(s: S) -> Data:
      match s:
        case SNat{}:
          Nat

    def nat_of(s: S, n: Nat) -> Maybe<&2, M(s)>:
      match s:
        case SNat{}:
          Some{n}

`bend mini.bend -o mini.mjs`, then from JS:

    nat_of({$: "SNat"}, 7n).value   ->  7        (typeof "number"; expected a BigInt)

The emitted wrapper marshals both arguments and nothing else:

    "nat_of": run_lib((a0, a1) => { const r = (run_loop($nat_of$((a0), nat_host(a1)))); (a0); BigInt(a1); return r; }, 2),

With a concrete return type the result is marshalled, and the Nat is converted:

    def concrete(n: Nat) -> Maybe<&2, Nat>:
      Some{n}

    "concrete": run_lib((a0) => { const r = $0m0(run_loop($concrete$(nat_host(a0)))); BigInt(a0); return r; }, 1),
    concrete(7n).value   ->  7n

Seen in a real program: `dec(s: Schema, r: Raw) -> Maybe<&2, Meaning(s)>` in a schema
library returns `{ $: "Some", value: 6 }` for a Nat while the declaration it emits for the
same module says `bigint` — `Meaning(s)` is a type family, so the result is unmarshalled.

Same shape as #1105 (a value on a path the marshal does not resolve keeps the runtime's
representation), and the value is exact either way (a Nat is at most 2^48-1 < 2^53), so
this is a representation bug rather than a wrong number. It is reachable from any def whose
return type the marshal cannot resolve, and the fix has to be at the boundary: a caller
cannot tell an internal number from a host number.

title: Conversion without blowups on numerals, same calls and shared graphs, at no cost to ordinary checks (#1071, #1075)
body:
| Objection | This change |
|---|---|
| "Identical first" is quadratic when nested | Every step still asks it (generated proofs need it: see below), but no walk is repeated: a walk remembers the calls it found different and its answer at share cells, so a nested step that meets them answers at once. Linear in the terms, not quadratic. |
| …or slows every comparison by a constant | A walk starts only if a side is a call; it first checks the two heads and arities without allocating, and stops at the first difference. Measured cost on `bench/checker/*`: within ±4% of main, the same range as the version that asked only at the top;. |
| Capping (4096 visits) trades one problem for another | No cap. The only threshold is *when* the sharing record switches on (after 256 steps of one conversion). |
| `F(100000 * 2) == F(100000 + 100000)` still unrolls | Base's `Nat.add`, `Nat.mul`, `Nat.cmp` and `U32.to_nat` on numerals return the literal their definitions compute. |
| Blowups come from shared graphs walked as trees | Past 256 steps, a conversion records the pairs it settles where a side is a share cell (the only node reachable twice), so a DAG is compared once. |

### What changed (`bend2/bend.ts`)

1. **Numerals** (`term_wnf`): when a `Ref` to `Nat.add`, `Nat.mul`, `Nat.cmp` or `U32.to_nat` is about to unfold and every argument is a numeral *as written* (share cells and annotations seen through, nothing evaluated), it returns the result as a literal; results above 2^32 − 1, and any other argument, unfold as today. Base's definitions stay the specification — this is the same kind of extension as Agda's `BUILTIN NATURAL` or Lean's kernel `Nat`, limited to Base's own functions. Evidence: a set of agreement laws covering these ops checks on main by plain unfolding and on this branch through the shortcut; false laws (e.g. `Nat.mul(6n, 6n) == 35n`) are still rejected. (Kept out of the repo to keep the diff small; happy to add them.)
2. **Same term** (`term_compare`): at every step, before normalizing, if a side is a call and both sides are written the same way (variables by level; calls, constructors, datatypes, equalities, `refl`, `absurd` walked like #1075's check), they're equal. The walk checks heads and arities first, compares arguments first to last, and remembers the calls it found different and its answer at share cells, so no walk is repeated.

   Why every step and not just the top: generated proofs (bend-ssz) pass evidence for `ok_X(s, dv) == True` where `Bool.and(A, B) == True` is expected and `ok_X` is defined as `Bool.and(A, B)`. The identical `B`s meet only one unfold down, and `B` contains a check over 2^13 roots; asking only at the top normalizes both copies (the BeaconState root overflowed the stack).
3. **Sharing record** (`term_compare`): each top-level conversion counts steps; past 256 it records `(lhs, rhs, mode, depth) → result` for pairs where a side is a share cell and answers repeats from the record. The record is dropped when the top-level conversion returns.

In short, this is #1075 but without quadratic complexity.
### Numbers

Apple M-series laptop (idle), CPU time (user + sys) of `bend <file> --check-only`, 7 interleaved rounds of main (b2111cf4) and this branch, medians; ±4% is noise here.

| bench/checker | main | this |
|---|---:|---:|
| compute_1600 | 2.05 s | 2.13 s (+2%) |
| defs_12800 | 1.83 s | 1.79 s (−2%) |
| generics_3200 | 1.84 s | 1.88 s (+2%) |
| proofs_3200 | 4.03 s | 4.10 s (+2%) |
| trees_400 | 2.56 s | 2.66 s (+4%) |
| hashes_4 | 8.80 s | 0.40 s |
| shared_4 | 0.38 s | 0.35 s |

bend-ssz (generated SSZ proofs, checked today on Bend 2.0.28 + #1075), `proofs/obj/big_root_BeaconState.bend` (12,882 definitions), with this change ported onto the same 2.0.28 base, both run side by side on a 48-core Linux box: #1075 384 s CPU, this 342 s; every definition checks. Asking the identity question only at the top overflows the stack on it.

A symbolic-leaf Merkle root, loop form vs recursive form (`root_loop(d, x) == root_rec(d, x)` for a variable `x`: nothing closed to state as a literal, each side a chain of `d` shared nodes):

| depth | main | this |
|---|---:|---:|
| 16 | 0.8 s | 0.5 s |
| 20 | 7.2 s | 0.5 s |
| 24 | 70 s | 0.4 s |
| 32 | > 300 s (killed) | 0.5 s |

Measured earlier on an Apple M-series machine against a previous revision of this branch (same three mechanisms):

| case | main | #1075 | this |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| hashes_100 | 150 s | 0.41 s | 0.41 s |
| #1071 a / b, jeromelaurens' closed bound | stack overflow | ~0.17 s | ~0.17 s |
| `100000n + 100000n`, `F(100000*2) == F(100000+100000)` | stack overflow | stack overflow | 0.17 s |
| aldeni fold, 16 / 20 steps, old copying `max` | 4.4 / 54 s | 0.92 / 8.2 s | 0.23 / 0.19 s |
| false equality inside the copying fold | rejected, 11.8 s | rejected, 11.9 s | rejected, 3.4 s |

A real proof book (bend-collections, 36 roots, being ported to 2.0.32): main checks 29, this 34; five roots that time out at 900 s on main check in 18–59 s; the 29 roots that check on both use 53% less CPU; none that checks on main fails here.

Soundness: all 1,510 files under `tests/` give the same `--check-only` output on this commit as on the previous revisions, which matched main on every file (identical error output on the failing ones).

### What it doesn't fix

- Numerals past 2^32 − 1 unfold as before.
- Two different closed expressions with the same value that aren't these Nat functions still evaluate fully — your literal pattern remains the answer there.
- Terms duplicated as separate objects (not shared) are still walked twice.

title: Base says the same with fewer helpers, and U32.log2 takes five native shifts instead of thirty-two
body:
Replaces #1059 by @jnadeau207-collab, rebased onto main without the U64 commit (#1057, closed as WONTFIX). The first commit is Jesse's simplifications, credited to them; the second replaces the U64-based `U32.log2`; the third puts back main's `Map.has` and `Map.del`, which were slower in the simplified form.

### What changes

- **Simplifications (Jesse Nadeau):** `Cmp.is_lt`, `is_eq`, `is_gt`, `is_le` and `is_ge` answer one constructor and fall through for the rest; `Bool.full_add` is xor and majority; `Nat.sub` and `Map.diff` merge their empty cases; `Nat.div`, `Nat.mod`, `String.eq` and `String.order` project with `Pair.fst`/`Pair.snd` instead of a `.fin` each; `Map.set`, `Map.get` and `Map.pop` fall through on a miss.
- **`U32.log2`** halves its search for the top bit: five steps of `U32.shrn` and `U32.is_ne` (natives) instead of thirty-two of `shr` and `is_lt`. The step stays branchless, as the old one was: a match needs its own def, and BendTT rejects a call that descends through one.
- **Kept as main has them:** `Map.has` through `Map.seek` copies the leaf's key to compare it, and `Map.del` through `Pair.fst` passes the popped value boxed; together they cost 6% in C. `U32.div` and `U32.mod` also stay: they run as natives by name on every lane, so the generic `Word.div`/`Word.mod` would add no speed, and they belong to the U64 design.

`base.bend`: +29 / −76.

### Performance (macOS, medians of 7 runs, this branch against main 35b71e37)

| | C | JS |
|---|---|---|
| 20M `U32.log2` | 0.09 s against 0.22 | 0.17 s against 0.33 |
| 300k Map has/get/del/set, 1000 keys | 1.05 s against 1.05 | 7.84 s against 7.96 |
| 2M `String.eq`/`is_lt`/`order` | 4.63 s against 4.68 | 9.08 s against 8.83 (noise: min 8.72 against 8.59) |
| 200M `Nat.is_*`, `Nat.div`, `Nat.mod` | 0.30 s against 0.30 | 12.57 s against 12.45 |

title: A shared Array's redirect is read without a race and without an atomic on the device, once per spin (#975)
body:
Fixes #975. Supersedes #997, #999 and #1084, and takes a piece from each.

## What changes

- **`blk_loc`:** reads a fork's redirect word as one relaxed 64-bit atomic on the CPU, and plainly on Metal and CUDA.
  - On arm64 and x86-64 the relaxed load compiles to the same `ldr`/`movq` as a plain read.
  - The target bits never change while a handle is live, so even a torn read finds the target.
  - Main (2.0.32) reads the word through `rfc_view`'s two atomic halves. That makes the shared-array path about 2× slower on the CPU and 4.5× slower on Metal.
- **The spin hoist, from #999:** a spin takes, beside each box word, the storage its caller already resolved. A handle equal to the one the spin entered with reads that storage instead of the redirect.
  - With no Array shared (`BLK_SHR 0`), nothing changes.
  - Ported by hand onto the reorganised `comp.ts`.
- **Tests:**
  - #997's race reproducer, `tests/run/array_redirect_race.bend`.
  - #1084's `tests/reg/spin_array_hold.bend`: a spin that swaps its two arrays each turn, plus holds over a fork's shared handle.
- **Not taken:** #997's split-redirect layout, which the `blk_loc` read makes unnecessary, and #1084's compile-time hoist (its author suggested #999's instead).

## Race check

ThreadSanitizer, 5 runs each at 1, 2, 4 and 8 workers.

- On the old plain read (`6a77e124`), the reproducer reports a race in every run at 2 or more workers.
- On main and on this branch, it reports none. The same holds for `array_fork`, `array_fork_unshare` and `stencil3d`.

## Measurements

Apple M4, `cc -std=c11 -O3`, interleaved rounds.

**Scaled `stencil3d`** (2^21 cells, 128 leaves, 160 passes). Best of 10 rounds, since load was high in that run:

| lane | main | `blk_loc` fix alone | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 thread | 1095 ms | 692 ms | 447 ms |
| 16 threads | 250 ms | 160 ms | 110 ms |
| Metal | 28.9 s | 4.9 s | 1.42 s |

The old racy plain read was 522 ms, 127 ms and 7.43 s.

**The 16 `bench/runtime` programs:**
- All are `BLK_SHR 0`, and each emits the same C as main except the dead `blk_loc` body. Every output matches its pin.

title: A file's names are keyed ns:name inside the compiler, so no declaration lands in another file's namespace and a foreign CID(None) keeps meaning Base's None (#1045)
body:
Closes #1045. Closes #1124. Closes #1184. Supersedes #1095.

## The bug

A file's names were keyed `namespace + "." + name`. The entry file's namespace is `""`, so its names are keyed bare. As a result, the entry's declaration `lib.None` got exactly the key that `lib.bend`'s own `None` would have. Two things then went wrong:

- `lib.bend`'s Bend code was resolved while `lib.bend` was parsed, so its `None` meant Base's `None`.
- Its foreign C/JS source is resolved after every file has loaded. There, `CID(None)` tries `lib.None` first and so took the entry's constructor.

The same spelling meant two different constructors in the two halves of one library. The result was the wrong `match` arm, and on C, a read of the allocator's bump word plus a free into the wrong size class:

| `import ./lib.bend as Q` + `type Evil is Data: lib.None{}` | interp | JS | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| main | `Some ` | `Some ` | `Some 97` |
| this PR | `None` | `None` | `None` |

## The fix

The ambiguity was in the key encoding, so this fixes the encoding. #1095 instead kept the ambiguous keys and made `c_ids` compute an ownership scope per foreign source to work around them.

- **Keys:** inside the compiler, a namespace now joins its names with `:`. A name is words joined by dots and a namespace is a path, so neither can contain `:`, and a key always names its file: `lib.bend`'s `None` is `lib:None`, and the entry's `lib.None` stays `lib.None`.
- **Lookups:** `parse_qual` joins with `:`, an alias expands to `ns:name`, `c_ids` tries `ns:k` then `k`, and `name_show` splits a key at its `:`.
- **Output:** the `:` never leaves the compiler. `name_key` spells `ns:name` as `ns.name` everywhere a key is written out:
  - messages, and the unsafe/foreign and out-of-scope lists;
  - a printed `main` value, in `SHOW_NAMES` for C and in the JS show table;
  - JS constructor tags, effect ids and `.mjs` exports;
  - BendTT names.

  Every output reads exactly as on main.
- **Size:** after the rebase, `bend.ts` +114 ttok, `comp.ts` +96 (63,213 → 63,309, under its 64k cap), `safe.ts` +37, `main.ts` +4.

## Also fixes #1124

The same encoding caused #1124 from the other side. `Word.bend`'s namespace is `Word`, so its bare `Nil` was first looked up as its own `Word.Nil`, which is Base's `Word.Nil`. With `ns:name` keys the file's own guess is `Word:Nil`, which no file declares, so `Nil` is List's. Likewise, `String.bend`'s bare `eq`, which nothing declares, is now refused as undefined, instead of silently binding Base's `String.eq`.

Only a sibling of the entry file gets a bare family name as its namespace (`libs/Word.bend` is `libs/Word`), so the test sits next to its entry:

- `tests/import/base_family_file.bend` imports a sibling `tests/import/Word.bend` and prints `1n` on every lane. On `main` the check, JS and C lanes all fail with the `Word.Nil` error.
- `gates/repo.ts` now allows capital letters in a test's file name, so a test can be named like the family it stands for.

## Behaviour changes

- **Newly accepted:**
  - The entry may declare `lib.x` next to `lib.bend`'s `x`; main refuses it as a duplicate.
  - A file may be named like a Base type, e.g. `U32.bend` declaring `show`; main clashed it with Base's `U32.show`.
  - A file may declare its own name, e.g. `lib.bend` declaring `lib.lib`.
- **Now refused:** a file reaches another file's names only through its own aliases. Spelling another namespace directly, e.g. filling `lib.bend`'s law with `def lib.one()` instead of `def L.one()`, now says the name isn't in scope. This is #1184: an imported `X.bend` no longer answers to `X.f` when its alias is `Z`.
- **Same printed name:** the only case where two distinct keys print alike is the first one above. There, the entry's `lib.x` and `lib.bend`'s `x` both print as `lib.x`. The program still behaves correctly because the keys differ. In JS, two such foreign effects fail loudly ("two effects register"), and two such `.mjs` exports share one export name.

## Verification

Each program was run on this branch and on main (`ef66a7cc`) through the interpreter, `--check-only`, `-o .js` + node, native `-o` + run, `--verdict` and `-o .bendtt`, and all outputs were diffed. The programs:

- all 1578 under `tests/`, `bench/runtime` and `demos`;
- a generated matrix of 120: 4 layouts (sibling, subdirectory, `../` climb, chain with diamond) × 4 name shapes (bare, `Geo.x`, `lib.x`, `A.B.x`) × def/type/constructor, working and with errors;
- 67 adversarial cases: hub packages through `BEND_LIB`, hyphenated paths, cycles, one file under two aliases, colliding aliases, laws and `LAWS`/`PROOF`, templates, operators, `.mjs` interop, foreign effects in `sub/deep` and `../shared`, `@unsafe` in nested files, and every error message that names a key;
- this PR's regression test.

Results:

- **No `:` in any output:** in the output of all 1773 programs (every lane's output and the emitted `.c`, `.js`, `.mjs` and `.bendtt`, string literals included), no `name:name` token appears that isn't in main's output.
- **Identical to main** except for:
  - the #1045 repro and `tests/io/cid_capture` (fixed);
  - the three newly accepted declaration cases above;
  - the canonical-spelling fill case above (now refused);
  - a JS-lane timeout under load, which matches when rerun serially;
  - the netcode demo, which needs a relay and depends on timing.
- **No existing test changes.**
- **Regression test:** `tests/io/cid_capture` is from #1095 (by @oxura). It forges `None` and a three-field `Con` over a `List` node and prints `None` / `6` on every lane (main: `Some ` / `Some 97`).
- **Repo gate:** `gates/repo.ts` passes, 49 / 49.

## After the rebase onto main (`607a095a`)

- **Conflicts:** only in `comp.ts`, all against #1235's rewrites and the newer comment-skipping `CID` scan. Each hunk keeps `main`'s code with this PR's `name_key` and `:` applied. `main`'s 31 new commits add no namespace joins or key printing of their own.
- **The `has no tag` message:** this PR had broken it over three lines to fit `name_key`, which changed the emitted JS text. It now keeps `main`'s layout, with the two names computed first.
- **`tests/io/cid_capture_lib.bend`** had no `#|` lines, but in the check lane it prints the usual "2 defs rely on unsafe or foreign code" error, so the gate would have failed it. It now pins that error, as the other foreign-code helpers do.
- **Sweep:** all 1603 `.bend` files under `tests/`, `bench/` and `demos/`, comparing `--check-only` output, `.c`, `.js`, `.bendtt` and every log against `main`:
  - **Real differences:** only `cid_capture` (fixed).
  - **Log paths:** 37 `.bendtt` logs differ only by the output path written into them.
  - **JS function names:** 17 `.js` files differ only there. A `:` in a key is mangled as `$058` (`$alias_lib$058two$`). That keeps the entry's `lib.two` and `lib.bend`'s `two` as two JS functions, so it is intended. It does mean the `.js` above is identical to `main` only up to these internal names.
- **Tests:** the new test and both `cid_capture` files pass the gate's check lane, run as its aggregator, and their JS and C lanes. `tsc` reports the same 12 errors as `main`. `gates/repo.ts` passes, 50 / 50.

## Not run

- The cluster gates (test, perf, safe): the minis refused my session's key.

title: safe.ts loses erased constructor-field types in match arms, causing two --verdict false negatives
body:
# `safe.ts` loses erased constructor-field types in match arms, causing two `--verdict` false negatives

## What I did

On Bend 2.0.32 (`4f856f61`, Darwin arm64), I checked two small files containing a match over a constructor with an erased function field:

```text
bun bend2/main.ts safe_erased_field_quantity.bend --check-only
bun bend2/main.ts safe_erased_field_quantity.bend --verdict
bun bend2/main.ts safe_erased_field_head.bend --check-only
bun bend2/main.ts safe_erased_field_head.bend --verdict
```

Neither file imports Base or uses `@unsafe`, foreign code, recursion, holes, templates, or open laws.

## What happened

Both source files pass Bend's checker:

```text
ALL PROOFS CHECK
Use --verdict for mathematical validity.
```

Both fail `--verdict` with the generic implementation/kernel mismatch. They expose two symptoms of the same lost field metadata.

### 1. The erased field is emitted as a live binder

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type Wrap is Data:
  Mk{-f: Unit -> Unit}

def SelfEqF(-f: Wrap -> (Unit -> Unit)) -> Data:
  {f == f : Wrap -> (Unit -> Unit)}

law erased_field_identity:
  SelfEqF({\{Mk: f => f} : Wrap -> (Unit -> Unit)})

def erased_field_identity():
  {==}
```

The constructor declaration is emitted with a Q0 field:

```text
λ{.Mk: Σ-x0 : ∀x0 : Unit -> Unit -> <()>; λ{}}
```

but the match arm binds that field at Q1:

```text
λ{.Mk: λ{(,): λx0 => λ{(): x0; λ{}}}; λ{}}
```

Running the BendTT kernel directly reports:

```text
SOME PROOFS FAIL
In erased_field_identity:
a λ of its binder's liveness
```

As a control, changing only that generated field binder from `λx0` to
`λ-x0` makes the same BendTT book return `ALL PROOFS CHECK`.

### 2. Applying the same erased field loses its head type

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type Wrap is Data:
  Mk{-f: Unit -> Unit}

def SelfEq(-u: Unit) -> Data:
  {u == u : Unit}

law erased_field_call:
  SelfEq(
    {({\{Mk: f => f(U{})} : Wrap -> Unit})(
      Mk{u => u}
    ) : Unit}
  )

def erased_field_call():
  {==}
```

`-o` reports:

```text
BendTT: out of scope, so not in safe_erased_field_head.bendtt:
- erased_field_call: an application past its head's known type
```

The definition is consequently absent from the emitted book.

## Expected behavior

Both files should return `ALL PROOFS CHECK` under `--verdict`. A match arm for `Mk{-f: ...}` should retain `f`'s Q0 quantity and its function type while elaborating dead source terms.

## Cause

In `safe.ts`, a match arm's constructor fields are represented by a `Chain` that carries only a field count and convoy variables. When `tree` reaches one of those field lambdas without an `All` annotation, it defaults both pieces of missing metadata:

```ts
let q = all === null ? 1 : quant(all.q);
let s2 = scope_kq(
  scope_bind(s1, { $: "Var", l }, all?.A ?? null, true),
  l,
  q,
);
```

The default `q = 1` produces the first mismatch. The null scope type makes `args` unable to elaborate `f(U{})`, producing the second. Threading each constructor field's telescope type and quantity through the match-field chain should address both symptoms.

## Environment

```text
bend 2.0.32
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.0.123.102)
```

title: The kernel puts a λ argument into a type annotated with its domain, so a + let of Equal.cong over a function checks (#1133)
body:
Fixes #1133 in the kernel. Supersedes #1136, which annotated in the elaborator and made `inferable` stricter than `Term.infer`.

### What fails

`Term.infer`'s App rule returns `B[x]`. When `x` is a λ or λ-match (the η-long form `safe.ts` gives a function argument), each call `(f a)` in `B` becomes a redex with a λ head. `Term.infer` can't type a bare λ, and `elim` only covers a variable argument. A `+` let checks its inferred type as Data, which infers those calls:

```
!+x3 = (Equal.cong -(Pair -U32 -Bool) -Bool -λx3 => (snd_of x3) -x1 -(mk x0) x2); x3
```

`V = {((λx3 => snd_of x3) x1) == ((λx3 => snd_of x3) (mk x0)) : Bool}`. Checking `V : *2` reaches `infer (λx3 => …)` on the right side and fails with `expected: an annotated term`. bend2 accepts, because its HOAS substitution β-reduces.

### The change

```lean
def Term.arg (x A : Term) : Term :=
  if Term.takes x then Ann x A else x
...
      pure (Term.inst B (Term.arg x A))
```

The rule has just checked `x : A`, so it puts `{x : A}` into `B`. Every such call then has an annotated head, which the ordinary App rule infers. That covers any arity, partial applications, arguments that don't infer (constructors), and types that depend on the argument.

### Proofs

`Typed` is unchanged. `{x : A}` reduces to `x` in one `Par.unann` step, so `chk`'s App case adds one conversion. `lean bendtt.lean` elaborates with no `sorry`, and `consistent`, `book_check`, `sr`, `progress`, `halts`, `empty` and `confluent` depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

### Checks (macOS arm64, Lean 4.34.1)

- `tests/proof/cong_lambda_argument.bend` covers one and two arguments, a partial application (`fst_snd(x) : U32 & Bool -> Bool`) and a constructor argument (`Bool.not(True{})`). It prints `True` and `--verdict` says `ALL PROOFS CHECK`. The kernel on `main` rejects it.
- Three arguments and an inline lambda also check (not added as tests).
- Over all tests, the old and new kernel give the same verdict on every emitted `.bendtt` (1026) except the new test.
- Cost: 6560 arguments are annotated over the tests, but only 46 annotations land in a type. The rest go into a `B` that doesn't mention the argument, so the type comes out the same as without it. Over the suite the kernel retires 98.16G instructions against `main`'s 98.27G (−0.11%). A build that never annotates is at +0.05%, so the difference is noise.
- `bendtt.lean` is at 63901 ttok. `gates/repo.ts` passes 49 / 49.

Not run: `gates/safe.ts` and `gates/test.ts` on the cluster.

A λ-headed redex written directly into `.bendtt` text still doesn't infer, as on `main`. The elaborator never emits one, because bend2's checked terms are already β-reduced.

title: A let the kernel reads at quantity 2 goes out with bend2's type, since the kernel checks the type it infers against *2 before any β-reduction
body:
Fixes #1133, the way @nicolas-abril's analysis on #1136 lays out; thank you for it, it was the explanation I was missing. `inferable` stays as it is, the mirror of `Term.infer`.

### What happens

For a let at quantity 2 (a `+` let, or one `let_term` promotes when the kernel counts more than one use), the kernel infers the value and checks the type it inferred against `*2`. That type comes from plain substitution, with no β-reduction, so a `+` let of `Equal.cong(A, B, f, x, mk(n), h)` gives `{((λx => f x) x) == ((λx => f x) (mk n)) : B}`: the left side passes by the `elim` rule for a `Var` argument, the right side sends the kernel to infer the λ, and it refuses `expected: an annotated term`. bend2's instantiation β-reduces as it builds, so it never meets that term.

### The change

`let_term` annotates a let whose emitted quantity is 2, the promoted case included, with the type bend2 knows for its value, unless the value already carries one. The type's elaboration is kept as a thunk from the let's own scope, so nothing is built for the lets that don't need it. Nothing else moves: `inferable`, the self-call re-binding and the "no known type" refusal are as on main.

```
!+x2 = {(Equal.cong -Nat -Nat -λx2 => (.Succ, (x2, ())) -x0 -(.Zero, ()) x1) : {(.Succ, (x0, ())) == (.Succ, ((.Zero, ()), ())) : Nat}}; x2
```

### Checks (Linux x86-64, kernel binary 7f6ef51c)

- `tests/proof/cong_plus_let.bend` holds both shapes reported: #1133's pair domain with a def as the function, and @nathanneuro's `Nat` case with a λ at the source. On main, `bend f.bend` says `ALL PROOFS CHECK` and `--verdict` says `SOME PROOFS FAIL`; here both say `ALL PROOFS CHECK`, and so does the kernel binary on the emitted `.bendtt`.
- Over `tests/proof`, `tests/check` and `tests/spec` (338 files), `--verdict` answers the same on main and here, file by file.
- The test prints `True` on the interpreted, JS and C lanes; `gates/repo.ts` passes 49 / 49; `safe.ts` is at 19776 of its 24000 ttok.

Not run: `gates/safe.ts` on a cluster, and macOS.

title: A CID(...) inside a comment of an effect's .c or .js fails the build with "CID(...) names no constructor or def"
body:
### What you did

bend main.bend -o main

### What happened

```text
Error: CID(...) names no constructor or def
```

The effect's `.c` is sound; the id it registers, `CID(answer)`, names a def of the file. What tripped the build is a comment in that `.c` quoting the error message itself. The same comment in the `.js` twin fails the JS and interpreted lanes the same way, since they read the twin.

`c_ids` in `comp.ts` resolves `CID(k)` and `FID(k)` by a regular expression over the whole source text, comments included, so any `CID(` followed by a name in a comment or a string literal is resolved as an id. A comment that documents an id, or quotes this very refusal, cannot be written. I hit it with a comment that said what happens on a wrong id.

A sibling of #1049 (the `undefined` guard reading the effect sources): the sources are hand-written, and their comments may say anything.

### The file

`main.bend`:

```python
import Base

law answer:
  U32 -> IO(U32)

def answer(n):
  import "./answer.c"
  import "./answer.js"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    a : U32 <- answer(40)
    IO.print(U32.show(a))
```

`answer.c`:

```c
// A wrong id fails the build with "CID(...) names no constructor or def".
Term answer_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  return (Term)((u32)f[0] + 2);
}

static void __attribute__((constructor)) answer_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(answer), answer_run, 0);
}
```

`answer.js`:

```js
function answer(n) {
  return (n + 2) >>> 0;
}

io_eff(CID(answer), answer);
```

Reword the comment's `CID(...)` and it prints `42` on every lane.

### bend --version

bend 2.0.32

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 22.1.8

title: A CID(k) in an effect source's comment is left alone: the ids are resolved in the code, not in the comments
body:
Fixes #1160.

### What happens

`c_ids` resolves `CID(k)` and `FID(k)` by a regular expression over the whole effect source, comments included. So a comment in a `.c` or `.js` twin quoting the refusal "CID(...) names no constructor or def" failed the build with that very line, on every lane that reads the source (the C build, and the JS and interpreted lanes through the `.js` twin), while the effect itself was sound. The sibling of #1049, where the `undefined` guard read the effect sources too.

### The change

The regular expression matches a `//` or `/* */` comment first and hands it back as it is; an id outside a comment resolves as before. Four lines in `comp.ts`, nothing else touched; a string literal that says `CID(...)` still resolves, as before.

### Test

`tests/io/effect_cid_in_comment` (`.bend`, `.c`, `.js`, the shape of `effect_undefined_word`): the C and JS twins each quote the refusal in a comment. On main the interpreted, JS and C lanes fail with `CID(...) names no constructor or def`; here they print `42`.

### Checks (Linux x86-64)

- The new test passes the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes 49 / 49; `comp.ts` is at 63937 of its 64000 ttok (the cap is close, so I kept the change to the regular expression alone).

title: Chan.try_send and Chan.try_recv answer at once: the send and receive that do not wait, shared with Chan.send and Chan.recv
body:
Implements #1147, asked by @LucasGois1, with two departures from its sketch said below.

### Why

`Chan.send` parks while the channel is full and `Chan.recv` while it is empty, and `IO.within` does not cancel the loser (WONTFIX), so a receive under a deadline still takes the next value once it arrives. Two programs need an operation that answers now: a writer that drains everything already queued into one transaction, then commits and blocks for the next; and a queue that drops under load rather than block its producers. Neither can be a hub package: the answer lives in the channel's row inside the runtime.

### What changes

```python
def Chan.try_send(-A: Type, chan: Chan(A), value: A) -> IO(Bool)
def Chan.try_recv(-A: Type, chan: Chan(A)) -> IO(Chan.Poll<&1, A>)

type Chan.Poll<a, -A: Kind(a)> is Kind(a):
  Wait{}
  Closed{}
  Got{value: A}
```

- `try_send` answers whether the value went: to a parked receiver, or into the ring while it has room. `False` on a full or closed channel, and the value is dropped, as `Chan.send` drops it on a closed one.
- `try_recv` answers `Got{value}` from the ring or from a parked sender, `Wait{}` while nothing is ready, `Closed{}` once the channel is closed and drained. Three answers, since `Maybe` cannot tell `Wait` from `Closed`, and a poller on a closed channel would never stop.

Where this departs from #1147's sketch, and why: `try_send` answers `Bool` like `Chan.send` rather than handing the value back in a `Maybe`, so the two sends read alike and a `None` does not mean "sent"; and the type's cases are `Wait`/`Closed`/`Got` (`Empty` is already a type in Base).

In both runtimes the step that does not wait is now one function each way, `chan_put` and `chan_get`; `Chan.send` and `Chan.recv` are that step followed by the park, and the two new effects are that step followed by an answer. `chan_send_run`/`chan_recv_run` and their JS twins lose their copies of it.

### Checks (Linux x86-64)

- `tests/io/chan_try.bend`: a channel with room for one (a send that goes, one that does not, a receive that takes, one that waits, one that finds it closed), and one with no room (a parked sender hands its value to `try_recv`, a parked receiver takes `try_send`'s, a `try_send` to nobody does not go). It prints its lines on the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes.
- The seven other channel tests (`chan_*`, `channel_*`, `nat_host_chan`) answer as on main; `channel_send_recv` is an io pin that fails on main alike.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes 49 / 49. The guide is at 7968 of its 8000 ttok, so I left it alone; a clause on the two in the channels paragraph would fit if you trim elsewhere.

Not run: macOS.

title: Every compiled IO program carries ~1 MiB of zeros: io_eff_rows is baked into .data.rel.ro by clang
body:
## Summary

Every natively compiled Bend program that does any IO carries about 1 MiB of
zero bytes. A program that only prints `hello` compiles to **1,089,008
bytes**. With a small change to the runtime C emitted by `bend2/comp.ts` it
is **40,504 bytes**, with identical behaviour.

## Reproduce

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print("hello\n")
```

```
$ bend hello.bend -o hello && stat -c %s hello
1089008
$ nm -S hello | grep io_eff_rows
000000000000fb60 0000000000100000 d io_eff_rows
```

A program with no IO (`def main() -> U32: 42`) is 27 KB. The megabyte
appears as soon as an effect is registered.

## Cause

`bend2/comp.ts:5464` (at c97ebd53b7) emits

```c
static IoEff io_eff_rows[1 << 16];
```

That is 65,536 × 16 bytes = 1 MiB. Effects are registered into it by
`__attribute__((constructor))` functions that store constants
(`io_eff(CID_IO_PRINT, io_print_run, 0)`). At `-O2`/`-O3`, clang evaluates
those constructors at compile time. Because the stored values are known, it
turns the table from zero-initialized `.bss` into an initialized 1 MiB
object in `.data.rel.ro`, most of it zeros, written into the file. gcc does
not do this: the process-spawning drill below, built from the same emitted C with
`gcc -O2`, keeps the table in `.bss` and is 93,264 bytes.

It costs file size only. The hello binary has just 19 relative relocations, and the zero pages
are never touched, so startup and resident memory are unaffected. But it
applies to essentially every compiled IO program, and it is the first thing
someone sees when they compile hello world and check the size.

## Suggested fix

Allocate the table instead of declaring it as a static array. A `calloc` in
a constructor that runs before the registering ones cannot be evaluated at
compile time, so nothing is baked into the binary. Lookups and the existing
`run == NULL` checks are unchanged.

```diff
-static IoEff io_eff_rows[1 << 16];
+static IoEff* io_eff_rows;
+
+// Allocated, not a static array: clang evaluates the effect-registering
+// constructors at compile time and would otherwise store all 1 MiB of the
+// mostly-empty table in the binary. Priority 101 runs before them.
+static void __attribute__((constructor(101))) io_eff_init(void) {
+  io_eff_rows = calloc(1 << 16, sizeof(IoEff));
+  if (io_eff_rows == NULL) {
+    fprintf(stderr, "host allocation failed\n");
+    exit(1);
+  }
+}
```

Measured on the emitted C, patched by hand and built with
`clang-19 -std=c11 -O3 … -lpthread -lm` (Bend's own flags):

| program | before | after | output |
|---|---|---|---|
| print `hello` | 1,089,008 B | 40,504 B | identical |
| a process-spawning drill (7 effects) | 1,126,208 B | 77,736 B | identical, exit 0 |

The error branch could use `err_fail` if it is declared before this point
in the emitted C; I used `fprintf`/`exit` so the snippet stands alone.
Sizing the table to the number of registered effects would also work, but
it touches more code.

Environment: Bend 2.0.32, Ubuntu clang 19.1.7, Linux x86-64.

title: --verdict fails on programs bend2 accepts: safe.ts splices terms at stale binder levels, so scope_move captures and uses over-counts
body:
### What you did

bend capture_reject.bend --check-only | bend capture_reject.bend --verdict 

### What happened

```text
$ bun bend2/main.ts capture_reject.bend --check-only
ALL PROOFS CHECK
Use --verdict for mathematical validity.

$ bun bend2/main.ts capture_reject.bend --verdict
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Sorry - this is a mismatch between the TypeScript implementation, and the formalized BendTT kernel. Your proofs may or may not be correct, and we cannot validate them yet. [...]
```

### The file

```python
import Base

def qof2(f: Nat -> Nat) -> Quant:
  &1

def k(f: Nat -> Nat, g: Nat -> Nat, -A: Kind(qof2(f)), b: Bool) -> Nat:
  match b:
    case True{}:  f(g(0n))
    case False{}: f(g(1n))

def main() -> Nat:
  k((y => y), (z => z), Unit, True{})
```


Root cause: k's -A: Kind(qof2(f)) specializes f, so safe.ts elaborates k as a per-instance tree and splices the column argument (y => y). The splice happens in [arm](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L1053): the column value is elaborated by the term(e, si, v, false) call at [safe.ts:1067](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L1067), at a stale binder level, then spliced under more binders. Two level-based passes then misfire:

[scope_move's mv (safe.ts:534-539)](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L534-L539) renames every Var at a level, bound or free, so convoying g rewrites the identity's body: f(g(0)) is emitted as (λ_.g)(g(0)).
[uses (safe.ts:1277)](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L1277) counts a λ's own bound var as a use of an outer level (the Lam case never checks o.l === l); [lams (safe.ts:1269)](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L1269) and [let_term (safe.ts:1196)](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L1196) then promote the binder to +, and a + binder of type Nat -> Nat fails the kernel's *2 check.
Currently masked — and un-masking it turns this into a wrong-program PASS

On this file, --verdict FAILs today because of a sibling bug: a root instance references its root constant before that constant is emitted. Fix that emit-ordering bug in isolation and this capture stops failing and instead passes --verdict with a body that computes something different from what bend2 checked, at the (still-correct) declared type. The minimal value-changing form needs no λ-headed redex. So this should be fixed together with the emit-ordering bug, not independently of it.

Severity / soundness

This is a fidelity/completeness bug, not a soundness hole. The capture corrupts a def's body, never its declared type: declared types are elaborated on a separate, capture-free path ([def_emit, safe.ts:296](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L296)), which scope_move never touches. Since the kernel re-typechecks each body against that faithful declared type and canonicity forbids an inhabitant of an uninhabited type, there is no path from this bug to a proof of Empty — the worst case is a well-typed body that computes the wrong thing (the "wrong-program PASS" above, once the masking bug is fixed).

Fix direction

Elaborate a spliced term at the depth where it lands, or re-level it on entry. Guarding mv/uses at binders with l === a (and Rwt's l/l+1) is only a partial fix. ~ arguments avoid the problem entirely because [arm substitutes them before elaboration (safe.ts:1055-1057)](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/v2.0.32/bend2/safe.ts#L1055-L1057).

Related: distinct root cause from bendlang/bend#1138 (kernel rejects what bend2 accepts) — not a duplicate; this pinpoints the splice/relevel mechanism.

### bend --version

bend 2.0.32

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

_No response_

title: The host grows its column to a row per thread, so a 10-thread pool drains 80 units, not 16
body:
## The idle time

- **One drain turn:** `hashmap` at 10 threads, on the CPU, runs as a single drain turn over 256 top-level tasks.
- **16 work units:** before the drain, `cube_run` grows the host's column only until there is a unit per thread, `(P + 7) / 8` rows. That is 2 rows at P = 10, and each row is 8 drain units, so the drain has 16 units of 16 tasks each.
- **The imbalance:** six workers take two units (about 460 ms) and four take one (about 270 ms), then wait for the turn to end.
- **Instrumented:** 780 ms of 4.4 s worker time is idle.

The allocator and the bank lock take no samples.

## The change

The host's column grows to a row per thread, so the drain has 8 units per thread, and a worker that finishes early takes another. The two expressions become one:

```diff
-      if (f * (CUBE_T / LINE) < pool_size) {
-        row_grow((Env){ H, ALC[0] }, io_stk, 0, CUBE_G,
-          (pool_size + CUBE_T / LINE - 1) / (CUBE_T / LINE));
+      if (f < pool_size) {
+        row_grow((Env){ H, ALC[0] }, io_stk, 0, CUBE_G, pool_size);
       }
```

- **Size:** `comp.ts` 63,794 → 63,762 ttok.
- **Emitted C:** the same as main's except this hunk and its comment.
- **GPU lane:** `gpu_pass` doesn't use this path.

## Measurements

These are from an Apple M4 laptop (4 performance and 6 efficiency cores), CPU only (`--gpu off`), with the builds interleaved.

**`bench/runtime` at 10 threads, the default here, median of 5.** Every output matches main.

| bench | main | this PR | |
|---|---|---|---|
| bfs | 0.604 s | 0.510 s | 1.18x |
| editdist | 0.514 s | 0.438 s | 1.17x |
| gameoflife | 1.433 s | 1.295 s | 1.11x |
| hashmap | 0.508 s | 0.440 s | 1.15x |
| kmeans | 0.475 s | 0.474 s | 1.00x |
| lexer | 0.455 s | 0.408 s | 1.11x |
| mandelbrot | 0.849 s | 0.736 s | 1.15x |
| merkle | 0.934 s | 0.835 s | 1.12x |
| nbody | 1.032 s | 0.912 s | 1.13x |
| queens | 0.985 s | 0.880 s | 1.12x |
| raytrace | 0.866 s | 0.780 s | 1.11x |
| symreg | 0.576 s | 0.507 s | 1.14x |
| terrain | 0.411 s | 0.366 s | 1.12x |
| tree-bitonic | 1.403 s | 1.465 s | 0.96x (median of 9) |
| tree-matmul | 0.505 s | 0.454 s | 1.11x |
| tree-radix | 0.860 s | 0.777 s | 1.11x |

**Other thread counts:** these come from the same rule measured earlier by patching the emitted C, median of 3.

| threads | effect |
|---|---|
| 3 | 1.08x on most |
| 5 | 1.19x on most |
| 6 | 1.03x to 1.06x |
| 8 | the same as main (main's rule already splits 8 units evenly there), except `tree-bitonic` 0.95x and `queens` 0.98x |
| 1, 4 | the same as main |

**Two others considered:**
- **The fewest rows whose units divide evenly among the threads.** It ties this at 3 and 5 threads, but is 1–3% slower than main at 6 and 1–4 points behind this at 10. With mixed fast and slow cores, more, smaller units balance better than an exact split.
- **4 units per thread.** It sits between main and this.

## Tests

- **Every program:** all 1,584 under `tests/`, `bench/runtime` and `demos`, on the native lane at the default thread count, `--threads 3` and `--threads 5`. They print the same as main. The exception is `demos/io_rollback_netcode/walkers_test`, which answers from whatever relay is running, as it does on main.

title: IO.poll: run an act until it answers or would wait
body:
Base has one non-blocking API per type (`TCP.poll`, `UDP.poll`, and #1162's `Chan.try_send`/`try_recv`); this is one mechanism for every effect.

### API

```python
type IO.Poll<-A: Type> is Type:
  Ready{value: A}
  Late{value: A}

def IO.poll(-A: Type, ms: U32, act: IO(A)) -> IO(IO.Poll<A>)
```

`IO.poll(ms, act)` runs `act`, but any effect in `act` that would wait more than `ms` before it starts is **cancelled** instead. It answers at once without running, and `act` goes on with that answer:

- a channel send answers `False` (its value dropped), a receive `None`;
- a sleep answers at once;
- an effect on a socket answers `(socket, Fail{ECANCELED})`, so the socket comes back to be closed.

`IO.poll` answers `Ready{x}` if `act` answered `x` with nothing cancelled, else `Late{x}`.

- **Nothing is left behind.** A cancelled receive took nothing, a cancelled send delivered nothing, and no waiter or timer stays on the channel. So a loop simply issues the call again next turn.
- **`IO.poll(0, act)` never waits** and reads no clock.
- **A cancel yields** to the other computations, as a wait would. Every 64 cancels also give the loop a non-blocking turn to see its timers and sockets, so a computation spinning on `IO.poll(0, _)` can't starve sleepers or socket readers.
- **A poll inside `act` waits no longer** than the enclosing one.
- **Runs to its end, past `ms`:**
  - an effect that has already started (a send half written, a connect, work on the IO threads);
  - a read the OS reported ready and then found empty;
  - an effect that declares no wait.
- **#1162's cases:**
  - `IO.poll(0, Chan.recv(c))`: `Ready{Some{v}}` got a value, `Ready{None}` closed, `Late{None}` nothing yet;
  - `IO.poll(0, Chan.send(c, v))`: `Ready{True}` sent, `Ready{False}` closed, `Late{False}` full.

  A receive with a timeout is `IO.poll(ms, Chan.recv(c))`.
- **`TCP.poll` and `UDP.poll`** are now Bend definitions over `IO.poll`, with the same behavior, sharing `Socket.polled`. Their effect files are gone.

An earlier version held the waiting effect in a `Wait{rest}` with `IO.resume`/`IO.cancel` (df031d60 replaced it). The cost of cancelling on the spot:
- a pending operation is re-issued rather than resumed;
- a cancelled send drops its value, as #1162's `try_send` does.

### How

- **Frames:** each computation keeps a stack of poll frames, `(k, until, late, own)`.
  - A nested frame's `until` is clipped to the enclosing frame's when that one is earlier, and `own` is the frame whose deadline it is. A cancel turns late every frame up to that one; on a tie, the cancel is the inner poll's own.
  - A polled act runs in place with the loop's own `Emit` continuation, on both lanes, so the `Emit` that ends it pops its frame.
  - A request whose continuation is that end answers the frame directly, whether it ran or was cancelled.
- **Cancelling before it starts:** under a frame, a request is checked before it runs. It can be cancelled if it's a channel step or a sleep, or if its effect declares `IO_IN`/`IO_OUT` in C or `{ fd: "in" | "out" }` in JS: its handle first, `(handle, Result)` back.
  - Readiness is checked with `select`, as `io_wait` does.
  - Past the deadline, the request is answered cancelled and the computation is requeued. Every 64 cancels, the loop gets a non-blocking turn (`io_wait`'s `peek`).
- **Before the deadline:**
  - a socket request waits on its fd and the clock together. If it's woken but its fd is no longer ready, it waits again until the deadline;
  - a sleep either ends in time or is cancelled at the deadline;
  - a channel step parks on its row, with a deadline timer **owned by the waiter**. Waking the waiter disarms the timer right away, and at the deadline the timer finds its waiter by identity.
- **User effects** opt in the same way. `guide/EFFECTS.md`'s section "A pollable effect" has the contract, the declaration on each lane, and what a wrong declaration breaks. Nothing checks a declaration against the def's type yet.
- **Size:** the core has only hooks. `comp.ts` is 63987 / 64000 on the branch, and 63958 / 64000 merged with current main. The rest is `effs/io_poll.c` and `effs/io_poll.js`, plus a waiter's timer in `chan.c`/`chan.js`.

### Cost

1M loops on an M-series Mac, median of 7, interleaved:

| loop | C | JS |
|---|---|---|
| `Chan.send` + `Chan.recv`, unpolled | 56 ms | 300 ms |
| both polled with 0 ms, both ready | 93 ms | 414 ms |
| `IO.poll(0, _)` that answers `Late` | 67–73 ms | 372–399 ms |

- **Per poll:** about 18 ns on C on top of the operation. That's the `IO.poll` request itself (one more trip through the evaluator than a `try_*`), a frame push/pop, and the `Ready`/`Late` box.
- **Against #1162's `try_*`,** on loops that do nothing but the channel: about 1.5–1.8× on C and 1.4–1.5× on JS.
- **Programs that don't use `IO.poll`** run as on main.

### Checks

- **Tests,** passing on the check, interpreted, JS and C lanes:
  - `io_poll.bend`: channels, sleep with deadlines, several effects in one act;
  - `io_poll_tcp.bend`: accept and receive;
  - `io_poll_deadline.bend`: receive in time; receive late, with the late value still there; send drained in time;
  - `io_poll_cancel.bend`: sockets come back from a cancel; a composite act goes on after one;
  - `io_poll_drop.bend`: a cancelled send is never delivered, and a cancelled receive leaves no waiter;
  - `io_poll_timers.bend`: an early-answered timed poll followed by a plain receive, a second timed poll, and another computation's poll;
  - `io_poll_yield.bend`: a 0 ms polling loop lets its sender run, including a sender that sleeps first;
  - `io_poll_nested.bend`: an inner poll is limited by the outer one's deadline, and a tie is the inner poll's own;
  - `io_poll_order.bend`: a poll runs its act in place, so both lanes interleave computations alike;
  - `io_poll_try.bend` and `io_poll_writer.bend`, by @aldeni;
  - `io_poll_foreign.bend` (+ `.c`, `.js`): a foreign effect written from EFFECTS.md's section.

  `io_poll_timers`, `io_poll_yield` and `io_poll_nested` come from @Lorenzobattistela's review, and each fails on the head before f605c67c. The sleeping sender, the tie and `io_poll_order` come from a later code review; each fails on the head before ae092263 (`io_poll_order` on JS).
- **Existing tests:** the full suite answers as on main on both lanes, `tcp_poll`, `udp_poll` and `tcp_recv_max_zero` included.
- **Memory (C):** 1M polls stay at 1 MB. 300k early-answered timed polls: 1 MB (75 MB before f605c67c).
- `tsc` is clean, and `gates/repo.ts` passes 49/49.

### Open

- [ ] Linux and the GPU binaries are not re-run on this version.
- [ ] A deadline above 0 waits on the loop's clock, so it's subject to #1122.
- [ ] Nothing checks a pollable declaration (`IO_IN`/`IO_OUT`, `{ fd }`) against the def's type.
- [ ] `GUIDE.md` doesn't mention `IO.poll`. The guide is at 7968 / 8000 ttok.
- [ ] Waking a channel waiter that a timed poll armed scans the park list to disarm its timer, which is O(parked items).
- [ ] `io_poll_cancel` takes a request apart the way `io_exec` does, as a second copy of that logic. A shared helper would cost 55 ttok in `comp.ts`, which has no room for it.

title: The kernel checks a self-call's descent as bend2's term_descend does, so a constructor rebuilt around a smaller part of its input descends (#1167)
body:
Fixes #1167. Rebased on #1192, which made the room for it.

### What fails

bend2 accepts a self-call whose argument rebuilds a constructor around smaller parts of the input (`term_descend`: same constructor, each field no bigger, one smaller; or no bigger than some field of the pattern). The kernel on main only accepts a rebuild of the input itself or of one of its pieces. So `height(Node{rest})` under `Node{Cons{x, rest}}` goes out as `height (.Node, (x1, ()))` and fails with `affine live code, calls that descend`.

### The change

`Term.fit` replaces `Term.pos`/`Term.piece` and follows `term_descend`. An argument meets its column's piece top down and returns how much smaller it is (`Except (failed field) slack`):

- **Variable:** fits at or below its tag, and the slack is the depth.
- **Label:** fits where a match hit it.
- **Constructor** (a pair at a field position): compares its fields in turn down its right spine. When one fails, it is tried at a site below the piece outside that field (bend2's `bad`), with its fields compared the same way, so searches nest as bend2's do. `Term.sites` finds the candidate sites from the constructor's first part.

`Arg.cmp` reads the result as error → gt, 0 → eq, more → lt. One difference is deliberate: bend2 skips the failed field again at every level it searches through, the kernel only at the top. So the kernel can accept more than bend2, never less.

### Proofs

The termination measure was already the size of the argument values, so the proof keeps its shape:

- `fit_ok` shows that, under σ, the argument is a closed value whose size plus the slack is at most the piece's size.
- `get_drop` (a piece n levels up is bigger by n) replaces `get_le`, and `cmp_size` reads the result.
- `desc_lex`, `hcl` and the rest of the termination section are unchanged.

title: A template over a constructor-less datatype vanishes from --verdict and -o with no oos entry
body:
### What you did

BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bend tv.bend --check-only, then --verdict, then -o tv.bendtt

### What happened

Both gates print `ALL PROOFS CHECK` (exit 0), but the emitted BendTT contains only `V` and `V.arms` — `tv` is absent from the book **and** from the out-of-scope report (`-o` prints no "out of scope" line). So a template whose `~` parameter type is a constructor-less datatype is silently never kernel-checked: zero enumerated values → zero instances → no def, no warning, no oos entry.

For comparison, other zero-instance situations (e.g. an impossible ~ parameter that is a stuck type) at least surface through oos ("no model"/"out of scope" lines); this one is fully silent.

### The file

```python
import Base

type V is Data:

def tv(~x: V) -> Nat:
  0n
```

`bend tv.bend --check-only` → `ALL PROOFS CHECK`; `bend tv.bend --verdict` → `ALL PROOFS CHECK`; `bend tv.bend -o tv.bendtt` → book holds only `V.arms` and `V`.

The body is still checked once generically by bend2 (a false body fails `--check-only`), so this is a verifier-completeness gap rather than a soundness hole — but the verdict claims to have kernel-checked a def it never emitted, silently.

title: A spliced inline lambda applied to a rebuilt column emits an un-annotated beta-redex, so --verdict rejects what bend2 accepts
body:
### What you did

BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bend inl2b.bend --check-only, then --verdict

### What happened

`--check-only` prints `ALL PROOFS CHECK`; `--verdict` fails with the TypeScript/kernel mismatch banner. The emitted BendTT contains an un-annotated beta-redex: a Kind-specialized parameter's inline-lambda value is spliced into the instance body and applied to a column-rebuilt tuple, emitting `App(Lam, Tup)` with no Ann around the lambda — the kernel's inference then fails with "expected an annotated term". When the same spliced lambda is applied to a plain variable instead, the kernel's bidirectional App-on-Var rule handles it and the file passes both gates.

Minimal shape (the erased `-A: Kind(q1(f))` parameter forces `f`'s field to specialize, splicing `(y: Nat) => 1n` into the body of `run3`'s instance):

```python
import Base

type Box is Type:
  Mk{fn: Nat -> Nat}

def q1(f: Box) -> Quant:
  match f:
    case Mk{g}: &1

def run3(f: Box, -A: Kind(q1(f)), +x: Nat) -> Nat:
  match f:
    case Mk{g}:
      match x:
        case 0n: g(x)
        case 1n+p: g(p)

def obs() -> Nat: run3(Mk{(y: Nat) => 1n}, Nat, 0n)
```

Emitted (the `case 0n` arm): `(λx0 => (.Succ, ((.Zero, ()), ())) (.Zero, ()))` — the lambda applied to the rebuilt tuple with no annotation, which the kernel rejects; the `1n+p` arm's `(λx0 => ...) x1` (variable argument) is accepted via the kernel's special App-on-Var rule.

Both gates agree on the trivial non-specialized variant, so this is specifically the spliced-lambda-at-non-Var-argument emission path.
