title: A Hypervisor for Bend in Bend
body:
# A separation kernel for Bend on ARM64, with its trap shim proved on ARM64 semantics

`hypervisor` → `main`

## A Bend Hypervisor

`demos/hypervisor` is an EL2 separation kernel for ARM64 on QEMU virt.
It runs up to four bare-metal guests at EL1, one vCPU each. Each guest
gets a static partition of 2 MiB blocks under stage-2 translation, and
the guests are scheduled round-robin on a GICv3 timer slice. A demo guest
talks to the kernel only by `hvc`: yield, print a character, quit.
Nothing else is emulated.

The kernel is a pure Bend function (`main.bend`). It takes one guest exit
and returns the next machine and the actions the hardware must perform. A
simulator runs those actions in Bend, and `bare.bend` applies them at EL2
through C effects (`hv_state.c`, `hv.c`). An instance hands off to a fresh
runtime through a two-slot handoff record, so a fail-stop loses no guest
work.

## Proven Parts

Everything below is proved in Bend and confirmed by the BendTT kernel
(`--verdict`). No def in the demo is `@unsafe`.

- **The model**: the 29 laws in `LAWS.bend`. They cover isolation and
  noninterference, that a guest's step cannot reach another guest's
  blocks, and that the handoff decoder accepts only records the kernel
  could have written.
- **The hardware step**: `Isa.bend` is an ARM64 subset. Over it, one EL1
  step touches no memory outside the guest's stage-2 map, no system
  register but its own (and those an exception entry writes), and not its
  own map.
- **The trap shim**: the 8 laws in `SHIM_LAWS.bend`. They cover the enter
  path, both exit paths and the five arms of the exit decoding, on the
  shim's real instruction words.

Trusted (SPEC.md §2): `Isa.bend`'s fidelity to ARM64; the C outside the
shim (stage-2 tables, GIC and timer, the handoff slots); the bare host;
the Bend toolchain and clang. Liveness is not proved. No effort was made 
to prove the C as most of it is expected to be replaced by native Bend 
soon.

`diff.sh` tests `Isa.bend` rather than trusting it. It runs one guest set
on QEMU and on the semantics, and compares every action and all 55 saved
registers at each of 14 exits. It has already caught one bug: a dropped
write-back that no shim proof could have found. Proving Isa.bend would be 
possible but was outside of the scope of this work.

The shim proof is 1.37 MB of generated Bend (`Segments.bend`) because the
kernel's per-def fuel runs out after about seventeen symbolic steps, and
the shim's paths are 68 and 80 steps. Each path is cut into segments,
which `Chain.bend` joins. Nothing the generator writes is trusted:
everything it writes gets checked.

## The Compilter Change to Support Custom Hosts

The runtime can now be built without an OS, and nothing in that build is
specific to ARM64 or to the demo:

- `-DBEND_HOST='"x.c"'` skips the OS headers and `main`.
- It includes x.c once, in place of the runtime's OS host. The OS host is
  now its own file, `bend2/effs/host.c`, which the C runtime splices in.
- The host's contract is written in `host.c`'s header. A host defines
  `io_take`, `io_work`, `io_wait` and the `f32` text functions, plus an
  entry that calls `io_loop(corpus_setup(false, 1, span))`.
- Any libc the host lacks comes in through `-include`.

The demo is one such host. `boot.c` is the host, `bare.c` is its libc,
and `build.sh x.bend x.elf` builds any program without `!` for EL2.
Moving the OS host out makes `comp.ts` smaller: 62,378 ttok against
`main`'s 63,951 (22 lines in, 178 out). A normal build's C differs from
`main`'s only in comments and the order of a few headers.

## Checking it

`sh demos/hypervisor/gate.sh` has six checks and passes in about seven
minutes, almost all of it the kernel on the shim. The demo has its own
gate because it needs QEMU, and its kernel runs take minutes, past the
30s cap. `gates/repo.ts` passes 50 / 50. The test and perf gates have 
not run on this branch.

## Commits

- `364c5424`: the separation kernel, its model laws, the simulator and
  the bare host on QEMU.
- `d593daea`: the ARM64 semantics, its QEMU differential test, and the
  shim's proof in kernel-checked segments.
- `3e80b20c`: the runtime's freestanding-host build, with the demo as one
  host.
- `93181199`: `main` merged in.
- `2f08c3a5`: the OS host moved to `bend2/effs/host.c`, which keeps
  `comp.ts` under its cap; the bare host follows `main`'s `io_wait`.

title: Process.run JS lane times out after the direct child exits with inherited pipes
body:
### What I did

On macOS arm64, I ran the existing `tests/io/process_run.bend` fixture against the source interpreter, emitted JS, and a native binary built from `main` at `a3b0dfe`:

```sh
BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun bend2/main.ts tests/io/process_run.bend
BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun bend2/main.ts tests/io/process_run.bend -o /tmp/process-run.js
bun /tmp/process-run.js
BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1 bun bend2/main.ts tests/io/process_run.bend -o /tmp/process-run-native
/tmp/process-run-native
```

I repeated the interpreter check with Bun 1.4.0 and 1.4.2. The subsequent `main` commit `1159f0b` does not change `process_run.js`, `process_run.c`, this fixture, or the guide's contract.

### What happened

The native binary prints the fixture's expected output (all 16 checks are `True`). Both the interpreter and emitted JS disagree on the two descendant cases:

```text
expected: inherited pipe: True
actual:   inherited pipe: unexpected failure

expected: descendant output: True
actual:   descendant output: unexpected failure
```

The first case is `Process.run("/bin/sh", ["-c", "sleep 3 & echo hi"], "", 128, 1500)` in the existing fixture. A direct `Bun.spawnSync` probe for that command returned `exitCode: 0` and `exitedDueToTimeout: true` after about 1500 ms, with `stdout: "hi\n"`. That is consistent with the inherited pipe remaining open after the direct child exits; I have not determined which part of Bun's process lifecycle sets the timeout flag. The `yes & echo hi` case is also observed failing here, but its output volume is scheduling-sensitive, so the `sleep` case is the cleaner regression.

`process_run.js` currently maps `exitedDueToTimeout` to `Fail`. The guide says a descendant holding an inherited pipe open does not extend `Process.run`'s wait. Since `gates/test.ts` compares this fixture in interpreter, C, and JS lanes, the observed JS output disagrees with the checked-in expectation.

### Prior work / question

#1051 reported the opposite mismatch (C failed where JS succeeded), and #1054 changed the native path. Its review already noted Linux/Bun differences; this report adds a macOS reproduction of the remaining JS-side mismatch. I did not find an open issue or PR that changes `process_run.js` for this case.

Should the JS lane keep the documented direct-child behavior here? If so, I would treat this as a process-lifecycle fix plus a focused regression, not as a reason to relax the fixture's expectation. I have not proposed a patch yet because swapping process APIs or changing timeout handling without agreeing on the intended behavior could create new leaks or hangs.

### Environment

- Bend: 2.0.35
- Bun: 1.4.0 and 1.4.2
- `uname -sm`: `Darwin arm64`
- Clang: `Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.4.4.1)`

title: BendTT fits ∀s by their parts, as bend2's LE does, so the kernel, not safe.ts, fits Nat -> Kind(&2) to Nat -> Type
body:
Stacked on #1203 (base: `kernel-kind-terms`).

## Why

bend2's LE goes under a binder. It compares a function type's domains swapped and its codomain along, so:
- `g : Type -> Nat` fits `Kind(&0) -> Nat`;
- `K : Nat -> Kind(&2)` fits `Nat -> Type`;
- a rewrite of type `Nat -> Kind(&0)` fits a `Nat -> Type` goal.

The kernel fitted only at the top, so on #1203 `safe.ts` bridged the gap:
- a self-call's argument went η-long where its domains or kinds differed from the column's (`qsig_eq`);
- a rewrite went out at its own type (`rwt_type`).

`--verdict` trusted that bridge, and all three divergences that review found were in it. This moves the rule into the kernel, with proofs, so the kernel decides those fits itself.

## Kernel (`bend2/bendtt.lean`)

- **`Fits` is inductive:** conversion, kinds (`*(g)` fits `*(h)` where `g` is `.Q2` wherever `h` is, as before), enums (fewer labels), **`∀q A B` fits `∀q C D` when `C` fits `A` and `B` fits `D`**, and transitivity. Transitivity is a rule, so the old nine-way `fits_trans` is gone.
- **`Fits.at` / `fits_at`** read a fit at a former, in both directions. If `T` converts to a former `X`, then `U` converts to a `Y` that fits `X` part by part, and the same from `U`'s side. `fits_all`, `fits_conv`, `fits2` and `fits_former` follow from it. They replace the case analysis of the old disjunction, including `fits_conv`'s "any non-kind fit converts", which a ∀ rule breaks.
- **`Term.fits`** threads fuel, as `qge` does, and fits two `∀`s of one quantity by their parts. `fits_sound` proves it.
- **Subject reduction and progress** take the rule:
  - β casts the argument along the domain fit and the result along the codomain's;
  - a split, a hit and a miss do the same;
  - a λ-match on an enum may now receive a smaller enum;
  - `lab_in` reads a label through a fit.
- Every claim (`consistent`, `book_check`, `confluent`, `sr`, `progress`, `halts`, `empty`) checks with no `sorry` under Lean v4.34.0 (the pinned version) and v4.34.1. Each depends only on `[propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound]`. The claim statements are unchanged; the typing judgment they quantify over is now more general.
- 63,988 ttok, against the cap of 64,000. The next kernel change has to simplify first.

## Elaborator (`bend2/safe.ts`)

- `qsig_eq` compares binder quantities only, since the kernel's fit still needs them equal.
- `rwt_type` and the annotation it added are gone.

## Checks

- Hand-written books, run through the built kernel:
  - **Rejected:** `K : <A> -> *1` at `<A> -> *2`; `∀(∀ *1 -> <A>) -> <A>` at `∀(∀ *2 -> <A>) -> <A>`; a function on `<A>` at `<A, B>`; a `∀` at a `∀+`.
  - **Accepted:** each fit in the sound direction, including two levels of contravariance.
- #1203's kind tests (`kind_*`, `meet_*`) pass. In `kind_none_is_type`, the self-call now passes `K0` whole, and the kernel fits `∀ Nat -> *(.Q0)` to `∀ Nat -> *(.Q1)` itself; on #1203 it went out as `λx2 => (K0 x2)`.
- Cluster gates on this head:
  - `repo` PASS 50 / 50, `test` PASS 1551 / 1551.
  - `perf`: the cluster was noisy. `main` itself scored 89 / 124 and this branch 49–110 / 124 in back-to-back runs. This branch doesn't touch `bend.ts`, `comp.ts` or `main.ts`, which are all perf measures.
  - `ping` was skipped: there is no site repo here.
  - `gates/safe.ts tests` with this kernel: per file, identical to `main`'s table plus #1203's new tests (999 agree, 69 unsafe, 491 bend2 rejects, 2 out of scope, 1 false reject: #1193).
- The snippets in the open issues give the same results as #1203's head.
- `tsc`: the same 12 errors as `main`.
- Not measured: kernel time. The fit now recurses through `∀`s instead of converting them, and fewer arguments go out η-long.

## Paper

`bend2/docs/BendTT/main.typ` and `paper/BendTT.pdf` give the `∀` rule:
- in the kinds section, with Bend examples;
- in Figure 3's caption for `U <= T`, together with transitivity;
- in the subject-reduction sketch, where a fit is inverted at a type former, so β casts along the domains' and codomains' fits.

The Lean line count is now 4,157.

title: book_promises returns early on a book with no promise, and its walk set is reach
body:
Follow-up to #1334, from its review.

- **Early return:** when no def is `@unsafe` or foreign (`bad` is empty), `book_promises` returns `[]` right away. The result is the same as before: the old code started the walk empty and returned nothing. Base's own `@unsafe` defs (`Array.fork`, `Array.join`) are in every book that imports Base, so this return only fires on books without Base.
- **`q` → `reach`:** since #1334, this one `Set` is both the pending list and the visited set, and the walk relies on `for…of` visiting entries added while it runs. Calling it `q` invited turning it back into an array or iterating a copy, which would silently stop the walk after one level.

**Checked:** `--check-only` gives identical output on main and this branch for all 1,631 `.bend` files in `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`: 82 report defs relying on unsafe or foreign code, 1,047 pass, the rest fail checking the same way on both. `main.ts` is 10,080 → 10,087 ttok.

title: JS effect marshaller overflows the host stack when recursion is nested under Array
body:
### What you did

Run the program below on the JS lane, then build and run it on the native lane:

```sh
bend main.bend
bend main.bend -o main && ./main
```

### What happened

On the JS lane, a depth of 5,000 prints `ok`, but 10,000 fails with:

```text
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
```

The native lane prints `ok` at depth 20,000. A control with the same 10,000-deep
recursive ADT but a direct `next: Tree` field also prints `ok` on JS. The failure
appears only when the recursive occurrence is under `Array`.

The generated marshaller makes a direct recursive field iterative, but the
wrapped occurrence remains a host call inside the array converter:

```js
"kids": ((a) => (a.forEach((x, i) => a[i] = $0m0(x)), a))(v["kids"])
```

This looks distinct from the JS non-tail-call limitation in WONTFIX.txt
(#798/#802): `grow` is tail-recursive and completes, while the host stack grows
only in compiler-generated marshalling at the effect boundary. Direct recursive
marshaller paths are already emitted as a loop, and #1304 tested a 50,000-deep
recursive Nat round trip; nesting that path under `Array` bypasses the loop.

Reproduced on current `main` at `565d7fdec289b1f2f5f5037bb58b5afb6738ff1d`.

### The files

`main.bend`:

```python
import Base

type Tree is Type:
  Leaf{}
  Node{n: Nat, kids: Array<Tree>}

def grow(n: Nat, tree: Tree) -> Tree:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      tree
    case 1n+p:
      grow(p, Node{0n, ALeaf{tree}})

law touch:
  for tree: Tree
  IO(Unit)

def touch(tree):
  import "./main.c"
  import "./main.js"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    u : Unit <- touch(grow(U32.to_nat(20000), Leaf{}))
    IO.print("ok")

#|ok
```

`main.js`:

```js
function touch(tree) {
  return {$: CID(Unit)};
}
io_eff(CID(touch), touch);
```

`main.c`:

```c
Term touch_run(Env e, Term* f, IoWork* w) {
  return term_pak(CID(Unit), 0);
}
static void __attribute__((constructor)) touch_use(void) {
  io_eff(CID(touch), touch_run, 0);
}
```

title: The pool's claim word has one layout, checked to fit, and POOL_WAIT is one statement
body:
Cleanup from reviewing #1092 against what #1269 put on main. No behavior change: for a forking test and for tree-bitonic, the emitted C compiles to byte-identical assembly before and after this PR.

**The claim word.** `pool_row` packs a turn's number, whether it grows, its row count, and the claims taken so far. `pool_rows`, `pool_work` and `pool_turn` each spelled that layout as bare shifts and masks (`c & 32767`, `c >> 15 & 255`, `c >> 23 & 1`, `c >> 24`, `turn << 24 | grow << 23 | n << 15`), so changing a field meant editing three functions in step. `CLAIM(turn, grow, rows)` and `CLAIM_TURN`, `CLAIM_GROW`, `CLAIM_ROWS`, `CLAIM_TAKEN` now hold the layout in one place.

**Checked to fit.** The 8-bit row field and the 15-bit claim field only fit because `CUBE_LOG` never exceeds 7 and `pool_size` never exceeds `CUBE_T`. Nothing stated that before: the 7 was `CUBE_LOG`'s initializer, and CUDA's `gpu_shape` clamped to a literal 128. Both now use `CUBE_LOG_MAX`, and a `_Static_assert` checks the largest case: at most `CUBE_G` rows, at most `CUBE_T` claims per row on a drain, plus one claim per thread past the end. Raising `CUBE_LOG_MAX` to 8 now fails the build with "the claim word's rows or claims overflow their fields".

**`POOL_WAIT`** was a multi-statement macro called without a semicolon. It is now wrapped in `do { } while (0)`, so a call is a single statement and is safe under an `if`.

Verification:
- Emitted C differs from main only in the pool section and in `gpu_shape`, which is compiled only on CUDA.
- `cc -std=c11 -O3 -S` gives identical assembly on main and this branch for `tests/io/process_run_parallel.bend` and `bench/runtime/tree-bitonic`.
- No `-Wall -Wextra` warnings in the new code.
- The CUDA path (`gpu_shape`) was not compiled: there is no CUDA toolchain here.
- `tsc`: no errors in `comp.ts`. `comp.ts` goes from 62,984 to 63,217 tokens, under its 64,000 cap.
- Gates: `repo` 50/50, `test` 1559/1559, `perf` 124/124. One earlier run got 121/124 on the same binaries. `ping` was skipped because there's no site checkout here.

title: A closed book overflows the stack after all its proofs check, in the recursive walk `book_promises` → `term_refs` over the elaborated terms (2.0.35)
body:
### What you did

Bend 2.0.35 (`79df8d9c`), Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64, with
`BUN_JSC_maxPerThreadStackUsage=16777216` (a 16 MiB JavaScript stack),
`BUN_JSC_useFTLJIT=false` (Bun's FTL tier off, the other tiers on) and
`ulimit -s 32768`.

```python
import Base

def Bounds(low: Nat, +high: Nat) -> Type:
  {Nat.is_le(low, high) == True{} : Bool} &
  {Nat.is_le(Nat.add(high, 2n), 30005n) == True{} : Bool}

def bounds() -> Bounds(30000n, 30001n):
  ({==}, {==})
```

```sh
bend repro.bend             # Error: the machine stack overflowed (…), exit 1
bend repro.bend --verdict   # the same; the kernel is never reached
```

Add any open claim to the file (`law open: {1n == 1n : Nat}`) and the same
command prints `SOME PROOFS FAIL` / `Error: 1 TODO found.` cleanly: the
proof of `bounds` was checked and accepted. Replace `30000`/`30001`/`30005`
by `20000`/`20001`/`20005` and the closed file prints `ALL PROOFS CHECK`.

### What happened

With `book_err` printing the stack, the `RangeError` comes from repeated
`term_refs` frames (`bend2/main.ts:776` in 2.0.35), called by
`book_promises`, called by `cli_verdict` from `book_run` (a book without
`main`). `term_refs` recurses through every field of the elaborated term
but `s`, including the `v` of each `Var` cell; `Check` (`bend.ts`) wraps
every checked subterm in `Ann(tm, Var("_", -1, undefined, ty))`, so the
elaborated term keeps the checked types with their memo cells. Reducing
`Nat.add(high, 2n)` under `Nat.is_le`, with `high` a reusable parameter bound
to `30001n`, forces the literal one successor at a time and each step is
memoised in a fresh cell (`fr.l.v = …` in the `VAR` frame of `term_wnf`):
the cell of `high` ends up holding a chain of about 60 000 nodes (`Succ` and
cell alternating). The elaborated term of `bounds` has 1.6 million nodes for
the 100 000 variant, depth 200 012 (measured by an iterative walk added for
the diagnosis). `term_refs` then overflows the stack on that chain.

`Nat.is_le(high, 30005n)` in place of `Nat.is_le(Nat.add(high, 2n), 30005n)`
leaves no chain and passes at 100 000; so does the same proof when each
comparison is a lemma of its own applied in the tuple (the elaborated
components then compare literal against literal). An open claim anywhere
skips the walk (`book_read` throws on `hols > 0` before `cli_verdict`),
which is why the overflow shows only on the final, closed book.

On `main`, #1334 (merged) and #1345 (open) change how `book_promises`
collects the definitions it walks; `term_refs` is the same recursion there.

### What you expected

`ALL PROOFS CHECK`, since the proof is accepted; or, at least, the same
outcome with and without an open claim.

A possible fix, for what it is worth: the walk without the machine stack,
an explicit worklist, with visited nodes recorded by identity (a `Set` of
objects) so that a shared node is walked once, and every field still
visited, the checked annotations and the memo cells' values included, so
that the reference set, and therefore every verdict, stays exactly the same.
Skipping the memo cells' values or the annotations, or walking the parsed
bodies instead of the elaborated terms, would also avoid the chain, but
nothing here shows that no dependency would be lost: the annotations are
where a type-only dependency lives (PR #990 keeps them for that reason;
#1205 shows a dependency missed when part of a type is not walked).

title: `-o`/`--verdict` leave out a def that copies a hypothesis of computed type after a match refined it ("a λ that uses a variable twice") (2.0.35)
body:
### What you did

Bend 2.0.35 (`79df8d9c`), Bun 1.3.14, macOS arm64, kernel built from
`bend2/bendtt.lean` (digest `e15042434e73aab0`).

```python
import Base

type Spine is Data:
  SpineEnd{}
  SpineCon{head: Nat, tail: Spine}

def AtEnd(rest: Spine, b: Nat) -> Type:
  match rest:
    case SpineEnd{}: {Nat.is_le(b, 7n) == True{} : Bool}
    case SpineCon{x, r}: Unit

def PairAtEnd(rest: Spine, +b: Nat) -> Type:
  match rest:
    case SpineEnd{}:
      {Nat.is_le(b, 7n) == True{} : Bool} & {Nat.is_le(b, 7n) == True{} : Bool}
    case SpineCon{x, r}: Unit

def duplicate(rest: Spine, +b: Nat, proof: AtEnd(rest, b)) -> PairAtEnd(rest, b):
  match rest:
    case SpineEnd{}:
      +copy = {proof : {Nat.is_le(b, 7n) == True{} : Bool}}
      (copy, copy)
    case SpineCon{x, r}: Unit{}
```

```text
$ bend copy.bend
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend copy.bend -o copy.bendtt
BendTT: out of scope, so not in copy.bendtt:
- duplicate: a λ that uses a variable twice, of a type whose fields are not Data (a ~ argument)
$ bend copy.bend --verdict
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Sorry - this is a mismatch between the TypeScript implementation, and the formalized BendTT kernel. …
```

### What happened

bend2 accepts `duplicate`: in the `SpineEnd{}` arm the type of `proof` is the
equality `{Nat.is_le(b, 7n) == True{} : Bool}`, which may be copied. The
translation sees the declared type `AtEnd(rest, b)`, which does not reduce
to a datatype while `rest` is a variable, and leaves the def out.

Two controls pass both checkers: the same arm calling a helper
`pairProof(+b: Nat, +proof: {Nat.is_le(b, 7n) == True{} : Bool})` that returns
`(proof, proof)`; and a hypothesis of computed type consumed once in each
arm, without a copy (whether the match refines its type or not).

### What you expected

The kernel checking `duplicate`, the copy being rebuilt at the type the
match refined it to (an equality, which is data); or, failing that, the
limitation listed in `WONTFIX.txt`, since `--verdict` alone only prints the
generic mismatch notice.

title: A taken kernel name gets a number, not one more underscore: n instances of a def cost O(n log n) characters of names, not O(n²)
body:
`fresh` makes a kernel name unique by appending `_` until it is free, so the k-th instance of a def is named with k underscores: n instances cost O(n²) characters of names, and as many characters hashed to find them. It now tries `n_1`, `n_2`, …. The first name of each def is unchanged; later ones go from `x_`, `x__` to `x_1`, `x_2`.

This matters for books with many template instances. Ours is a 2.4 MB generated proof book (square packings, every lemma generic over an ordered field), where `FieldRing.of_nat` alone has ~300 instances. `bend PROOF.bend -o` and then the kernel, on main (ffeddf06), same machine, back to back:

| of which `qvv_…` names | 320 MB  | 10 MB   |

title: fix(compiler): register datatypes of boxed constructors
body:
Native compilation can emit a boxed constructor without discovering its dependent datatype, leaving its `CID_*` undefined. This affects U32/F32 Word tails and user-defined dependent families such as `V.Nil`/`V.Con`.

Register the datatype of each emitted constructor in the reachable source map before native constructor IDs are collected. Keep the existing runtime roots and reserved-name policy. Retain the original Word regression and add F32, dependent-vector, and nested boxed-call regressions.

Fixes #1252.

Validation:

- All four regressions pass check-only, interpretation, emitted JS on Bun and Node, native CPU with one/four threads, and forced Metal GPU mode.
- 276 local fixtures pass across `compile`, `eval`, `run`, `base`, `show`, and `spec`: 253 native runs, 253 emitted-JS runs, and 22 forced Metal runs. The other 23 fixtures use the existing gate's exclusion for unprintable mains.
- All 17 runtime benchmarks emit byte-identical C compared with current main (`ef6278149`).
- Repository gate passes, 50/50. `comp.ts` is 63,719 ttok, within its unchanged 64,000 cap.
- Two independent correctness reviews found no remaining actionable issues.

The mini-cluster gates were not rerun for this revision because the local machine cannot resolve `cluster`. CUDA was not tested.

title: A library target for the browser: pure defs as WebAssembly, with parallel calls on Web Workers
body:
### What Bend should do Build a program's pure defs as WebAssembly that a web page imports and calls, with parallel calls running on Web Workers. This is close to the shape @pjcavalcanti sketched when closing #866, which he gave as an illustration rather than a decided API: ```sh bend heatpar.bend --library -o heatpar.wasm.js ``` ```js import {steps} from "./heatpar.wasm.js"; // the page owns the canvas and the frame loop, and calls Bend once a frame function frame() { grids = steps(1n, grids); draw(grids.fst); requestAnimationFrame(frame); } ``` What a page would need from it: - the same calling convention as the `-o x.mjs` module has today, so a page can switch between the two builds by changing one import - `Array` and `Array` readable from JS without a copy (a typed-array view on the wasm heap would do), since a game draws them every frame - parallel calls on Workers when the page is cross-origin isolated, and on one thread when it is not, because many hosts cannot send the COOP and COEP headers and the page should still run there - no page, canvas or UI of its own ### Why A falling-sand game in the browser, in the style of Noita, runs a few kernels over flat arrays every frame: the cell rules, heat and air pressure. Bend's native lane already runs this kind of kernel well. In the browser, the only option today is the JS lane. It is single-threaded by design, and on the kernel below it is 13 times slower than the native build on one thread and 38 times slower than the native build on four threads. The kernel is `heatpar.bend` (below): heat spreading on a 512 × 512 grid of F32 for 100 steps, with the grid split 6 times using `Array.fork`. Measured on an Apple M2 Pro (10 cores) with Bend 2.0.35 and Node 26.5.0. Each figure is the median of 7 runs, and every build prints the same centre value (3.9639938). | How `heatpar.bend` runs | Time for 100 steps | |---|---| | native binary, `--threads 1` | 28 ms | | native binary, `--threads 4` | 10 ms | | native binary, `--threads 10` | 10 ms | | `-o heatpar.mjs`, imported by Node | 378 ms | | the same module with the index patch below | 165 ms | | `bend heatpar.bend` | 1,095 ms | For scale, the same kernel written as a plain loop takes 22 ms in C (clang -O3) and 60 ms in JS over a `Float32Array`. ### A smaller fix for the JS lane Most of the JS lane's time on this kernel goes to wrapping the index. `bend2/comp.ts` (lines 245 and 246) emits `$0[$1 % $0.length]` for `Array.get` and `Array.set`, and `array_rmw` uses `i % a.length`. As far as I can see, every JS-lane array has a power-of-two length: `array_new` makes `2 ** d` elements, `array_node` joins two halves of equal length, and `Array.clone` copies. If that holds, `$0[$1 & ($0.length - 1)]` reads the same element. It also does so for U32 indexes of 2^31 and above, because `&` keeps the low bits and the block class cap is 31. I replaced the expression in the generated modules with `perl -pe 's/% (_\w+)\.length\]/& ($1.length - 1)]/g'`. That took `heatpar.mjs` from 378 to 165 ms. It also took the same kernel without the fork (a single sweep) from 408 to 150 ms. The output was the same in both cases. I have not rebuilt Bend itself with the change.
heatpar.bend ```python import Base # Heat spreading on a 512 x 512 grid (2^18 cells, row-major), from one array into the other: each # cell moves a fifth of the way toward its four neighbours (indexes wrap round the edges). Each read # hands the array back beside the value, and a computed pair can only be taken apart as a parameter, # so the stencil is a chain of defs, one read each, written bottom-up (a def calls only defs above it). def s5(+c: F32, l: F32, rt: F32, u: F32, r: Array & F32) -> Array & F32: (a, d) = r (a, (c + 0.2 * (l + rt + u + d - 4.0 * c) : F32)) def s4(+i: U32, +c: F32, l: F32, rt: F32, r: Array & F32) -> Array & F32: (a, u) = r s5(c, l, rt, u, Array.get(F32, a, (i + 512 : U32))) def s3(+i: U32, +c: F32, l: F32, r: Array & F32) -> Array & F32: (a, rt) = r s4(i, c, l, rt, Array.get(F32, a, (i - 512 : U32))) def s2(+i: U32, +c: F32, r: Array & F32) -> Array & F32: (a, l) = r s3(i, c, l, Array.get(F32, a, (i + 1 : U32))) def s1(+i: U32, r: Array & F32) -> Array & F32: (a, c) = r s2(i, c, Array.get(F32, a, (i - 1 : U32))) def cell(+i: U32, a: Array) -> Array & F32: s1(i, Array.get(F32, a, i)) # one sweep: ov is the old grid beside the value worked out for the cell before i def sweep(n: Nat, +i: U32, ov: Array & F32, b: Array) -> Array & Array: match n: case 0n: (a, v) = ov (a, Array.set(F32, b, (i - 1 : U32), v)) case 1n+p: (a, v) = ov sweep(p, (i + 1 : U32), cell(i, a), Array.set(F32, b, (i - 1 : U32), v)) # a stretch of len cells from lo: the same sweep over a part of the grid def range(n: Nat, +i: U32, ov: Array & F32, b: Array) -> Array & Array: match n: case 0n: (a, v) = ov (a, Array.set(F32, b, (i - 1 : U32), v)) case 1n+p: (a, v) = ov range(p, (i + 1 : U32), cell(i, a), Array.set(F32, b, (i - 1 : U32), v)) # (a leaf works out its first cell before the loop, which then writes each cell as it works out the # next, and the last at the end: every write stays inside the leaf's own stretch, so leaves never race) def leaf(+lo: U32, +len: U32, a: Array, b: Array) -> Array & Array: range(U32.to_nat((len - 1 : U32)), (lo + 1 : U32), cell(lo, a), b) def joined(x: Array & Array, y: Array & Array) -> Array & Array: (xa, xb) = x (ya, yb) = y (Array.join(F32, xa, ya), Array.join(F32, xb, yb)) # split the grid in two k times, each half on its own core, every task sharing both arrays def par(+k: Nat, +lo: U32, +len: U32, ap: Array & Array, bp: Array & Array) -> Array & Array: match k: case 0n: (a1, a2) = ap (b1, b2) = bp _ = a2 _ = b2 leaf(lo, len, a1, b1) case 1n+p: (a1, a2) = ap (b1, b2) = bp +h = U32.shr(len) x y = par(p, lo, h, Array.fork(F32, a1), Array.fork(F32, b1)) par(p, (lo + h : U32), h, Array.fork(F32, a2), Array.fork(F32, b2)) joined(x, y) def flip(r: Array & Array) -> Array & Array: (x, y) = r (y, x) def steps(k: Nat, ab: Array & Array) -> Array & Array: match k: case 0n: ab case 1n+p: (a, b) = ab steps(p, flip(par(6n, 0, 262144, Array.fork(F32, a), Array.fork(F32, b)))) def second(r: Array & F32) -> F32: (a, v) = r v def probe(r: Array & Array) -> F32: (a, b) = r second(Array.get(F32, a, 131328)) def main() -> IO(Unit): do IO: a : Array = Array.set(F32, Array.new(F32, 18n, 0.0), 131328, 1000.0) t0 : Nat <- IO.now() r : Array & Array = steps(100n, (a, Array.new(F32, 18n, 0.0))) t1 : Nat <- IO.now() IO.print("centre " ++ F32.show(probe(r)) ++ " after 100 steps; " ++ Nat.show(Nat.sub(t1, t0)) ++ " ms") ```
The Node timing script ```js // heatpar.bend built with `bend heatpar.bend -o heatpar_out.mjs`, run under Node: the module as built, // and the same module with `% a.length` replaced by `& (a.length - 1)` (median of 7 runs each). const med = (xs) => xs.sort((a, b) => a - b)[xs.length >> 1]; for (const file of ['heatpar_out.mjs', 'heatpar_mask.mjs']) { const B = (await import('./' + file)).default, ts = []; let c = 0; for (let w = 0; w < 7; w++) { const a = Array(1 << 18).fill(0), b = Array(1 << 18).fill(0); a[131328] = 1000; const t0 = performance.now(); const r = B.steps(100n, { $: 'Tuple', fst: a, snd: b }); ts.push(performance.now() - t0); c = r.fst[131328]; } console.log(`${file.padEnd(18)} median ${med(ts).toFixed(0)} ms (min ${Math.min(...ts).toFixed(0)}) centre ${c}`); } ```
Written by Claude (Anthropic) at Ben Sturgeon's request. The numbers are from his machine.

title: Calls passing a source lambda run a specialized def with the lambda's captures as parameters
body:
**Draft: `comp.ts` is 64,306 ttok, 306 over the 64,000 cap.** Opened to decide whether this is worth the tokens.

Follows #1288, which made calls with a known callback skip the closure by inlining the callee at each call site. That needed a fuel budget and couldn't handle recursive callees, so it was closed. This does the same thing in `comp.ts` only, with no fuel and no language change. The JS lane is unchanged.

## What it does

A call that passes a lambda written in the source, in a declared live parameter position, runs a specialized def `callee$cbN` instead of building a closure:
- **The specialized def:** its body is the callee's with the lambda substituted for that parameter, and the lambda's captured variables become its leading parameters.
- **Sharing:** specializations are keyed by the lambda's code with captures abstracted and types dropped, plus its parameters' layouts, so the same lambda code at different call sites shares one def.
- **When they're created:** only while the book is read. During emission, calls only look them up.
- **Beta reduction:** `anf` reduces the callback's applications, binding each argument.

**Termination, by construction.** A substituted lambda carries a marker span (`CB`). A lambda that contains one is never used as a key, except the substituted lambda itself passed on unchanged. So every key is a pair of a callee and a lambda written in the source, and both sets are finite. A callback that a recursion wraps, as in `go(n - 1, y => f(g(y)))`, keeps its closure.

## Results

The fixtures from #1288 (by @mizchi) are included unchanged. Each prints `42` in the interpreter, JS and native (1 and default threads), and builds no closures beyond the runtime's baseline (main builds 9 and 2). `known_callback_shapes.bend` covers:
- mutual recursion passing the callback unchanged
- a callee that ignores its callback
- a callback before a tuple-destructured parameter
- `Array` and `List` captures
- two lambdas in one call
- a recursion that wraps its callback

**Speed** (M4, 10⁸ steps, median of 7, run alone; the same at 1 and default threads):

| program | main | this | hand-written |
|---|---|---|---|
| helper called each step with a fresh capturing lambda | 0.25 s | 0.07 s | 0.07 s |
| callback passed down 10⁸ steps, called once | 0.07 s | 0.07 s | 0.07 s |

**Regression** (1,644 programs in `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`, main vs this):
- **Unchanged:** every JS file is identical, no build fails, and no bench's C changes.
- **Changed C:** 47 programs (40 tests, 7 demos). All 40 tests give main's output natively and match their `#|` lines, and all 7 demos build.
- **Closures:** across the changed programs, closure builds go from 1,820 to 1,548. Their C grows 1.3%.

**Compile time** (median of 3): `app_slash_boss_3d` 1.13 → 1.15 s, netcode `walkers_test` 0.32 → 0.35 s; others unchanged.

## Not covered

- **IO continuations:** `IO.bind` applies its callback to more arguments than the lambda has, which would need let-floating. `Maybe.bind`, `Result.bind` and `String.word` are covered.
- **Only one lambda per call** is specialized.
- **A callback in a raised (undeclared) parameter position** is skipped.

## Cost and how it could fit the cap

+1,174 ttok:
- `cb_spine`: 757 in total (rejection checks 122, key and captures 278, building the def 275, redirecting the call 82)
- `def_inst`, which instantiates the callee's body and type: 203
- `anf` beta reduction: 146
- hooks and `File` fields: ~130

A review pass on `cb_spine` found only about 6 safe tokens to cut. Getting under the cap would need one of these:
1. **Key by the lambda's source position instead of its code.** This saves about 100–150 tokens. Identical lambdas at different call sites would no longer share a def. A source lambda that ends up in two type contexts would then need its own guard.
2. **Drop callbacks after a matched parameter** (`def_inst`'s `Mat` case). This loses `String.word.go`-style matchers that take a continuation.
3. **Free tokens elsewhere in `comp.ts`.**

## Open risks

- **Stale annotations:** annotations above the substituted parameter still mention it. Emission reads inner annotations, so this hasn't mattered, but a U32 match table could read the stale type.
- **Capture identity:** captures are identified by probe index plus name, because `term_higher` copies probe variables. A collision cancels the specialization; it doesn't miscompile.

Not run: the cluster gates and CUDA.

title: Roots share their ~ constants, so a template goes to the kernel once instead of once per root that uses it
body:
## Problem

`--verdict` checks a template like `def pair(~a: Nat, ~b: Nat)` at made-up constants `pair~a`, `pair~b`. Every root gets its own made-up constants, and every template it calls is copied at them. So in

    def pair(~a: Nat, ~b: Nat) -> Nat: Nat.add(a, b)
    def other(~x: Nat, ~y: Nat) -> Nat: pair(~x, ~y)

`pair` goes to the kernel twice: once at `pair~a, pair~b`, once at `other~x, other~y`. A template used by 18 roots goes 18 times, with everything it calls.

## Fix

A root reuses the constant an earlier root made for the same place and type. Above, `other` checks at `pair~a, pair~b`, and `pair(~x, ~y)` is the copy that is already there.

This is safe because:

- the kernel knows nothing about a made-up constant, so a proof at it holds for every value, whichever root made it;
- two parameters of one root are at different places, so they still get different constants (`{a == b}` still does not check).

## Numbers

Our book (generated square-packing proofs, 2.4 MB), on main (d052d4f3), same machine:

|                              | main         | this PR  |
| ---------------------------- | ------------ | -------- |
| text sent to the kernel      | 237 MB       | 23.5 MB  |
| memory to write it (`-o`)    | 14.7 GB      | 4.5 GB   |
| kernel memory                | 8.6 GB       | 0.85 GB  |
| kernel time (two runs, busy) | 24 to 63 min | 57 s     |
| our CI job                   | 27 min       | 7.6 min  |

`gates/safe_node.ts` on all 1580 files in `tests/` prints exactly the same output as main.

## Note on #1263

#1263 lets a root change the models of its constants after the fact. With shared constants, that change would also affect other roots, so a root that needs such a change should get its own constants again. If #1263 lands first, I will add that to this PR.

title: UDP gets the byte twins TCP and File already have: send_bytes_to, recv_bytes_from and their try_ twins
body:
## What changes

`UDP.send_to` and `UDP.recv_from` carry UTF-8, so a binary datagram does not survive them. Four effects carry the bytes as they are, with the types and rules of `TCP.send_bytes` / `TCP.recv_bytes`:

| text | bytes |
|---|---|
| `UDP.send_to` | **`UDP.send_bytes_to`** |
| `UDP.try_send_to` | **`UDP.try_send_bytes_to`** |
| `UDP.recv_from` | **`UDP.recv_bytes_from`** |
| `UDP.try_recv_from` | **`UDP.try_recv_bytes_from`** |

```python
def UDP.send_bytes_to(sock: Socket, host: String, port: U32, data: List<&2, U32>) ->
  IO(Socket & Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String) & List<&2, U32>, Unit>)

def UDP.recv_bytes_from(sock: Socket, max: U32) ->
  IO(Socket & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, String & U32 & List<&2, U32>>)
```

`List<&2, U32>`, one cell per byte, as `File.read_bytes` and `TCP.recv_bytes` use. A value past 255 fails with `EINVAL` before anything is sent and the list comes back whole, as in `TCP.send_bytes`. No new type and no new helper: `io_list`, `io_cbuf` and `io_unlist` are the ones TCP uses.

## Why

On `main`, a datagram holding the byte 200 is read by `UDP.recv_from` as U+FFFD (the same in the interpreted, JS and C lanes), and `UDP.send_to` writes a char 200 as two bytes. So nothing binary can go over UDP today: DNS, NTP, RTP, QUIC, STUN.

WONTFIX keeps DNS out of Base and says to build such things as hub packages over bytes (#846); TCP got its bytes for that. A resolver is a UDP protocol, and a package cannot carry it over text. This is what a library cannot build without its own foreign code: the socket is Base's.

Every UDP API I know takes bytes: Python's `sendto(bytes)`, Go's `WriteToUDP([]byte)`, Rust's `send_to(&[u8])`, Node's `dgram` with a `Buffer`, Java's `DatagramPacket(byte[])`, Erlang's `gen_udp` with a binary.

## How

Each pair shares its effect file, in the shape `tcp_send.c` and `tcp_recv.c` have:

- `udp_send_to.c`: `udp_send_to_with(e, w, more, make)` is the old step with the function that hands the datagram back passed in (`io_str` or `io_list`); `udp_send_to_at` reads the address for both starts; the bytes start refuses a value past 255 before it allocates.
- `udp_recv_from.c`: `udp_recv_from_with(e, w, more, read)`, and `udp_recv_from_start` takes `more`.
- The `.js` twins take the same parameter (`io_text` or `io_list`); `udp_send_to_with` takes the bytes already made, so both callers share it.
- `base.bend`: the four defs, each after its text twin.

The text effects behave as before. `bend.ts` and `comp.ts` are untouched.

## Tests

`tests/io/udp_bytes.bend` (12 lines): 0, 255, the two bytes of "á" and a lone 128 arrive byte for byte; text sent by `UDP.send_to` arrives as its UTF-8 bytes; an empty datagram is `[]`; a `max` of 2 keeps 2 of 5; a value past 255 and a malformed address fail with 22 and hand the list back; the `try_` twins answer `Wait{}`, `Ready{Done{}}` and `Ready{Fail{}}`; a `max` of 0 fails with 22.

On Linux x86-64 (clang 21, bun), built from this branch:

- `udp_bytes` prints its lines in the interpreted, JS and C lanes.
- The other 27 `udp_*`, `tcp_*`, `file_*` and `port_bound` tests keep their output in the three lanes (`file_size_no_ffi` is JS-only by design).
- `gates/repo.ts`: PASS 50 / 50.

Beyond the suite, in the three lanes:

- All 256 byte values to and from Python's `socket`: identical both ways.
- A real DNS query (A, example.com) to 127.0.0.53 and to 8.8.8.8: the reply parses, and its addresses are the ones `getaddrinfo` gives.
- Datagrams of 1472, 9000 and 65507 bytes over loopback arrive whole (size and sum); 65508 fails with `EMSGSIZE` and the list comes back whole (C and JS).

Not tested: macOS (I have no Mac), and the cluster gates.

title: Tests that could not fail now check what they name
body:
Closes #1311.

Each of these tests kept passing when the behavior it names was broken. No change outside `tests/`.

## Printer

- **`printer/offload_bang_g`, `_h`**: `f` was the identity, so `main` normalized to `n => n` and the `!` never reached the printer. `f` now matches on its argument, so `f!(n)` on a variable is stuck and the printed snf keeps the mark: `n => f!(n)` and `n => Nat.add(f!(n), f(n))`. title: A constructor's fields compile with their declared types, so a Word folded out of a U32 literal emits
body:
Closes #1100. ## Cause The C emitter folds calls on constant arguments at compile time. When the argument is a U32 literal and the callee matches it as `U32{w}`, the body receives the literal's `Word(32n)`. That word is a `WCon{…WCon{…}}` chain the compiler built itself, so none of its nodes carry a type annotation. `emit_ctr` compiled every field with type `null` and relied on each field carrying its own annotation. The chain's inner `WCon` belongs to the parametrized `Word.Con

`, so `ctr_adt` died with `a constructor outside a datatype`. The interpreter and the JS backend print the value. Minimal repro (no pair or datatype needed): ```python import Base def word_of(u: U32) -> Word(32n): match u: case U32{w}: w def main() -> IO(Unit): do IO: IO.print(Nat.show(Word.to_nat(32n, word_of(5)))) ``` ## Change - **`emit_ctr`:** passes each field its domain from the constructor's telescope, filled with the datatype's arguments (`ctr_doms(ctr, adt.x)`, as `facts_ctr` already does). All three branches do this: the generic one, the U32/F32/Nat one and the Array one. The second commit covers the last two. No current program reaches them with an untyped parametrized constructor, so that commit is defensive. The domains are computed on demand, so constructors already in the constant cache skip them. - **`emit_each`:** takes an optional `tys` list alongside the layouts. - **`comp.ts`:** 63,464 → 63,510 ttok (cap 64,000). - **Compile time:** emission does one telescope fill per parametrized constructor node it emits, about 2 µs each. A 100×100 list constant goes from 0.17 s to 0.19 s, and the big demos (`app_slash_boss_3d`, `pure_hvm5_mini`) from 1.17 s to 1.20 s and 0.38 s to 0.39 s (best of 5). ## Tests - **New:** `tests/reg/u32_literal_word_field` covers the word alone, in a box, in a pair behind a parametrized datatype (the shape #1100 reported), in a field whose type names an earlier field (`Sized{n: Nat, w: Word(n)}`), and stored by `Array.new` and `Array.set`. Each shape dies on `main` with the error above. Here the test prints `5 6 7 8 10` on the interpreter, native and JS lanes. - **Corpus:** I emitted C for all 1,587 tests under `tests/` with and without the change. Every other test's C is byte-identical (727 files), and every run's output and exit code are identical. - **Not run:** the cluster gates. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: safe.ts and comp.ts stop reducing types they never read or already reduced, and safe_pass dedups book.order in one pass
body:
`--verdict`'s elaborator spent most of its time on big books in two places it didn't need to. The compiler reduced a computed type once per annotation that mentions it, instead of once per def signature.

**`safe.ts`**
- **Order dedup:** `safe_pass` found each root with `book.order.lastIndexOf(k) === i`, which is O(n²). On the checker benches `book.order` holds 42–54k entries, and this one line was 55–80% of elaboration. It now builds one `Map` of last indices.
- **Unused whnfs:** reductions whose result is never read, which can re-run a proof by computation bend2 already checked:
  - `arg_term` and `tree` skip `all_of` for a term bend2 never types as a function (`NOT_FN`: types, quantities, constructors, literals, `{==}`).
  - `ctr_term` skips the goal's whnf for a family with no parameters.
  - `root_cols` no longer reduces the return type past the last parameter.
  - `arm` builds its template map only for a def with `~` parameters.

**`comp.ts`**
- `term_spine` skips `tele_unbind` on a node with no applications. It was reducing a leaf's annotation type it never reads.
- **A def's signature is reduced once, in its telescope.** `term_wnf` has no per-object result cache (sharing lives in argument cells, built fresh per call), so every fresh copy of `T(ev(…))` was reduced again.
  - `tele_unbind`, already memoized per def in `FL.teles`, now stores each domain reduced.
  - `fun_of` takes a fully applied def's return type from it.
  - `file_book` reads the datatypes of a def's own λs and body, and of a call's head, off that reduced telescope (`tele_adts`), instead of reducing each annotation's copy of the signature. They come out in the order `type_adts` walks a ∀ (domains, then return type), so constructor ids keep their numbering.
  - Other annotations, such as an `App`'s or a `Ctr`'s per-site type, are scanned as before.
- An earlier revision of this PR memoized `ty_wnf` by structural key instead. That was unsound: @Lorenzobattistela's `tests/reg/wnf_memo_bound_key.bend` shows a bound `X` sharing a key with a free `X`, so a count was lost and memory freed early. The memo is gone; the test stays as a regression guard and passes natively, in JS, and in the interpreter.

**Timings** (median of 3, Apple M4):

| | `--check-only` | `-o .bendtt` main → branch | `--verdict` main → branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| defs_12800 | 0.32 s | 2.78 → 0.61 s | 7.09 → 5.05 s |
| generics_3200 | 0.40 s | 4.38 → 0.85 s | 7.82 → 4.24 s |
| proofs_3200 | 0.84 s | 3.65 → 1.59 s | 9.04 → 6.98 s |
| app_win_is_bug_2d/PROOF | 0.30 s | 0.71 → 0.31 s | 1.24 → 0.82 s |

Most of what's left in `--verdict` on the benches is the kernel: `Book.index` is a linear scan, run once per def and once per live call. That fix needs the proofs updated and will come as a separate PR.

**Where `comp.ts` speeds up:** nothing in the corpus has a computed type in live code, so its compile times don't move (`.c` 98.6 → 98.4 s, `.js` 91.5 → 91.4 s over the whole corpus). On a program built for it, live `p(x: Nat) -> T(ev(200000n))` and `q(x: Nat, u: T(ev(200000n)))` called from `main`, with a 0.35 s check, `-o .c` goes 1.55 → 0.84 s and `-o .js` 1.59 → 0.75 s. In `safe.ts`, the same kind of return type takes `-o .bendtt` from 0.78 → 0.36 s.

**Checked:**
- Over all `.bend` files in `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`, the output is byte-identical to main's: `-o .bendtt` for all 1,154 files that emit it, `-o .c` for all 762 that build, and `-o .js` for all 786.
- `tsc` reports no new errors.
- Merged onto main 7ed3424b (repo, test and ttok on f9012d59; the rest on a90ef7d7, since f9012d59 only drops comments):
  - The output is still byte-identical to main's for every file that builds on both: 1,152 `.bendtt`, 764 `.c` and 788 `.js`. The new test is the only extra file.
  - repo 50 / 50, ping 47 / 47, test 1576 / 1576.
  - safe (tests): 1017 agree, 74 u, 491 bend2 rejects, 4 out of scope, 1 false reject (agree_32, also on main). Main has 1016 agree; the new test is the extra one.
  - perf 123 / 124: raytrace's COMPILER cell is 1.16x. Main misses one cell in the same session too (mandelbrot GPU 1.16x), with raytrace's COMPILER at 1.14x.
  - `safe.ts` 22,019 → 22,117 ttok, `comp.ts` 63,553 → 63,838.

title: A bang that may reach F32.show or F32.read runs on the host
body:
Closes #1128.

## Bug

The device has no libc, so `F32.show` and `F32.read` are stubs under `#if DEVICE` that post `ERR_FIDS`. A `!` call whose code reaches either was sent to the GPU anyway and fail-stopped with `a function the device does not hold`, while the CPU lanes gave the right answer. This also happened when the call reached them through a closure argument.

## Fix

The bangs that go to the device are now picked from the ones that can't reach a host-only op. Everything is in `comp.ts`:
- The `f32_show` and `f32_read` rows in `OPERATIONS` are marked `host`, and `emit_intr` marks the segment that emits one.
- `compile_book` finds every segment that can reach a marked one. A bang is kept off the device if its own segment is one of these, or if its parameter may hold a closure and some closure can reach a marked segment.
- Those bangs lose their `FID_T` bang bit, so `corpus_eval` runs them on the host. They're also left out of the device's reach and out of `BANGS`.

Every other bang still goes to the GPU. In the new test's emitted C, `sq` keeps its bit and `sh` doesn't.

## Checked

- **`tests/compile/gpu_reach_host`** (new): `sh!` and `rd!` reach the ops directly, and `ap!` reaches `F32.show` through a closure. All three run on the host, while `sq!` still goes to the device. The interpreter, `--gpu off` and `--gpu on` all print `49 1.5 2.25 v=2.5`. On main, `--gpu on` fail-stops.
- **The issue's program:** it prints `1.5` with the GPU on.
- **Gates:** repo 50/50, test 1574/1574, perf PASS (121/124). ping was skipped: the site repo isn't checked out on this machine.

This doesn't implement `F32.show` or `F32.read` on the GPU; a call that reaches them now runs on the CPU. The fuzzer's `metal-host-only` skip isn't in this repo, so it still needs to be dropped wherever the fuzzer lives.

title: A value past 2^24-1 live copies fail-stops with its own message, and WONTFIX names the cap
body:
Refs #1267. The cap stays: this makes it visible. Once this merges, #1267 should be closed as not planned, like the other RUNTIME entries.

## Why

On the C lane, copies of a `+` value share it through one 24-bit count, so a value can have at most 2^24 − 1 live copies. Past that, the program fail-stops with the generic `bend: runtime fail-stop`, which doesn't say which limit was hit. JS keeps no count and runs on. The BendRT paper lists the cap among its limitations, but WONTFIX didn't, which is why #1267 looked like an undocumented `Array.new` limit.

The cap isn't specific to arrays. `Array.new(T, d, x)` makes 2^d copies of `x`, so it hits the cap at depth 24, but so does a list holding 2^24 copies of one computed string.

## Change

- **Error message.** The overflow now posts its own `ERR_CNTS`, both from `rfc_bump` and from `blk_new`'s depth-24 check:
  ```
  bend: a value has more than 2^24-1 live copies: keep fewer alive at once, or build it again for some of them (each build counts its own copies)
  ```
  `ERR_RFCS` keeps its generic text for its other two uses, sharing a closure and `span_fade`'s sealed-field check. Neither is a count overflow.
- **WONTFIX.** The RUNTIME section has a new entry next to #779. It states the cap and the JS difference, and gives the workaround: build the value again for each group of copies, for example an `Array.new` at depth 23 per build, joined with `ANode`.

## Checked

On the C lane:

| Program | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `Array.new(String, 23n, F32.show(1.0))` | `1n` | `1n` |
| the same at depth 24 (and with `F32.show(12.375)`) | `runtime fail-stop` | the message above |
| a list of 2^23 copies of one computed string | `1n` | `1n` |
| a list of 2^24 copies | `runtime fail-stop` | the message above |

JS prints the answer in every case, as before.

There's no new test: every lane must print the same `#|` lines, and here JS and C differ by design.

title: fix(verdict): build inlined recursive let arguments at each use
body:
Fixes #1326.

A let inlined into a recursive call kept kernel binders allocated where the let was declared. A later convoy could rename those levels and certify a different value. Store its original Bend term using the existing specialized-argument mechanism, then elaborate it at each use's depth and mode.

title: Preserve match-refined Data views in copyable lets
body:
Closes #1349.

A `+` binder whose type is a match-refined view (for example `proof: AtEnd(rest, b)` refined to an equality in a match arm) was left out of the kernel text when used twice. `tree()` in `bend2/safe.ts` chose how to handle a binder used twice from the declared kind of its type's head (`AtEnd ... -> Type`), not from the type it reduces to. So it sent the binder to `rebuild`, which can't rebuild an equality, and `--verdict` said SOME PROOFS FAIL even though bend2 accepted the program.

Fix: in `tree()`, reduce the binder's type first. If it reduces to an equality or to Data, the binder copies it (q=2) instead of rebuilding it. This uses the existing q=2 path, and the kernel already checks that a q=2 binder's type is Data, so no new trust is added. There is no special case in `let_term`. `duplicate` now goes out as `λ+x1 => (x1, x1)`.

This also covers a refined copy passed to a self-call. After #1368 such a let is rebuilt at each use, so a fix at the let site loses the view there.

Test: `tests/proof/refined_proof_copy.bend` covers the reported equality pair, the helper call, the consumed-once boundary, a Bool refinement, and the self-call case (`walk`). It fails on main and checks with this change.

Verification (main f1a69ec4, BendTT kernel b9f3e025):
- repo 50/50, ping 47/47, test 1583/1583 (main 1582 + the new test)
- safe gate: 1024 agree (main 1023, +1 = new test); unsafe, rejects, out of scope and the one known false reject (agree_32) are the same as main
- perf: same as main (only GPU/raytrace flicker, 124/124 on rerun)
- 1,137 emitted .bendtt files byte-identical to main except the new test
- #1326 repros and `tests/check/let_put_depth.bend` still pass
- ttok: safe.ts +58

No changes to the kernel, `bend2/bend.ts`, gates/caps, GUIDE, or CHANGELOG. No GPU cluster run (safe.ts doesn't affect runtime).

title: Make Array-wrapped JS marshalling stack-safe
body:
Closes #1346.

Memoize Array converters alongside ADT converters and give composite converters one shared explicit work stack. Nested arrays and mutually referenced converters no longer invoke each other recursively. Work items use a flat stack rather than allocating a tuple per field; scheduling visits fields/elements left-to-right. Existing ownership stays unchanged: arrays are converted in place, ADT nodes are copied, and absent array elements are skipped.

The permanent regression traverses 20,000 nodes through singleton Arrays. The foreign effect checks each Nat and changes the leaf; Bend checks the entire returned tree. Both the JS twin and the real C twin perform that transformation.

Verification on Linux:
- Corrected regression on unchanged main: `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)`.
- Source IO CLI and emitted JS under Bun 1.3.13 / Node 22.23.1: `ok`.
- Native binary with 1 and 4 CPU threads: `ok`.
- Exported host API: 20,001 nodes and two branches, BigInt round trip and existing array identity preserved, on Bun and Node.
- Existing Nat, closure and 50,000-value marshalling fixtures exercised.
- Repository gate: `PASS: 50 / 50`, including the staged new fixtures.

No changes to `bend2/bend.ts`, native runtime/emitter, gates/caps, GUIDE or release changelog. No macOS/GPU/mini-cluster verification claimed.

title: Keep JS Process.run bounded by the direct child
body:
Closes #1343.

Replace Bun.spawnSync's inherited-pipe lifecycle with synchronous POSIX spawn/poll/waitpid through Bun FFI, matching the existing native contract. Feed stdin and capture both streams concurrently, enforce the combined byte limit and a monotonic deadline, reap the direct child, then drain only already-buffered output. Descendants retaining the pipes do not extend the wait. Timeout/output failures kill and reap the child and close all parent descriptors.

Keep literal argv, spawn errno, signal exit codes and child SIGPIPE defaults. Relocate pipe fds below 3 before setting up child stdio. Handle Darwin arm64's stack-based variadic ABI for fcntl and ioctl. No expectation in the existing process fixture is relaxed; add a real closed-parent-stdin regression with JS/C twins.

Verification on Linux (Bun 1.3.13, Clang 22):
- Existing 16-check process fixture: every check `True` in source IO CLI, emitted JS and native CPU binary.
- Existing parallel process fixture: `True`.
- Closed-parent-stdin regression: `0:payload:` on JS and native with 1/4 threads.
- Real-process stress: 100 timeouts under forced GC, exact 4,000-byte environment value preserved, stable open-fd count, no unreaped direct children.
- Repository gate: `PASS: 50 / 50` including staged fixtures.
- Clang `arm64-apple-darwin` ABI probe verifies the padded FFI call places ioctl's pointer on the same stack slot as a real variadic call. This is code-generation evidence, **not a macOS runtime test**.

MacOS runtime verification remains for the project CI/maintainer; no Mac, GPU or mini-cluster run is claimed. No native runtime, gates/caps, GUIDE or release-changelog changes.

title: BendTT's Book holds its defs and a name table, so a lookup is one map read, not a scan of the book
body:
`Book.index` was `bk.findIdx? (·.k == k)`, a scan of the defs list. The checker ran it once per def for the fresh-name check and once per live call in `Term.called`, which was 77–95% of the kernel's time on the checker benches.

- **`Book`** is now a structure: its `defs` and their `lib`, a `Std.HashMap String (Nat × Def)` holding each name's first def at its index. The list stays because a def's index still orders its live calls.
  - The invariant is an equation, `ok : lib = Book.table 0 defs`, so `Book.of` (used by the parser) proves it by `rfl`. Part 1 gains no theorem.
  - `Book.table`, the builder, sits next to the structure in Types, since the field names it.
- **Lookups:** `Book.get` and `Book.index` read `lib`. `Book.length` keeps every `bk.length` as it was.
- **No `Lib`:** the checker (`Term.wnf` … `Term.check`) takes the `Book` where it took a `Lib`, and `Book.check` passes the book itself and `Book.of` of its transparent copy. So `Lib`, `Lib.of` and `lib_get` are gone, and one map build per book with them.
- **Proofs:**
  - Part 2's claims and every theorem statement are unchanged.
  - New in PROOF's Checker section: `table_at` (the table holds `findIdx?`'s index and `find?`'s def), and `get_find`, `index_find`, `index_lt`. They give the few proofs that read list facts off the old definitions those facts back (`book_check`, `ok_called`, `hcl`, `consistent`).
  - `Sees` is stated over `Book.get`.

**Timings** (kernel alone on each bench's BendTT, median of 3, Apple M4):

| | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| defs_12800 | 4.29 s | 0.27 s |
| generics_3200 | 3.28 s | 0.32 s |
| proofs_3200 | 5.07 s | 0.84 s |
| trees_400 | 1.49 s | 1.35 s |
| compute_1600 | 0.93 s | 0.89 s |

End to end, `bend bench/checker/defs_12800/main.bend --verdict` takes 0.90 s, after the cached kernel rebuilds once.

**Checked:**
- `bendtt.lean` elaborates with Lean v4.34.0 with no errors, warnings or `sorry`.
- `--verdict` output (exit code, verdict and failure text) is identical with main's kernel and this one on all 1,664 `.bend` files in `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`.

title: A `!` build finds CUDA at $CUDA_PATH and /opt/cuda too, so Arch's CUDA is no longer skipped
body:
## What changes

`cli_build` takes the first of `$CUDA_HOME`, `$CUDA_PATH`, `/usr/local/cuda` and `/opt/cuda` that holds `include/nvrtc.h`, instead of `$CUDA_HOME`, else `/usr/local/cuda`. GUIDE.md says CUDA 12 or 13 and names the paths.

## Why

Arch's `cuda` package installs at `/opt/cuda`, and its `/etc/profile.d/cuda.sh` exports `CUDA_PATH=/opt/cuda`, not `CUDA_HOME`. On `main`, a `!` program there builds CPU-only with no message: no `.gpu` beside the binary, and every `!` runs on the cores. `CUDA_HOME=/opt/cuda` fixes it, but nothing tells the user to set it.

The guide named CUDA 12 only. CUDA 13.4 builds and runs (comp.ts already branches on `CUDA_VERSION >= 13000`).

## Behavior

| environment | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `CUDA_HOME=/opt/cuda` | GPU | GPU |
| `CUDA_PATH=/opt/cuda`, no `CUDA_HOME` (Arch's default) | CPU, silently | GPU |
| neither set, CUDA at `/opt/cuda` | CPU, silently | GPU |
| `CUDA_HOME=/nonexistent`, CUDA at `/opt/cuda` | CPU, silently | GPU |
| no CUDA anywhere (`/opt/cuda` hidden with bwrap) | CPU | CPU |

`$CUDA_HOME` and `/usr/local/cuda` keep their priority, so a machine that built a GPU program before builds the same one. A `$CUDA_HOME` with no `nvrtc.h` now falls through to the next candidate instead of to the CPU.

## Tested

Arch Linux, CUDA 13.4.2 at `/opt/cuda`, RTX 4070 Ti SUPER (open driver 615.71.09), clang 23.1.1, bun 1.4.2:

- each row of the table above, every binary run with `--gpu on`;
- the 24 tests under `tests/` that use `!`, compile, and need no foreign effect, built with this `main.ts` and no `CUDA_HOME`: each emits its `.gpu` and prints its `#|` lines under `--gpu on` and `--gpu off`;
- `tsc -p bend2/pack/tsconfig.json`: no error in `main.ts` (the errors in other files are the same as on `main`);
- `ttok`: GUIDE.md 7981 / 8000 (was 7968), main.ts 10178 / 16000.

I did not run the gates, which need the cluster.

title: C backend: a def whose last parameter is erased compiles its parallel let as two sequential calls
body:
### What you did

bend erased_last_bad.bend -o bad && time ./bad --threads 1 && time ./bad --threads 16

### What happened

```text
$ time ./bad --threads 1
3942408568
real 1.013s  user 1.010s
$ time ./bad --threads 16
3942408568
real 1.010s  user 1.006s
 
No speedup with 16 threads. The only difference from a program that scales is
one ERASED parameter, -z, at the end of tree's parameter list, passed unchanged:
 
                                           --threads 1   --threads 16
erased_last_ok.bend    tree(+d, +i)            1.01 s        0.17 s
erased_last_bad.bend   tree(+d, +i, -z)        1.01 s        1.01 s
erased_middle_ok.bend  tree(+d, -z, +i)        1.02 s        0.17 s
 
All three print 3942408568.
 
In the emitted C (bend X.bend -o x.c), erased_last_ok and erased_middle_ok have
the join FID_TREE_J2 for the parallel let; erased_last_bad has only the
continuations FID_TREE_K2 and FID_TREE_K3, so the second call runs after the
first returns.
 
Also reproduced on main at 0ad47fc (bun bend2/main.ts).
 
Files: https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/docs/upstream/erased_last_ok.bend
       https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/docs/upstream/erased_last_bad.bend
       https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/docs/upstream/erased_middle_ok.bend
 
Where it bit us: in bend-ml, Bands.matvec carries an erased proof
(-e: {rr == r : Nat}); with -e last the bands of a matrix-vector product ran one
after another. With a runtime parameter after it, GPT-2's 50257 x 768 logits
product went from 26.7 ms to 3.3 ms on 16 threads.
```

### The file

```python
# The same program with one extra ERASED parameter, -z, at the end of tree's parameter list,
# passed unchanged. The parallel let is compiled as two sequential calls: --threads 16 takes
# as long as --threads 1. Moving -z before the runtime parameter i (erased_middle_ok.bend),
# or adding any runtime parameter after it, restores the fork.
#
#   bend erased_last_bad.bend -o bad && time ./bad --threads 1 && time ./bad --threads 16
import Base
 
def work(n: Nat, acc: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      work(p, (acc * 1103515245 + 12345 : U32))
 
def tree(+d: Nat, +i: U32, -z: Nat) -> U32:
  match d:
    case 0n:
      work(600000000n, i)
    case 1n+q:
      a b = tree(q, (i * 2 : U32), z) tree(q, (i * 2 + 1 : U32), z)
      (a + b : U32)
 
def main() -> U32:
  tree(4n, 1, 0n)
```

### bend --version

bend 2.0.35

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 22.1.8

title: IO.fork computations run their pure work on one core; the guide says "in parallel, on every core"
body:
### What you did

bend io_fork_parallel.bend -o f && time ./f --threads 1 && time ./f --threads 16

### What happened

```text
$ time ./f --threads 1
real 1.681s  user 1.678s
$ time ./f --threads 16
real 1.684s  user 1.681s
 
Four IO.fork computations; each reads the clock inside the fork and then runs a
flat loop seeded with it, so the work can only happen inside the forked
computation (not when the action is built, and not in the joiner). They take the
same time with 1 and 16 threads, and user time equals real time:
 
                                                     --threads 1   --threads 16
io_fork_parallel.bend      4 IO.fork, then 4 join       1.68 s        1.68 s
io_fork_sequential.bend    the same 4 jobs in a row     1.68 s        1.68 s
io_fork_parallel_control   same loops, 2 parallel lets  1.69 s        0.85 s
 
Also on main at 0ad47fc.
 
The guide (IO and Concurrency) says: "A Bend program is a set of computations
interleaved by one event loop, as in Node.js: each runs its pure code (in
parallel, on every core) up to its next effect". We read it as forked
computations running their pure parts at the same time on different cores, and
loading GPT-2's 12 layers with one IO.fork each was slower than in sequence
(6.6-7.1 s against 5.1-5.6 s), the same with 1 and 16 threads.
 
If forks are meant to take turns on the event loop, a sentence in the guide
saying so would help; if they are meant to overlap, this shows they do not.
 
Files: https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/docs/upstream/io_fork_parallel.bend
       https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/docs/upstream/io_fork_sequential.bend
       https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/docs/upstream/io_fork_parallel_control.bend
 
Not a duplicate of #831 (fixed in 2.0.13): that one was about parallel lets after a
closure call; here there are no parallel lets in the forked work, the forks are
IO.fork computations, and the parallel-let version (io_fork_parallel_control) scales.
```

### The file

```python
# Four IO.fork computations. Each reads the clock INSIDE the fork and then runs a flat loop seeded with it,
# so the work can only happen in the forked computation (not when the action is built, and not in the
# joiner). On Bend 2.0.35 and on main (0ad47fc) this takes the same time with --threads 1 and --threads 16,
# and the same time as io_fork_sequential.bend, which runs the four jobs one after another.
#
#   bend io_fork_parallel.bend -o f && time ./f --threads 1 && time ./f --threads 16
import Base
 
def work(n: Nat, acc: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      work(p, (acc * 1103515245 + 12345 : U32))
 
# the forked computation needs the value for its own effect, so it cannot leave the work to the joiner
def job(+seed: U32) -> IO(U32):
  do IO<U32>:
    +now : Nat <- IO.now()
    +v : U32 = work(4000000000n, (seed + U32.from_nat(now) : U32))
    IO.print(U32.show(v))
    return v
 
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    +t : Nat <- IO.now()
    a : Chan(U32) <- IO.fork(U32, job((U32.from_nat(t) + 1 : U32)))
    b : Chan(U32) <- IO.fork(U32, job((U32.from_nat(t) + 2 : U32)))
    c : Chan(U32) <- IO.fork(U32, job((U32.from_nat(t) + 3 : U32)))
    d : Chan(U32) <- IO.fork(U32, job((U32.from_nat(t) + 4 : U32)))
    x : U32 <- IO.join(U32, a)
    y : U32 <- IO.join(U32, b)
    z : U32 <- IO.join(U32, c)
    w : U32 <- IO.join(U32, d)
    IO.print(U32.show((x + y + z + w : U32)))
```

### bend --version

bend 2.0.35

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 22.1.8

title: A read-only borrow of an Array for a parallel let, without @unsafe
body:
### What Bend should do

```python
# A read-only view of an Array that many tasks can read at once, checked by the
# type system, so a library that publishes laws can share a weight matrix
# across a parallel let without copying it and without @unsafe.
#
# For example (the name and shape are only a suggestion):
#
#   Array.borrow(a: Array<T>, f: ReadOnly<T> -> R) -> Array<T> & R
#
# where ReadOnly<T> is Data (so it can go down both sides of a parallel let
# with +) and only offers get and size. No write can reach the shared block.
 
# rows i0 .. i0+n-1 of W · x, reading W through the view
def rows(+w: ReadOnly<F32>, +x: ReadOnly<F32>, +k: U32, i0: U32, n: Nat) -> List<&2, F32>:
  ...
 
def halves(+w: ReadOnly<F32>, +x: ReadOnly<F32>, +k: U32, +i0: U32, +n: Nat) -> List<&2, F32>:
  # both halves read the same W, nothing is copied
  a b = rows(w, x, k, i0, Nat.div(n, 2n)) rows(w, x, k, (i0 + U32.from_nat(Nat.div(n, 2n)) : U32), Nat.sub(n, Nat.div(n, 2n)))
  List.append(&2, F32, a, b)
```

### Why

In matrix · vector (the inner loop of LLM inference) every weight is read once. To run it on several cores each task must read part of the weight matrix, and today a library that proves laws has no good way to do it:
 
| way | cost | problem |
|---|---|---|
| `Array.clone` per task | O(n) per task per call | costs more than the products: 2304 × 768 with 8 tasks takes 10.4 ms, the sequential product 0.80 ms |
| `Array.fork` / `Array.join` (#885) | O(1) | `@unsafe`: `--check-only` and `--verdict` report `SOME PROOFS FAIL: 1 def relies on unsafe or foreign code` |
| split the matrix into one array per task, once | one copy at load time | works and is proved, but the split is fixed when the matrix is loaded |
 
The guide's Ownership section (`guide/SHADERS.md`) says "The compiler borrows a boxed parameter (not an `Array`) that the def only matches or passes to a borrower": arrays are the one kind of data a library cannot share read-only between tasks without copying or `@unsafe`.
 
What we do today in [bend-ml](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml) is the third row (`Bands<r, c>`, a tree of row bands, each its own Array). Time per product, 16 threads, Bend 2.0.35, Intel Core Ultra 7 155H:
 
| W | sequential | clone per task (8) | 16 bands |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2304 × 768 | 0.80 ms | 10.4 ms | 0.32 ms |
| 3072 × 768 | 1.07 ms | 23.5 ms | 0.42 ms |
| 50257 × 768 | 25.1 ms | 337 ms | 6.1 ms |
 
A read-only borrow would give the same speed without fixing the split at load time, and would let operations that need the whole matrix (an embedding lookup, a transposed product for training) read it directly. It matches two items of the roadmap (2026-09-29): "way better support for shared atomic arrays" and "more parallelism options (not just fork/join)".
 
Benchmark and numbers: [bench/mv_bands.py](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/bench/mv_bands.py), [full table](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/bench/results/mv_bands-2026-10-05.txt), [NOTES.md](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/0a875a59dbb412956fdc662e76ffadb1df2958f1/NOTES.md) (experiments 9 and 11).

title: An erased last argument no longer cuts its call, so a def whose last parameter is erased keeps its fork (#1374)
body:
Fixes #1374.

## Cause

`anf`'s `spine` cut the call prefix before every argument, live or erased. In `tree(q, i, z)` with `z` erased, the prefix `tree(q, i)` already carries every live argument, so `term_spine` reads it as a complete call. `anf` cut it into a sequential `h = tree(q, i)`, the parallel let's values became plain variables, and the let compiled with continuations and no join. With `-z` anywhere else, the prefix before it isn't a complete call, so nothing was cut. That's why only an erased *last* parameter showed it.

The same cut also hit tail calls into a def that isn't flat. `Word.add_comm.go` ends each arm with `Word.add_comm.arm(p, at, bt, k, h)`, whose last parameter `-h` is erased, so each of its eight arms was emitted as a cut plus a continuation (`FID_WORD_ADD_COMM_GO_K4` … `K11`) instead of a tail call.

## Change

In `anf`, only a live argument over-applies a call, so the prefix is cut only before one. An erased argument stays in the application, as it already did when it sat in the middle. Variables keep their rule: a variable applied to erased arguments is the variable. The header comment above `anf` now says "a live over-application".

- **Size:** `comp.ts` 63,849 → 63,858 ttok (+9; cl100k_base, ttok's default). `gates/repo.ts` passes 50 / 50.
- **New test:** `tests/compile/fork_erased_last.bend` is a parallel let in a def whose last parameter is erased. Its C now has the join (`FID_TREE_J4`), and main's has none. Stdout can't show a fork, so main prints the same `#|` line: the test runs the forked shape on every lane but doesn't catch a revert, and its header says so. The evidence for the fork is the C and the timings below.

## Checked

Linux x86-64 (Core Ultra 7 155H, 22 threads), bun 1.4.2, clang 22.1.8. Main is 0ad47fc0.

**The repros from #1374** (best of 3; all print `3942408568`):

| program | join in the C (main / this PR) | `--threads 1` (main / this PR) | `--threads 16` (main / this PR) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tree(+d, +i)` | J2 / J2 | 1.010 / 1.027 s | 0.165 / 0.170 s |
| `tree(+d, +i, -z)` | none / J2 | 1.010 / 1.017 s | 1.013 / **0.169 s** |
| `tree(+d, -z, +i)` | J2 / J2 | 1.010 / 1.058 s | 0.169 / 0.170 s |

The two controls emit byte-identical C on main and here, so their timing differences are noise.

**Same output elsewhere.**
- **C and JS:** for all 1,659 `.bend` files under `tests/`, `bench/runtime/` and `demos/`, each lane builds the same files as main (770 C, 794 JS), and every error message is identical. Every emitted JS file is byte-identical. Two C files differ:
  - `proof/word_add_comm`: the eight cuts above become tail calls;
  - `reg/erased_call_cut`: one local is renamed (`_h_0` → `_v0_0`), and its binary is byte-identical to main's.
- **`.mjs` and binaries:** built with `-o t.js -o t.mjs -o t` for all 1,593 tests. Every `.mjs` is byte-identical. Of the 736 binaries, two differ: `proof/word_add_comm` and the new test.
- **Runs:** every test, run with the interpreter, as a C binary and as JS under bun, prints the same output on main and on this branch (1,593 interpreter runs, 736 C, 760 JS). The 16 that don't match their `#|` lines fail identically on main: display tests, `io/process_run`, `io/chan_try_late`, and helper modules under `tests/import` and `tests/reg/respelled`.
- **`--checkup`** on `reg/erased_call_cut`, `proof/word_add_comm` and the new test prints their `#|` lines.
- **`tsc -p bend2/pack`:** the same 12 errors as main, none in `comp.ts`.

**Performance.** For each of the 17 `bench/runtime` programs I ran SEQ-CPU (`--threads 1 --gpu off`) and PAR-CPU (`--threads 32 --gpu off`) after one warm run, taking the median of 5 runs interleaved with main. For every bench:
- the emitted C and the binary built with the perf gate's cc line are byte-identical to main's;
- every output is the same.

| | main → this PR |
|---|---|
| runtime, geomean of the 17 benches | SEQ 0.999, PAR 1.004 (identical binaries, so noise) |
| compile time (`-o main.c`), geomean | 1.007; peak RSS the same |
| `bench/checker`, min of 3 | 0.97 to 1.00 |

**Memory.** A side effect, not pinned by any test, since output can't show it. A tail-recursive loop that forks in its body and has an erased last parameter got one continuation per iteration on main. Over 3M iterations, peak RSS was 30 MB on main and 12 MB here at 1 thread, and 104 MB against 14 MB at 16 threads. The output is the same.

**Not run:** the cluster gates (`gates/test.ts`, `gates/perf.ts`, `gates/safe.ts`, `gates/ping.ts`), Metal and CUDA. This machine has no access to the minis and no Apple GPU.

title: fix(runtime): size effect table to program constructor IDs
body:
Fixes #1163. Clang can fold effect constructors into an initialized 65,536-slot callback table, adding 512 KiB to small native programs with `-fno-common`.

Size `io_eff_rows` by the generated `CID_T` rows, as requested in [maintainer review](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1378#issuecomment-6039452745). Generated effect IDs and dispatched requests already share that metadata domain. The runtime diff is one declaration; registration, dispatch, external linkage and diagnostics remain unchanged.

The two regression fixtures cover native artifact size below 256 KiB and IO without registered effects. They are unchanged from the initial PR. The native size regression is compiler-dependent: Apple Clang's default common-symbol behavior already passes the original fixture; `-fno-common`, Homebrew Clang and Linux Clang reproduce the failure. CLI and JS lanes measure their source entries.

Validation:
