title: On Linux a window paces at the display's refresh rate, not 60 Hz, as the Mac's display sync does
body:
## What changes

On Linux, `Window.frame` paced every frame to a fixed 60 Hz tick (`window_pace`, "as the Mac's display sync"). It now paces at the display's refresh rate: `Window.open` reads the rate RandR reports (`XRRGetScreenInfo` + `XRRConfigCurrentRate`) and keeps its period in the window.

libXrandr is loaded at run time with `dlopen`, so a build needs no `libxrandr-dev` and no new link flag. When it cannot be loaded, or the display reports no rate in 24..1000 Hz (Xvfb reports 0), the period stays 60 Hz. The library stays loaded: `XRRGetScreenInfo` registers a close hook on the display, which `XCloseDisplay` in `Window.close` runs.

## Why

On the Mac, `displaySyncEnabled` paces a window at the screen's rate. On Linux every window ran at 60 FPS whatever the screen, so on a 144 Hz monitor a program that draws a frame in 4 ms still showed 60 a second.

## Behavior

300 frames of a 640x360 window that then closes itself (so `Window.close` and the close hook run), timed with `IO.now`; `main` and this PR both built from source:

| display | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| XWayland on a 143.88 Hz monitor (RandR reports 144) | 5001 ms (60 FPS) | 2084 ms (144 FPS) |
| the same, libXrandr unloadable (`/dev/null` bound over it) | 5000 ms | 5001 ms |
| Xvfb (RandR reports 0) | 5000 ms | 5001 ms |
| Xvfb, libXrandr unloadable | 5001 ms | 5000 ms |

Every run exits 0. On the same monitor, a 1920x1080 starfield that draws in about 4.2 ms went from 60 to about 110 FPS; the rest of its frame is the host fill and the `XPutImage` of 8 MB.

## Notes

- `dlopen` is in libc from glibc 2.34, the floor the guide already names for `Process.run`; on an older glibc a window program would need `-ldl`.
- RandR 1.1 reports one integer rate for the screen, so with two monitors of different rates a window paces at that one.
- A program that moves a fixed step per frame now runs faster on a fast screen: `demos/app_pong_game_2d` (3 px per frame) runs 2.4x faster at 144 Hz, as it already does under the Mac's display sync on a 120 Hz screen.

## Tested

Arch Linux, Hyprland (XWayland), 1920x1080 at 143.88 Hz, clang 23.1.1, bun 1.4.2: the table above. I did not run the gates, which need the cluster.

title: BendTT's parser reads the text's UTF-8 bytes at a position, not a List Char, so it parses twice as fast in a quarter of the memory
body:
Follow-up to #1372. With `Book.index` a map read, parsing became the kernel's biggest cost on large books: 0.47 s of `proofs_3200`'s 0.82 s.

`Parse` was `StateT (List Char) (Except String)`:
- the text became one cons cell per char, 320 MB for `proofs_3200`'s 8 MB of BendTT;
- every `take` built its word with `w.toList` to test a prefix;
- every step walked the list with `drop`.

**What changed (Parser section only):**
- `Parse` is `ReaderT ByteArray (StateT Nat (Except String))`: the text's UTF-8 bytes, read at a position.
- `skip`, `take` and `name` move the position. A word is compared byte by byte (`Parse.at`, `Parse.sees`), and a name is one `extract`.
- `Term.parse` dispatches on the next byte as before. Only a non-ASCII byte checks for `∀`, `Σ` or `λ`.

**Same input, same output:**
- Spaces are the same 4 chars: `Char.isWhitespace` is `' '`, `'\t'`, `'\r'`, `'\n'`.
- Name chars are the same: `Char.isAlphanum` is ASCII-only. So reading bytes classifies every char as before.
- A parse error still quotes the next 30 *chars* (counted by UTF-8 lead bytes), so every message is the same.
- Nothing in Part 2 names the parser; the claims are about the parsed `Book`.

**Timings** (median of 3, Apple M4):

| | parse, main → branch | kernel, main → branch | `--verdict`, main → branch |
|---|---|---|---|
| proofs_3200 | 0.47 → 0.23 s | 0.82 → 0.63 s | 2.43 → 2.18 s |
| generics_3200 | 0.20 → 0.10 s | 0.31 → 0.24 s | 1.12 → 1.02 s |
| defs_12800 | 0.18 → 0.09 s | 0.26 → 0.20 s | 0.89 → 0.80 s |

Peak memory parsing `proofs_3200` goes from 320 MB to 76 MB.

**Checked:**
- `bendtt.lean` elaborates with Lean v4.34.0 with no errors, warnings or `sorry`.
- The kernel's full output (exit code, verdict, message) is identical on main and this branch for 591 `.bendtt` books:
  - the checker benches' books;
  - 23 table edge cases: duplicate, forward and unknown names, an empty book, 20,000-def books;
  - 544 random mutations of 68 real books: duplicated, moved, swapped, deleted or renamed defs, retargeted references, toggled `opaque`;
  - 14 parser cases: comments, mixed whitespace, truncated and unclosed input, stray multi-byte chars, `opaque` at the end of the input, and long error snippets with multi-byte chars.
- `--verdict` output is identical on main and this branch for all 1,664 `.bend` files in `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes 50 / 50: `bendtt.lean` 60,818 → 61,325 ttok.
- `gates/test.ts` passes 1581 / 1581.

title: External linting rules for tooling
body:
# External lint rules with checker context and source fixes

May supersede [#1367](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1367). If it merges first, this PR builds on its diagnostic changes.

This PR lets external JS/TS rules use Bend's checked types, local contexts and source spans to produce diagnostics and fixes. Capturing those facts during checking gives tools a shared interface instead of making each consumer instrument the checker or reconstruct its context, and because rules can run asynchronously, this could enable a tool to run very deep(possibly LLM-or-any-external-service-assisted) suggestions.

Two executable examples:

- [Semantic cleanup](tests/lint/erasure.js): removes redundant annotations using resolved aliases, generic parameters and dependent types.
- [Formatting](tests/lint/format.js): generates spacing fixes that an editor can offer individually or a formatter can apply together.

The implementation adds two optional recording points, a sequential rule loop and fields to the existing diagnostic machinery. Compiler and loader growth totals **172 net lines against current `main`, or 103 if #1367 merges first**; another 617 lines are tests and examples.

Validated locally in WSL: edited programs recheck with identical elaborated bodies, and both rules are idempotent.

title: Lift every JS continuation body into a standalone global function
body:
Fixes #1086. Replaces the periodic lifting approach rejected in #1096 with normal lifting of every emitted continuation body.

Every live Lam/Mat/Efq closure now emits its body in a standalone global factory function, so nested continuation bodies no longer occur inside the parent's source. The factory takes the closure's captures as parameters: the variables its body reads from an outer depth, collected while the body is emitted (no scan of the emitted text). Word/Char/F32 VIEW operands capture the underlying variable. `run_clo` sets `j.f = f` so `run_tail` unwraps only its own wrappers.

C and JS names now come from one scheme, `name_id`, which no longer uppercases. A closure is named after its def, `c` and a file-wide count (`$main_c1`, `FID_main_c18`). Names that differ only by `.` versus `_` get a `_1` suffix. `effs/process_run.c` wrote `CID_CON` by hand and now uses `CID(Con)`.

No period, parser/stack flag, source splitting, language-core edit, runtime ABI change or gate/cap change.

Tests: `io/do_deep` (400 ordered IO steps, previously a Node stack overflow on load), `compile/js_closure_views`, `js_closure_captures`, `js_closure_def_name`, `js_def_names`, `io/js_closure_host`.

Verified on macOS: repo 54/54, ping 55/55, test 1612/1612, cluster perf 124/124. `comp.ts` is 63,257 tok (main 63,067). Compile time for 1000/2000 IO steps is linear (2000 steps used to overflow the stack). The original Linux checks are in the PR history. Linux, CUDA, Metal and `--verdict` were not rerun after this revision.

title: safe.ts walks each term once for its uses and skips the out-of-scope pass when nothing is out of scope
body:
Two costs in `--verdict`'s elaborator that grew with the program instead of the work. Both changes are in `bend2/safe.ts` and leave the BendTT byte for byte as it was.

- **Use counts:**
  - A λ (`tree`), a let chain (`let_term`), `lams` and a match (`tree`, `swi`'s default) each counted their levels' live uses by walking the whole term they build. That term holds the terms already counted below it, so a match `d` deep was walked `d` times.
  - `o_uses` now keeps the counts of a term it counts on its own, in `Safe.uses` (a `WeakMap` on the built term, beside `consts`; nothing changes a term after it is built). It reads them wherever its walk reaches that term again.
  - `uses`, `lams` and `tree`'s match go through `o_uses` as before, now taking `e`.
  - Callers only read the counts, and the one that lists their keys sorts them, so the output can't depend on the cache.
- **Out-of-scope pass:** the loop that drops a def naming one out of scope ran `o_refs` over every def out even when no def had failed. It now starts only when one has.

**Timings** (elaboration only, `-o .bendtt` minus `--check-only`, median of 3, Apple M4):

| | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| tests/compile/nat_pattern_deep | 0.44 s | 0.05 s |
| tests/flatten/literal_rows_cubic | 0.67 s | 0.11 s |
| tests/proof/nat_literal_unfolds | 0.58 s | 0.10 s |
| bench/checker/proofs_3200 | 0.67 s | 0.62 s |
| bench/checker/generics_3200 | 0.38 s | 0.35 s |
| demos/app_slash_boss_3d/bend3d | 0.13 s | 0.11 s |

End to end, `--verdict` on `nat_pattern_deep` goes 0.75 → 0.36 s and on `literal_rows_cubic` 1.27 → 0.71 s.

The big benches gain less. Most of what's left of their elaboration is in `bend.ts`: re-materializing a λ's body at each `x.f(y)`, and reducing types.

title: A native build lets go of the compiler's memory before clang runs, so its peak is the larger of the two, not their sum
body:
`bend x.bend -o x` writes the C, then waits on clang with `spawnSync`. All that time the compiled book's `File` (`FL`: every segment's lines, the memo tables, the facts) stayed reachable, and the waiting process allocates nothing, so nothing collected it: bend's emission heap sat beside clang for the whole C compile.

`compile_book` now leaves `FL` as a fresh `File` once the C is built, and `cli_emit` collects (`Bun.gc(true)`) before `cli_build`. The C and the binary are unchanged.

### Memory

AMAGE Eco's CPU reference renderer (`Chromi/examples/eco/reference.bend` from [amage-si](https://github.com/amage-si): 1,759 segments, 4.1 MB of C), `bend reference.bend -o ref`, RSS sampled every 0.2 s, on a Ryzen 7 5800H (32 GB, Linux) with Bun 1.4.2 and clang 22:

| | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| bend while clang runs | 1.69 GiB | 0.80 GiB |
| bend and clang together, peak | 2.37 GiB | 1.68 GiB (bend's own, before clang) |
| wall | 47.3 s | 47.9 s |

With only `Bun.gc(true)`, bend held 1.47 GiB during clang: most of what it kept was `FL`. Adding `Bun.shrink()` after the collection changed nothing measurable.

### Same output

- The binaries built by main and by this branch are byte-identical (same output name; the temporary C's name ends up in the binary).
- `compile_book`'s result is untouched: for all 1,668 `.bend` files under `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`, the emitted `.c`, `.js` and `.mjs` and the exit status and stderr of every file are the same as main's.
- `gates/test.ts`'s shard script run locally (Linux, no display, no CUDA), on the previous main (eebc18cd): 1579 / 1581 with all three PRs of this work applied, and the same on main: the misses are `io_chan_try_late` [c] (a timing race on this machine) and `io_process_run` [interp, js] (its inherited-pipe cases, under the local runner).
- `comp.ts` is 63,972 ttok (main: 63,940) and `main.ts` 10,285 (main: 10,280). `tsc -p bend2/pack` reports the same 12 errors as main, and `gates/repo.ts` passes, 50 / 50.

Found while building AMAGE Eco, a UI toolkit written in Bend 2 ([amage-si](https://github.com/amage-si)).

title: compile_book emits a def again only when a fact it missed was added, so the passes after the first cost what changed, not the whole program
body:
`compile_book` emits every live def in every pass until a pass adds no fact (`own`, `hot`, `stat`). Big programs take several passes, and each one re-emits everything, although after the first pass or two only a few defs see a new fact. This PR emits a def again only when a fact it missed was added. The C output is the same.

### How

- `hot` and `stat` are a `Set` subclass, `Facts`, whose `has` records each miss of the def being emitted (`TRACE`).
- `brw_of` records each row it hands out, and the `own` facts that would turn its borrowed slots owned.
- In a later pass, a def none of whose misses was added is skipped; its row asks and its lends are replayed in its place.
- When a pass adds no fact, one more pass emits every def. Its C is the result, so the output is always a full emission at the fixpoint, as before.

Foreign defs, which main now emits in the same loop, are traced and skipped the same way.

This branch is the core commit only, rebased on main. The two token-trim commits are dropped.

### Same output

- All 1,726 `.bend` files under `tests/`, `demos/`, `bench/` and `evals/`: same exit codes and stderr as main, and every emitted `.c` (803), `.js` (833) and `.mjs` (1,139) is byte-identical.
- AMAGE Eco (`amage-si/chromi`, `examples/eco/main.bend`): byte-identical C (13.3 MB).

### Speed

`bend main.bend -o main.c` on an Apple M-series Mac, Bun 1.4.0, median of 3 interleaved runs:

| program | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| AMAGE Eco | 13.6 s | 6.8 s |
| `demos/app_slash_boss_3d` | 1.12 s | 0.93 s |
| `demos/pure_hvm5_mini` | 0.39 s | 0.39 s |
| small programs | 0.07-0.19 s | same, within noise |

Eco's passes emit 2,526, 1,849, 545, 197, 86, 54, 24 and 2 defs, then the final 2,526 (main: every pass emits all 2,526). Peak memory on Eco: 3.17 GB on main, 2.79 GB here.

### Checks

- `gates/repo.ts` 54/54, `comp.ts` at 63,998 ttok (cap 64,000)
- `gates/test.ts` 1623/1623, `gates/ping.ts` 58/58, `gates/perf.ts` 124/124
- Not run: CUDA, Linux, Windows.

title: mat_lits compares a word match's default with its replay node by node, up to where they meet, not as two JSON strings
body:
At every single-arm level of a U32 match's 32-level bit tree, `mat_lits` decides whether the level's default is the covering default replayed. It did this by comparing `JSON.stringify(term_lower(·))` of both sides, which lowers and prints the rest of the match twice per level. In a multi-column match with literals inside constructor patterns, the rest of the match is large. On the AMAGE Eco demo ([amage-si](https://github.com/amage-si); 1,253 live defs, 7.7 MB of C), `mat_lits` took 8.1 s of the 17.9 s of C emission.

The two sides are nearly always equal, and they share most of their nodes as the same objects. `same` walks both the way `term_lower` would: λs opened with the same variable at the same depth, then applications, constructors and matches field by field. It returns true at the first shared object and false at the first difference. Any other node it compares by the old key, lowered at its depth. So it gives the key comparison's answer without printing the rest of the match.

### Speed

`bend lits.bend -o lits.c` with the generator below. Apple M4 Pro, Bun 1.4.0, medians of 5 interleaved runs:

| program | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `step`, 8 arms | 1.10 s | 0.66 s |
| `step`, 16 arms | 2.06 s | 1.13 s |
| `step`, 32 arms | 4.20 s | 2.35 s |
| AMAGE Eco demo (Ryzen 7 5800H, Linux, author's run) | 18.2 s | 12.2 s |

The repository's own programs have no match of this shape. Their perf gate results are unchanged (124 / 124).

```sh
n=32; { cat <<'EOF'
import Base

type Tag is Data:
  Tag{kind: U32, open: Bool, close: Bool, a: U32, b: U32, c: U32}

type Doc is Data:
  Doc{depth: U32, xs: +List<U32>, y: U32, w: U32, h: U32, z: U32, status: U32, count: U32}

def step(t: Tag, d: Doc) -> U32:
  match t d:
    case Tag{0,True{},False{},a,b,c} Doc{_,xs,y,w,h,z,1,count}:
      U32.add(a, count)
    case _ Doc{_,_,_,_,_,_,1,_}:
      1
EOF
for i in $(seq 1 $((n-1))); do
  echo "    case Tag{$i,True{},False{},a,b,c} Doc{_,x <> more,y,w,h,z,0,count}:"
  echo "      U32.add(U32.add(U32.add(a, b), U32.add(c, x)), U32.add(U32.add(y, w), U32.add(U32.add(h, z), U32.add(count, $i))))"
done
cat <<'EOF'
    case _ _:
      0

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(step(Tag{3,True{},False{},1,2,3}, Doc{0,[7, 8],2,3,4,5,0,6})))
EOF
} > lits.bend
time bun bend2/main.ts lits.bend -o lits.c
```

### Same output

- For all 1,706 `.bend` files under `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/`, main and this branch give the same exit status, stdout and stderr. Every emitted `.c` (803) and `.js` (833) is byte-identical. The generator's C is byte-identical at 8, 16 and 32 arms.
- Every comparison `mat_lits` made while compiling all of the above was done both ways, with any disagreement logged. That covered 205,970 comparisons (201,496 equal, 4,474 not), and `same` agreed with the key on all of them.
- New test `tests/compile/word_match_cover_fields.bend` has an odd arm and a default that differ only in a constructor, or only in a nested match's last arm. Before this, a `same` that skipped constructor names or a match's rest would pass every test.

### Gates

`comp.ts` is at 63,968 ttok (cap 64,000). Results: repo 54 / 54, test 1624 / 1624, perf 124 / 124, ping 58 / 58. Not run: CUDA, Linux, Windows.

Found while building AMAGE Eco, a UI toolkit written in Bend 2.

title: Large native builds: every segment takes the widest record's words, the C is one translation unit, and its names shift with every edit
body:
## Summary

Building [AMAGE Eco](https://github.com/amage-si) natively (a UI toolkit written in Bend 2; its demo is 1,253 live defs from 12 libraries, 2,582 segments, 7.7 MB of C), three properties of the emitted C set most of the build time, and the first also costs at run time:

1. **Every segment takes the widest one's words.** One flat 104-word record makes all 2,582 segments take 188 `Term` parameters. Boxing datatypes wider than 32 words halves clang's time on the demo (59.9 s to 29.8 s) and runs a 1,759-segment program in 200 ms instead of 274 ms, with the same output.
2. **The C is one translation unit,** so clang uses one core: that 1,759-segment program, split into 9 units, builds in 7.4 s on 8 cores instead of 28.8 s.
3. **Names are positions,** so an edit renames most of the program and no per-unit cache survives it.

All numbers were taken on main at 0ad47fc0, and main at 51ab8e8e emits the same C for both programs, with and without `BEND_FLAT_MAX=32`; run from source with Bun 1.4.2: Ryzen 7 5800H (8 cores, 16 threads), 32 GB, Linux 7.2, clang 22.1.8.

## 1. Every segment takes the widest one's words

Every segment is a host function entered by `musttail`, directly or through `wl_tab`, so all of them share `WL_SIG`: as many words as the widest segment's parameters or the widest return value (`WL_RESW`). A non-recursive datatype stays flat up to `WIDE` (247) words, so one wide record anywhere sets the signature of every segment, and a wide record is passed word by word through each call that takes or returns it. In the demo, the UI model is 104 words: `WL_RESW` is 104 and every segment takes 188 `Term`s.

A 7-line opt-in, `BEND_FLAT_MAX=n`, boxes datatypes wider than `n` words as `WIDE` does (a word's bit chain, `Word.Con`, stays flat): [Iann29/bend@flat-max-reference](https://github.com/Iann29/bend/compare/main...flat-max-reference). With 32:

| | default | `BEND_FLAT_MAX=32` |
|---|---|---|
| demo C | 7.67 MB | 6.02 MB |
| demo `WL_SIG` `Term`s / `WL_RESW` | 188 / 104 | 71 / 31 |
| demo, `clang -std=c11 -O3 -c` | 59.9 s, 1.41 GiB | 29.8 s, 0.86 GiB |
| reference renderer C | 4.07 MB | 3.95 MB |
| reference renderer `WL_SIG` `Term`s / `WL_RESW` | 111 / 104 | 62 / 31 |
| reference renderer, `clang -std=c11 -O3` (bend's line) | 28.8 s, 0.64 GiB | 18.2 s, 0.54 GiB |
| reference renderer binary | 2.04 MB | 1.98 MB |
| reference renderer run, median of 10 | 274 ms | 200 ms |

The reference renderer (`Chromi/examples/eco/reference.bend`) loads a TTF, decodes a PNG and an SVG in Bend, lays out the demo's first frame and paints it on the CPU; both builds write the same PPM (SHA-256), and the paint step takes 77 ms in both. Eco's own C effects still call the three-argument `io_eff` of 2.0.35, so for the two demo `clang -c` rows that argument was dropped from the emitted C; the reference renderer has no foreign C and builds with `bend -o` as is.

Where the run time goes is not `FID_EXIT`'s copies: with `WL_SAVE`/`WL_TAKE` replaced in the emitted C by ladders that copy only the `n` result words (as `WL_LOAD` does), the reference renderer takes 277 ms against 274 ms. That agrees with aldeni's measurement in #1069 that a wider bank costs nothing by itself. What the boxed build changes is that those records travel as one word each instead of up to 104.

Options, from least to most work:

1. Box datatypes wider than a small bound by default (the branch above, with a default instead of a variable). It changes data layout: with 32, AMAGE Eco's 13 test suites that build on main print the same as without, and so do both reference frames (900x560 and 640x760); with 16 the 900x560 frame is the same too.
2. Make `FID_EXIT` copy what it carries instead of `WL_RESW` words. Measured above: no gain on this program, so not worth it alone.
3. Keep the `musttail` signature at a fixed K words and pass a segment's words past K through a per-lane spill area, so only wide segments pay for their width. This is the spill #1069 describes, applied to every segment rather than only past `WIDE`.

Per-segment signatures are not possible as such: `musttail` needs the caller's and the callee's prototypes to match, and dynamic jumps go through one table type (see the comment in #1069 on LLVM's `tailcc`).

## 2. One translation unit

clang compiles the program as one unit, on one core. On the host every segment is already its own function, so the file splits with little change: the mutable globals defined in one unit and `extern` in the others, the head's static prototypes and the segment functions given hidden external linkage, static inline code repeated where it is used. AMAGE Eco's build tool does this to bend's output ([eco-build](https://github.com/amage-si/eco-build), `ecobuild/csplit.py`). On main's C for the reference renderer:

| | one unit | 9 units on 8 cores |
|---|---|---|
| `clang -O3` | 28.8 s, 0.64 GiB | 7.4 s, 0.24 GiB per clang |
| with `BEND_FLAT_MAX=32` | 18.2 s | 4.4 s |
| run, median of 10 | 274 ms | 274 ms |

The split binary writes the same PPM. Emitting the units from `comp.ts` (or splitting in `cli_build`) would be simpler than splitting afterwards.

## 3. Names shift with every edit

Segment names carry the program-wide segment count (`seg_name`: `def$k` + `FL.segs.length`), spins are numbered in order of first use (`spin_` + `FL.spun.size`), and FIDs, CIDs and static offsets are positions. An edit anywhere renames most segments and spins, so a cache of compiled units never hits. eco-build renames segments by their order inside their def, spins by a hash of their text (their locals renumbered, since a spin takes them from the def that first emitted it), and makes FIDs link-time constants; then an edit of the demo, of logic or of a value, recompiles one unit of 18 (measured with eco-build on 2.0.35). Per-def counters in `seg_name` and spins named by their content in `comp.ts` would give the same without the post-processing.

## Related

From the same work, three PRs that keep the emitted C byte for byte: #1386 (a def is emitted again only when a fact it missed was added), #1387 (`mat_lits` compares a default with its replay without JSON) and #1385 (a native build lets go of the compiler's memory before clang runs). The `BEND_FLAT_MAX` branch above is a reference for this issue, not a PR.

## Reproduce

```sh
for r in ankra auvia chromi dithra kairo mokko ocula runika splina syllo tessra voltra; do
  git clone https://github.com/amage-si/$r ${r^}    # the libraries import each other as ../Runika etc.
done
git clone https://github.com/bendlang/bend
git clone -b flat-max-reference https://github.com/Iann29/bend bend-flat-max
bun bend/bend2/main.ts Chromi/examples/eco/reference.bend -o ref
BEND_FLAT_MAX=32 bun bend-flat-max/bend2/main.ts Chromi/examples/eco/reference.bend -o ref32
cd Chromi && mkdir -p build && ../ref && ../ref32    # each writes build/eco-reference-900x560.ppm
bun ../bend/bend2/main.ts examples/eco/main.bend -o eco.c && grep -m1 'WL_RESW' eco.c
```

Library commits measured: ankra c3a8c94, auvia 511eda4, chromi 4c45e6b, dithra 30930b5, kairo 7d87a92, mokko 1935d1d, ocula f44281d, runika 131874b, splina a8ab0e3, syllo 51b948a, tessra f40c025, voltra 45daa19.

title: adds bend-lint tool
body:
# Add bend-lint, a standalone linter for Bend 2 with user-written rules

This moves the userland diagnostics work into a tool. Nothing in
bend2/ changes.

`tools/bend-lint` checks a file with bend's own checker, then runs rules on
it. A rule is a TS module or a Bend file. It reads the source text, the
checker's result for each term (type, scope, depth, quantity, uses), or
both, and returns findings with fixes. The CLI prints them in bend's error
layout, and `--fix` applies the safe fixes:

```sh
bun tools/bend-lint/src/lint.ts file.bend --rules my_rules.ts --rules my_rule.bend
```

How it gets the checker's results without changing bend: when bend-lint
loads `bend2/bend.ts` (Bun only), it wraps `term_infer` and `term_check` in
memory so they record what they return, and gives bend.ts an fs and path
whose real paths use "/", so imports also resolve on Windows. For rules
written in Bend, it exports `RUNTIME_MAIN` and `js_sat` from comp.ts, so a
rule is compiled once. The files on disk do not change, `bend` and the
gates never load this, and checking gives the same results.

It does not drift silently. Each patch anchor must match exactly once, a
self-check runs at load, and `bend.pin` holds the git blob hashes of
bend.ts and comp.ts. Any mismatch stops it with a DriftError. To bump:
`BEND_LINT_UNPINNED=1 bun test tools/bend-lint`, then `--pin`.

It intentionally does not add anything to `bend`'s CLI, run in the gates,
serve LSP, or give codes to bend's own errors (they are all `bend/check`).
The only file outside tools/bend-lint is gates/repo.ts: three allow lines.

Validation:

- `bun test tools/bend-lint` (45 tests: patch anchors, span mapping, TS and
  Bend rules, CLI, and 12 tests from tests/ against drift), on Linux, WSL
  and Windows
- `bunx tsc -p tools/bend-lint/tsconfig.json --noEmit` (no errors in
  bend-lint; the two it reports in bend2/bend.ts are on main too)
- `git diff --check`

title: o_uses keeps its own counts, so uses, lams and tree take no Safe and Safe has no uses
body:
Follow-up to #1384, which merged with the kept use counts as a field of `Safe`. Every use count then had to be passed the elaboration: `uses(e, o, l)`, `lams(e, ps, b)`, `o_uses(e, o, …)`, and their callers.

- The counts are now `o_uses`'s own. A term it counts on its own keeps its counts in `o_counts`, a `WeakMap` beside `o_uses`, and its walk adds them where it reaches that term again.
- `Safe.uses` is gone. `uses`, `lams`, `tree`, `swi` and `let_term` call `o_uses` exactly as they did before #1384.
- Against the file before #1384, the whole change is now the out-of-scope skip, `o_counts` and the head of `o_uses`.

**Checked:**
- `-o .bendtt` is byte-identical on main and this branch for all 1,164 `.bend` files in `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/` that emit it.

title: JS Process.run parks on the child's pipes and exit, not Bun.spawnSync
body:
Fixes #1343. Supersedes #1371.

Bun 1.4 changed `spawnSync` to wait for the child's pipes to close, as Node's `spawnSync` always has, instead of for the child to exit. A background grandchild holding stdout open (`sh -c "sleep 3 & echo hi"`) now runs `Process.run` into its timeout. On Bun 1.3.14, main passes; on 1.4.2 it fails `inherited pipe` and `descendant output`. The 1.4 release notes don't mention the change.

No `spawnSync` call gives the documented behavior, and the JS runtime's loop is synchronous, so Bun's async `spawn` callbacks never run. The JS lane therefore does what `process_run.c` does, over `bun:ffi`, but parks on the loop instead of blocking it.

**What changed:**
- `process_run.js`:
  - `posix_spawnp` on close-on-exec pipes, moved above fd 2, with SIGPIPE back at its default.
  - Parks on stdin, stdout, stderr and an exit descriptor: a pidfd on Linux, a kqueue on macOS, or a 50ms tick when neither is available.
  - Reads one chunk (64KB) per pipe per wake, so a descendant that keeps writing (`yes &`) can't keep the call from seeing the exit. Once the direct child is reaped, it reads at most each pipe's capacity more (what it could hold at the exit) and answers: 64KB on macOS, `F_GETPIPE_SZ` on Linux.
  - Like the C lane, it needs glibc 2.34+ on Linux (`posix_spawn_file_actions_addclosefrom_np`).
- `io_park_on` (`comp.ts`, +22 tokens): in place of `fd`, it also takes a list of `[fd, out]` pairs and wakes on the first one ready. Waiting stays on the one `select` loop: no epoll, and no kqueue beyond the exit notification. Existing callers are unchanged.
- Other computations now run while a child does, on the JS lane as on the C lane. Before, the JS lane blocked the whole loop.
- Docs: `GUIDE.md` and `EFFECTS.md` are updated.

**Compared to #1371:**
- It parks on the event loop instead of running its own `poll` loop.
- It wakes on the child's exit fd instead of polling `waitpid` every 50ms.
- One reused read buffer, with chunks copied out of it, so tiny reads don't each hold 8KB.
- The argv/env memory stays referenced until the call ends.
- No kill after `ECHILD`, so it can't hit a reused pid.
- No spinning in the last millisecond before the deadline.
- One read path and one kill-and-reap path.

It keeps #1371's closed-stdin regression test (its author is credited as co-author).

**New test:** `process_run_beside` checks that `main` prints while a forked `Process.run` child is still running. Main's code fails it: the order flips.

**Checked (macOS arm64):**
- Bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.2: `process_run`, `process_run_parallel`, `process_closed_stdin` and `process_run_beside` pass in the interpreter, emitted JS and native lanes.
- 55 IO tests on Bun 1.4.2, interpreter and emitted JS: output is identical to main, except the two #1343 checks (now `True`) and the two new tests.
- Extra checks: 3MB through `cat`; a child that ignores 3MB of stdin (EPIPE); `yes` over the limit (`Fail 27`); a child that closes its pipes and exits 200ms later; 64KB on each of stdout and stderr written just before exit, and 500KB.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: 50 / 50.

**Not checked:**
- **Linux has not been run.** The pidfd call (syscall 434), `addclosefrom_np`, `F_GETPIPE_SZ` (1032) and `O_NONBLOCK` 0x800 are only checked against headers.
- `comp.ts` is at 63,997 of its 64,000-token cap.

title: Process.run reads until stdout and stderr close, as Node's and Bun 1.4's spawnSync do
body:
Fixes #1343. Supersedes #1391.

Bun 1.4 changed `spawnSync` to read its pipes until they close, as Node's does ([oven-sh/bun#33832](https://github.com/oven-sh/bun/pull/33832)). Bun treated the old behavior as a bug: output a grandchild wrote after the direct child exited was silently lost. The PR adds no option to keep it.

Bend's contract ("waits for the direct child … a descendant holding an inherited pipe open does not extend the wait") was Bun 1.3's behavior, adopted for the C lane in #1054. This PR moves the contract to what Node, Bun 1.4 and, as far as I know, Python, Go and Rust do by default, and makes every lane follow it on any Bun version.

**What changed:**
- `process_run.c`: reads until stdout and stderr both close, then reaps the child, all within the deadline. The `FIONREAD` drain from #1054 goes. The exit descriptor (kqueue/pidfd) stays, but it's polled only after both pipes close: before that, the child may already have exited, and the descriptor would stay readable and make `poll` spin. Without kqueue or pidfd, it checks `waitpid` every 50ms, as before.
- `process_run.js`: Bun 1.3's `spawnSync` returns when the direct child exits, so the JS lanes no longer use it. A worker runs the async `Bun.spawn`, which reads each pipe to its end on any Bun version. It enforces the timeout (clamped to 2³¹−1 ms, the most `setTimeout` takes) and the combined output limit; on either, it kills the child, cancels both readers and waits for the child to exit, as the C lane does. Each call passes the current `process.env`, which the worker would otherwise copy only when it starts. The main thread blocks on `Atomics.wait` (as long as `spawnSync` blocked it) and takes the answer with `receiveMessageOnPort`. The worker, its channel and the flag are made on the first call and reused; the worker is `unref`'d. If no answer comes within the timeout plus 1s (the worker failed to load or died), the call drops the worker and answers `Fail` EIO instead of hanging. No FFI and no `comp.ts` change, unlike #1391.
- `GUIDE.md`: the call returns once the child exits and stdout and stderr close, so a descendant holding a pipe open delays it, up to the timeout.
- `tests/io/process_run.bend`:
  - `inherited pipe` (`sleep 3 & echo hi`, now with a 300ms timeout) expects a timeout failure.
  - `descendant output` is now `printf A; (sleep 0.2; printf B) & exit 0` and expects `"AB"`.
  - `runaway descendant` (`yes & echo hi`) now expects `Fail 27` (output limit), the reverse of #1051's fix. Its `contains_answer` helper is gone.
  - New `closed stdio` (`exec >&- 2>&-; sleep 3`, 300ms) expects a timeout: once the pipes close, the timeout still bounds the wait for the child to exit.
  - New `largest timeout` (`/bin/echo hi` with a timeout of 4294967295 ms) expects `Done`.

**Trade-off:** a sloppily backgrounded process holding stdout (`cmd &` in a shell one-liner) now runs `Process.run` into its timeout. That's the same footgun as in Node. Well-behaved daemons redirect their stdio.

**Bun version:** none required. The JS lanes give the same answers on Bun 1.3.14 and 1.4.2, so the release and the cluster can stay on 1.3.14 for this.

**Size (ttok, from the merge base):** `process_run.c` −196, `process_run.js` +480, `process_run.bend` +138, `GUIDE.md` +3; +425 in all.

**Checked (macOS arm64):**
- `process_run` (19 lines) and `process_run_parallel`: interpreter, emitted JS and native all pass on Bun 1.3.14 and on 1.4.2.
- `process_run` through a `bun build --compile` binary on 1.3.14 (the worker loads from a blob URL): passes.
- No stray `yes` after `runaway descendant`: cancelling the readers closes the pipes.
- A child that closes its stdio and runs 2s: 17 involuntary context switches, against about 1,600 with a 1ms `waitpid` loop.
- In a standalone benchmark, about 0.85ms per call on either Bun version, plus about 5ms once to start the worker.
- With `process_run.js` in a harness, on both Bun versions: a child sees an env var set after the worker started; a child killed on timeout is reaped before the call answers; a worker that throws on load answers `Fail 5` after the timeout plus 1s.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: 50 / 50.

**Checked (Arch Linux x86_64, glibc 2.44):**
- `process_run` and `process_run_parallel`: interpreter, emitted JS and native all pass on Bun 1.3.14 and on 1.4.2. No stray `yes` after.
- The harness checks above (env, reaping, a broken worker) pass on both versions; a timeout answers 110.
- A child that closes its stdio and runs 2s: 4 context switches in 1.8s across all threads, so the native lane blocks on the pidfd.

title: Metal: non-tail recursion under a bang faults at 1023 list elements; CPU completes through 100000
body:
A `!` call whose body recurses non-tail over a list (Base's `List.append`, one frame per element of its first list) dies on the Metal lane with `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)` once the list has 1023 elements. 1022 passes in the recorded runs. The same binary with `--gpu off` completes at the tested lengths through 100000. There are no parallel calls inside the `!`; it is one sequential def.

## Program (`deep.bend`)

```python
import Base

# [n-1, ..., 1, 0], built with a tail loop.
def Gen(n: Nat, +k: U32, acc: List<&2, U32>) -> List<&2, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      Gen(p, (k + 1 : U32), k <> acc)

# Sum with a tail loop.
def Sum(xs: List<&2, U32>, +acc: U32) -> U32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      acc
    case Con{h, t}:
      Sum(t, (acc + h : U32))

# The only non-tail recursion: List.append over n elements.
def Deep(n: Nat) -> U32:
  xs = Gen(n, 0, [])
  ys = List.append(&2, U32, xs, [7])
  Sum(ys, 0)

def Run(m: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> IO(Unit):
  match m:
    case Some{n}:
      IO.print(U32.show(Deep!(U32.to_nat(n))))
    case None{}:
      IO.die(Unit, 2, "usage: deep <n>")

def Args(args: List<String>) -> IO(Unit):
  match args:
    case Con{_, Con{n, _}}:
      Run(U32.read(n))
    case _:
      IO.die(Unit, 2, "usage: deep <n>")

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    Args(args)
```

## Commands and output

```
$ bend deep.bend -o deep
$ ./deep 1022
521738
[exit 0]
$ ./deep 1023
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
$ ./deep 1023 --gpu off
522760
[exit 0]
$ ./deep 100000
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
$ ./deep 100000 --gpu off
704982711
[exit 0]
```

The 1022/1023 boundary is exact and deterministic (3 of 3 runs each). The program and these commands are the whole repro.

## Relation to earlier issues

- #918 (right spine of forks, fixed in 2.0.23) and #930 (fork-leaf handoff, fixed in 2.0.24) hit the same message. This one has no forks at all. The [close note on #930](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/930#issuecomment-5755631695) says "a bang's root and a fork kid still run on the lane stack on the device". My inference, not a runtime diagnosis: about two words a frame on that 2048-word lane stack would fit the observed boundary. This may be the known remaining limit rather than a regression.
- What I would ask for: either the lane stack spills to the heap (the general answer #930 mentions), or the fault names the cause ("non-tail recursion deeper than the device lane stack under `!`"), or the guide states the limit. Today a program that runs with `--gpu off` dies with the GPU on, and the message does not say why.

## Environment

- bend 2.0.34 (`bend version`). Later releases are untested here, including [2.0.36](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/releases/tag/v2.0.36); this report makes no claim about their behavior.
- macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), Apple M3 Ultra, Darwin arm64; clang on PATH: Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101).
- Built with `bend deep.bend -o deep`; the `.gpu` program sits beside the binary.

title: Metal: one `!` over a two-leaf fork tree (a 365-fork spine beside a 3-fork spine) faults; each leaf alone, a balanced 365+365, and `--gpu off` all pass
body:
A `!` call over a small binary tree whose two leaves are fork spines of very different lengths dies on the Metal lane with `bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)`. Each leaf alone passes under `!`, two equal leaves (365 + 365) pass, and the CPU pool (`--gpu off`) runs every shape. The fault is deterministic (3 of 3 runs of `365 3`, and every shape below gave the same result on each rerun of the transcript), and `--gpu 48GB` does not change it.

Shape: the tree is `Tree(WTwo{a, b})` → `x y = Tree(a) Tree(b)`; each leaf of size k is a spine of k nested parallel calls `a b = Spine(p, ...) Leaf(i, ...)`; each `Leaf` appends a generated list of `d` numbers to one of `w` numbers with Base's `List.append` (so `d` non-tail frames) and folds the result with a tail loop. All input is generated in code.

## Program (`forks.bend`)

```python
# Repro: one `!` call over a small, unbalanced fork tree faults on Metal,
# while each of its parts passes alone, a balanced tree of the large part
# passes, and the CPU runs every shape.
#
#   bend forks.bend -o forks
#   ./forks <w> <d> <a> <b> ...            # Metal: one `!` over items a, b, ...
#   ./forks <w> <d> <a> <b> ... --gpu off  # CPU
#
# Every input is built in code. An item of size k is a "spine": k nested
# parallel calls, each pairing the rest of the spine with one leaf job. A leaf
# job appends a generated list of d numbers to one of w numbers with Base's
# List.append (d non-tail frames, under the 1022 that one lane holds when
# it is a bang's root, per the companion deep-recursion repro), then folds the
# result with a tail loop. The items sit as the leaves of a balanced binary
# tree, and the whole tree is one `!` call.

import Base

# [n-1, ..., 1, 0] plus a seed, built with a tail loop.
def Gen(n: Nat, +k: U32, acc: List<&2, U32>) -> List<&2, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      Gen(p, (k + 1 : U32), k <> acc)

# A small mixing fold, tail recursive.
def Mix(xs: List<&2, U32>, +acc: U32) -> U32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      acc
    case Con{h, t}:
      Mix(t, ((acc * 31 : U32) + h : U32))

# One leaf job: append a generated list of d numbers to one of w numbers
# (List.append: d non-tail frames), then fold the result.
def Leaf(+i: U32, +w: U32, +d: U32) -> U32:
  Mix(List.append(&2, U32, Gen(U32.to_nat(d), i, []), Gen(U32.to_nat(w), i, [])), i)

# An item of size k: k nested parallel calls along a spine.
def Spine(n: Nat, +i: U32, +w: U32, +d: U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      0
    case 1n+p:
      a b = Spine(p, (i + 1 : U32), w, d) Leaf(i, w, d)
      (a + b : U32)

type Work is Data:
  WNone{}
  WOne{k: Nat}
  WTwo{l: Work, r: Work}

# Pair neighbours, one level up.
def Pairs(ws: List<&2, Work>) -> List<&2, Work>:
  match ws:
    case Con{a, Con{b, t}}:
      WTwo{a, b} <> Pairs(t)
    case _:
      ws

def Join(n: Nat, ws: List<&2, Work>) -> Work:
  match n ws:
    case _ Nil{}:
      WNone{}
    case _ Con{w, Nil{}}:
      w
    case 0n _:
      WNone{}
    case 1n+p _:
      Join(p, Pairs(ws))

# The items as a balanced binary tree; both halves of a node run in parallel.
def Tree(t: Work, +w: U32, +d: U32) -> U32:
  match t:
    case WNone{}:
      0
    case WOne{k}:
      Spine(k, 0, w, d)
    case WTwo{l, r}:
      a b = Tree(l, w, d) Tree(r, w, d)
      (a + b : U32)

def Item(m: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> U32:
  match m:
    case Some{n}:
      n
    case None{}:
      0

def Items(args: List<String>, acc: List<&2, Work>) -> List<&2, Work>:
  match args:
    case Nil{}:
      List.reverse(&2, Work, acc)
    case Con{s, t}:
      Items(t, WOne{U32.to_nat(Item(U32.read(s)))} <> acc)

def Run(+w: U32, +d: U32, ws: List<&2, Work>) -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(Tree!(Join(32n, ws), w, d)))

def Args(args: List<String>) -> IO(Unit):
  match args:
    case Con{_, Con{w, Con{d, t}}}:
      Run(Item(U32.read(w)), Item(U32.read(d)), Items(t, []))
    case _:
      IO.die(Unit, 2, "usage: forks <leaf width> <leaf depth> <size> ...")

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    Args(args)
```

## Commands and output

`w = 64`, `d = 800` unless noted.

```
$ bend forks.bend -o forks
$ ./forks 64 800 365
4280936846
[exit 0]
$ ./forks 64 800 3
2078004979
[exit 0]
$ ./forks 64 800 365 365
4266906396
[exit 0]
$ ./forks 64 800 365 3
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
$ ./forks 64 800 365 3 --gpu off
2063974529
[exit 0]
$ ./forks 64 800 173 3
2170616609
[exit 0]
$ ./forks 64 800 174 3
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
$ ./forks 64 800 365 3 3 3 3
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
$ ./forks 64 417 365 3
2125310752
[exit 0]
$ ./forks 64 418 365 3
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
$ ./forks 64 800 365 3 --gpu 48GB
bend: memory fault (machine stack overflow?)
[exit 1]
```

The corresponding `--gpu off` runs complete and print numeric checksums rather than the Metal fault. The program and these commands are the whole repro.

What the boundaries say, as far as I can read them:
- With two leaves `N 3` and `d = 800`, N = 173 passes and N = 174 faults.
- With leaves `365 3`, d = 417 passes and d = 418 faults, while a single leaf of 365 passes at d = 800 (and the single-lane limit for the same `List.append` from a bang's root is 1022 frames, see the companion issue). So in the unbalanced tree, a leaf job seems to get about half the lane stack it gets otherwise. [My inference from the numbers, not from reading the runtime.]
- Equal leaves (365 + 365) pass at d = 800; small equal leaves (3 3 3 3 3; 1 1) pass; 10 + 3 passes, and so do 10 or 30 beside four 3s; 100 + 100 and 100 + 50 pass; 365 + 200 faults.

## Relation to earlier issues

- #918 (a right spine of ~1000 forks, fixed in 2.0.23): here a spine of 365 alone passes, and only the pairing with a short spine faults.
- #930 (fork-leaf handoff, fixed in 2.0.24): its close note says a fork kid still runs on the lane stack on the device. This may be the same lane stack shared by two tasks once the tree is unbalanced, but I have not confirmed it.

## Environment

- bend 2.0.34 (`bend version`). Later releases are untested here, including [2.0.36](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/releases/tag/v2.0.36), whose notes include a work-pass change after a grow (#1132). This report does not establish whether the fault persists there.
- macOS 26.5.2 (25F84), Apple M3 Ultra, Darwin arm64; clang on PATH: Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101).
- Built with `bend forks.bend -o forks`; the `.gpu` program sits beside the binary.

title: comp.ts sheds 443 tokens of redundant code
body:
`bend2/comp.ts` drops from 63,975 to 63,532 ttok (−443) through simplifications, not minimizations: dead special cases, duplicated logic folded into one place, and helpers reused instead of copied. No identifiers are shortened and no comments are cut to save tokens.

## What changed
- **Compiler (A–C):** a match's uses fold in the generic kids walk; `lay_box` is gone (only W32/W64/BOX have no arms, so it was `x === BOX`); `seg_open` renames a binding's words in place; `compile_book` opens defs and foreign defs in one loop and indents a segment with one `seg_text`; `emit_fork` picks frame bindings with one filter; a few dead guards confirmed unreachable by instrumenting the corpus.
- **JS backend and runtime:** one function emitter for foreign and filled defs; one tag test in `js_match`; a pure main's show descriptor is one array; `show_chr` takes the character.
- **C runtime:** a host `WL_AGAIN` is `WL_JMP`; `blk_wcls` is the one word-class rule; `task_deal` picks a ring in one expression; `corpus_map` loops its hints and falls back through `pool_mmap`; `io_str` drops a no-op `io_seal`; `io_loop` takes both of its every-64-steps checks under one test; `main` reads a missing flag value as `""`, so `--threads`/`--gpu` need no NULL checks; `show_f32`/`show_val` are simpler; `gpu_hash` lives in the CUDA branch, its only user.

## Output changes
- The C and JS runtime text changes, so every emitted `.c` and `.js` differs in those runtime lines.
- `js_def`'s shared emitter gives a foreign def the trailing blank line every other def has, so `.js`/`.mjs` files with a JS foreign def gain one blank line after it (this also fixes a `}export default {` run-on).
- Everything else emits byte-identical output, and every compile-error log is identical to main's.

## Verification
- **Output:** all 1,074 tests, benches and demos were compiled to C, JS and .mjs and compared with main; the only differences are the ones listed above.
- **Tests:** every Base test on the JS and native (clang + Metal) lanes gives the same result as main.
- **Gates:** repo 50/50, ping 46/46, test 1587/1587. perf: every cell over 1.15x also fails on main (raytrace's COMPILER TIME sits at 1.15–1.18x on main; PAR-GPU mandelbrot/merkle up to 1.19x).
- **Speed:** the C runtime changes keep instruction counts; CPU cycles are within ±0.5% on all 17 benches, Metal within noise. Dropping `term_const`'s fieldless-constructor shortcut slowed raytrace's compile by 3%, so it stays; raytrace now compiles in the same time as on main.
- **Review fixes:** `ctr_build` keeps its `has` check (a constructor and a def can share a name, and `book_fam` returns the constructor's own name when its type is no ADT); `term_uses` still skips `DUMMY`; `io_loop` reads the clock only when something is parked.
- **Not tested here:** the CUDA build (the CUDA change only moves `gpu_hash` into its branch and inlines `gpu_shape`).

Rejected for costing speed: a merged copy loop in `ctr_take` (5–10% faster on CPU, slower on Metal), `WL_ARGS` pushing N words (+1% queens), and removing `WL_FRAME`'s `wtw` temporary (breaks an ldp/stp pairing).

title: io_chan_try_late: the pinned scheduler interleaving flips 10/10 on a fast Linux box (try_recv deadline loses the 1 ms sender)
body:
### What you did

Ran the repo's own `tests/io/chan_try_late.bend` through the C lane, natively, on a fast idle Linux box (48 cores):

```
bend tests/io/chan_try_late.bend -o t && ./t
```

### What happened

The pinned interleaving **inverts 10 out of 10 runs on the idle machine**: `Chan.try_recv` answers `Ready{Some{7}}` instead of `Wait{}`, the 7 is consumed before the program's second `Chan.recv`, and the program then ends in a deadlock:

```
B: 767263360
S: sent
A: ready got 7
bend: deadlock: every computation waits on a channel      (exit 1)
```

The pin is:

```
B: 767263360
A: wait
A: then got 7
S: sent
```

Statistics on this machine:
- C lane, idle: flipped 10/10 (last line `bend: deadlock…`, exit 1)
- C lane, under heavy parallel load: pinned ~1 in 4 runs — the result flips with machine speed
- JS lane: pinned 10/10 (the test's premise holds there because the JS lane blocks while a computation runs)

### Analysis

The test's comment documents the guarantee under test: "a try_ deadline that passes in the same loop pass as an earlier timer still withdraws its waiter before anything runs, on every lane". The construction relies on `busy` (allocating a 50,000,000-cell unary Nat, then spinning) holding the event loop past **both** the sender's 1 ms sleep and the receiver's 10 ms deadline. On this machine the busy computation does not hold the loop long enough: the sender's 1 ms timer is processed while the receiver's 10 ms deadline is still in the future, the send lands in the channel first, and `try_recv` legitimately answers Ready when its deadline does expire.

Each individual outcome is internally consistent with the effect semantics — what varies is machine speed, i.e. the test is timing-brittle by construction on fast machines. As multi-core CI/Linux machines get faster, this test will fail more often, and it fails in the confusing direction (a deadlock message after "ready got 7").

Suggestions (either would fix it):
- Make the busy hold deterministic relative to the timers (a far larger spin, or gate the sender's sleep on the busy computation having reached the loop), or
- Weaken the pin to accept both interleavings and keep the deadline-withdrawal guarantee pinned by a construction that doesn't race wall-clock timers against worker-thread throughput.

### The file

`tests/io/chan_try_late.bend`, unchanged from the repo at commit 1d895ca (2.0.36).

### bend --version

bend 2.0.36

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

Ubuntu clang version 21.1.8 (6ubuntu1)

title: A pure main forces deep_thunk_chain's 262144-link Nat thunk chain in the source interpreter, which its IO main left to the JS lane
body:
Closes #1316.

`tests/eval/deep_thunk_chain.bend` pins the interpreter collapsing a lazy accumulator deeper than the host stack, but its main is IO, and `bend file.bend` runs an IO main through `Comp.io_run`, i.e. the JS emitter. So the chain that comment describes only ever gets forced by the strict JS lane; the interpreter never sees it. Only a pure main goes through `term_snf`.

This adds `tests/eval/deep_thunk_chain_pure.bend`: same `Nat.pow2`, same `go`, same head demand through a match, but main answers a Bool instead of printing. The interpreter now has to collapse the 262144-link `Nat.add(acc, 1n)` chain itself before the match can pick an arm. I kept the match rather than returning the Nat so the test pins thunk forcing alone, not the printer's walk over a 262144-deep Succ chain, which is a separate concern.

Ran it the way the gate does, from the repo root:

- `--check-only`: ALL PROOFS CHECK
- aggregator `--checkup` with `BUN_JSC_maxPerThreadStackUsage=33554432`: prints `True{}` under the file header, 1.1 s
- `-o t.js` + bun, and `-o t` + `./t`: both `True{}`, well under the 5 s alarm
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS

It also passes with a 512 KB JSC stack, so the forcing really is off the host stack. I couldn't rerun it from before the LAZ-frame law landed: the tree at that point predates `law`, so the parser rejects the file.

A missing or check-failing `.bend` import fails the bundle with a formatted error and a nonzero exit, per the CLI's own contract ("any input gets a graceful formatted error, never a silent wrong output").

title: A Nat match with N literal-numeral rows costs ~quadratic checker memory: 2000 rows → 1.4 GB, 3000 → 3.6 GB (a valid program that runs); succ-pattern rows cost 83 MB
body:
### What you did

Checked (then ran) a fully valid program whose `main` matches a `Nat` through N literal-numeral rows:

```bash
python3 -c "
N=2000
rows='\n'.join(f'    case {i}n:' for i in range(N))
print('import Base\n\ndef main(x : Nat) -> Nat:\n  match x:\n' + rows
  + '\n' + '\n'.join(f'      {i}n' for i in range(N)) + '\n    case other:\n      0n')
" > rows.bend
/usr/bin/time -f "t=%es rss=%MkB exit=%x" bend rows.bend
```

(shape: `case 0n:` … `case 1999n:` each answering its numeral, `case other:` answering `0n`)

### What happened

Memory (and time) that grows ~quadratically in N — for a **valid, exit-0 program**:

```
N=2000 (attached repro):   t=2.9-6.7s  rss=1.43-1.45 GB  exit=0    (runs, prints)
N=3000, valid, --check-only: t=6.4s   rss=3.64 GB
N=5000 (no default):        rss=4.78 GB, then the formatted "machine stack overflowed"
```

Scaling table (no-default variants, each measured, 3000-row re-measured twice):

| N | peak RSS | time |
|---|---|---|
| 250 | 97 MB | 0.2s |
| 500 | 167 MB | 0.4s |
| 1000 | 427 MB | 0.9s |
| 2000 | 1.32 GB | 3.8s |
| 3000 | 3.11 GB | 7.8s |
| 5000 | 4.78 GB | 8.7s |

The blowup is specifically the **literal-numeral pattern path**: the same 3000 rows written `case 1n+p{i}:` (succ-pattern, no literal) check and run in 0.2s / 83 MB, so the literal rows appear to materialize ~i-node succ chains inside the coverage/exhaustiveness matrix (≈ Σ i ≈ N²/2·~800 B). A ~70 KB hand- or machine-written decision table then needs ~5 GB and, at 20k rows, an extrapolated ~75 GB. The JS emitter additionally stack-overflows on the 3000-row valid book (`-o out.js`, exit 1 after 3.25 GB).

Possibly the same underlying mechanism as #1266 (String keyword rows, quadratic in keyword length) — reported separately because the scrutinee path (Nat numeral rows vs String defaults) and the observable limits differ; also adjacent to the WONTFIX "the checker is not optimal" entry (#993/#1075), but that entry is about conversion cost on differing terms, while this is source-size-proportional cost on a single match.

### Expected

Checking a match should cost ~O(rows), or a documented bound a la the guarded parser-depth limit ("machine stack overflowed" at ~10k nesting).

### The file

Generator command above (the 2000-row file is ~65 KB; happy to attach if wanted).

title: An Array of a concrete function type (Array<(U32 -> U32)>) checks and runs on the interpreter but stops both emitters with "an open Array element type" (follow-on to #1130)
body:
### What you did

Checked and ran a program holding an array whose elements are **closures** — a fully concrete element type — then tried to build it:

```python
import Base

def mkA() -> Array<(U32 -> U32)>:
  ALeaf{(x => ((x + 41 : U32)))}

def callOld(r: Array<(U32 -> U32)> & (U32 -> U32)) -> U32:
  (a2, old) = r
  old(7)

# (main swaps a closure out and calls it; full file below)

```

```
bend t.bend           # interpreter
bend t.bend -o t.js   # JS lane
bend t.bend -o t      # native lane
```

### What happened

The lanes split:

```
bend t.bend           → 48      (exit 0 — the checker accepts, the run works)
bend t.bend -o t.js   → Error: an open Array element type   (exit 1)
bend t.bend -o t      → Error: an open Array element type   (exit 1)
```

Both emitters stop at `lay_el`'s `die("an open Array element type")` while the checker and the evaluator accept the same book and produce the right answer (verified in isolation, plus 14/14 generated variants: every function-element array fails this way; nested `Array<U32>` compiles fine). This is the same wall as the closed #1130 (an Array of an *equality* type), which was fixed for equalities — a concrete **function** element type still refuses, and unlike `tests/reg/array_open_element.bend` (which pins the refusal for a *generic* `Array<T>` element), here the element type is fully known: `U32 -> U32`.

One design trade-off is worth stating: `tests/reg/array_open_element.bend` documents that a generic element refuses loud at emission because "one untyped segment cannot serve two representations" — that rationale does not reach this case, since closures and boxed words are alike one-word heap references, which is exactly why the evaluator runs the program.

### Expected

Either the checker rejects `Array<(U32 -> U32)>` (so no lane pretends the program is legal), or the layout treats a one-word heap-referencing element the way the evaluator already does.

### The file

Full repro (`32-array-of-closures-uncompilable.bend`, ~15 lines):

```python
import Base

def mkA() -> Array<(U32 -> U32)>:
  ALeaf{(x => ((x + 41 : U32)))}

def callOld(r: Array<(U32 -> U32)> & (U32 -> U32)) -> U32:
  (a2, old) = r
  old(7)

def sumA(a: Array<(U32 -> U32)>) -> U32:
  match a:
    case ALeaf{x}:
      x(1)
    case ANode{xs, ys}:
      (sumA(xs) + sumA(ys) : U32)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    a : Array<(U32 -> U32)> = Array.new(U32 -> U32, 2n, x => (x * 2 : U32))
    b : Array<(U32 -> U32)> = mkA()
    IO.print(U32.show(callOld((Array.swap(U32 -> U32, a, 0, x => (x + 1 : U32))))))
```

bend 2.0.36

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

Ubuntu clang version 21.1.8 (6ubuntu1)

title: fix(cli): a native build that fails before clang removes its /tmp/bend-* dir (#1402)
body:
Fixes #1402.

## Why

`cli_emit` creates the build's temp dir with `fs.mkdtempSync`, then writes the C file with `Comp.compile_book(book)` before the `try` whose `finally` removes the dir. When `compile_book` throws (a book with no `main`, or a foreign import pointing at a missing file), the error is printed but the empty `/tmp/bend-XXXXXX` dir stays behind. A loop or CI over failing books keeps adding more.

## Change

In `bend2/main.ts`, the C file path, the `writeFileSync`, and the `Bun.gc(true)` call now sit inside the existing `try`, so the same `finally` removes the dir on every path, as it already did for a clang failure. Only `mkdtempSync` stays outside the `try`, so the `finally` only runs once the dir exists. The behaviour of a successful build doesn't change.

## Verification

With `TMPDIR` pointed at an empty dir, I ran `bun bend2/main.ts <book> -o out.bin` on both reproductions from the issue:

| Book | Error printed | Dirs left without this fix | Dirs left with it |
| --- | --- | --: | --: |
| no `main` | `Error: no main to run` | 1 | 0 |
| `main` calling a def that imports `./nothere.c` | `Error: ENOENT ... lstat .../nothere.c` | 1 | 0 |

The printed errors are the same as before.
