title: perf(js): avoid rebuilding strings in String.contains
body:
String.contains rebuilds the remaining input before each prefix check. On the JavaScript backend, this makes even an absent one-character search quadratic. A local search for `"b"` in 1,024,000 `"a"` characters took 7,209 ms.

Add a JS intrinsic that checks prefixes at Bend Char boundaries and advances an index through the original string. Reuse `char_len` with an optional offset. This preserves arbitrary U32 Char codes and prevents matches inside their packed representation. Base definitions and their proof reductions stay unchanged.

On Apple M5 Max with Bun 1.3.14, the same search took 5.45 ms with the change. Both figures are medians of three calls; they exclude input creation and compiler startup. This removes suffix reconstruction, but repeated long prefixes can still require O(N*M) comparisons.

Add two Bend regressions: character and partial-application cases with an unfolding proof, and a two-million-character absent search under the existing test gate timeout.

Validation:

- New regressions pass through the CLI, emitted Bun/Node, and native C. The long search exceeds the existing five-second limit on unmodified main and passes with the change.
- 15 existing String/Char fixtures pass on emitted Bun and Node.
- 50,625 U32-token substring cases pass against an independent reference on each runtime.
- C output is byte-identical for two probes.
- Repository gate: 54/54. comp.ts: 64,185 tokens, below the unchanged 66,000 cap.
- TypeScript diagnostics match unmodified main. The full cluster gates were not run.

title: Revert "fix(base): stop list searches when the result is known (#1548)"
body:
Fixes #1616.

Reverts #1548 (32d23b43). After #1548, `List.all/any/find/contains` match the tail before the head's result is used, so with an erased tail (`h <> t`) the call stays stuck even when the head decides it. Lemmas like `List.all(f, 5n <> t) == False` stopped checking, and bend-mathlib lost 23 defs.

We tried keeping the early stop in Base only (checking the head before the tail). That fixed the one-element case but not `1n <> 5n <> t`, which v2.0.37 proved. Matching the flag first is rejected by the termination check, so the shape can't be fixed without a checker change.

Cost of the revert: list searches on very long lists (50k) overflow the stack again and lose the early stop. That overflow is the known host-stack limit in WONTFIX.txt.

Test: `tests/base/list_search_head.bend` (one- and two-element head-decides cases) fails on main and passes here. `tests/base/list_search.bend` from #1548 is removed with the revert.

Gates: repo 54/54, test 1648/1648, perf 124/124, ping 62/62. Not run: safe, Linux, CUDA.

title: test(base): pin the native U32, Nat and Bool ops to Base's defs
body:
The compiler runs U32's arithmetic, bitwise, shift and comparison ops, Nat's ops and `U32.to_nat` as native C and JS (`comp.ts` `OPERATIONS`), not as Base's defs. No test pinned the natives to the defs at edge values. These three tests do:

* `tests/base/u32_native_model.bend`: 204 calls of `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `mod`, `and`, `or`, `xor`, `min`, `max`, `inc`, `shl`, `shr`, `not`, `shln`, `shrn`, `pow` and `from_nat`, at 0, 1, 2^31−1, 2^31, 2^31+1, 2^32−2, 2^32−1, and shifts by 0, 1, 31, 32 and 33.
* `tests/base/u32_native_compare.bend`: 40 calls of `is_eq`, `is_ne`, `is_lt`, `is_le`, `is_gt`, `is_ge` and `is_zero`.
* `tests/base/nat_native_model.bend`: 65 calls of `Nat`'s `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `mod`, `min`, `max`, `double` and `pow`, plus `U32.to_nat`.

Each has the same shape:

```python
def calls() -> List<U32>:
  [U32.add(4294967295, 1), ...]

def model() -> {calls() == [0, ...] : List<U32>}:
  {==}

def main() -> List<U32>:
  calls()

#|[0, ...]
```

So the test gate checks that every lane prints the values, and `--verdict` checks that the values are what Base's defs compute.

**What I ran** (Linux x86_64 under WSL2, `main` at `e5527d5`):

* All three files: the interpreted, JS and C runs print their `#|` lines, and `--verdict` prints ALL PROOFS CHECK (≤1.1 s each).
* With `u32_mul` deliberately broken in a copy of `comp.ts` (C `+` for `*`, JS `+1`): the JS and C lanes of `u32_native_model.bend` fail. The interpreted lane (which runs Base's defs) and `--verdict` still pass.
* The values come from a larger run of 3,774 calls, where the C, JS and interpreted results all agreed and the kernel proved each one by `{==}` from Base's defs.

**Not run:** the minis (Metal, CUDA). F32 isn't covered, since Base has no model to compare against.

Found and tested with Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5, during an audit of `--verdict`.

title: perf(cli): an opt-in check cache for --check-only (BEND_CACHE, #1234)
body:
Closes #1234 if you want it in this form; otherwise it's a reference for your own version. It's an opt-in check cache for `--check-only`. It adds 34 lines to `main.ts` and changes 5 (+421 tokens, 11,952 of the 16,000 cap), and doesn't touch `bend.ts`.

**Idea.** `book_valid(book, done)` already takes the first `done` order entries as validated. A file's imports load before its own entries and can't name them, so the imports' entries check the same whatever the file adds. With `BEND_CACHE=<dir>` set, a successful `--check-only` records two keys:

* the prefix it checked before its own entries;
* its whole order (so a file that imports this one can skip all of it).

A later run that loads the same prefix starts `book_valid` after it.

**What the key covers.** A sha256 of `VERSION`, `bend.ts`, `base.bend`, the path and contents of every loaded file, and the exact list of entry names in the prefix. If any of these changes, it's a miss and a full check. The file's own entries are found by `b`, which marks Base's entries, so a file without `import Base` gets an empty prefix.

**Scope.** Only `--check-only`:

* `--verdict` needs every def's elaborated term, so it never uses the cache;
* a plain run and `-o` builds never use it either.

`book_promises` falls back to the def's body as written when a cached def has no elaborated term, so `@unsafe` and foreign-effect dependants are still reported.

**Measured** on the reproduction in #1234 (a library of 800 proofs, 10 small clients):

| | stock | cached |
|---|---|---|
| client_0, first run | 1.22 s | 1.44 s (writes the cache) |
| client_0, again | 1.22 s | 0.13 s |
| clients 1–9, each for the first time | 12.13 s | 1.07 s |

**Tested** on a copy of `main` at e5527d5 (this branch's `main.ts` is byte-identical to it):

* All 1,666 `.bend` files under `tests/`, `--check-only` text compared against stock: 0 differences cold, and 0 warm with one cache shared across all of them.
* Unsafe propagation through an imported body (`lib` has an `@unsafe` def, a client calls it): stock, cold, warm, and warm-from-another-client's-cache all report the same 3 dependent defs. `--verdict` still fails.
* A broken library proof is caught after the library changes, and so is a false law in a client.
* A failing file without `import Base`, checked right after a passing one with the same entry count, still fails.
* `gates/repo.ts`: PASS 54 / 54. `tsc --noEmit` reports the same errors as on `main`, all in `bend.ts` and `safe.ts`, none in `main.ts`.

Not run: `gates/test.ts` and `gates/safe.ts` on the minis.

**Limits:**

* The cache trusts its directory. Anyone who can write to it can mark a prefix as checked, so it's opt-in and should be a private directory.
* It caches whole prefixes, not single defs: an edit to a library re-checks everything after it in load order.

Happy to change the interface (a flag instead of an env var, a default directory) or the scope.

Found and tested with Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5, during an audit of `--verdict`.

title: Proposals for bend.ts: clearer messages for seven common mistakes
body:
`AGENTS.md` keeps `bend2/bend.ts` human-written, so these are proposals for the team to review and implement, not a PR. Each comes with a minimal reproduction, the current output on `main` (`e5527d5`), and where the change would go. Happy to help with any of them in the form you prefer. A companion issue, #1633, covers checking speed (content-keyed template instance names).

The checker already supports a `Note:` line (`Err`'s `nte`), and the `+`-parameter error uses it well:

```text
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
Note: +f can be used many times, so its type must be Data.
```

Each case below would gain the same kind of explanation, and most of the information is already computed at the throw site.

### 1. A misspelt name: suggest the closest names

```python
import Base

def double(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  Nat.ad(n, n)
```

```text
- expected : a defined name
- observed : Nat.ad
```

**Proposed:** keep the message, and add `Note: did you mean Nat.add?`, listing names in `book.tlds` within an edit distance of 2, same namespace first. **Where:** infer-ref, `bend.ts:3315`. The search runs only on the error path, so it costs nothing on success.

### 2. A value used twice: point at the uses, and say what to do

```python
import Base

def both(f: U32 -> U32) -> (U32 -> U32) & (U32 -> U32):
  (f, f)
```

```text
- expected : f
- observed : f (consumed more than once)
Location: both
3>| def both(f: U32 -> U32) -> (U32 -> U32) & (U32 -> U32):
  |          ^
```

The caret points at the binder, and "expected f, observed f" reads as a contradiction. **Proposed** (prototyped, output below):

```text
- message  : f is used 2 times (at 4:4, 4:7), but a plain binding is used at most once
Location: both
3 | def both(f: U32 -> U32) -> (U32 -> U32) & (U32 -> U32):
4>|   (f, f)
  |       ^
5 | 
Note: a +f binding may be used many times if its type is Data; otherwise use it once (a function or another Type value cannot be copied).
```

**Where:** `uses_close`, `bend.ts:3478`. `Uses` keeps quantities, not positions, so on this error path the prototype re-walks the checked body for the variable's `Var` nodes, skipping an `Ann`'s type as `uses` does. Its two callers (the `Lam` case and the `Let` loop) pass `f_chk.tm` as one extra argument. It runs only on failure.

What the prototype showed, on a scratch copy of `main`:

* `f(f(f(x)))` reports 3 uses, with the caret on the second.
* A use in each of two match arms is not flagged (`uses` joins arms), and neither is a mention in a type annotation.
* A `let`-bound value used twice is flagged the same way.
* All 19 tests whose expected output contains "consumed more than once" get the new message (none fall back to the old one), so their expected output would need regenerating with the change.

One refinement it needs: when the variable is bound by a pattern, the `+` goes on the matched parameter, not the pattern variable. In `match k: case 1n+p:`, using `p` twice is fixed by writing `+k: Nat`, so the Note should say that in that case.

### 3. A missing match case: drop the internal term, name the missing pattern

```python
import Base

def pred(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:
    case 1n+p:
      p
```

```text
- expected : cases for Zero
- observed : \{}
```

`\{}` is an internal term. **Proposed:**

```text
- message  : this match doesn't cover Zero
Note: add `case 0n:` (or `case _:`).
```

using the surface spelling where one exists (`0n` for `Zero`, `[]` for `Nil`). **Where:** `bend.ts:3628`.

### 4. A recursive call that doesn't shrink: name the argument

```python
import Base

def loop(a: Nat, b: Nat) -> Nat:
  match a:
    case 0n:
      b
    case 1n+p:
      loop(1n+p, b)
```

```text
- expected : a decreasing self-call (arguments are read left to right: each passed unchanged until one shrinks)
- observed : loop
```

**Proposed:**

```text
- message  : loop's 1st argument, 1n+p, is not smaller than a
Note: pass p, a part of a, or mark the def @unsafe to skip the termination check.
```

**Where:** `bend.ts:3336`. The loop just above already computes `ord` per argument (`term_descend(lhs.qs[j], sp[j], cols[j])`), so the first `j` where it isn't `EQ` and the reason (`GT` or not comparable) are already known.

### 5. A false `{==}`: say which side is which

```python
import Base

def add3(n: U32) -> U32:
  U32.add(n, 3)

def bad() -> {add3(4) == 8 : U32}:
  {==}
```

```text
- expected : 7
- observed : 8
```

**Proposed:**

```text
- message  : {==} needs both sides to compute to the same value
- left     : add3(4)  ⟶  7
- right    : 8        ⟶  8
```

**Where:** check-rfl, `bend.ts:3665` (`throw Err(book, ctx, t_wnf.a, t_wnf.b, …)`). Showing `t_wnf.a`/`t_wnf.b` as written next to their normal forms makes large equations readable.

### 6. A missing argument: say how many

```python
import Base

def add2(a: U32, b: U32) -> U32:
  U32.add(a, b)

def main() -> U32:
  add2(1)
```

```text
- expected : U32
- observed : @b:U32 -> U32
```

**Proposed:** keep it, and add `Note: add2 takes 2 arguments, 1 given (missing b : U32).` when the observed type is a `∀` and the expected type isn't. **Where:** check-infer's final comparison (`throw Err(book, ctx, ty, x_inf.ty, …)`, just before `def_check`).

### 7. A pair where Data is expected: say why `A & B` is Type

```python
import Base

def f(xs: List<&2, U32 & U32>) -> List<&2, U32 & U32>:
  xs
```

```text
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
  |                    ^^^^^^^^^
```

**Why it's Type.** `A & B` is short for `Sigma<&1, &1, A, _ => B>` (GUIDE.md, short forms), and `Sigma<a, b, ..>` is `Kind(a <&> b)`. So the shorthand pair is `Kind(&1)`, which is Type, whatever `A` and `B` are. A pair of two Data types is Data only when spelled with `&2`: `Sigma<&2, &2, U32, _ => U32>` and `+Sigma<U32, _ => U32>` both check. The natural spelling `+(U32 & U32)` is rejected by the parser:

```text
- expected : a quantified datatype after + (+D<..> sets D's leading quantities to &2)
- observed : '>'
```

I tried each of `U32 & U32`, `Bool & Nat`, `U32 & (Bool & Nat)` and `(U32 & Bool) & Nat` as a list element: all fail the same way, with no hint of the fix.

**Proposed:**

* **(a) A Note**, when the observed `Type` is a `Sigma` at `&1`: `Note: A & B is Sigma<&1, &1, ..>, which is Type. Write +Sigma<A, _ => B> for a pair that is Data.` **Where:** the kind comparison that throws expected Data. The check is on the error path only.
* **(b) Optionally, accept `+(A & B)`** in the parser as `Sigma<&2, &2, A, _ => B>`, matching what `+D<..>` does for named datatypes. This changes the language, so it's your call. (a) alone already removes the dead end.

### 8. A file declaring a name Base has: let the file's declaration win

Base's type and constructor names are global, so adding a name to Base breaks every package that declares the same name. Two cases I hit:

* A Base `Poll` with constructor `Ready` broke a hub package that had its own `Ready`.
* A `U8`/`U16` section for Base, with byte helpers that pass Base, all three lanes, and `--verdict`, can't land as it is: 11 hub files declare their own `type U8` and 3 declare `type U16`, among them both published versions of an integer kit and several UTF-8 packages.

**Proposed:** let a file's own declaration shadow a Base name inside that file and its importers, as an import alias does, rather than conflict with it. Base could then grow without breaking published packages. This is a language decision, and I'd understand if you'd rather keep names global and coordinate additions instead. A Note on the conflict naming the Base declaration would help in either case.

Found and measured with Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5, during an audit of `--verdict`.

title: Proposal for bend.ts: content-keyed template instance names, for parallel and cached checking
body:
`AGENTS.md` keeps `bend2/bend.ts` human-written, so this is a proposal for the team, not a PR. The measurements are on `main` (`e5527d5`). A companion issue, #1632, covers error messages.

**Idea.** `book_valid(book, done)` already treats the first `done` entries as validated. So a worker can check a contiguous range `[a, b)` by loading the file, keeping `book.order` up to `b` and calling `book_valid(book, a)`. The result of a parallel check is then the failure with the smallest entry index. Every entry before it passed, so its context is the sequential one, and its error is the one the sequential check reports. Workers past that index can be cancelled. Loading is cheap next to checking (13–112 ms against up to 3.7 s here). And since `HTerm`s hold closures and can't cross workers, each worker reloading from source is the natural design. That part needs no change to `bend.ts`.

**Measured** (contiguous ranges, 8 workers simulated in one process, `main` `e5527d5`):

| File | Sequential | Slowest of 8 | Speed-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| bend-mathlib `sort.bend` | 148 ms | 79 ms | 1.9× |
| `typed/examples.bend` | 2,476 ms | 1,816 ms | 1.4× |
| `dynamic_array/proof.bend` | 541 ms | 424 ms | 1.3× |
| `aes/inverse.bend` | 3,719 ms | 4,935 ms | 0.8× |

The gains are capped by two things:

* single heavy defs (one def is 51–61% of `inverse.bend` and `examples.bend`);
* **each worker re-checking the template instances it calls.**

`def_inst` names an instance by first use (`tm.k + "~" + String(is.size)`), so the same instance gets different names in different workers, and in different runs, and its check can't be shared.

**Proposed bend.ts change:** name an instance by its content, for example `tm.k + "~" + <short hash of key>` (`key` is already computed there). With deterministic names:

* workers, and separate runs, can share an instance's checked result, which is what parallel checking needs to beat sequential on template-heavy files;
* per-instance caching gets stable keys;
* error messages and `-o` output stop depending on check order.

The cost is that instance names in messages and `-o` text become hash-based (e.g. `keep~3f2a` instead of `keep~0`).

My suggestion is to treat this as an enabler. Cross-file caching of whole import prefixes doesn't need it: #1631 does that today for `--check-only`. Per-instance caching, and parallel checking that beats sequential on template-heavy files, both do.

Found and measured with Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5, during an audit of `--verdict`.

title: fix(js): invalid Nat inputs report a misleading 2^48-1 limit
body:
## Summary

Exported JavaScript functions reject invalid `Nat` arguments with a message claiming the value is past `2^48-1`, even when the invalid input is negative, fractional, or a BigInt. The same function accepts valid numeric inputs above that stated limit, through `2^53`. This report concerns the diagnostic wording; the tested invalid inputs are correctly rejected.

## Steps to reproduce

Using either tested build from Runtime or environment, save the following files in the same directory.

### The file

`interop.bend`:

```python
import Base

def ident(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  n
```

`interop-test.mjs`:

```javascript
import M from './interop.mjs';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';

for (const n of [0, 5, 2 ** 48, 2 ** 53]) {
  assert.equal(M.ident(n), n);
  console.log('accepted', n);
}
for (const [name, n] of [
  ['bigint', 5n], ['negative', -1], ['fraction', 1.5],
  ['above-range', 2 ** 53 + 2], ['infinite', Infinity], ['nan', NaN],
]) {
  assert.throws(() => M.ident(n), (error) => {
    console.log('rejected', name, String(error));
    return true;
  });
}
```

### What you did

For the release executable, run:

```sh
bend interop.bend -o interop.mjs
bun interop-test.mjs
```

For the source checkout, replace the first command with `bun /path/to/checkout/bend2/main.ts interop.bend -o interop.mjs` and run the same consumer.

## Expected behavior

A rejected host `Nat` argument should receive a diagnostic consistent with the host input contract: a JavaScript number that is a whole number from 0 through `2^53`. It should not imply that the supported exported-function input ceiling is `2^48-1` or that every rejected value exceeded an upper bound.

## Actual behavior

### What happened

Both compilers and both consumer runs exited 0; the consumer catches and asserts each rejection. Both runs printed:

```text
accepted 0
accepted 5
accepted 281474976710656
accepted 9007199254740992
rejected bigint bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1
rejected negative bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1
rejected fraction bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1
rejected above-range bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1
rejected infinite bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1
rejected nan bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1
```

## Evidence

- Expected source: The [JS host conversion in `bend2/comp.ts`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/e5527d5be0c441d00f1f7d2fb61eb464fa478e5c/bend2/comp.ts#L492-L494) accepts integer numbers from 0 through `2 ** 53`; `host()` routes exported Nat inputs through that function. The [JS side guide](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/e5527d5be0c441d00f1f7d2fb61eb464fa478e5c/guide/EFFECTS.md#L99-L109) states the same whole-number range for Nat effect answers. [PR #1506](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1506) explicitly describes that range for exported Nat arguments too.
- Failure source: The inline consumer produced the output above on both tested builds. In the source checkout, `nat_in()` delegates every invalid value to `nat_chk(Infinity)`, whose emitted diagnostic uses the immediate-Nat limit.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

## Restoration check

Run the same consumer. All six invalid inputs must remain rejected, with a diagnostic that describes the JavaScript Nat input contract without the misleading immediate-Nat bound. Keep the valid `2 ** 48` and `2 ** 53` assertions passing so a narrower accepted range cannot mask the wording defect.

## Runtime or environment

- Latest published release tested: Bend 2.0.37, tag `v2.0.37`, revision `4ff8545f19b09b7d2b8ca2303668100eac8efd66`, using the official Darwin ARM64 release executable in an isolated installation.
- Current default branch tested: `main`, at the revision pinned in the source links above, invoked through `bun bend2/main.ts` in a fresh checkout.
- Version command used: `bend version` printed `bend 2.0.37`.
- `uname -sm`: `Darwin arm64`.
- JavaScript runtime: Bun 1.4.3 for both source compilation and both emitted-module consumer runs.
- Native compilation was not involved.

## Triage assessment

- Impact level: P3
- Assessment status: supported
- Impact basis: The observed defect is misleading error wording for invalid JavaScript Nat arguments; valid boundary values still round-trip and the invalid inputs are rejected.
- Workaround status: available
- Workaround basis: Callers can validate that inputs are JavaScript integer numbers from 0 through 2^53 before calling the exported function; the inline valid controls demonstrate that the documented boundary values work.

title: fix(issues): bug form requests an unsupported version command
body:
## Summary

The Bug issue form labels its required version field `bend --version`, but that command fails on both tested builds. The supported `bend version` command prints the requested version. This is a wording defect in the reporting form.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Open the Bug issue form for this repository and inspect the required version field.
2. Run the command shown by its label using either tested build from Runtime or environment.

```sh
bend --version
```

3. As a control, run the version command listed by `bend --help`.

```sh
bend version
```

No `.bend` input file is needed.

## Expected behavior

The required version field should direct reporters to a command that prints the version on the current release.

## Actual behavior

The form label says `bend --version`. On both tested builds, that command exits 1 and prints this to stderr:

```text
bend: unknown option --version (see bend --help)
```

On both builds, the control command exits 0 and prints:

```text
bend 2.0.37
```

## Evidence

- Expected source: The CLI's own `bend --help` output lists `bend version` as the command to print the version; the command was executed successfully on both tested builds.
- Failure source: [The required version field in `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/e5527d5be0c441d00f1f7d2fb61eb464fa478e5c/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug.yml#L27-L33) instructs `bend --version`, which produced the observed rejection above.
- Evidence provenance: observed
- Local verification: reproduced
- Reproduction completeness: complete

## Restoration check

Follow the version field's command on the current release and confirm it exits successfully and prints the installed Bend version. The label should agree with that working command. Keep the version field required so the reporting workflow still collects its intended information.

## Runtime or environment

- Latest published release tested: Bend 2.0.37, tag `v2.0.37`, revision `4ff8545f19b09b7d2b8ca2303668100eac8efd66`, using the official Darwin ARM64 release executable in an isolated installation.
- Current default branch tested: `main`, at the revision pinned in the form source link above, invoked through `bun bend2/main.ts` in a fresh checkout.
- `uname -sm`: `Darwin arm64`.
- Source execution runtime: Bun 1.4.3.
- Native compilation was not involved.

## Triage assessment

- Impact level: P3
- Assessment status: supported
- Impact basis: The observed failure is a wrong command in the issue form's field label; it adds a failed command while gathering version information without changing program behavior.
- Workaround status: available
- Workaround basis: `bend version` printed the version with exit status 0 on both builds, and `bend --help` lists that command.

title: F32.to_nat returns zero for representable Nats at and above 2^32
body: On main e5527d5, F32.to_nat(4294967296.0), F32.to_nat(4294967808.0), and F32.to_nat(281474959933440.0) all return 0 on both generated JS and native C. Each input is an exact F32 integer and fits the documented 48-bit Nat bound. F32.to_nat currently goes through F32.to_u32, whose range ends at 2^32. The conversion loses valid Nat values before U32.to_nat sees them. I reproduced this by compiling an IO.print/Nat.show program with bun bend2/main.ts probe.bend -o probe.js -o probe, then running both outputs on Linux x86-64 (Bun 1.3.13, clang 22.1.8). I will preserve the existing low-range conversion and split wide finite inputs into high and low 32-bit parts.

title: JS String.contains still scans ordinary text character by character
body: The packed-Char boundary handling in #1628 is needed, but every ordinary string still takes the per-character startsWith loop. On main e5527d5, a real exported Bend contains(s: String, p: String) -> Bool takes 77-79 ms to reject a 1024-character almost-matching needle in one million ASCII characters (Bun 1.3.13, Linux x86-64). The UTF-16 packed-Char sentinel is U+DC00. When the haystack contains no such code unit, native includes can search without a false match inside a packed Char. I am testing that fast path while retaining the existing boundary walk whenever the sentinel occurs, including an astral pair containing U+DC00. This does not change the String API or the behavior of non-scalar Chars.

title: JS F32 bit casts allocate a fresh buffer and typed views on every call
body: On main e5527d5, f32_bits and f32_from_bits each create a backing buffer and two typed-array views per call. A real exported Bend function bits(x: F32) -> U32 takes about 294-308 ms for one million warmed calls on Bun 1.3.13/Linux x86-64. This is unnecessary allocation on numeric code paths: the cast is synchronous and its backing storage never escapes. I am testing one private four-byte DataView reused by both helpers, with actual exported-module calls covering signed zero, subnormal values, and the largest finite F32. No representation change or NaN-payload guarantee is intended.

title: feat(cli): --profile, per-entry check times
body:
Adds `bend <file.bend> --profile`: it checks the file as `--check-only` does, one order entry at a time, lists the 20 slowest entries with file and line, then gives `--check-only`'s verdict and exit code. It adds 77 lines to `main.ts` (+958 tokens, 12,489 of the 16,000 cap) and doesn't touch `bend.ts`. It's independent of #1631: the two merge cleanly, and together leave `main.ts` at about 12,900.

```text
$ bend proofs/crypto/aes/inverse.bend --profile
583 of 583 entries checked in 3901 ms; the slowest:
   3759.4 ms  96.4%  inverse_unit_bits (proof)  proofs/crypto/aes/inverse.bend:12
     13.8 ms   0.4%  inverse_zero (proof)  proofs/crypto/aes/inverse.bend:573
      6.6 ms   0.2%  U32.pow  Base:1624
...
ALL PROOFS CHECK
Use --verdict for mathematical validity.
```

**How it works.** `book_valid(book, done)` takes the first `done` entries as validated. `cli_profile` cuts the order after entry `i` and calls `book_valid(book, i)`, so each call checks one entry against the entries before it, on the same book. Checked bodies and template instances stay in the book, so the times are the full check's, split by entry.

`book_valid` hides the bodies of the defs in the order it's given until their last entry. Because the order is cut at each step, `cli_profile` hides every body up front, as the full check does. Without that, a later def's body would be visible early and a forward reference would check. A law's statement entry keeps its body hidden, so its proof is timed once, at its fill, and rows are labelled `(statement)` or `(proof)`. After the last entry it counts TODOs and calls `cli_verdict`, as `--check-only` does.

This is the loop from a standalone tool I published at https://github.com/ScottMoore0/bend-prof, offered here so it ships with `bend`.

**Tested** on `main` at e5527d5 (this branch's `main.ts` is byte-identical to the tested copy):

* All 1,666 `.bend` files under `tests/`: `--profile`'s output, with the table removed, is identical to `--check-only`'s, and so is the exit code. This includes forward references, unfilled laws, TODOs and `@unsafe` dependants.
* `--check-only` output is unchanged by the patch (first 400 test files compared).
* Per-entry times add up to about a plain check: 3.9 s against 4.0 s on `aes/inverse.bend` (583 entries), and 1.2 s against 0.9 s on a `dynamic_array` proof (1,851 entries; each call has a small fixed cost).
* `--profile` with any other option fails with "--profile takes no other option".
* `gates/repo.ts`: PASS 54 / 54. `tsc --noEmit` reports the same errors as on `main`, none in `main.ts`.

Not run: `gates/test.ts` and `gates/safe.ts` on the minis. There's no test file for it, since its output is timings.

Happy to change the flag name, the row count or the output format, or to drop the verdict at the end.

Found and tested with Claude Code, running Claude Opus 5.5, during an audit of `--verdict`.

title: Let an empty String prefix reduce without inspecting the haystack
body: On main e5527d5, a generic law {String.starts_with(s, "") == True{} : Bool} cannot close with {==}: starts_with matches s before the empty pattern. A prefix consisting of one known character likewise stays stuck after that character has matched, when the haystack tail is unknown. A case split can prove the identity, but callers must inspect an unrelated tail after the entire prefix has matched. Reproduced with bun bend2/main.ts proof.bend --check-only. Deciding the pattern first can retain the public type and runtime answers, with regressions for empty prefixes, known prefixes over arbitrary tails, and early head mismatches. This is a Base normalization improvement, not a soundness report.

title: JS String.ends_with reverses the whole haystack even for a one-character or empty suffix
body: On main e5527d5, String.ends_with runs the Base definition through two String.reverse calls. In a real exported Bend suffix(s: String, p: String) function, a 50,001-character haystack takes about 5-8 ms per call on Bun 1.3.13/Linux, including a missing one-character suffix or an empty suffix. The result is correct, but it constructs reversed strings unnecessarily. A JS intrinsic can use native endsWith and validate the candidate start as a Bend Char boundary when a packed-Char marker occurs. The C and checked Base definitions can stay unchanged. I measured the existing implementation before changing it and will keep non-scalar and astral-boundary regressions.

title: fix(base): preserve wide finite values in F32.to_nat
body:
Fixes #1636.

`F32.to_nat` went through `U32`, so it returned 0 for every value at or
above 2^32. It now keeps the direct cast below 2^32 and, for
`2^32 <= a < 2^48`, combines the high and low 32-bit words. At or above
2^48 no Nat fits (the runtime's largest is 2^48-1), so it gives 0 as before
rather than aborting on the Nat overflow; +inf and NaN also give 0. The
public type is unchanged.

| F32 input | Before, C and JS | After, C and JS |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4294967296 | 0 | 4294967296 |
| 4294967808 | 0 | 4294967808 |
| 281474959933440 | 0 | 281474959933440 |
| 281474976710656 (2^48) | 0 | 0 |
| 1e20, +inf | 0 | 0 |

`tests/base/f32_to_nat_wide.bend` pins all of these, plus fractional
truncation and a negative input.

Gates, merged onto main c7b20300 on the mini cluster: repo 54/54, test
1655/1655, perf 124/124, ping 62/62; safe 1077 agree, 0 false rejects.

title: perf(js): stop allocating buffers for each F32 bit cast
body:
Fixes #1638.

The JS bit casts share a four-byte buffer instead of allocating one for every call. They reuse the cast functions from bend.ts, with no second implementation or endian flags.

Kept the round-trip table for signed zero, subnormals, finite bounds and infinities; removed the unrelated `lib.bits(0.75)` call. No new NaN-payload guarantee.

Local generated-module smoke: `0` / `16777216`. Repo gate: 54/54. The maintainer ran the full gates on the previous head; I haven’t rerun the private gates locally.

title: perf(js): use native search when String.contains needs no packed-Char walk
body:
Fixes #1637.

Keep #1628's boundary walk when a haystack contains U+DC00. Otherwise native substring search is safe: there cannot be a match inside a packed U32 Char. An astral pair containing U+DC00 conservatively keeps the existing path.

Measured through an actual exported Bend function on Bun 1.3.13/Linux, rejecting a 1024-character almost-match in one million ASCII characters:

| Call | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| `String.contains` | 77–79 ms | 0.30–0.37 ms |

Added consumer regressions for ordinary text, empty patterns, astral characters, a match inside a packed payload, a false UTF-16 match across an astral boundary, and a genuine match after a packed Char. Generated C and JS print all seven expected answers. Repository gate: 54/54. Mini-cluster/Metal/CUDA not run. AI-assisted.

title: fix(base): stop prefix checks at the matched prefix
body:
Fixes #1640.

`String.starts_with(s, "")` previously stayed stuck when `s` was unknown. Matching a known prefix also unnecessarily required inspecting the remaining haystack.

Match the prefix first, returning `True` as soon as it is exhausted. Preserve existing signatures and short-circuit on character mismatches.

Adds proof regressions for arbitrary strings and tails, plus runtime coverage for empty strings, exact matches, longer prefixes, mismatches, and Unicode.

Validation:

- All 36 Base tests match their expected output.
- All five string tests pass in the interpreter, generated JavaScript, and native C.
- BendTT validates the new regression test and existing `string_contains` and `string_kit` tests.

title: perf(js): check String.ends_with without reversing the inputs
body:
Fixes #1641.

JS no longer builds two reversed strings for a suffix check. The new intrinsic uses native `endsWith`, then checks that a matching suffix starts at a Bend Char boundary when U+DC00 occurs. The C implementation and checked Base definition stay unchanged.

A local exported-module probe uses 50,001 characters (ASCII plus an emoji):

| Case | Before | After, warmed |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Present suffix | 5–7 ms | 0.056–0.063 ms |
| Missing suffix | 5–9 ms | 0.053–0.081 ms |
| Empty suffix | 5–9 ms | 0.054–0.125 ms |

Bun 1.3.13/Linux x86-64; whole API calls including host string handling, not a cross-platform benchmark. Boundary regressions cover ordinary text, empty and whole patterns, astral characters, packed payloads and a false UTF-16 match beginning inside an astral pair. AI-assisted.

title: fix(base): normalize exhausted string prefixes
body:
Fixes #1640.

Once a prefix has been consumed, `String.starts_with` should not need to inspect the remaining haystack just to return True. The old haystack-first recursion left generic empty-prefix and known-prefix laws stuck.

This puts the internal recursion in pattern-first order while keeping the public `(s, p)` argument order. A separate internal `go` is needed because Bend does not allow matching an earlier binder after a later one. The old internal helper is removed, not aliased.

The new test checks empty prefixes, one- and two-character prefixes over arbitrary tails, and an early mismatch over arbitrary tails. The same empty-prefix program fails `--check-only` on e5527d5 and passes after this change. This is a normalization improvement, not a soundness fix. AI-assisted.

Checked with the independent Lean 4.34 kernel: both the new generic prefix laws and the existing `string_contains` laws report ALL PROOFS CHECK. The new program also runs on C and JS; the existing string-kit program keeps all 36 expected outputs on both targets.

title: C backend: a memory-bound loop's speed depends on unrelated code (flipping BLK_SHR in a program that never forks makes it 10-18% faster)
body:
### What you did

docs/upstream/matvec_schedule.sh (builds matvec_schedule.bend's emitted C twice, once as is and once with only `#define BLK_SHR 0` changed to 1, then times both on one pinned thread)

### What happened

```text
The same program gets 10-18% faster when I flip BLK_SHR in its emitted C, although
it never forks (so the flag only changes which runtime code is compiled around the
loops). Same result, more instructions, fewer cycles: clang schedules the hot loop
differently.

matvec_schedule.bend multiplies a 50,257 x 768 matrix by a vector, 38 times, through
bend-ml-tensor-array@0.1.11.0 from BendHub (op 0: Mat.matmul_nt with one row, op 1:
Bands.matvec), on one thread pinned to a P-core (taskset -c 3). ms for the 38 products:

                    bend 2.0.37                     main e5527d5b (bun bend2/main.ts)
                    as built     BLK_SHR 1           as built     BLK_SHR 1
op 0, 3 rounds      751-762      677-680             774-804      661-667
op 1, 3 rounds      781-794      696-706             823-873      684-686

Every run prints checksum=90.09511.

perf stat, op 0, 2.0.37:
                    as built     BLK_SHR 1
instructions        19.25 G      20.79 G
cycles               4.13 G       3.58 G
LLC load misses      404 k        29.5 k

Both spend their time in spin_47 (the dot product, four partial sums). perf annotate,
the loads and the add of one step:

as built                                 BLK_SHR 1
movss (%r11,%rcx,4),%xmm3     4.77%      movss (%r10,%r15,4),%xmm2    10.08%
mulss (%rbx,%r10,4),%xmm3     3.24%      mulss (%r10,%r8,4),%xmm4     15.27%
addss %xmm6,%xmm3            41.75%      addss %xmm7,%xmm4             7.17%

As built, the loop waits on one addss right after its load. With the flag, both loads
index off one base register and the wait is spread. -falign-loops=64 does not change
it. A smaller Base-only program with the same loop shape shows no gap, so it depends
on the code around the loop.

I don't think this is a bug in Bend's semantics: it's clang's schedule of the C Bend
emits. But the emitted C decides it, so maybe the backend could steer it, e.g. by
emitting a loop's array accesses from one hoisted base pointer (the form the faster
build ended up with), so a memory-bound loop's speed stops depending on unrelated code.

Where it bit me: I compare every change in bend-ml and llama.bend against the previous
build. In a variant of this program the gap was 21%, and in llama.bend not keeping
the per-layer activations moved one-thread time by 4-6% with the hot loop's
instructions unchanged, only shifted 16 bytes (-falign-loops=64 closed most of that
one). Swings of this size are the size
of what I'm measuring, so I now check every small gap with counters and the hot loop's
disassembly before calling it a cost.
```

### The file

https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/d6034030d34daf18e0a8689c6a6425c3d77d2df9/docs/upstream/matvec_schedule.bend
https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/d6034030d34daf18e0a8689c6a6425c3d77d2df9/docs/upstream/matvec_schedule.sh

### bend --version

bend 2.0.37 (and main e5527d5b)

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64 (Intel Core Ultra 7 155H)

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 22.1.8

title: Reduce compiler report allocation and reuse C generation work
body:
This change reduces allocation while collecting unsafe and foreign-effect references. The higher-term traversal uses the compiler's existing fresh-variable operation and preserves the dependent-reference report.

The normal C and native build paths reuse generated C when the compiler, source closure, foreign inputs, and relevant environment match the stored identity. Foreign-only refresh validates the receipt, manifest structure, and artifact digest before applying one exact source substitution. Invalid or incomplete cache entries trigger ordinary generation. Diagnostic requests execute the compiler to preserve diagnostics.

A changed foreign fragment containing compiler-owned CID/FID transforms triggers generation. Cache authority checks require a private, user-owned directory and reject symlinks throughout its ancestor chain. The manifest and artifact digests validate each reused result.

Structural opening, use, and spine memo entries survive definition boundaries within a compiled book. Definition-specific let entries are evicted at those boundaries, and the set of those entries is cleared when a new book starts. Probe indices remain valid across the book, so this change removes the per-definition probe-table reset. Peak memory for large books still needs measurement.

Remote validation with pinned Bun 1.3.14:

- The dependent-reference report regression passes.
- The bounded cache fixture passes 45 checks, including identity changes, diagnostic bypass, foreign refresh, corrupt artifacts and metadata, UTF-8 byte counts, CID edits, permissions, and symlinked ancestors.
- 85 programs generate byte-identical C with fresh cache directories: 12,263,641 bytes per arm. Five JavaScript backend samples are also identical.
- Sequential compiles of three books in one process match fresh-process results, including interleaved books.
- The changed compiler identity produces a new cache entry; both identities show a compile followed by a hit with identical C artifacts.
- Paired heavy-fixture runs measured approximately 6-13 percent lower generation time. Memory changes varied by fixture and round; boss_3d increased 4.4 and 9.2 percent. The shared host had load 20-26 during those runs.

These measurements cover bounded fixtures. Full repository validation, Main-scale memory behavior, and a full Main cache-hit measurement remain pending.

title: Port fixed-point and report compiler improvements to Bend 2.0.25
body:
This branch publishes compiler changes qualified against Baton’s pinned Bend 2.0.25 source lineage. It includes the default facts-only fixed-point path, deferred foreign C emission until facts stabilize, indexed iterative reachability, and direct HTerm reference collection in `cli_report`. It also adds report-reference fixtures and a stress script.

The source is based on the upstream `v2.0.25` tag and carries the pinned Baton compiler changes needed by the qualified candidate. It is separate from PR #1649, which targets current upstream and covers report allocation plus the proven C-output cache.

The focused report fixtures and compiler checks passed against the pinned remote toolchain. The fixture shell and generator syntax were checked on this branch. No full upstream suite or release qualification is claimed here. The branch is intended for source review and normal toolchain qualification before Baton pins it.

title: fix(js): reuse a 4-byte DataView for F32 bit casts
body:
Resolves #1638.

`f32_bits` and `f32_from_bits` in the emitted JS runtime each allocated a fresh `Float32Array`/`Uint32Array` pair per call. Reuse one private 4-byte `DataView` for both, removing the per-call allocation on numeric code paths.

Behavior is unchanged: little-endian (matching the previous typed-array view), so signed zero, subnormals, the largest finite F32, and Infinity round-trip identically. NaN-payload guarantees are unchanged (the JS lane does not preserve them, per WONTFIX).

I verified equivalence against the previous implementation for a range of values (signed zero, subnormals, 3.4e38, Infinity, NaN, and arbitrary u32 bit patterns) with a standalone script.

title: fix(js): String.length walks Char width instead of expanding the string
body:
Resolves #1612.

The JS `string_length` intrinsic was `[...str_out($0)].length`, which builds a whole expanded copy of the string just to count its Chars — O(n) temporary storage, including a second representation of every supplementary character.

Replace it with a `string_length(s)` helper that walks the string with the existing Char-width decoder (`char_len`) and a counter: O(n) time, O(1) space. This reuses the same `char_len` the runtime already trusts (e.g. `string_contains`), so it counts a packed U32 Char (4 UTF-16 units) as one Char and an astral scalar (2 units) as one Char, exactly as before.

Verified equivalence against the previous `[...str_out(s)].length` for ASCII, astral, and packed-U32-Char strings.

title: fix(effects): scan CID/FID with the source's own comment rules
body:
Resolves #1604. Supersedes #1606, which takes the same approach; its C test cases are folded in here.

`c_ids` resolves `CID(k)`/`FID(k)` by scanning the text of an effect source, and it applied C's line-continuation rule to every source:

- **JS**: a `//` comment ending in a backslash swallowed the next line, so a following `io_eff(CID(...))` was left unresolved and the effect died at runtime with `ReferenceError: CID is not defined`.
- **C**: the continuation only matched `\` + LF, so a CRLF `// ... \` comment did not continue, and a quoted `CID(...)` on the next line leaked out of the comment and failed the build. A `CID` token split by a backslash-newline was not resolved either.

Fix (`bend2/comp.ts`): `effect_srcs` splices a C source's backslash-newline (`\`, optional trailing blanks, CR? LF; clang and gcc splice the same) before scanning, and leaves JS alone. The `//` pattern stays `//.*`, so a comment still ends at CR, LS and PS. This matches what each host does: C keeps a continuation inside a comment, JS does not.

Test: `tests/io/effect_comment_backslash` runs on both lanes. The JS twin has a `// C:\` comment right before `io_eff(CID(answer), ...)`. The C twin is CRLF and has continued comments that quote ids, one with trailing spaces, and a `CID` split across lines. Both fail on main and print `42` here.

Gates on main bedc9646: repo 54/54, test 1657/1657, perf 124/124, ping 62/62, safe: 0 false rejects. comp.ts 64,178 → 64,237 ttok.

title: fix(issues): bug form requests the supported `bend version` command
body:

The Bug issue form's required version field was labeled `bend --version`, but that command fails on current builds with `bend: unknown option --version (see bend --help)`. The supported command — listed by `bend --help` itself — is `bend version`, which prints `bend 2.0.37` and exits 0.

title: fix(runtime): make the SIGSEGV/SIGBUS trap async-signal-safe
body:
Part of #1624

## The problem

`err_trap`, the host `SIGSEGV`/`SIGBUS` handler, ended in `err_fail`, so it called `fflush(stdout)` and `fprintf(stderr, ...)` from inside a signal handler. Two things could go wrong:

- A fault inside stdio could fault again in the flush. SIGSEGV is blocked inside the handler, so that second fault either killed the process with no numbered line (Linux) or hung it (macOS).
- A fault and a fail-stop on two threads, or two faults at once, raced to print. The wrong cause could win, or the line could be printed twice.

## The fix

- **`err_claim` picks one thread to end the process.** It records the first caller's `pthread_self()` in an atomic with a compare-and-swap, and only that thread flushes stdout. Any other thread waits a second (`nanosleep`, resumed after a signal) for that thread's `_exit`. It may be holding the very lock the claimer is flushing on, so after the second it prints its own line and exits rather than hang. A second fault on the claiming thread's own exit path skips the flush and goes straight to the line. `err_claim` needs no setup and allocates nothing, on any thread. Both `err_fail` and `err_trap` call it.
- **The trap never waits.** It flushes stdout only if `ftrylockfile` succeeds. Then it writes the constant `bend: <ERRS[7]>\n` (the text the JS trap already uses) with one `write(2)`, and calls `_exit(1)`. Stdout goes before the line, so a log that combines stdout and stderr keeps its order.
- **A fault inside that flush still prints the line.** The trap is installed with `SA_NODEFER`, so a fault in the flush re-enters it. `err_claim` returns 0 on re-entry, so the flush is skipped and the line goes out. The altstack is `4 * SIGSTKSZ` so the nested frame fits.
- **`err_fail` still prints with `fprintf`, so a message of any length goes out whole.** It is now `OUTLINE` (cold, never inlined) and `err_claim` is `FAR`. When `err_fail` was inlined at its call sites, its larger body made editdist and merkle SEQ-CPU 1.24x and 1.32x slower on the minis, in three runs each.
- **`io_errs` and `IO.print` send the text and its newline in one write.** They use the byte `io_cbuf` leaves for the NUL, so a fail-stop cannot land between the text and its newline.

`tests/io/stack_fault_trap.bend` prints `BEFORE` before the deep call and expects `#|BEFORE` above the error line. That pins the trap's flush against removal (stdout is buffered when it goes to a pipe).

## Verification

Gates on b66cf640 over main b0d1ca60:

- repo 54/54 (comp.ts 65,489 / 66,000)
- test 1692/1692
- ping 63/63
- perf 124/124
- safe: 0 false rejects

A C harness ran the emitted `err_claim`, `err_fail` and `err_trap` verbatim, with stdout and stderr captured as one stream:

| case | output | exit |
|---|---|---|
| plain fault | `BEFORE`, line | 1 |
| 7 threads fault at once | `BEFORE`, exactly one line, 100/100 runs | 1 |
| a fail-stop while another thread faults | `BEFORE`, `bend: <the fail-stop's message>` only | 1 |
| a fault inside the trap's flush | line | 1 |
| a fault inside `err_fail`'s flush | line | 1 |
| a fault on a thread holding stdout while another is in `err_fail` | line after 1s (hung before this change) | 1 |
| the same, with a handled signal sent to the waiting thread every 50ms | one line after the full second | 1 |
| the faulting thread holds the stdout lock | `BEFORE`, line | 1 |
| another thread holds stdout | line (the flush is skipped, never waited on) | 1 |
| main returns while another thread is faulting | line (was exit 0 with no line under a wait-based version) | 1 |
| a thread that never set up an altstack faults | line, and a `malloc` hook saw no allocation in the handler | 1 |

The harness ran on macOS (arm64) only. The glibc path has not been run.

## Trade-offs

- **The trap drops the flush if another thread holds stdout at that instant.** Waiting inside a signal handler lets the program keep running past the fault.
- **A second failing thread waits only a second for the first one's flush.** If stdout is a pipe that is slow to drain, it can exit before the flush finishes, cutting stdout short; the line is still printed. Waiting longer brings back the hang this avoids.
- **A flush that blocks forever on a pipe nobody reads hangs before the line,** as main does. Writing the line first would put it ahead of stdout in a combined log.

## Out of scope

- **Re-raising the signal** (the issue's second option). `stack_fault_trap` requires the numbered line and `exit 1`, never death by signal.
- **A fatal hook for embedders** (the issue's first option), and the atexit/termios restore. Both are still open in #1624.
- **`io_help` threads have no altstack,** so a stack overflow there still dies silently. That is true on main too.
