title: The test and perf gates run `!` on Metal only; CUDA-specific behaviour goes unnoticed
body:
### What Bend should do

Run the CUDA lane in the gates, even on one small machine running the `!` tests, so CUDA-specific changes and regressions show up before a release.

### Why

The test gate builds every runnable test with Metal and runs its `!` on the minis, and the perf gate pins its GPU cells on `apple_m4`; GitHub Actions runs only `repo-gate`. Nothing runs the CUDA lane, and it differs from Metal in ways the gates cannot see: managed memory over PCIe instead of unified memory, the shared memory reserved at launch, register counts and occupancy, and NVRTC's code generation. Three things I found on an RTX 4050 Laptop (Bend 2.0.37 and main 881cb2e5) that no gate would report:

- the device loops' error poll costs up to 20x on tight loops on CUDA (#1776);
- #1393's lane-stack fault reproduces on CUDA at the same depths (my comment on PR #1439: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1439#issuecomment-6279729706);
- from 2.0.37 to today's main, which has PR #1602, CUDA kernels moved by 0.92-2.2x, both ways: 2M reads a leaf of a 32-number Array 2.02 -> 0.92 s, a tiled 512x512x4096 matmul 216 -> 234 ms (idle machine, 5 alternated rounds).

title: CUDA: the leaves of a balanced fork tree land on threads in an order that changes from run to run, so a layout cannot be coalesced
body:
### What Bend should do

Would it be possible to deal a balanced tree's leaves in a fixed order (leaf k on thread k, or any documented order), or to give a bang's code its thread index (like `threadIdx`/`blockIdx`, or CubeCL's `ABSOLUTE_POS`) so that a program can choose its layout? Either would let flat loops over shared blocks read coalesced.

### Why

`SHADERS.md` asks for one leaf per lane and flat loops; the speed of such a loop on a GPU then depends on neighbouring threads reading neighbouring addresses. To lay data out that way I need to know which thread runs which leaf. I measured it:

```python
import Base

@unsafe
def launch(+d: Nat, +t: U32, +y: Array<U32>) -> Array<U32>:
  match d:
    case 0n: Array.set(U32, y, t, t)
    case 1n+p:
      l r = launch(p, (t * 2 : U32), y) launch(p, ((t * 2 : U32) + 1 : U32), y)
      Array.join(U32, l, r)
# main: launch!(14n, 0, Array.new(U32, 14n, 0)), then print every cell
```

In the C that main (881cb2e5) emits for it I patched that write, on the device only, to store `blockIdx.x * 128 + threadIdx.x` instead of `t`, built it as `bend -o` does, and ran it three times (Bend 2.0.37 gave the same picture):

- every leaf runs on its own thread, all on the GPU;
- every block of 128 threads gets exactly one aligned range of 128 leaves, in every run;
- inside the block the order changes: 6,048 and 6,660 of the 16,384 leaves were on the same thread as in the first run;
- a warp's 32 leaves spread over the block's whole range, so a read of element j of leaf t at `j * 16384 + t` touches 16 sectors of 32 bytes per warp in every run (Nsight Compute on main: 15.9 sectors a request; 4 would be coalesced).

The layout matters even with this order: 200,000 reads a leaf over one shared 2^26-number block take 112-113 ms interleaved (element j of leaf t at `j * 16384 + t`), 230-235 ms with each leaf's cells contiguous and 175-196 ms interleaved by the bit-reversed leaf index (main 881cb2e5, idle machine, driver 615.78.08, 5 alternated rounds); an empty bang over the same tree takes 1.35 ms.

What it costs: a tiled matmul (512x512x4096, a 4x4 block of C a leaf) whose layout assumes neighbouring leaves on neighbouring threads reads 16.45 sectors a request (Nsight Compute) against 8.5 for the same kernel handwritten in CUDA. Renumbering the leaves with a permutation of the low 7 bits that fits the observed order (in all six maps, Bend 2.0.37's and main's, a warp then touches ~5 sectors) gets it to 9.59 and makes the product 1.58x faster (4.62-4.72 -> 2.82-2.96 ms, the same results), but that is a guess about a run-time order: for the 8x4 version, a tree of depth 13, the same permutation is slower (3.44-3.54 -> 3.58-3.70 ms).

title: A tiled matmul in Bend runs about 4x slower than the same kernel handwritten in CUDA: where the time goes
body:
### What Bend should do

These are questions more than a request; the measurements are under Why.

- Could a balanced tree's leaves be dealt to threads in a fixed order, or could a bang expose the thread's index? (#1780)
- Could the tree be grown on more than one group, or could a bang over a known balanced tree skip the grow?
- Is there a way to keep a bang's blocks on the device between bangs (no host touches until the result is read)?
- Could a spin's array masks be computed once per spin when its arrays are passed unchanged (the common case in a flat loop over one block)?
- Would a separate, smaller kernel for leaf-only spins be possible, so a flat loop does not inherit the runtime's 80 registers?

Programs and Nsight reports available on request; I can rerun anything on this GPU.

### Why

I wrote a tiled matmul with the one-block pattern of `tests/run/stencil3d.bend` (`Array.fork`/`Array.join`, one block per array, one 4x4 block of C a leaf over 2^14 leaves, A stored transposed so lanes read neighbouring cells), and the same kernel in CUDA (same thread mapping, layouts and data, compiled with NVRTC, `--fmad=false` as Bend's device build). RTX 4050 Laptop, driver 615.78.08, main 881cb2e5 (with #1602), idle machine, 5 alternated rounds; the results are the same bits in both:

| ms a product | Bend | handwritten | ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 512x512x4096, 4x4 a leaf | 4.62-4.72 | 1.08-1.23 | 4.3x |
| 512x512x4096, 8x4 a leaf | 3.44-3.54 | 0.78-0.82 | 4.4x |
| 256x1536x576, 4x4 a leaf | 2.10-2.17 | 0.224-0.226 | 9.4x |

From K = 1024 to 4096 (512², 4x4): ~0.97 µs a K step in Bend against ~0.27 µs, plus ~0.7 ms a bang, which is why the smaller product does worse. This is where the time goes, with Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute.

#### A bang's fixed cost (~1.3 ms empty)

Each bang is five `bend_dev` launches back to back, then the host's turn. Nsight Systems, medians of 19 bangs:

| ms | grow, 1 group | grow, 128 groups | main pass | final | host, between bangs |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| an empty bang over a 2^14-leaf tree | 0.55 | 0.10 | 0.11 | 0.007 | 0.58 |
| the 512² matmul (4x4) | 0.32 | 0.15 | 5.06 | 0.009 | 0.30 |

(the fifth launch, between the grows and the main pass, takes ~1 µs). The first launch grows the fork tree on one group of 128 lanes, so a balanced 2^14 tree costs up to 0.55 ms before any leaf runs, and the host's turn adds about as much. On 2.0.37 I counted hundreds of CPU page faults a bang in that turn (Bend's heap is managed memory), while the host only reads a result.

#### The main pass

Nsight Compute on main, application replay (kernel replay restores device memory, and with Bend's managed heap that makes every replay fault its pages back in):

| | Bend | handwritten |
|---|---:|---:|
| warp instructions | 175.7 M | 95.5 M |
| SASS instructions a K step | 83 | ~45 |
| registers; blocks of 128 per SM | 80; 6 (registers) | 39-48; 10-12 |
| warps active a cycle | 21.6 | 23.6 |
| sectors a load request | 16.45 | 8.5 |

The step carries, besides the 8 loads and 32 float operations:

- the error poll (`YIELD`, `BSSY`/`BSYNC`, a counter and a branch every step; #1776);
- ~30 address instructions: every `Array.get` masks its index (`i & (2^cls - 1)`) and the mask is rebuilt from the block's class bits each step (`blk_at` reads `blk_cls(a)` of an array that is a loop variable), so the compiler cannot turn `base + i` into a pointer plus a fixed offset;
- a 64-bit counter for the `Nat` fuel.

And the whole runtime is one kernel, so the matmul's loop runs with the register count of the largest path in it (80), which caps the resident lanes at 6 blocks per SM.

The largest single part is coalescing: Bend's loads cost 16.45 sectors a request against the twin's 8.5, because the warps do not hold the leaves the layout assumes. Each block of 128 threads runs one aligned range of 128 leaves, but inside the block the leaves are dealt in an order that changes from run to run (#1780). Renumbering the leaves to fit the order I observed (a permutation of the low 7 bits) brings the loads to 9.59 sectors a request, with the same instructions:

| 512², 4x4, ms a product | |
|---|---:|
| as built | 4.62-4.72 |
| leaves renumbered | 2.82-2.96 |
| renumbered, poll split (#1776's patch) | 3.14-3.30 |
| renumbered, poll removed | 2.16-2.22 |
| handwritten | 1.08-1.23 |

The last Bend row minus the ~0.7 ms a bang costs (~1.5 ms) is where the handwritten kernel lands once it copies Bend's index mask, poll and occupancy: 1.36-1.47 ms at 6 blocks per SM (2026-10-18, busy CPU; the mask alone +20%). Copying Bend's addressing further (both masks rebuilt every step, a 64-bit counter) costs the twin nothing measurable. Ruled out: the leaf count (4,096 to 16,384 leaves give the same ratio), unrolling (the twin without unrolling is not slower), managed memory (the twin in one managed heap runs as fast) and the data layout (the same in both).

One thing I did not expect: with the leaves renumbered, #1776's split poll is slower than the plain poll (3.14-3.30 against 2.82-2.96 ms), while on the matmul as built it is faster (222-227 against 230-237 ms for 50 products). I have not looked at why.

title: Calling a def written below its caller reports "an unfilled law is a dead claim", not the ordering rule
body:
### What you did

```sh
bend fwd.bend --check-only
```

### What happened

```text
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : a filled definition (an unfilled law is a dead claim: live code cannot use it)
- observed : b
Context:
- x : Nat
Location: a
3 | def a(x: Nat) -> Nat:
4>|   b(x)
  |   ^
5 | 
```

`bend fwd.bend` prints the same, and both exit 1.

`b` is not a law. It is a def with a body, written below its caller `a`. Moving `b` above `a` makes the file check, and `bend fwd.bend` then prints `2n`.

The message is about laws, so it sends the reader looking for a missing proof, and it never mentions order. The guide states the rule only indirectly, where it says an `@unsafe` def "may call a def written below it". A name that doesn't exist gets a clear message: with `c(x)` in place of `b(x)`, the error is `expected : a defined name` / `observed : c`.

### Expected

When the name is a def written later in the file, the error names the ordering rule, for example:

```text
- expected : a def written above a
- observed : b, which is written below it (move b above its first caller)
```

The code involved is the same in 2.0.37 and on `main` (`881cb2e5`):

- [`book_valid`](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/881cb2e5823260927380eb5c9c7129cbe9a1a42c/bend2/bend.ts#L3804-L3814) clears every def's body and restores the bodies in file order. While `a` is checked, `b` has `v === null`, as a law with no proof does.
- [infer-ref](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/881cb2e5823260927380eb5c9c7129cbe9a1a42c/bend2/bend.ts#L3321-L3323) throws the law message for any such `Def`.
- A `law` declaration is parsed with `l: true` ([bend.ts:2581](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/881cb2e5823260927380eb5c9c7129cbe9a1a42c/bend2/bend.ts#L2581)), so infer-ref could tell an unfilled law from a def written below and choose the message.

### The file

`fwd.bend`:

```python
import Base

def a(x: Nat) -> Nat:
  b(x)

def b(x: Nat) -> Nat:
  1n+x

def main() -> Nat:
  a(1n)
```

### bend version

bend 2.0.37

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

title: A call to a def written below its caller names the file order, not an unfilled law (#1782)
body:
Fixes #1782.

## What changes

`book_valid` clears every def's body and restores the bodies in file order. So while a def is checked, a def written below it has `v === null`, as an unfilled law does, and infer-ref refused both with the law message: "a filled definition (an unfilled law is a dead claim: live code cannot use it)". A reader with no law in sight went looking for a missing proof.

infer-ref now refuses every bodiless def with one message that is true in each case:

```text
- expected : a def whose body is implemented before the def is used (defs are checked in file order, and an unfilled law has none)
```

It covers:

- a def written below its use (the issue's case);
- a law filled below its use, in the same file;
- a law filled by an importing file, used inside the file that declares it;
- a law never filled.

The issue's `fwd.bend` now prints:

```text
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : a def whose body is implemented before the def is used (defs are checked in file order, and an unfilled law has none)
- observed : b
Context:
- x : Nat
Location: a
3 | def a(x: Nat) -> Nat:
4>|   b(x)
  |   ^
```

The rule itself does not change, only the message. The diff in `bend2/bend.ts` is that one string: no new field, and `book_valid` is as on main.

Earlier rounds chose between a file-order message and the law message, first by `tld.l`, then by a `w` mark on `Def` recording where a body is written. Both needed state the checker has no other use for, so they were replaced by the single message.

## Tests

The tests that expected either message now expect the new one:

- `tests/check/unsafe_forward_safe.bend` and `tests/comptime/later_def.bend` (a def below its use, direct or as a `~` argument);
- `tests/check/forward_reference.bend`, `forward_reference_scope.bend` and `assert_fill_scope.bend` (a law filled below its use);
- `tests/check/axiom_use.bend`, `axiom_whitelist.bend`, `axiom_import_warn.bend`, `axiom_runtime_capture.bend` and `tests/compile/axiom_runtime.bend` (a law never filled).

The headers of the first five say the refusal names the file order, without changing their line counts.

## Checks

On 87035a88 merged onto main e2a7f603: test PASS 1826 / 1826, repo PASS 54 / 54, ping PASS 81 / 81, safe 0 false rejects; perf 121 / 124 against 120 / 124 on main (the same pin drift).

title: IO.model: a pure interpreter for laws about a program’s observable IO behavior
body:
### What Bend should do

Provide a pure way to interpret an IO program against an explicit modeled world, so laws can describe its observable behavior: exit status, stdout, stderr, and decisions based on arguments, environment variables, or terminal properties.

For example, a small command-line program could prove that an unknown option writes an uncolored diagnostic to stderr and exits with status 2:

```bend
# Proposed API sketch, not code supported by Bend today.
# Main.main is the same entry point used by the executable.
law usage_error:
  {IO.model(
    World{
      args: ["pkg", "--frob"],
      env: [],
      stdout_tty: False{},
      stderr_tty: False{}
    },
    Main.main())
   == Ran{
     code: 2,
     out: "",
     err: "error: unexpected argument '--frob' found\n"
   } : Ran}
```

`World`, `Ran`, and `IO.model` are illustrative names; the request is for the capability, not this exact API.

### Why

Laws over a program's pure core can prove parsing, validation, and formatting while leaving mistakes in the IO shell uncovered: sending a diagnostic to the wrong stream, returning the wrong exit status, continuing after an exit, or emitting color into a pipe. Those behaviors currently need execution tests, often with separate TTY fixtures.

Bend already supports laws equating IO terms: [the hello-world demo](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/main/demos/io_hello_world/LAWS.bend) equates `main()` with `IO.print("Hello, world!")`. The missing piece is a pure semantics that supplies effect results and reduces the resulting observations to data, allowing a law to reason about a whole interaction.

There is also an import boundary: user-defined host effects anywhere in a proof's import graph make the verdict fail, even when unused. [#1558](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1558) explicitly preserves that rule. An IO shell using such effects therefore cannot simply be imported into its laws. Terminal queries are one concrete example, discussed in [#1464](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/1464).

### A useful first scope

- Supply `IO.args` and `IO.get_env` results from the modeled world, with defined behavior for missing variables.
- Interpret `IO.print`, `IO.write`, and `IO.print_err`, preserving exact output and newline behavior on each stream.
- Model normal completion, `IO.exit`, and `IO.die`, including their exit codes, diagnostics, and the fact that termination skips the remaining continuation.
- Supply terminal properties independently for stdout and stderr, so a redirected stream and a terminal can coexist in one fixture. Since these queries currently require custom effects, define a supported way to give an effect a pure model without bringing its host implementation into the proof graph.

The model should interpret the same program used in production. Maintaining a separate pure copy of the IO shell would leave the connection between the two unproved. Unsupported effects should be rejected or explicitly represented as unsupported, never silently treated as successful.

A small demo could prove the example above, then show that swapping stdout and stderr, changing the exit code, or adding an ANSI escape to the piped diagnostic breaks its proof. Additional laws could cover successful help output and an environment-controlled color choice.

These would be proofs about the program under the stated effect model. Tests comparing the model with the C and JS implementations would still be needed to establish that those implementations follow the modeled contract.

title: A dotted name an imported file resolved once is not resolved again
body:
Closes #1514.

`parse_var` resolves a dotted name once and returns a `Ref` holding the key (`lib:Cell.At`). Three sites then pass that key to `parse_reso` again: the `<..>` family head, the `\{..}` arm names and the `(.. : T)` operator namespace. When the name is already in the book, `parse_reso` returns the key unchanged; for a datatype declared later in an imported file, `parse_qual` adds the namespace a second time and the term keeps `lib:lib:Cell.At`, a key no file declares. So a file that checks on its own fails as soon as it is imported.

A source name never contains `:` (`char_is_name` allows letters, digits, `_` and `.`), so a key that has one is already resolved, and `parse_reso` now returns it as is. That covers all three sites in one place.

The guard and the two tests are @viridale's from the issue thread; I'm sending them as a PR since they'd been sitting there. Tests, in `tests/import/`: a module whose def names a dotted datatype and constructor declared below it, and an entry that imports it. On `main` the entry fails with `unknown: forward_dotted_lib.forward_dotted_lib:Cell.At`; here it prints 5, and the module alone still prints 7.

What I ran: every file under `tests/` through `bend <file>` on `main` (34003e6f) and on this branch, 1,688 shared outputs identical, the two new tests the only additions; `bun gates/repo.ts` 54/54. Not run: the cluster gates.

title: comp.ts sheds 1,012 tokens: tighter comments and four small simplifications
body:
comp.ts goes from 65,931 to 64,919 ttok, out of its 66,000 cap. That frees 1,012 tokens without changing what the compiler emits.

## Comments (about −920 ttok)

32 long comment blocks are tightened. Each keeps its facts and drops narration, restatement of the code beneath it, and benchmark anecdotes:
- "56 to 369 ms"
- "3.05 s against 2.51 s"
- "15 MB -> 68 MB"
- "#1475: 3.2 s -> 1.1 s"
- "bitonic 1.35x without"

One `term_drop` comment line also comes back under 80 columns.

## Code (about −94 ttok)

- **`f32_text`** builds the decimal form in one loop over the digit places, with a point before place −1. This replaces three `memmove`/`memset` cases (`ex < 0`, `ex < p`, else). The scientific branch now returns directly.
  - Old and new give the same text and length for all 2^32 f32 bit patterns, checked in a C harness.
  - `p` never reaches 9, so `char d[9]` cannot overflow.
- **`bend_dev`**: CUDA's early `turn_groups` return moves into the CUDA `#else` branch. The back-to-back `#endif` / `#ifndef __METAL_VERSION__` pair goes. The text after preprocessing is the same on Metal, CUDA and the host.
- **JS `io_run`** requeues a step that has run 64 effects through `io_push(op.kont, x, false, io)`, the helper `io_wait` already uses. Before, it mutated and re-pushed `s`.
- **`term_open` and `open_of`** return a named `type Open`, replacing the literal type written three times. `emit_native` reads `f.h`, which is always `fun_of(k).h`.

Two changes were left out because #1576's review restored them: dropping the trailing `#undef WL_X`, and `emit_jump`'s `seg_ref`.

All 1,773 programs under `tests/`, `bench/` and `demos/` were built to `.c`, `.js` and `.mjs` with main's comp.ts and with this one:

- **`.c` and `.js`:** they differ only in comment lines and the three runtime edits above. The compiler's own output (tables, spins, segments, JS program text) is byte-identical.

## Gates (on main 257f8969)

- repo 54/54
- test 1688/1688
- ping 63/63
- perf 123/124 on two branch runs, against 123/124 for main run between them. The one failing cell, mandelbrot SEQ-CPU at about 1.33x, fails on main too. Geomeans per column match main within noise.

title: A do-block bind or let without its type annotation reports an unrelated error
body:
### What you did

`bend a.bend --check-only`, then the same for `b.bend` and `c.bend` below. The syntax reference writes a do-block bind as `x : A <- m` and a let as `x : A = v`; each file leaves the `: A` off, the way a Haskell or Python user writes it the first time.

### What happened

```text
a.bend
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : a defined name
- observed : x
Location: main
4 |   do IO<Unit>:
5>|     x <- IO.pure(U32, 1)
  |     ^

b.bend
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : a pattern (a binder or a constructor)
- observed : {x : IO(Unit)}
Location:
4 |   do IO<Unit>:
5>|     x = 1
  |     ^

c.bend
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : Type
- observed : U32
Context:
- n : U32
Location: f
```

None of the three mentions the annotation. `a.bend` says `x` is undefined, which sends the reader looking for a declaration of `x`; `c.bend` says a `U32` was used where a `Type` goes, which has nothing to do with the bind; `b.bend` quotes a term the file does not contain. Adding `: U32` after `x` (or `n`) makes each file check, and `bend a.bend` then prints `1`.

### The file

`a.bend`, a bind of a new name:

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    x <- IO.pure(U32, 1)
    IO.print(U32.show(x))
```

`b.bend`, the same with a let:

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    x = 1
    IO.print(U32.show(x))
```

`c.bend`, a bind of a name that already exists:

```python
import Base

def f(n: U32) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    n <- IO.pure(U32, 1)
    IO.print(U32.show(n))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  f(2)
```

### Expected

The cause is in `parse_term_do_stmt` ([bend.ts:2248](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/34003e6f/bend2/bend.ts#L2248)). The statement's first term is read with `parse_term`, and only a `:` after a variable makes the statement a bind or a let. So `x <- m` is read as the exec form `A <- m` with `x` as the type: for a new name that is "a defined name", for a `U32` parameter it is a `U32` where a `Type` goes. And `x = v` is read as the block's result `{x : IO(Unit)}`, after which the `=` has nowhere to go. The exec form itself is fine (`Unit <- IO.print("a")` and `U32 <- IO.pure(U32, 1)` both run); it is the lowercase name that gives the intent away.

When a statement is a bare name that is not a declared type, followed by `<-` or `=`, the error could say that the annotation is required, for example:

```text
- expected : a typed bind (x : A <- m) or let (x : A = v)
- observed : x <- IO.pure(U32, 1)
```

That check would sit right after `typed` is computed, before `parse_term` reads the right-hand side, so an exec statement with a real type on the left keeps working.

### bend version

bend 2.0.37, and `main` at 34003e6f

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2)

title: fix(compiler): box wide continuation and closure captures
body:
Large continuation and closure captures can fail native compilation with `an arity over 247`. This change boxes captures before saving them.

Use one helper for function parameters and captures. Box the widest values until their width fits. Cache a flag for each parameter boxed by that helper, and preserve only those incoming boxes. Closure arguments and match fields use their normal layouts. Update capture bindings in place while retaining owners of borrowed arguments.

The regression tests cover calls, forks, closures, shared fields, and parent reads. Native layout assertions detect boxing every capture and unboxing a retained parameter. The original compiler comments are restored.

Related to #1069. Hundreds of separate one-word values and oversized combined call results can still exceed the limit.

Validation:

- 53 repository test programs pass native execution at 1, 4, and 8 threads, plus JS.
- Scalar closure and match probes pass. Generated C no longer keeps or sinks a raw scalar closure argument.
- Native layout assertions fail on the earlier implementation.
- The TypeScript check reports the same 11 existing diagnostics, with none in `comp.ts`. `git diff --check` passes.
- Full cluster and GPU gates were not run.

The token gate is pending: restoring the comments puts `comp.ts` at 66,464 of 66,000 tokens. The requested upstream reduction, #1829, was closed without merging. This branch still needs that reduction before it can pass the gate.

title: Base: read a number from a string (U32.of_string, F32.of_string)
body:
Base can print a number (`U32.show`, `F32.show`) but cannot read one back. Every data layer needs it: a CSV cell is bytes, and `"5.1"` is not an `F32`.

**What it costs today.** `bend-kit-f64` says it outright: *"Decimal text is not here."* So the number parsers live inside the packages that need them (the JSON kit, the CSV kit) and every other package that reads data writes its own. That is the whole gap.

**The shape I would use**, the same one Base uses for its own errors:

```python
def U32.of_string(s: String) -> Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, U32>:
  # Fail{(code, message)} when the text is not a number
```

and `F32.of_string(s: String) -> Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, F32>` for a decimal (a sign, a fraction, and an exponent, or a documented subset of them).

**The law that comes with it**, and it is provable by the kernel:

```
law of_string_show:
  for x: U32
  {U32.of_string(U32.show(x)) == x : U32}
```

(The `F32` round trip is not a law: `F32.show` rounds, so the text is not the number. The `U32` one is exact.)

**Alternatives, for the record**: `bend-kit-parse` is a parser-combinator library and would do the work, and the JSON kit already has a private number parser. Both are workarounds for a missing prelude function.

I am working on a machine-learning library for Bend 2 (the data layer of scikit-learn's surface), where this is the first thing in the way, and I would be glad to send a draft pull request with the parser and the law. Say the word and I will.

title: Device lane spill: a loop at the exact fill depth spills and restores the whole stack on every call (~200x slower)
body:
Since #1439, a `!` job whose lane stack fills moves the words below the calling def to a heap block and moves them all back when it returns to that point. If code keeps calling right at the depth where the stack fills, each call spills about 2,048 words and each return restores them, so the lane comes back full every time.

Repro (Apple M4 Pro, Metal, `-o` build):

```python
import Base

def inc(n: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      0
    case 1n+p:
      (inc(p) + 1 : U32)

def loop(m: Nat, +acc: U32) -> U32:
  match m:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+q:
      a = inc(1n)
      loop(q, (acc + a : U32))

def down(n: Nat, +m: Nat) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      loop(m, 0)
    case 1n+p:
      (down(p, m) + 1 : U32)

def hi(+m: Nat) -> U32:
  down(2042n, m)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(hi!(200000n)))
```

| depth in `hi` | GPU | `--gpu off` |
|---|---|---|
| 2041 | 0.22 s | - |
| 2042 | 48.7 s | 0.00 s |
| 2043 | 0.22 s | - |

All three print the right result. Before #1439, depths like this faulted, so this is not a regression; it is the cost model of the spill.

A fix would spill only the bottom part of the stack, so that a restore leaves room. The hard part is that the exit frame must sit on a frame boundary, and at runtime the lane does not know where its frames start and end: each frame's size depends on its segment. Spilling part of the stack needs either frame sizes recorded on the stack or per-segment size tables to walk it.

title: fix(lsp): preserve match scopes across forall bodies
body:
## Problem and fix

A column-zero `@` in a match-arm's forall type clears the formatter's remembered match scope. A later `case` is then dedented outside the match, turning valid Bend into a parse error; the shared layout fingerprint accepts that output.

Reset scopes on actual `def`, `type`, and `law` tokens in the existing delimiter-depth-zero scan. This also preserves declaration boundaries when `@unsafe` is split across lines or the declaration keyword is indented.

## Blast radius

Two files in `tools/bend-fmt-lsp`: one scope-reset condition in `src/formatter.ts` and fixtures in its existing CLI-backed test. This affects match indentation during document formatting and its layout fingerprint. No public API or language compatibility break; the compiler, parser, and repository gates are unchanged.

## Regression evidence

Four added fixtures cover a column-zero forall body, a grouped forall with an `unsafe` binder, and split/indented decorated declarations with and without comments. Each source runs before formatting; all three indentation styles must change the text, preserve the expected output (`7` or `20`), and be idempotent.

The updated test fails against main with a misindented `case` parse error. It also fails if the fix merely removes `@` from the old reset condition, catching the lost decorated-declaration boundary.

## Checks

- `npm test`: build and all 33 tests pass, zero skips, including the LSP stdio session.
- `npm pack --dry-run`: build passes; 14-file package inventory.
- `bun gates/repo.ts` with CI-pinned `ttok` 0.3: 54/54.
- `git diff --check`: passes.

## Validation limits

Local checks ran on macOS arm64 with Node 26.8.2 and Bun 1.3.11. No Linux run or interactive editor-client check. The CLI regressions use Bend's source interpreter; compiled CPU/GPU lanes and the cluster/performance gates were not run for this formatter-only change.

title: perf(c): hoist the node allocation every match arm makes
body:
## What changes

This is commit 2 of #1596 on its own, as asked in the closing review there, now merged with main at b8664b0a. Everything is in `bend2/comp.ts`.

1. **Hoist the node allocation every match arm makes.** When each arm of an `if`/`else` chain opens with its one node allocation, all of one size class, with no inner block, `emit_chain` allocates the node once before the chain. Before, the inline `heap_alloc` fast/slow branch in each arm kept clang from merging the arms. Now their stores become selects instead of a branch on the tag.
   - An arm qualifies only if its first line is its alloc, so nothing in it (a free, a jump, an exit) runs before the alloc. An arm that frees a node and then allocates one keeps reusing the slot it just freed.
   - `ctr_build` and `seg_clo` write the class as a literal (`heap_alloc(e, 2)`, not `heap_alloc(e, cls_fit(3))`), so arms are compared by class.
   - The JS backend never emits `heap_alloc`, so on `FL.js` the arm callback returns right after the arm's body and scans nothing.
2. **Keep comp.ts under its cap.** Main is at 66,000 / 66,000, and the hoist adds 179 tokens. These comment sentences come out, each restating code near it, which brings comp.ts to **65,998**:
   - the header's "The C and JS runtimes close the file" (the RuntimeC and RuntimeJs section headers);
   - the C-only ops' list of their own four names (shortened to "intr_of skips an op with no JS, so a JS file runs Base's def");
   - `compile_book`'s "the datatypes of the constructors a pure main prints are roots too" (the `file_book` call below it);
   - the Compile comment's "An effect source is read once, in one namespace" (`effect_src`'s `FL.effs` check and its error);
   - the Globals comment's device-program sentence (`BEND_SRC`, below it);
   - the Gpu comment's "a launch loads it or compiles" (both `gpu_load` bodies);
   - `gpu_pass`'s "A bang launches 1, 2, 4 .. 64 rounds between syncs, until the pack empties the frontier" (its loop);
   - the C Io comment's request and parked-request sentences (`io_step`, `io_wait_on` and `io_wait`);
   - `io_loop`'s "A busy loop still checks due timers, and fds periodically" (the block below it);
   - `io_list`'s "io_unlist answers null if a value is past 255" (`io_unlist`, a few lines down).

## Checks

- `bun gates/repo.ts`: 54 / 54.
- `tsc -p bend2/pack/tsconfig.json` (TypeScript 5.9.3): the same 11 errors as main, none in `comp.ts`.
- `gates/test.ts`, run locally: 1705 / 1707. The two failures, gfx_clicks and gfx_window, expect "no display". This Mac has a desktop session, so they fail the same way on main here.
- Every `.bend` file under `tests/`, `bench/` and `demos/` built to C and JS with main and with this branch (866 build to C, 910 to JS; the same builds fail on both):
  - JS: outside comment lines, identical in all 910.
  - C: 49 chains with 98 arms in 35 programs are hoisted. After writing main's `cls_fit(n)` as its class and undoing every hoisted chain (putting the shared `heap_alloc` back in each arm), 865 of the 866 programs are main's C outside comment lines. The last, `fork_leaf_result_loop`, differs only in how its `_nd_` locals are numbered.
- Of the 17 runtime benches, only tree-bitonic and tree-radix change, with one chain each. The other 15 compile with the gate's `cc -std=c11 -O3` to the same machine code as on main (`otool -tX` text identical); only `BEND_SRC`'s embedded text differs. That includes symreg, whose chain has an arm that computes a predecessor before its alloc, and editdist, kmeans and tree-matmul.
- C emission time (`bend main.bend -o main.c`, the whole `bun` run, 7 interleaved rounds, medians): merkle takes 0.183 s on main and 0.188 s here, and tree-bitonic takes 0.112 s on both. The ranges overlap (merkle 0.174–0.196 s on main, 0.178–0.198 s here).

## Benches (the hoist alone)

These were measured on an Apple M3 Max, not the minis' M4, with main at b8664b0a against this branch's head. Builds use the gate's `cc -std=c11 -O3 main.c -lpthread` and run with `+RTS --threads N --gpu off`. Each binary runs once to warm up. Then main and this branch alternate, for 5 rounds on SEQ (`--threads 1`) and 9 rounds on PAR (`--threads 16`). Ratios are PR / main, so lower is faster. Every run printed the pinned output.

| bench | mode | main (s, median) | PR (s, median) | PR / main, min | PR / main, median |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| tree-bitonic | SEQ | 9.921 | 8.211 | 0.827 | 0.828 |
| tree-radix | SEQ | 9.316 | 9.106 | 0.941 | 0.977 |
| tree-bitonic | PAR | 1.367 | 1.129 | 0.850 | 0.826 |
| tree-radix | PAR | 0.479 | 0.463 | 0.975 | 0.967 |

Notes:

- **tree-bitonic**
  - SEQ is steady. Main ran 9.89–9.97 s in four rounds and 12.68 s in one. This branch ran 8.19–8.23 s every round.
  - PAR is noisier: main took 1.21–1.45 s and this branch 1.03–1.33 s.
- **tree-radix**
  - SEQ is bimodal in both builds. Most rounds take 9.0–9.4 s and a few take 7.1–7.8 s, so the minimum only shows which build drew a fast round. Read the median, 0.98.
  - PAR is a steady 0.97.
- **Layout:** an earlier run, main at 10256a7b against f6c6d216, also built both sides with `-falign-functions=64`, which takes function layout out of the comparison. The aligned medians were 0.79 (SEQ) and 0.80 (PAR) for tree-bitonic, and 0.99 and 0.97 for tree-radix. So the gain is not a layout effect.
- **symreg** measured 0.98–0.99 at f6c6d216. It now compiles to main's code.
- **tree-matmul and kmeans** have the same machine code as main here, so their −7% and −3% in the #1596 table came from the other commits.
- **editdist**'s code is also unchanged, so commit 3's regression is gone.

title: Compile constructor tails with destination passing and owned-node reuse
body:
> This is garbage code produced by GPT, but the idea of this optimization is very well known (tail modulo cons, tail modulo async, etc) and shows significant performance improvement. The ideas should be taken from here and rewritten from scratch, ideally with the agent not having access to this PR's code itself.

Constructor tails currently wait for their children and then allocate/rebuild the parent. On sequential paths this retains constructor continuations down the recursive spine; on parallel paths results travel through the join before becoming constructor fields. This change allocates the parent first, lets children fill its fields, and reuses a consumed node when the existing ownership analysis permits it.

The selected implementation is destination passing with fused sibling continuations and owned-node reuse. It is enabled automatically in the C emitter; CPU, Metal and CUDA share the emitted runtime. The JS emitter and language/checker are unchanged.

**Draft / merge blocker:** `comp.ts` is 67,278 tokens against the permanent 66,000-token cap. The repository gate reports that failure; the cap has not been changed. Removing the experimental switches saved 91 tokens, but another 1,278 must be removed by simplification before merging. This PR preserves the measured design for review rather than claiming the size gate passes.

## Transformation

For an eligible constructor tail:

```text
left, right = f(a), g(b)
return Node(left, right)
```

the operational transformation is:

```text
parent = reuse_owned_node_or_allocate(2)
root = Node(parent)

sequential:
  publish root into the incoming destination, or save it in a root frame
  redirect the final child's destination to parent[1]
  save g's arguments and a continuation:
    parent[0] = returned_value
    tail-jump g(b)
  tail-jump f(a)

parallel:
  retain root in an ordinary join record
  launch f(a) with destination parent[0]
  launch g(b) with destination parent[1]
  return root only after both children complete
```

A unary constructor tail needs no sibling continuation: it stores the parent, updates the current destination and tail-jumps to its child. Self-tail calls become worker-loop iterations; cross-function tails use the existing tail-transfer machinery. Branching retains only pending sibling work. There is no subtree merging or shared scope-wide completion counter.

## Chosen design: all pieces

1. **Conservative eligibility in `emit_dps`.** The current segment and callees return one boxed value. The body is an unshared, non-native constructor whose boxed fields are exactly the call-result variables, once each and in order. Calls are statically known, have no explicit bang and no borrowed parameters. Constructor and argument arities leave room within `WIDE`. Everything else keeps the existing lowering.
2. **One allocation/reuse helper.** `node_alloc` extracts the existing size-class matching logic from `ctr_build`. Both ordinary constructors and destination parents use it. Arguments are captured and dead bindings processed before selecting a spare; selection happens before flushing the other spares. A possibly static node retains the existing `HEAP_OFF` check, so static storage is never overwritten. This adds no new ownership analysis or free list.
3. **Allocate before descending.** Each eligible tail constructs its parent reference before starting the children. Reused storage follows the same destination protocol as fresh storage.
4. **Packed sequential continuations.** A continuation word holds the 16-bit function id below a 40-bit heap destination. `WL_RETN` masks the id before dispatch. An existing destination is filled immediately and redirected to the final child's field. At an ordinary caller boundary, a two-word root frame saves the result root and its final destination. The compiler's existing function-id limit bounds the encoding.
5. **One root-return segment.** `Dps~ret` stores the final result into its destination and returns the saved root. Its returned value is captured as a segment input before `WL_OPEN` resets output registers.
6. **Fused sibling continuations.** Each pending sibling saves its argument words and one packed continuation word. That segment stores the preceding child's result and immediately tail-jumps to the sibling. There is no separate `Dps~put` frame or handler per child.
7. **Ordinary parallel joins remain the completion boundary.** The parent root occupies the first join payload slot; the following slots retain child tasks for the scheduler. A `TAG_DST` continuation identifies result delivery into the parent's field. `task_deliver` resolves that destination through the join's root, writes the result, and uses the existing release/acquire completion protocol. The ready join returns the root; a consumer never receives a partially filled tree.
8. **Small runtime surface.** The runtime adds one continuation tag, destination selection in delivery, and the return-id mask. `DPS_ASYNC` is emitted from segment reachability so the delivery branch can disappear when unused. It is not a user-facing switch. There are no cloned destination entries, per-return root checks, cascading joins, benchmark-specific rules or additional compiler pass.

## Runtime measurements

Elapsed seconds, median of five measured runs after a warm-up. Each cell is **production baseline → selected**, followed by elapsed-time change; negative is better.

| Workload | CPU, 1 thread | CPU, 8 threads | Metal |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| tree-matmul | 2.0141 → 2.0576 (+2.2%) | 0.4455 → 0.4375 (-1.8%) | 0.8786 → 0.8661 (-1.4%) |
| kmeans | 4.0420 → 3.9030 (-3.4%) | 0.8592 → 0.8382 (-2.4%) | 0.6296 → 0.4894 (-22.3%) |
| tree-bitonic | 5.7602 → 5.7409 (-0.3%) | 1.4044 → 1.3712 (-2.4%) | 1.7313 → 1.6150 (-6.7%) |
| tree-radix | 3.7028 → 3.0531 (-17.5%) | 0.7223 → 0.5903 (-18.3%) | 1.1702 → 0.8339 (-28.7%) |

These compare the whole transformation against baseline commit `99a3d5fb42455f5c9cc75a6c2c459b2cd0a06172`. Reuse's incremental contribution over fused destination passing is smaller: Metal matmul improves 4.6%, radix 2.0%, and kmeans 0.5% in the final paired batch. CPU radix improves another 2.9%/3.0% at one/eight threads.

Single-thread matrix multiplication still regresses about 2.2% against production. Allocation reduction does not guarantee lower elapsed time. Bitonic's Metal result varies across batches, including a sign change in the incremental reuse comparison; the final number is not a robust universal gain. Small differences are exploratory.

Hardware: Apple M4 minis, 10 cores, 16 GiB, Apple clang 21, `-O3 -std=c11`. Variants rotate/reverse order on the same leased mini for each comparison. Every run checks output. Times include process startup; Metal archives are built before timing. Metal uses eight host threads and 4 GB spans for matmul/radix, 1 GB otherwise. There is no thermal control.

CPU data come from the phase2 reuse variant, whose full assembly matches the simplified candidate under clang 17 and 21. This PR's default-enabled source emits byte-identical C to that candidate for all 17 runtime benchmarks and three pure demos. Metal data come from the final paired baseline/fused/selected batch. Earlier clang 17 timing investigations are excluded from this table.


## Profiles and compiler cost

Untimed, single-thread matrix instrumentation:

| Counter | Fused destination passing | With reuse |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Heap allocations | 244,669,839 | 125,578,383 |
| Heap frees | 244,669,839 | 125,578,383 |
| Explicit stack writes | 5,235,850,887 | 5,235,850,887 |
| Generated segment entries | 3,815,571,348 | 3,815,571,348 |

Reuse removes **48.7% of allocation/free calls**. Relative to production, destination passing reduces matrix segment entries from 4,183,573,524 and stack writes from 5,806,776,711. These are semantic counters, not hardware instruction/cache measurements.

A fresh 100,000-node unary-chain check returns the same result with **5 explicit worker-stack words instead of 100,003**. This bounds the recursive construction spine, not heap usage or all branching programs. The earlier Metal stress check also completed with the destination design where baseline exhausted its stack.

Fresh compiler timings for the default-enabled PR source use seven measured repetitions plus warm-up on the four workloads above and three pure demos. Sum of per-workload medians:

| Stage | Baseline | PR | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `compile_book`, after checking | 672.05 ms | 675.01 ms | +0.44% |
| Whole Bend-to-C CLI | 1,067.83 ms | 1,071.36 ms | +0.33% |
| Native C compilation | 2,229.19 ms | 2,232.51 ms | +0.15% |
| Generated C, aggregate | 1,551,849 bytes | 1,551,052 bytes | -0.05% |

There is no claimed compiler-speed improvement. The choice favors runtime gains with one shared allocation helper and no specialization pass.


## Tried and discarded

The four later optimizations—reuse, known-destination specialization, root-return inlining and cascading join completion—were profiled and timed individually and together. Further batches tested combinations and bounded forwarding. Comparisons below use each experiment's paired fused-DPS control unless stated otherwise.

| Attempt | Evidence and reason to discard |
| --- | --- |
| Shared scope/counter prototype | Added synchronization instead of making the sequential constructor tail a loop; severe Metal kmeans regression. Replaced by destination passing with ordinary per-fork completion boundaries. |
| Separate destination frames / `Dps~put` | Genuine destination passing, but extra frames and dispatches caused the early matrix regressions. Replaced by stores fused into sibling continuations. Those earlier timings used a different CPU toolchain and are not mixed into the final table. |
| Known-destination entry specialization | Alone was mixed. With reuse it improved matrix CPU1/CPU8/Metal by 5.7%/5.3%/4.7% against fused, but Metal radix was 6.3% slower than reuse alone. Adds cloned entries and compiler machinery; not chosen as a general default. |
| Root-return inlining into every return | Removed 121,335,936 matrix segment entries but slowed matrix CPU1/CPU8 by 13.2%/9.8%. The extra return-path work outweighed fewer dispatches. |
| Cascading completed joins | Metal kmeans went from 0.4866 s to 3.9067 s, about 8.0× slower. GPU occupancy/divergence was not measured, so the precise hardware cause remains unknown. |
| All four together | Matrix CPU1/CPU8 slowed 19.9%/11.7%; Metal kmeans retained a roughly 7.8× regression. |
| At most one parent forwarded | Removed the catastrophic kmeans regression (0.4893 s versus fused 0.4950 s), but other gains were small/mixed and required more runtime machinery. |
| Reuse + specialization + root-return inlining | Matrix CPU1 slowed 19.3% in the combination batch. Fewer destination tests/entries did not make it faster. |

Reuse alone is the selected additional optimization. No tested combination won on every workload/backend.


## Validation

- Default-enabled PR compiler: **PASS 1678 / 1678** through the cluster test gate.
- Added fixtures cover unary and mutual constructor tails, sibling destinations with unequal leaf work, completion before consumption, and mutually recursive names also exercised by the discarded specialization experiment.
- All 17 runtime benchmarks and three pure demos matched baseline outputs at one/eight CPU threads: 40 checks on the measured candidate, with byte-identical generated C verified again for this PR.
- Every timed CPU/Metal variant checked outputs; deep-chain stack behavior was rechecked on this PR.
- Whitespace checks pass for the implementation and tests. Repository gate **fails only the compiler token cap: 67,278 > 66,000**.
- CUDA and interactive window/network demos were not benchmarked. This is not a claim that the full perf/ping gate suite passed.

title: IO.get_env with a "=" in the name reads part of another variable on the C lane and Node
body:
### What you did

bend envq.bend -o envq -o envq.js, then A='B=C' ./envq, A='B=C' node envq.js, A='B=C' bun envq.js

### What happened

```text
$ A='B=C' ./envq          # C lane (glibc)
A=Done:B=C
A=B=Done:C
$ A='B=C' node envq.js    # Node
A=Done:B=C
A=B=Done:C
$ A='B=C' bun envq.js     # Bun
A=Done:B=C
A=B=Fail:2
```

`IO.get_env("A=B")` names a variable that does not exist, so it should fail with ENOENT, as it does on Bun. On the C lane and on Node it answers `Done("C")`, the tail of `A`'s value: glibc's `getenv` compares the name up to its length and then wants a `=`, so `"A=B"` matches the entry `A=B=C`. Node's `process.env` goes through the same `getenv`. Bun looks the exact key up in its own object and fails. So the lanes disagree, and a name built from input (`"PATH=x"`, say) can read a variable the program never named. macOS's `getenv` stops the name at the first `=` instead, so there `get_env("A=B")` likely answers all of `A`'s value (not verified here).

This is the `=` twin of #1449 (a NUL in the name). `get_env.c` already rejects a NUL with `io_nul` before calling `getenv`; a `=` can never be part of a variable name either (POSIX `setenv` refuses one with EINVAL).

### The file

```python
import Base

law report:
  for tag : String
  for r   : Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String), String>
  IO(Unit)

def report(tag, r):
  match r:
    case Done{value}:
      IO.print(String.append(tag, String.append("=Done:", value)))
    case Fail{error}:
      (code, message) = error
      IO.print(String.append(tag, String.append("=Fail:", U32.show(code))))

law main:
  IO(U32)

def main():
  do IO<U32>:
    a : Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String), String> <- IO.get_env("A")
    x : Unit <- report("A", a)
    b : Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String), String> <- IO.get_env("A=B")
    y : Unit <- report("A=B", b)
    return 0
```

### bend version

Bend 2.0.37 (main at 10256a7)

### uname -sm

Linux x86_64

### clang --version (the first line)

clang version 23.1.1 (Node v26.10.0, Bun 1.4.3)

title: fix(io): get_env rejects a name with a "="
body:
<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"orezraey"} -->
## Problem

Closes #1794.

`IO.get_env` passed a name containing `=` straight to the host. glibc's `getenv("A=B")` matches the entry `A=B=C` and answers `C`, so on the C lane and on the Node lane (whose `process.env` uses `getenv`) the call read part of another variable's value, while Bun, which looks up the exact key, failed with ENOENT. The lanes disagreed, and a name the caller built could read a variable it never named.

| Lane | `A` (with `A='B=C'`) | `A=B` (before) | `A=B` (after) |
|---|---|---|---|
| C | `Done("B=C")` | **`Done("C")`** | `Fail(ENOENT)` |
| Node | `Done("B=C")` | **`Done("C")`** | `Fail(ENOENT)` |
| Bun | `Done("B=C")` | `Fail(ENOENT)` | `Fail(ENOENT)` |

## Change

- `bend2/effs/get_env.c`: reject a name containing `=` with the same ENOENT the NUL guard (`io_nul`) and the unset path already return, before calling `getenv`.
- `bend2/effs/get_env.js`: the same check next to the NUL check from #1449.
- `tests/io/get_env_eq.bend` (+ `get_env_eq.c` / `get_env_eq.js`): a foreign `put_eq` effect sets `BEND_ENV_EQ=x=y`; the test pins `exact=x=y` and `eq=unset` for `get_env("BEND_ENV_EQ=x")`.

Valid names, values containing `=`, own-property semantics and the error codes are unchanged: the guard only fires on a name no variable can have.

## Verification

On Linux x86_64 (clang 23.1.1, Bun 1.4.3, Node v26.10.0), each test checked and interpreted with `bun bend2/main.ts <t>.bend`, then built with `-o t.js -o t.c` and run under Bun, Node and the clang binary:

- `tests/io/get_env_eq.bend` before the fix: interp and Bun print `eq=unset`, Node and C print `eq=y`. After: all four print `exact=x=y` / `eq=unset`. So the test discriminates the bug.
- `tests/io/get_env.bend`, `get_env_nul.bend`, `get_env_own.bend`, `nul_bytes.bend`: unchanged output on all four lanes.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: `PASS: 54 / 54` (the new files match `tests/...` and `bend2/effs/[a-z0-9_]+\.(c|js)`; no capped file is touched).
- `--check-only` refuses the test the same way it refuses `tests/io/exit_status.bend` (it depends on a foreign effect).
- `get_env.js` merges cleanly with the open #1549, which edits the line above.

title: Keep FID presence guards from rooting entries
body:
Follow-up to #1714.

A presence guard used to bring its own FID target into the build, so it was always true. Preprocessor queries no longer root entries. `#define` bodies still do: a macro-expanded call must keep its target.

The new runtime fixture covers absent/present guards, continued/commented directives, C digraphs, and a macro call across a multiline comment. It failed in clang before the fix and now builds and prints 42.

The JS twins now use `FID(imul)` to dispatch to the real `Math.imul`, instead of returning a constant. The C twins still invoke the Bend entry.

Locally, all four affected/boundary fixtures pass checkup, the interpreter, emitted JS, and native C. No private-cluster run claimed.

Repo gate: 54/54; all caps unchanged.

title: fix(cli): reject hard-linked input files as outputs
body:
`bend main.bend -o out.js` can overwrite `main.bend` when `out.js` is a hard link to it. The current output check resolves paths, but hard links have distinct paths. The command succeeds and replaces the source with compiled JavaScript.

Use the existing `same_file` helper to compare each existing output with the program's inputs by device and inode. Reject a match before writing the output. Keep the current path and directory checks.

The regression test covers the entry file, imported Bend files, and foreign JS and C files. It checks direct paths, symbolic links, hard links, output formats, directories, and valid output creation and replacement. Each rejected output must leave all inputs unchanged.

Validation:

- The new regression test prints `3` before the fix and the expected `0` after it.
- Seven fixtures pass in the CLI and compiled JS. Two also pass as native binaries: 16 local runtime checks.
- The repository gate passes: `PASS: 54 / 54`.
- TypeScript reports the same 11 diagnostics on current `main` and this change. The full type check does not pass on either version.
- Cluster gates were not run.

title: IO.args turns non-UTF-8 arguments into U+FFFD, so a program can't open a file it was given
body:
### What you did

```bend
import Base

def codes(s: String) -> String:
  match s:
    case SNil{}: ""
    case SCon{head, tail}:
      String.concat([" ", U32.show(Char.to_u32(head)), codes(tail)])

def show_open(name: String, r: Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, File>) -> IO(Unit):
  match r:
    case Done{file}:
      do IO<Unit>:
        IO.print(("open: ok" : String))
        File.close(file)
    case Fail{(code, msg)}:
      IO.print(("open: " ++ msg : String))

def report(args: List<String>) -> IO(Unit):
  match args:
    case Nil{}: IO.print("no argument")
    case prog <> rest:
      match rest:
        case Nil{}: IO.print("no argument")
        case +name <> more:
          do IO<Unit>:
            IO.print(("code points:" ++ codes(name) : String))
            r : Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, File> <- File.open(name, "r")
            show_open(name, r)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    report(args)
```

On Linux (Debian bookworm, aarch64), with the C that Bend 2.0.37 emits:

```sh
bend args.bend -o args.c
clang -O2 args.c -o args -lm -lpthread
touch "$(printf 'caf\xe9.txt')"     # a Latin-1 name: bytes 63 61 66 E9 …
./args "$(printf 'caf\xe9.txt')"
./args "$(printf 'caf\xe8.txt')"
```

### What happened

```
code points: 99 97 102 65533 46 116 120 116
open: No such file or directory
code points: 99 97 102 65533 46 116 120 116
open: No such file or directory
```

The file exists, but the byte `E9` reaches the program as U+FFFD, so it
can't open the file it was given, and two different names arrive as the
same `String`. A UTF-8 name works (`code points: 99 97 102 233 …`,
`open: ok`). A native build on macOS and the JavaScript build under Bun
print the same code points.

### Why it matters

On Linux and other POSIX systems, arguments and file names are byte strings:
an argument may hold any byte but NUL, and a file name any byte but NUL and
`/`. Programs that take paths from a shell glob, `find` or `xargs` (copy,
archive, rename and search tools) can be handed names that aren't UTF-8,
from old Latin-1 media or archives made elsewhere, and today they can
neither open nor tell apart those files.

### Possible shapes

`String` is text (#1248) and files and sockets decode with the WHATWG
decoder (#809), so this doesn't ask to change either. Two options:

1. Byte twins, as TCP got: `IO.args_bytes()` answering `List<List<U32>>`,
   plus path effects that take bytes (`File.open_bytes` and so on). Exact,
   but it doubles every effect that takes a path.
2. Lossless decoding only where the OS hands over names (argv, environment
   variables, paths), as Python's `surrogateescape` does (PEP 383): a byte
   that isn't part of valid UTF-8 decodes to U+DC00 plus the byte
   (U+DC80–U+DCFF), and encoding a `String` for the OS turns those code
   points back into the byte. Valid UTF-8 decodes exactly as today, and
   every effect that takes a path keeps its signature.

On the JavaScript lane, Node and Bun decode `process.argv` before a program
sees it, so that lane may be unable to recover the bytes either way.

title: A non-UTF-8 argument reaches the program as bytes and opens its file (#1798)
body:
Fixes #1798.

## What changes

This takes the issue's first shape: byte twins, like the ones TCP, UDP and `File.read` already have. `String` stays text (#1248), and bytes cross as `List<&2, U32>`.

- `IO.args_bytes() -> IO(List<List<&2, U32>>)` gives the entries `IO.args` gives, as bytes, with no UTF-8 decoding. In C it is `IO.args`'s loop with `io_list` where `IO.args` uses `io_str`.
- `File.open_bytes(path: List<&2, U32>, mode: String)` opens the path's bytes as they are. A value past 255 fails with EINVAL, as `TCP.send_bytes` does, and a 0 fails with EILSEQ, as a NUL in `File.open`'s path does. It shares `File.open`'s code in both lanes: `io_cbuf` with `CID(Con)` in C, and `io_unlist` in JS.

Each twin lives in its sibling's effect file (`args.c/.js`, `file_open.c/.js`) under its own `#ifdef CID(...)`, as `file_read.c` does.

**The JS lane.** Node and Bun decode `process.argv` before the program runs, so there `IO.args_bytes` is each argument's UTF-8: a byte that isn't UTF-8 arrives as U+FFFD's UTF-8, EF BF BD. The doc comment in `base.bend` says so. The C lane keeps every byte.

`IO.get_env` and `Process.run`'s program and arguments also take Strings, as do the other path effects. This PR leaves them alone: each could get a twin the same way if one is wanted.

## The issue's program

Rewritten for the twins:

```bend
import Base

def hex(xs: List<&2, U32>) -> String:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}: ""
    case x <> rest: " " ++ U32.show(x) ++ hex(rest)

def show_open(r: Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, File>) -> IO(Unit):
  match r:
    case Done{file}:
      do IO<Unit>:
        IO.print(("open: ok" : String))
        File.close(file)
    case Fail{(code, msg)}:
      IO.print(("open: " ++ msg : String))

def report(args: List<List<&2, U32>>) -> IO(Unit):
  match args:
    case Nil{}: IO.print("no argument")
    case prog <> rest:
      match rest:
        case Nil{}: IO.print("no argument")
        case +name <> more:
          do IO<Unit>:
            IO.print(("bytes:" ++ hex(name) : String))
            r : Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, File> <- File.open_bytes(name, "r")
            show_open(r)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<List<&2, U32>> <- IO.args_bytes()
    report(args)
```

The C binary on Linux, with `caf\xe9.txt` present:

```
$ ./args "$(printf 'caf\xe9.txt')"
bytes: 99 97 102 233 46 116 120 116
open: ok
$ ./args "$(printf 'caf\xe8.txt')"
bytes: 99 97 102 232 46 116 120 116
open: No such file or directory
```

In the JS lanes (`bun`, `node`, `bend args.bend`) both print `99 97 102 239 191 189 …`. A UTF-8 name (`caf\xc3\xa9.txt`) gives `99 97 102 195 169 …` and `open: ok` in every lane.

## Tests

- `tests/io/args_bytes.bend` is `args.bend` for the twin: every lane sees its program, as bytes, and no argument. The harness passes no arguments, so the gate can't reach the Latin-1 argv case; the C run above checks it by hand.
- `tests/io/file_open_bytes.bend`: UTF-8 bytes open the file that `File.open`'s String names; a 256 fails with EINVAL, and a 0 with EILSEQ.

## Checks

Merged onto main e9055f75: `gates/test.ts` PASS 1696 / 1696, `gates/repo.ts` 54 / 54, `gates/ping.ts` 73 / 73, `gates/safe.ts` 0 false rejects, and `gates/perf.ts` the same cells as main. `comp.ts`, `bend.ts` and `main.ts` don't change.

`guide/GUIDE.md` is left for a human. If you want the twin mentioned there, one sentence after the `IO.args` one could read: "`IO.args_bytes` answers the same entries as bytes, for a name that isn't UTF-8, and `File.open_bytes` opens one."

title: Bend 2.0.38
body:
- **A compiled program's runtime options go between `+RTS` and `-RTS`**
  (#1466, PR #1530 by viridale). **Breaking:** `./main --threads 4` now
  passes `--threads 4` to the program (`IO.args`); write `./main +RTS
  --threads 4 -RTS`. A trailing `-RTS` may be left off, `BENDRTS` holds
  options too (the command line wins), `--` stops option reading and
  reaches the program, and an unknown option inside the bracket is an
  error. `--threads` takes digits, `--gpu` takes `on`, `off` or a size in
  `GB` or `MB`.
- **JS modules keep their names apart.** **Breaking for JS hosts:** a
  constructor's JS tag is its name in the file that declares it, so a
  value crosses modules and matches the right arm (#1105, PR #1488 by
  oxura); imported export keys and foreign JS def ids keep their `:`
  (#1758, #1759, #1766, PR #1760 by oxura).
- **`TCP.send` and `TCP.try_send` hand back unsent bytes**, a
  `List<&2, U32>` to resume with `TCP.send_bytes`, so a write cut inside a
  UTF-8 character loses nothing (#1764, PR #1765 by oxura). **Breaking**
  for code that read the residue as a String.
- **Native windows emit `Text` events** with the typed characters on
  Linux and macOS (#1019, PR #1441 by oxura).
- **A `Char` holds any u32 on every lane**; a non-scalar becomes U+FFFD
  only where text leaves Bend (#1080, PR #1411 by oxura).
- **`--verdict`**:
  - The verdict says why each def it lists relies on unsafe or foreign
    code (PR #1531 by MattCozendey), and hints when those defs come only
    through unused imports (#1463, PR #1558).
  - A def specialized at a finite `~` parameter is checked by the kernel
    over each value, so an empty type no longer passes unchecked (#1186,
    PR #1225 by nicolas-abril); a `~` constant takes its model from the
    template's instances (PR #1580 by nicolas-abril).
  - The kernel accepts a self-call on a constructor rebuilt around a
    smaller part of its input, as the checker does (#1167, PR #1200 by
    nicolas-abril).
  - Fixes: annotations under η and let inlining (#1665, #1669, PR #1666 by
    aaaxn); a bare constructor in a type (#1619, PR #1620 by ScottMoore0);
    shared group prefixes (PR #1704 by sebastian-griego); kernel failures
    show their details (#1535, PR #1536 by viridale).
- **Faster**:
  - A GPU bang chains its rounds on the device, three command buffers in
    flight, with no host round trip per stage (PR #1447 by nicolas-abril).
  - A flat generic def's spin takes words at its instance's layouts
    (#1195, PR #1588).
  - `String.order` walks both strings once: 8x on C, and `String.eq` of
    long strings no longer overflows the JS lane (PR #1459 by aldeni);
    `String.contains` is linear on JS (PR #1628 by sebastian-griego).
  - Emission allocates 40% less on large files (PR #1617 by
    nicolas-abril); word matches with many literals compile faster (PR
    #1387 by Iann29).
  - `U32.pow` by squaring and `F32.show` without a second conversion on C
    (PRs #1567 and #1591 by sebastian-griego); `F32.read` rejects bad input
    in linear time (PR #1625 by toprameen); expired channel waiters leave
    in constant time (PR #1671 by sebastian-griego).
  - CUDA keeps its L1 cache in `bend_dev` (PR #1602 by wakamex).
- **Fixes**:
  - Metal: a full lane stack spills to the heap, so non-tail recursion
    under `!` no longer faults at 1023 frames (#1393, #1394, PR #1439 by
    totaland).
  - C: a shared word is written back to its fork frame slot (PR #1615 by
    viridale); a recursive spine is freed cell by cell (#1307, PR #1438 by
    oxura); native channels free their rows and unread values (#1268, PR
    #1532 by oxura); Nat powers and bit widths take checked paths (#1709,
    #1710, PR #1713 by oxura); functions only an effect calls stay
    reachable (#1711, #1712, PR #1714 by oxura); the crash trap is
    async-signal-safe (PR #1655 by adeerkhan).
  - IO: ready effects yield to other computations every 64 (#1719, PR
    #1723 by oxura); `IO.exit` flushes buffered output (PR #1519 by
    vicmcorrea); file and JS stream writes fail on zero progress (#1445,
    PRs #1446 by oxura and #1747 by vicmcorrea); nested JS IO schedulers
    are isolated and resume their own channel waiters (#1524, #1761,
    #1770, PRs #1525 and #1762 by oxura); UDP receive buffers are bounded
    (#1695, PR #1698 by oxura); `TCP.connect` checks its arguments on JS
    (PR #1618 by vicmcorrea); JS `Audio.write` counts whole frames and
    paces on monotonic time (PRs #1683 by toprameen and #1597 by
    vicmcorrea).
  - Base: `List.any`, `all`, `contains` and `find` stop once the answer is
    known (#1726-#1729, PR #1730 by oxura); prefix checks stop at the
    prefix (#1640, PR #1645 by EpsilonPhoenix); `F32.round` keeps negative
    zero and rounds once (#1611, PRs #1613 by oxura and #1547 by
    vicmcorrea); `F32.lerp` stays finite and keeps its endpoints (#1607,
    #1749, PRs #1608 and #1754 by oxura); `F32.to_nat` keeps wide values
    (#1636, PR #1642 by oxura); JS `U32.to_f32` keeps zero positive and
