title: fix(formatter): raw apostrophe literals keep their boundaries
body:
The formatter now preserves raw apostrophe character literals. Previously, it mistook the payload apostrophe for the closing quote, which could stop formatting or turn valid source into a parse error.

For example, valid `[''',''']` previously became invalid `['' ',' '']`; it now formats as `[''', ''']`. The scanner consumes the payload before looking for the closing quote.

Tests verify literal spelling, comment and escape boundaries, idempotence, and unchanged execution across three formatting styles. All 35 formatter/LSP tests and the repository gate pass.

title: fix(comp): C comments keep Unicode separators
body:
Foreign C effects containing U+2028 or U+2029 inside a `//` comment can fail compilation when later comment text resembles a `CID` or `FID` placeholder.

The scanner now uses each language’s comment boundaries while sharing the remaining pattern. The existing fixture tests retained C comments and live JavaScript code after a separator.

Local source, compiled CLI, Bun/Node and native checks pass. Repository gate: 54/54. Compiler tokens: 65,960 → 65,998. TypeScript retains seven baseline diagnostics.

title: fix(comp): correct fork/join captures after borrowing spins
body:
### Summary

A parallel `let` whose first call owns a value, while a sibling's argument runs a spin that borrows the same value, fails in C at 2+ threads with `bend: frontier drained without a result` (#1953). One thread, the interpreter and JS print the right answer.

`emit_fork`'s two paths disagreed on whether that value lives until the join. This PR makes the fork path release it the way the serial path already does. It is two lines in `emit_fork` plus a regression test.

### Root cause

`emit_fork` emits a fork path (`if (!seq)`) and a serial path that meet in one join segment, so the fork's captures must equal the join's leading parameters.

- In the fork path, each call's arguments are emitted with every *other* call in `rest`. After `Items.keep(xs)` pops its owned share (`term_keep`), the spin `Items.copy(xs, ..)` in the sibling's argument still sees `keep(xs)` as a later use. `xs` is left bound, so it lands in `hold` and is captured into the join.
- In the serial path, the spin's `bind_dead` (from #1243) sinks `xs` right after the spin.
- The join segment opens from the serial path's live set, `[a, b]`, so `task_node` sizes it at arity 2. The fork path fills `[xs, a, b]`. The second task's ref is written to slot 2, the join's continuation word. `task_deal` scans only the first `arity` slots, so that task never runs, `rem` stays at 1 and the root never gets a value.

Instrumenting the generated C confirmed this at runtime. One thread takes the serial path, and 2+ threads take the fork path with the overwritten continuation.

`e4a53903` stated this invariant ("the fork's parallel hold set is carried by every sequential step so both paths share one joiner") and guarded it with `die("a fork's paths hold different values")`. That guard went in `87a1e9c9`, before #1243 added the early sink.

### Fix

After the arguments are emitted, the fork path calls `bind_dead` with the only things that can still use a binding: the sibling tasks' borrowed variable arguments and the body.

```ts
bind_dead(pl, [...calls.flatMap((c) => c.xs.filter((a, i) =>
  brw_of(c.k!)[i] && term_strip(a).$ === "Var")), o.b]);
```

The join then holds an owned value only for a sibling task that borrows it or for the body. A spin in an argument runs to completion in the parent before any task exists, so the value it read is sunk before the fork, as the serial path does. The owning task keeps its own `term_keep` reference. Values a sibling task borrows stay held, as `borrow_fork_hold` and `dead_param_fork` pin.

I also tried the opposite direction, carrying `hold` into the serial path's `emit_args`. It turned `Xs.sum` in `dead_param_fork` into a self-sustaining lend, so it is not used here.

### Regression coverage

`tests/reg/fork_spin_owner.bend` prints `2 3 6 3` from four shapes:

1. The issue's shape: an owner first, then a spin in the sibling's argument.
2. A three-way `let` with spins in two siblings.
3. Two lists, each borrowed by its own spin in the second call.
4. An owner between two spins.

### Validation

All local, on macOS arm64 with Apple clang 17, against `main` at `f1273d30`.

- **The new test.** On `main`, the interpreter and JS pass, and C passes at 1 thread but fails 5/5 at 2 and 8 threads. With this PR it passes all lanes at 1, 2 and 8 threads.
- **Related tests.** All 56 `tests/reg` files matching `fork|spin|borrow|brw|hold|dead_param|lent` pass interpreted, as JS, and as C at 1, 2 and 8 threads (5 runs each).
- **Edge cases.** 13 programs (variants of the issue, 3-way lets, two borrowed lists, deeper nesting, body uses, dead results, a 3,000-cell list, a task borrower) were run 10 times each at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. All pass. `main` fails the 6 that hit this bug at 2+ threads.
- **Generated code.** C is byte-identical to `main` for all 881 tests that emit C, and JS for all 930 that emit JS.
- **Typecheck.** `tsc` reports no errors in `comp.ts`, and the same pre-existing errors as `main` elsewhere.
- **`bun gates/repo.ts`.** 53/54, the `comp.ts` ttok cap fails (below). `main` is 54/54.
- **Not run.** The mini-cluster gate (`gates/test.ts`), the GPU (Metal/CUDA `!`) lanes and Linux.

### Token-limit note

`ttok -m gpt-3.5-turbo` agrees under ttok 0.3 (CI's) and 1.0:

- `main` (`f1273d30`): 65,960
- This PR: 66,005
- Cap: 66,000

The fix adds 45 tokens and puts `comp.ts` 5 over the cap, so the repo-gate check will fail. I asked how you'd like to handle it on #1953 and haven't trimmed unrelated code to make room. The cap is unchanged.

### Related issue

Addresses #1953.

title: fix(io): validate UDP send addresses before FFI setup
body:
An invalid UDP host or port can stop a JavaScript program with an FFI error before Bend returns `Fail(EINVAL)`. Validate the destination before loading the system interface, as `TCP.connect` already does.

The regression test covers all four UDP send functions. Its JavaScript helper injects an FFI failure before each invalid send. It checks invalid hosts and ports, returned text and bytes, and `Ready{Fail}` for timed sends. A valid send after the failures checks that the socket still works.

Validation:

- The regression failed before the fix with `Error: no ffi on this host`.
- All 16 focused tests passed on their supported local backends: direct execution, emitted JavaScript, and native C.
- The repository gate passed: `54 / 54`.
- JavaScript syntax checks and `git diff --check` passed.

The full cluster gates were not run.

title: fix(cli): reject overlapping output paths before writing
body:
A build with multiple `-o` paths can exit successfully while one output silently overwrites another. For example, if `result.mjs` links to `result.js`, requesting both replaces the runnable JS with the module output.

Preflight all requested outputs before writing, resolving symlinks (including dangling links and linked parent directories) and comparing hard-link identities. Include GPU sidecars only when the generated program and platform/toolkit detection select a GPU build; CPU-only `-o program -o program.gpu` remains valid. Reuse generated C when preflight needs it.

Validation on Linux:
- Extended `output_input_links` regression fails on upstream main and passes interpreted and as emitted JavaScript.
- Covers duplicate paths, symlinks, hard links, simulated CUDA sidecar collisions, two CPU binaries, and the no-CUDA `!` fallback. The native CPU binaries print `42`.
- Mixed native, JS, and C output build passes; native and JS print `42`.
- Repository gate: **54/54**. `git diff --check` passes.
- Independent GPT-6.1-Terra medium review using `review-agent`: no findings after correcting its initial CPU-sidecar finding.

Actual Metal/CUDA execution and the mini-cluster gates were not run. The collision guard is a preflight; it does not protect against concurrent filesystem changes after the check.

title: fix(io): release abandoned JS channel waiters when their run ends
body:
A nested JavaScript IO run can exit or throw while a channel sender is parked behind a live waiter. Its abandoned queue entry keeps the payload and continuation reachable until it reaches the head, allowing repeated nested runs to retain them indefinitely.

Register parked channel waiters with their owning run and release them when that run ends. Waking or timing out a waiter removes its cleanup registration. Queue compaction keeps abandoned entries bounded behind a waiter that stays live.

Validation on Linux:
- New blocking/timed sender regression covers nested exit and throw paths: `piled up: 999` on main, `bounded` with the fix. Passes interpreted and as emitted JS, independently rerun by the parent agent.
- Five related channel/timeout fixtures pass across interpreter, emitted JS and native C; re-entry and timer regressions also pass.
- Repository gate: **54/54**; `git diff --check` passes.
- GPT-6.1-Terra medium `review-agent` review: no findings.

The new regression is JS-only because it exercises nested host IO and inspects queue retention. The mini-cluster gate could not start because the cluster hostname did not resolve; GPU lanes were not run.

title: fix(bundle): encode virtual module names for quoted HTML filenames
body:
An HTML page whose filename contains a double quote fails to bundle an inline module importing Bend: serialization of the generated module `src` changes the virtual path, and Bun reports `Could not resolve`.

Encode the page basename in generated inline-module names so it survives HTML attribute serialization. The module keeps its original directory, and diagnostics still point to the source page.

Validation on Linux:
- Extended `bundle_inline` regression returns `9` on main and `0` with this fix; interpreted and emitted-JS runs both pass, independently rerun by the parent agent.
- Bundles and executes Bend imports from page names containing a quote, an HTML character reference, a percent escape, and Unicode; also checks a diagnostic in a quoted filename.
- Repository gate: **54/54**; `git diff --check` passes.
- GPT-6.1-Terra medium `review-agent` review: no findings.

The regression uses a JS-only foreign effect. The mini-cluster gate could not start because its hostname did not resolve.

title: On Metal, the shared-node half of a take is a call, not code inlined into the taken match
body:
Fixes #1954.

**What fails.** On an M1 Max (macOS 27.2, Xcode 27.1) the reproducer from the issue fails every run on Metal, on current main and back to v2.0.37: mostly `a function the device does not hold`, sometimes `frontier drained without a result`, once a hang. `--gpu off` and the interpreter print `57798656`. The same program passed 466/466 on raramos9's M1 under macOS 15.6.1 and fails 400/400 on that same M1 after its update to 27.2; on Lorenzo's M4 Pro under macOS 26.5.2 it passes 100/100. So the trigger is the machine code the macOS 27.2 Metal compiler produces, seen so far on the M1 and the M1 Max; whether an M4 on 27.2 is affected is unknown.

**Where.** Bisected on the failing machine (every step rebuilt from main and run 10 times):

- the reporter's variant with a heap-built `Seg` instead of the constant passes, and its shader is 208 KB instead of 1011 KB; the only device-side difference in the emitted C is one `ctr_take` call on the static `Seg`
- `ctr_take` not inlined (`static`, or `__attribute__((noinline))`): passes, shader 214 KB / 294 KB
- only the shared-node branch of `ctr_take` (acquire, last-holder free, or fade) as a real call: passes, shader 304 KB
- `span_fade` alone as a real call, the copy loop not unrolled, every `OUTLINE` function as a real call on Metal, `maxTotalThreadsPerThreadgroup = 128`, the language version pinned to 3.2 or 4.0, 16 or 64 threadgroups per pass instead of 128: all still fail

**The branch that moves never runs in this program.** The static `Seg` is a plain constructor word (`term_ctr` sets no `RFC_BIT`), so at that site `ctr_take` always returns from the owned path. A counter in the CPU build confirms it: the program makes 16 `ctr_take` calls in all and none enters the shared-node branch, at this site or at the two four-field sites. Deleting that branch for two-field takes only, on top of main, therefore changes nothing the program executes, and the GPU result goes from wrong 10/10 to right 10/10 (shader 1011 KB to 297 KB).

So the Metal compiler at its default level inlines the shared-node branch of `ctr_take` into the taken match, the shader grows about five times, and on the M1s under macOS 27.2 the live code around that dead branch runs wrong. Code that never runs changing the result of code that does is a compiler defect, unless the live code has undefined behaviour the newer compiler exploits differently; nothing found points at the second, and the same shader is right under the older compiler, on the M4 Pro, on the CPU and in the interpreter. The corruption is there before dispatch, as raramos9 saw on the M1: captured at the failing dispatch here, the entry word is `0x72f3baae7b12e2fa` and the like, function id `0xf3ba` in a program with 40 functions, the same pattern within a few bits across six runs. Shader validation (`MTL_SHADER_VALIDATION=1`) rewrites the shader and fails every variant, main included, so it is not a usable check here.

**The change.** The shared-node branch moves from `ctr_take` into `span_fade`, which already is the shared path's out-of-line function, and `span_fade` is a real call on Metal (`FAR`) rather than a `static` the compiler inlines anyway. Host and CUDA keep `OUTLINE` as before, with the last-holder free now inside it. `ctr_take` is the copy and one branch. 18 lines in, 15 out; `bun gates/repo.ts` passes (comp.ts 65990 of 66000 ttok).

**Evidence on the M1 Max** (32-core GPU, 64 GB, macOS 27.2 build 26B123, Xcode 27.1, bun 1.4.2):

- reproducer: 50/50 at the default level, 10/10 with `+RTS --gpu 1GB`, 5/5 compiled from source with no cached `.gpu`, clean under `MTL_DEBUG_LAYER=1`; `--gpu off`, `--threads 1` and the interpreter print `57798656`; the heap-built variant still passes 10/10; the shader archive goes from 1011 KB to 304 KB
- the 17 `bench/runtime` programs: same checksums as main on GPU and on CPU, times below, medians of 3 runs, or of 5 alternating runs on an idle machine where a first pass had moved; CPU is `+RTS --gpu off` on all cores
- the 45 tests that use a `!` call, built natively (clang, Metal): 43 pass; the other 2 (`printer/offload_bang_g`, `_h`) have mains the compiler refuses to print, so they are check-only, as on main
- `tests/run` and `tests/rfc`, built natively: 124 files: 113 pass, 7 are error tests whose expected output is the build error and `exit 1`, 4 are check-only; all 11 give byte-identical build logs on main

|---|---|---|---|---|---|

**Rejected alternatives**, both pass the reproducer:

- compile the whole device program at `MTLLibraryOptimizationLevelSize` on the M1 family (`supportsFamily:MTLGPUFamilyApple7` without Apple8), the shape I announced in the issue: raytrace 0.47 s to 0.55 s here, lexer unchanged, and it gates on the GPU family when raramos9's update shows the compiler version is the variable

title: Metal: large continuation dispatcher crashes MTLCompilerService in LLVM allocation
body:
Compiling a large Bend program for Metal repeatedly aborts `MTLCompilerService` in LLVM allocation/vector growth. The native executable is produced, but shader compilation fails and no `.gpu` archive is produced. Splitting the generated continuation dispatcher into smaller functions makes the same application build and pass our recorded CPU/Metal comparisons.

This report concerns a **shader compilation failure**, before any application input executes. It is an application-sized reproducer, not a minimal test case.

**Source-only reproducer:** [bend-metal-dispatcher-reproducer.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34202783/bend-metal-dispatcher-reproducer.zip) (7.7 MB)

### Version and environment

- Bend base: official `v2.0.39`, with the attached small downstream patch `bend-2.0.39-metal-loops.patch`. The version string is `2.0.39+writha-metal-loops.1`.
- That patch makes short generated tail loops `noinline` on Metal. It was already needed for a separate runtime failure; it does not split the dispatcher. This is **not a claim of an unmodified-release reproduction**.
- Apple M1 Pro, Darwin arm64. Environment read during report preparation on 2026-10-30: macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple clang 21.0.0 (clang-2100.3.34.2). The failed builds and crash records are from 2026-10-29.
- Upstream `main` at `f1273d300840c9b167104985efb71fd08f79126e` was inspected during issue preparation, but this application has not been compiled or run against that revision. No current-main reproduction is claimed.

### What happened

The original command was equivalent to:

```sh
bend tests/metal_classifier_entry.bend -o classifier
```

The build ended with exit status 1 after 1,454.45 seconds:

```text
bend: Compilation failed due to an interrupted connection: XPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_INTERRUPTED. This error occurred after multiple retries.
```

Four retained `MTLCompilerService` crash summaries show `EXC_CRASH` / `SIGABRT`, with these frames:

```text
llvm::report_bad_alloc_error(char const*, bool)
llvm::SmallVectorBase<unsigned int>::grow_pod(void*, unsigned long, unsigned long)
```

These frames identify where the service aborted; they do not establish whether the underlying cause is memory exhaustion, an internal compiler limit, or another compiler defect.

The embedded C/Metal source is 20,925,129 bytes. After device preprocessing, its single dispatcher contains 5,749 cases and its function text occupies 16,489,628 bytes. A native binary alone is not a successful GPU build: this attempt produced no GPU archive and performed no GPU classification.

Expected: compile the program successfully, or report an actionable supported limit. Repeated compiler-service aborts followed by the generic interrupted-connection message do not identify which generated-code limit was exceeded.

### Retained reproduction artifact

The accompanying `bend-metal-dispatcher-reproducer.zip` contains the **exact generated source extracted from the failed executable**, the complete source for the successful dispatcher-splitting comparison, the two downstream compiler patches, checksums, and compact evidence records. It contains no native executables or GPU archives.

The failing source was rechecked during issue preparation: its SHA-256 matches the original extraction receipt, and its complete bytes followed by a NUL occur verbatim in the retained failed native executable.

```text
source/loops1-embedded.c
SHA-256: 9e722f25ac961d87f8e0e14747880046b7bef05a58c87ac2d03220bee77c56b6
```

The generated file embeds itself using `#embed __FILE__`, so it can be rebuilt without the Writha checkout or the Bend compiler:

```sh
clang -DBEND_METAL=1 -x objective-c -fobjc-arc -fmodules \
  -std=c11 -O3 source/loops1-embedded.c -lpthread -lm \
  -framework Metal -framework Foundation -o classifier
./classifier +RTS --gpu-build
```

This is the standalone replay recipe derived from Bend 2.0.39's build/runtime code. It has **not been rerun during report preparation**; the failure above comes from the original completed build. The shader build does not need application input. The original retries took about 24 minutes, so a replay may be lengthy.

### Experiments and workaround

| Generated-code variant | Recorded result |
| --- | --- |
| v2.0.39 plus Metal tail-loop call boundaries | Build fails after 1,454.45 s; four retained compiler-service aborts; no GPU archive |
| Also keep all generated flat calls and the Metal work loop out of line | Build still fails after 1,425.57 s with the interrupted-connection message; no GPU archive |
| Separate size-optimization experiment | Compiler crash observed; a later retry was deliberately stopped. This is not recorded as a naturally completed failure sequence |
| Tail-loop patch plus dispatcher split into at most 64 continuation IDs per function | Build succeeds; 102 chunks, largest preprocessed chunk 443,792 bytes |

The split dispatcher passes an explicit lane-state record containing the environment, stack cursor, sequence flags, return width, continuation ID, error-poll counter, and continuation registers. A completion flag distinguishes a jump to another chunk from a final result. The segment bodies and continuation semantics are retained; the change is confined to the Metal dispatcher.

Recorded checks for that candidate include eight complete CPU/Metal result-graph comparisons, composition and series-division arithmetic regressions, and source checks showing identical preprocessed CPU/CUDA paths and each Metal case present exactly once. These checks support this workaround on the tested workloads; they are not a compiler-correctness proof or a performance comparison. The 64-ID chunk size is a working downstream choice, not an established hardware limit or a proposed universal tuning value.

### Related reports and request

- [PR #1433](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1433) reports lost results/wrong branches from large inlined Metal kernels on M1. That is relevant context for our earlier runtime workaround, but this report supplies a separate **compile-time LLVM allocation abort** and its retained source.
- [Issue #1154](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/1154) concerns a small parallel sum and an M2 shader compiler crash on Bend 2.0.32. Our program, version, and recorded abort signature differ.
- [Issue #1195](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/1195) concerns code growth from generic record boxing and long Metal compilation. We have not established that boxing is the cause here.

I did not find an existing issue or PR matching this dispatcher-size/allocation-abort report in the open and closed searches performed on 2026-10-30. Could Bend bound or partition the generated Metal dispatcher, or expose a supported limit with a useful diagnostic? Guidance on reducing this exact retained source further would also help.

title: Array<T> accepts a mixed-depth ANode that the compiled runtime cannot represent
body:
**Bend 2.0.38**, Linux x86-64.

`Array<T>` is a binary tree whose type admits an `ANode` whose two children have different depths. The compiled runtime cannot represent one: it keeps an array as one flat block of 2^c cells and checks the halves' lengths. So a value the type accepts and the plain run produces is refused by `-o`, and the same value inside an `IO` block is refused by the JS lane too.

## The program

```bend
import Base

def sz(r: Array<F32> & U32) -> U32:
  (a, n) = r
  n

def main() -> U32:
  sz(Array.size(F32, ANode{ALeaf{0.0}, ANode{ALeaf{1.0}, ALeaf{2.0}}}))
```

Three leaves, the right child one level deeper than the left.

## What happens

| lane | result |
|---|---|
| `bend mixed.bend` (JS, no `-o`) | prints `2` |
| `bend mixed.bend -o mixed && ./mixed` (C) | `bend: runtime fail-stop`, exit 1 |
| the same size printed with `IO.print(String.append(..., U32.show(...)))` on the JS lane | `bend: runtime fail-stop` |

`bend --check-only` accepts all three. A balanced `ANode{ALeaf{0.0}, ALeaf{1.0}}` works everywhere.

So the value is reachable three ways: accepted by the checker, produced by the JS lane when nothing else touches it, and refused by the C lane and by the JS lane once it crosses the `IO` boundary.

## Why it is not simply "a crash"

`array_node` in `bend2/comp.ts` checks `a.length !== b.length` and raises the fail-stop, so the C runtime is refusing on purpose. The bug is the mismatch between that invariant and the type: `ANode{xs, ys}` takes two `Array<T>` and cannot tell a leaf from a node, so there is no way to write the invariant in the type as it stands.

This is the same question as #1934 asks from the other side (whether Base should state `Array`'s own facts). It also matters for the value law in `bend-ml`: the counterexample that makes `get_other_set` need `ASet.Apart` is exactly this tree, `ANode{ANode{ALeaf{0.0}, ALeaf{1.0}}, ALeaf{2.0}}` (bend-ml#26), which means the counterexample itself can only be run on the JS lane.

## What I would ask for

One of:

- a type that cannot express a mixed-depth `ANode` (a depth index, or `Array<T>` as a perfect tree only, with a separate type for the general binary tree the laws want); or
- a runtime that represents it (the JS lane already does when the value stays pure); or
- a diagnostic at check time that says an `ANode` of two different depths is not representable, rather than a fail-stop after the program has been accepted and run.

The first is a language decision and above my call; the third would at least make the failure arrive before the run.

Reported here because the message is a `runtime fail-stop` with no detail, so the failing program is not obvious from the error. I have not changed anything in `bend2/` (`AGENTS.md` keeps it human-written).

title: app_triangle_2d: PROOF.bend passes after an edit that stops presses on the triangle from counting
body:
### What you did

`bend PROOF.bend` in `demos/app_triangle_2d`, after editing only `main.bend`. This is the follow-up #1931 left for its own issue. `LAWS.bend` and `PROOF.bend` are unchanged.

```diff
@@ -17,10 +17,13 @@
 def Tri.side(+ax: U32, +ay: U32, bx: U32, by: U32, px: U32, py: U32) -> Bool:
   ((bx - ax) * (py - ay) - (by - ay) * (px - ax) > 2147483647 : U32)
 
-def Tri.inside(+x: U32, +y: U32) -> Bool:
+def Tri.shape(+x: U32, +y: U32) -> Bool:
   (Tri.side(256, 64, 64, 448, x, y) && Tri.side(64, 448, 448, 448, x, y)
     && Tri.side(448, 448, 256, 64, x, y))
 
+def Tri.inside(+x: U32, +y: U32) -> Bool:
+  False{}
+
 def Tri.out(
   +ax: U32, +ay: U32, +bx: U32, +by: U32, +x0: U32, +y0: U32, +x1: U32,
   +y1: U32
@@ -29,7 +32,7 @@
     || Tri.side(ax, ay, bx, by, x0, y1) || Tri.side(ax, ay, bx, by, x1, y1)))
 
 def Tri.color(+x: U32, +y: U32, n: U32) -> U32:
-  Tri.pick(Tri.inside(x, y), 16744499,
+  Tri.pick(Tri.shape(x, y), 16744499,
     Tri.pick(((y < 8) && (x < 16 * n) && U32.is_eq((x .&. 8 : U32), 0) : U32),
       16777215, 3362125))
 
@@ -39,8 +42,8 @@
   +y1 = (y0 + s : U32)
   +strip = ((y0 < 8) && (x0 < 16 * n) : U32)
   (strip && (s <= 8 : U32)) || (Bool.not(strip)
-    && ((Tri.inside(x0, y0) && Tri.inside(x1, y0) && Tri.inside(x0, y1)
-        && Tri.inside(x1, y1))
+    && ((Tri.shape(x0, y0) && Tri.shape(x1, y0) && Tri.shape(x0, y1)
+        && Tri.shape(x1, y1))
       || Tri.out(256, 64, 64, 448, x0, y0, x1, y1)
       || Tri.out(64, 448, 448, 448, x0, y0, x1, y1)
       || Tri.out(448, 448, 256, 64, x0, y0, x1, y1)))
```

### What happened

On `main` at 9e8d7b79:

```text
$ bend PROOF.bend
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend PROOF.bend --verdict
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend PIXEL.bend
(256, 300) drawn orange, press -> count 0
(440, 300) drawn teal, press -> count 0
```

`PIXEL.bend` reads each color from the quadtree `Tri.view` draws. The page still draws the triangle at (256, 300), but a press there no longer counts. On the unedited demo, the first line ends in `count 1`.

### Why it happens

Both click laws state their hypothesis with `App.Tri.inside`, the test `main.bend` itself uses, and `PROOF.bend` rewrites with that hypothesis. So the laws hold whatever `Tri.inside` is. #1915 and #1932 fixed the same shape in four other demos; #1931 left this one out because it needed a choice: the drawing lives in `main.bend` too.

### The file

<details>
<summary>PIXEL.bend</summary>

```python
import Base
import ./main.bend as App

def at.pick(right: Bool, down: Bool, tl: Image, tr: Image, bl: Image, br: Image) -> Image:
  match right down:
    case False{} False{}:
      tl
    case True{} False{}:
      tr
    case False{} True{}:
      bl
    case True{} True{}:
      br

# the color the page draws at (x, y), read from the quadtree of depth d
def at(d: Nat, img: Image, +x: U32, +y: U32) -> U32:
  match d img:
    case _ Pix{c}:
      c
    case 0n Qua{tl, tr, bl, br}:
      0
    case 1n++e Qua{tl, tr, bl, br}:
      +h = U32.shln(1, e)
      at(e, at.pick((x >= h : U32), (y >= h : U32), tl, tr, bl, br),
        (x .&. (h - 1) : U32), (y .&. (h - 1) : U32))

def name.if(orange: Bool, teal: Bool) -> String:
  match orange teal:
    case True{} _:
      "orange"
    case False{} True{}:
      "teal"
    case False{} False{}:
      "other"

def name(+c: U32) -> String:
  name.if(U32.is_eq(c, 16744499), U32.is_eq(c, 3362125))

def drawn.at(+x: U32, +y: U32, v: U32 & Image) -> String:
  (n, img) = v
  name(at(9n, img, x, y))

def drawn(+x: U32, +y: U32) -> String:
  drawn.at(x, y, App.Tri.view(0))

def counted(r: Maybe<U32>) -> String:
  match r:
    case Some{n}: U32.show(n)
    case None{}: "quit"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print("(256, 300) drawn " ++ drawn(256, 300) ++ ", press -> count " ++ counted(App.Tri.event(Press{0, Tool.Mouse{}, 256.0, 300.0, 0, 0, True{}}, 0)))
    IO.print("(440, 300) drawn " ++ drawn(440, 300) ++ ", press -> count " ++ counted(App.Tri.event(Press{0, Tool.Mouse{}, 440.0, 300.0, 0, 0, True{}}, 0)))
```

</details>

### A fix, and what it leaves

#1982 adds `SPEC.bend` with the triangle's corners and points both laws at `Spec.inside`. `main.bend` keeps its own `Tri.inside`. I considered having `main.bend` import `Spec.inside` instead, and went with 1570e072's direction, where `pure_par_sum` kept its own `pow2` so that "SPEC.bend no longer reaches into the program". `PROOF.bend` doesn't change: the checker unfolds `Spec.inside` and `Tri.inside` to the same expression, so the rewrite still applies, and the edit above now fails at `Laws.click_inside`.

What it leaves: the laws pin which presses count, not where the triangle is drawn. Moving only the drawing still checks. With `Tri.color` testing `Tri.inside((x - 100 : U32), y)`, `PIXEL.bend` prints `(256, 300) drawn teal, press -> count 1` and `(440, 300) drawn orange, press -> count 0`. Pinning the picture would take a law about `Tri.view`'s quadtree, which means proving that every cell `Tri.flat` paints in one color lies inside the triangle. That looks out of reach to me, so the PR narrows the two law comments to "SPEC.bend's triangle", as #1915 scoped the flag law.

`pure_hvm5_mini` and `app_slash_boss_3d`, also named in #1931, are still to check. I'll file them separately if they have the same gap.

### bend version

Bend 2.0.39 (`main` at 9e8d7b79)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

title: fix(demos): app_triangle_2d's click laws read the triangle from SPEC.bend
body:
Fixes #1981.

`SPEC.bend` holds the triangle: `inside` tests a point against its three corners with `side`. It has the header the other demos' `SPEC.bend` files use. Both click laws state their hypothesis with `Spec.inside`, and their comments now say "SPEC.bend's triangle".

`main.bend` keeps its own `Tri.inside`, as `pure_par_sum` keeps its own `pow2` after 1570e072, so `SPEC.bend` doesn't reach into the program. `PROOF.bend` doesn't change: `Spec.inside` and `App.Tri.inside` unfold to the same expression, so the existing rewrites apply. Unlike `pow2`, nothing here recurses, so no bridging lemma is needed. If you'd rather have the bridge spelled out, `inside_same(x, y) : {Spec.inside(x, y) == App.Tri.inside(x, y) : Bool}` proves by `{==}` and the two click proofs rewrite with it first; I tried it and left it out.

What it leaves, as the issue says: the laws pin which presses count, not where the triangle is drawn.

### What I checked

On 9e8d7b79, macOS arm64:

- `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) print ALL PROOFS CHECK, `bend SPEC.bend` checks, and `bend main.bend -o` builds.
- The issue's `PIXEL.bend` prints `(256, 300) drawn orange, press -> count 1` and `(440, 300) drawn teal, press -> count 0`, as on `main`.
- The issue's edit now fails at `Laws.click_inside`.
- Redefining `Tri.inside` as a triangle 100 px to the right, for the drawing and the presses alike, fails the same way.
- Moving only the drawing (`Tri.color` testing `Tri.inside((x - 100 : U32), y)`) still checks, and `PIXEL.bend` shows (440, 300) drawn orange with a press there leaving the count at 0. That is the limit above.
- I ran these edits in throwaway copies, as for #1932.

`repo-gate` passes in CI. Not run: the cluster gates, Linux.

title: Run path: File.read_bytes / read_at / read commit `max` bytes per call since 2.0.37 (an 8-byte file read with a 1 GiB cap costs ~1 GB; 40 reads: 0.25 s / 113 MB -> 12 s / 3 GB)
body:
## Summary

Since **2.0.37**, on the run path (`bend file.bend`, the JS lane), each `File.read_bytes(f, max)` / `File.read_at(f, off, max)` / `File.read(f, max)` costs memory and time proportional to **`max`**, not to the bytes actually read. A program that reads small files with a generous cap (a common "read the whole file" idiom: `File.read_bytes(f, 1073741824)`) now uses gigabytes and runs 40-50x slower. 2.0.36 ran the same program in 0.25 s / 113 MB. Native builds (`-o`) are not affected.

macOS 26 arm64 (Apple M2 Pro), release tarballs from GitHub.

## Repro (Base only)

```bash
printf 'a,b\n1,2\n' > small.csv     # 8 bytes
```

```bend
import Base

# read an 8-byte file 40 times with File.read_bytes(f, 1 GiB) and print the byte count each time
def got(r: File & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, List<&2, U32>>) -> IO(Nat):
  (f, res) = r
  match res:
    case Fail{(code, msg)}:
      do IO<Nat>:
        File.close(f)
        return 0n
    case Done{bs}:
      do IO<Nat>:
        File.close(f)
        return List.length(&2, U32, bs)

def opened(o: Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, File>) -> IO(Nat):
  match o:
    case Done{f}:
      do IO<Nat>:
        r : File & Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, List<&2, U32>> <- File.read_bytes(f, 1073741824)
        got(r)
    case Fail{(code, msg)}:
      IO.pure(Nat, 0n)

def once(+path: String) -> IO(Nat):
  do IO<Nat>:
    o : Result<&1, &1, U32 & String, File> <- File.open(path, "r")
    opened(o)

def loop(n: Nat, +path: String) -> IO(Unit):
  match n:
    case 0n:
      IO.pure(Unit, Unit{})
    case 1n+p:
      do IO<Unit>:
        k : Nat <- once(path)
        IO.print(Nat.show(k))
        loop(p, path)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  loop(40n, "small.csv")
```

```bash
/usr/bin/time -l bend readbig.bend
```

Every version prints `8` forty times. Two runs each:

| version | wall | max RSS |
|---|---|---|
| 2.0.36 | 0.25 s / 0.26 s | 113 MB / 118 MB |
| 2.0.37 | 13.4 s / 15.1 s | 2.9 GB / 2.8 GB |
| 2.0.38 | 10.9 s / 11.8 s | 3.6 GB / 3.0 GB |
| 2.0.39 | 10.3 s / 12.2 s | 3.1 GB / 2.9 GB |
| 2.0.39, `bend readbig.bend -o x && ./x` | 0.41 s | 1 MB |

With the cap at 1 MiB, all versions are ~0.2 s / <130 MB. `File.read_at(f, 0, 268435456)` × 40 shows the same thing: 2.0.36 0.23 s / 115 MB, 2.0.39 1.6 s / 1.3 GB.

In a real program (a CSV reader test suite that reads ~100 small fixture files through such a helper) this went from 2.6-3.5 s / 0.5 GB on 2.0.36 to 14-25 s / 4.4-5.7 GB on 2.0.39.

## Where it comes from (as far as I can tell)

`bend2/effs/file_read.js` allocates the whole cap up front, in 2.0.36 through 2.0.39 and still on `main` after #1845:

```js
const len = Math.min(max, 2147483647);
const b = new Uint8Array(Math.max(len, 1));
```

That file did not change between 2.0.36 and 2.0.37, but the embedded runtime did (the binaries report Bun v1.3.14 in 2.0.36 and Bun v1.4.0 in 2.0.37-2.0.39). On 2.0.36 the untouched 1 GiB buffer apparently never became resident; from 2.0.37 it does, so each read pays for zeroing/committing `max` bytes.

A possible fix: don't size the buffer by `max`. For example, cap the first allocation at `min(max, fstat size - position)` for regular files, or read into a bounded chunk (64 KiB, doubling) and grow until `max`/EOF. The fill loop from #1845 already has the right shape for growing a buffer.

## Related

#1894 (the run path is the JS lane). #1845 / #1881 changed this file after 2.0.39 but still allocate `max` up front.

title: --verdict / -o .bendtt: stack overflow since 2.0.38 on a named Σ type over two computed equations (16-line Base repro; 2.0.37 passes)
body:
## Summary

Since **2.0.38**, `--verdict` and `-o X.bendtt` fail on a 16-line Base-only program that bend2 accepts. The error is `Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)`, with no location. 2.0.36 and 2.0.37 translate it and the kernel accepts it. It fails in under a second, so there is no size threshold. The translation appears to recurse without end.

macOS 26 arm64 (Apple M2 Pro), release tarballs from GitHub.

## Repro

```bend
import Base

type T is Type:
  A{}
  B{}

def f(b: T) -> T:
  match b:
    case A{}:
      B{}
    case B{}:
      A{}

def P(c: T) -> Type:
  &z: T -> {f(c) == z : T} & {f(z) == c : T}

def p() -> P(A{}):
  (B{}, {==}, {==})
```

| version | `bend r.bend` | `bend r.bend --verdict` | `bend r.bend -o r.bendtt` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0.36 | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ok (1105-byte .bendtt) |
| 2.0.37 | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ok (1105-byte .bendtt) |
| 2.0.38 | ALL PROOFS CHECK | **stack overflowed** | **stack overflowed** |
| 2.0.39 | ALL PROOFS CHECK | **stack overflowed** | **stack overflowed** |

## What is needed to trigger it

Each of these is required. Every variant listed passes on 2.0.39:

- **A named `-> Type` def is used as the return type.** Writing the same Σ inline in `p`'s signature passes, and so does `P()` with no parameter.
- **Both equations compute `f`:** one applies it to the def's parameter (`f(c) == z`) and the other to the bound variable (`f(z) == c`). Their order doesn't matter. These pass: `{f(c)==z} & {z==f(c)}`, `{f(c)==z} & {f(c)==z}`, `{f(z)==c} & {f(z)==c}`, `{c==z} & {f(z)==f(c)}`, a single equation, and a plain pair of equations without the bound `z`.
- **`f` has a `match`.** An identity `f` passes.
- **The def is proven with a concrete witness**, `(B{}, {==}, {==})`.

## Context

I found this in a real proof set: a round-trip predicate `def FZW(c: Column) -> Type: &z: Fz -> {fz(c) == z : Fz} & {unfz(z) == c : Column}`, used as the return type of several lemmas. In that ~21k-line proof set, `--verdict` printed ALL PROOFS CHECK on 2.0.37 (91 s). On 2.0.38 and 2.0.39 the same file overflows after ~16 s, and nothing says which def caused it. The missing location made it expensive to find, so it would help if the overflow named the def being translated.

#1892 and #1896, merged after 2.0.39, change how `safe.ts` η-expands types with no finite η-long form. I have not built `main` to check whether they also cover this case. It may be a different path, because this program's type does have a finite form and it translated fine on 2.0.37.

title: fix(io): a JS File.read's max is a cap, not its buffer size (#1983)
body:
Fixes #1983.

## What

On the JS lane, `file_read_with` (`File.read`, `read_line`, `read_bytes`, `read_at`) allocated a `Uint8Array` of the whole `max` on every call. Since Bun 1.4.0 (2.0.37), those pages are committed. A "read the whole file" call capped at 1 GiB therefore costs about 1 GB and 0.3 s, even when the file holds 5 bytes.

`max` is now a cap, not a size:
- The buffer starts at a regular file's size + 1, so it fills in one buffer and sees EOF without growing. Anything else (a pipe, a terminal, `/dev/zero`) starts at 64 KiB.
- When the buffer is full and still below `max`, it doubles, never past `max`.
- The fill loop from #1845 (EINTR, partial bytes on a later error, line mode, a 0-byte read still making its syscall) is unchanged.

The C lane's `malloc(max + 1)` is left alone. Its pages are never touched, so they are never committed: the native build of the test below peaks at 6 MB.

## Test

New `tests/io/file_read_cap.bend`:
- reads a 5-byte file 40 times with `File.read_bytes(f, 1073741824)`, then prints the total: `200`;
- reads 300000 bytes from `/dev/zero`, which has no size, so the buffer grows through 64K → 128K → 256K → 300000: prints `300000`.

| | output | wall | max RSS |
|---|---|---|---|
| emitted JS, `main` | 200 / 300000 | 60.4 s | 1.5 GB |
| emitted JS, this PR | 200 / 300000 | 0.09 s | 43 MB |
| native C, this PR | 200 / 300000 | 0.79 s | 6 MB |

On `main` the test runs far past the gate's 5 s alarm.

## Validation (macOS arm64, Bun 1.4.0)

- The #1983 repro through `bend2/main.ts` (the run path): 26.0 s / 2.6 GB on `main`, 0.88 s / 79 MB with the fix.
- Every `tests/io` test that reads a file (24 of them, including `file_read_short`, `file_read_line`, `file_read_line_interrupted`, `file_read_after_error`, `file_read_no_ffi`, `file_open_fifo_peer`, `read_bytes`) passes before and after the change, both interpreted (`bend t.bend`) and as emitted JS (`-o t.js`).
- `git diff --check` is clean. The new test matches `gates/repo.ts`'s allow list. I could not run the token count (no `ttok` here); it only covers capped files, which this PR does not touch.

title: Native heap: freed memory is reused only within its size class (peak = sum of per-class high-water marks)
body:
## Summary

In native builds (`bend x.bend -o x`), heap memory freed by blocks of one size class is never reused by
blocks of another class, never coalesced or split, and never returned to the OS. A program whose live data
changes shape over time (many small arrays, then one big one; or a big one, then many small ones) peaks at
the **sum** of the per-class high-water marks instead of the largest live set. Bend 2.0.39, macOS 26 arm64
(Apple M2 Pro), `--threads 1` and `--threads 4` alike.

The repro below keeps 4096 arrays of 2^12 U32 (64 MB) alive, frees them, then allocates one array of
2^24 U32 (64 MB). Peak footprint (`/usr/bin/time -l`, "peak memory footprint"):

| mode | what | peak |
|---|---|---:|
| `small` | 4096 x 2^12 words, freed | 65 MB |
| `big` | one 2^24-word array | 65 MB |
| `same` | small, freed, small again | 65 MB (same class: reused) |
| `both` | small, freed, then big | **129 MB** |
| `rev` | big, freed, then small | **129 MB** |

## Where it comes from (generated C)

`heap_free(e, cls, loc)` pushes the block on the per-lane free list of its class `cls` (blocks are 2^cls
words); a full list is handed to the shared bank of the same class. `heap_alloc_miss` takes a block of the
requested class from the lane's cold list or `bank_pop(H, cls)`, and otherwise bumps `H_BUMP`
(`corpus_grow`). Nothing merges two free class-c buddies into a class-(c+1) block, splits a larger free block,
or `madvise`/unmaps freed pages.

## Why it matters

Any pipeline that builds many small pieces and then one big result (a parallel parser whose lanes each build
a part of every column, then a concatenation) pays parts + result, even though the parts are dead before the
result is complete. In bend-frame (a dataframe library), reading an 85 MB CSV peaks at ~300 MB for ~110 MB of
final columns, mostly for this reason, and every later allocation of a new size class grows the heap again.
Coalescing buddies on free (or splitting a larger free block on a miss), or returning long-idle pages with
`madvise(MADV_FREE)`, would let the peak follow the live set.

## Repro (Base only)

```bend
# Freed heap memory is reusable only by blocks of the same size class (Base only).
#   bend allocclass.bend -o allocclass
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./allocclass small   # 4096 arrays of 2^12 U32 alive at once (64 MB), then freed
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./allocclass big     # one array of 2^24 U32 (64 MB)
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./allocclass both    # small, freed, then big: peak ~128 MB, not ~64 MB
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./allocclass same    # small, freed, then small again: peak ~64 MB (same class reused)
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./allocclass rev     # big, freed, then small: peak ~128 MB (a big free block is not split)
# Each phase prints a checksum, so nothing is dead code.
import Base

# sum of a[0..n), a consumed
def sum.go(n: Nat, +i: U32, +s: U32, r: Array<U32> & U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      (a, x) = r
      s
    case 1n+p:
      (a, +x) = r
      +j = U32.inc(i)
      sum.go(p, j, U32.add(s, x), Array.get(U32, a, j))

def sum(+d: Nat, a: Array<U32>) -> U32:
  sum.go(U32.to_nat(U32.shln(1, d)), 0, 0, Array.get(U32, a, 0))

# k arrays of 2^d words, all alive at once
def many(+k: Nat, +d: Nat, acc: List<&1, Array<U32>>) -> List<&1, Array<U32>>:
  match k:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      many(p, d, Array.new(U32, d, U32.from_nat(p)) <> acc)

def sums(+d: Nat, xs: List<&1, Array<U32>>, +s: U32) -> U32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      s
    case a <> t:
      sums(d, t, U32.add(s, sum(d, a)))

def small() -> U32:
  sums(12n, many(4096n, 12n, Nil{}), 0)

def big() -> U32:
  sum(24n, Array.new(U32, 24n, 1))

def show(+x: U32) -> IO(Unit):
  IO.print(U32.show(x))

def run(+is_small: Bool, +is_big: Bool, +is_same: Bool, +is_rev: Bool) -> IO(Unit):
  match is_small is_big is_same is_rev:
    case True{} False{} False{} False{}:
      show(small())
    case False{} True{} False{} False{}:
      show(big())
    case False{} False{} True{} False{}:
      do IO<Unit>:
        show(small())
        show(small())
    case False{} False{} False{} True{}:
      do IO<Unit>:
        show(big())
        show(small())
    case _ _ _ _:
      do IO<Unit>:
        show(small())
        show(big())

def go(+m: String) -> IO(Unit):
  run(String.eq(m, "small"), String.eq(m, "big"), String.eq(m, "same"), String.eq(m, "rev"))

def arg(xs: List<&1, String>) -> String:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      "both"
    case h <> Nil{}:
      "both"
    case h <> a <> t:
      a

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    go(arg(args))
```

```bash
bend allocclass.bend -o allocclass
for m in small big same both rev; do /usr/bin/time -l ./allocclass $m 2>&1 | grep -E "^[0-9]+$|peak memory"; done
```

title: 16 bytes per character: String and the byte APIs are cons lists, no packed byte/string type
body:
## Summary

A `String` costs **16 bytes per character** on the native heap (one `SCon` cell per character), and so does
every byte API (`File.read_bytes`, `TCP.recv_bytes`, `IO.args_bytes`: `List<U32>`, one cell per byte). The
only compact element storage in Base is `Array<U32>` (4 bytes per slot). There is no packed byte or
string type. Bend 2.0.39, native build, macOS 26 arm64.

Measured with the repro below (2^20 freshly built strings, all alive at once; "peak memory footprint" from
`/usr/bin/time -l`):

| characters per string | peak | per character |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 17.2 MB | (the list itself) |
| 16 | 273.3 MB | 16.0 B |
| 32 | 529.4 MB | 16.0 B |

## Why it matters

Text-heavy data is 16x its UTF-8 size in memory (Arrow / Polars: ~1 byte per ASCII character plus a 4- or 8-byte
offset per string). In bend-frame, reading a 1M-row CSV of distinct ~15-character keys peaks at ~450 MB; the
keys alone are ~15M characters, ~240 MB as `String`s. Polars holds that column in ~15 MB (the whole
three-column frame in ~31 MB). A library can pack code points into
`Array<U32>` itself (4 B per character), but then loses every `String` function in Base. Would a packed
representation be possible, either for `String` or as a separate `Bytes` / `Array<U8>` type that the byte
APIs return?

## Repro (Base only)

```bend
# The heap cost of a String per character (Base only).
#   bend strmem.bend -o strmem
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./strmem 20 0     # 2^20 empty strings in a list (the list's own cost)
#   /usr/bin/time -l ./strmem 20 16    # 2^20 strings of 16 characters, all alive at once
# (peak(16) - peak(0)) / (2^20 * 16) is the cost of one character. Each string is built fresh
# (its first character depends on its index), so nothing is shared.
import Base

# a fresh string of k characters, the first one 'a' + (i mod 26)
def str.go(+k: Nat, +i: U32, acc: String) -> String:
  match k:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      str.go(p, i, SCon{Chr{U32.add(97, U32.mod(U32.add(i, U32.from_nat(p)), 26))}, acc})

def strs(+n: Nat, +k: Nat, acc: List<&1, String>) -> List<&1, String>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      strs(p, k, str.go(k, U32.from_nat(p), SNil{}) <> acc)

# every character counted once all strings exist (the list is consumed)
def total(xs: List<&1, String>, +s: Nat) -> Nat:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      s
    case x <> t:
      total(t, Nat.add(s, String.length(x)))

def nat(m: Maybe<&2, Nat>, +d: Nat) -> Nat:
  match m:
    case None{}:
      d
    case Some{v}:
      v

def args2(xs: List<&1, String>) -> Nat & Nat:
  match xs:
    case _ <> d <> k <> t:
      (nat(Nat.read(d), 20n), nat(Nat.read(k), 16n))
    case _:
      (20n, 16n)

def run(r: Nat & Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  (+d, +k) = r
  IO.print(Nat.show(total(strs(U32.to_nat(U32.shln(1, d)), k, Nil{}), 0n)))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    run(args2(args))
```

```bash
bend strmem.bend -o strmem
for k in 0 16 32; do /usr/bin/time -l ./strmem 20 $k 2>&1 | grep -E "^[0-9]+$|peak memory"; done
```

title: Question: using LAWS.bend with a TypeScript / React Native app
body:
### What Bend should do

Support using LAWS.bend from a TypeScript / React Native app: prove laws in Bend, then call the proven code from TypeScript through the JavaScript target, running under Hermes (no Node APIs). Concretely:

a documented way to import a module from Bend’s JS target into TypeScript, with generated .d.ts types;
guidance on whether laws can state ordering rules over a sequence of events (state machines), not only pure functions.

Sketch of what we’d write (syntax approximate):

```python
# LAWS.bend
law no_registration_after_logout:
  for events: List<Push.Event>                 # any order of login, logout, request results
  s = Push.replay(Push.start(), events)
  {Push.is_settled(s) == True{} -> Push.registered_user(s) == Push.session_user(s) : Bool}
```

```typescript
// React Native (TypeScript)
import { replay, start } from './generated/push.bend.js'
const next = replay(state, [event])
```

### Why

We build a large React Native app in TypeScript. Our hardest bugs are ordering bugs (“a request in flight at logout must not land after cleanup”). Today we check them with TLA+/TLC plus fast-check property tests. TLC checks a hand-written model, so the model can drift from the real code. Proving laws on the same Bend code that the app then runs would close that gap. The README says Bend works best on the backend, so we’d like to know whether this frontend/mobile path is feasible, or on the roadmap

title: `bend PROOF.bend` fails on four unedited demos: their main.bend holds `@unsafe` defs that no law uses
body:
### What you did

`bend PROOF.bend` in every demo that has one, on `main` at faeb02ea, with no edits.

### What happened

Four of the fifteen print SOME PROOFS FAIL and exit 1. The other eleven print ALL PROOFS CHECK.

```text
$ bend PROOF.bend        # demos/io_http_server
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error: 2 defs rely on unsafe or foreign code:
defs that depend on @unsafe: main.http_serve, main.main
Hint: no law or proof uses these defs. Move them to a file this proof does not import, and the proofs will check: main.http_serve, main.main
```

| demo | defs the error names |
|---|---|
| `io_http_server` | 2: `http_serve`, `main` |
| `io_tcp_echos` | 4: `echo_conn`, `serve_next`, `serve`, `main` |
| `app_slash_boss_3d` | 4: `Play.loop`, `Play.run`, `Main.mode`, `main` |
| `pure_hvm5_mini` | 35, from `term` to `app` |

### Why it happens

Each of these `main.bend` files holds both what the laws are about (`http_response`, `echo_step`, ...) and `@unsafe` defs, such as the io demos' accept loops. `LAWS.bend` imports `main.bend`, so those defs are among `PROOF.bend`'s imports, and since 4eb344b6 any def there that relies on `@unsafe` fails the run, whether a law uses it or not. With the checker from just before 4eb344b6, `bend PROOF.bend` in `io_http_server` printed `All terms check.` and exited 0, and only `bend main.bend --check-only` listed the loop (`All terms check, but 2 defs rely on unsafe or foreign code:`). #1472 listed these four demos, and #1558 kept the failure and added the hint, which names exactly these defs.

The README asks for `bend PROOF.bend` after every edit, and on these four demos it can't print ALL PROOFS CHECK. A broken proof starts with the same line: in `io_tcp_echos`, making `echo_step` drop the data (`case Done{m}: None{}`) prints SOME PROOFS FAIL with `expected : None{}` and `observed : Some{SCon{c, t}}` at `Laws.echoes_data`.

### Two ways out for the io demos

I tried both on copies of `io_http_server` and `io_tcp_echos` at faeb02ea:

| | fuel | split |
|---|---|---|
| change | the loops take a `Nat` fuel, and `main` passes `4294967295n`, as `App.run` does | `http_response` and `echo_step` move to their own files, which `LAWS.bend`, `PROOF.bend` and `main.bend` import |
| files | `main.bend` only (+34/-23 over both demos) | 4 per demo, 1 of them new (+26/-20 over both) |
| `bend PROOF.bend`, `--verdict` | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |
| `bend main.bend --check-only` | ALL PROOFS CHECK | still the `@unsafe` error |
| the running server | stops after 4294967295 connections | runs until killed, as now |
| follows | GUIDE.md: "A loop bounded by the outside world, like a server's, counts down a `Nat` fuel argument instead" | #1558's hint, and the layout of `tests/proof/app` |

#1990 takes the fuel way for the two io demos, and #2039 for `app_slash_boss_3d`, whose only `@unsafe` def is its frame loop. `pure_hvm5_mini` is bigger (its 35 defs sit between lines 790 and 1915 of its `main.bend`), so I'll look at it on its own.

### bend version

bend 2.0.39 (`main` at faeb02ea)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

title: fix(demos): the io server loops count down a fuel, so their proofs check
body:
Part of #1989.

`io_http_server` and `io_tcp_echos` print SOME PROOFS FAIL unedited, because their `@unsafe` loops sit in the `main.bend` that their laws import. This drops `@unsafe` instead of moving the loops: each loop takes a `Nat` fuel and counts it down, as GUIDE.md suggests for a server's loop and as `App.run` does with `4294967295n`.

- `io_http_server`: `http_serve` takes the fuel and closes the listener at zero. `main` passes `4294967295n`.
- `io_tcp_echos`: `serve` does the same. `echo_conn`, the recv loop of each connection, takes a fuel too and closes its socket at zero. `serve_next` starts each one with `4294967295n`.
- The header comments say the loops count down a fuel, where they said `@unsafe: it runs until killed`. `LAWS.bend` and `PROOF.bend` don't change.

For someone running them, one thing changes: a server stops after 4294967295 connections, and a connection closes after 4294967295 recvs.

The issue compares this with the split from #1558's hint, which keeps the loops running until killed. If you'd rather have the split, I have it ready.

### What I checked

On faeb02ea, macOS arm64:

- In both demos, `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) print ALL PROOFS CHECK, and so do `bend main.bend --check-only` and `bend main.bend --verdict`.
- `bend main.bend -o` builds a binary and an `.mjs` for both.
- I ran both binaries. Three `curl` requests to 8080 each got the hello page with its headers, and three `nc` connections to 7777 each got their line back.
- With the fuel at `2n`, the HTTP server answered two requests, refused the third, and exited 0.

`repo-gate` passes in CI. Not run: the cluster gates, Linux.

title: C backend: Base's `Array.to_list` copies both halves at every level, ~190 instructions a cell (a loop of `Array.get` takes ~35)
body:
### What I see

On the C backend, `Array.to_list` of an `Array<F32>` costs about 190-208 user-mode instructions and 11-15 ns per cell on one thread, 13-15x a C loop that builds the same list. A plain Bend loop of `Array.get` that reads from the last index down and conses each number builds the same list for about 35 instructions and 2.6-4 ns a cell.

The repro (`array_to_list_walk.bend`, below) fills 64 fresh arrays of 2^20 F32, converts each one and sums the list. MODE 0n uses `Array.to_list`, MODE 1n the `Array.get` loop. Bend 2.0.39, clang 23.1.3, Core Ultra 7 155H, one thread pinned with `taskset -c 3`, `+RTS --threads 1 -RTS`, 5 alternated runs (instructions from `perf stat -e instructions:u`, wall time from `/usr/bin/time`):

| | instructions | per cell (fill + convert + sum) | time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `Array.to_list` | 12,826-12,834 M | 191 | 0.86-0.87 s |
| loop of `Array.get`, last index down | 2,318-2,326 M | 34.6 | 0.23 s |

Both print the same sum (23.789732). Per cell, `Array.to_list` alone is about 157 instructions and 9.6 ns more than the loop.

Across sizes (my bench, the conversion of a fresh `Array.new` of 2^d F32 plus the sum of its list, per cell, against a C loop that writes the same list into an arena and sums it):

| cells | `Array.to_list` | C |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2^12 | 192 instr, 11.3 ns | 14 instr, 1.4 ns |
| 2^16 | 195 instr, 11.7 ns | 14 instr, 1.4 ns |
| 2^20 | 199 instr, 13.1 ns | 14 instr, 1.8 ns |
| 2^24 | 208 instr, 15.2 ns | 14 instr, 5.5-6.2 ns |

### Why, as far as I can tell

`Array.to_list.go` matches the array: `ANode{xs, ys}` → `to_list.go(xs, to_list.go(ys, acc))`. In the C lane matching `ANode` is `blk_half` twice, and each call allocates a block for its half and copies the cells into it (the high call frees the source). So every level of the tree allocates and copies, down to one block per leaf: 2n - 1 allocations and frees and about n log2 n copied cells for an n-cell array. The copies are cheap per cell (that is why the count grows only from 192 to 208 between 2^12 and 2^24); the block per node is most of the cost.

The JS lane had the same shape and got a flat walk in #1661: reading the flat array backward and prepending list nodes. The same thing would work in C: `Array.to_list` on a flat block is n reads and n conses with no new blocks. A Bend-level version of it is the MODE 1n loop above, which is what I use in my own code now; it needs the array's size, which Base gets from `Array.size`.

### Repro

```python
# MODE 0n: Array.to_list; MODE 1n: the same list read by index, from the last cell down, so it needs no reverse.
# Each run fills 64 fresh arrays of 2^20 F32 (Array.new), converts each one and sums the list.
import Base

def lsum(xs: List<F32>, acc: F32) -> F32:
  match xs:
    case Nil{}:
      acc
    case Con{+h, t}:
      lsum(t, (acc + h : F32))

# n + 1 cells ending at index i, read from i down onto acc
def by_get(n: Nat, +i: U32, acc: List<F32>, r: Array<F32> & F32) -> List<F32>:
  match n r:
    case 0n Tuple{a, +v}:
      v <> acc
    case 1n+p Tuple{a, +v}:
      by_get(p, (i - 1 : U32), v <> acc, Array.get(F32, a, (i - 1 : U32)))

def conv(m: Nat, a: Array<F32>) -> List<F32>:
  match m:
    case 0n:
      Array.to_list(~F32, a)
    case 1n+q:
      by_get(1048575n, 1048575, Nil{}, Array.get(F32, a, 1048575))

def go(k: Nat, +acc: F32) -> F32:
  match k:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      go(p, (lsum(conv(MODE, Array.new(F32, 20n, acc)), 0.0) * 0.000001 : F32))

def main() -> F32:
  go(64n, 1.0)
```

```sh
sed 's/MODE/0n/' array_to_list_walk.bend > m0.bend && bend m0.bend -o m0
sed 's/MODE/1n/' array_to_list_walk.bend > m1.bend && bend m1.bend -o m1
perf stat -e instructions:u taskset -c 3 ./m0 +RTS --threads 1 -RTS
perf stat -e instructions:u taskset -c 3 ./m1 +RTS --threads 1 -RTS
```

I haven't checked `Array<T>` of boxed values or the GPU lane. If a flat walk in C is welcome, I can try it as a PR with the same measurements.

title: CUDA: about 0.6 ms of every `!` goes to page faults on the pages the host wrote since the last bang
body:
I run a small Llama (SmolLM2 135M and 360M) with its weight products under `!`, about 120 bangs a token. Each bang costs about 1 ms on the device even when the product is small, and I wanted to know where that millisecond goes before trying to batch more work per bang.

With `nsys` (CUDA trace plus unified-memory faults), weights already resident, medians over the second half of the run:

| | 135M | 360M |
|---|---|---|
| `cuLaunchKernel`, each (5 a bang) | 3.9 µs | — |
| kernel 0 (pass 0, 1 block) | 645 µs | 657 µs |
| of which servicing GPU page faults | 588 µs | — |
| kernel 1 (pass 0, 128 blocks: the product) | 282 µs | 462 µs |
| first launch to last kernel's end | 1,042 µs | 1,280 µs |
| host time between two bangs | 572 µs | 668 µs |

So launches (about 20 µs a bang) and `cuCtxSynchronize` are not the cost. The fixed part is kernel 0, the one-block pass that starts each bang: about 650 µs on both models and every product size, 92% of it under page-fault handling. That is about 88 faults a bang on about 11 distinct 4 KB pages: the pages the host wrote since the previous bang (the input vector and the heap blocks the host allocator reused). Between bangs the host faults back about 14 pages too.

As far as I can read `gpu_map` in `comp.ts`, the corpus is one `cuMemAllocManaged` region with the device as preferred location and no prefetch, so every host write before a bang migrates on demand, one fault at a time, inside the first kernel.

My question: would the runtime take a prefetch of the pages the host touched (`cuMemPrefetchAsync` on the dirty ranges, or on the request's root region) before launching a bang, or keeping a bang's inputs in device memory? I don't know whether the runtime tracks which pages the host wrote, so I may be missing why it is done this way. On my side nothing in Bend code reaches it: the products that read one vector are already stacked four to a bang, and the rest depend on each other.

I can share the `nsys` reports and the program if useful.

title: perf(js): avoid backtracking in GPU size validation
body:
The emitted JS runtime takes quadratic time to reject a long `+RTS --gpu` value without a valid size suffix. Make the fractional digit run conditional on its decimal point, preserving accepted spellings such as `.5GB` and `5.GB`, match captures, and the existing diagnostic. Factor the unit conversion on the same validation line; the compiler token count stays unchanged.

On macOS, rejecting a 60,000-digit argument without a unit takes about 1.5 seconds on Bun and Node before this change, versus 0.01–0.05 seconds afterward, including process startup.

Validation:
- The new regression launches a freshly emitted program and checks rejection, output and deadline. It fails on unchanged code and passes through source CLI, emitted Bun/Node, a freshly compiled CLI and aggregate checkup.
- Ordinary size boundaries, accepted spellings and argument retention agree before and after; independent Astra review found no actionable issues.
- Repository gate: 54/54. `comp.ts`: 65,998/66,000 tokens before and after.
- TypeScript reports the same seven baseline diagnostics. Full cluster and ping gates were not run.

title: fix(io): retry interrupted JavaScript file writes
body:
JavaScript file writes currently return `Fail` when `fs.writeSync` raises `EINTR`, even after writing part of the data. Retry the interrupted call at the current buffer position, matching the native backend and preserving positioned-write offsets.

Extend the existing interruption regression to inject errors in the JS lane before and after a short write, and cover `File.write_at` alongside text and byte writes.

Validation: regression passed with checkout-generated JavaScript under Bun and Node and with native C; related binary and positioned-write tests passed under Bun and native C. `bend demos/io_hello_world/PROOF.bend` passed, though it does not prove foreign effects. Mini-cluster/macOS gates and actual signal-induced host interruptions were not tested.

title: fix(js): allow timer waits without Bun FFI
body:
A generated program containing `IO.sleep(1)` fails under Node with `Cannot find module bun:ffi`: the scheduler loads libc even when it is only waiting for a timer. Use `Atomics.wait` for waits with no file descriptors; socket waits continue to use `select`, and runnable work keeps its nonblocking poll. This also enables timer-backed channel deadlines and `IO.within` under Node.

The regression makes the FFI table inaccessible and checks forked sleep ordering and `IO.within` races. Nearby runtime comments are shortened to stay within the existing compiler token cap.

Validation:
- New regression fails before the fix and passes under Bun and Node afterward.
- `sleep_timer`, `sleep_order`, `within`, `within_busy`, and `chan_try` pass under Bun and Node.
- `spawn_sleep`, `select_eintr`, `tcp_try`, `udp_try`, `tcp_backlog_timer`, and `udp_backlog_timer` pass under Bun.
- Repository gate: 54/54. Hello-world proof project passes (does not prove runtime effects).
- Independent Terra medium review: no findings.

`chan_try_wake_timers` produces its expected deliberate deadlock and exit code 1 with both the old and new wait implementations. Mini-cluster and macOS gates were not run.

title: [complexity, checker] O(n^2) parameter substitutions — Every constructor value repeats the same substitutions
body:
Consider these programs:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type N<-A: Data> is Data:
  Z{}
  S{p: N<Unit>}

def test() -> N<Unit>:
  S{Z{}}
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type N<-A: Data, -B: Data> is Data:
  Z{}
  S{p: N<Unit, Unit>}

def test() -> N<Unit, Unit>:
  S{S{Z{}}}
```

In the second program, the outer `S`, inner `S` and `Z` are all checked against
`N<Unit, Unit>`. Yet Bend separately substitutes `A := Unit` and `B := Unit` for each
of those three values: six parameter substitutions in total.

With `k` datatype parameters and `d` nested `S` values, there are `d+1` values
including `Z`, giving `k(d+1)` substitutions. When `k=d=n`, the amount of syntax
grows linearly, but these substitutions grow as `n(n+1)`: O(n²). The datatype `N`
still has only two constructor declarations, `S` and `Z`.

**Cause.** Constructor checking calls `tele_fill` for every value. It starts from
the constructor declaration and substitutes the datatype arguments again, even
though those arguments are unchanged throughout this chain.

Bend also rebuilds each constructor's result type, `N<Unit, ...>`. Finding its
parameter values requires walking a linked list: O(n²) list visits per value,
or O(n³) across this family. Thus the quadratic substitution count understates
the full checking cost.

**Repeating this work for every value may not be necessary.** The field type and
datatype arguments are unchanged throughout the chain. Preparing the field type
once and reusing the already-known result type could give O(k+d) work here,
rather than repeating the substitutions and list searches at each value.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either program as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [parameter substitution][source1], [constructor checking][source2].

title: a match binder that shadows a parameter is reported with the name printed twice and no scope
body:
## What

A `match` arm whose pattern binder has the same name as a parameter is reported with that name printed twice in the
context, no scope on either, and no line for the parameter. The reader has to guess which of the two the error is
about, and the first place anyone looks — the parameter — is the one that is fine.

Bend 2.0.38, `bend file.bend`. The message is unchanged in `bend2/bend.ts` on `devel`: `ctx` prints a binder as
`name : type` with nothing else.

## Repro

```bend
import Base

type Box is Data:
  Box{rate: Nat}

def f(+rate: U32, b: Box) -> U32:
  match b:
    case Box{rate}:
      rate
```

```
$ bend shadow.bend
SOME PROOFS FAIL
Error:
- expected : U32
- observed : Nat
Context:
- rate : U32
- rate : Nat
Location: f
 8 |     case Box{rate}:
 9>|       rate
   |       ^^^^
```

## Why it is worth a fix

- The two `rate`s are different values, and nothing says which is the parameter and which the arm's binder. Here the
  types happen to differ; when both are the same type the context is literally two identical lines.
- The caret is at the use, and the parameter has no line at all, so the message points at the arm while the mistake is
  usually "I meant the parameter".
- This cost three wrong edits while writing a `Conv2d` (the padding `p` shadowed by a param binder `p`, where the
  message read `expected Nat, observed Lin` and the context was two `p`s).

Two other shapes of the same family exist and are separate: a bare constructor name as a pattern is a catch-all binder
when the datatype comes from another file (#1328), and a missing match case drops the internal term (#1632 item 3).

## Proposed

At the binder, a note that names the shadowing:

```
 8 |     case Box{rate}:
   |              ^^^^ Note: this match binds `rate` again, hiding the `U32` parameter of `f`
```

and scoped context lines:

```
- rate : U32 (parameter of f)
- rate : Nat (binder of this arm)
```

With both types equal, the scopes are what carries the message; the note is what makes it discoverable. This is item 10
of #1632; it is filed here on its own because it is a wrong-scope message rather than a wanted-feature proposal, and
because a comment on a proposals list is not a place a fix gets scheduled from.

title: [complexity, checker] O(n log n) — Unused parameters still copy paths through variable maps
body:
Consider these programs, which leave every parameter unused:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

def example(x1: Unit, x2: Unit) -> Unit:
  U{}
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

def example(x1: Unit, x2: Unit, x3: Unit) -> Unit:
  U{}
```

Let `n` be the number of parameters: 2 and 3 above. Opening and closing them
copies O(n log n) nodes in the maps of variables and use counts, within the
supported index range.

**Cause.** Each variable has a number. `pmap_set` follows it through a binary tree
and copies the path, preserving the old tree. `ctx_bind` does this to add parameters;
`uses_close` does it again to record zero uses when leaving an unused parameter.

Variable number `i` has `floor(log2(i+1)) + 1` nodes on its path: numbers 0, 1 and 2
need 1, 2 and 2 nodes. For n consecutive parameters, the total grows as n log n.
This follows from repeatedly halving the index, rather than a timing fit. Checking
types and bodies adds further updates.

**Copying these paths may not be necessary for every binding.** The active variable
context could update one indexed entry and restore it when leaving a scope.
Bindings needed for later error messages could stay in a shared list. Usage
counts could keep their existing maps, but closing an already absent variable need not
insert a zero. For these unused parameters, opening and closing scopes could then
take O(n) updates instead of copying O(n log n) tree nodes.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either program as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [path copying][source1], [variable binding][source2], [closing uses][source3],
[lambda scopes][source4].

title: [complexity, parser] O(n * 2^n) — Nested annotation types are read twice
body:
Consider these programs:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

def example() -> Type:
  {_ => Unit : Unit -> Type}(U{})
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

def example() -> Type:
  {_ => Unit : {_ => Unit : Unit -> Type}(U{}) -> Type}(U{})
```

Both return the type `Unit`. In the second, the inner call computes the outer
function's argument type. The braces are actual type annotations.

Let `n` be the nesting depth of the annotations: 1 and 2 above. The innermost
`Unit -> Type` is read `2^n` times, although each level adds a fixed amount of source.
Repeated column searches also traverse longer prefixes, giving O(n * 2^n)
character visits in those searches for these one-line bodies.

**Cause.** While reading the lambda body, `parse_body` reads the following
`: ...` as a possible type for a local binding. Finding `}` rather than `=`,
it goes back. The enclosing brace annotation then reads that same type again.
Each level contains the inner type once but parses it twice.

**Reading the same type twice may not be necessary.** A local binding needs an
`=` after its type, before the surrounding group closes. If there is no such
`=` outside nested brackets, strings and comments, the parser need not read the
type to rule out a local binding. One source scan could identify these positions.
The enclosing annotation would then read the type once, in its correct scope.
This would remove the doubling here, but not the separate column searches.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either program as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [body reader][source1], [brace annotation][source2], [lambda body][source3].

title: [complexity, parser] O(n^2) — Nested lambdas repeat line and whitespace searches
body:
Consider these functions:

```bend
def one(A: Type) -> A -> A:
  (x => x )
```

```bend
def two(A: Type) -> A -> A -> A:
  (x => y => y  )
```

Let `n` count both the lambdas and the spaces immediately before `)`: one of each
in the first function, two of each in the second. The source grows linearly with
`n`, but parsing repeats two searches whose work grows as O(n²).

**Cause.** Each lambda body asks for its column. `parse_col` searches back to the
previous newline each time. The lambdas start farther and farther along the same
line, so the lengths searched add up to O(n²).

As parsing returns through the lambdas, `parse_nl` repeatedly checks whether the
whitespace before the same closing `)` contains a newline. Each check scans the
same `n` spaces. O(n) checks of O(n) spaces give another O(n²) cost.

The spaces contribute independently: with `l` lambdas and `s` spaces, those
repeated checks read O(l*s) space characters. More spaces increase the work even
when the function itself stays the same.

**These repeated searches may not be necessary.** Remembering the current line
start would let column queries use subtraction. Remembering the newline answer
while the source position stays unchanged would let the whitespace be scanned
once. Together, these could reduce the two scans to O(n) work for this family.
Moving backwards must restore or invalidate the remembered information.
Leaving either scan unchanged leaves quadratic work in this same example.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either snippet as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [lambda body reader][source1], [column helper][source2],
[whitespace scan][source3].

title: Make List.map work with reusable lists
body:
`List.map` was fixed to affine lists, so a `List<&2, A>` was refused. It now takes a leading `~a` and `~b`, one quantity per list, with `A` at `Kind(a)` and `B` at `Kind(b)`:

```bend
def List.map(
  ~a: Quant, ~b: Quant, ~A: Kind(a), ~B: Kind(b), ~f: A -> B, xs: List<a, A>
) -> List<b, B>:
```

This breaks every existing call: `List.map(~A, ~B, ~f, xs)` becomes `List.map(~&1, ~&1, ~A, ~B, ~f, xs)`. Reusable lists use `~&2`. The list can also change quantity, for example an affine list of tickets to a `List<&2, U32>`, or a reusable list to an affine element type.

I updated the six existing template fixtures and the formatter test's call, and noted the breaking change in the changelog. No checker, compiler, kernel or cap changes.

## Checked

- Linux, on the earlier one-quantity version: Bun, standalone Node JS and native CPU kept reusable word and string inputs intact and let the mapped lists be reused. Affine tickets and empty lists worked too. The native `tmpl` consumer printed `50005000`.
- macOS, on this version, under Bun: `tests/base/list_map_quantities.bend` and the six `tests/comptime` fixtures print their expected output, and `tools/bend-lint/rules/format.test.ts` passes 37/37.
- `--verdict` with the real kernel on the new fixture, on this version: `ALL PROOFS CHECK`.
- An affine or function output type is refused at `~&2` with `expected: Data`. This isn't pinned by a test yet.
- `gates/_run.ts` merged with `main` `db64cf76`: `repo` 54/54, `test` 1820/1820, `perf` 124/124.
- `gates/_run.ts` on this branch: `repo` 54/54, `test` 1816/1816. Next to `test`, `perf` missed one cell in 3 of 13 runs, against none in 8 on the base commit, and passed 124/124 on 2 solo runs. The one miss logged was `merkle` compiler time at 1.15x, whose median was no slower here (0.655 s vs 0.677 s on the base commit).

## Not run

`gates/safe.ts`, including its `hub` mode, so the effect on published packages is unknown. Also GPU, and `gates/ping.ts`, which was skipped for a missing site repo.

Fixes #1994.

title: [complexity, parser] O(n^2) — Each field name is compared with every earlier name
body:
Consider these types:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type Fields is Type:
  Make{field1: Unit}
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type Fields is Type:
  Make{field1: Unit, field2: Unit}
```

Let `n` be the number of fields in the constructor: 1 and 2 above. Main makes
`n(n-1)/2` name comparisons: O(n²). Counted runs found 0 for 1 field, 1 for 2 fields,
and 523,776 for 1024 fields. This counts name comparisons, not bytes compared inside
strings; larger number suffixes also make names longer. The count comes from the
search itself, not a curve fitted to loading times.

**Cause.** The field reader uses `tele.some` to reject names already used in the
constructor. Distinct names force it to compare each new name with all earlier
names: 0, 1, 2, and so on. Every field has the same ordinary datatype, `Unit`. The
count isolates duplicate field-name comparisons; resolving those type names adds separate parsing work.

**This repeated search through earlier names may not be necessary.** For example, a
set could record the names seen in the constructor. With constant expected lookup
and insertion cost, these checks would take expected O(n) work. Reading and hashing
the names would still cost work.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either snippet as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [field reader][source1].
