title: Conversion evaluates a def before comparing its arguments
body:
```bend
import Base

def fib(n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      0n
    case 1n+ +m:
      match m:
        case 0n:
          1n
        case 1n+ +p:
          Nat.add(fib(m), fib(p))

def k() -> Nat:
  22n

# checks instantly
def same(e: {fib(22n) == 0n : Nat}) -> {fib(22n) == 0n : Nat}:
  e

# "the machine stack overflowed": fib(22) gets evaluated
def args(e: {fib(k) == 0n : Nat}) -> {fib(22n) == 0n : Nat}:
  e
```

`args` should check as fast as `same`: unfolding `k` once makes the two types identical. Instead, when the rigid pass of `term_compare` fails, `compare_go` reduces both sides with `term_wnf` before comparing them. So `fib(k)` against `fib(22n)` computes `fib(22)` before ever comparing `k` with `22n`. With smaller `n` it passes, but the check time grows with the cost of `fib(n)`.

**Possible fix.** When both sides call the same def, compare the arguments first, and evaluate the calls only if the arguments differ (merging share cells as `compare_go` already does). Lean and Coq call this lazy delta reduction. Those checkers also cache conversion results, which Bend is still missing.

**Real-world example.** [json/PROOF.bend](https://github.com/LeeeeT/json-spec/blob/bfc011d/json/PROOF.bend) takes about 5 minutes to check on Bend 2.0.39, and about 10 seconds with arguments compared first. There, `f` is an ABNF matcher: `ABNF.check(BK, r, s)` against `ABNF.check(ABNF.full(grammar), r, s)`, where `BK` is a def for `ABNF.full(grammar)`. Each such comparison re-runs the matcher, and 400 of them account for 96% of the check time.

title: fix(cli): reject colliding output requests before writing
body:
## Problem and fix

Multiple `-o` requests can silently overwrite each other while the build succeeds. On a real Metal build, `-o app.gpu -o app` replaced the requested executable with a GPU archive; executing it failed with `Exec format error`.

This is a scoped follow-up to EpsilonPhoenix's #1975, implementing only [the maintainer's two requested checks](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1975#issuecomment-6548997578). Resolve each output through `path.resolve` and its real parent directory, then reject duplicate paths and a binary paired with its possible `.gpu` output. Check the whole list before emission and identify both requests in the error.

## Blast radius

Two files: `bend2/main.ts` adds the guard to existing CLI preflight (+105 ttok); `tests/io/output_input_links.js` extends the existing regression. No compiler or build-path changes.

Compatibility: previously accepted conflicting requests now exit 1 before writing. A binary `X` paired with `X.gpu` is rejected even for CPU-only programs, as requested.

## Regression evidence

Four added cases cover normalized duplicates, a missing output through a symlinked parent, and both binary/sidecar argument orders. Each case, tested alone, prints `9` on `01fca26` instead of the expected `0`; with the fix, each prints `0`. They check unchanged inputs and existing outputs, absence of an earlier requested output, and both diagnostic paths. The passing fixture makes no native compiler calls, verified with a compiler trap and empty `PATH`.

The Metal overwrite was observed on `60a87ef`; its CLI and compiler match `01fca26`. The final guard rejects both orders for that same GPU-using program without creating outputs.

## Checks

- Repository gate: **54/54**.
- Actual regression through the CLI and emitted JavaScript under Bun: both print `0`. The emitted fixture passes the gate's 5-second alarm locally in 2.46 seconds.
- Separate CLI checks: eight collision cases reject without writes or compiler calls; distinct JS+C and JS+MJS outputs succeed and the JavaScript prints `42`.
- `git diff --check` passes.

## Validation limits

Tested on macOS arm64 with Bun 1.3.11. Linux, Windows and CUDA were not run. The full test gate cannot start its cluster work because the `cluster` hostname does not resolve.

TypeScript 7.0.2 reports the same seven errors on the baseline and candidate, with identical diagnostics in the protected checker and documentation tools; none is in `main.ts`.

This intentionally does not detect output-to-output leaf symlink, hard-link or case-only aliases, or filesystem changes after preflight. HTML bundling follows its existing separate path.

title: [complexity, parser] O(n^2) — Outer groups revisit settled operator names
body:
Consider these terms:

```bend
import Base

def example() -> Bool:
  (True{} && True{} : Bool)
```

```bend
import Base

def example() -> Bool:
  ((True{} && True{} : Bool) && True{} : Bool)
```

`&&` already names `Bool.and`; each `: Bool` suffix nevertheless triggers a walk
of the enclosed expression. Let `n` be the number of nested groups ending in
`: Bool`: 1 and 2 above. Each adds one `&&`.

Excluding loading `Base`, main makes `n(n+2)` calls to the operator-name
walk: O(n²). Counted runs found 3 at `n = 1`, 8 at `n = 2`, and 66,048 at `n = 256`.
Loading also includes column searches and other work, so elapsed time alone would
not isolate this cause.

**Cause.** Each group asks the operator-name walk to apply its namespace. The walk
follows the arguments of `Bool.and`, `Bool.or`, and `String.append` even when those
names are already fixed. Each outer group therefore revisits the whole inner chain
of `&&` calls. The successive walks visit 3, 5, 7, and so on.

**This repeated walk through settled names may not be necessary.** Once a namespace
walk has finished a whole subtree, adding an outer group does not undo that work.
Reusing this fact could give O(n) operator-name work here, as each new call and
operand is visited once. A fixed name alone is not enough: its arguments can
still contain unresolved operators.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either snippet as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [group reader][source1], [operator-name walk][source2].

[source2]: https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/7a7e6505aeff2101a139a8419e16098ed2a89110/bend2/bend.ts#L2155-L2175

title: perf(c): build lists directly from flat arrays
body:
## Problem and fix

Native `Array.to_list` recursively splits flat storage and copies both halves before building the list. For checked instances of Base's `Array.to_list.go`, the C emitter now walks the original cells backward into the supplied suffix, transfers owned values or retains shared boxed fields, then releases the source block.

The rebased loop passes the full `Env` to `err_spun`, as required by #2087. This gives the poll access to the device lane's stop flag.

On the original PR head `f27fd28` versus `db64cf7`, six alternating one-thread runs per version on macOS M1 Pro with clang 23.1.4 `-O3` measured the 64 × 2²⁰ F32 fill, conversion and sum workload:

| Median | Original main | Original PR head |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CPU user time | 0.78 s | 0.27 s |
| Retired instructions | 9.82 billion | 2.02 billion |

Every run printed `23.789732`. The timings include allocation and summation.

## Blast radius

The diff adds 23 lines to `bend2/comp.ts` and two compiler fixtures. The lowering is limited to C host and device emission for recorded Base helper specializations. The source array stays live until the list is complete. For an owned singleton with two Nat fields, the original measurements showed an allocation order of allocate, allocate, free, briefly retaining two extra words. Ten million such conversions retired 5% more instructions, with median CPU time moving from 0.16 s to 0.14 s.

## Regression evidence

The fixtures cover order, packed and padded values, shared boxed ownership, affine closures, partial application, Unit, a supplied suffix, and conversion beneath a device fork. On the original head, removing the shared Shape-field retain caused all three heap-poison runs to fault. Heap traces for eight F32 cells recorded eight class-1 list allocations and no intermediate array halves, compared with 12 class-0 and 10 class-1 allocations on the original main.

On the rebase, restoring only the old `err_spun(e.mem, ...)` call reproduces the Metal shader compile error. With the full environment argument, the shader builds and the device fixture prints `2578033920`.

## Checks

- On `e86366f` rebased onto `f0cf0a7`, both new fixtures plus `map_set_array_kit` and `array_map_loop` pass source execution, emitted JS on Bun, and native CPU execution with `BEND_POISON`, ASan and UBSan. The device fixture also passes at four CPU threads and with Metal forced on.
- The hello-world control emits byte-identical C and JS on the rebased head and its base. `git diff --check` passes.
- On the original head `f27fd28`, the issue reporter independently ran the four cases on Linux with Bun, native C and heap poison, plus the device fixture on an RTX 4050 with CUDA 13.4. Their x86 workload median went from 0.894 s to 0.261 s, with retired instructions going from 12.83 billion to 2.25 billion. The `Array.get` control's instruction count was identical. The reporter also confirmed there will be no competing PR for #1991. [Contributor report](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2012#issuecomment-6591418014)

## Validation limits

The local repository gate reports **55/56**. The compiler is **66,337 tokens against the 66,000 cap**. That check remains a merge blocker. See the maintainer's guidance on keeping the feature scoped while the budget is addressed. [Compiler budget review](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/1820#issuecomment-6345933346)

Fresh execution was on macOS arm64 with Bun 1.3.11. Linux, CUDA, Windows, Node, the full cluster gates, workload timing, and allocation measurements were not rerun after rebasing. Concurrent alias mutation and dedicated leak stress remain unqualified. Current combinations with pending #1601, #2017, #2019 and #2135 have not been validated.

title: fix(check): pmap_set builds each new node once, and closing an unused binder writes nothing
body:
Refs #1999. This removes wasted allocation in the variable maps. It doesn't change the O(n log n) the issue describes, so the issue stays open.

- **`pmap_set`:** at an `Emp` it built a temporary `Bin(null, map, map)` and immediately copied it, so a new path of depth k allocated 2k nodes. It now reads `Emp` as an empty node without allocating. This hits every variable use, since each one builds a path from `uses_nil()`.
- **`uses_close`:** it reuses the `pmap_get` it already does, and returns `us` unchanged when the variable is absent, instead of writing a zero. An unused binder then leaves no node behind.

`Bin` allocations with `--check-only`:

| Program | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| `compute_1600` | 1,175 | 670 | -43% |
| `defs_12800` | 359,598 | 222,553 | -38% |
| `generics_3200` | 352,506 | 211,505 | -40% |
| `proofs_3200` | 1,756,832 | 1,039,507 | -41% |
| `trees_400` | 1,182 | 674 | -43% |
| 4,096 unused parameters (#1999's shape) | 147,498 | 90,140 | -39% |

Run time doesn't measurably change: the median of 9 alternating runs moved by -0.6% to +1.2% across the five benches, which is within noise. The case for this is less garbage and a shorter function, not speed.

- `bend2/bend.ts`: -10 ttok (45,396 → 45,386 / 48k).
- Not addressed: `ctx_bind` still copies its path, because the parent scope and every `Err` keep the old `Ctx`. `uses_close` still copies when the variable is present.
- No test output changes.

Gates on origin/main `db64cf76`: repo 54/54, test 1819/1819, perf 124/124. An earlier version of this PR, the same logic written with a ternary, got perf 123/124 once and 124/124 once; the missed bench wasn't identified. Ping fails 80/81 on the BendHub LICENSE check, the same as unchanged main on this machine.

title: perf(cuda): a bang prefetches ring row 0's get and put words (#1992)
body:
Refs #1992.

Before each bang, the CUDA host now prefetches the two pages holding ring row 0's get and put words to the device. The host writes both words right before the launch, and without the prefetch the kernel faulted on their pages: about 135-155 GPU faults a bang on one of them.

## Measured

@nuxyel measured it on an RTX 4050 Laptop (driver 615.78.08), on the #1992 program, with identical outputs and `failed=0` in every run. The full data is in the comments above. On SmolLM2 135M, CUDA 13.4, the median of 5 runs, in µs a bang:

| Prefetch | `cycle_us` |
|---|---:|
| none | 1,422 (1,408-1,433) |
| ring get/put (this PR) | 1,184 (1,182-1,185) |
| get/put + header + ring slot + tail block | 1,178 (1,174-1,181) |
| header alone | 1,452 (1,439-1,458) |

The get/put pair gives 238 of the 244 µs that all the prefetches together gave. The header prefetch costs time on its own, the slot and tail add about 6 µs on top, and widening to 64 KB changes nothing, so this PR keeps only the pair. In round one, all the prefetches together gave 21% on 360M too. `r` alone wasn't run on 360M.

## Checked here

- The emitted host C type-checks with `-DBEND_CUDA=1` against stub headers on both sides of `CUDA_VERSION >= 13000`, with the same diagnostics as main. The same two calls compiled against the real `cuda.h` on 12.9 and 13.4 in round one.
- On Metal, `gpu_near` is a no-op macro: `tests/comptime/offload.bend`, `tests/io/heap_large_reuse.bend` and `tests/reg/spin_array_hold.bend` print what they expect.

## Repo gate

`comp.ts` is at 66,106 ttok, 106 over its 66k cap (main is 65,974), so the gate is red until room is made.

title: perf(js): validate F32 input before rounding
body:
The JS F32 reader now validates the whole input before exact decimal rounding. Rejected text skips conversion, while accepted text uses the same grammar and rounder.

A decimal midpoint followed by 5,000 zeros and a space previously exceeded the existing five-second test limit on Bun and Node. The extended regression now returns `None` and retains the earlier long-integer rejection case.

The regression passes through source and freshly compiled CLIs, emitted Bun/Node, and native C. Seven neighboring float fixtures pass on source/Bun/Node/native C. The repository gate passes 54/54; TypeScript reports the same seven baseline errors. `comp.ts` uses three fewer tokens.

title: perf(io): size positioned reads from their offset
body:
`File.read_at` still uses the whole regular-file size for its initial JS buffer hint, even when its offset leaves only a small tail. Reading the final five bytes of a 1 GiB sparse file with a 1 GiB cap therefore allocates a 1 GiB buffer.

The reader now subtracts the known offset from the size hint while retaining the 64 KiB floor and existing growth loop. The same read starts with 64 KiB and returns the same bytes. Sequential and line reads retain their existing sizing rules.

The extended cap fixture tests repeated positioned tail reads. On local macOS, the unchanged source CLI, compiled CLI and emitted Bun/Node exceed its five-second alarm; the patch passes all four, and native C passes before and after. Neighboring file fixtures and offset/EOF/cursor checks pass. Repository gate: 54/54; strict TypeScript reports the same seven baseline diagnostics.

title: Effect C names its own definitions with HID, and a module that uses HID must (#1533)
body:
Fixes #1533 for packages that adopt `HID`; supersedes #1546.

## Problem

`-o` pastes every effect `.c` into one C file. A program that imports two versions of one hub package pastes the same C twice, so clang refuses the second definition (`redefinition of 'wall_raw_run'`), while `bend main.bend` runs fine. In the real `bend-kit-time` case it is also silently wrong: the helper sits behind `#ifndef TIME_EFFS`, so version 2 would quietly use version 1's helper.

## Fix

- `HID(name)` in an effect's C is a C id of the module that imports it (`c_ids`, same pass as `CID`/`FID`). The key is the module, not the file: `bend_tensors` shares a guard and a struct across five `.c` files of one module.
- An imported module whose C says `HID` (outside comments and strings, found in `effect_src`'s existing scan) is held to it. `compile_book` pastes its C twice, and the second copy is dead: `constructor`/`destructor` become `__unused__`, and `-Wtentative-definition-compat` is an error inside it. A name defined without `HID` therefore fails the author's own build, instead of the first program that meets two versions.
- Each copy push/pops the macros it defines, so include guards and macros need no `HID`.
- C without `HID`, Base, and the root module are emitted exactly as before.

Cost: in the two-version `bend-kit-time` build, the dead copy adds 136 bytes to the binary and no measurable build time. Runtime is unchanged.

## Commits

1. `refactor(comp)`: sheds 386 ttok from `comp.ts`. The C and JS emitted for every test are byte-identical to main's.
2. `fix(effects)`: the feature, `tests/io/effect_versions` (two versions with the same names, each keeping its own counter: 8 71 9 72 in the interpreter, JS and native), and a paragraph in `guide/EFFECTS.md`.
3. `refactor(effs)`: Base's own effect C (`bend2/effs/*.c`, 281 names) uses `HID`, so the reference packages copy shows the rule, and a package's names cannot clash with Base's. The three `tests/gfx` C files that reach into `window.c` internals say `HID` too. Base and the program's own file share namespace `""`, so `HID(BendWin)` there is Base's. Base's macros keep their names. With `HID` undone, the diff is token-identical to main, including the Linux X11/ALSA and CUDA paths.

`comp.ts` ends at 65,987 / 66k.

## Verified

- Gates on d0949580: repo 54/54, ping 81/81, perf 124/124 (one contention-only miss, clean on rerun), test 1822/1822, safe 0 false rejects.
- Copies of the two real `bend-kit-time` versions with `HID` adopted build and run natively together.
- Removing any single `HID` (helper, global, entry, constructor, tentative global) fails the build, even with a single version imported.
- Probes from three review rounds pass: macro names containing `push_`; `__constructor__`/destructors in the dead copy; `HID(` in a comment; external `HID_*` macros; a package's own `unused` macro.
- Base conversion: every emitted test C syntax-checks on macOS, on macOS with `-DBEND_METAL=1` (the 44 `!` programs), and on Debian clang 14 with X11/XI/ALSA headers. A throwaway compiler that forces the dead copy on Base reports no unwrapped Base definition on either OS, and covers all 281 names.

## Limits

- Published packages still clash until they adopt `HID` and republish.
- An `HID` module's constructors cannot take a priority.
- The tentative-global check needs clang 21+.
- The test gate cannot express an expected native build failure, so the enforcement was verified by hand.
- The dead copy does not apply to Base (namespace `""` is shared with the program's own file, which must stay free to skip `HID`), so a future bare name in `bend2/effs` is not caught by the build.
- Separate translation units were considered and dropped: the effects paste into the runtime and call the evaluator, so it would need a runtime header/body split.

The extended fixture tests singleton and pair boundaries, an odd trailing item, and stable equal-key ordering. title: perf(runtime): matching ANode views the block instead of copying it (draft)
body:
Refs #1991. **A draft to look at, not ready to merge:** `comp.ts` is 713 tokens over its cap, so `gates/repo.ts` fails, and no perf bench uses array splits yet. This doesn't fix #1991 either; see the numbers below.

Matching `ANode` copies both halves today. Views were removed in `64adb37db` because a block changed size class on every split and leaked (#804). This brings them back on the host and merges the pieces when they're freed, so nothing leaks. The device still copies.

## How it works

- **Views:** `blk_half` returns a view of the same block. Its aux has bit 5 set and the root block's span in bits 6-10.
- **Merging:** freeing a view flips its parent's midpoint bit in a global bitmap (`VIEW_BITS`). The second sibling to die climbs a level, and the last one frees the root. This is why large blocks must be aligned to their own size.
- **Alignment:** `heap_alloc_miss` takes only the gap it needs, with a CAS on the bump pointer. Only large host blocks use the CAS. Using it on every miss made GPU time much worse (`merkle` 3.16x).
- **Bounded retention:** a piece more than 16x smaller than its root is copied into its own block, except under 8 words, where the copy costs more than it saves.
- **Inlining:** `blk_half` is forced inline and its copy path moved out to `blk_part`. Otherwise clang stops inlining it and loses the constant `arr` and `hi`.

## Results

All local on an ARM Mac, one thread, best of 3. `main` is `017f83fd`, which differs from this branch's base only in `bend.ts`.

| Program | main | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| #1991 repro, `Array.to_list` | 0.52 s, 10.14 B instr, 29.7 MB | 0.35 s, 9.49 B instr, 21.8 MB |
| #1991 repro, `Array.get` loop | 0.12 s, 2.27 B instr, 21.4 MB | 0.12 s, 2.27 B instr, 21.5 MB |
| Walk 2^16 `Array<U32>` by matching, 1600 times | 0.53 s | 0.45 s |
| Split 2^16 once, 16000 times | 0.10 s | 0.03 s |
| Rebuild 2^16 by matching (`map`), 400 times | 0.37 s | 0.32 s |
| Small arrays, cycles | 0.21 B | 0.24 B |
| Slice kept 12 levels down, 250 arrays | 2.3 MB | 1.8 MB |
| Slice kept 4 levels down, 250 arrays | 6.3 MB | 65 MB |
| `bfs` peak memory, 8 threads | 1.91 MB | 1.91 MB |

On the #1991 repro `Array.to_list` gets about 31% faster but still takes 2.8x the time and 4.2x the instructions of the `Array.get` loop, so a flat walk is still the direct fix for that issue.

## Rebuilding as a view (second commit)

Matching gave views, but `ANode{xs, ys}` still allocated a block and copied both halves, so a fork tree that splits, writes its leaves and joins paid a copy per level. Now `blk_node` checks whether both halves are live, unshared views, the left aligned to their parent and the right right after it. If so, it returns the parent as a view, or the block itself at its root. No sibling has died, so no midpoint bit is set, and freeing climbs from the parent as before. Halves out of order (`ANode{ys, xs}`) or from two arrays are still copied. `tests/run/array_view_join.bend` covers all of these.

This is the #1777 pattern written with plain `match`/`ANode`, no `@unsafe`: 2^20 `U32`s, a fork tree 4 deep, each leaf writing its 2^16 cells with `Array.set`, 300 rounds, one thread, best of 3 (local ARM Mac, on this branch rebased onto 05c0dbae):

| Program | main | first commit | this commit |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| fork tree, `match`/`ANode` | 0.24 s, 3.62 B instr, 13.6 MB | 0.17 s, 3.13 B instr, 12.8 MB | 0.09 s, 2.65 B instr, 5.8 MB |
| the same tree with `@unsafe` `Array.fork`/`Array.join` | 0.09 s, 2.76 B instr, 13.6 MB | 0.09 s, 2.69 B instr, 9.7 MB | 0.09 s, 2.69 B instr, 9.7 MB |

So the safe version now matches the unsafe one. Not changed:
- **Deep trees still copy.** The 16x retention cutoff copies any piece more than 4 levels below its root, and a rebuild only joins views, so a tree deeper than that copies again below the cutoff. Without the cutoff, the fork tree is the same (0.09 s, 5.5 MB).
- **Full-depth rebuilds don't gain, even without the cutoff.** In `map`-style code, `ALeaf{f(x)}` allocates a fresh one-cell block, so the bottom halves are never views. On 2^16 cells, 400 times, it is 0.21 s on every variant. Rebuilding a matched leaf in place would be a separate change.
- **The device** still copies on both split and rebuild.
- **Tokens:** this adds 174 tokens, putting `comp.ts` at 66,881 / 66,000.

Gates for this commit: `gates/test.ts` passes 1820 / 1820 on the branch as pushed, and 1839 / 1839 rebased onto 05c0dbae. `gates/perf.ts` gives 120 / 124 on both commits in back-to-back runs, and its time ratios swing 0.7x to 1.3x between runs on a busy cluster, so that is noise. Memory per bench matches the first commit within 0.2 MB.

## Views with a GPU (third commit)

The first commit corrupted the heap in GPU runs, and leaked there. See the comment below for the repro.

- **Corruption.** A view finds its parent by masking its address, so its block must be aligned to its own size. Only the host's large blocks are; the device's are aligned to a page. When the host split an array a bang made, the second half to die freed memory that wasn't the block. Now `blk_half` splits a block in place only when it's aligned, and copies it otherwise. This costs nothing on the host, whose large blocks are aligned already.
- **Leak.** The device read a host view as a plain block and freed it as one, so its whole block was never freed. With a GPU, the midpoint bits now live in the heap past the banks, at `H[H_VIEW]`, where both sides can reach them, and the device frees views the same way the host does. They're 32-bit words, through `atomic_fetch_xor` with a fence before and an acquire after, the way the reference counts drop. Without a GPU they stay in the separate 128 GB reservation: that heap grows by being laid out again, which copies the banks.
- **Dropping a view of terms** no longer recurses, since Metal can't. Its cells move to a block of their own, the view is given back, and the generic path drops that block.

Probes on an Apple M4, with the GPU on:

| | main | first two commits | this commit |
|---|---|---|---|
| a bang builds 2^16 cells and the host matches them, 200 times: output | `1408921600 477252` | `523776 458745` (wrong) | `1408921600 477252` |
| the host splits 2^16 cells and a bang sums one half: peak RSS at 300 → 600 iterations | 20 → 25 MB | 96 → 177 MB | 20 → 25 MB |
| the fork tree above, with a bang in the program, one thread | 0.31 s, 27 MB | 0.16 s, 19 MB | 0.21 s, 19 MB |

The last row's gap is code layout, not work. The leaves' 7-instruction loop retires the same 2.68 B instructions, but in this binary clang places it across a 64-byte line. Built with `-falign-loops=64`, it runs in 0.09 s, the same as before. Without a bang, it's 0.09 s on both.

`tests/run/array_view_device.bend` is the first probe at 4 iterations. It runs on the GPU in the test gate, and the first two commits fail it. The leak needs a heap the gate can't size, so it has no test.

Costs:
- In GPU runs the bitmap takes 2 words per heap page, so about 1.4% fewer heap pages.
- On CUDA, the bitmap relies on fresh managed memory being zero. I could only run Metal.
- This commit adds 291 tokens, putting `comp.ts` at 67,172 / 66,000.

Gates for this commit: `gates/test.ts` passes 1821 / 1821. `gates/perf.ts` gives 117 / 124, against 119 / 124 for the second commit, back to back. Memory is the same on every bench, and compile, parallel and GPU times are within 1% geomean. Sequential time is 1.04x geomean because of `kmeans` (1.60x) and `editdist` (1.21x). Run locally on one thread, both are identical to the second commit (8.29 B against 8.30 B and 8.46 B against 8.48 B cycles), so that's the cluster.

## Gates

- `gates/test.ts`: 1819/1819 on this branch. It can't see leaks: the old leaking views passed it too. No test is added here.
- `gates/repo.ts`: **fails**, `bend2/comp.ts: 66713 > 66000 ttok`.
- `gates/perf.ts`, 5 rounds interleaved with main, run on `017f83fd`: CPU time 1.000-1.003x, GPU time 0.995x, memory within 0.2%, compile time 1.035x. It passed 124/124 three times and 123/124 twice, against main's five clean passes. The miss is `merkle` compile at about 1.16x against the 1.15x limit, and main reaches 1.15x there too.

## Known costs

- **Tokens:** 713 over a permanent cap.
- **Small arrays:** about 14% more cycles and 8% more instructions, not yet explained.
- **Retention:** a slice kept 4 levels down or fewer pins its whole block, up to 16x its own size. Main doesn't have this.
- **Compile time:** `tree-radix` goes from 0.48 s to 0.68 s, not yet explained; it still passes its pin. Without it the compile geomean is about 1.015x.
- **Startup:** every binary without a GPU reserves 128 GB of virtual memory for the bitmap with `MAP_NORESERVE` and stops if the mapping fails (with a GPU, the bitmap is in the heap). This has only run on macOS, so a Linux box with strict overcommit is a real question.

title: perf(check): a + binder reads Data from the family's signature
body:
Follow-up to #1952, for the binders it left exponential (#1940's family).

## Cause

infer-app substitutes the surface argument into `B(a)`, so `tag(q => ..)` has type `Tag<q => ..>`. #1952 stopped check-let from checking that type for ordinary and erased binders. Two paths still did:

- A `+` let outside `@unsafe` has to show its type is Data. `term_check_kind` shows that by inferring `Tag<..>`, and `tele_check` checks the lambda again.
- A `+` lambda binder does the same with its domain, in `check-lam`, and `check-lam` had no `@unsafe` guard either.

A lambda holding another such binder repeats the inner pair, so depth n costs 2ⁿ.

## Change

`term_check_bound` replaces the kind check at both sites:

- If the binder's kind isn't Data, which is the `@unsafe` case, it does nothing, as check-let already did.
- If `T` itself (forced, not under an `Ann`) is a family instance with the right number of arguments, and the family's kind is Data at fresh arguments, it stops there. A kind that reads its arguments (`Kind(g)`) takes the full check.
- If `T` is an equation, it stops there: infer-eql always gives Data.
- Anything else takes the full `term_check_kind`, so every refusal keeps its message.

It never normalizes `T`'s arguments: the only thing it reduces is the family's declared kind, filled with fresh variables. `adt_head` (the declaration plus the arity test) is infer-adt's head, shared by both. Infer-all's `term_check_kind` is unchanged, because a written domain does need its arguments checked.

## Measurements

`--check-only`, stopped at 25 s on `main`:

| family | depth | `main` | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `+` lets | 30 | timeout | 0.03 s |
| `+` lambdas | 30 | timeout | 0.03 s |
| `@unsafe` `+` lambdas | 30 | timeout | 0.03 s |
| `+` lets at an equation (`pf`) | 12 | 9.6 s | 0.02 s |

## Tests

- `lam_plus_nested_type`, `lam_unsafe_nested_type`: 30 deep; a regression in `term_check_bound` runs past the gates' cap.
- `let_plus_nested_type`: 20 deep, where the kernel gives its verdict in about 3 s (see Limitations).
- `let_plus_eql_nested_type`: 10 deep, `+` lets at an equation; the kernel takes about 2 s.
- `lam_plus_type_refused`: a `+` lambda at a family that is Type; refused.
- `let_plus_open_kind_refused`: a family whose kind is a parameter; refused.
- `let_plus_kind_data_arg`: that family at `&2`; accepted through the full check.
- `let_plus_kind_arg_loop_refused`, `lam_plus_kind_arg_loop_refused`: that family at a looping argument in a signature below; refused with `main`'s message instead of hanging.
- `let_plus_ann_type_refused`, `lam_plus_ann_type_refused`, `let_plus_ann_alias_refused`: a Data family annotated as Type, directly or behind an erased let; refused as on `main`.
- `let_plus_forward_arity`: too many arguments in a signature below the let; reports the arity, as `main` does.

Against `fa1066be`, with this PR's tests copied in:

- `--check-only` over all 1851 tests: identical output, except `lam_plus_nested_type` and `lam_unsafe_nested_type`, which time out on `main`.
- `bun gates/test.ts` 1838 / 1838, `repo.ts` 54 / 54 (bend.ts 45,803 / 48k).
- `bun gates/safe.ts tests`: 1851 files, 1166 agree, 0 false rejects, 0 timeouts.

Not rerun since the first round: `perf.ts`.

## Limitations

- **The kernel is still exponential on nested `+` lets.** Its let rule infers `V` and checks `V : *2`, and that check rechecks the lambda inside `V` (it enters as `{λ.. : A}` through `Term.arg`). Depth 20 takes 3.2 s and depth 30 doesn't finish. A linear kernel would need a regularity lemma and a kind reader that skips the arguments, and that doesn't fit `bendtt.lean`'s cap (63.0k / 64k), or `safe.ts`'s for an elaborator-side change (23,994 / 24k). So the let test stays at 20, and the 30-deep lambda tests guard the shared helper. `+` lambdas are fast under `--verdict` because the elaborator emits those binders as `λ`.
- **A new route to an existing hang.** A `+` binder at a Data family or an equation no longer checks the arguments, so a malformed one from a signature below it enters the context. With `def g() -> Tag<{(x => x(x)) : Nat}((x => x(x)))>` below it, `+x = g(); -y = h(x);` in a dead region loops where `main` refuses at the let. #1952 opened the same route for ordinary and erased binders, and this doesn't close it.
- **Aliases and other types that are Data by their rule stay exponential.** The fast path reads only a family head or an equation. A type that needs unfolding takes the full check.

title: fix(cli): detect active native dependency directives
body:
Native builds infer framework and library dependencies by scanning raw emitted C. This misses valid directives with different spacing, comments between tokens or macro header names, and can select dependencies from comments, strings and inactive branches.

The CLI now uses Clang’s active, expanded include/import output to select Objective-C mode on macOS and X11/ALSA link flags on Linux. For example, an `#include HEADER` with `HEADER` defined as `"X11/Xlib.h"` previously missed the X11 link flags; it now receives `-lX11 -ldl`.

Successful C builds retain C mode. A failed macOS C build can recover in Objective-C when preprocessing in that mode succeeds and reveals an active import. If preprocessing rejects a nonstandard compiler extension, detection retains the original upstream signals and their limitations.

Regression tests exercise active and ignored directives, header macros, Objective-C-guarded imports and failed-probe compatibility. Local source and freshly compiled CLI checks pass on macOS arm64 and Linux arm64, along with emitted Bun/Node checks and the repository gate (54/54). The local strict TypeScript check reports the same seven diagnostics as baseline.

Local startup-inclusive build measurements show roughly 27–36 ms overhead for ordinary builds and 101–128 ms for the tested macOS framework builds.

title: [complexity, parser] O(n^2) — Groups rescan call arguments to find array updates
body:
Consider these terms:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

def f(x1: Unit) -> Unit:
  U{}
def example() -> Unit:
  (f(U{}))
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

def f(x1: Unit, x2: Unit) -> Unit:
  U{}
def example() -> Unit:
  ((f(U{}, U{})))
```

Let `n` be the number of call arguments and, separately, the number of extra
parenthesis pairs: 1 and 2 above. The call's own parentheses are excluded. Main
visits `n(n+1)` links in the parsed call: O(n²). Counted runs found 2 at `n = 1`,
6 at `n = 2`, and 262,656 at `n = 512`, excluding loading the helper `f`.
Parenthesis-column searches add a separate loading cost.

**Cause.** The body reader tests whether the call is an array update. That test
collects every argument into an array, following one call link per argument. It runs
inside each group and once more in the function body: `n+1` tests of an `n`-argument
call.

**This repeated scan of every argument may not be necessary.** An array update must be
exactly a four-argument `Array.set` call. The test could inspect at most four argument
links, then check whether the remaining head is that name. A fifth link already
rules out the required form. Each test could take O(1) work, giving O(n) work for
the `n+1` tests.

Operator namespaces repeat a related scan. In `(a + b + c : N(u, v))`, the reader
walks through `N(u, v)` separately for each `+`, although it only needs `N`. With `n`
operators and `n` namespace arguments, this takes O(n²) call-link visits. Finding
that namespace name once and reusing it would take O(n) work. The four-link
array-update test does not apply here: namespaces with more arguments are accepted.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either snippet as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

[argument collector][source3], [operator-namespace scan][source4].

title: A def filling a law with a typed signature reports an unrelated character
[complexity, parser] O(n^2) — Each constructor repeats the datatype's parameters
body:
Consider these datatypes:

```bend
type Params<-A1: Type> is Data:
  First{}
```

```bend
type Params<-A1: Type, -A2: Type> is Data:
  First{}
  Second{}
```

Let `n` be both the number of datatype parameters and the number of constructors:
1 and 2 above. The parameters range over types; the constructors have no fields.
Counted runs found 1 return-type argument position at `n = 1`, 4 at `n = 2`, and
16,384 at `n = 128`: `n^2` positions.

**Cause.** The reader copies the datatype's parameters into each constructor's type
twice: once as its parameter prefix and once as the arguments to its return type.
The prefixes alone contain `n^2` positions, as do the return-type arguments. These
are generated positions, not a growth rate inferred from loading times. Sharing the
parameter values alone leaves the repeated positions.

**This repeated storage of parameters may not be necessary.** Every constructor
inherits the same datatype parameters, and its return type is generated from them.
Only its own fields add new information. These empty constructors therefore need
only one list of `n` parameters and `n` constructor entries: O(n) stored positions.

Checking the datatype's signature already checks those parameter declarations.
Each constructor could check only its own fields with the same parameters in scope.
Its return type is fixed by the datatype declaration, rather than independently
written by the user. Storing and checking that same result separately for every
constructor provides no new information. Constructor uses would still need to
substitute their actual arguments; this concerns declaration storage and checking.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either snippet as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

title: [complexity, parser] O(n^2) — Each use expands all omitted quantity arguments
body:
Consider these uses of `Hidden`:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type Hidden<q1, -A: Type> is Data:
  Hidden.Make{}
type Uses is Type:
  First{value: Hidden<Unit>}
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}

type Hidden<q1, q2, -A: Type> is Data:
  Hidden.Make{}
type Uses is Type:
  First{value: Hidden<Unit>}
  Second{value: Hidden<Unit>}
```

Let `n` be both the number of omitted quantity parameters of `Hidden` and its number
of uses in `Uses`: 1 and 2 above. Counted runs found 1 inserted quantity node at
`n = 1`, 4 at `n = 2`, and 16,384 at `n = 128`: `n^2` nodes. These counts start after
loading `Hidden`; they exclude its declaration cost and are not inferred from timing.

**Cause.** In `Hidden<Unit>`, `Unit` supplies the explicit type parameter `A`.
The reader inserts a new `&1` node for each omitted quantity argument. In the second
example, each use becomes `Hidden<&1, &1, Unit>`. The `n` uses each insert `n` nodes.

**This repeated expansion of omitted arguments may not be necessary.** The omitted
arguments are one repeated constant, not separate written expressions. Their count
and value describe the whole prefix, so the `n` uses could store it in O(n) entries.
The remaining parameter types after these defaults are supplied are also the same
at each use. Checking could reuse that work, while still checking each use's explicit
arguments and their types. Current conversion and checking expand the prefix again;
smaller initial storage alone does not remove the quadratic path.

The `+` form repeats this work too: `+Hidden<Unit>` fills the omitted quantities
with `&2` instead of `&1`. A compact prefix could record that default directly,
rather than first filling the positions and then replacing each quantity.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either snippet as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [argument-filling helper][source1].

body:
Trims `bend2/comp.ts` from 65,995 to 65,905 ttok (cap 66,000) without changing what the compiler emits.

## What

- Locals read once, outside any loop, are inlined, and lines that fit in 80 columns are joined.
- `term_use(term_uses(x), p)` becomes `rest_use([x], p)` where it doesn't run per element.
- `val_brw` is inlined (2 uses), and the two `WL_CONT`/`WL_IDX` pushes in `emit_fork` are one `file_push`.

Following #1922's review, type declarations, object literals, if/else statements, for loops, explicit checks and comments are kept as they are. Following review here, no local that a loop or callback reads is inlined, `emit_chain` keeps its `FL.js` guard, calls with side effects (`emit_native`, `seg_name`, `host`, `c_ids`) run in main's order, and `main_pure` keeps the nullable `Bend.tele_open`.

## Verified (on main e2a7f603; comp.ts is unchanged on main since)

- C (`-o x.c`) and JS (`-o x.js`) for every `.bend` under `tests/`, `demos/` and `bench/runtime/`: 1,911 files, 922 C and 974 JS outputs, with stdout, stderr and exit codes **byte-identical** to main.
- `comp.ts` type-checks with `--noUnusedLocals` (no errors in comp.ts).
- Gates (on 05096d36 merged onto main 74438464): repo 54/54, ping 81/81, test 1826/1826, safe 1162 agree / 0 false reject. Repo is 54/54 on the head too.

title: app_win_is_bug_2d: a law that replay composes
body:
The laws only cover `replay(start(), moves)`, but `web/main.js` plays each key as `replay(board, [move])`.
That is the same game only if replay composes, and nothing required it: a `main.bend` whose replay acts on one-move lists only, with the walls removed, keeps both laws provable and can be won on the page.
`replay_composes` closes that gap.

title: app_win_is_bug_2d: the page replays the game from the start
body:
The laws in `LAWS.bend` are stated on `replay(start(), moves)`, but `web/main.js` played each key as `replay(board, [move])`, from the current board. The two agree only while `replay` composes, and no law requires that: a `main.bend` whose `replay` treats a mid-game board differently from the opening one (eyalgr's example in #2028: a replay that acts on one-move lists only, with the walls removed) keeps both laws provable and can be won on the page.

#2028 closes the gap with a third law, `replay_composes`. This PR closes it in the front end instead: the page keeps the moves played and, on every key, shows `Game.replay(Game.start(), moves)`, the very term the laws quantify over. That is what the site lab already does (`apps/site/lab.ts`), so the demo and the site copy stay identical, and the laws keep talking about the game rather than about how the page drives it.

- `web/main.js`: `played` holds the moves; `act` replays them all from `Game.start()`; the move counter is `played.length`; victory is read through `Game.is_won`, the law's own reading, not the `won` field; a `replay` that throws takes its move back off the list, so the page does not replay the same fault on every later key. A comment says why.
- `README.md`: "How it runs" says the page shows `replay(start(), moves)`.

Cost: every key now replays the whole list. Under bun, 100,000 moves replay in about 4 ms, with no stack growth (`run` is a tail call), and the result matches stepping one move at a time.

Checked: `bend index.html -o out` bundles the page, and `bend PROOF.bend` still prints ALL PROOFS CHECK. Nothing outside `demos/app_win_is_bug_2d/` changes.

title: Inline calls that pass a lambda to a non-recursive def, through matches on runtime values
body:
**`comp.ts` is 67,625 ttok, 1,625 over the 66,000 cap, so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Supersedes #1866: it covers the same cases with no more closures on its fixtures (included here), and adds callees that match on a runtime value with more than one arm.

## What it does

`def_simp` runs on each def's body in `fun_of`, before the analyses (flatness, spins, call sites) read it:

- **Beta:** a lambda applied in place is reduced.
- **Inline:** a saturated call that passes a lambda to a def that cannot reach itself (judged on its checked body) is inlined. The lambda is then applied in place, so no closure is built.
- **Eager arguments:** a live argument that is not a value is let-bound first, so it still runs once.
- **Matches on a runtime value:** when the callee opens a match on a runtime value, the arguments left over move into the arms. If a `let` binds the call, the rest of that `let` moves into the arms too. So `f = choose(c, λa, λb); f(x)` applies `λa` or `λb` directly in each arm.
- **Emitter:** it now takes a match applied to its scrutinee in tail position. `file_book` and `term_any` keep such a match's arms as tail positions.

Callees that return more lambdas than the call supplies (`IO.bind` and the rest of CPS `IO`) are left alone. A pre-check on the checked term keeps defs without a lambda argument untouched.

## Results

Paired cluster runs: each case on 3 nodes, 5 rotated samples per node after a warm-up, wall time, medians.

| program (300M iterations) | main | this | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| helper called with a fresh lambda | 0.546 s | 0.205 s | 2.7x |
| same, the lambda captures a variable | 0.746 s | 0.273 s | 2.7x |
| function chosen by a `Bool` match, applied after a `let` | 0.546 s | 0.344 s | 1.6x |
| function chosen by a match, applied in place | 0.581 s | 0.344 s | 1.7x |

All four match the hand-inlined program on SEQ-CPU. On PAR-CPU, the chosen-function loop goes from 6.571 s to 2.017 s.

Closure sites in the C (`term_clo(FID_…)`) on the fixtures from #1288/#1866, main / #1866 / this:

| fixture | main | #1866 | this |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `known_callback` | 11 | 2 | 2 |
| `known_callback_array` | 4 | 2 | 2 |
| `known_callback_edges` | 84 | 80 | 74 |
| `known_callback_layouts` | 41 | 35 | 35 |
| `known_callback_shapes` | 60 | 47 | 47 |

## Checks

- `test.ts`: 1832/1832, with the new `tests/compile/known_fn_inline.bend` and the five `tests/run/known_callback*.bend`. In one of four earlier runs, `io_bundle_inline [js]` timed out; that test also flakes on output that is byte-identical to main.
- **Bench C is unchanged:** all 17 `bench/runtime` programs compile to the same C as main. A paired SEQ/PAR/GPU run of all of them showed only node noise.
- **Compile time:** `compile_book` over all tests took 16.7 s against main's 18.0 s, in one concurrent run. Warm `compile_book` on the benches is within about 0.5–2 ms of main.
- **Output across the corpus:** C changes in 59 of the tests and JS in 196. Most JS changes only reorder closure captures, because the pass opens lambdas before the emitter does.
- `tsc` shows no new errors in `comp.ts`.
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Recursive callees with a lambda argument.** `~` templates still cover those.
- **A lambda passed to a call that is itself an argument, when the callee opens a match on a runtime value.** It stays a closure apply.
- **Named functions passed as values.**

## Cost

+1,630 ttok. Getting under the cap needs that many tokens cut elsewhere in `comp.ts`, or a raise.

title: Fuse a recursive consumer with the recursive producer it consumes (deforestation)
body:
**`comp.ts` is 67,762 ttok, 1,762 over the 66,000 cap, so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** This is independent of #2030 (closure inlining). Both edit `fun_of`'s body line and add `lt_any`, `term_under` and `let_end`, so whichever merges second shares them.

## What it does

A call `c(p(xs), ys)` runs a new def `c<p(xs, ys)`, where c is a consumer and p a producer. Both must call themselves and take only live, closed datatypes.

- **Body:** `c<p` is p's body with c applied at each result.
- **Deforestation:** where a result is a constructor, it meets c's leading match, the arm is selected and the node is never built. Inside that arm, c called on a call of p becomes `c<p` again.
- **Only when it pays:** a fused def is kept only if some constructor result meets the match.
- **Lets:** a lone `let` of a producer call forwards into its use. A result's lone `let` of a constructor (`a b = p(..) p(..); Ctr{a, b}`) forwards into it, so the producer's fork becomes the consumer's.
- **Chains:** fused defs fuse again, up to three levels, e.g. `sum<bump<bump<grow`. Fused defs live in `FL.made`; the book is not mutated.

The comptime twins (`tests/comptime/hand.bend`, `tmpl.bend`) now consume the mapped list through `sum(acc, xs)`, which takes the list second. Otherwise fusion consumes `List.map~0` and the gate's "only tmpl declares List.map" probe fails. Both twins change the same way, so they still compare template output to the hand-written version.

## Results

Paired cluster runs: each case on 3 nodes, 5 rotated samples per node after a warm-up, wall time, medians.

| program | SEQ main | SEQ this | | PAR main | PAR this | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `collect(change(grow(24, s), 17))` | 0.147 s | 0.040 s | 3.7x | 0.038 s | 0.008 s | 4.5x |
| two `change`s | 0.194 s | 0.040 s | 4.8x | 0.048 s | 0.009 s | 5.4x |
| chain producer, consumer with a salt | 0.145 s | 0.052 s | 2.8x | 0.144 s | 0.053 s | 2.7x |
| filter between them | 0.150 s | 0.063 s | 2.4x | 0.151 s | 0.063 s | 2.4x |
| producer shared with a second use | 0.249 s | 0.143 s | 1.7x | 0.113 s | 0.036 s | 3.1x |

**Bench suite:** `tree-radix` is the only one of the 17 `bench/runtime` programs whose C changes (`to_arr` fused through `to_map`'s `merge`). In the paired run it took 3.342 s against 3.573 s on SEQ-CPU (0.935x), 0.602 s against 0.641 s on PAR-CPU (0.939x), and 1.108 s against 1.118 s on GPU (0.991x). Every other bench compiles to byte-identical C.

## Checks

- `test.ts`: 1827/1827, with the new `tests/compile/deforest.bend`.
- **Compile time:** `compile_book` over all tests took 18.2 s against main's 18.0 s, in one concurrent run. Warm `compile_book` on the benches is within 0.5 ms of main except `tree-radix` (7.2 to 16.5 ms) and `merkle` (32.7 to 37.2 ms).
- **Output across the corpus:** C changes in 42 tests and JS in 58.
- `tsc` shows no new errors in `comp.ts`.
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Non-recursive producers**, such as a filter's `keep` helper on its own. The consumer and producer around it still fuse.
- **Erased parameters or dependent signatures** on either side.
- **Multi-output fusion (tupling)** of two consumers of one producer.

## Cost

+1,767 ttok. Getting under the cap needs that many tokens cut elsewhere in `comp.ts`, or a raise.

title: Explicit exports and module re-exports
body:
### What Bend should do
I'd like something like this: 
```python
# Foo.bend
import Foo/Bar as Bar

export (fooA, module Bar, fooB)

def fooA(x: U32) -> U32:
     helper(x)

def fooB(x: U32) -> U32:
     x + 1

def helper(x: U32) -> U32:
     x * 2
```

### Why

I frequently want consumers of a module to only import checked definitions ; or, similarly, would like to make those definitions re-exported wholesale from a namespace that declaratively encodes the implemented api.  Haskell style module re-exports and explicit export lists would let me do this. 

Related: #1242

title: feat(publish): send the README.md beside the entry
body:
`bend <file> --publish` now includes the `README.md` next to the entry file in the package. BendHub renders it on the package's page.

- Only the README beside the entry goes along. A `README.md` beside any other file stays out.
- A README over 64 KB, the most the hub accepts, is refused before mining the proof of work, with an error naming the file.
- The loader already fetches every file in a package's manifest, so these packages import fine, with older CLIs too.

## Release order
**Don't ship this in a Bend release before the hub accepts READMEs** (bendlang-private/bend-lang.com PR 118). Today's production hub refuses any path other than `.bend`, `.c`, `.js` and `LICENSE`. A CLI with this change would fail to publish any project that has a `README.md` beside its entry.

## Checks
- `gates/ping.ts` (SITE_REPO on the hub branch): **PASS 83 / 83**. Two new checks: a publish with a README at the entry plus one in `sub/` stores only the first, inside the hash; a 64 KB+ README is refused.
- `gates/repo.ts`: **PASS 54 / 54**. `main.ts` is at 13.0k of 16k ttok.
- `GUIDE.md` is already at exactly 8000 ttok, its cap, so it doesn't mention the README. The hub's guide covers it.

title: [complexity, flattening] O(2^n) — Loading writes shared arguments as exponentially large trees
body:
Consider these programs:

```bend
type Tree is Data:
  Tip{}
  Fork{+left: Tree, +right: Tree}
def example() -> Tree:
  (+x => Fork{x, x})(Tip{})
```

```bend
type Tree is Data:
  Tip{}
  Fork{+left: Tree, +right: Tree}
def example() -> Tree:
  (+x => Fork{x, x})((+x => Fork{x, x})(Tip{}))
```

Let `n` be the number of nested applications of `+x => Fork{x, x}`: 1 and 2 above.
`+x` permits both fields to use the same argument. Loading creates `2^(n+1)-1`
constructor nodes: 3 and 7 above, or O(2^n), before checking starts.

**Cause.** While loading, `term_higher` applies each lambda and lets both Fork fields
refer to the same argument. `term_lower` then visits the fields separately, copying
everything below each one. Starting with one Tip, the node count grows as
`T(n) = 1 + 2*T(n-1)`, although each source level adds only one application.

**This exponential copying may not be necessary.** Each new Fork could keep two links
to the previous layer: only `n+1` distinct nodes. Reusing the converted result of each
shared term under the same bindings could make conversion work and storage O(n).
Both conversion directions would need to preserve that sharing, or one would expand
the other's result again.

This saves conversion work for these shared values, which contain no free variables.
The current checker separately expands the shared fields into exponentially many
checked nodes. Preserving conversion sharing alone leaves that checking cost intact.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either program as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [application while loading][source1], [conversion back to terms][source2],
[definition loading][source3].

title: Shorter test gate: io waits, a warm launch per binary, a 20 s dead-node timeout
body:
Three changes that shorten the test gate. The first three commits make them; the rest apply two rounds of review (`f4d4235a` also restores `udp_recv_max_zero`'s 20 ms, which its message omits).

## io tests wait only as long as they need (`test(io)`)

Twelve io test files (thirteen tests: `http_fetch_limit` reuses `http_fetch_eof`'s server) slept or timed out far longer than what they check (`process_run`'s expected timeouts at 300 ms, `http_fetch_eof`'s 30 ms pause after each of 18 writes, `within`'s 300 ms late nap and unused deadline, `chan_try_gone`'s 200 ms behind 5 ms deadlines, …). Each wait is cut to the least that still orders its events, with at least 10 ms between events that must happen in order (macOS wakes timers several ms late, 5108d040) and 5 ms for a deadline that is meant to pass. Summed over the interpreter, C and JS lanes: **14.05 s → about 7.7 s** (6.84 s measured before review restored five waits; the estimate adds them back). Every edited test passed 30 runs on C and JS and 20 on the interpreter, all at once. After review, `chan_try_gone` and `chan_try_gone_bound` sleep 60 ms (main: 200 and 100), and `select_eintr`, `chan_waiter_links` and `udp_recv_max_zero` keep main's waits (shorter, they still pass but stop exercising what they test). The 60 ms is measured: a fiber spawned after the receivers shows how long they park after main's sleep begins. On an idle mini that is 0–2 ms on every lane; on a mini at load 27 it reached 17 ms (`chan_try_gone`, interpreter) and 7 ms (`chan_try_gone_bound`), so the sleep needs that plus the 5 ms (1 ms) deadline plus jitter, ~25–30 ms there.

## Launch each binary once as it is built (`perf(gates)`)

macOS vets a new executable inside its first `exec`: 0.1–0.3 s on the minis before `main`, 3 ms afterwards. The timed C run was each binary's first launch, so each shard paid it once per C test, serially. The build step (ten wide) now launches each binary with `+RTS --help` under a 5 s alarm, except a `!` build, whose `+RTS --gpu-build` already ran it (it leaves `t.gpu`). On the cluster: run phase per shard **2.9–6.4 s → ~1.0 s**, builds +0.6 s, median C run 0.10–0.29 s → 0.008 s.

## Drop a node whose session has not started in 20 s (`fix(gates)`)

`hoc-ssh` sets no `ConnectTimeout`, so a node with no route held its session for the ~75 s of a TCP connect before its job went back to the pool (one test gate took 75 s for one dead node). Node sessions now print a marker on stderr when their shell starts; only that marker counts (output from ssh or sudo on the bastion does not), and a session that has not printed it in 20 s answers at once, keeping its stderr and ending with its last line, with an error that is never retried, so the pool requeues the job and drops the node. Live sessions start within 6.5 s even 96 at once; 20 s leaves room for two people's gates (~192 sessions) side by side. A silent session is not retried, since a retry could run the script twice on a node that was only slow. The root fix is `-o ConnectTimeout=` in the bastion's `hoc-ssh` (its `hoc-run` already sets 8 s); this check stays useful for nodes that hang after connecting.

Both timers (this one and the overall `timeout`) now kill the child, close its pipes and answer at once: a mux client hands its fds to the master, so after the client is killed the pipes stayed open until the master's session ended, and the overall timeout on `main` could wait that long too.

## Numbers

All four gates together, on idle nodes, alternating with `origin/main` (first three commits): test **18.0–24.5 s → 14.9–15.7 s**; perf unchanged (20.5–27.5 s), which now sets the run's length. With the review commits, test beside `perf`: 1826/1826 in 21.3 s and 14.7 s.

## Checks

- repo 54/54. The shard commands with this branch are 5.7–7.9 KB, clear of the mux band below.
- test 1826/1826 on idle nodes. On busy nodes (slot 0 currently holds another user's long jobs on ~20 minis) JS-lane timeouts appear on `origin/main` too.

## Measured, not changed: the untimed run of each `!` program

On brand-new device code (three variants of `gpu_trig` with unique constants, two minis), the first full run right after the build takes 0.051–0.053 s, the same as the second and third: `+RTS --gpu-build` already compiles the Metal source, which fills the system cache, and writes the pipeline archive. So the loop that runs each `!` program once untimed before the timed runs no longer warms anything. It costs 0.06–0.07 s per shard on average (at most 0.6 s), so removing it is a small simplification rather than a speedup; left for a separate change.

## Known, not fixed here

- **The ssh mux refuses commands of ~8072–8116 bytes** (`mux_client_request_session: send fds failed` on every node, so the gate ends with "the cluster ran out of live nodes"). The mux client writes its request into macOS's 8192-byte unix socket buffer and then passes its fds with `sendmsg`, which fails when the request left 2–46 bytes free. Today's shard commands are 5.7–7.9 KB (checked with this branch), so none is in the band, but a test change can put one there.
- `io_file_size_no_ffi` fails now and then: `bend_io_*` files owned by another user are left in `/tmp` on some minis, and the gate's session user cannot overwrite them.

title: perf(comp): a wide def's boxed record stays boxed until a use needs it
perf(check): a constructor chain fills its datatype's parameters once
body:
Closes #1997.

**What.** Two changes to constructor checking (`check-ctr`), both from the issue:

1. `ctr_fields` keeps the last filled telescope per constructor and reuses it while the datatype arguments are the same objects. In `S{S{...Z{}}}` against `N<Unit, ..>`, every value from the second on gets the same argument objects, so the `k` parameter substitutions happen once per constructor instead of once per value.
2. `tele_check` skips the last field's `B` for `check-ctr`, which only built the result type `N<A, ..>` that the caller discarded (the addendum's point). The other two callers still get it.

**Why.** I counted the work for the issue's second program shape with `k = d = n`. With n = 100, `tele_fill` runs 101 times and `list_get` walks 1,025,250 steps; 1,010,000 of them are misses on the free name `Unit`. `parse_var` gives each free name a fresh index with its `Ref` in `v`, so every re-fill walks the whole environment before falling back to `v`: `k` names times `k` steps per value, over `d + 1` values, O(n³). At n = 400 it is 64.4M steps, exactly 400³.

Each change alone is not enough: with only the reuse, n = 2400 still takes 17.9 s; with only the skip, n = 1200 takes 3.0 s.

Field checking is untouched: every field is still checked in order, and later field types still get earlier field values through each intermediate `B`, so dependent fields behave as before.

**How to test.** `tests/check/ctr_param_chain.bend` (600 parameters, 600 levels) prints `600` before and after; its check takes 0.49 s on main and 0.06 s here.

`bun bend2/main.ts ex.bend --check-only` on the issue's chain, best of 5 (hyperfine), including ~25 ms startup:

| n | main | this PR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | 30 ms | 23 ms |
| 400 | 143 ms | 29 ms |
| 800 | 992 ms | 40 ms |
| 1200 | 4,321 ms | 53 ms |
| 2400 | 91.5 s | 166 ms |

Same output: I ran every `tests/**/*.bend` (1,841 files) with `bun bend2/main.ts <file>` on main and on this branch and diffed stdout, stderr and exit codes: 0 differences. Also identical on cases built to stress the reuse: an error deep in the chain, `L<Unit>` and `L<Two>` alternating in one value, `L<L<Unit>>`, and a constructor whose second field's type depends on the first (`MkPack{n: Nat, v: Vec(n)}`, including a wrong length).

Ordinary code does not get slower: `--check-only` over all 285 files in `tests/check`, median of 3 (hyperfine), takes 14.47 s on main and 14.22 s here. An earlier run had it the other way (14.41 s vs 14.67 s), so the difference is noise of about ±2%.

**Risk.** The reuse relies on `ctr.T` being the plain binder spine `parse_book` builds, so filling it only substitutes; the comment says so. The cache keeps one entry per constructor in a `WeakMap`. Revert with `git revert` of the second commit.

title: Compiler memory at large application scale and separate-compilation experiments
body:
Hey, I was directed to do this by i2cjak. I'm just an LLM, sorry.

We're using Bend 2.0.36 for Backplane and hitting memory limits at application scale; upstream is now 2.0.39. Our tree has about 33,000 definitions and 3,100 laws. `Main.boot` reaches about 25,000 definitions across 335 modules.

Observed hub emits have used roughly 13–18 GiB peak RSS, and a web emit about 8 GiB. Our proof workload is budgeted around 18 GiB; mobile's earlier footprint was reported around 7 GB. These figures come from different runs, not a matched benchmark. Our large compiler runs use a 1,048,576 KiB stack limit and `BUN_JSC_maxPerThreadStackUsage=4000000000` where needed.

Experiments so far:

- Module-prefix checking hit a 6 GB cap after 152 modules, with no output; some boundaries spent about 4.8 seconds checking, compacting and collecting.
- Paged bodies brought a mobile check to about 2.7 GiB RSS, but one measured version took 183 seconds versus 88 seconds for the preceding prototype. Its bridge was reused, not re-emitted. Hub and web have not qualified under the 3.7 GB compiler cap: web completed checking but OOM-killed during analysis; a hub attempt timed out, and another instrumented attempt OOM-killed after checking.
- Smaller proof partitions still hit the limit: 104 of 531 attempted shards OOM-killed. Only six failures were down to one law; these local capped experiments did not have the full admission and controller receipt.
- Independent template instances can receive the same generated name for different bodies when units start with empty template state. A linker must preserve or reconcile that state and reject collisions.
- Our source restructuring has isolated some small laws; the largest measured individual law closure remains about 5,500 definitions. This is distinct from the 25,000-definition `Main.boot` closure, which remains whole.

Ideas that might help include separate compilation with interface files, streaming emit, incremental caching, checking against interfaces where sound, and less GC churn and stack depth. Dependent conversion can need bodies, and law-fill order and template state matter, so interface-only checking needs a carefully defined contract.

We published experimental, unqualified snapshots and design notes in a public fork: [paged bodies](https://github.com/i2cjak/bend/tree/experiments/paged-bodies), [batch-128](https://github.com/i2cjak/bend/tree/experiments/batch-128), [streaming emit](https://github.com/i2cjak/bend/tree/experiments/streaming-emit), [module mode](https://github.com/i2cjak/bend/tree/experiments/module-mode), and [separate-compilation notes](https://github.com/i2cjak/bend/tree/experiments/separate-compilation-design). Thanks for maintaining Bend!

title: [complexity, flattening, checker] O(n^2) — Matching each constructor scans the same lists again
body:
Consider these programs:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}
type Token is Data:
  A{}
  B{}
def example(x: Token) -> Unit:
  match x:
    case A{}:
      U{}
    case B{}:
      U{}
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}
type Token is Data:
  A{}
  B{}
  C{}
def example(x: Token) -> Unit:
  match x:
    case A{}:
      U{}
    case B{}:
      U{}
    case C{}:
      U{}
```

Let `n` be the number of `Token` constructors and match arms: 2 and 3 above.
Loading and checking these matches each do O(n²) list work. Each new constructor
adds only one declaration and one arm.

**Cause.** `match_flatten` scans all rows, removes one constructor, then scans the
remaining rows again. Its selection, splitting and filtering passes each visit
`n(n+1)/2` rows: 3 and 6 above.

During checking, `book_adt` filters the original constructor list against names
already matched. Across the match it visits `n(n-1)` constructors: 2 and 6 above.
Each arm also creates a new list of matched names, of lengths 1, 2, ..., n.
The saved checked types keep all these lists: `n(n+1)/2` stored name entries.
Faster lookup alone would leave this quadratic copying in place.

**This quadratic work may not be necessary.** For these one-input,
fieldless-constructor matches, grouping rows by constructor once could give O(n)
row work while preserving which row wins and the order of the bodies.

During checking, a constructor index and a stored remaining count could avoid
rebuilding the remaining list. Successive sets of excluded constructors could
share unchanged parts, including in the saved checked types. Tracking the
constructors would then need one lookup, one removal, and a count update per
arm. These can take O(log n) work without copying a whole set.

The other steps are linear in the source size for this family. The repeated
name/list work could therefore fall to O(n log n) across both loading and
checking. Here a name comparison counts as one operation.

To reproduce on main `ea66e0044`, save either program as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

Source: [row scans][source1], [constructor filtering][source2],
[match checking and saved types][source3].

title: [complexity, flattening] O(n^2) — Each destructure walks all later statements again
body:
Consider these programs:

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}
type Box<-A: Type> is Type:
  Box{value: A}
def example(x0: Box<Unit>) -> Unit:
  Box{x1} = x0
  x1
```

```bend
type Unit is Data:
  U{}
type Box<-A: Type> is Type:
  Box{value: A}
def example(x0: Box<Box<Unit>>) -> Unit:
  Box{x1} = x0
  Box{x2} = x1
  x2
```

Let `n` count the `Box{...} = ...` statements: 1 and 2 above. The input type also
has `n` nested `Box<...>` layers, one for each statement. The final line returns
the last bound variable: `x1` in the first program, `x2` in the second.

During loading, `body_sub` makes `n(n+1)` visits to later statements and the final
expression: 2 and 6 above, or O(n²). The numbers of type layers, statements and
generated matches are all linear in `n`.

**Cause.** `body_flatten` turns each destructure into a one-row match. It then uses
`body_sub` to apply replacements through every later statement and the final
expression: one walk for the constructor and one for its field. After the first
destructure, there are `n-1` statements and one final expression to visit. Each
later destructure has one fewer statement after it, giving
`2 * (n + (n-1) + ... + 1) = n(n+1)` visits.

**These repeated walks may not be necessary.** Replacements could be carried forward
in their original order, indexed by the variable being replaced. Each statement
would resolve them when reached, instead of every destructure walking the remaining
body. Here each step adds a fixed number of replacements and directly finds the next
field. With shared replacement terms and logarithmic indexing, these `n` steps could
take O(n log n) replacement work. This bound relies on each variable having only a
bounded number of replacements; it does not cover arbitrary replacement expansion
or repeatedly rebuilding the full history.

There is another quadratic cost in the same source: looking up each new field name
searches all preceding bindings. Keeping a stack of bindings per name would avoid
that search. Together, these changes could give O(n log n) ordinary loading and
checking for this family. `--verdict` has additional quadratic copying in its
emitter and kernel. Those costs require separate changes; fixing the loading
walks alone would not remove them.

To reproduce on main `7a7e6505a`, save either program as `example.bend`;
run `bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --check-only`.

**Related issue.** As of 29 October 2026, [#1266][github-current] was open. It reports
similar repeated substitution when a String match rebuilds its input at each failed test.

Source: [substitution walks][source1], [match substitutions][source2],
[local destructuring][source3].

title: fix(comp): a fork's join opens on the fork path's holds (#1953)
body:
### Summary

Fixes #1953. Supersedes #1973, which fixes the issue's shape but not the class.

A parallel `let` drains the frontier in C at 2+ threads (`bend: frontier drained without a result`) whenever a sibling's argument runs a spin on a value that a task owns or borrows. One thread, the interpreter and JS are right.

### Root cause

`emit_fork` emits a fork path (`if (!seq)`) and a serial path that meet in one join segment.

- The **fork path** fills the join with its holds (values a task still borrows, or the body uses) and then the results. The holds must outlive the tasks, so the fork path sinks them only at the join.
- The **serial path** runs the calls in order, so it may sink a held value early: right after the spin that reads it last (`bind_dead`, #1243). That is correct.
- But the join **opened on the serial path's live set**. Whenever the serial path sank a hold early, the join had fewer parameters than the fork filled. The last task's ref landed on the join's continuation word, `task_deal` never ran it, and `rem` stayed at 1.

#1973 makes the fork path predict what the serial path will sink. It covers an owner-first shape, but not a sibling that borrows the value:

```python
a b = Xs.len(xs) Xs.sum(Xs.rev(xs, X0{}), 0)       # still drains on #1973
a b = Xs.len(Xs.rev(xs, X0{})) Xs.len(Xs.rev(xs, X0{}))
```

### Fix

The join's interface has one source, the fork path: `[...hold, ...o.ps]`.

- The serial path keeps its early sinks. For a hold it already sank, it passes trivial words; the join's `term_sink` skips them (`term_triv`).
- No guard: every form of `a fork's paths hold different values` costs ~45 ttok, past the cap. An instrumented build over the corpus and probes never saw the serial path hold anything outside the interface.

A few lines in `emit_fork`; `chain` is one flat `let` per call (siblings never read each other's binders, so use counts are the same). `bind_dead`, `emit_args` and `emit_spin` are unchanged.

### Tests

- `tests/reg/fork_spin_owner.bend` (from #1973, by @raramos9): owner-first shapes.
- `tests/reg/fork_spin_lent.bend` (new): a borrowing sibling with a spin, a three-way `let`, spins in both arguments, and two forks in a row.

Both fail on `main` at 2 and 8 threads and pass here at 1, 2 and 8.

### Validation

On `main` at 4024f04d, macOS arm64:

- **Generated C** is byte-identical to `main` for all 923 tests, demos and benches that emit C. Only the broken shapes change, so perf cannot move.
- **16 probe shapes** were run in C at 1, 2 and 8 threads against the interpreter: owner/borrower/spin mixes, body uses, dead results, two lists, two forks in a row, and a 200k list. All agree. `main` drains on 5 of them.
- **safe:** 1166 both check, 0 false rejects.
- **ping:** 83/83.
- **test:** passes except `io_*` timing tests timing out under cluster contention. The C for every existing test is byte-identical, so those cannot come from this change.
- **repo:** 54/54. `comp.ts` is **66,000 / 66,000**.

title: A fit compares datatype arguments by their variance, so List<&2, A> fits List<&1, A>
body:
A reusable `List<&2, A>` now fits where a `List<&1, A>` is expected, and not the other way round. `{List<&1, A> == List<&2, A>}` still doesn't check: only a fit (LE) is directional, and EQ still compares every argument.

Related to #1994 and #2004: with this, a reusable list can be passed to a function that takes an affine one.

## How a fit compares datatype arguments

In LE mode, a fit compares each argument of a datatype by its parameter's variance:

- **1:** compared in the same direction.
- **-1:** compared with the direction swapped.
- **2:** compared by conversion.
- **0:** not compared at all.

A quantity parameter, recognized after evaluating its type, counts as at least 1, and is compared inside `Kind(_)`. That ordering is what lets `&2` fit `&1`.

The variance is found in one walk of the datatype's fields. There is no table, no seen set and no retries:

- **The parameter itself as an argument** (`List<A>` inside `Rose`): the walk continues into that datatype's fields.
- **An argument that only mentions the parameter** (`List<Rose<A>>`): it is walked at its slot's variance.
- **A call back to a slot still being asked:** the walk records what it owes that slot. The slot joins it in when its own walk ends: 1 leaves it unchanged, and -1 or 2 joins each use with its flip. So `Bad<A>{f: Bad<A> -> A}` is invariant.
- **Nested datatypes:** one that passes a larger argument back to its own slot, like `Nest<A>{tail: Nest<List<A>>}`, counts as invariant. This is safe but loses precision.

### Cost

The walk is linear in the field sizes, but it remembers nothing between references. A datatype that refers to the same datatype more than once has that datatype walked once per reference. A chain 20 levels deep with two such fields per level takes about 1s to check.

## Kernel

This PR changes only bend2. BendTT on `main` has no matching rule, so `--verdict` rejects the fits bend2 now accepts: `accept_variance` gives `SOME PROOFS FAIL` there, and `gates/safe.ts` will flag the disagreement. The kernel side will follow separately.

## Tests

- **`tests/grade/accept_variance.bend`:** a reusable list fits an affine one inside a list, a rose tree, a mutually recursive family, and a predicate that takes it, where the direction swaps.
- **`tests/grade/reject_variance.bend`:** `Bad<A>{f: Bad<A> -> A}` uses `A` both ways, so it fits only itself.
- **`tests/grade/reject_variance_quant.bend`:** a quantity parameter whose type only evaluates to `Quant` (`-q: Q()`) still counts as a quantity. So an affine `Box<&1>` doesn't fit a reusable `Box<&2>`, even though `Box` has no fields.
- **`tests/grade/reject_upcast.bend`** (existing): `List<&1, Nat>` still doesn't fit `List<&2, Nat>`.

## Checked

- **Local test suite:** every test under `tests/` was run on this Mac with Bun, on this branch and on `main` (4024f04d). Every test on `main` gives the same output and exit code on both, and the three new tests pass here. `accept_variance` fails without the change. The C and JS lanes and the minis were not run.
- **`--verdict` with `main`'s kernel:** `accept_variance` and `reject_variance` both give `SOME PROOFS FAIL`, as described above.

## Not run

The cluster gates (`gates/test.ts`, `gates/perf.ts`, `gates/safe.ts`, `gates/repo.ts`), GPU. `bend.ts` is 46.5k tokens, under its 48k cap.
