title: fix(demos): app_slash_boss_3d's laws read their measures from SPEC.bend
body:
Fixes #2066.

`SPEC.bend` holds what `LAWS.bend` measures: `steps` (n ticks, each one `Slash.Game.step`), `fade` (n ticks of a countdown, with a `dec` of its own) and `cat` (a frame's events joined). It has the header the other demos' spec files use. `LAWS.bend` and `PROOF.bend` import it and name `Spec.steps`, `Spec.fade` and `Spec.cat`; the laws and the proofs are otherwise unchanged. `main.bend` loses its `# Spec` section, which only those two files used, as #1932 did for `pure_par_sort` and `pure_par_sum`.

`SPEC.bend` imports `main.bend` only for `Game.step` and the game's types, as the `SPEC.bend` of `pure_par_sort` and the `BOARD.bend` of `app_win_is_bug_2d` do. `fade` counts with its own `dec`, the body of `Sim.dec` (as `pure_par_sum`'s `SPEC.bend` keeps its own `pow2` since 1570e072), so an edit to `Sim.dec` can't move the measure. The checker unfolds both countdowns to the same `R.word`, so the proofs didn't change beyond the names. `cat` is its own append.

What it leaves, as the issue says: the laws pin `Game.step`, not the loop that runs it.

### Before and after

The same edits on `main` and on this branch, with `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) giving the same answer in each cell:

| | `main` at ae7341dd | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| the issue's edit (a paused clock runs, the measure and `PROOF.bend` edited to match) | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.pause_freezes` |
| `Sim.dec` gives 6 for 7 and 0 for anything else, which `dec_floor` still accepts | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.pause_freezes` |
| nothing edited | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |

On this branch the measure lives in `SPEC.bend`, so the first row applies only the bug and the `PROOF.bend` edit. The bug is in the game on both sides, so the issue's `CHECK.bend` prints `after 3 ticks: time 3` on both; unedited, it prints `time 0` on both.

### What I checked

On ae7341dd, macOS arm64:

- `bend main.bend --check-only`, `bend main.bend --verdict` and `bend SPEC.bend --check-only` print ALL PROOFS CHECK. `bend LAWS.bend` alone reports 7 TODOs, as on `main`.
- Moving only the loop to another stepper still checks, which is the limit above.
- `bend main.bend -o` builds, and `SLASH_PROBE=120` runs headless and exits 0. The loop is unchanged, so I didn't open the window.
- Every other demo's `PROOF.bend` prints what it prints on `main`: ALL PROOFS CHECK, except `pure_hvm5_mini`, kept `@unsafe` in #1989.

`repo-gate` passes in CI. Not run: the cluster gates, Linux.

title: perf(flatten): a destructure defers its substitutions instead of walking the rest of the body (#2041)
refactor(bendtt): simplifications, 63.0k -> 60.1k ttok
body:
A round of simplifications in `bend2/bendtt.lean`: **63,038 → 60,051 ttok** (−2,987; the cap is 64k). +446 / −631 lines, in that file only.

The definitions keep `main`'s style (sequences of `let`s, full calls), and everything before Show is exactly as on `main`. Part 1 changes only in structure; most of the saving is in the proof.

## What changes

**Part 1, structure only**
- `Term.show` takes its depth first.
- One `Parse.upto` loop replaces `gap.eol`, `Parse.span` and `Char.is_name`. `Parse.fail` decodes 120 bytes, cut at a character's start, and takes 30 characters, so `Parse.next` goes.
- `Parse.label` takes a flag for the `.k` key form, so `Parse.key` goes.
- `<` eats its bracket where it is matched, so `parse_enum` drops its `ks.isEmpty` test.
- `parse_tup` takes a `top` flag, so `parse_paren` is its top-level call and the tuple tail isn't written twice.
- The `App q f (Var v)` step of a case-tree walk moves from `Term.run` into `Term.fire`, so `run` builds its leaf in one place. It takes no fuel in `fire`, because it comes only from `run`, which has taken it, so the fuel spent per step is the same as on `main`.
- `Term.check` and `Term.tree` read that step's test through `Term.node`.
- `Def.check` and `Book.check_from` take `(bk tb : Book)` instead of `ls : Book × Book`, whose first half was always `bk`.

**Part 3, the proof (~2,750 ttok, two rounds)**
- `reach` runs halts, progress and sr once, for both `consistent` and `adequate`, which are now a few lines each.
- `lab_in`, `canon_enu`, `value_form`, `rfl_conv` and `canon_eql` take the type itself, not a `Conv` to it that all but two callers gave as `crefl`. `rfl_conv` replaces `eql_inj`, and `spine_ft` is stated for calls, so `tform_call` goes.
- `sr`'s and `ev`'s congruence cases each share one script. `progress`, `eval_value`, `table_at` and `chk` lose special cases.
- `pat_below` inducts on the pattern instead of a fuel and passes its fields step to `below_tup` in place. `desc_lex`'s size step is one disjunction. `tp` simplifies its hypotheses once.
- `LiveV` ranges over tags. `ref_sub` reads `LiveV`, so `head_used` goes. `bud_once` is one script, so `once_if` goes. `bool_imp` reads `!a || b` as an implication, so `qlive` goes.
- Lemmas folded into their only uses: `conv_all`/`conv_sig` (into `conv_bin`), `lab_fix`, `labels_app`, `vm_up`, and `wnf_pars`'s `R1` and `F`.

**CLAIMS is byte-identical.** `consistent` and `adequate` still depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`.

## Is the executable part the same?

**Show, the evaluator, the checker, the live check and the validator are proven equal to `main`'s.** The theorems below keep `main`'s version of each changed total definition under `Old.*`, beside the new one, and prove each equal, up to

```lean
theorem E_book (bk : Book) : Old.Book.check bk = Book.check bk
```

`Book.check` is the whole verdict, error text included: every refusal string comes from `Ctx.fail`, `Ctx.fit` and `Term.show`, which are covered.

One definition does change on some inputs: the new `Term.fire` steps `App q f (Var v)`, which the old one didn't. So `E_eval` proves `wnf`, `run` and `val` equal at every fuel, and `fire` equal on every other term. `wnf` never hands `fire` an App, and `run`'s App step gives the old result through the new route.

**The parser is reviewed and tested, not proven.** Its functions are `partial`, so Lean can't reason about them.
- **Review:** each hunk preserves the order of effects and every error text; only `Parse.fail`, `Parse.upto`, `Parse.label`, `<`, and `parse_tup` change.
- **`Parse.fail`:** the input is `s.toUTF8` of a `String` (`IO.FS.readFile` checks UTF-8). At a character boundary, both versions decode the same 30 characters: they fit in 120 bytes, and the slice ends at a character's start. Inside a character, both start at a continuation byte and give `''`.
- **Differential test:** one binary holds `main`'s parser (as `Old.*`) and the new one. For each text it compares the error message, or `repr` of every parsed def (name, opaque flag, type, body). A canary that changes one new error string is caught.

| inputs | parses | differ |
|---|---|---|
| the 1,322 books exported from `tests/`, plus 3,954 seeded mutants | 5,276 | 0 |
| 375 books under 2.5 KB: every character prefix, and each of the first 600 one-character deletions | 495,283 | 0 |
| 8,364 grammar-aware fuzz mutants (1–5 inserted, deleted, copied or truncated tokens, including `∀ Σ λ`, `<&>`, `(,)`, `#` comments and 2- to 4-byte characters) | 8,364 | 0 |
| 63 hand-written edge cases, with all their prefixes and deletions | 1,358 | 0 |
| 1,152 errors followed by runs of 2-, 3- and 4-byte characters at every offset (540 cut the 120-byte slice inside a character) | 1,152 | 0 |

The fuzz reaches every parse error message (`a name`, `':'`, `')'`, `'->'`, `'.'`, `';'`, `'='`, `'}'`, `'=>'`, `'1'`, `a pair after a quantity mark`, `a fresh label`), and the checker on the books that parse.

Separately, compiled kernels from `main` and this branch give byte-identical output and exit status on the 5,276 books and mutants (3,256 refused).

**Cost:** the proof check still takes about 8.5 s, as on `main`. Parsing may be slightly slower (the `Parse.upto` closure).

<details>
<summary>Reproducing the equivalence proof</summary>

The proof can't live in the repo (the repo gate allows no new files), so here it is. Save the two files, then:

```sh
git show origin/main:bend2/bendtt.lean > old.lean
python3 mkeqv.py old.lean bend2/bendtt.lean equiv_thms.lean eqv.lean
lean eqv.lean   # Lean 4.34.0; no output means every theorem checks
```

`mkeqv.py` puts `main`'s version of each changed non-parser definition under `namespace Old`, before CLAIMS, and appends the theorems.

`mkeqv.py`:

```python
# mkeqv.py OLD NEW THMS OUT: NEW with OLD's changed total defs under
# namespace Old (before CLAIMS), then THMS, which prove them equal
import re, sys
def blocks(path):
    out, cur, buf, mut = {}, None, [], False
    for l in open(path).read().split("\n"):
        if l.startswith("-- CLAIMS"): break
        m = re.match(r"^(?:partial )?(def|abbrev|instance|structure|inductive|theorem|mutual|end)\b\s*([^\s:(]*)", l)
        if m and not (mut and m.group(1) in ("def", "abbrev", "theorem")):
            if m.group(1) == "end" and mut:
                buf.append(l); mut = False; continue
            if cur: out[cur] = "\n".join(buf).rstrip()
            buf, cur, mut = [l], (m.group(2) or m.group(1)), m.group(1) == "mutual"
            if mut: cur = "mutual@"
            continue
        if mut and m and cur == "mutual@": cur = "mutual:" + m.group(2)
        if cur: buf.append(l)
    if cur: out[cur] = "\n".join(buf).rstrip()
    return out
old, new = blocks(sys.argv[1]), blocks(sys.argv[2])
keep = [k for k in old if (k not in new or old[k] != new[k]) and not k.startswith("Parse.")
        and k not in ("Char.is_name", "mutual:Term.parse", "Book.parse_defs")]
body = "\n\n".join(old[k] for k in keep)
body = re.sub(r"([^.A-Za-z_])Min([^A-Za-z_])", r"\1Term.Min\2", body)
s = open(sys.argv[2]).read(); i = s.index("\n-- CLAIMS")
open(sys.argv[4], "w").write(s[:i] + "\n\nnamespace Old\n\n" + body + "\n\nend Old\n" + s[i:] + open(sys.argv[3]).read())
print("Old:", ", ".join(keep))
```

`equiv_thms.lean`:

```lean
set_option linter.unusedSimpArgs false

-- Equivalence of the old and new executable definitions
-- =====================================================

theorem E_show (t : Term) (d : Nat) : Old.Term.show t d = Term.show d t := by
  induction d, t using Term.show.induct <;> simp_all [Old.Term.show, Term.show]

theorem E_eval (ck : Book) (cl : Bool) (n : Nat) :
    (∀ t xs, Old.Term.wnf ck cl n t xs = Term.wnf ck cl n t xs) ∧
    (∀ t e xs, Old.Term.run ck cl n t e xs = Term.run ck cl n t e xs) ∧
    (∀ t e xs, (∀ q f v, t ≠ App q f (Var v)) → Old.Term.fire ck cl n t e xs = Term.fire ck cl n t e xs) ∧
    (∀ b q t, Old.Term.val ck b n q t = Term.val ck b n q t) := by
  induction n using Nat.strongRecOn generalizing cl with
  | _ n ih =>
  have W : ∀ m < n, ∀ c t xs, Old.Term.wnf ck c m t xs = Term.wnf ck c m t xs := fun m h c => (ih m h c).1
  have R : ∀ m < n, ∀ c t e xs, Old.Term.run ck c m t e xs = Term.run ck c m t e xs := fun m h c => (ih m h c).2.1
  have V : ∀ m < n, ∀ b q t, Old.Term.val ck b m q t = Term.val ck b m q t := fun m h => (ih m h cl).2.2.2
  have F : ∀ m < n, ∀ c t e xs, (∀ q f v, t ≠ App q f (Var v)) → Old.Term.fire ck c m t e xs = Term.fire ck c m t e xs :=
    fun m h c => (ih m h c).2.2.1
  refine ⟨?_, ?_, ?_, ?_⟩
  · intro t xs
    cases n with
    | zero => rw [Old.Term.wnf.eq_def, Term.wnf.eq_def]
    | succ n =>
      rw [Old.Term.wnf.eq_def, Term.wnf.eq_def]
      cases t <;> simp (disch := first | omega | simp) [W, R, V, F]
      all_goals (repeat' split) <;> simp_all (disch := first | omega | simp) [W, R, V, F]
  · intro t e xs
    cases n with
    | zero => rw [Old.Term.run.eq_def, Term.run.eq_def]
    | succ n =>
      rw [Term.run.eq_2]
      by_cases hv : ∃ q f v, t = App q f (Var v)
      · obtain ⟨q, f, v, rfl⟩ := hv
        rw [Old.Term.run.eq_2, Term.fire.eq_1]
        simp only [Term.node]
        have : (App q f (Var v)).takes = false := rfl
        split <;> rename_i h <;> simp [h, R n (by omega), this]
      · have ht : ∀ q f v, t ≠ App q f (Var v) := fun q f v h => hv ⟨q, f, v, h⟩
        rw [Old.Term.run.eq_3 _ _ _ _ _ _ ht, F n (by omega) cl t e xs ht]
        split <;> simp (disch := omega) [R] <;> split <;> rfl
  · intro t e xs ht
    rw [Old.Term.fire.eq_def, Term.fire.eq_def]
    cases n <;> cases t <;> (try cases xs) <;> (try exact absurd rfl (ht _ _ _)) <;> simp (disch := omega) [W, V]
    all_goals split <;> (try split) <;> simp_all
  · intro b q t
    cases n with
    | zero => simp [Old.Term.val, Term.val]
    | succ n =>
      rw [Old.Term.val.eq_def, Term.val.eq_def]
      cases b <;> cases q <;> simp (disch := omega) [W] <;> split <;> simp (disch := omega) [V]

theorem E_wnf (ck : Book) (cl : Bool) (n : Nat) (t : Term) (xs : List Arg) :
    Old.Term.wnf ck cl n t xs = Term.wnf ck cl n t xs := (E_eval ck cl n).1 t xs

theorem E_run (ck : Book) (cl : Bool) (n : Nat) (t : Term) (e : Env) (xs : List Arg) :
    Old.Term.run ck cl n t e xs = Term.run ck cl n t e xs := (E_eval ck cl n).2.1 t e xs

theorem E_fail : @Old.Ctx.fail = @Ctx.fail := by
  funext α c x o; simp [Old.Ctx.fail, Ctx.fail, E_show]

theorem E_fit : Old.Ctx.fit = Ctx.fit := by
  funext ck c U T; simp [Old.Ctx.fit, Ctx.fit, E_show]

theorem E_chk (ck : Book) (n : Nat) :
    (∀ c t, Old.Term.infer ck n c t = Term.infer ck n c t) ∧
    (∀ c t T, Old.Term.check ck n c t T = Term.check ck n c t T) := by
  induction n using Nat.strongRecOn with
  | _ n ih =>
  have I : ∀ m < n, ∀ c t, Old.Term.infer ck m c t = Term.infer ck m c t := fun m h => (ih m h).1
  have C : ∀ m < n, ∀ c t T, Old.Term.check ck m c t T = Term.check ck m c t T := fun m h => (ih m h).2
  constructor
  · intro c t
    cases n with
    | zero => rw [Old.Term.infer.eq_def, Term.infer.eq_def]
    | succ n =>
      rw [Old.Term.infer.eq_def, Term.infer.eq_def]
      cases t <;> simp (disch := omega) [I, C, E_fail, E_fit, E_show]
  · intro c t T
    cases n with
    | zero => rw [Old.Term.check.eq_def, Term.check.eq_def]
    | succ n =>
      rw [Old.Term.check.eq_def, Term.check.eq_def]
      cases t <;> simp (disch := omega) [I, C, E_fail, E_fit, E_show]
      rename_i q f x
      cases x <;> simp (disch := omega) [I, C, E_fit, Term.node] <;> rfl

theorem E_check (ck : Book) (n : Nat) (c : Ctx) (t T : Term) :
    Old.Term.check ck n c t T = Term.check ck n c t T := (E_chk ck n).2 c t T

theorem E_tree (g : Guard) (ps : List Tag) (t : Term) : Old.Term.tree g ps t = Term.tree g ps t := by
  induction g, ps, t using Term.tree.induct <;> rw [Old.Term.tree.eq_def, Term.tree.eq_def] <;>
    simp_all (config := { zetaDelta := true }) [Term.node]

theorem E_defcheck (bk tb : Book) (i : Nat) (d : Def) :
    Old.Def.check bk (bk, tb) i d = Def.check bk tb i d := by
  simp [Old.Def.check, Def.check, E_check, E_tree]

theorem E_from (bk tb : Book) (i : Nat) (ds : List Def) :
    Old.Book.check_from bk (bk, tb) i ds = Book.check_from bk tb i ds := by
  induction ds generalizing i <;> simp [Old.Book.check_from, Book.check_from, E_defcheck, *]

-- the kernel's verdict on a book is unchanged
theorem E_book (bk : Book) : Old.Book.check bk = Book.check bk := by
  simp [Old.Book.check, Book.check, E_from]
```

</details>

- `lean bend2/bendtt.lean`: checks, no `sorry`, about 9 s.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: 56 / 56.

title: fix(comp): a host miss reuses banked cells in address order (#1007)
body:
Fixes #1007.

## Cause

A long-running program slows down with the same instruction count. On the #1007 repro at 4 threads, a round goes from 31 ms to 813 ms, with output and RSS unchanged.

The bank hands generations back in LIFO order. Allocations that don't free anything in place keep shuffling addresses round after round, for example a static string literal on the left of `++`: the copy allocates, but the literal frees nothing. After many rounds a chain's cells are scattered across the heap. Threads make it worse, because shuffled generations move between lanes through the bank.

The same LIFO free list written in plain C degrades the same way, so this is LIFO allocator aging and not codegen.

## Change (host CPU heap only)

**Layout and free map**
- Small classes (`< NCLS`) are bumped in 4096-word windows aligned to 4096 words, one class per window (`heap_bump`).
- A free map (`fm_*`) tracks free words:
  - a bit per free word;
  - a counter per window;
  - per class, a bit per offered window (`FM_SUM`);
  - per class, a bit per nonzero `FM_SUM` word (`FM_TOP`).
- A window is offered once an eighth of it is free.

**What a miss does, in order**
1. Takes the lowest offered window. With nothing offered, this reads one `FM_TOP` word per 4096 windows.
2. Else COLD, as before.
3. Else pops one banked generation:
   - It peeks at the first 64 links. If 7/8 of them stay within a window, the generation is in order and becomes the chain, as on main.
   - Otherwise it is poured into the map, and the miss takes again.
4. Else fresh memory.

**Unchanged**
- Frees, `heap_hand` and COLD reuse are untouched and stay O(1).

**Reservation**
- The map is reserved `PROT_NONE` for the most windows a u32 page count or `RLIMIT_AS` allows.
- It is opened with `mprotect` as the corpus grows. A failed open fails the grow.

**Fallback**
- GPU runs, device code, a `QUANTUM` that isn't a window, and a failed reservation all keep the old path.

## Numbers (M4 Pro, main f0ddfe7b)

#1007 repro, ms per round. Rows 1–12 are the young process, row 96 the aged one; v1 is this PR's first commit.

| threads | | main | v1 | **now** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | rounds 1–12 | 62 … 92 | 77 … 91 | **67 … 69** |
| 1 | round 96 | 197 | 109 | **82** |
| 4 | round 96 | 813 | 53 | **44** |
| 14 | round 96 | 713 | 44 | **34** |

Young process with a big live heap: a 1.4 GB string held across 24 rounds of the repro (`big.bend`), at 1 thread.

| | main | v1 | **now** |
|---|---|---|---|
| round 1 → 24 (ms) | 64 → 160 | 76 → 98 | **67 → 71** |

**Runtime benches**
- All 17 at 1 and 14 threads, best of 3, are within noise. tree-bitonic and histogram were re-timed ×6 at 14 threads.
- Outputs are identical.
- Peak RSS is within +3%, except tree-radix at +4% (682 → 710 MB).

**Linux** (arm64 container):
- Under `ulimit -v` 12–16 GB the map shrinks and stays on: round 96 at 1 thread is 135 ms, vs 206 on main.
- Under `vm.overcommit_memory=2` on a 7 GB VM, main itself fails to reserve its corpus.

**Sanitizers:** ASan+UBSan are clean on the repro at 8 threads.

## Gates (on main f0ddfe7b)

- **test:** `PASS: 1849 / 1849`.
- **ping:** `PASS: 83 / 83`.
- **perf:** `124 / 124` once and `123 / 124` three times, against main at 124/124 in each run.
  - The failing cell is merkle's **compiler** time: 1.16x vs main's 1.13x on the same nodes, with a limit of 1.15x.
  - The cause is the added runtime C: about +14 ms of clang on the Metal host build, after making the `fm_*` functions `noinline`.
  - Runtime cells match main.
- **repo:** `bend2/comp.ts: 68037 > 66000 ttok` (+~2k over main). This needs Taelin's call on the cap, or cuts.

Variants I tried that were worse:
- **Bitmap on every overflow free:** +17–55% on tree-radix.
- **Sorting each generation at hand-off:** 2x the cost on a fresh heap.
- **Per-window LIFO lists:** the repro degrades again.
- **A 1/16 or 1/32 offer mark:** cuts tree-radix RSS to +2.5%, but the repro ages again (t4 round 96: 80 vs 48 ms).

### What you did

`bend PROOF.bend` in `demos/app_slash_boss_3d`, after editing only `main.bend` and `PROOF.bend`. `LAWS.bend` is unchanged. This is the point the review of #2067 left for its own issue (https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2067#issuecomment-6681849972): the laws are stated only through functions in `main.bend`, and they pin `Game.step` rather than the loop.

In `main.bend`, `Game.events` answers `None{}` for every frame. In `PROOF.bend`, `esc_quits` becomes `{==}` and its helper `esc_arm` goes.

```diff
-      Laws.esc_quits(rest, post, g)
-    case Leave{id} <> rest:

-    case Close{} <> rest:
-      {==}
+  {==}
 
 # Sanity

```

</details>

### What happened

On `main` at 266b02ee:

```text
$ bend PROOF.bend
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend PROOF.bend --verdict
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend CHECK.bend
a frame with only w pressed: the game quits
```

Built with `bend main.bend -o` and run from the repo root, the window closes after 0.4 s with exit 0. Unedited, it is still open when `timeout 8` stops it, and `CHECK.bend` prints `the game keeps running`. The same edit gives the same results on the branch of #2067.

### Why it happens

`esc_quits` says that a frame with an Esc anywhere ends the game. A `Game.events` that ends the game on every frame satisfies it, and no law says that a frame with no Esc and no Close keeps the game running.

More generally, each law reaches the game only through functions of `main.bend` (names as on #2067's branch):

| law | stated through |
|---|---|
| `pause_freezes` | `Spec.steps` (each tick one `Game.step`), `Spec.fade` |
| `pause_twice` | `Game.pause`, `Game.paused` |
| `esc_quits` | `Game.events`, `Spec.cat` |
| `back_to_title` | `Game.route`, `Game.init` |
| `pause_toggles` | `Game.pause`, `Game.paused`, `Game.fresh`, `Game.init` |
| `dec_floor`, `dec_is_spec` | `Sim.dec` (and `Spec.dec`) |
| `arrows_are_wasd` | `Key.mask` |

So a law can keep holding in two ways while the game changes: the function it names stops doing its job (`Game.events` above), or the loop stops calling that function. #2067 states the second for `pause_freezes`: with `Live.steps` going through a stepper that runs the clock in a pause, `PROOF.bend` still prints ALL PROOFS CHECK, with `--verdict` too, on that branch.

title: An LE-only compare walks two shared function types as a tree, exponential in their depth (2.0.40)
body:
### What I did

```text
bun bend2/main.ts le_only.bend
```

`le_only.bend` builds two equal function types, `A` and `B`, as let chains: each level is `t -> t` of the level below, so both are shared graphs with one cell per level. It then checks `x => x` against `A -> B`, which compares `A` against `B` in LE. The separate `fa`/`fb` make the rigid pass fail, so the full-book pass does the work. This is the file at 24 levels:

```bend
import Base

def fa(-t: Type) -> Type:
  t -> t

def fb(-t: Type) -> Type:
  t -> t

def P(-X: Type) -> Type:
  -a0 = X
  -a1 = fa(a0)
  -a2 = fa(a1)
  -a3 = fa(a2)
  -a4 = fa(a3)
  -a5 = fa(a4)
  -a6 = fa(a5)
  -a7 = fa(a6)
  -a8 = fa(a7)
  -a9 = fa(a8)
  -a10 = fa(a9)
  -a11 = fa(a10)
  -a12 = fa(a11)
  -a13 = fa(a12)
  -a14 = fa(a13)
  -a15 = fa(a14)
  -a16 = fa(a15)
  -a17 = fa(a16)
  -a18 = fa(a17)
  -a19 = fa(a18)
  -a20 = fa(a19)
  -a21 = fa(a20)
  -a22 = fa(a21)
  -a23 = fa(a22)
  -b0 = X
  -b1 = fb(b0)
  -b2 = fb(b1)
  -b3 = fb(b2)
  -b4 = fb(b3)
  -b5 = fb(b4)
  -b6 = fb(b5)
  -b7 = fb(b6)
  -b8 = fb(b7)
  -b9 = fb(b8)
  -b10 = fb(b9)
  -b11 = fb(b10)
  -b12 = fb(b11)
  -b13 = fb(b12)
  -b14 = fb(b13)
  -b15 = fb(b14)
  -b16 = fb(b15)
  -b17 = fb(b16)
  -b18 = fb(b17)
  -b19 = fb(b18)
  -b20 = fb(b19)
  -b21 = fb(b20)
  -b22 = fb(b21)
  -b23 = fb(b22)
  -A = fa(a23)
  -B = fb(b23)
  A -> B

def p(-X: Type) -> P(X):
  x => x
```

### What happened

The file checks, but the time doubles with each level:

| Levels | Check time |
| ---: | ---: |
| 18 | 0.10 s |
| 20 | 0.14 s |
| 22 | 0.33 s |
| 24 | 1.09 s |
| 26 | 4.18 s |
| 28 | 16.75 s |

As a control, the same two graphs compared in EQ (`P` returns `{A == B : Type}`, proved by `{==}`) check in 0.06 s at 24 levels, and at any depth.

### Why it happens

`compare_go` only links two share cells into one class in its EQ branch ([bend.ts:3196-3204](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/7442eee6ea7a4840fc263c7fff180de2fa264a90/bend2/bend.ts#L3196-L3204)). The class check at the top ([bend.ts:3183-3186](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/7442eee6ea7a4840fc263c7fff180de2fa264a90/bend2/bend.ts#L3183-L3186)) runs in either mode since #2052, so an LE compare benefits once an EQ compare has linked the cells. But when the graphs are only ever compared in LE, nothing links them. Each `All` compares its domains (swapped) and its codomains in LE ([bend.ts:3267-3272](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/blob/7442eee6ea7a4840fc263c7fff180de2fa264a90/bend2/bend.ts#L3267-L3272)), and with `t -> t` both are the same pair of cells, so the walk is `C(n) = 2 C(n - 1)`.

This is the LE counterpart of #993, which the class links fixed for EQ. It's distinct from #984, which duplicates global quantity references while normalizing, with no share cells involved.

### What was tried

In #2052, a filled-cell pair in LE first tried an EQ compare, which links on success. That fixed this file (0.06 s at 24 and 40 levels), but a failed EQ attempt isn't remembered, so the LE walk retried it at every level. A type built by passing a growing `Nat -> t` through an argument (`F(p, Nat -> t)`), checked against the same type ending in `Type` instead of `Data`, went from 0.06 s to 1.04 s at 4,000 levels: quadratic where it was linear. It was reverted (bd0ccbf2).

### Expected behavior

LE should compare a shared graph once, as EQ does. Two possible fixes:

- **Keep the EQ attempt and remember its failures.** A field `n?: Cell` on a class root, where `r.n = l` records that an EQ compare between the classes rooted at `r` and `l` failed under the full book. Rigid-pass failures aren't recorded, since unfolding can turn them into successes. Only the LE pre-attempt would read it, so it only skips a redundant attempt and never changes an EQ or LE answer. That makes the `F(p, Nat -> t)` chain linear again.
- **A memo of LE results** per pair of classes and pass, including failures. That's more general, since it also covers leaves that fit both ways without being equal (`Kind(q <&> r)` against `Kind(r <&> q)`), where no EQ attempt can succeed.

A test for this can't catch a slowdown in CI until BendTT shares cells (#1555): `--verdict` on this file takes 0.9 s at 16 levels and 15.7 s at 20, while the tree walk stays under the test gate's 5 s alarm until about 27 levels.

### Version

```text
bend 2.0.40
commit 7442eee6ea7a4840fc263c7fff180de2fa264a90
Bun 1.3.14
Darwin arm64
Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.4.2)
```

title: Native String.cmp rebuilds both strings on a shared prefix
Map.get re-walks the key from its head at every trie level
body:
Bend 2.0.40 and main `266b02ee40a2`, Darwin arm64, Homebrew clang 22.1.8.

`Map.get.go` calls `Map.bit(key, q)` at each level, and each call walks the key from its first character (`Map.bit.go`). #1725 stopped that walk rebuilding the key; the walk itself remains. So a lookup costs depth x prefix length, which matters for keys sharing a long prefix (paths, URLs, namespaced names). This does not ask to change the trie encoding.

Positions only grow on the way down, so each level can continue from the character the previous level read. The program below does that in user code, over the same `MNode`/`MLeaf` and the same bit layout, and compares the whole key at the leaf as `Map.get` does.

4096 keys, a shared prefix of P characters plus 4 letters, 200,000 hits, seven alternating process pairs, time inside the program. The checksum is 409307552 on both, and equals an independent Python sum.

| Keys | `Map.get` 2.0.40 | Cursor 2.0.40 | `Map.get` main | Cursor main |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| P = 16 (20 chars) | 221 ms | 158 ms | 217 ms | 157 ms |
| P = 64 (68 chars) | 902 ms | 454 ms | 896 ms | 451 ms |

The machine was busy (load 7-15), so read the ratios: 1.4x and 2x. What remains is mostly `String.cmp` at the leaf (reported separately). The same idea should apply to `Map.set` and the other descents; I only measured `get`.

Save as map_cursor.bend (64n is P; replace `get2` in `look` with `Map.get` for the current behaviour):

```bend
import Base

# keys: P copies of 'a', then 4 letters from the low 16 bits of i
def pre(n: Nat, t: String) -> String:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      t
    case 1n+p:
      SCon{Chr{97}, pre(p, t)}

def hex(+i: U32, +s: Nat) -> Char:
  Chr{(97 + U32.and(U32.shrn(i, s), 15) : U32)}

def key(+p: Nat, +i: U32) -> String:
  pre(p, SCon{hex(i, 12n), SCon{hex(i, 8n), SCon{hex(i, 4n), SCon{hex(i, 0n), SNil{}}}}})

def build(n: Nat, +i: U32, +p: Nat, m: Map<&2, U32>) -> Map<&2, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      m
    case 1n+k:
      build(k, (i + 1 : U32), p, Map.set(&2, U32, m, key(p, i), i))

# Map.get with a cursor: positions only grow on the way down, so each level
# continues from the character the last level read.
def drop(n: Nat, s: String) -> String:
  match n s:
    case 0n s:
      s
    case 1n+k SNil{}:
      SNil{}
    case 1n+k SCon{c, t}:
      drop(k, t)

def bit_at(rest: String, off: Nat) -> Bool:
  match rest:
    case SNil{}:
      False{}
    case SCon{c, t}:
      match c off:
        case Chr{x} 0n:
          True{}
        case Chr{x} 1n+b:
          Map.bit.u(x, Nat.sub(31n, b))

def go(-V: Data, node: Map<&2, V>, d: V, +key: String, +rest: String, +ci: Nat, b: Bool) -> Map<&2, V> & V:
  match node b:
    case MNode{p, MTip{}, hi} False{}:
      (MNode{p, MTip{}, hi}, d)
    case MNode{p, MLeaf{k, v}, hi} False{}:
      Map.lo(&2, V, V, p, hi, Map.get.leaf(V, d, v, String.cmp(key, k)))
    case MNode{p, MNode{+q, x, y}, hi} False{}:
      +cq = Nat.div(q, 33n)
      +r2 = drop(Nat.sub(cq, ci), rest)
      Map.lo(&2, V, V, p, hi, go(V, MNode{q, x, y}, d, key, r2, cq, bit_at(r2, Nat.mod(q, 33n))))
    case MNode{p, lo, MTip{}} True{}:
      (MNode{p, lo, MTip{}}, d)
    case MNode{p, lo, MLeaf{k, v}} True{}:
      Map.hi(&2, V, V, p, lo, Map.get.leaf(V, d, v, String.cmp(key, k)))
    case MNode{p, lo, MNode{+q, x, y}} True{}:
      +cq = Nat.div(q, 33n)
      +r2 = drop(Nat.sub(cq, ci), rest)
      Map.hi(&2, V, V, p, lo, go(V, MNode{q, x, y}, d, key, r2, cq, bit_at(r2, Nat.mod(q, 33n))))
    case MTip{} b:
      (MTip{}, d)
    case MLeaf{k, v} b:
      Map.get.leaf(V, d, v, String.cmp(key, k))

def get2(-V: Data, d: V, m: Map<&2, V>, +key: String) -> Map<&2, V> & V:
  match m:
    case MTip{}:
      (MTip{}, d)
    case MLeaf{k, v}:
      Map.get.leaf(V, d, v, String.cmp(key, k))
    case MNode{+p, lo, hi}:
      +cq = Nat.div(p, 33n)
      +r2 = drop(cq, key)
      go(V, MNode{p, lo, hi}, d, key, r2, cq, bit_at(r2, Nat.mod(p, 33n)))

def look(n: Nat, +i: U32, +p: Nat, +acc: U32, r: Map<&2, U32> & U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      (m, v) = r
      (acc + v : U32)
    case 1n+k:
      (m, v) = r
      look(k, (i + 1 : U32), p, (acc + v : U32), get2(U32, 0, m, key(p, U32.and((i * 7 : U32), 4095))))

def run(+p: Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    m : Map<&2, U32> <- IO.pure(Map<&2, U32>, build(4096n, 0, p, Map.new(&2, U32)))
    start : Nat <- IO.now()
    sum : U32 <- IO.pure(U32, look(200000n, 0, p, 0, (m, 0)))
    end : Nat <- IO.now()
    IO.print(U32.show(sum))
    IO.print(Nat.show(Nat.sub(end, start)))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  run(64n)
```

```sh
bend map_cursor.bend -o map_cursor && ./map_cursor
```

title: perf(js): String.eq compiles to ===
body:
On JS, Base's `String.eq` was compiled as written, `Cmp.is_eq(String.order(a, b))`: a loop that takes four `slice`s and allocates a `Cmp` per character. It is now one `===` (a JS-only entry in `OPERATIONS`, like `string_append`; C keeps Base's def).

`===` is exact, not a fast path: a String's JS text is canonical. `char_new` writes a Unicode scalar as itself and any other code as a lone `\uDC00` marker followed by three units below `0x800`, which `fromCodePoint` never produces, and a String literal is only a `Lit` when all its codes are scalars. So two Bend Strings are equal exactly when their JS texts are. (`String.order` cannot use `<` the same way: UTF-16 order is not code-point order.)

- `tests/base/string_eq.bend`: empty, prefixes, astral chars, non-scalar codes (the marker form), surrogate pairs vs the astral char, built and sliced Strings vs literals; passes on interp, JS and C.
- The 22 runnable tests that use `String.eq`/`String.order` print the same on JS; `gates/repo.ts` passes (comp.ts 65,977 -> 65,992 ttok).
- 2M comparisons of 17-character strings on JS: 1.92 s -> 0.01 s.

Context: #2038. Backplane writes string dispatch as `String.eq` helper chains because string-literal patterns blow up compilation (#1266); this makes that workaround fast at runtime.

title: Peak Memory Explooooosion (bend 2.0.40 requires too much memory)
body:
### What you did

Used bend 2.0.40 for the first time. Immediately crashed memory. 

Reproduction:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/dmbarbour/glam-in-bend
cd glam-in-bend && git checkout 9922172
cd spike && bend kernel.bend -o kernel.c
```

### What happened

Peak memory measured in a cgroup of its own (`memory.peak`).

- bend 2.0.39: peak 1.9 GB, 18 s.
- bend 2.0.40: killed at a 6 GB cap after 20 s, and at a 7 GB cap. With
  `BUN_JSC_forceRAMSize=1000000000` it finishes at 7.6 GB, 38 s.

The emitted C is about the same: 3.57 MB against 3.91 MB, and 2,332
`spin_` functions against 2,327. `--check-only` takes 0.9 GB. The JS
target is unaffected: on a smaller program, 1.2 GB against 1.1 GB.
Programs that call into a smaller part of the same code grow faster than
their output: for 0.4 to 1.1 MB of C, 1.9 to 3.0 GB under 2.0.40 against
1.0 to 1.2 GB under 2.0.39.

The likely cause is in `comp.ts`. In 2.0.39, `FL.memo` held the
`opens`, `uses`, `folds` and `spines` caches, and `memo_gc()` cleared
them for each definition the emit loop visited. In 2.0.40 those caches
live on `FL`, along with the new `ground` and `ty_opens`, and only
`FL.folds` is cleared, in `unit_emit`. The caches are `Map`s keyed by
term objects (all but `ty_opens`), so they keep every unit's terms
alive. I emitted the C for a program of 1.1 MB of output, then forced a
full GC (`Bun.gc(true)`):

| | 2.0.39 | 2.0.40 |
|---|---|---|
| heap used | 459 MB | 1,754 MB |
| `ground` entries | (cleared) | 2.28M |
| `opens` entries | (cleared) | 1.02M |
| `spines` entries | (cleared) | 266K |
| `uses` entries | (cleared) | 251K |

To test it, I patched the bundle inside the release binary to clear the
caches alongside `folds`:

```js
function unit_emit(u) {
  FL.folds.clear();
  [FL.opens, FL.uses, FL.spines, FL.ground, FL.ty_opens].forEach((m) => m.clear());
```

I ran the patched bundle under the binary's own Bun (`BUN_BE_BUN=1`).
The C it emits is byte-identical to the release's. Peak memory:

- the kernel: 2.8 to 3.0 GB in three of four runs (the fourth 6.2 GB),
  30 s;
- the 1.1 MB program: 3.0 GB down to 1.8 GB.

A `WeakMap`, as `FL.keys` already is, might do as well.

What remains above 2.0.39 (1.9 GB, 18 s) I haven't traced. The units
that fill the caches most are a template-heavy rewrite
(`krules:rewrite_id~0` to `~3`): 165K `opens` and 324K `ground` entries
in one unit.

One more difference between the releases: 2.0.40's binary embeds Bun
1.3.14, while 2.0.39's embedded 1.4.0.

(Issue co-authored by Opus.)

title: Package Extras or Carry-Ons
body:
### What Bend should do

When building and publishing a package, support packing some extra files beyond the default `*.bend` files, LICENSE, and README. Perhaps something like: 

```sh
bend --publish ... --extra_files ... # or
bend --publish ... --manifest ManifestFile # etc.
```

### Why

I'm developing [a preprocessor for Bend, called Blend](https://github.com/dmbarbour/blend), that supports compile-time objects with multiple inheritance and mixins, and better control of function sharing. It's a thin layer that supports imports of both `.bend` and `.blend` files, but will parse `.blend` files to support inheritance and override. 

I'd like to integrate cleanly with the Bend package system, i.e. such that Bend users can access the generated `.bend` files and Blend users can inherit from `.blend` objects. But, at the moment, `bend --publish` filters all files that aren't `.bend` excepting a README and LICENSE.

I have several workarounds available, but each is awkward in its own way:
- I could include blend source as a comment within the `.bend` file or an associated file.
- I could include blend source as a definition within a `.bend` file, perhaps compressed.
- I could maintain `blend --publish` based on reading `bend` sources, attempt to keep up with API changes.

But the solution I feel best about is to just include the `.blend` files and model publishing as a relatively thin wrapper around `bend` like everything else `blend` does.

title: A task ring pop can mix up two tasks when its slot gets reused
body:
## What you did

I pulled `ring_push` and `monk_step` out of the C that Bend emits (`bun bend2/main.ts bench/runtime/histogram/main.bend -o hist.c`, at 266b02e) and ran them through two memory model checkers: GenMC 0.20 and herd7 7.58 with Arm's official model. The code is the same on main today (be236f3).

## What happened

Each task in a ring is stored in two halves. To pop one, `monk_step` does three things:

1. reads the top half (acquire)
2. reads the bottom half
3. bumps `get` to say "this slot is free now" (relaxed store, comp.ts:4459)

Nothing forces step 3 to wait for step 2. On ARM the CPU is allowed to make the `get` bump visible before the bottom-half read has finished. If a pusher sees that bump, it can write a new task into the same slot, and the late read picks up the new task's bottom half. The pop then runs the top of one task glued to the bottom of another.

Shortest way it happens, on a 2 slot ring:

1. pusher writes task 1 into slot 0, then task 2 into slot 1
2. popper reads task 1's top half from slot 0
3. popper's "slot 0 is free" bump shows up early
4. pusher sees it, writes task 3's bottom half into slot 0
5. popper's bottom-half read lands: it gets top 1 + bottom 3

This is the ARM code clang 18 emits at `-std=c11 -O3`: `ldar` (top), `ldr` (bottom), `str` (`get`), and nothing ties the `ldr` to the `str`. Arm's model says the mixed result can happen:

```
AArch64 TornPop
{ lo=1; hi=1; get=0;
  0:X4=hi; 0:X5=lo; 0:X6=get; 1:X4=hi; 1:X5=lo; 1:X6=get; }
 P0           | P1           ;
 LDAR W0,[X4] | LDR W0,[X6]  ;
 LDR W1,[X5]  | CMP W0,#1    ;
 MOV W2,#1    | B.NE LC00    ;
 STR W2,[X6]  | MOV W1,#3    ;
              | STR W1,[X5]  ;
              | MOV W2,#3    ;
              | STLR W2,[X4] ;
              | LC00:        ;
exists (0:X0=1 /\ 0:X1=3 /\ 1:X0=1)
```

```text
Observation TornPop Sometimes 1 2
```

Make that `STR` an `STLR` and it says `Never`.

There's a second way in that only matters under plain C11 rules: with two pushers, since `get` is passed around relaxed on both ends, an older push's write to the slot can land after a newer one's. That's why the push side needs an acquire too.

GenMC on the emitted code, with 1 to 3 pushers, rings of 2 and 4 slots, and both the host build and the device build's fences:

- as is: mixed-up pop under ARMv8 every time, and under C11 rules whenever there are 2+ pushers
- with the fix below: clean everywhere, up to 501k orderings checked
- either half of the fix alone still fails somewhere

**How likely is it:** low. I haven't seen it on real hardware (I'm on x86, where it can't happen). The ring has to be completely full right then, because the slot being refilled has to be the one being popped. With 1024 slots that's 1023 tasks queued. It can happen though: the work pass does push into rings whose owners are popping them (`task_deal` through `ring_flip`). Same kind of thing as #975, except here Arm's model says the bad result is actually allowed on the code clang emits.

**Which platforms:**

- x86 (Intel/AMD): safe. GenMC's x86 model finds nothing on the code as is (up to 229k orderings), since x86 never lets a store jump ahead of an earlier read.
- ARM CPUs (Apple Silicon, Graviton, Linux arm64): affected, per GenMC's ARMv8 model and Arm's own model above.
- NVIDIA GPUs: probably affected. The device build has no `FENCE()` between the bottom-half read and the `get` bump, and GPUs reorder more freely than ARM. My GenMC run of the device path (its fences written as C11 fences) fails too, but that's an approximation of PTX, not the real thing.
- Apple GPUs (Metal): probably, same reasoning. There's no public formal model to check against.
- Any platform, through the compiler: C11 lets clang reorder those two accesses itself. It doesn't at `-O3` today, but nothing stops it.

The two-pusher case only exists under C11's rules: on ARM hardware the pusher's room check is a branch, and ARM keeps a write after the read that its branch depends on.

## The fix

```diff
@@ ring_push
-  if (pos - a32_load(ring_get(H, r)) >= RING_LEN) {
+  if (pos - a32_load_acq(ring_get(H, r)) >= RING_LEN) {
@@ monk_step
-  a32_store(get, *get + 1);
+  a32_store_rel(get, *get + 1);
```

On x86 this compiles to exactly the same instructions as today. On ARM the store becomes `stlr` and the load `ldar`. On the GPU both go through `FENCE()`.

## bend version

bend 2.0.40

## uname -sm

Linux x86_64

## clang --version (the first line)

Ubuntu clang version 18.1.3 (1ubuntu1)

title: fix(comp): a ring pop publishes get with release, a push reads it with acquire (#2078)
body:
Fixes #2078.

## What was wrong

Popping a task off a ring is three steps: read the top half, read the bottom half, then bump `get` to say the slot is free. The bump was a relaxed store, so on ARM it could become visible before the bottom-half read finished. A push that saw the bump could then refill that same slot, and the pop would end up with the top of one task and the bottom of another. The push side checked for room with a relaxed load of `get`, which under C11's rules lets a second pusher's old write land after a newer one.

The full walk-through, the herd7 test against Arm's model and the GenMC results are in #2078.

## The change

Two lines in `bend2/comp.ts`:

- `monk_step`: `a32_store(get, ...)` becomes `a32_store_rel(get, ...)`, so the bump waits for both reads.
- `ring_push`: `a32_load(ring_get(...))` becomes `a32_load_acq(ring_get(...))`, so a push sees everything the pop did before its bump.

Both helpers already exist and are used the same way elsewhere in the runtime. On the GPU they go through `FENCE()`.

## How I checked it

- GenMC on the C this branch emits (ring code pulled out verbatim): no errors under C11 (RC11) or ARMv8 rules, host and device paths, where main fails under ARMv8 every time.
- On x86 the two functions compile to exactly the same instructions as before (clang 18, `-std=c11 -O3`), so nothing changes there.
- histogram, bfs, hashmap, kmeans, queens and tree-radix built for the CPU print the same output as main.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS 56 / 56.

## Not checked yet

- Speed on ARM: the store becomes `stlr` and the load `ldar`, once per pop and push. I'm measuring the benches on Apple Silicon (GitHub's M1 runners) and will post numbers here.
- The test and perf gates on the minis, which I can't run.

title: fix(err): a context row hidden by a later binder of its name says (shadowed)
body:
Closes #1998.

A `match` binder that reuses a parameter's name printed two context rows with the same name and nothing to tell them apart. When the types agree, the two rows are the same text. Now a row hidden by a later binder of the same name ends in `(shadowed)`:

```
Context:
- rate : U32 (shadowed)
- rate : Nat
```

This is smaller than the issue's proposal: it marks which row is hidden, but doesn't say it is `f`'s parameter, and adds no note at the binder. Both of those would need to track where each binder came from.

- `bend2/bend.ts`: in `err_show`, a row is hidden when it isn't the last of its name in scope (`bnd.lastIndexOf(k) !== i`). This is the test `expr_show` already uses to write a hidden variable as `x^i`.
- `tests/check/ctx_shadowed_binder.bend`: the issue's repro.
- `tests/page/context_dedup_shadow.bend`: its outer `x` row gains the marker.

`bun gates/test.ts` 1845 / 1845, `bun gates/repo.ts` 56 / 56.

title: 2.0.40: on the CPU, every take of a shared node is a call (#1978), +10% instructions on a list-heavy program
body:
#1978 fixed the M1 Metal miscompile by moving the shared-node half of `ctr_take` into `span_fade` and making `span_fade` `FAR`. The PR body says "Host and CUDA keep `OUTLINE` as before, with the last-holder free now inside it", but the C that 2.0.40 emits for the host has `FAR u64 span_fade`, so on the CPU the change is more than a move:

- **2.0.39:** `ctr_take` checks the count inline and frees a last-held node in place. Only a node that really is shared calls `span_fade`, which is `OUTLINE` (cold, `preserve_most`).
- **2.0.40:** every take of a node with the RFC bit calls `span_fade`, a plain `noinline` with the normal calling convention. The count check runs inside it.

I saw it on a BPE tokenizer (`bend-ml-bpe-tokenizer@0.1.3.0`, 256 merges learned from a 4,096-word text, then a 32,768-word text encoded). The repro and a script that counts both releases are in https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/devel/docs/upstream/bpe_encode.bend and [`bpe_encode.sh`](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/devel/docs/upstream/bpe_encode.sh). The setup was one thread pinned to a P-core of a Core Ultra 7 155H, clang 23.1.3 with the `-std=c11 -O3` that `bend -o` uses, and `perf stat` in user mode. The output is the same on every build.

- 2.0.39 runs 177.7 G instructions and 2.0.40 runs 194.2 G (+9.3%). Cycles go from 33.7 G to 43.1 G, part of which is a second, separate regression (#2082).
- I bisected it to #1978. At that commit the count goes from 177.9 G to 196.3 G instructions (+10.3%), and from 33.6 G to 39.1 G cycles. L1 misses stay where they were.
- I added a counter to the C. The program calls `span_fade` 1.21 G times on 2.0.40, against 39.5 M times on 2.0.39. 1.15 G of those calls are takes of a last-held node, which 2.0.39 handles inline.
- With `ctr_take` and `span_fade` put back as in 2.0.39 in `comp.ts` at v2.0.40 (only that text, built with `bun bend2/main.ts`), the program runs 173.6 G instructions. That is 10.6% fewer than the release and 2.3% under 2.0.39.
- Keeping 2.0.40's shape but marking `span_fade` `OUTLINE` makes it worse: 209.1 G instructions. `preserve_most` is then paid on every one of those 1.2 G calls. On the host, the last-holder check has to stay inline.

My suggestion is to keep 2.0.39's `ctr_take` and `span_fade` outside Metal, and #1978's shape under `__METAL_VERSION__` only. I can't test the M1 side. The CUDA build goes through the same `FAR` and may want the same split, but I haven't measured it.

title: 2.0.40: after #2036, a BPE training loop takes 5.6x the L1 misses (+11% cycles)
body:
This is the second of two regressions I found in the same program. The first is #2081, about the take on the host, and it accounts for the instructions. This one accounts for most of the cycles. The program is a BPE tokenizer (`bend-ml-bpe-tokenizer@0.1.3.0`, 256 merges learned from a 4,096-word text, then a 32,768-word text encoded). The repro and a counting script are in https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/devel/docs/upstream/bpe_encode.bend and [`bpe_encode.sh`](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/devel/docs/upstream/bpe_encode.sh); run it with `EVENTS=instructions:u,cycles:u,mem_load_retired.l1_miss:u`. The setup was one thread pinned to a P-core of a Core Ultra 7 155H, clang 23.1.3 with `-std=c11 -O3`, and `perf stat` in user mode. The output is the same on every build.

**What I measured.** I bisected between the tags on L1 load misses and it stopped at #2036 (3c1f0d3a). Against its parent (4024f04d):

- Instructions go down 1.1% (196.3 G to 194.2 G), so #2036 does what it says.
- Cycles go up 11% (39.1 G to 43.4 G).
- L1 load misses go from 0.22 G to 1.24 G, and almost all of them hit in L2 (`mem_load_retired.l2_miss` stays at 0.005 G).

**What I could pin down.** #2036 changes three functions in this program's C. `merge.go` and `count.go` now keep a list element's token (`B{n}`/`M{k}`) boxed and share it with `term_keep`, where before they took it apart and built a fresh node. `bump.go` reuses the taken `Cnt` node in place. I put one function at a time back to its pre-#2036 C, inside 2.0.40's own C:

- `merge.go` and the `peek` it calls, as before: the misses go back to 0.22 G and cycles to 39.2 G. Instructions go up to 198.9 G, since the old `merge.go` does the extra unboxing.
- `count.go` as before: no change (1.24 G).
- `bump.go`'s reuse or free order as before, each one alone and both: no change (1.24 G).
- With this one and #2081's take both put back, 2.0.40 is at 2.0.39 again: 177.1 G instructions, 33.9 G cycles, 0.23 G misses.

The misses are not in `merge.go` itself, though. The sampled profile (`mem_load_retired.l1_miss:pp`) puts them in `bump.go`, the walk over the pair counters during training. There are two reads:

- `heap_alloc` reading a free block's next pointer (`ALC_AT(e, cls) = e.mem[h]`): 118 M to 630 M.
- `term_peek` reading a redirect cell: 7 M to 465 M.

The allocation counts barely move (class 0: 1.262 G to 1.153 G). How long a one-word block waits on its free chain before it is handed out again has almost the same histogram before and after.

**What I haven't proven: why.** My guess is the heap layout that each merge pass leaves for the counting pass after it. Before #2036, `merge.go` rebuilt every token node in list order. Now the old nodes stay where they were, and the counter list's nodes come from free chains in another order, spread over more cache lines. I haven't measured lines touched or data addresses, so take it as a lead. It may also just be what this one program does; I haven't looked for it in others.

title: Executable Packages and Bend scripting
body:
### What Bend should do

```python
bend foo@1.0.0.0/foo.bend ...
bend 0x.../foo.bend

bend --script "import foo@1.0.0.0/foo.bend\n..." ...
```

### Why

Ergonomics. Consistency of naming. Convenience of access. Scriptability.

title: fix(io): a JS TCP.recv's max is a cap, not its buffer size
body:
On the JS lane, `TCP.recv` (and `recv_bytes`, `try_recv`, `try_recv_bytes`) allocated a `Uint8Array` of the whole `max` on every call. Since Bun 1.4.0 those pages are committed, so a receive capped at 1 GiB costs about 1 GB even when 8 bytes arrive. This is the TCP twin of #1983, which #1985 fixed for `File.read`.

The buffer is now `min(max, 64 KiB)`, and the one `recv` reads into it. So one receive answers at most 64 KiB, which TCP already allows (a short read); the rest comes on the next receive. Parking, the `try_` deadline, EINTR, EOF and errors are unchanged. The `INT32_MAX` cap and its comment go, since 64 KiB is below it.

I first tried growing the buffer up to `max` with more `recv` calls, as `file_read.js` does, so one receive could answer more than 64 KiB like C's single `recv(max)`. I dropped it: the extra `recv` can consume a pending `ECONNRESET` (64 KiB arrive, then a reset), and the next receive then answers EOF instead of the error.

The C lane is unchanged. Its `malloc(max)` pages are never touched, so 1000 receives of 8 bytes with a 1 GiB max take 0.01-0.36 s and 2 MB there. It can still answer more than 64 KiB in one receive, where JS now answers at most 64 KiB; both are valid short reads, and no test in `tests/io` expects more than 8192 bytes from one receive. I did not measure bulk throughput (e.g. 10 MB through `TCP.recv(s, 1 MiB)`): it now takes more receives of 64 KiB, but each one no longer commits 1 MiB.

New `tests/io/tcp_recv_cap.bend`: 1000 rounds send 8 bytes over loopback and receive them with a 1 GiB max, then print the byte count (`8000`). It reuses `tcp_bytes.bend`'s helpers, like the other TCP tests, and, like them, expects a small loopback send to arrive in one receive. It prints `8000` on `main` too: what fails there is the gate's 5 s alarm, since the JS lane takes 7-8 s on macOS.

**Environments**

| | macOS | Linux |
|---|---|---|
| Machine | Apple M4 Pro | same Mac, Docker 29.7.2 (4 CPUs, 6 GB) |
| OS | macOS 26.5.1 | Debian 13 (`python:3.12` image), aarch64 |
| Bun | 1.4.2 | 1.4.2 |
| C compiler | Apple clang 17 | clang 19.1.7 |

**`tests/io/tcp_recv_cap.bend` on the JS lane** (`bun bend2/main.ts tests/io/tcp_recv_cap.bend`, 3 rounds alternating `main` and this PR, median with the range)

| | macOS `main` | macOS this PR | Linux `main` | Linux this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Time | 7.85 s (7.43-8.29) | **0.10 s** (0.10-0.10) | 22.76 s (18.55-23.53) | **0.10 s** (0.08-0.13) |
| Peak RSS | 7229-7677 MB | **100-106 MB** | 5546-5666 MB | **94-104 MB** |

`tests/io/tcp_*.bend` pass on the JS and C lanes on macOS. In the Linux container they pass too, except `tcp_text_residue`, which fails the same way on `main` and on both lanes there. Repository gate: 56/56.

title: perf(js): char_len reads the code point once
body:
`char_len` reads the code point once and drops the `s[at]` read and string compare before it. It runs twice for every `SCon` match on the JS lane (head and tail slice), and it was the top self-time function of `bench/runtime/lexer` there: 47.5% of a profile at size 19.

`codePointAt` alone answers both questions: on a packed Char's lone `\uDC00` lead it returns `0xDC00`, and a surrogate pair returns 0x10000 or more, never `0xDC00`. So `c === 0xDC00 ? 4 : c > 0xFFFF ? 2 : 1` gives the same width at every integer offset, which is all the runtime passes. Old against new on every UTF-16 unit followed by each of 7 units, at offsets 0-2, plus 1,000,000 random packed Chars: 2,376,256 cases, no difference, on Bun and Node.

`comp.ts` goes from 65,977 to 65,979 ttok, under its 66k cap. The C lane does not use `char_len`.

New `tests/run/string_walk_char_widths.bend` walks a string with ASCII, an astral code point, a non-scalar code and two surrogate code points (each packed in four units on JS), one `SCon` match per Char, and prints the count and an order-sensitive hash: `(7, 751504163)` on the interpreter, the JS build and C, on `main` and on this branch (`bun bend2/main.ts tests/run/string_walk_char_widths.bend`). The 34 `tests/run` files that use `String` pass on the JS and C lanes.

**`bench/runtime/lexer` (size 23) on the JS lane**, `bun bend2/main.ts bench/runtime/lexer/main.bend`, 3 rounds alternating, median (range). Apple M4 Pro with macOS 26.5.1, and Linux in Docker on the same Mac (Debian 13 aarch64, 4 CPUs, 6 GB); Bun 1.4.2 on both.

| | macOS `main` | macOS this PR | Linux `main` | Linux this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Time | 36.74 s (36.22-37.57) | **30.12 s** (30.09-30.31) | 38.45 s (37.26-38.90) | **32.02 s** (30.98-33.04) |
| Peak RSS | 118-120 MB | 119-120 MB | 113-117 MB | 114-116 MB |

Both print `2401049475`, the bench's expected checksum.

title: fix(comp): reduce native emitter cache retention
body:
Refs #2076.

When Bend emits C for the reported Glam kernel, compiler caches keep temporary terms from earlier functions alive. Under a 6 GiB memory limit on Linux arm64, current main was killed before it wrote the C file. The patched compiler emits byte-identical C and peaked at 3.93 and 4.25 GiB in two separate runs.

The C emitter uses weak keys for opened binders, preserving their cached bodies while the terms are live. Before emitting each ordinary or generated native function, it clears the cache of constant-tree checks if it holds more than 262,144 entries.

Two macOS series measured a 42–43% drop in median peak memory on the reported kernel. Median emission time went from 10.05 to 10.07 seconds in one series and from 9.89 to 10.34 seconds in the independent repeat. Some of the memory gap relative to Bend 2.0.39 remains.

Nine fixtures passed native and Bun execution in the independent review, the local compiler-state checks passed, and the repository gate passed 56/56.

title: fix(runtime): a device lane that misses the heap stops at its next step (#1924)
body:
Fixes #1924.

## Cause

A failed device allocation posts ERR_HEAP and hands out HEAP_OFF, page 0, which every failing lane shares. The lane only learned of the error from the poll every 4096 steps, so it kept running on nodes other lanes were overwriting. A fork or bang that missed also returned its task straight out of `work_loop`, and `monk_step` dealt it to other lanes' rings without polling at all. The shared-flag fixes proposed on the issue (and on the HIP branch) don't cover that second path.

## Change

- On a miss, the lane sets a private latch (`Env.stop`, device only). `err_spun` reads it at every step: in the dispatch loop, in looping spins, and in `term_drop`.
- `monk_step` reads the error word whenever `work_loop` returns a task, before dealing or pushing it. This replaces its 4096-step counter.
- Spins that never loop no longer poll, since the next step of their segment does. Polling at the entry of every spin cost gameoflife 8% on an M4.
- On the host, `err_spun` is `0`, as `err_post` exits there.

The latch is the same idea as oxura's branch on the issue.

## Results

**Misses** (Metal, `--gpu 512MB`, instrumented): tree-radix 18.7M → 5.0k, hashmap 377k → 1.6k, i.e. about one miss per lane.

**AMD** (RX 6600M, the HIP branch rebased onto this; 5 runs a case):

| case | no fix | this fix |
|---|---|---|
| tree-radix 512MB / 768MB / 1GB | faults 15/15 | out of memory 15/15 |
| tree-bitonic 512MB | faults 5/5 | out of memory 5/5 |
| tree-matmul 768MB | faults 5/5 | out of memory 5/5 |

The fault was `Memory access fault by GPU … Page not present` after about 17 s. With the fix, the run stops in 0.17 s.

**Perf:**
- **CPU:** the host machine code is identical to main for all 17 benches. The only difference is the file name.
- **Metal:** perf gate 124/124, over two runs each of main and this PR. Most benches are within noise; the steadiest costs are queens +4%, symreg +5%, tree-bitonic +5%, tree-matmul +4% and lexer +3%.
- **HIP:** the private latch costs tree-matmul +10% and tree-radix +6%. One `__shared__` slot per lane brings that back to within about 1%.
- **CUDA:** untested. It shares the HIP code path (`BEND_RTC`), so it needs measuring (see the comment below).

## Gates

- repo 56/56, test 1845/1845, perf 124/124.
- comp.ts is at 65,999 of 66,000 tokens.

title: refactor(comp): a round of simplifications, 65,994 -> 65,940 ttok
body:
A round of simplifications in `bend2/comp.ts`: **65,994 → 65,940 ttok** (−54; the cap is 66k), in that file only.

The file has been through many rounds already; four independent passes (compiler front, compiler back end, C runtime, JS runtime) found little left that simplifies rather than golfs. Everything here keeps the file's style, and no cache is touched.

## What changes

**C runtime**
- `f32_text` writes the fixed form with `snprintf("%.*f", p - ex)`, which rounds at the same place, 10^(ex − p), as the scientific form did; a whole number moves the digits over the point and pads with zeros. This replaces copying the digits into `d[9]` and rebuilding the string place by place.
- The host's globals and their device stand-ins (`KEEP_WORDS`, the `f32_show` / `f32_read` stubs, `corpus_grow`) share `Globals`' one `#if !DEVICE … #else` split, instead of three separate ones.

**Compiler**
- `facts_hot` names its forced recursion `hot`, built only in the branch that uses it, instead of repeating `facts_hot(def, x, true, local)` three times.
- `nat_is_lt` needs no `$o` substitution.
- `ctr_adt` uses the existing `tld_of`.
- `anf`'s `Lam` case binds the instantiated body `all.B(DUMMY)` once instead of computing it twice.

## Verification

- **Emitted programs:** `bend f -o f.c` and `-o f.js` on all 1,935 test, demo and bench programs, against `main` (ca77ef28). Every compile error is identical. Every `.js` is identical to `main`'s, and every `.c` differs from it by the same single diff, which is exactly the C runtime edits above. So no compiler change alters any output.
- **`f32_text`:** compared bit for bit with the old function on every float32 from 0x33000000 to 0x63000000, both signs (about 1.6 billion values, past both cut-offs), every denormal, inf and nan: 0 differences.
- **Machine code:** for all 17 benches, the host CPU objects are byte-identical, the Metal AIR is byte-identical, and the host Metal build differs only in the embedded source's size.
- **Gates:**
  - `gates/repo.ts`: 56 / 56.
  - `gates/test.ts`: 1,847 / 1,847. An earlier run on the same commit had 4 misses that didn't repeat.
  - `gates/perf.ts`: 124 / 124 on a rerun. The first run's one miss, queens PAR-CPU at 1.39x, read 1.02x on the rerun, and also 1.02x on `main` run right after.
- Not tested: CUDA (no edit touches its code) and Linux. glibc's `%f` is exact too, so the `f32_text` argument holds there, but it was run only on macOS.

title: test(io): every test file gets a fresh /tmp name, and a gate's shard its own directory
body:
Two test runs at the same time (two agents, for example) raced each other in three ways:

- The io tests wrote fixed paths such as `/tmp/bend_io_file.tmp`, while a few tests already drew random names, so the tests did not agree with each other.
- Each gate shard reused `$HOME/bend-test/<shard>` after an `rm -rf`, so a second gate on the same mini deleted the first one's builds.
- Every shard deleted all of the user's `/tmp/bend_io_*` and `bend_gfx_*` files before and after it ran, including files a running gate was still using.

## Changes

- **Tests:** every io/gfx test that opens a file draws a random number at the top of `main` and uses one fresh path:
  ```
  def tmp(salt: U32) -> String:
    "/tmp/bend_t_io_<name>_" ++ U32.show(salt)
  ...
    +salt : U32 <- IO.try(U32, IO.random_u32())
  ```
  Only the `U32` salt is shared: a shared `String` path would make `SCon` hot and move the tests off the cold `io_str` path they check. Every changed test compiles to the same hot constructors and `rfc_` count as on `main`.
  Helpers take the salt as an argument instead of a fixed name or a `path()` def. A test that needs a second file adds a suffix (`_append`, `_excl`, `_missing`, `_mode`). `path_utf8` and `file_open_bytes` keep the `é` at the end of the name.
- **`file_write_at_append_fd`:** `Fd.append(path)` takes the path it opens in both the C and JS twins.
- **FIFO twins:** `fifo_eof`, `file_read_short` and `file_open_fifo_peer` already named their FIFOs by process ID and deleted them right after opening, so they are unchanged.
- **New prefix:** files are named `bend_t_io_*` / `bend_t_gfx_*`. A gate run from an older branch still deletes every `bend_io_*` file, which would remove this branch's files mid-test, and the new prefix is outside that pattern.
- **Cleanup:** each test deletes its own files as `main` ends (`rm -f` through `Process.run`, found in `PATH`), then returns `main`'s original result, so the expected output is unchanged. `file_binary` is the exception: it already shares a list, and linking `Process.run` would make `String` hot there, so its file is left for the sweep.
- **`gates/test.ts`:**
  - Each shard builds in `mktemp -d $HOME/bend-test/<shard>.XXXXXX` and exits if that fails, instead of unpacking into `$HOME`.
  - One sweep at the start deletes test files older than an hour (including older gates' `bend_io_*` / `bend_gfx_*` leftovers) and shard directories older than a day, which catches what a crashed run left behind. `$d` is touched after unpacking, so the archive's timestamp can't make it look old.
  - Each gate writes its shard logs to a fresh `mkdtemp` directory under `/tmp/bend-test/` and prints that path to stderr when tests fail or the cluster run throws, in `--gate` mode too. It deletes log directories older than a day and skips any that another gate deleted first.

## Testing

- `bun gates/test.ts`: PASS 1847 / 1847

title: perf(js): char_new takes fromCharCode below the surrogates
body:
`String.fromCodePoint` was 18% of the JS lexer's self time. Below 0xD800 a Char is a single UTF-16 unit, and `String.fromCharCode` (which JSC inlines) produces the same string. Codes from 0xD800 up go through the same paths as before.

## Numbers (JS lane, `bench/runtime/lexer`, local M4 Max)

| size | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 19 (medians of 5 interleaved runs) | 2.73 s | 2.09 s (−23%) |
| 23, the bench's size (one run each) | 45.1 s | 38.0 s (−16%) |

Output is `2394243056` / `2401049475` on both. The C lane is untouched.

## Tokens

`comp.ts` goes from 65,994 to 65,997 ttok. The comment above `char_new` is rewritten: "non-scalar" covers the surrogate codes that the old "past the Unicode scalars" missed; "its u32 in three pieces" replaces "three 11-bit pieces", since the first piece (`c >>> 22`) holds 10 bits; and "the JS runtime copies this function" says why `char_new` must stay self-contained. The ternary now has one case per line, like the file's other chains.

Extending the fast path to 0xE000–0xFFFF would put `comp.ts` at 66,008, over the cap, and the lexer (all ASCII) measured the same with it, so it waits for room.

## Gates

- repo 56/56, ping 83/83, test 1847/1847 (alone, on slot 0).
- perf 121/124: the three failing cells are `queens` (COMPILER 1.29x, SEQ-CPU 1.21x, PAR-CPU 1.28x). A clean `origin/main` fails the same three cells in the same run conditions (1.21x, 1.18x, 1.31x), so `queens` has already regressed on main and it isn't from this change.
- A full `gates/_run.ts` puts the test gate on slot 1, where minis 50+ hold another user's `/tmp/bend_io_*` files, and 4–5 io tests fail with `Permission denied`; #2089 addresses that.

## Not done here

The rest of the walk's cost (`char_len`, ~31% self time) is rope flattening plus a substring for each tail, paid by whichever helper reads a fresh string first. Calling `char_len` once per match, or reading the code without copying the head, measured no faster, so they're left out.

title: fix(comp): a large device program splits its dispatch into parts by call order (#1979)
body:
Fixes #1979, and makes split programs faster on the GPU.

## Root cause

On the device, `work_loop` is one function: a `for (;;) switch (fid)` with a case for every device segment. Metal's compiler takes time and memory superlinear (about quadratic) in that one switch, and a wide register bank multiplies the cost. Measured with the runtime's own Metal build path (`newLibraryWithSource`, then a binary-archive pipeline), on main:

| device cases | bank | back end | compiler peak |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1,504 | narrow | 57 s | 1.9 GB |
| 3,004 | narrow | 270 s | 4.7 GB |
| 3,007 | 165 | 458 s | 4.6 GB |

The report's program has 5,749 cases and a 165-wide bank (`WL_RESW 165`). At that size the compiler needs well over 16 GB, hence the `bad_alloc` abort in `MTLCompilerService`. The report's workaround of splitting the dispatcher into chunks of 64 avoids it for the same reason this fix does.

## Fix

A device program that needs more than one part (9 device cases or more) splits its segments into `noinline` parts of about `2^PART` (8). Each part is its own function with its own `switch`.
- **Grouping:** segments go into parts in the order control reaches them from the bangs: a segment, then what it calls, then its own function's continuations. A function of up to 32 device segments stays whole in one part, so a hot loop doesn't cross parts. A constant table `WL_GRP` maps each id to its part.
- **Jumps:** a jump inside a part is unchanged. A jump to an id outside the part saves the lane's state in a `Wl` and returns. `work_loop` then calls the next part directly through `wl_hop`. An id no part holds reports `ERR_FIDS`, as `work_loop`'s default does on main.
- **Copies:** a part copies only the registers its segments take or pass on, at a width fixed when compiling. The copies fold to straight-line code. Most parts copy 1–2 registers.
- **Small programs:** programs of 8 device cases or fewer keep one switch and the same device code as main, plus unused macros.

What the design rests on:
- **`noinline` is required.** With parts of 256 inlined, the 3,007-case wide program's back end takes 157 s and 3.7 GB, against 22 s with the same parts out of line.
- **The copy width must be a constant.** Copying only the target's registers with a count decided at runtime made Metal's front end take 301 s and 5.5 GB on an 1,800-case program.
- **Grouping by id loses.** An earlier version of this PR grouped by id. Forced on the benches, it made `symreg` 5× slower, because its hot functions were spread over many parts. Grouping by call order fixes that.
- **Parts of 8.** Bigger parts compile slower and lose the runtime gain; see the comment below for the sweep over 8–128.
- **Splitting a program that fits in one part only costs.** In one part, `queens` is 5% slower and `histogram` 2% slower, with no gain.

## Measurements (M4 mini)

**Metal compile**, the 3,007-case, 165-wide program (front + back end, compiler peak): 493 s and 4.6 GB on main, 16 s and 1.2 GB with this PR.

**Perf gate**, 12 clean alternating rounds against main:

| | main | this PR | change |
|---|---|---|---|
| runtime, all cells | 86.04 s | 83.92 s | −2.6% (p < 0.001) |
| compile, all cells | 10.42 s | 11.18 s | +7.1% (p < 0.001) |
| checker | 2.52 s | 2.52 s | no change |

GPU runtime cells that changed significantly:

| bench (device cases) | change |
|---|---|
| lexer (15) | −77% |
| tree-matmul (72) | −17% |
| symreg (40) | −8% |
| tree-radix (26) | −1.3% |
| histogram (32) | +2.4% |
| queens (13) | +7.5% |

Compile cells that changed most: `tree-matmul` +54%, `symreg` +32%, `mandelbrot` +25%, `histogram` −8%. Each is under 0.3 s. `kmeans` read +37% here but −5% in an earlier run, while main's own time on that cell moved from 0.80 s to 0.56 s, so that cell is unreliable. CPU cells don't change.

**910-case synthetic benchmark** (300 functions, 16,384 lanes, a call chain that jumps between functions on almost every call), mean of 5 runs: narrow bank 384 ms on main, 240 ms with this PR; 165-wide bank 507 ms against 283 ms.

## Testing

- **Test gate:** 1847/1847. Also 1847/1847 with every test program split, bang tests included.
- **GPU checks:** split programs of 117–397 parts, up to 165 wide, give the same output on the GPU as on the CPU and the interpreter.
- **Not tested:**
  - CUDA. The code path is shared under `DEVICE`.
  - The report's own program. It is built with a downstream patch, so I used synthetic programs of the same size and bank width.
  - Why `lexer` gains 4×. It gains only when split into 2 or more parts; in one part it doesn't change. My guess is register pressure in the one big switch, not verified.

## Token cap

`comp.ts` goes from 65,943 to 67,190 ttok, over the 66,000 cap, so `gates/repo.ts` fails on that one check. The fix and grouping need about 1,250 tokens. This needs either a cap raise or savings elsewhere in `comp.ts`.

title: Emission exhausts the host stack on a finite 4096-let chain (reproduced in 2.0.36, 2.0.39 and 2.0.40)
body:
## Summary

On official Bend 2.0.36, 2.0.39 and 2.0.40, the identical Base-only program generated below passes `--check-only`, but both native compilation and JS emission exit 1 with:

```text
Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)
```

The program has 4096 sequential `U32.add` bindings and takes its initial value from `IO.args`. It has no recursive type alias, large Nat/string literal, application imports, or host FFI. The largest numeric literal in the generated Bend source is `1`.

## Reproducer

Save the following as `gen.py`, then run `python3 gen.py`:

```python
from pathlib import Path

n = 4096
source = """import Base

def number(m: Maybe<&2, U32>) -> U32:
  match m:
    case Some{n}: n
    case None{}: 0

def input(args: List<String>) -> U32:
  match args:
    case Nil{}: 0
    case path <> tail:
      match tail:
        case Nil{}: 0
        case value <> rest: number(U32.read(value))
"""
source += "\ndef work(x: U32) -> U32:\n"
previous = "x"
for i in range(n):
    source += f"  v{i} = U32.add({previous}, 1)\n"
    previous = f"v{i}"
source += f"  {previous}\n"
source += """
def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    result : U32 = work(input(args))
    IO.print(U32.show(result))
"""
Path("deep.bend").write_text(source)
```

The generated file is 112,930 bytes, SHA-256 `a743afea20b6b3a0512f6f86f621fe7fb1e261f97823a94d17a4669c38baf702`.

```sh
bend version
# bend 2.0.40

bend deep.bend --check-only
# ALL PROOFS CHECK
# Use --verdict for mathematical validity.
# exit 0

bend deep.bend -o deep.native
# Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)
# exit 1

bend deep.bend -o deep.js
# Error: the machine stack overflowed (a deep recursion, or a literal too large to expand)
# exit 1
```

The check-only output establishes typed compatibility, not mathematical validity.

| Official release | Typed check | Native emission | JS emission |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0.36 | exit 0, ALL PROOFS CHECK | exit 1, stack exhaustion | exit 1, stack exhaustion |
| 2.0.39 | exit 0, ALL PROOFS CHECK | exit 1, stack exhaustion | exit 1, stack exhaustion |
| 2.0.40 | exit 0, ALL PROOFS CHECK | exit 1, stack exhaustion | exit 1, stack exhaustion |

The 2.0.36 and 2.0.39 rows are fresh controlled runs on the byte-identical source, same host, same selected CC, and unchanged OS/VM stack budgets. The 2.0.40 row reuses the previously recorded identical-source/binary observation; it was not rerun merely to reconfirm failure.

**This reproducer does not establish a newly introduced 2.0.40 regression.** It also does not compare the maximum passing depth across versions. A smaller 768-binding native compilation completed on 2.0.40; I have not established the smallest failing length.

## Narrowed cause

Using the tagged 2.0.40 sources at `624dd9f4607cd29b0871a9b96d413bfb11e92f52` with external Bun 1.4.4 and diagnostic-only original exception reporting, C emission fails with `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`.

The expanded stack shows nested use analysis:

```text
term_uses -> term_kids -> let_live -> rest_use -> term_uses -> ...
```

The immediate top of that standalone trace is `term_higher`, reached by `term_open`; the enclosing use/liveness calls account for the repeated depth. On a larger real application, the trace directly repeats the `term_uses` child-reduction frames at `comp.ts:538`.

This source diagnostic used an external Bun, not an assertion that it is identical to the official binary's embedded runtime. No compiler stack-budget override was used for the failing source or official-binary reproductions. Increasing the number of captured stack frames was diagnostic-only, not an increase in the VM stack budget.

## Focused repair experiment

An experimental iterative use-analysis change eliminates this failure. The repaired source compiler builds the reproducer; its native and emitted-JS programs both print `4103` for argument `7`.

After compiling with that experimental repair:

```sh
./deep.native +RTS --threads 1 -RTS --RTS 7
# 4103
bun deep.js 7
# 4103
```

On the real application, the repaired compiler at ordinary resources emits C byte-identical to the unmodified source compiler with an explicitly enlarged stack budget. The resulting native application also passes focused execution/reuse/corruption controls. Small ownership, let-liveness, closure-capture and match controls retain their original C and native/JS outputs; an invalid `Bool` body for an `IO(Unit)` main is still rejected.

I am minimizing the compiler-only patch before proposing it. This is not a claim that every recursive compiler helper becomes stack-safe, and the installed official release has not been patched.

The reduced prototype changes only `comp.ts` (+36/-8 lines), but it currently measures 66,246 tokens using the gate's `gpt-3.5-turbo` counting model, against the permanent 66,000 cap. This is not a ready-to-merge PR, and I am not requesting a cap increase.

## Relation to existing decisions

I read the closure discussions, not only the issue titles:

- [#791](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/791#issuecomment-5733085716) already mentions approximately 4000 sequential do-block statements failing. Its maintainer closure identifies the Nat-checking case as a duplicate of #779; [#779's final note](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/779#issuecomment-5733558598) fixes Nat literals while retaining the general depth limitation. I am not claiming the first report of long-body stack exhaustion.
- [#1127](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/1127#issuecomment-5858034040) was closed by its reporter citing the WONTFIX policy for emitter recursion on a large expanded literal; I do not treat that as a separate maintainer decision on this use-analysis patch.
- [#993](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/993#issuecomment-5855957778) explains the deliberate common-path tradeoff for exponential equality checking.

I understand those limits and am not requesting a beta-optimal checker or unlimited term depth. The standalone failure is already present in all three tested releases. Source-level diagnosis on 2.0.40 isolates the use-analysis traversal on ordinary sequential bindings, including a real-application failure without a giant literal; no old-release throw-site identity is claimed.

**Is this specific `term_uses`/Let-liveness case already tracked, and would a focused iterative repair be welcome if it preserves emitted output and fits the existing source-size cap? Or is this case also intentionally covered by the existing WONTFIX policy?**

## Environment

- Official Bend 2.0.36, 2.0.39 and 2.0.40 distributions; source-level diagnosis and repair are specifically against 2.0.40 tag commit `624dd9f4607cd29b0871a9b96d413bfb11e92f52`.
- macOS 26.6.2, Darwin arm64.
- Compiler OS/VM stack budgets were not increased for the reproductions or patched-source passes.
- Source diagnostics and source-fork checks: external Bun 1.4.4. Official embedded-runtime equivalence was not established.
- Diagnosis, reproducer, patch and focused checks were prepared with AI assistance; the commands above are reproducible independently.

title: Metal: IR evaluator works on CPU but fails on M1 Max
body:
## Reproducer

https://github.com/IlyaGulya/bend-metal-repro

Includes the source, build/run instructions, pinned compiler version, and candidate patch.

The input is three IR nodes:

```bend
[Ir.ISlot{0}, Ir.IInt{1}, Ir.IAdd{0,1}]
```

State slot 0 contains `2`. The full evaluator module is included: a smaller standalone evaluator did not reproduce the failure. No model checking or BFS runs in this example.

## Results

CPU and Metal use the same original binary.

| Input node | Original CPU | Original Metal | Patched Metal |
|---|---|---|---|
| `0` | `2` | fails | `2` |
| `1` | `1` | fails | `1` |
| `2` | `3` | fails | `3` |

The recorded error is `frontier drained without a result`. Earlier runs also produced `a function the device does not hold` or `memory fault (machine stack overflow?)`.

Environment: M1 Max, 32 GPU cores, Darwin 25.6.0, Apple clang 21. C generated on Linux with Bun 1.4.4. Native runs use `--threads 4` and `--gpu 512MB`.

## Candidate workaround

[Patch](https://github.com/IlyaGulya/bend-metal-repro/blob/master/patches/bend-device-work-dispatch.patch)

The patch replaces device Work self-loops with VM redispatch, reloading entry/frame arguments. It leaves the original inliner, host path, and native flat loops unchanged.

This makes the reproducer pass on actual Metal, without CPU fallback. The same patch passed 23 full-checker CPU/Metal cases and 23 comparisons against TLC.

This is a workaround, not a confirmed root-cause fix. It may avoid a Metal compiler defect rather than repair invalid Bend lowering. Current main, CUDA, and general performance impact were not tested.

Possibly related: #1954 and #1978. A shared root cause has not been established.
