title: perf(js): an Array index wraps with a mask, as C's blk_at does
body:
On the JS lane, `Array.get`, `Array.set`, `Array.swap` and `array_rmw` (which the JS atomics also use) wrapped the index with `i % a.length`, an integer division on every array access. A Bend `Array` is a 2^d tree: `ALeaf` has length 1, `ANode` joins two halves of equal length (`array_node` throws otherwise), and `array_new` is `Array(2 ** d)`. So the length is always a power of two, and `i & a.length - 1` reaches the same cell, as C's `blk_at` already does.

The index is a U32 (0 to 2^32 - 1). `&` first turns it into a signed 32-bit integer, which keeps its low bits, and `a.length - 1` is at most 2^31 - 1, so the result equals `i % a.length` for every index: 0 differences over every power-of-two length up to 2^31, at the edges and 20,000 random indices per length. `tpl` only substitutes variables and constants (`op_bare`, else `emit_hold`), so no substituted expression changes the precedence. An array handed in by foreign JS with another length is outside the `Array` layout and not covered.

`comp.ts` goes from 65,943 to 65,976 ttok, under its 66k cap; 33 of those are the comment that states the invariant. The C lane is unchanged.

New `tests/run/array_wrap_high_index.bend` does a get, a set and a swap at 2^32 - 1, 2^31 + 6 and 2^32 - 4 on four cells, the indices where the 32-bit conversion goes negative, and prints `13991007` on the interpreter, the JS build and C, on `main` and on this branch. It passes on `main` too: it pins the wrap the mask has to keep. The 23 `tests/run` files and 57 other test files that use arrays print the same on the JS lane as on `main`.

**`bench/runtime/bfs` on the JS lane**, median of alternating rounds (5 on macOS, 3 on Linux). Apple M4 Pro with macOS 26.5.1, and Linux in Docker on the same Mac (Debian 13 aarch64, 4 CPUs, 6 GB); Bun 1.4.2 on both. Both print `651176970`.

| | macOS `main` | macOS this PR | Linux `main` | Linux this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Built JS (`-o bfs.js`, `bun bfs.js`) | 32.25 s | **23.08 s** | 31.24 s | **22.05 s** |
| `bun bend2/main.ts bench/runtime/bfs/main.bend` | 34.92 s | **32.06 s** | 35.43 s | 34.94 s |
| Peak RSS, built JS | 54-78 MB | 60-78 MB | 60-62 MB | 60-61 MB |

The built JS, the file `-o x.js` writes, gains about 30% on both machines. Run through `main.ts`, the same bench is slower to begin with and gains about 8% on macOS and 1% on Linux; I have not found why the two paths differ. `editdist` and `terrain` through `main.ts` stayed within run-to-run noise (3 rounds each on macOS).

Revert: the `get` and `set` templates, `array_rmw` and the comment in `bend2/comp.ts`, and the new test.

title: perf(js): Array.swap and the atomics hand array_swap a value, not a closure
body:
On the JS lane, `Array.swap` compiled to `array_rmw(a, i, () => (v))` and every `Array.atomic.*` to `array_rmw(a, i, (o) => ...)`, so each write allocated a closure. The one helper is now `array_swap(a, i, v)`: it stores `v` and returns the old cell.

- `swap` passes its value: `array_swap(a, i, v)`.
- An atomic passes its new value, with the old cell read inline where its text says `$o`: `add` is `array_swap(a, i, (a[i & a.length - 1] + v) >>> 0)`.
- `exch` is just its value, the same call as `swap`.
- `AT`, the masked cell read, is shared by `set`, `get` and the atomics.

The JS lane runs one thread, so reading the cell in the argument and again in `array_swap` sees the same value. The C lane is unchanged. `comp.ts` stays at 65,974 ttok, as on `main`.

No new test: the 52 test files that use `Array.swap`, `set`, `get` or the atomics and build print their `#|` lines on the JS lane, among them `tests/run/array_fork.bend` (every atomic) and `tests/reg/array_function_element.bend` (function values swapped in and called).

**`bench/runtime/terrain` on the JS lane** (built JS, `bun terrain.js`), 3 rounds in rotating order on an Apple Mac, on top of #2097. All print `2572468224`.

| | median | runs |
|---|---:|---|
| `main` | 44.4 s | 38.2, 48.5, 44.4 |
| this PR | **37.8 s** | 35.4, 37.8, 39.9 |

No bench calls the atomics; in a micro-bench (5e7 `add`/`cas` calls) they drop from 200-330 ms to as low as ~72 ms, though bun's inlining makes single runs bimodal.

Revert: `AT`, the `swap` and atomic JS templates and `array_swap` in `bend2/comp.ts`.

title: fix(verdict): ignore template binder names in instance keys
body:
`--verdict` rejects equal template applications when their lambda parameter names differ. In #2092, `List.map(~Bool, ~Bool, ~(x => x), xs)` and the same call with `y => y` produce separate recursive kernel definitions.

The elaborator now omits binder names from specialization keys. It keeps variable levels, quantities, global names, constructor names, and literal values. Root constants reuse the existing key helper. The regression covers renamed lambdas, nested lambdas, and function types. It also checks that different variable levels and constructors remain distinct.

Fixes #2092.

Validation:

- Built the current BendTT kernel with Lean 4.34.0. The new regression and both reproductions fail before the fix and pass after it.
- Compared 134 local verdict runs: 122 existing proof files, 9 check files, the new regression, and 2 reproductions. The other 131 files have identical output and exit status. No timeout occurred.
- The repository gate reports `PASS: 56 / 56`. `safe.ts` is 23,998 / 24,000 tokens. `git diff --check` passes.
- Independent key checks preserve semantic fields and the equality relation across 168 root-key examples. Deliberately removing variable levels or constructor names makes the regression fail.
- TypeScript checking reports the same five errors in the unchanged baseline and this patch, in `bend.ts` and `comp.ts`. Cluster gates were not run.

title: fix(demos): app_slash_boss_3d's laws keep a frame with no Esc and no Close going
body:
Part of #2071. #2101 covers the other half of the same issue. The two PRs change different lines, so they merge in either order.

### Why

#2071 came out of the review of #2067 (https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2067#issuecomment-6681849972). It shows two ways that a law of `app_slash_boss_3d` keeps holding while the game changes:

1. The function that a law names stops doing its job. The review's example: if `Game.events` answers `None{}` for every frame, `esc_quits` still holds, and its proof becomes `{==}`. The built game then closes on its first frame.
2. The loop stops calling the function that a law names. #2101 covers this half.

This PR covers the first half. `esc_quits` says that a frame with an Esc anywhere ends the game. No law says the other side: that a frame with no Esc and no Close keeps the game. So a `Game.events` that ends the game on every frame satisfies every law.

#2071 left the choice of laws to you. This is the smallest law I found that closes its example. I'm happy to restate it, or to close this PR.

### What changes

- `LAWS.bend`: a new law, `calm_keeps`. For any game and any list of events with no Esc and no Close, `Game.events` answers `Some{...}`, so the game goes on. The header of the file lists the new law.
- `SPEC.bend`: `Calm(es)` says which lists of events count. It is a type: `Unit` when the list holds no Esc and no Close, and `Empty` when it holds one. `Calm.key` handles a single key.
- `PROOF.bend`: the proof `Laws.calm_keeps` and its helper `calm_arm`.
- `README.md`: the Laws paragraph names the new law.

`main.bend` doesn't change.

### How the proof works

`Laws.calm_keeps` uses the same induction over the events as `Laws.esc_quits`, and `calm_arm` mirrors `esc_arm`:

- An empty list gives `Some{g}`.
- A key that isn't Esc goes through `Game.quit(False{}, ...)`, which keeps the game. The rest of the list follows by induction.
- For an Esc key or a Close, `Calm` reduces to `Empty`, so an empty `match` closes the case.

`Calm` is a type and not a `Bool` because of that last step. `tests/proof/exists_witness.bend` uses the same pattern for `IsEven`.

### What it doesn't cover

- A Close: no law says that a Close ends the game, before or after this PR. If you want a `close_quits` law beside `esc_quits`, I can add it here.
- The loop: #2101 covers it.

### Before and after

Each row edits `main.bend`, and `PROOF.bend` where the old proof no longer fits. `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) give the same answer in each cell.

| edit | `main` at f0ddfe7b | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| #2071's `Game.events` that answers `None{}` for every frame (`esc_quits` proved by `{==}`) | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.calm_keeps` |
| `Game.event` also ends the game on `w` (`Laws.esc_quits` passes the new test to `esc_arm`) | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.calm_keeps` |
| nothing edited | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |

#2101 alone catches the first row, through its frame law, but not the second. A frame that holds keys needs this law.

### What I checked

On f0ddfe7b, macOS arm64:

- `bend main.bend --check-only` and `bend SPEC.bend --check-only` print ALL PROOFS CHECK.

title: fix(demos): app_slash_boss_3d's laws pin the loop's ticks through Live.steps and Live.after
body:
Fixes #2071, together with #2100 (merged).

### Why

#2071 came out of the review of #2067 (https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2067#issuecomment-6681849972). It shows two ways that a law of `app_slash_boss_3d` keeps holding while the game changes:

1. The function that a law names stops doing its job. #2100 covered this half.
2. The loop stops calling the function that a law names.

This PR covers the second half. `pause_freezes` pins `Game.step`, but no law pins that the running game ticks through `Game.step`, or how many ticks a frame runs.

Terms used below:

- A tick is one `Game.step`.
- A frame is one call of `Live.after`. It takes the game after the frame's events and the time since the last frame. It works out the ticks that the frame owes (60 a second, from at most 100 ms of the time), and runs them with `Live.steps`.
- The loop is the chain that the game runs every frame: `Play.loop`, `Play.blit`, `Play.turn` and `Play.next` run in IO, and then `Live.after` and `Live.steps` run as pure functions.

### What changed after the review

The first version (6fbe3045) added two laws about a paused game, `pause_freezes_live` and `pause_freezes_frame`. The review (https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2101#issuecomment-6751581263) showed that they were too weak: the frame law only said that some number of ticks exists, and the tick law only covered a paused game. This version replaces them with the two laws the review asked for, and adds one more.

### What changes

- `LAWS.bend`: three new laws.
  - `live_steps`: for any number of ticks `n` and any game `g`, the game that `Live.steps` leaves is `Spec.steps(n, g)`, which is `Game.step` applied `n` times. The previous game and the cues can be anything.
  - `live_after`: a frame that goes on with game `g` leaves `Spec.steps(Spec.owed(stamp, debt, now), g)`. The law has no `exs`, so the proof cannot pick the number of ticks.
  - `empty_keeps`: `Game.events(Nil{}, g)` is `Some{g}`. A frame with no events keeps the game as it is.
- `SPEC.bend`: `game_of` reads the game that a `Live` holds. `frame_game` reads the game that a frame leaves, or `None{}` when the frame ends the game. `owed` is the number of ticks a frame owes, stated once.
- `PROOF.bend`: the three proofs.
- The headers of `LAWS.bend` and `PROOF.bend` and the README's Laws paragraph describe the new laws. The header of `LAWS.bend` lists what the laws leave open, and the README points there.

`main.bend` doesn't change.

### The empty frame: two options

`live_after` starts from `Some{g}`, the game after the frame's events. The first version's frame law started from `Game.events(Nil{}, g)`, so it also said that an empty frame hands the game on unchanged. With `Some{g}`, no law says that any more: `calm_keeps` only says that some game comes back. A `Game.events` that answers an empty frame with the title screen then checks (row 6 of the table).

I weighed two ways to state it:

1. Write `Game.events(Nil{}, g)` in place of `Some{g}` inside `live_after`.
2. Keep `live_after` as the review wrote it, and state the fact as a law of its own.

I took the second. I assume the review took the events out of the frame law to keep two facts apart: what the events do to the game, and how many ticks the frame runs. The second option keeps them apart. It also pins `Live.after` for every `Some{g}`, not only for the game that an empty frame hands on, and a failure names the function that broke. Its cost is one more law. `empty_keeps` is a commit of its own, so it is easy to take out if you'd rather not have it.

### How the proofs work

- `Laws.live_steps` is an induction over the ticks. At each tick the game moves one `Game.step` on, the old game becomes the previous game, and `Cue.list` adds to the cues. The recursive call takes those three as they are.
- `Laws.live_after` unfolds `Live.after`, then rewrites the ticks with `Laws.live_steps` at the count that `Live.after` computes. That count and `Spec.owed` reduce to the same term, so `{==}` closes it.
- `Laws.empty_keeps` computes.

### What it doesn't cover

- `live_steps` and `live_after` read only the game in a `Live`. Its `prev`, `stamp`, `debt` and `cues` are not pinned. A `Live.after` that passes a debt of 0, or keeps the old `stamp`, still checks (rows 7 and 8). A law over the whole `Live` can be a follow-up.
- The IO part of the loop. If `Play.next` passes the frame to some function other than `Live.after`, `PROOF.bend` still checks (row 10).
- A frame that holds events. `esc_quits` and `calm_keeps` are the only laws about it, so a `Game.event` that answers a mouse move with the title screen still checks (row 9).

### Before and after

Each row edits `main.bend`, and `PROOF.bend` where the old proof no longer fits. `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) give the same answer in each cell. The middle column is 6fbe3045 merged with `main`.

| # | edit | `main` at 335f239a | before the review | now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Live.after` never ticks | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.live_after` |
| 2 | `Live.after` skips the ticks while the game is paused | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.live_after` |
| 3 | `Live.after` always runs one tick | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.live_after` |
| 4 | `Live.after` runs 30 ticks a second with no 100 ms cap | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.live_after` |
| 5 | `Live.steps` runs two `Game.step`s a tick outside a pause | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.live_steps` |
| 6 | `Game.events` answers an empty frame with the title screen | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.pause_freezes_frame` | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.empty_keeps` |
| 7 | `Live.after` passes a debt of 0 | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK (a limit above) |
| 8 | `Live.after` keeps the old `stamp` | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK (a limit above) |
| 9 | `Game.event` answers a mouse move with the title screen | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK (a limit above) |
| 10 | `Play.next` passes the frame to another after function | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK (a limit above) |
| 11 | nothing edited | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |

Rows 1 to 5 are the cases from the review. In a failing cell, the proof was adapted the same way as in the passing cells of its row (the new count or the new stepper in place of the old one).

### What I checked

On the branch with `main` at 335f239a merged in, macOS arm64:

- `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` print ALL PROOFS CHECK after each of the four commits.
- `bend main.bend --check-only` and `bend SPEC.bend --check-only` print ALL PROOFS CHECK.
- `bend LAWS.bend` alone reports 12 TODOs, three more than on `main`.
- `bun gates/repo.ts` prints PASS: 56 / 56 (ttok 0.3).

Not run: the cluster gates, Linux.

<details>
<summary>The first version's table (6fbe3045), which the review refers to</summary>

Each row edits `main.bend`, and `PROOF.bend` where the old proof no longer fits.

| edit | `main` at f0ddfe7b | the first version |
|---|---|---|
| `Live.steps` goes through a stepper that runs the clock in a pause | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.pause_freezes_live` |
| `Live.steps` stays, and `Live.after` goes through another steps function with that stepper | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.pause_freezes_frame` |
| #2071's `Game.events` that answers `None{}` for every frame (`esc_quits` proved by `{==}`) | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.pause_freezes_frame` |
| `Play.next` passes the frame to another after function | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |
| nothing edited | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |

Since #2100, `calm_keeps` rejects the third row on `main` as well.

</details>

title: A host drain hangs when a push finds the ring full: the reserved slot is never written and the loop doesn't check err_seen
ring_push can post a false ERR_RING when it reads an old get
body:
## What you did

Read `ring_push` (`bend2/comp.ts:4211`, main at d60b4c68) while reviewing #2079. I found this by reading the code against C11's rules. I haven't seen it happen.

## What happened

`ring_push` reads `get` once to check for room. If the ring looks full, it posts `ERR_RING`, which ends the run:

```c
u32 pos = a32_add(ring_put(H, r), 1);
if (pos - a32_load(ring_get(H, r)) >= RING_LEN) {   // a32_load_acq after #2079
  err_post(H, ERR_RING);
  return;
}
```

That load can return an old `get`. #2079 makes it an acquire, which orders what comes after it but doesn't make the value any newer. C11 and ARM both allow a load to miss a store that just happened on another core.

Say a ring holds `RING_LEN - 1` tasks and its owner has just popped one, so `get` has advanced. A pusher on another core can still read the old `get`, see `pos - get >= RING_LEN`, and fail the program with `ERR_RING`, even though the ring has a free slot.

The window is short and needs the ring to be nearly full, so this would be rare. When it does happen, it's a fatal false error.

## What should happen

`ERR_RING` should only fire when the ring is really full. Two options:

- After seeing "full", read `get` again a bounded number of times before posting the error. The slot at `pos` is already reserved, so waiting for `get` to move is safe, as long as the pusher isn't the ring's own popper.
- Or treat a full ring as backpressure rather than a fatal error.

This interacts with #2102 (the reserved-but-unwritten slot on the error path), so the two should probably be fixed together.

title: row_grow reads ring put/get with plain loads while other threads update put atomically (C11 data race)
body:
## What you did

Read `row_grow` (`bend2/comp.ts:4669`, main at d60b4c68) while reviewing #2079.

## What happened

`row_grow` reads each ring's `put` and `get` with plain, non-atomic loads:

```c
put0[i] = *ring_put(H, base + i * stride);
has += put0[i] != *ring_get(H, base + i * stride);
```

Other threads can be changing those `put` words at the same time. When a grow takes longer than 1 ms, `monk_step` is called with base 0, stride `CUBE_G` and the global `H_CURSOR`, so it pushes to rings in every row, and so do drain-turn deals with stride 0 (`ring_flip(g)`). `ring_push` updates `put` with `a32_add`. A plain read racing an atomic write is a data race under C11, which makes it undefined behavior. It's the same kind of bug #2079 fixes for `get`.

In practice the compiler is unlikely to do anything bad with a single aligned 32-bit load. But this site is formally unsound, and the GenMC run in #2078 doesn't cover it. A wrong `put0` would also feed straight into `monk_step`'s stop bound.

The host drain loop has the same pattern on `get` (`*ring_get(e.mem, rg)`, comp.ts:4761). That one is fine as long as only the owner writes `get`, but it's worth reading through `a32_load` too so every cross-thread ring word goes through one path.

## What should happen

Use `a32_load` (relaxed is enough for a snapshot) for `put` and `get` in `row_grow`. On x86 and ARM this compiles to the same instructions, so it costs nothing.

title: perf(base): Map.get carries a key cursor from level to level (#2074)
body:
## Summary

Fixes #2074.

`Map.get.go` called `Map.bit(key, q)` at every trie level, and each call walked the key from its first character. A lookup with a shared prefix of P characters therefore cost depth x P, although positions only grow on the way down.

`Map.get.go` now threads a cursor into the key: the descended key, the suffix at the current position, that position, and the bit read at it. Each level drops only the characters between its position and the child's (`String.drop`), and reads the bit from the first character of the suffix with a small `Map.get.bit`. Positions strictly grow, so the cursor reads the same bit `Map.bit(key, pos)` would. The leaf still compares the whole key, the public signature is unchanged, and the key is taken once at the top.

`tests/base/map_get_cursor.bend` covers a 64-character shared prefix, hits, misses past the end, empty and short keys, keys that prefix each other, characters past U+10FFFF and the map returned by one lookup answering the next one.

## Measurements

Apple M2 Pro, macOS 27.2, Apple clang 21.0.0, Darwin arm64. Warmed alternating process pairs, 200,000 hits over 4,096 keys, time inside the program (includes building each key, as in #2074). The baseline is the pre-change `Map.get` copied into the bench; the checksum is `409307552` on both, the issue's independent Python sum.

| Keys | `Map.get` before | `Map.get` after | Speedup |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| P = 16 (20 chars) | 219-221 ms | 171-174 ms | 1.27x |
| P = 64 (68 chars) | 873-907 ms | 484-505 ms | 1.8x |

## Test plan

- [x] `bun bend2/main.ts tests/base/map_get_cursor.bend` (interpreter)
- [x] `-o /tmp/mgc` and run natively (C, clang -O3)
- [x] `-o /tmp/mgc.js` and run under `bun` (JS)
- [x] Existing map tests on all three lanes: `tests/base/map_ops.bend`, `tests/base/map_prefix_keys.bend`, `tests/base/map_set_array_kit.bend`, `tests/run/map_set_ops.bend`, `tests/run/map_bit_native.bend`
- [x] `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS 56/56; `bend.ts`, `comp.ts` and the capped files are unchanged

Full cluster and GPU gates were not run.

AI-assisted.

title: perf(io): skip file size checks for small JS reads
body:
Each small JS file read calls `fstatSync` to size its buffer. The initial `room` is 65,536 bytes, and the stat result can only increase it. For a read cap at or below 65,536, `min(len, room)` is always `len`. Skip the stat call in this case.

This keeps the buffer-sizing design from #1985 and #2016. Zero-byte reads still call `readvSync`, so an invalid handle still returns an error.

A local test made 200,000 sequential eight-byte reads from a regular file. Medians from seven alternating before/after pairs were 365 → 267 ms on Bun and 417 → 327 ms on Node. Every run returned the same checksum. The number of `fstatSync` calls fell from 200,000 to zero.

Validation:

- Repository gate: 56/56 passed.
- Existing file tests: 21/21 passed on Bun; 18/18 available tests passed on native C.
- Extra Node runs: 14 passed. The other seven produced the same output and status on unchanged main, including Bun-only foreign fixtures and existing platform differences.
- 432 buffer-size cases matched on Bun and Node, including caps around 65,536, positioned reads, and stat errors. FIFO reads and zero-byte invalid-handle reads also matched.
- `git diff --check` passed.

title: fix(comp): a bit-trie level runs arm_self only on a row it keeps (#2076)
body:
Part of #2076. Since #1817, `mat_lits` runs `arm_self` on the default arm at every level of a U32/Nat bit trie, then compares those rebuilt arms (`term_same(cov(w), inst(w))`) to decide whether the level needs its own row. That cost dominates large C builds:

- Each call `term_map`s the whole default arm. On glam-in-bend's kernel that is 149K calls, 15M nodes walked and 2.07M Lam/Let binders rebuilt.
- The rebuilt binders have lazy bodies (`(y) => go(s.f(y))`), so the comparison re-maps them on every instantiation (330K more times).
- The two sides no longer share nodes, which the comparison relied on ("a default and its replay share most nodes"). Each comparison visits ~75 nodes instead of ~11.
- Each rebuilt term is fresh, so the file-long `opens`/`ground` caches keep every one.

`emit_match → mat_rows → mat_lits` was 61% of the kernel build. The excess peak memory over 2.0.39 is not retained data: forcing a full GC shows 2.0.39 holding more (median 982 MB vs 718 MB). It is this garbage outliving Eden collections.

The row decision now compares the raw defaults, as in 2.0.39, and `arm_self` runs only on the rows that are kept. If the raw defaults are equal, the deeper row is covered by its parent, so skipping it is sound. The two orderings can still disagree, in either direction, because `arm_self` rewrites against each level's own bit path. Where the raw defaults differ but the rewritten ones match, a redundant row is emitted. Where the raw defaults match but only the child's rewrite would reuse the scrutinee, the child row is dropped and its inputs take the parent's row, which rebuilds the value instead of reusing `self`. Both cases compile correctly and only lose an optimization, which is also what 2.0.39 did. On every input below the decisions are the same.

An earlier version of this PR bounded the caches at 200K opens. That is gone: with this change `opens` grows ~5K per pass on the kernel and never reaches the bound.

**glam-in-bend `spike/kernel.bend`** (3.5 MB of C), M-series Mac, 16 GB, bun 1.4.4:

| | time | peak RSS | live heap after each pass (`Bun.gc(true)`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0.39 | 5.8 s | 2.9–3.1 GB | – |
| main | 10.8–17.7 s | 7.0–7.3 GB | 2.4 → 3.8 → 5.3 GB |
| 200K cache bound (first version) | 7.9–8.2 s | 4.2–7.5 GB | 0.60 → 0.74 GB |
| this PR | 2.7–2.8 s | 2.6–2.9 GB | 1.12 → 1.16 GB |

**Unchanged elsewhere**
- The kernel's C is byte-identical to main's.
- Every test and demo emits byte-identical C and JS (1,886 outputs that build), and every program exits with the same code.
- boss_3d: 0.55 s, identical C.
- `gates/repo.ts`: 56/56. comp.ts drops to 65,942 ttok (main: 65,965).

**Not run:** the test and perf gates on the cluster.

The 2.0.40 binaries embed bun 1.3.14 because `release.ts` builds with the Bun that runs it, and the release Mac has 1.3.14 (CI pins 1.4.0). That is a separate fix.
