title: refactor(comp): arm_self walks its arm itself, and term_map is gone
body:
`term_map` was a generic term rewrite with a single caller, `arm_self`. It hid a recursive pass behind a callback, and every Lam/Let it rebuilt got a lazy body (`(y) => go(s.f(y))`) that re-ran the whole rewrite each time the body was instantiated. That laziness is part of what made #2076's kernel build slow.

`arm_self` now walks the arm itself, in one pass:
- The leading field lambdas, through `Ann`s, are opened and recorded as before. A `Ctr` that rebuilds the scrutinee becomes `self`, and only the path to a rewrite is rebuilt.
- A rebuilt Lam or Let is pre-opened with its rewritten body in `FL.opens`, as `let_open` does, so `term_open` never re-runs the rewrite.
- Its HOAS function re-runs the rewrite on the original body. The first version kept the original body there, unrewritten. The C emitter opens an erased lambda by applying that function (`emit_body`, `emit_expr`, `anf`). When `arm_self` had dropped the fields, the body still named them, and the build died in `bind_pop`. `tests/reg/arm_self_erased_lam.bend` covers it. Across every test, demo and bench, that function is applied only in the new test (8 times).

**Checked**, on `main` (bc136949) + this change:
- `gates/test.ts`: 1853/1853. `gates/repo.ts`: 56/56.
- comp.ts is 65,938 ttok (`main`: 65,963).
- The new test prints `13` in the interpreter, under JS and under C. Without the second commit, the C build throws `undefined is not an object (evaluating 'b.n')`.
- glam-in-bend's `spike/kernel.bend` (bun 1.3.14), three runs each: the C is byte-identical to `main`'s, about 5.3 s and 2.8 GB on both. A per-arm cache of `back(ps)` made no difference there either, so it is left out.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: perf(comp): stop term searches before opening child expressions
body:
`term_any` prepares child terms before it tests the current term. When `emit_unfold` rejects a lambda, this still opens the lambda body even though the predicate already determines the result. Test the predicate first and return before child discovery when it succeeds.

On an Apple M5 Max with Bun 1.3.14, two generated closure workloads showed these compile times:

| Workload | Before | After |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| 40 closures, 80 additions per closure | 25.18 ms | 23.44 ms |
| 120 closures, 150 additions per closure | 63.72 ms | 50.33 ms |

These are medians from 13 alternating before/after pairs after two warm-up pairs. The timer covers only `Comp.compile_book`, after parsing and checking. Each workload returns closures in a constructor, gives each closure a distinct constant capture, and sums the closure results. Generated C was identical. Both versions returned the expected results with one and four CPU threads.

Validation on main `335f239a`:

- Compared C and JS output, status, and diagnostics for all 362 fixtures in `tests/base`, `tests/run`, `tests/compile`, and `tests/comptime`. No differences: 316 emitted identical C and JS; 46 had identical existing diagnostics.
- Twelve existing closure, erased-argument, and fold tests passed through the direct runner, Bun, Node, and native C.
- The existing compiler-state and comptime checks passed.
- Repository gate: 56/56 passed. `comp.ts` is 65,986 tokens, below its 66,000-token cap.
- `git diff --check` passed.

title: perf(base): String.ends_with compares the last length(p) chars instead of reversing both strings
body:
`String.ends_with(s, p)` reversed both strings and ran `starts_with` on the copies, so every call built a reversed copy of `s` and of `p`. It now drops the first `length(s) - length(p)` characters of `s` and compares what is left with `String.eq`:

- an empty `p` returns `True` without reading `s`, as the reversing body did, so `{String.ends_with(s, "") == True{} : Bool}: {==}` still checks for an abstract `s`;
- a `p` longer than `s` drops nothing (`Nat.sub` stops at 0), and `String.eq` then compares strings of different lengths, which is `False`.

This is in Base, so it runs on every lane; #1641 asked for a JS-only `endsWith`, and this does not add one.

**C lane**, Apple M4 Pro, macOS 26.5.1, Apple clang 21, on `335f239a`. Each iteration calls `ends_with` with `"abcd"` (a hit), `"abce"` (a miss) and `"zabcd"` (a miss); the text is `x` repeated, then `"abcd"`. Time inside the program with `IO.now`, median of 9 runs (nine of `main`, then nine of this PR); both print the same checksum.

| text | calls | `main` | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 12 chars | 600,000 | 76 ms | **45 ms** |
| 104 chars | 60,000 | 74 ms | **43 ms** |
| 10,004 chars | 600 | 49 ms | 49 ms |

Short strings, the usual case for a suffix test such as a file extension, take 40% less time. Long ones stay the same: both versions are one walk of `s`. Peak RSS is the same (1.5 MB). The JS lane also gets faster in these runs (243 → 130 ms, 125 → 102 ms and 115 → 87 ms, medians of 3).

**Tests.** New `tests/base/string_ends_with.bend`, shaped like `string_starts_with.bend`: the empty-suffix proof above, and empty, longer, equal, missing, astral and non-scalar (`\u{ffffffff}`) suffixes. It prints its `#|` lines on the interpreter, JS and C, on `main` and on this PR. Separately, every pair from the 40 strings of length ≤ 3 over `a`, `b` and `\u{ffffffff}` (1,600 pairs) gives the same answer as the reversing body on all three lanes. `tests/base` prints the same as on `main`. I have not run the cluster gates or `--verdict`.

**One difference in what the checker can prove.** The `Bool` is the same for every pair of concrete strings, but the comparison now starts at the front of the suffix instead of the back, so a few equalities over abstract characters reduce differently. `{String.ends_with("a", SCon{c, "b"}) == False{} : Bool}: {==}` checked before (the reversed strings compare `'a'` with `'b'` first) and now stops at `'a'` against the abstract `c`. The other way round, `{String.ends_with("", SCon{c, t}) == False{} : Bool}` did not check before and does now. No file in the repo relies on either.

Revert: the body of `String.ends_with` in `bend2/base.bend`.

title: Use atomic ring snapshots in row_grow
A datatype name makes a valid GPU call fail at runtime
body:
Save this program as `example.bend`:

```bend
import Base

type Ch<-n: Nat> is Data:
  End{}
  Link{next: Ch<(1n + n : Nat)>}

type Chfalse is Type:
  Fn{f: U32 -> U32}

type Duo is Type:
  Duo{chain: Ch<0n>, callable: Chfalse}

def use(d: Duo) -> U32:
  match d:
    case Duo{chain, callable}:
      match callable:
        case Fn{f}:
          f(41)

def main() -> U32:
  use!(Duo{End{}, Fn{x => (x + 1 : U32)}})
```

This program should return `42`: `Fn` holds `x => (x + 1 : U32)`, and `use`
calls that function with `41`. The `use!` call requests execution on the GPU.

CPU execution returns `42`, even with the bug. To exercise the failure, use a
Metal or CUDA GPU and require GPU execution instead of allowing CPU fallback:

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts example.bend -o example.bin
./example.bin +RTS --gpu on
```

If no GPU is available, this command reports that rather than running on the CPU.

The compiler excludes the function from the GPU program. When the GPU reaches
`f(41)`, its function dispatcher has no code for `f` and takes the missing-function
error path:

```text
bend: a function the device does not hold
```

Renaming every `Chfalse` to `Callable` makes the compiler include the function.
A datatype's name should not determine whether this valid call can run.

The compiler searches datatype fields for functions that may be passed to the
GPU. It remembers visited types by joining the datatype name and a string
representing its arguments. When following recursion makes that argument string
longer, it uses `false` for the argument part of the lookup key. For `Ch<n>`
this produces `Chfalse`, the same key as the unrelated type `Chfalse` with no
arguments. The search therefore treats that type as already visited and misses
its function field.

title: Prevent collisions in the keys used to remember visited datatypes
body:
Fixes #2112.

The compiler uses `ty_holds` to search datatype fields for functions that may
run on the GPU. The search remembers visited datatype instances in `w.seen`;
finding an existing key makes it skip that instance's fields.

The change is in how that key is built in `comp.ts`. It has two parts: the
datatype name (`t.k`) and its argument strings (`xs`). When following recursion
makes an argument string grow, the existing rule uses `false` for the argument
part instead. Replace direct concatenation with a JSON-encoded pair:

```diff
- const key = t.k + (!re && xs);
+ const key = JSON.stringify([t.k, re ? false : xs]);
```

Previously, `"Ch" + false` and `"Chfalse" + []` both produced `"Chfalse"`.
The new keys are `["Ch",false]` and `["Chfalse",[]]`: the datatype name remains
separate from the argument part.

The search therefore visits the unrelated datatype `Chfalse` instead of
mistaking it for an already visited instance of `Ch`. It finds that datatype's
function field and includes the required function in the GPU program, avoiding
the missing-function runtime error. The traversal and the rule for growing
recursive arguments are unchanged.

Validation: five existing recursive-datatype and closure-reachability tests pass in JS and native CPU execution before and after; their generated C and JS are unchanged. The issue's reproducer now includes its closure in GPU dispatch; GPU execution still needs checking on hardware.

title: Keep shared-node takes inline on the CPU
body:
Closes #2081.

CPU takes were paying a `FAR` call even for a last-held shared node. Use the existing `DEVICE` switch: keep that helper out of line on Metal/CUDA devices, but let the host inline it. No helper body, memory ordering or cap changes.

Using [nuxyel’s BPE repro](https://github.com/nuxyel/bend-ml/blob/devel/docs/upstream/bpe_encode.bend), three alternating before/after runs pinned to CPU0:

| `perf stat` median | main `335f239a` | This change | Change |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| User instructions | 193,352,682,977 | 172,577,214,225 | −10.74% |

All six runs print `256`, `31633`, `2633430213`. Linux x86_64, i7-11700, clang22.1.8, `-std=c11 -O3`; PMU counters ran over99% of the interval. Cycles were noisy, so this only claims the instruction reduction.

Build the linked repro with each checkout’s `bun bend2/main.ts bpe_encode.bend -o bpe`, then run `taskset -c 0 perf stat -e instructions:u,cycles:u ./bpe`.

Repo gate passes56/56; `comp.ts` is65987/66000 tokens. Full unchanged gate bundle was also run: `test`/`perf` fail because this machine cannot resolve the `cluster` bastion; `ping` skips because the site checkout is unavailable. Keeping this draft for mini/platform qualification. No GPU, macOS or Windows execution claim.

@nuxyel also checked this head on [the original Core Ultra 7 machine](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2114#issuecomment-6798627073). The three output lines and instruction reduction held; full host inlining beat the proposed split. Their cycles are directional because the machine was busy, and they measured a larger binary. This is their independent CPU check, not locally rerun mini or GPU qualification.

Thanks @nuxyel for the repro and measurements. AI-assisted with omp / GPT-6.1 Sol; no subagents.

title: Allow a local variable to have the same name as a constructor
body:
Save as `example.bend`:

```bend
type T is Data:
  C{}

def main() -> T:
  C : T = C{}
  C
```

Run:

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts example.bend
```

The parser rejects the first `C` in the local binding:

```text
a braced constructor pattern (C is a constructor: write C{}, or rename the binder)
```

In `C : T = C{}`, the left `C` is intended as a local variable name; `C{}`
constructs its value, and the final `C` returns the bound value. The parser
rejects the binding because a constructor already has that name. Renaming
the variable to `x` makes the program run and return `C{}`.

Allow this program to return `C{}`. A bare name in a pattern would always
bind a variable, while braces would distinguish constructor patterns.

title: Allow constructor names as bare pattern binders
body:
Fixes #2115.

The parser deliberately rejects a bare pattern name when a visible constructor
has that name, suggesting braces or a different binder. This PR relaxes that
language rule: if datatype `T` declares constructor `C{}`, then in
`C : T = C{}` the left `C` may bind the value constructed by the right `C{}`.

In `bend.ts`, remove the constructor lookup and error from `parse_patt`'s
variable branch, leaving:

```ts
case "Var": {
  return parse_bind(p, t);
}
```

`parse_bind` creates a variable binding. Because `parse_patt` also handles
`case` patterns and recursively parses constructor fields, bare names in those
positions can likewise bind variables even when a constructor uses the name.
Braced patterns still take the separate `Ctr` branch and match a constructor.

The trade-off is losing the diagnostic for forgotten braces: `case C:` now
binds the whole input instead of prompting for `case C{}:`.

Validation: typed, untyped and reusable lets, a catch-all case, and a nested constructor pattern now run with constructor-named binders. Seven existing parser/import controls keep identical results before and after. The full cluster gates have not been rerun for this standalone patch.

title: BendTT rejects equality between a returned matcher and its inline body
body:
Save as `example.bend`:

```bend
type U is Data:
  U{}

def make() -> U -> U:
  \{U: U{}}

def witness() -> {make() == (\{U: U{}}) : U -> U}:
  {==}
```

`make()` takes no declared arguments. It returns a function that matches
`U{}` and returns `U{}`. The proof `witness` compares that returned function
with the same function written inline.

Run:

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts example.bend
bun bend2/main.ts example.bend --verdict
```

Bend's checker accepts the proof, but `--verdict`, which also checks the
translated program with BendTT, rejects the equality. Both should accept it:
unfolding `make()` gives exactly the matcher on the right side.

title: perf(comp): fold and unfold stop walking terms once the answer is known
body:
Follow-up to #2109: the fold and unfold paths stop walking terms once the answer is already known.

- `emit_fold`'s fuel pass stops at the first node that leaves fuel negative, and the fold pass is skipped when that happens. Only the sign of `fuel.n` is ever read, so the result is unchanged.
- `emit_fold` skips `emit_unfold` when fuel is already negative. On that path the result was always `null` (the fuel pass charges at least one node), so this only drops the work of folding the arguments and building a body that would be thrown away.
- `emit_unfold`'s `bad` walks each let's value once per probe instead of once per use, so an argument used k times is no longer walked k times.
- `term_any` is one expression again. The tail-tag test stays a substring match: it is the fewest tokens of the seven forms measured, and no term tag in `bend.ts` matches it without being one of `Ann`, `Lam`, `Mat`, `Rwt`.

This doesn't make the merged #2109 path any faster. `term_any` is not where compile time goes:

| Workload | `term_any` calls | unfolds | compile time |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 363 fixtures (before the no-fuel skip) | 796,188 → 793,432 | | |
| fold chain that runs out of fuel | 978,378 → 952,528 | 40,744 → 39,076 | 295.6 → 295.0 ms |
| matched arm using a large runtime argument 300 times | 53,596 → 38,774 | 3,040 → 3,036 | 167.5 → 163.8 ms |

Times are whole-CLI `-o x.c` means of 21 runs (hyperfine, 3 warm-ups). The differences are within noise.

Validation, rebased on main `d18110b6`:

- C and JS output, exit status and diagnostics are identical for all 363 fixtures in `tests/base`, `tests/run`, `tests/compile` and `tests/comptime`.
- Both workloads emit identical C and print the same results when built natively.
- Repository gate: 56/56 passed. `comp.ts` is 65,941 tokens, 3 over main.
- The typecheck shows the same errors as main.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Preserve returned function values in the BendTT translation
body:
Fixes #2117.

`--verdict` first checks a Bend program with the checker in `bend.ts`.
Then `safe.ts` translates the checked program into BendTT, and the BendTT
checker in `bendtt.lean` checks that translation. This PR changes `safe.ts`;
the rules of both checkers remain unchanged.

The Bend program reported in #2117 defines a type `U` with one constructor,
`U{}`, and these two definitions:

```bend
def make() -> U -> U:
  \{U: U{}}

def witness() -> {make() == (\{U: U{}}) : U -> U}:
  {==}
```

`make()` takes no arguments and returns a matcher. `witness` proves that
`make()` equals that matcher written directly. Before this PR, Bend's
checker accepts `witness`, but the BendTT checker rejects its translation.
There are two reasons for that rejection.

First, before this PR, `arg_term` in `safe.ts` translates the two equality
sides differently. In Bend syntax, the resulting BendTT forms are:

```bend
x => make()(x)       # Translation of make().
\{U: U{}}           # Translation of the inline matcher.
```

The BendTT checker has no rule equating these two function forms.

Second, the BendTT checker cannot unfold `make()(x)`. Before replacing a
named call with its body, the BendTT checker tries to bind the call's
arguments at the body's leading lambdas and select its match arms. If a
match cannot select an arm, the checker leaves the named call unchanged.
Before this PR, the translated body of `make` is the matcher itself. The
BendTT checker therefore treats `x` in `make()(x)` as an argument that
`make` itself must match before unfolding. But `make()` takes no arguments;
`x` is the input to the function it returns. Since `x` has no known
constructor, this extra match prevents `make()` from unfolding.

This PR makes two changes to `safe.ts`:

1. `arg_term` applies its existing expansion rule to inline lambdas and
   matchers as well as named calls. For the inline matcher above, the result
   is `x => ({\{U: U{}} : U -> U})(x)`. The `U -> U` annotation supplies the
   function type needed to translate the matcher application inside this
   lambda.
2. `tree` puts a BendTT `Ann` type annotation around a definition's returned
   function. For `make`, the translated body is `{\{U: U{}} : U -> U}`.
   The BendTT checker stops processing argument patterns at `Ann` and
   allows the named call to unfold. Its evaluator then removes the
   annotation. This lets `make()` unfold while `x` remains unknown.

With both changes applied, `safe.ts` produces these equality sides, again
shown in Bend syntax:

```bend
x => make()(x)
x => ({\{U: U{}} : U -> U})(x)
```

The BendTT checker unfolds `make()` and removes the annotations, leaving
both lambda bodies as `(\{U: U{}})(x)`. The match on `x` remains unevaluated,
but the bodies are identical, so the equality succeeds.

To place the annotation at the end of the declared arguments, this PR
changes how `arm` in `safe.ts` initializes `Scope.cols`. The list starts with
one entry per remaining declared argument, including a `null` entry when
its value is unknown. Unknown values must still count as arguments.

Matching a constructor can introduce fields that also need binding. These
field bindings still belong to the argument pattern. `tree` inserts `Ann`
only when `cols` and its existing constructor-field stack `fs` are both
empty. It then continues translating inside the annotation with
`cols: null`; leaving `cols: []` would trigger the same annotation again.

The added tests check the reported equality directly and when passing the
returned function together with an erased proof of that equality to another
function. A further test checks that constructing the expanded function
form does not execute the call that returns the function.

title: A RangeError that is not a stack overflow is reported as one
fix(formatter): preserve spacing after %
body:
The formatter preserves the whitespace boundary after `%` that distinguishes modulo from rewrite syntax, including when a comment follows the marker.

Three regression programs retain their outputs after formatting with default spaces, four spaces, and tabs. All 35 formatter/LSP tests and 56 local repository checks pass.

title: fix(cli): only a stack overflow prints the stack overflow message (#2120)
body:
Fixes #2120.

`book_err` in `bend2/main.ts` printed every `RangeError` as "the machine stack overflowed". JSC also throws `RangeError` for things that are not a full stack (`Out of memory`, an invalid array length, a BigInt too big), so 2.0.40's `FL.ground` blowup (#2076) read as a deep recursion, and raising the stack limit could not help. Now only "Maximum call stack size exceeded" prints the stack-overflow message. Any other `RangeError` prints its own text, as `RangeError: Out of memory`.

**Checked**
- On a program that hits #2076, built at 624dd9f4 (before #2107), it now prints `RangeError: Out of memory` where it printed the stack-overflow message.
- #2093's repro, rebuilt byte for byte, still prints the stack-overflow message: that one is a real stack overflow (`Maximum call stack size exceeded` in `term_wnf`).
- The 550 tests whose expected output has an error print exactly what main prints.
- `gates/repo.ts`: 56/56. `main.ts` drops to 13,034 ttok (main: 13,036): 3 lines added, 5 removed.

title: app_slash_boss_3d: the laws hold for a game that ignores a Close, or an Esc release
body:
### What you did

`bend PROOF.bend` in `demos/app_slash_boss_3d`, after one edit of `main.bend`, with `PROOF.bend` edited only where the old proof stopped fitting. `LAWS.bend` and `SPEC.bend` are unchanged. These are the two gaps that the review of #2100 named (https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2100#pullrequestreview-5832477100).

Two edits, each on its own:

1. A Close does nothing. `Game.event` loses its `Close{}` arm, so a Close falls to `case _: Some{g}`.
2. An Esc release keeps the game. `Game.event` ends the game on a key-down only.

<details>
<summary>Edit 1</summary>

```diff
--- a/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/main.bend
+++ b/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/main.bend
@@ -2679,8 +2679,6 @@
   match e:
     case Key{code, down}:
       Game.quit(U32.is_eq(code, 27), Game.key(g, code, down))
-    case Close{}:
-      None{}
     case _:
       Some{g}
 
--- a/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend
+++ b/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend
@@ -153,7 +153,7 @@
     case Focus{on} <> rest:
       Laws.esc_quits(rest, post, g)
     case Close{} <> rest:
-      {==}
+      Laws.esc_quits(rest, post, g)
 
 # A calm frame goes on
 # ---------------------
```

</details>

<details>
<summary>Edit 2</summary>

```diff
--- a/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/main.bend
+++ b/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/main.bend
@@ -2678,7 +2678,7 @@
 def Game.event(+e: Event, g: Game) -> Maybe<Game>:
   match e:
     case Key{code, down}:
-      Game.quit(U32.is_eq(code, 27), Game.key(g, code, down))
+      Game.quit(Bool.and(down, U32.is_eq(code, 27)), Game.key(g, code, down))
     case Close{}:
       None{}
     case _:
--- a/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend
+++ b/demos/app_slash_boss_3d/PROOF.bend
@@ -133,7 +133,7 @@
     case Nil{}:
       {==}
     case Key{+code, +down} <> rest:
-      esc_arm(U32.is_eq(code, 27), Slash.Game.key(g, code, down),
+      esc_arm(Bool.and(down, U32.is_eq(code, 27)), Slash.Game.key(g, code, down),
         Spec.cat(rest, Key{27, True{}} <> post),
         s => Laws.esc_quits(rest, post, s))
     case Text{text} <> rest:
@@ -177,12 +177,34 @@
     case False{}:
       ih(g, e)
 
+law calm_up:
+  for d: Bool
+  for b: Bool
+  for g: Slash.Game
+  for -rest: List<Event>
+  for e: Spec.Calm.key(b, Spec.Calm(rest))
+  for ih: @s: Slash.Game -> Spec.Calm(rest) -> &g2: Slash.Game -> {Slash.Game.events(rest, s) == Some{g2} : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
+  exs g2: Slash.Game
+  {Maybe.bind(&1, Slash.Game, Slash.Game, Slash.Game.quit(Bool.and(d, b), g),
+      s => Slash.Game.events(rest, s)) == Some{g2} : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
+
+def calm_up(d, b, g, rest, e, ih):
+  match d b:
+    case True{} True{}:
+      match e:
+    case True{} False{}:
+      ih(g, e)
+    case False{} True{}:
+      match e:
+    case False{} False{}:
+      ih(g, e)
+
 def Laws.calm_keeps(es, g, e):
   match es:
     case Nil{}:
       (g, {==})
     case Key{+code, +down} <> rest:
-      calm_arm(U32.is_eq(code, 27), Slash.Game.key(g, code, down), rest, e,
+      calm_up(down, U32.is_eq(code, 27), Slash.Game.key(g, code, down), rest, e,
         s => c => Laws.calm_keeps(rest, s, c))
     case Text{text} <> rest:
       Laws.calm_keeps(rest, g, e)
```

</details>

### What happened

On `main` at d18110b6, with either edit:

```text
$ bend PROOF.bend
ALL PROOFS CHECK
$ bend PROOF.bend --verdict
ALL PROOFS CHECK
```

`bend EVAL.bend` (the file below) prints what the game does with a frame that holds only that event:

| | a frame with only a Close | a frame with only an Esc release |
|---|---|---|
| unedited | ends | ends |
| edit 1 | goes on | ends |
| edit 2 | ends | goes on |

So with edit 1 a Close no longer ends the game, and the laws still check. I evaluated `Game.events` only. I did not run the built game and click its window.

### Why it happens

Three laws speak about a frame's events. None of them covers a Close or an Esc release.

| a frame's events hold | law | the law says |
|---|---|---|
| an Esc key-down | `esc_quits` | the game ends |
| an Esc release and no key-down | none | |
| a Close and no Esc key-down | none | |
| no Esc and no Close | `calm_keeps` | the game does not end |
| nothing | `empty_keeps` | the game stays as it is |

`esc_quits` names `Key{27, True{}}`. `calm_keeps` takes a `Spec.Calm(es)`, and `Spec.Calm` is `Empty` at a `Key{27, _}` with either flag and at a `Close{}`, so `calm_keeps` says nothing about those frames.

### The file

<details>
<summary>EVAL.bend</summary>

```python
import Base
import ./main.bend as Slash

def goes_on(m: Maybe<Slash.Game>) -> String:
  match m:
    case None{}:
      "ends"
    case Some{g}:
      "goes on"

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(goes_on(Slash.Game.events([Close{}], Slash.Game.init())))
    IO.print(goes_on(Slash.Game.events([Key{27, False{}}], Slash.Game.init())))
```

</details>

### What might close it

The review suggested a `close_quits` beside `esc_quits`. #2124 adds it, and lets `esc_quits` range over the key's flag.

### bend version

Bend 2.0.40 (`main` at d18110b6)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

title: fix(demos): app_slash_boss_3d's laws say a Close quits, and an Esc release too
body:
Fixes #2123.

This PR adds one law, `close_quits`, and widens one law, `esc_quits`. With it, a game that ignores a Close fails `bend PROOF.bend`, and so does a game that an Esc release no longer ends. `main.bend` and `SPEC.bend` don't change.

### Why

The review of #2100 named two gaps in the laws about a frame's events (https://github.com/bendlang/bend/pull/2100#pullrequestreview-5832477100):

> `esc_quits` covers only `Key{27, True{}}` while `Calm` rules out any `Key{27, _}`, so an Esc release falls under neither law; a `close_quits` beside `esc_quits` would also be welcome as a follow-up.

#2123 shows both gaps on `main`. With either edit of `main.bend`, `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` print ALL PROOFS CHECK.

### Terms

- An Esc is a `Key` event with code 27. `Key{27, True{}}` is its key-down. `Key{27, False{}}` is its release.
- A Close is the `Close{}` event.
- A frame's events are the `List<Event>` that the loop passes to `Game.events` one time per frame.
- A frame ends the game when `Game.events` returns `None{}`. A frame goes on when `Game.events` returns `Some{g2}`.
- A frame is calm when `Spec.Calm(es)` is `Unit`. In `SPEC.bend`, `Spec.Calm(es)` is `Empty` when `es` holds a `Key{27, _}` or a `Close{}`.

### The gaps on `main`

| a frame's events hold | law | the law says |
|---|---|---|
| an Esc key-down | `esc_quits` | the frame ends the game |
| an Esc release and no key-down | none | |
| a Close and no Esc key-down | none | |
| no Esc and no Close | `calm_keeps` | the frame does not end the game |
| nothing | `empty_keeps` | the game stays as it is |

`calm_keeps` takes a `Spec.Calm(es)`. That type is `Empty` for the two middle rows, so `calm_keeps` says nothing about them.

### What changes

**1. `LAWS.bend` gets `close_quits`.** It is `esc_quits` with a Close in the place of the Esc.

```python
# LAW: a Close anywhere in a frame's events quits, whatever the events
# before and after it and whatever the game.
law close_quits:
  for pre: List<Event>
  for post: List<Event>
  for g: Slash.Game
  {Slash.Game.events(Spec.cat(pre, Close{} <> post), g) == None{}
    : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
```

**2. `esc_quits` ranges over the key's flag.** The law had `Key{27, True{}}`. It now has `Key{27, down}` for any `down`, so it covers the release also.

```diff
 law esc_quits:
   for pre: List<Event>
+  for down: Bool
   for post: List<Event>
   for g: Slash.Game
-  {Slash.Game.events(Spec.cat(pre, Key{27, True{}} <> post), g) == None{}
+  {Slash.Game.events(Spec.cat(pre, Key{27, down} <> post), g) == None{}
     : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
```

**3. `PROOF.bend` proves both laws with one induction, `quits_anywhere`.** The section below describes it.

**4. The headers and the README name the new law.** The header of `LAWS.bend`, the header of `PROOF.bend` and the Laws paragraph of the README say that an Esc or a Close quits.

### The laws after this PR

| a frame's events hold | law | the law says |
|---|---|---|
| an Esc, key-down or release | `esc_quits` | the frame ends the game |
| a Close | `close_quits` | the frame ends the game |
| no Esc and no Close | `calm_keeps` | the frame does not end the game |
| nothing | `empty_keeps` | the game stays as it is |

Do the first three rows leave a frame out? I did not prove that from the three laws. I proved one more statement on a copy of this branch: a frame that is not calm ends the game.

```python
law not_calm_quits:
  for es: List<Event>
  for g: Slash.Game
  for n: Spec.Calm(es) -> Empty
  {Slash.Game.events(es, g) == None{} : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
```

It prints ALL PROOFS CHECK under `bend` and `--verdict`. So, for the game on this branch, a calm frame goes on and a frame that is not calm ends the game. This law is not in the PR. The second choice below says why.

### How the proofs work

On `main`, `Laws.esc_quits` is an induction over `pre`, the events before the Esc. This PR gives that induction a name and one more parameter: the event that quits.

```python
law quits_anywhere:
  for pre: List<Event>
  for e: Event
  for post: List<Event>
  for g: Slash.Game
  for h: @s: Slash.Game -> {None{} == Slash.Game.event(e, s) : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
  {Slash.Game.events(Spec.cat(pre, e <> post), g) == None{} : Maybe<Slash.Game>}
```

`h` says that `e` ends every game. The induction has three kinds of arm:

1. `pre` is empty, so the frame starts with `e`. The proof rewrites `Slash.Game.event(e, g)` to `None{}` with `h(g)`. Then `Maybe.bind` of `None{}` computes to `None{}`.
2. `pre` starts with a key. `esc_arm` splits on whether the key is an Esc. If the key is an Esc, the frame ends there. If the key is not an Esc, the induction hypothesis takes the rest. This arm is the same as on `main`.
3. `pre` starts with any other event. If the event is a Close, the frame ends there. If the event is not a Close, `Game.event` keeps the game, and the induction hypothesis takes the rest.

After that, each law is one line:

```python
def Laws.esc_quits(pre, down, post, g):
  quits_anywhere(pre, Key{27, down}, post, g, s => {==})

def Laws.close_quits(pre, post, g):
  quits_anywhere(pre, Close{}, post, g, s => {==})
```

`s => {==}` proves `h`. `Game.event(Key{27, down}, s)` computes to `None{}` for any `down` and any `s`, and `Game.event(Close{}, s)` computes to `None{}` for any `s`.

### Two choices

**The Esc release.** `Game.event` ends the game on a `Key{27, _}` with either flag. So the widened `esc_quits` states what the game does today. The other way is to let an Esc release keep the game. Then `Spec.Calm` rules out the key-down only, and `Game.event` changes. I did not take that way, because it changes the game. The release is the second commit, so you can drop it without the first.

**Two laws, not one.** The law `not_calm_quits` above closes both gaps with one statement. It also reads the quit side from `Spec.Calm`, the same definition that `calm_keeps` reads. So the two sides cannot disagree. The Esc release gap was such a disagreement. I kept two named laws for three reasons:

- `esc_quits` and `close_quits` name the Esc and the Close in the law. `not_calm_quits` names them only through `Spec.Calm`.
- The proof of `not_calm_quits` adds 42 lines to `PROOF.bend`. This PR adds 19.
- The review asked for a `close_quits` beside `esc_quits`.

`Spec.Calm` and the two laws are in files that stay fixed when someone rewrites the game. So an edit of `main.bend` cannot make them disagree. If you prefer the single law, tell me. The proof is ready.

### What it doesn't cover

`calm_keeps` says that a calm frame does not end the game. It does not say which game comes back. If `Game.event` answers an event that is no key and no Close with the title screen, `PROOF.bend` still checks (the third row below). The header of `LAWS.bend` states this limit, and this PR only adds `close_quits` to the laws that the sentence lists.

### Before and after

Each row edits `main.bend`, and `PROOF.bend` where the old proof no longer fits. `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) give the same answer in each cell. #2123 holds the first two edits.

| edit | `main` at d18110b6 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| a Close does nothing | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.close_quits` |
| an Esc release keeps the game | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.esc_quits` |
| an event that is no key and no Close resets the game | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK (the limit above) |
| nothing edited | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK |

After the first commit alone, the first row fails and the second row still checks.

I also evaluated what each edited game does. With the first edit, `Game.events([Close{}], Game.init())` is a `Some`, so the game goes on after a Close. With the second edit, `Game.events([Key{27, False{}}], Game.init())` is a `Some`. Unedited, both are `None{}`.

### What I checked

On d18110b6, macOS arm64:

- `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` print ALL PROOFS CHECK after each of the two commits.
- `bend main.bend --check-only` and `bend SPEC.bend --check-only` print ALL PROOFS CHECK.
- `bend LAWS.bend` alone reports 14 TODOs, one more than on `main`.
- `bun gates/repo.ts` prints PASS: 56 / 56.

Not run: the cluster gates, Linux, and the built game's window. I evaluated `Game.events` only.

title: io_http_server: the laws hold for a server that sends another body, no status line, or a 500
body:
### What you did `bend PROOF.bend` in `demos/io_http_server`, after one edit of `http_response` in `main.bend`, with `PROOF.bend` edited only where the old proof stopped fitting. `LAWS.bend` is unchanged. Then I built each edited server and sent it one request. ```sh cd demos/io_http_server # apply one of the three edits below bend PROOF.bend bend PROOF.bend --verdict bend main.bend -o http_server && ./http_server & curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080 ``` The demo has two laws, and both are about `http_response(page)`, the text that the server sends for a page: - `page_after_blank`: the response is some head, then a blank line (`"\r\n\r\n"`), then the page. - `response_inj`: two equal responses come from equal pages. Three edits, each on its own: 1. The head holds a blank line of its own, with text after it. 2. The response has no status line and no headers. 3. The status line says 500.
Edit 1: a blank line inside the head ```diff --- a/demos/io_http_server/main.bend +++ b/demos/io_http_server/main.bend @@ -12,7 +12,7 @@ # the response for a page: the status line, the headers, a blank # line, then the page def http_response(page: String) -> String: - "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" ++ page + "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n

Not the page

\r\n\r\n" ++ page def http_sent(m: Socket & Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String) & List<&2, U32>, Unit>) -> IO(Unit): (s, r) = m --- a/demos/io_http_server/PROOF.bend +++ b/demos/io_http_server/PROOF.bend @@ -7,7 +7,7 @@ import ./LAWS.bend as Laws def Laws.page_after_blank(page): - ("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close", {==}) + ("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n

Not the page

", {==}) # the text after its first n characters def drop(n: Nat, s: String) -> String: @@ -22,4 +22,4 @@ drop(p, t) def Laws.response_inj(a, b, e): - Equal.cong(String, String, s => drop(63n, s), Srv.http_response(a), Srv.http_response(b), e) + Equal.cong(String, String, s => drop(88n, s), Srv.http_response(a), Srv.http_response(b), e) ```
Edit 2: no status line and no headers ```diff --- a/demos/io_http_server/main.bend +++ b/demos/io_http_server/main.bend @@ -12,7 +12,7 @@ # the response for a page: the status line, the headers, a blank # line, then the page def http_response(page: String) -> String: - "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" ++ page + "\r\n\r\n" ++ page def http_sent(m: Socket & Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String) & List<&2, U32>, Unit>) -> IO(Unit): (s, r) = m --- a/demos/io_http_server/PROOF.bend +++ b/demos/io_http_server/PROOF.bend @@ -7,7 +7,7 @@ import ./LAWS.bend as Laws def Laws.page_after_blank(page): - ("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close", {==}) + ("", {==}) # the text after its first n characters def drop(n: Nat, s: String) -> String: @@ -22,4 +22,4 @@ drop(p, t) def Laws.response_inj(a, b, e): - Equal.cong(String, String, s => drop(63n, s), Srv.http_response(a), Srv.http_response(b), e) + Equal.cong(String, String, s => drop(4n, s), Srv.http_response(a), Srv.http_response(b), e) ```
Edit 3: the status line says 500 ```diff --- a/demos/io_http_server/main.bend +++ b/demos/io_http_server/main.bend @@ -12,7 +12,7 @@ # the response for a page: the status line, the headers, a blank # line, then the page def http_response(page: String) -> String: - "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" ++ page + "HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" ++ page def http_sent(m: Socket & Result<&1, &1, (U32 & String) & List<&2, U32>, Unit>) -> IO(Unit): (s, r) = m --- a/demos/io_http_server/PROOF.bend +++ b/demos/io_http_server/PROOF.bend @@ -7,7 +7,7 @@ import ./LAWS.bend as Laws def Laws.page_after_blank(page): - ("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close", {==}) + ("HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close", {==}) # the text after its first n characters def drop(n: Nat, s: String) -> String: @@ -22,4 +22,4 @@ drop(p, t) def Laws.response_inj(a, b, e): - Equal.cong(String, String, s => drop(63n, s), Srv.http_response(a), Srv.http_response(b), e) + Equal.cong(String, String, s => drop(82n, s), Srv.http_response(a), Srv.http_response(b), e) ```
### What happened On `main` at d18110b6, with each edit: ```text $ bend PROOF.bend ALL PROOFS CHECK $ bend PROOF.bend --verdict ALL PROOFS CHECK ``` The client gets something else each time. This is what `curl -i` prints. Nothing edited: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html Connection: close

Hello, world!

``` Edit 1. The body is not the page. It starts with the text that the edit put in the head: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html Connection: close

Not the page

Hello, world!

``` Edit 2. `curl` refuses the response and exits with 1: ```text curl: (1) Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed ``` Edit 3. The server answers every request with an error status: ```text HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error Content-Type: text/html Connection: close

Hello, world!

``` I built each server with its port changed to 18080, because 8080 was taken on my machine. ### Why it happens `page_after_blank` asks for some head: ```python law page_after_blank: for +page: String exs head: String {head ++ ("\r\n\r\n" ++ page) == Srv.http_response(page) : String} ``` A proof of a law with `exs head` is a pair: a value for `head`, and a proof for that value. So the proof picks the head. In each edit above, the proof gives the new text as the head, and `{==}` checks. | edit | the head that the proof gives | |---|---| | nothing edited | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close` | | 1 | the same text, then `\r\n\r\n

Not the page

` | | 2 | the empty text | | 3 | `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close` | So the law holds for every `http_response` that puts some text and a blank line before the page, whatever that text is. `response_inj` does not look at the head. It says that two equal responses come from equal pages. Every response starts with the same text, so the law holds whatever that text is. Its proof drops that text from both sides, and each edit changes only the count of characters to drop (88, 4 and 82 in place of 63). Two comments say more than the laws do: - The header of `LAWS.bend` says that the laws pin "the bytes sent for a page". They pin only the bytes after the head. - The comment of `page_after_blank` says "a client that cuts at the blank line reads the page back". A client cuts at the first blank line. With edit 1, the first blank line is inside the head, so the client reads another body. The `exs head` has the same shape as the `exs n` in the first version of #2101: the proof gives the value that the law leaves open. The review of #2101 asked for a count stated in `SPEC.bend` in place of that `exs n`. ### What might close it #2126 states the head one time in a `SPEC.bend`, and `page_after_blank` reads it, so the law has no `exs`. The other way is to keep the law and narrow the two comments, as 2.0.32 did for `io_http_fetch` (#1119). ### bend version Bend 2.0.40 (`main` at d18110b6) ### uname -sm Darwin arm64 ### clang --version (the first line) Apple clang version 21.0.0 (clang-2100.1.1.101)

title: fix(demos): io_http_server's page_after_blank law reads the head from SPEC.bend
body:
Fixes #2125. This PR states the head of a response one time, in a new `SPEC.bend`, and `page_after_blank` reads it. The law no longer has an `exs`. With it, `bend PROOF.bend` fails for a server that puts a blank line inside the head, for one that sends no status line, and for one that answers 500. `main.bend` doesn't change. ### Why #2125 shows three edits of `http_response`. On `main`, each one prints ALL PROOFS CHECK under `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict`, and each one changes what a client gets: | edit of `http_response` | what `curl -i` gets | |---|---| | nothing edited | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, body `

Hello, world!

` | | a blank line inside the head | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK`, body `

Not the page

`, a blank line, then `

Hello, world!

` | | no status line and no headers | `curl: (1) Received HTTP/0.9 when not allowed` | | the status line says 500 | `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error`, body `

Hello, world!

` | ### Terms - A response is the `String` that `http_response(page)` returns. The server sends it for each request. - A blank line is `"\r\n\r\n"`: the end of one line, then an empty line. - The head is the part of a response before its first blank line: the status line and the headers. - The page is the text that `http_response` takes. - The body is the text that a client reads after the first blank line. - A law pins a fact when an edit that breaks the fact makes `bend PROOF.bend` fail. ### How a client reads a response This is the response of the unedited server: ```text HTTP/1.1 200 OK the status line Content-Type: text/html a header Connection: close a header the first blank line

Hello, world!

the body ``` A client takes the text after the first blank line as the body (RFC 9112, section 2.1). So the body is the page only when the head holds no blank line of its own. ### The gap on `main` ```python law page_after_blank: for +page: String exs head: String {head ++ ("\r\n\r\n" ++ page) == Srv.http_response(page) : String} ``` The law says that some head exists. A proof of a law with `exs head` is a pair: a value for `head`, and a proof for that value. So the proof picks the head. On `main`, an edit of `http_response` needs only a new value in that pair: | edit | the head that the proof gives | |---|---| | nothing edited | `HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close` | | a blank line inside the head | the same text, then `\r\n\r\n

Not the page

` | | no status line and no headers | the empty text | | the status line says 500 | `HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close` | So the law holds for every `http_response` that puts some text and a blank line before the page, whatever that text is. The other law, `response_inj`, does not look at the head. It says that two equal responses come from equal pages. Every response starts with the same text, so the law holds whatever that text is. Two comments said more than the laws did: - The header of `LAWS.bend` says that the laws pin "the bytes sent for a page". On `main` they pin only the bytes after the head. - The comment of `page_after_blank` said "a client that cuts at the blank line reads the page back". If the head holds a blank line, the client cuts there, and the body is not the page. ### What changes | file | change | lines | |---|---|---| | `SPEC.bend` | new: the head | +10 | | `LAWS.bend` | `page_after_blank` reads `Spec.head()`, with no `exs` | +4 -4 | | `PROOF.bend` | the proof of `page_after_blank` is `{==}` | +4 -4 | **1. `SPEC.bend` holds the head.** ```python # the head of a response: the status line and the headers. It holds no # blank line, so the first blank line of a response is the one before # the page. def head() -> String: "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close" ``` **2. `page_after_blank` reads that head.** ```diff -# LAW: the response of any page is some head, then a blank line, then -# the page: a client that cuts at the blank line reads the page back. +# LAW: the response of any page is SPEC.bend's head, then a blank +# line, then the page. law page_after_blank: for +page: String - exs head: String - {head ++ ("\r\n\r\n" ++ page) == Srv.http_response(page) : String} + {Spec.head() ++ ("\r\n\r\n" ++ page) == Srv.http_response(page) : String} ``` The comment of the law now says only what the law states. The sentence about the client moved to the comment of `head`, where one can read it off the text. **3. The proof of `page_after_blank` is `{==}`.** ```diff def Laws.page_after_blank(page): - ("HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close", {==}) + {==} ``` `main.bend` and `response_inj` don't change. The header of `LAWS.bend` doesn't change either: with this law, the laws pin the bytes sent for a page, as that header says. ### Why a `SPEC.bend` `guide/GUIDE.md` ("Laws and Proofs") gives `LAWS.bend` to the human, and `main.bend` and `PROOF.bend` to the AI. If the head were only in `main.bend`, an edit of `main.bend` could change what the law means. Five demos keep such texts in a `SPEC.bend` beside `LAWS.bend`: `proof_insertion_sort`, `pure_par_sort`, `pure_par_sum`, `app_triangle_2d` and `app_slash_boss_3d`. This PR does the same, with the same two header lines. ### How the proof works `Spec.head() ++ ("\r\n\r\n" ++ page)` computes to 63 characters in front of `page`: the 59 characters of the head and the 4 of the blank line. `http_response(page)` computes to the same 63 characters in front of `page`. So `{==}` proves the law for any `page`. On `main`, the proof was a pair: a head and `{==}`. Now the law names the head, so the proof has no value to give. `Laws.response_inj` is the same as on `main`. It drops the first 63 characters of both responses, and the pages are left. ### What the checker prints for an edit With the first edit on this branch, `bend PROOF.bend` prints SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.page_after_blank`. The checker prints both sides as chains of `SCon`. Written as text, they are: ```text - expected : "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" ++ page - observed : "HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/html\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n

Not the page

\r\n\r\n" ++ page ``` ### Three choices **The exact head.** A weaker law keeps `exs head` and adds two conditions: the head holds no blank line, and the head starts with the status line. I did not build it. It needs a text search in `SPEC.bend` and a longer proof, and the header of `LAWS.bend` says that the laws pin the bytes. The exact head has a cost: a response with one more header needs an edit of `SPEC.bend`. **Not the comments only.** 2.0.32 narrowed the comment of `io_http_fetch` to what its law says (#1119). I built that version for this demo too. It changes the two comments and no law, and all three edits still check. Here the exact law is cheap, because the head is a closed text. **`main.bend` keeps its own head.** The program does not import `SPEC.bend`. The law ties the two texts: if they differ, `bend PROOF.bend` fails. 1570e072 did the same for the `pow2` of `pure_par_sum`. ### What it doesn't cover - The laws read `http_response` only. `http_reply` chooses the page that the server sends, and that choice is in the IO part. A server that sends another page still checks (the fourth row below). - The accept loop, the read and the close are in the IO part also. No law states them. - `io_http_fetch` states a limit of the same kind in its header. This PR does not touch it. ### Before and after Each row edits `main.bend`, and `PROOF.bend` where the old proof no longer fits. `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` (Lean 4.34.0) give the same answer in each cell. #2125 holds the first three edits and the full output of `curl -i`. | edit | `main` at d18110b6 | this branch | |---|---|---| | a blank line inside the head | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.page_after_blank` | | no status line and no headers | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.page_after_blank` | | the status line says 500 | ALL PROOFS CHECK | SOME PROOFS FAIL at `Laws.page_after_blank` | | the server sends another page | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK (the limit above) | | nothing edited | ALL PROOFS CHECK | ALL PROOFS CHECK | To run a row again: 1. Apply the edit from #2125 to `main.bend`. On this branch, change only the count in `drop(63n, s)` in `PROOF.bend`. 2. Run `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` in `demos/io_http_server`. 3. To see what a client gets, run `bend main.bend -o http_server && ./http_server`, then `curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8080`. ### What I checked On d18110b6, macOS arm64: - `bend PROOF.bend` and `bend PROOF.bend --verdict` print ALL PROOFS CHECK. - `bend main.bend --check-only` and `bend SPEC.bend --check-only` print ALL PROOFS CHECK. - `bend LAWS.bend` alone reports 2 TODOs, the same as on `main`. - The server built from this branch answers `curl -i` with `HTTP/1.1 200 OK` and the body `

Hello, world!

`. - `String.contains(Spec.head(), "\r\n\r\n")` evaluates to `False{}`, as the comment in `SPEC.bend` says. - `bun gates/repo.ts` prints PASS: 56 / 56 with `SPEC.bend` tracked. I built each server with its port changed to 18080, because 8080 was taken on my machine. Not run: the cluster gates, Linux, and the JS build of the server.

title: perf(io): borrow shared strings and bytes during native conversion
body:
`io_cbuf` can borrow an immutable shared string or byte list until conversion finishes, then drop its owned root once. This avoids incrementing and decrementing the next cell's reference count for every element.

The dispatcher checks the root's count once. A root with one owner keeps the existing consuming loop. `io_cbuf_go` lets clang specialize those two paths; putting the choice inside one loop regressed unique-input throughput in an earlier experiment. `term_word` already uses the same borrow-then-drop ownership pattern.

The held root owns its descendants even if another owner drops concurrently. The count only selects the optimization; lifetime safety does not depend on its remaining greater than one. UTF-8 encoding, invalid-byte rejection and the returned malloc buffer's ownership are unchanged. The helper covers stdout, file writes, socket sends and other existing native callers.

To stay under the repo gate's 66,000-token limit for `comp.ts`, the `// Io` header and the old `io_cbuf` comment are shortened. Handle packing is still visible in `io_hand`/`io_hand_v`, and the NULL-on-invalid-byte contract in the native callers.

## Results

This measures a complete native command: read a payload from a file and write it to stdout eight times while retaining the same String. Stdout goes to `/dev/null` to expose conversion cost. The control reads and writes once without sharing. Payloads are generated ASCII log records, sized at 64 KiB, 1 MiB and 8 MiB. These are serialization workloads, not measurements of HTTP latency, disk throughput or the whole runtime benchmark suite.

Each row has 20 fresh-process samples per side, interleaved with alternating first side, after two warm-ups per side. The table reports p50 / p80 / p95. OS caches are warm; startup, file loading, conversion and teardown are all included. Peak RSS is the process high-water mark, not attributed allocation volume.

For the shared 8 MiB payload (64 MiB written), median wall time falls from 0.434 to 0.223 s on macOS and from 0.750 to 0.311 s in Linux. Peak RSS is unchanged at the displayed precision. Large unique-input medians stay within approximately 1%. The 64 KiB unique Linux case moves from 1.4 to 1.5 ms; its distributions overlap, and process startup is a substantial part of that case. I do not count that control as a speedup.

## Tests

VERIFIED for the shared-output workload above, with preserved output and a repeatable wall-time reduction in both environments.

- Full SHA256 comparison against the exact expected byte stream for all six workloads, base and branch, in both environments: 24/24 pass. The largest shared output is 64 MiB.
- Fourteen IO tests, each run with base and branch through native C, generated JS/Bun and the interpreter on each OS: 168/168 lane checks pass. They cover non-scalar Unicode, NUL payloads and rejected NUL paths/hosts, byte values 0..255, invalid bytes, file writes and positioned writes.
- Extended `print_write.bend` covers shared computed UTF-8 text, a unique prefix over a shared tail, and later reuse of the original text. Extended `file_binary.bend` checks that a shared invalid byte list survives rejection; its existing shared-valid-byte check also passes.
- Temporary generated-C instrumentation confirms the tests execute borrowed shared roots, unique roots, refcounted roots with count one, shared valid bytes and shared invalid bytes. Both modified tests also pass against the baseline implementation.
- `bun gates/repo.ts`: PASS 56/56, including `comp.ts` at 65,996 of its unchanged 66,000-token limit. `git diff --check`: pass.
- `bunx --bun -p typescript tsc --project bend2/pack/tsconfig.json`: fails with the same 21 diagnostic lines on base and branch, including existing `HTerm.k` errors and missing canvas types. No new diagnostics. The repo has no configured lint command; the repo gate and C compilation were run.
- The cluster-only test/performance gates were not run. Their pure runtime workloads do not cover host text output; the standalone benchmark below exercises the changed public IO path.

Environment: base `d18110b6d6e9a70bb8814b2a8d8db092e301e540`, branch `9192bd0e0f392ee0653e4f85a76e613601f50189`; Apple M4 Pro, 24 GiB RAM; macOS 26.5.1 arm64, Bun 1.4.2, Apple clang 21.0.0; Linux arm64, Debian clang 19.1.7. <summary>Interleaved measurement driver</summary>

```python
"""Interleaved base/branch benchmark, the same on macOS and inside Linux containers.

usage: bench_pairs.py --pairs N --base "CMD" --branch "CMD" [--base-cwd D] [--branch-cwd D]
                      [--warmup K] [--metrics a,b] [--digest] --out FILE.csv

Each side has its own full command, so each side picks its own interpreter or build
(e.g. /base/.venv-linux/bin/python bench.py). Wall time is measured around the child
process only. peak_rss_mib is the largest resident set of one process: the child, or
the largest descendant it waited for (getrusage semantics). It is NOT the summed
memory of parallel workers, and it excludes GPU memory.

--metrics names values the child measures itself, printed on stdout as one line
`BENCH name=value name=value`. Use it when startup or data loading dominates the
process: e.g. `inner_s` (the timed call alone) and `rss_delta_mib` (how much the call
raised the peak RSS). Every listed metric must appear in every run.
--digest: the child also prints one line `DIGEST <hash>` of its output (e.g. md5 of the
results the user reads). Every measured run of both sides must print the same hash, or
the script reports "outputs differ" and exits 1: a speedup that changes output is a bug.
Exit 1 if any warm-up or measured run fails or a sample is invalid.
"""
import argparse, csv, math, os, platform, shlex, subprocess, sys, tempfile, time

RSS_UNIT_BYTES = 1 if sys.platform == "darwin" else 1024  # ru_maxrss: bytes on macOS, KiB on Linux


def run_once(cmd, cwd):
    with tempfile.TemporaryFile() as err_file:  # a file, not a pipe: a chatty stderr cannot block the child
        start = time.perf_counter()
        proc = subprocess.Popen(cmd, cwd=cwd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=err_file)
        out = proc.stdout.read().decode(errors="replace")  # drain before wait so the pipe never blocks the child
        _, status, usage = os.wait4(proc.pid, 0)
        wall = time.perf_counter() - start
        err_file.seek(0)
        err = err_file.read().decode(errors="replace")[-400:]
    code = os.waitstatus_to_exitcode(status)
    return wall, usage.ru_maxrss * RSS_UNIT_BYTES / 2**20, code, err, out


def child_metrics(stdout, names):
    found = {}
    for line in stdout.splitlines():
        if line.startswith("BENCH "):
            found.update(kv.split("=", 1) for kv in line.split()[1:])
    missing = [n for n in names if n not in found]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"child did not print BENCH {', '.join(missing)}")
    values = [float(found[n]) for n in names]
    if not all(math.isfinite(v) for v in values):
        raise ValueError("child printed a non-finite metric")
    return values


def child_digest(stdout):
    digests = [line.split(maxsplit=1)[1].strip() for line in stdout.splitlines() if line.startswith("DIGEST ")]
    if len(digests) != 1:
        raise ValueError(f"child printed {len(digests)} DIGEST lines, expected 1")
    return digests[0]


def main():
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--pairs", type=int, required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--warmup", type=int, default=1, help="unreported runs per side; 0 for cold-start cases")
    ap.add_argument("--base", required=True); ap.add_argument("--branch", required=True)
    ap.add_argument("--base-cwd", default="."); ap.add_argument("--branch-cwd", default=".")
    ap.add_argument("--metrics", default="", help="comma-separated names the child prints as BENCH name=value")
    ap.add_argument("--digest", action="store_true", help="child prints DIGEST <hash>; all runs must match")
    ap.add_argument("--out", required=True)
    a = ap.parse_args()
    if a.pairs < 1 or a.warmup < 0:
        ap.error("--pairs must be >= 1 and --warmup >= 0")
    metric_names = [m for m in a.metrics.split(",") if m]
    sides = {"base": (shlex.split(a.base), a.base_cwd), "branch": (shlex.split(a.branch), a.branch_cwd)}

    for name, (cmd, cwd) in sides.items():
        for _ in range(a.warmup):
            *_, code, err, _ = run_once(cmd, cwd)
            if code != 0:
                sys.exit(f"warm-up failed on {name} (exit {code}): {err}")

    failed = False
    digests = {"base": set(), "branch": set()}
    with open(a.out, "w", newline="") as f:
        f.write(f"# {platform.system()} {platform.machine()} python {platform.python_version()} warmup={a.warmup}\n")
        w = csv.writer(f); w.writerow(["pair", "side", "wall_s", "peak_rss_mib", *metric_names, "exit"])
        for i in range(1, a.pairs + 1):
            order = ("base", "branch") if i % 2 else ("branch", "base")  # alternate who goes first
            for name in order:
                wall, rss, code, err, out = run_once(*sides[name])
                extra = [""] * len(metric_names)
                if code == 0:
                    try:
                        extra = [f"{v:.6g}" for v in child_metrics(out, metric_names)]
                        if a.digest:
                            digests[name].add(child_digest(out))
                    except ValueError as e:
                        code, err = 99, str(e)
                w.writerow([i, name, f"{wall:.4f}", f"{rss:.1f}", *extra, code])
                f.flush()
                if code != 0:
                    failed = True; print(f"pair {i} {name} exit {code}: {err}", file=sys.stderr)
    if a.digest and len(digests["base"] | digests["branch"]) > 1:
        failed = True
        print(f"outputs differ: base {sorted(digests['base'])} branch {sorted(digests['branch'])}", file=sys.stderr)
    sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Considerations

The change is host IO only. JS and device execution are unchanged. It adds no cache, background task or tuning flag. Existing IO comments were shortened to fit the permanent compiler token cap; the macOS FIFO and leading-zero address warnings remain.

title: perf(base): compare Map leaf keys without rebuilding both strings
refactor(comp): the intrinsic table is keyed by Base's def name, intr_of has no flag, a spare carries its size class, and a fold walks its body once
body:
A simplification pass over `bend2/comp.ts`: **65,952 → 65,913 ttok** (−39; the cap is 66k), in that file only.

## What changes

- **The intrinsic table is keyed by Base's def name.** `OPERATIONS` had keys like `u32_add`, reached by lowercasing `U32.add` and replacing dots, with a cache (`FL.ops`) over that translation. The keys are now the Bend names (`"U32.add"`, `"Array.atomic.cas"`, `"Map.msb.u"`), so `intr_of` is a direct lookup and `op_name` and its cache are gone. No other cache is touched.
- **`intr_of` has no `js` flag.** An op is an intrinsic in a lane exactly when it has that lane's text. Before, a JS-only op (the String ones) counted as an ordinary def in the JS lane unless the caller passed `true`.
- **A spare carries its size class, not a word count.** The emitted free names the class as a number (`heap_free(e, 2, sp)`) instead of calling `cls_fit(3)` in C, as every emitted alloc already did.
- **`emit_fold` walks an unfolded body once.** It charged fuel in one walk and folded the inner calls in a second; one walk does both. When a body runs the fuel out, the inner calls visited before that point now stay folded, where the two walks discarded them; the folds are valid either way, and no program in the corpus changed.
- **The compiler's `cls_fit` gives class 0 for no words, as the runtime's does** (it gave 32). No caller reaches it with zero today; `lay_arr` drops its own guard for that case.

## Effect on emitted programs

Compared on all 1,944 test, demo and bench programs, `-o f.c` and `-o f.js`, against `main` (8ec4c889):

- **C:** every `.c` is identical once `cls_fit(n)` is read as its number. Every compile error is identical.
- **JS:** 46 of the 990 programs that compile to JS differ, all from the `intr_of` change:
  - Base's bodies of the String ops, and helpers reached only through them (`String.order`, `Cmp.is_eq`, `String.starts_with`), are no longer emitted, or are emitted at a different position.
  - Some closures take their captured variables in a different order, consistently at the definition and the call.

One edge not tested directly: in the JS lane, a U32 match whose arm goes through a String op no longer constant-folds through Base's body when building a lookup table. No program in the corpus changed its tables.

## Verification

- **Machine code:** the host objects (`clang -O3`) were byte-identical to `main`'s for all 938 programs that build. This was run on the first two changes, before the rebase over #2122, and not repeated; the later changes leave the C output as it was.
- **Gates:** `gates/repo.ts` 56 / 56 and `gates/test.ts` 1,853 / 1,853, run with the first three changes. The `emit_fold` and `cls_fit` changes came after and leave every `.c` and `.js` in the corpus byte-identical to that gated state; `gates/repo.ts` was rerun on the final commit. An earlier test run had one miss, a JS-lane timeout in `io_chan_reclaim_limit`, which did not repeat.
- **Not run:** `gates/perf.ts` on this branch, and CUDA.

title: perf(base): String.eq settles heads before tails, and Map.set walks the keys once
body:
Follow-up to #2128, from its review.

**String.eq.** It walks the strings itself with `Char.is_eq` instead of going through `String.order`, and settles each head before it opens the tails. `String.order.go` matched `a b c` left to right, so after two unequal heads it was stuck on `String.order.go(t, p, LT{})`, waiting on a symbolic tail. Now `String.eq(SCon{'a', SCon{'b', t}}, SCon{'a', SCon{'c', p}})` reduces to `False{}` (main fails that proof). Map.get, Map.has and Map.pop use it, and #2128's `Map.key_eq` is gone. Bend can't express this as one function: the termination check reads arguments left to right and a match can't open a later binder first, so it takes a helper def, as `String.cmp` and `String.starts_with` already do.

**Map.set.** `Map.set.fin` compared the new key with the closest leaf's through `String.cmp`, rebuilding both, then walked them again with `Map.diff` to find the split bit. `Map.diff` now does both in one tail-recursive walk: `None` if the keys are equal, else the first differing bit.

## Measurements

Native C on this Mac (apple_m4_max), median of 5 runs.

| Workload | main | branch |
|---|---|---|
| Map.set over an existing key, 1M, 64-char shared prefix | 2.29 s | 0.76 s (-67%) |
| Map.set a new key then Map.pop it, 1M, 64-char shared prefix | 2.02 s | 1.54 s (-24%) |
| Map.has hit on one leaf, 4M, 64-char prefix (vs #2128's key_eq) | 1.59 s | 1.63 s |
| String.eq, 400K compares of 257 chars, equal or differing at the end | 0.28 s | 0.30 s (+7%) |

String.eq costs one extra call per char on native. On JS it still compiles to `===`, so JS is unchanged.

The review on #2128 asked whether the leaf helpers' `+k` share piles up layers on a repeated miss. It does not: `+` is a reference count. 16M misses on one leaf, then a hit, run in constant memory (1.5 MB peak RSS), and the time grows linearly in N.

**Checked**
- `tests/base/map_leaf_eq.bend` gains two proofs: a shared head, then unequal known chars, then unknown tails, for `Map.has` and for `String.eq`.
- All 40 tests that use `String.eq`, `String.order`/`is_lt`/... or `Map.`: same interpreted, JS and C output as main. 34 pass in all three lanes. The other 6 expect a check error and print the same as main.
- `gates/repo.ts`: 56/56. The full test gate was not run (it needs the minis).

title: perf(c): borrow shared tails in String.drop
body:
String.drop now consumes unique cells as before and borrows the suffix once it reaches a shared cell. The C walker retains the selected tail before releasing its shared root. This avoids taking and releasing every skipped shared cell.

Base's definition, checker reduction and the JS backend are unchanged. The JS emitted for all 21 benchmark programs is byte-identical between base and branch.

## Results

The Map.get workload adapts [#2074](https://github.com/bendlang/bend/issues/2074): 4096 entries, keys with P copies of 'a' followed by four suffix letters, then 50,000 lookups. These are whole-process medians, including map construction, query creation, lookups and cleanup, against f311527776559ce40095108ad6a7514a6c34aaa1. The tested branch is b5ca68840fd9581e469ca19740c93b88ce0d790a.

| Added prefix P | macOS arm64, base → branch | Docker Linux arm64, base → branch |
|---|---|---|
| 0 chars | 12.0 → 11.0 ms (-8%) | 18.95 → 16.30 ms (-14%) |
| 16 chars | 24.8 → 20.7 ms (-17%) | 39.4 → 29.8 ms (-24%) |
| 64 chars | 61.5 → 46.9 ms (-24%) | 101.75 → 71.20 ms (-30%) |
| 256 chars | 204.85 → 137.40 ms (-33%) | 334.8 → 219.5 ms (-34%) |

All 20 pairs improve in each Map.get row above. Peak RSS is unchanged at the displayed precision for those rows. This is a time improvement, not a memory-reduction claim.

There are 21 cases per OS, each with 20 interleaved pairs: 1680 timed child processes in total. Pair order alternates; each side has two warm-ups, and every measured child is a fresh process. Each sample must print the independently expected checksum and exit successfully. An intentional wrong checksum makes the sampler reject the run.

The controls cover 16, 1024, 65,536, 1,048,576 and 8,388,608 characters, unique and retained/shared inputs, zero and overlong drops, and a 64 KiB private prefix over a retained 1 MiB tail, stopped before and after the handoff. Map.get also has a P64 miss case. Prefix lengths vary at a fixed 4096 entries; this is not entry-count scaling.

Dropping half an 8 Mi-character retained input, then counting the returned tail, takes 137.25 → 122.9 ms on macOS and 220.15 → 194.0 ms on Linux, including setup and the original-input check. The unique control is almost flat: 84.3 → 83.75 ms on macOS, 135.05 → 135.5 ms on Linux.

Small costs remain visible in the full tables:
- Linux unique 8 Mi-character half-drop: +0.45 ms / +0.33%, slower in 14/20 pairs.
- Linux unique 1 Mi-character overlong drop: +0.25 ms / +1.57%, slower in 15/20 pairs.
- Linux private-prefix/before-handoff control: inner median 10 → 11 ms; whole process 30.95 → 31.0 ms. IO.now has 1 ms resolution.
- Linux 1 Ki-character controls: +0.05–0.1 ms in process medians, dominated by startup; their median paired differences are zero.
- The largest median RSS increase is 0.4 MiB, below 1%. There is no claim of zero cost in every control.

The direct-control inner interval includes String.drop, String.length of its result and consumer cleanup. It is not isolated drop latency. Building the input occurs before the inner timestamp. A retained input is checked again after that interval; this check is inside whole-process time. The 16-character rows are startup/timer-resolution controls.

## Why this helps

In a separate instrumented P64 run, String.drop is called 703,167 times: 553,167 calls drop zero characters, and 3,350,000 skipped cells use the borrowed path. That instrumented binary is excluded from timing data. CPU sampling of a longer, 500,000-query P256 variant attributes the old drop cost to span_fade/term_drop; String.eq remains a large cost after the change. Query generation and map construction also remain, so this does not remove all lookup work.

The unique/refcount-one path still uses ctr_take and spare_free. Borrowed descendants are sealed or static, and the root stays alive until the result is retained. A fresh unique prefix can transition to the shared path partway through. term_triv is checked before reading a refcount.

## Tests

VERIFIED for the native CPU cases measured above.

- 10 fixtures on base and branch × C/Bun/Node/interpreter × macOS/Linux: 160 checks, all expected output lines matched. These include the existing string, suffix and map-cursor tests and the new native-drop fixture.
- Both OSes: existing string kit and new fixture on both sides with BEND_POISON and AddressSanitizer/UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. All passed, with leak detection disabled. Linux sanitizer libraries were added to a separate test-only image; timing used the unchanged image below.
- Both sides on real Metal: the new fixture passes with --gpu on. It checks a shared string across 16 parallel lanes. This is behavior coverage, not a GPU timing claim.
- Dynamic full-U32 Char, NUL, surrogate and astral values; empty, zero, exact, overlong and huge-count drops; preserved original values, unique inputs and unique-prefix/shared-tail inputs. Independent probes also covered RFC1, partial application and a first-class String.drop reference.
- Repo gate: 56/56. comp.ts: 65,999 / 66,000 ttok. The cap is unchanged. git diff --check passes.
- Typecheck is not green: strict TypeScript 7.0.2 reports the same 16 diagnostics (27 lines, after line-number normalization) on base and branch, including missing Node type declarations and existing term-type errors. No new diagnostic was added. No standalone lint command is configured here.
- The full mini-cluster/perf gates and CUDA were not run locally.

## Review guide

Start at str_drop in bend2/comp.ts, then its String.drop entry in OPERATIONS and tests/run/string_drop_native.bend. The remaining diff shortens existing ownership/emitter comments to fit the permanent source cap; it changes no compiler behavior. The public String.drop signature and representation stay the same. Revert the intrinsic entry and helper to restore the prior native path.

## Environment

macOS 26.5.1, Apple M4 Pro, 24 GiB RAM, Apple clang 21.0.0; Bun 1.4.2, Node 25.9.0, uv 0.13.7, Python sampler 3.14.5. C flags: -O3 -g -std=c11, linked with -lpthread -lm.

Linux arm64 is a Debian 13.7 VM on the same Apple Silicon Mac, not bare-metal Linux. Container limits: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB RAM, 8 GiB memory+swap (no extra swap). Debian clang 19.1.7, Bun 1.4.2, Node 25.9.0, uv 0.13.7, Python 3.12.16. The timed image ID was sha256:99df25fd443929b4bf3095c2dc763fde6c29cbe7bb2d458d79ec6e50523eced8. No other build ran alongside a timing batch. The benchmarks have no bang or GPU work. RSS is the child process high-water mark, not attributed allocations or GPU memory.

## Reproduction

The following files are self-contained. Save each under .scratch/perf/string-drop-20261112/ in a checkout of this PR, then run:

```sh
export BEND_NO_TELEMETRY=1
d=.scratch/perf/string-drop-20261112
printf '.scratch/\n' >> "$(git rev-parse --git-path info/exclude)"
git fetch origin f311527776559ce40095108ad6a7514a6c34aaa1
git worktree add --detach "$d/base" f311527776559ce40095108ad6a7514a6c34aaa1
node "$d/generate-final.mjs"
node "$d/build-final.mjs"
uv run python "$d/measure.py" mac 20 final all
```

The summarizer expects both OSes, so run its last command after the Linux batch. It writes final/results.json. Keep pilot and interrupted files outside final/. The sampler records wall seconds and RSS MiB; tables above convert wall and inner time to milliseconds.

For Linux, build the Dockerfile below and capture its immutable ID. Its pinned Python base and tool versions recreate the setup; package mirrors can change, so check clang --version before comparing numbers. The measured image ID is recorded above, rather than claiming a rebuilt image has the same ID.

```sh
docker build --platform linux/arm64 -f "$d/Dockerfile" -t bend-drop-repro "$d"
image=$(docker inspect bend-drop-repro --format '{{.Id}}')
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 --cpus=4 --memory=8g --memory-swap=8g \
  -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work "$image" sh -c \
  'set -eu; d=.scratch/perf/string-drop-20261112; sh "$d/build-linux.sh"; uv run python "$d/measure.py" linux 20 final all'
uv run python "$d/summarize-final.py"
```

```bend
import Base

# keys: P copies of 'a', then 4 letters from the low 16 bits of i
def pre(n: Nat, t: String) -> String:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      t
    case 1n+p:
      SCon{Chr{97}, pre(p, t)}

def hex(+i: U32, +s: Nat) -> Char:
  Chr{(97 + U32.and(U32.shrn(i, s), 15) : U32)}

def key(+p: Nat, +i: U32) -> String:
  pre(p, SCon{hex(i, 12n), SCon{hex(i, 8n), SCon{hex(i, 4n), SCon{hex(i, 0n), SNil{}}}}})

def build(n: Nat, +i: U32, +p: Nat, m: Map<&2, U32>) -> Map<&2, U32>:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      m
    case 1n+k:
      build(k, (i + 1 : U32), p, Map.set(&2, U32, m, key(p, i), i))

def look(n: Nat, +i: U32, +p: Nat, +acc: U32, r: Map<&2, U32> & U32) -> U32:
  match n:
    case 0n:
      (m, v) = r
      (acc + v : U32)
    case 1n+k:
      (m, v) = r
      look(k, (i + 1 : U32), p, (acc + v : U32), Map.get(U32, 0, m, key(p, U32.and((i * 7 : U32), 4095))))

def run(+p: Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    m : Map<&2, U32> <- IO.pure(Map<&2, U32>, build(4096n, 0, p, Map.new(&2, U32)))
    start : Nat <- IO.now()
    sum : U32 <- IO.pure(U32, look(50000n, 0, p, 0, (m, 0)))
    end : Nat <- IO.now()
    IO.print(U32.show(sum))
    IO.print(Nat.show(Nat.sub(end, start)))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  run(0n)
```
