title: Continuations with the same code are one segment, so a return through them has one target
body:
**`comp.ts` is 66,251 ttok, 251 over the 66,000 cap (main is 65,962), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run. Independent of #2135 and #2137.

## What it does

A non-tail call pushes a frame that ends in the id of its continuation, and the callee returns by jumping through the segment table on that id (`WL_RETN`). When two arms of a def continue the same way after their calls, each arm got its own copy of the continuation. The return then has two targets, and which one it takes depends on the arm that made the call, a whole subtree earlier, so the indirect jump predicts badly.

Continuation segments whose text is the same but for the names of their locals are now emitted once:

- **The key** is the segment's frame reads and its lines, with every local renamed by first appearance. Equal keys are the same code.
- **To a fixpoint:** fusing two continuations rewrites the frames that push them, which may make those segments alike too (`esize` in `symreg`: `k3 k7 k11 k15` fuse first, then `k1 k5 k9 k13`).
- **Only continuations** (segments entered through a frame). A def's entry, a closure and a join keep their own segment.
- **The device:** a fused segment is compiled for the device if any of its copies was.

In `queens`, `solve`'s two descending arms (`ret` is `Stat0` or `Stats`) differ before the child call and agree after it, so `solve$k1` and `solve$k3` were the same code. With one copy, every return from a child lands on the same segment.

## Results

One M4, GPU off. The machine was shared with other benchmark runs, so the numbers are instructions retired and cycles (`/usr/bin/time -l`), the two builds run in turn.

| bench | threads | instructions, main | this | cycles, main (min / median) | this (min / median) | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `queens` | 1 | 89.83G | 89.83G | 22.06G / 22.13G | 19.93G / 19.96G | 1.11x |
| `queens` | 8 | 89.88G | 89.88G | 24.84G / 25.14G | 22.57G / 23.20G | 1.10x |
| `symreg` | 1 | 50.78G | 50.76G | 12.46G / 12.72G | 12.28G / 12.33G | 1.01x |
| `symreg` | 8 | 50.81G | 50.79G | 14.18G / 14.39G | 13.86G / 14.28G | 1.02x |

10 runs each at one thread, 12 at eight. `queens`' wall time at one thread goes from 5.55 s to 5.01 s (the minimum of those runs; 5.63 s to 5.06 s the median). Wall time at eight threads moved too much with the machine's load to report.

**Placement:** the `queens` gain is in cycles at the same instruction count, and on this M4 cycles can move with where code lands, so both builds were swept. Nops at the head of `work_loop` (run once per task) move every segment by 4 bytes a step; `solve` and `solve$k1` sit at the same addresses in both builds at each step. 16 positions (64 bytes), 6 interleaved rounds, one thread, the minimum per position:

| build | min | median | max |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| main | 21.93G | 22.14G | 22.41G |
| this | 19.89G | 20.00G | 20.39G |

The ranges do not overlap: the slowest position of this build is 1.54G cycles under the fastest of main. Position by position the ratio runs from 1.09x to 1.11x, median 1.11x. Placement alone moves either build by about 2%.

**Mispredictions:** counted with Instruments' CPU Counters (`xctrace`, sampling every 20M cycles, so about 98% of each run is covered; two runs each, scaled to the full 89.83G instructions):

| build | mispredicted branches | of them indirect |
|---|---:|---:|
| main | 577M | 78.4M |
| this | 508M | 0.07M |

The indirect mispredictions are the returns through the segment table, and they are gone. The other branches mispredict 9M more often, so the total falls by 69M.

The other 15 `bench/runtime` programs compile to byte-identical C. `queens`' C twin runs 27.19G instructions in 15.11G cycles, so this takes its gap from 1.46x to 1.32x. In `symreg` only `esize`'s continuations fuse (6 segments); `eval`'s differ by their operator.

**Elsewhere:** `demos/pure_hvm5_mini` goes from 645 to 608 segments and `demos/app_slash_boss_3d` from 778 to 756; their C is 2.8% and 0.4% smaller. Of the 905 tests that emit C, 125 emit different C.

**Compile time:** emitting `app_slash_boss_3d`'s C takes 2.28 s against 2.29 s on main, and `pure_hvm5_mini`'s 1.03 s to 1.45 s against 1.08 s to 1.21 s over four rounds: no difference above the noise.

## Checks

All local, against main `011b54d3`:

- **Native lane:** every test was emitted by both compilers. 780 emit byte-identical C. The 125 that differ were built and run with the GPU off, at the default thread count and at one thread: 122 print their `#|` lines on both, 3 fail the same way on both (`gfx/window_open_args`, `io/http_fetch_limit`, `io/tcp_recv_max_huge`), none differs from main.
- **Memory:** each of those 125 built with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit: the same output, exit code and count as main on every one.
- **Metal:** the 3 of those 125 that make a `!` call print the same with `--gpu on`. A scratch program in which a host-only continuation and device-reached ones fuse, so the copy kept becomes a device segment, prints the same with the GPU on and off, on main and here.
- **JS lane:** unchanged (`compile_book` is the C emitter); the JS for the new test, `symreg` and `pure_hvm5_mini` is byte-identical.
- **New test:** `tests/run/fused_continuations.bend`: arms that fuse at once, arms that fuse only at the fixpoint, arms that differ by a constant or an operator (kept apart), the `queens` shape, and forking arms. Its numbers were computed apart in Python; it prints them on the C lane (default threads and one), and under `bend file.bend`.
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates and CUDA** have not run.
- **Joins and closures** with the same code are not fused, so two forking arms that agree keep their continuations apart (they lead to different joins).
- **Continuations that differ in one word** (`eval`'s four operators in `symreg`) keep their own segments, and their returns keep several targets.
- **`tsc`** was not run.

## Cost

+289 ttok. Getting under the cap needs 251 tokens cut elsewhere in `comp.ts`, or a raise.

## Where this came from

The direction explored was running sequential non-tail recursion as real C calls on the host. With `solve` rewritten by hand in the emitted C as a recursive C function, `queens` runs 19.13G to 19.39G cycles, 1.14x to 1.15x over main. This change reaches 19.93G, so most of what C calls gave `queens` was a return that predicts, and the rest is 1.03x to 1.04x. The same edit on `symreg`'s `eval` gave between 0.97x and 1.14x across two equivalent ways of writing the function and two optimisation levels (the spread is the shape clang picks), with 8% more instructions in the fastest one.

title: A countdown loop that calls a countdown loop each turn runs sixteen turns' calls side by side on the host
body:
**`comp.ts` is 68,071 ttok, 2,071 over the 66,000 cap, so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run. Independent of #2135 and #2137.

## What it does

A loop that counts a Nat down and calls, each turn, a second countdown loop over words is a chain of dependent steps: `mandelbrot`'s 64-pixel chunk (`hchunk`) runs 51 steps of `mit` for one pixel before it starts the next, and each step waits on the multiply before it. The pixels are independent, but clang vectorises neither the outer loop nor the inner one.

On the host, such a loop now runs the calls of its next sixteen turns side by side:

- **Enter:** each of sixteen lanes takes the arguments the inner loop would start with at one of the next sixteen turns. A helper between the two loops (`pix`) is emitted once more as a lane variant that stores those arguments instead of calling the loop.
- **Step:** while every lane holds the same count, the inner loop's lane variant (its body, with the self call replaced by a store) steps all lanes one round at a time. That is a plain loop over sixteen lanes of `u32` state, and clang vectorises it.
- **End:** the inner loop itself ends each lane (its zero row), and each of the sixteen turns then reads its result by its predecessor instead of making the call.

When it applies. All of these are read from the emitted natives, and each falls back to the code as it was:

- **The outer loop** is a flat def with a Nat every self call passes the predecessor of and whose zero row holds every result, so every turn it has left will run.
- **The call** stands at the top of the countdown's row (under no other match), and its arguments are words built from the predecessor and from parameters every self call passes back as they are, through operators alone.
- **The callee** is the inner loop, or a def whose every tail calls it. Both take and answer words only.
- **The inner loop** is a countdown of the same kind: it leaves only at zero and every self call passes the predecessor. Lanes whose counts differ are not stepped together; the inner loop runs each alone, as before.
- **The first turn's count decides once, before the loop:** a count clang can see at compile time, or one under 8, leaves the loop exactly as it was. Clang unrolls a short known loop and vectorises the outer one by itself, and under 8 steps the core overlaps the turns without help (measured below).
- **Host only:** all of it sits under `#if !DEVICE`.

## Results

One M4, GPU off, one thread, best of 5 interleaved runs (the machine was shared, so these are instructions retired and cycles from `/usr/bin/time -l`).

| bench | main, instructions / cycles | this | | C twin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `mandelbrot` | 43.45G / 19.76G | 28.34G / 11.50G | 1.72x | 34.59G / 16.60G |
| `gameoflife` | 172.35G / 31.81G | 172.39G / 22.18G | 1.43x | 158.61G / 27.70G |

Wall time, best of 5 (noisy, other jobs were running): `mandelbrot` 4.97 s to 2.92 s on one thread and 1.35 s to 0.82 s on eight; `gameoflife` 8.07 s to 5.57 s and 2.42 s to 1.93 s.

`mandelbrot`'s step vectorises (15G fewer instructions). `gameoflife`'s does not (the instruction count is the same); its gain is sixteen independent boards in flight where there was one.

**Bench suite:** of the 17 `bench/runtime` programs only these two compile to different C. The other 15 are byte-identical.

**All programs:** of the 1,943 `.bend` files under `bench/runtime`, `demos` and `tests`, 941 build on main and here; 938 emit byte-identical C, and the 3 that differ are the two benches and the new test.

**Where it does not pay,** on a small program made for it (a 4e8-step hash under an outer loop, the inner count hidden from clang), cycles:

| inner count | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 | 32 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| main | 0.698G | 0.506G | 0.523G | 0.675G | 0.969G |
| this | 0.696G | 0.524G | 0.323G | 0.295G | 0.299G |

Under 8 the lanes are off and the loop is the one main emits. With the count written as a literal clang can see (4 hash steps, 12 Newton steps over F32, 100 Collatz steps), the instruction counts equal main's: the lane code is dead and clang drops it. Before that test existed, the F32 case ran 1.5x slower with the lanes on, because clang had been vectorising its outer loop.

## Checks

All local, against main `011b54d3`:

- **Native lane:** every test that builds and passes on main (882) passes here, the GPU off.
- **JS lane:** the same 882 print their `#|` lines, and every test file gets the verdict it gets on main.
- **Memory:** the new test, built with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit: the same output and the same count as main. Every other test emits the C main emits.
- **New test:** `tests/run/countdown_lanes.bend` runs turns under, at and past sixteen; an inner count of zero, of 7, of 8 and one written as a literal; a count that differs by turn, or agrees only inside a block of turns (the lanes run alone); an inner loop that may leave early or has a third row, and an outer loop that leaves early, has a third row or a second countdown (none takes lanes); the loop called directly and through a helper; a countdown that is not the first parameter; a result of two words; F32 state; an argument that changes between turns. Its counts come back through a join so that clang cannot see them; a build that prints each batch confirms the lanes run in 10 of its 11 sites, stepped together and alone. It prints main's output on the C lane and under `bend file.bend`.
- **Metal:** `mandelbrot` and `gameoflife` build with `-DBEND_METAL=1` and print their checksums on the GPU (the lane variants are dead code there).
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates and CUDA** have not run. Linux and x86 have not been built; the lanes use `__builtin_constant_p`, which gcc and clang both have.
- **A fail-stop moves earlier:** the calls of the next fifteen turns run before the rest of the current turn. Every one of them would have run, so only a program that already dies (a Nat past 2^48-1 in a later turn) can die at a different point.
- **A count clang knows** gets no lanes even when it is long (51 written in the def that loops), since the test cannot tell a short known loop from a long one.
- **Arguments** must be operators over the predecessor and fixed parameters: a call whose argument is a `let` bound earlier in the turn, or another call's result, is left alone. So is a loop inside a segment (a def that forks), and a call under a second match.
- **`mandelbrot`'s second pass** forks one leaf per pixel, so there is no loop to take lanes; it is now most of the run.
- **`tsc`** was not run.

## Cost

+2,109 ttok. Compile time: emitting `mandelbrot`'s C takes 182 ms against 165 ms (two more natives and the lane block). `demos/app_slash_boss_3d`, whose C does not change, takes 1.72 s against 1.64 s, best of 15 on a loaded machine where single runs spread by 10%; the emitter's fixpoint takes the same three rounds.

title: fix(io): flush stdout before native IO jobs
body:
On the native runtime, `IO.print` and `IO.write` can leave output buffered until the event loop next polls. A later effect in the same fiber can start on a helper thread before that flush. A file write to stdout can then appear ahead of earlier output, or a subprocess can read redirected output before the earlier text reaches the file.

The runtime now flushes stdout before handing a job to a helper thread. The regression keeps another fiber runnable so the helper can finish before the next poll, then checks that stdout still follows program order. It fails on upstream and passes with the patch on macOS and Linux arm64.

title: fix(io): skip empty writes to JavaScript stdout
body:
With stdout redirected, each `IO.write("")` adds an empty buffer to the JavaScript output queue. The queue flushes at 64 KiB, but empty buffers add nothing to the byte count. A loop can exhaust the heap before it writes a single byte.

Skip encoding and queuing when the input string is empty. The regression test writes two empty strings between visible output and counts the empty buffers before the flush. It finds two on `main` and zero with this change.

### Reproduction

```bend
import Base

def repeat(n: Nat) -> IO(Unit):
  match n:
    case 0n: IO.print("ok")
    case 1n+p:
      do IO<Unit>:
        IO.write("")
        repeat(p)

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  repeat(U32.to_nat(1000000))
```

```sh
bend empty.bend -o empty.cjs
node --max-old-space-size=96 empty.cjs > out.txt
```

On `main`, Node runs out of memory before it prints `ok`. With the fix, it prints `ok` and exits 0.

### Measurements

Median peak resident memory across five alternating pairs, with the default heap limit and stdout redirected to a pipe.

| Runtime | main | This PR |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Node 24.15.0 | 572 MiB | 57 MiB |
| Bun 1.3.14 | 295 MiB | 92 MiB |

I also timed nonempty writes across eleven alternating pairs. For 800,000 one-byte writes, the median paired time increased by 1.7% on Node and 2.6% on Bun. For 750,000 mixed ASCII and UTF-8 writes, it decreased by 0.7% on Node and 3.3% on Bun. All output files matched their expected bytes.

### Checks

- The new test reproduced the bug on the Bend CLI and on emitted JavaScript under Bun and Node. All three passed after the fix.
- Fourteen stdout and stderr tests passed on the Bend CLI and Bun. All eleven with native support passed there. Twelve of thirteen Node tests matched the expected output. The existing `stderr_failure` test prints `errno 2` on Node on both branches.
- The local repository gate passed all 56 checks.

title: perf(io): File.read_line reads a regular file ahead and seeks back past its line
body:
## What

On the C lane, `File.read_line` made one `read(2)` per byte, so a program that reads a file line by line spent most of its time in syscalls. On a regular file it now reads up to 256 bytes per `read(2)`, cuts at the first `'\n'`, and seeks back over the bytes past it. The file position after each call is the same as before. A pipe, a terminal or a size-0 file such as `/proc/...` still reads one byte at a time, because only a regular file can seek back.

```
regular file:  read(256) -> "ab\ncd..."  -> keep "ab\n", lseek(-k, SEEK_CUR)
pipe / tty:    read(1) x n               -> unchanged
```

`File.read`, `read_bytes` and `read_at` pass step 0 and keep their old path. If the seek-back fails, the call answers `Fail` with that errno instead of dropping bytes without a trace.

## Why

A loop that counts the lines and bytes of a file with `File.read_line(f, 65536)`, built with `bend rl.bend -o rl` on an Apple M4 Pro (macOS, 12 threads). Each row is 3 interleaved base/branch pairs, warm. The output digest matches in every pair.

| input | base p50 | branch p50 | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 200k lines, 9.5 MB | 4.22 s | 1.67 s | 2.5x |
| 1M lines, 47.6 MB | 21.16 s | 7.94 s | 2.7x |
| 10k lines of ~4 KB, 42 MB | 12.18 s | 0.27 s | 45x |
| `./rl /dev/stdin < 200k lines` | 4.28 s | 1.65 s | 2.6x |
| `cat 200k lines \| ./rl /dev/stdin` | 4.47 s | 4.91 s | 0.91x |

The pipe row gets slower: every line now pays one `fstat` to learn it is not a regular file. That works out to about 2 µs per line, against roughly 22 µs per line that a pipe already costs. On the regular-file rows, sys time drops from 3.4 s to 1.3 s at 200k lines; I did not profile what remains.

## How to test

- `tests/io/file_read_line_rest.bend` (new): it reads a short line, a 300-byte line cut at 280 and then finished by the next call, a whole 300-byte line (two 256-byte chunks), and a line cut at `max`, then calls `File.read` for the rest of the file. The test passes on base and on the branch. On the C lane it goes red if the seek-back is off by one byte, or if the scan for `'\n'` starts at the start of the buffer instead of at the new chunk.
- `tests/io/file_read_line*`, `file_read_short`, `file_read_after_error`, `file_read_cap`, `file_read_stdout_order`, `read_bytes`, `file_open_fifo_peer` and `file_binary` pass on the interpreted, C and bun lanes. `file_read_line_interrupted` still interposes `read()` and sees the retry.
- Benchmark: `bend rl.bend -o rl && ./rl big.txt` before and after, on any file with many lines.

## Risk

- Two readers that share one open file description (a dup'd fd, a forked child) could move the offset between the `read` and the `lseek`. The byte-at-a-time path never had that window.
- Only macOS was measured. On Linux the same calls exist (`fstat`, `S_ISREG`, `lseek`), so I expect the same shape there, but I did not run it.
- The JS lane still reads one byte at a time: Node's `fs` has no `lseek`, and `bun:ffi` is missing on Node (#1881).
- To revert, revert the commit. The change is limited to `bend2/effs/file_read.c` and the new test.

title: fix(formatter): keep erased parameters glued to < and @
body:
## What

bend-fmt-lsp splits an erased or plus parameter from the `<` or `@` in front of it. It now keeps them glued.

| Source | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| `type Array<-T: Type> is Type:` | `type Array <- T: Type> is Type:` | unchanged |
| `-B: @-x: A -> Type` | `-B: @ -x: A -> Type` | unchanged |
| `for ~f: (@+x: U32 -> U32)` | `for ~f: (@ +x: U32 -> U32)` | unchanged |

## Why

The scanner reads `<-` in `Box<-T` as the bind arrow, so the formatter spaces it like `x <- f()`. The output still parses, but the type header now reads as a bind. `@` was only treated as a prefix before a name, so the space went in before `-x`.

Repro on main:

```sh
cd tools/bend-fmt-lsp
bun -e 'import {formatBend} from "./src/formatter.ts"; console.log(formatBend(require("fs").readFileSync("../../bend2/base.bend","utf8")))' | grep -nE "<- [A-Z]|@ -"
```

It prints `type Word.Con <- p`, `type Array <- T`, `type IO.OP <- R`, `type App <- S`, `@ -x` in `Sigma` and `Exists`, and `@ -R` in `IO`. Over the repo's `.bend` files, 155 have one of these lines. bend-lint's format rule already keeps them glued, so the two formatters disagree today.

## How

- `splitLine`: `<-` right after a word and before a name, with no spaces, is `<` and `-`, as in `Box<-T`. The existing rules then keep `<-T` together. A spaced bind (`x : U32 <- f()`) is unchanged.
- `unary`: `@` followed by a glued `-` or `+` is a prefix, so `@-x` stays together.

## How to test

```sh
cd tools/bend-fmt-lsp && npm ci && npm test
```

On main the new case `keeps erased parameters glued to their opener` fails. On this branch all tests pass.

Over all 1,973 `.bend` files in the repo, I compared the formatter before and after. 155 files change, and every changed line is one of the two patterns above. Formatting stays idempotent (0 files change on a second pass). On the 144 changed files under `tests/`, `demos/` and `guide/`, `bun bend2/main.ts --check-only` gives the same verdict before and after formatting.

## Risk

Low. Only the formatter changes, and only for `<-` glued to a name and `@` glued to `-` or `+`. One visible change: a bind written with no spaces before a name, `x : U32<-f()`, now stays glued instead of becoming `x : U32 <- f()`. Bend reads `<-` the same either way, so the meaning does not change. The repo has no such line. `a<-1` still becomes `a <- 1`. To revert, revert the commit.

title: fix(comp): retry a stale get before the ring's fatal error (#2103)
body:
`ring_push` reserves `pos` and then reads `get` once to decide whether the ring has room. That load may miss a `get` another core has just advanced, so a nearly full ring can look full and the host posts `ERR_RING`, which kills a valid run.

The slot at `pos` is already reserved, and on the host drain path the pusher is not that ring's popper. Retry the room check a bounded number of times (64) before the fatal error. A truly full ring still fails; #2102 is by design and the drain loop is unchanged.

## Cap

`bend2/comp.ts` is 65,996 / 66,000 ttok. `bun gates/repo.ts`: 56/56.

## Tests

Built and ran on the C lane with `+RTS --threads 16 -RTS`:

- `tests/run/fork_held_family.bend` (20 runs)
- `tests/reg/fork_spin_hold.bend` (20 runs)
- `tests/compile/fork_closure_stress.bend` (20 runs)
- `tests/run/array_fork.bend` (10 runs)
- `tests/run/array_atomic_fadd.bend` (10 runs)
- `tests/reg/brw_fork_push.bend` (10 runs)

All printed their `#|` lines. The stale-`get` window is rare and I could not make a deterministic regression; this is a memory-ordering retry rather than a change in the ring protocol.

Closes #2103.

title: Buffered file and stdout writes with a manual File.flush
body:
### Today

The two output paths behave differently:

| | C lane | JS lane |
|---|---|---|
| `IO.print` / `IO.write` (stdout) | buffered (stdio) | buffered when stdout is not a terminal (64 KiB batches) |
| `File.write` / `write_bytes` / `write_at` | a `write`/`pwrite` per call on a helper thread | a `fs.writeSync` per call |
| `IO.print_err` | direct | direct |

So many small file writes cost a syscall each, while stdout batches. The runtime orders the two by flushing stdout before a file or process job (#2155). Base has no flush effect, so a program can't do it itself.

### Proposal

Buffer both, the same way, with a manual flush, as C's stdio and Python do:

- `File.stdout` (and `File.stderr`) as `File` handles. `IO.print` is a write to `File.stdout`.
- A per-handle write buffer for files on both lanes.
- `File.flush(h)`: flushes `h`'s buffer, a no-op if it is empty.
- The runtime still flushes:
  - at `File.close` and at exit, so the tail of the output is not lost;
  - before a read, size or positioned write on the same handle, so a handle sees its own writes (C requires this of stdio too);
  - nowhere else, so stderr stays unbuffered.
- What stays manual is the case #2155 handles today: output reaching one destination through two handles or a child process (stdout redirected to a file the program also writes or reads, or a `Process.run` child that reads that file; the child's own stdio is piped, not inherited). The program calls `File.flush(File.stdout)` first, like `fflush` in C. #2155's automatic flush goes away.

### To decide

- Buffer size, and whether a terminal stdout is line-buffered (C) or unbuffered (the JS lane today).
- Whether a flush error (EPIPE on a closed pipe) is a `Result` from `File.flush` or ends the program as a short write on a standard stream does now.
- `guide/EFFECTS.md` and the guide on when to flush.

(`File.sync(h)`, durability to disk with `fsync`, is a separate question.)

title: perf(c): a host lane's chain count is kept less KEEP_WORDS, so a free tests its sign
body:
**`comp.ts` is 66,074 ttok, 74 over the 66,000 cap (main is 65,966; this adds 108), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run.

**What it buys:** fewer instructions on six benches (`tree-bitonic` -8.1%, `tree-radix` -6.2%, `lexer` -4.8%), none more on any. In cycles only `lexer` gains (-2.5%); `tree-bitonic` runs 1.2% more of them, by where its code lands (see Cycles).

Independent of the other open drafts: it branches from main `f0cf0a7c` and touches only the allocator's count. It was found while breaking down what `lexer` loses to its C twin, where a line of source is about 60 nodes allocated and 60 freed.

## What it does

A lane keeps, per size class, a free chain and the number of words in it. `heap_free` adds to the count and hands the chain off when it reaches `KEEP_WORDS`. `KEEP_WORDS` is a static the host sets once at start (`CHUNK` with a GPU, `CAP_WORDS` without), so every free loaded it and compared twice: six instructions on arm64 after the add.

Now the host keeps the count less `KEEP_WORDS`: an empty chain's count is `ALC_NONE` (`-KEEP_WORDS` on the host, 0 on the device), and the hand-off test is the sign of the count after the add, which the add's flags already hold. A free on arm64 goes from 12 instructions to 8 (`adds`, `str`, `b.mi` in place of `add`, `str`, `adrp`, `ldrb`, `cmp`, `b.ne`, `cmp`, `b.hs`).

- `heap_hand` and `heap_alloc_miss` set the count from `ALC_NONE`.
- `corpus_setup` gives every lane's row its start, after it sets `KEEP_WORDS`.
- `heap_alloc` is unchanged, and so is the device: there `ALC_NONE` is 0, the test is compiled out as before, and `dev_cut` reads the count as it did.

Nothing about the allocator's behaviour changes: the same chains, the same generations handed off at the same frees, the same address from every `heap_alloc`. That is what the checks below test.

## Results

One M4, one thread, GPU off, instructions retired from `/usr/bin/time -l`, the least of three interleaved runs. The runtime is part of every program's C, so all 17 `bench/runtime` programs were built with main and with this branch and run; every one prints the same result.

| bench | main, instructions | this | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `bfs` | 28.746G | 28.742G | -0.02% |
| `editdist` | 49.777G | 49.776G | -0.00% |
| `gameoflife` | 172.349G | 172.349G | +0.00% |
| `hashmap` | 18.496G | 18.187G | -1.67% |
| `histogram` | 44.369G | 44.369G | +0.00% |
| `kmeans` | 41.577G | 40.600G | -2.35% |
| `lexer` | 53.407G | 50.870G | -4.75% |
| `mandelbrot` | 43.446G | 43.446G | +0.00% |
| `merkle` | 47.321G | 47.304G | -0.04% |
| `nbody` | 39.787G | 39.787G | -0.00% |
| `queens` | 89.816G | 89.816G | +0.00% |
| `raytrace` | 82.953G | 82.953G | +0.00% |
| `symreg` | 50.767G | 50.732G | -0.07% |
| `terrain` | 44.568G | 44.568G | -0.00% |
| `tree-bitonic` | 148.712G | 136.634G | -8.12% |
| `tree-matmul` | 62.582G | 61.614G | -1.55% |
| `tree-radix` | 13.791G | 12.940G | -6.17% |

No program runs more instructions.

**Cycles: the gain in time is `lexer`'s alone.** The six instructions a free no longer runs were a load that always hits and two compares that are always predicted, so they cost little time, and on this machine where the code lands moves a run by a percent or two on its own. So each bench whose instruction count changed was built at 16 placements (the segments shifted in 4-byte steps), every placement run one to three times, alternating with main; the table has the least, the median and the most of the per-placement minimum, in cycles.

| bench | main: least / median / most | this: least / median / most | median |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `lexer` (3 rounds) | 8.398G / 8.449G / 8.938G | 8.141G / 8.236G / 8.649G | -2.5% |
| `tree-radix` (1) | 15.336G / 15.888G / 16.308G | 15.423G / 15.699G / 15.841G | -1.2% |
| `kmeans` (1) | 8.274G / 8.285G / 8.321G | 8.270G / 8.282G / 8.311G | -0.0% |
| `hashmap` (1) | 9.526G / 9.683G / 9.941G | 9.525G / 9.671G / 9.896G | -0.1% |
| `tree-matmul` (1) | 8.144G / 8.197G / 8.244G | 8.199G / 8.273G / 9.395G | +0.9% |
| `tree-bitonic` (2) | 20.317G / 20.373G / 20.605G | 20.486G / 20.622G / 20.740G | +1.2% |

`tree-bitonic` runs 8% fewer instructions and 1.2% more cycles, at every placement. That loss follows the code's offsets inside the functions (which shifting whole segments cannot vary), not the test: with two `nop`s after the count's store in `heap_free` it runs 142.0G instructions in 20.32G cycles, main's speed; with one, 20.52G; with three, 20.48G; with five (main's instruction count), 20.37G. Marking the hand-off unlikely (`__builtin_expect`), which moves its call out of line, gives 20.51G / 20.70G / 20.74G, so that is not the cause and it is not in this change. The same padding on `lexer` gives 8.11G to 8.28G, under main's 8.38G every time, so `lexer`'s gain is the work removed. Branch mispredictions on `tree-bitonic` (Instruments' CPU counters) go from 99.1M to 92.4M.

`editdist`'s instruction count does not change. A plain run of it is 20% faster here, which is main's binary sitting on the one bad placement in 16 (10.62G against 8.45G at the other 15, in both builds): not a gain.

## Checks

All local, against main `f0cf0a7c`:

- **The allocator behaves the same.** Each program is built with both runtimes and a hash over every `heap_alloc` result, every free, every hand-off and every miss, in order; at one thread that is deterministic. Of the 883 tests that pass on main and the 17 benches at full size, 885 give the same hash. The other 15 are IO tests (files, sockets, processes) whose hash changes from run to run on main itself; nine vary within three runs, and six runs of each of the other six on both runtimes give hashes from the same set. 25 programs hand chains off at one thread, 56,472 times in all.
- **The count, at any thread count.** A build that keeps main's plain count beside the new one and aborts if the two ever disagree, or if a hand-off happens when main's rule would not hand off (or the reverse): 899 programs at 1, 4 and 8 threads, no abort. `tree-bitonic` hands off 272,015 times at 4 threads. (The 900th is `heap_large_reuse`, whose private lane rows that build cannot index.)
- **Memory:** each of the 900 with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit: the same output and the same count as main.
- **Native lane:** every test that passes on main passes here, the GPU off; the 22 that do not pass on main in this local lane end the same way.
- **`tests/io/heap_large_reuse.c`** reads the allocator's cells: it built its private lane rows as zeros and tested a count for 0. It now starts a row's counts at `ALC_NONE` and tests for that. It passes with the GPU off and on (`KEEP_WORDS` is `CHUNK` there).
- **New test:** `tests/run/heap_generations.bend` frees several generations of 2-word, 4-word and 8-word nodes on one lane (by a walk and by a drop), builds again from what was handed off, frees blocks of 2^16 words, and forks so that one lane frees what another allocated. 620 hand-offs at one thread. It passes on the C lane at 1 and 8 threads, on Metal (its last round is `round!`) and in JS.
- **Wrong versions.** A miss that sets the plain count, a hand-off that resets to 0 and a bias off by two words each change the hash on the new test; the first two also fail `heap_large_reuse`. A lane row left at zero passes at one thread (a lane's first event in a class is a miss, which sets the count) and aborts the shadow build at 8 threads, where a lane frees what another allocated. So the new test alone does not prove the count; the hash and the shadow build do.
- **Metal:** all 17 benches print the same results with `--gpu on`.
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates, CUDA, Linux and x86** have not run.
- **`heap_alloc`'s side of the count** (a load, a subtract and a store per allocation) is still there. With no count at all, by hand edit of the emitted C, `lexer` runs 47.50G instructions (-11%); this collects 2.54G of that 5.91G.

title: perf(comp): a statement's call unfolds into a def that is not flat
body:
**`comp.ts` is 67,137 ttok, 1,137 over the 66,000 cap (main is 65,966; this adds 1,171), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run.

**What it buys:** `lexer` runs 25.5% fewer instructions and 22.9% fewer cycles (its gap to the C twin goes from 1.96x to 1.52x), `symreg` 0.8% fewer instructions; the other 15 benches emit byte-identical C.

Independent of the other open drafts: it branches from main `f0cf0a7c`. It was found while breaking down what `lexer` loses to its C twin: more than half of that gap is the line generator, a recursion over a template that is a literal.

## What it does

`emit_unfold` already unfolds a call whose constant arguments decide its matches, but only into a flat def, because its residue is emitted as an expression. `lexer`'s `gen` walks a literal template with a call that is not a tail call, so it is not flat: every line paid 39 frames, 39 returns through the segment table, and a comparison chain per template character to pick its slot, all on constants.

Now a call in statement position (a tail call, or the call a `let` binds, which is where ANF puts every call into a def that is not flat) unfolds into such a def too. Its residue is a statement, so ANF cuts the calls it makes, and they unfold in turn where they stand. Four things make the unfold go through there, all behind the one flag, so an expression's fold is what it was:

- **A flat argument folds to its end**, not one step, so `slot(105)` is `Id{}` by the time `expand` matches on it.
- **An op on constants is its constant** (a `U32` or a `Bool`, by the op's JS, as a match table's cells already are): `U32.is_eq(105, 105)` is `True{}`, and the template position `k + 1` is a literal.
- **A def with no match of its own unfolds if its body's tail call does**, and a residue's tail call unfolds in place: `gen.at(105, t, rest)` is `expand(slot(105), 105, t, rest)`, which is `ident(n, t, rest)`.
- **An argument that calls a def that is not flat is bound first**, so no later argument is held across it in a frame. An argument bound this way is typed by the arguments before it (the flat unfold types it by the callee's own parameter names), since its uses are read in the caller.

When it does not unfold:

- **No constant argument:** not tried.
- **The fuel** is `FOLD_FUEL`, as for the flat unfold: a unit for every term of every body unfolded, all of it or none. A try that fails gives its fuel back, and a def whose unfold ran out is not tried again in that unit.
- **A recursion the constants do not carry to its end:** a residue that keeps a call leading back to the def unfolded is refused, or the recursion would only be peeled once (`U32.show`'s digit loop, with its literal fuel, would be, in every program).
- **A residue that forks or bangs** is refused, so no segment starts or stops forking because of an unfold (a def that forks runs on the device, one that does not runs on the host).
- **A lambda argument, or a match left in the residue,** as before.

For `lexer` the whole of `gen`, `gen.at`, `expand`, `slot` and `slot.go` is gone from a line: its literal characters are `SCon` nodes built in place (the tail `" ;"` is static), and the seven identifiers and numbers are seven calls with one word, the line's seed, in each frame. It takes 5,451 of the 8,192 fuel, so a template half as long again would stay a call. `symreg`'s `gen(5n, h)` builds its 63-node candidate without a frame.

Elsewhere it is mostly `"literal" ++ x`: Base's `String.append` is not flat, and now a literal in front is consed on directly.

## Results

One M4, GPU off, instructions retired and cycles from `/usr/bin/time -l`, the least of five interleaved runs.

| `lexer` | main | this | | C twin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| instructions, 1 thread | 53.407G | 39.784G | -25.5% | 17.757G |
| cycles, 1 thread | 8.380G | 6.524G | -22.1% | 4.284G |
| wall, 1 thread | 2.08 s | 1.62 s | 1.28x | 1.01 s |
| cycles, 8 threads | 10.433G | 7.917G | -24.1% | |
| wall, 8 threads | 0.39 s | 0.30 s | 1.30x | |
| per line, generating it: instructions / cycles | 3,449 / 596 | 1,825 / 379 | | 1,087 / 248 |
| per line, lexing it: instructions / cycles | 3,012 / 522 | 3,012 / 522 | | 988 / 304 |

The per-line rows are from builds that generate 64 lines, then lex them, with a counter read between (so their cycles are a little above a plain run's).

The gain was checked against placement, since any change to the C moves the code: both builds at 16 placements (the segments shifted in 4-byte steps), three alternating rounds, the least per placement.

| build | least | median | most |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| main | 8.383G | 8.442G | 8.765G |
| this | 6.464G | 6.508G | 6.577G |

No overlap; -22.9% on the median.

**Bench suite.** 15 of the 17 `bench/runtime` programs emit byte-identical C. The other two:

| bench | main, instructions | this | | main, cycles | this |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `lexer` | 53.407G | 39.784G | -25.51% | 8.380G | 6.524G |
| `symreg` | 50.767G | 50.364G | -0.79% | 12.368G | 12.308G |

**Size and compile time.** Over the 883 tests that pass on main, the 17 benches and two more programs, 464 emit different C and 438 the same; the C is 0.02% larger in all (from 0.26x on `reg/show_shared_layout` to 2.16x on `base/list_sort`), and compiling them all takes 6% longer. Of the 15 demos with a `main.bend`, 8 emit the same C and 7 change: `app_slash_boss_3d` 2.92 MB to 3.07 MB of C (+5.1%) and 0.65 s to 0.94 s to emit it; `pure_hvm5_mini` +2.3% and 0.33 s to 0.42 s; `io_http_server` +4.0%; the other four shrink by 1% to 3%.

## Checks

All local, against main `f0cf0a7c`:

- **Native lane:** every test that passes on main (883) passes here, the GPU off; the 22 that do not pass on main in this local lane end the same way.
- **Every program whose C changes** (464 of 902: tests, benches at full size, the two new tests): built with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit, and run at one thread: the same output, the same exit code and the same count as main on every one; then at 8 threads: the same output.
- **JS:** the JS emitted is byte-identical to main's on 40 programs sampled from those whose C changes; the change is in the C emitter only.
- **New tests.** `tests/run/unfold_statements.bend`: a fold over a constant list whose step is not flat; an arm that drops a constant and frees a value; a value the caller keeps, shared by two arguments of a def that walks it, handed to an arm that drops it, and again at its last use; a def with no match that unfolds through its callee, with its character's class decided by ops on constants; a def that forks (it must stay a call); a count too long for the fuel and a call tree that is; Base's `String.append` and `List.append` on literals; an unboxed pair out of a def that is not flat; and a template expanded as `lexer`'s is. Its inputs come from a list built at run time, so C folds none of it. `tests/run/unfold_generic.bend`: a generic def unfolded over a literal list whose other argument is computed, bound and shared, with boxed elements, called from a def whose own type parameter has the same name and place. Both pass on the C lane at 1 and 8 threads, on Metal, in JS, and with poisoned frees and no live word at exit. In the emitted C the segments of `fold`, `step`, `pick`, `both`, `wrap`, `reads`, `two`, `gen`, `glue`, `twice` and `List.append` are gone, and those of `tsum`, `count` and `fib` are not.
- **Wrong versions the tests catch:** an op on constants folded to the wrong `Bool`, or to a `U32` one too high (the first test and `lexer` print wrong); a use the unfold adds not counted (the compiler stops); a residue that forks unfolded into a `!` def (Metal: stack overflow, the def now runs on the device). Found on the way and fixed: a bare reference to an op (no arguments) folded to a constant, which stopped the compiler on `tests/reg/array_clone_runs.bend`.
- **Wrong versions they do not catch:** a use the unfold drops left counted (`bind_dead` recounts the binding at the next statement, so nothing leaks); the argument that calls bound last (slower, not wrong); an argument bound with the callee's own type names, as the flat unfold does (no program I wrote makes it matter: a call nearby marks the same types shared).
- **Demos:** the four whose C changes and that run without a window (`proof_insertion_sort`, `proof_numerics`, `proof_typed_eval`, `pure_hvm5_mini`) print what they print on main.
- **Metal:** `lexer` (2.51 s to 1.48 s), `symreg` and the two new tests print the same results with `--gpu on`.
- **Hard inputs:** `fib`-shaped and million-deep recursions on literals, alone and as arguments: same output, same compile time, no unfold.
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates, CUDA, Linux and x86, `tsc`** have not run. `lexer`'s pin would move.
- **Compile time and size** grow where constants drive a recursion: 45% on the largest demo, more than twice the C on one test (`base/list_sort`, literal lists sorted). The fuel caps it for a unit, not for a program.
- **The fuel is a cliff.** `lexer`'s template takes two thirds of it; a longer one unfolds nothing.
- **A constant that reaches only a call that is not the tail** of a def with no match is not seen: `both(o, w) = kl_sum(w, step(o, w))` stays a call for a constant `o`.
- **An op whose result is a `Nat` or an `F32`** is not folded, so `ident(U32.to_nat(3), ...)` is not unrolled.
- **JS** gets none of this: the JS emitter does not go through `emit_body`.
- **Which programs gain** beyond the two benches and a literal in front of `++` was not measured.

title: CPU: automatic thread count ignores a nested cgroup-v2 quota
body:
### What you did

Ran a small `IO.thread_count()` program in a transient user service with `CPUQuota=100%`, without a `--threads` override.

```sh
bun bend2/main.ts thread-count.bend -o thread-count.c
clang -std=c11 -O3 thread-count.c -lpthread -lm -o thread-count
systemd-run --user --wait --pipe --collect \
  --property=CPUQuota=100% \
  /usr/bin/python "$PWD/quota-context.py" "$PWD/thread-count" \
  +RTS --gpu off -RTS
```

The helper only prints its own cgroup limit before executing the program:

```python
# quota-context.py
import os
import pathlib
import sys

for line in pathlib.Path("/proc/self/cgroup").read_text().splitlines():
    if line.startswith("0::"):
        group = pathlib.Path("/sys/fs/cgroup") / line[3:].lstrip("/")
        print("own cpu.max:", (group / "cpu.max").read_text().strip(), flush=True)
os.execv(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[1:])
```

### What happened

```text
own cpu.max: 100000 100000
16
```

Outside the service the program also prints `16`. I expected the automatic count inside it to be `1`: #1048 describes the default as the affinity mask under the cgroup quota. The kernel still enforces the quota; the issue is the pool size chosen by default.

`cpu_count()` reads `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max`, but this service's limit lives below its own cgroup directory. I haven't changed production code yet. This reproduction covers nested cgroup v2, not v1.

### The file

title: Wake only useful CPU workers for each turn
body:
Tiny parallel lets were waking the whole CPU pool. This starts workers only when needed, wakes a useful prefix, and uses per-worker pending notifications instead of the yield loop. The grow scan supplies the drain bound; the turn header now carries its stride rather than recalculating it for every claim.

Timings for 822ef948 on local Linux x86_64 / clang 22.1.8, against f0cf0a7c. Three alternating pairs with identical CPU affinities; loop times use public `IO.now`:

| 16-thread workload | main loop | patch loop | main system CPU | patch system CPU |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| #2141 repro | 129 ms | 105 ms | 821.7 ms | 7.7 ms |
| Bitonic sorts, depths 8 + 14 | 17 ms | 18 ms | 52.0 ms | 24.5 ms |

The dense case is a little slower locally, so I'm not calling this fully performance-qualified.

`bun gates/repo.ts` passes 56/56. Five fork cases pass in C at 1/2/4/8/16 threads and in Bun JS; all 42 before/after workload runs preserve their results. The new regression goes dense → 512 sparse rounds → dense again.

Review follow-up 437663cf seeds the wake bound from the current frontier before growing. Two rebuilt native consumers pass at 1/2/4/8/16/32 threads, and repo passes 56/56. I haven't remeasured performance for this follow-up; a diagnostic bitonic run didn't reach the exact `f == CUBE` skip-grow case.

Keeping this draft: no mini-cluster access here, and the required mini test/perf gates, Metal/CUDA runs and private installer/ping qualification are still missing. Local Linux checks aren't substitutes for those.

Fixes #2141

title: fix(parse): a fill written with a signature says it fills a law (#2023)
body:
Fixes #2023.

A def that fills a law takes bare names. Written with a full signature, like any other def, it got an error about a stray character, and each spelling failed somewhere else:

| written | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| `def claim(n: Nat) -> T:` | `expected : a name`, caret at the `->` | caret at the `:` |
| `def claim(n) -> T:` | `expected : ':'`, at the `->` | at the `->` |
| `def claim(-n):` and `(+n)` | `expected : ':'`, at the `)` | at the `-` / `+` |
| `def claim(~n):` | `expected : a name`, at the `~` | at the `~` |
| `def claim(n: Quant):` | accepted, the annotation is ignored | at the `:` |

All of them now say the same thing, at the character that is wrong:

```
- expected : bare parameter names and no '->' (def claim fills a law, which gives the types)
```

This is the change @raramos9 proposed in the issue, moved onto current main. `parse_tele` takes the fill's message and refuses where the parameter stops being a bare name, so `parse_def` no longer needs its two special checks (the `~` on the first parameter, and "every type is Quant" after the list).

One behaviour change, the one the issue already points out: `n: Quant` in a fill used to be accepted and ignored, and it's refused now like any other annotation. Nothing under `tests/`, `demos/` or `bench/` relies on it. If you'd rather keep it, tell me and I'll put that check back.

Tests:

- new in `tests/parse/`, one per spelling the issue lists that had no test: `law_fill_typed`, `law_fill_minus`, `law_fill_plus`, `law_fill_quant`. Each gives a different output on main.
- updated: `tests/parse/law_fill_arrow.bend` and `tests/comptime/err_law.bend`, which pinned the old messages.

What I ran, on main at f0cf0a7c:

- every `.bend` file under `tests/` (1,857 files) through `bend <file>` on main and on this branch: only those two change
- the 103 `.bend` files outside `tests/` with `--check-only`: same output
- 26 hand-written fills, right and wrong, on both: valid fills and ordinary defs behave the same, and `def f(match)` and "a name for each ~ clause" keep their own messages
- all 17 runtime benches compile to byte-identical C
- repo gate 56/56, `bend.ts` 45,949 → 45,992 ttok (cap 48,000)

Not run: the cluster gates.

If you'd like the message worded differently, I'm happy to change it. Let me know.

title: Allow extra text files in published packages
body:
Lets a package carry `LAWS.bend`, `PROOF.bend` or `.blend` source without adding them to the entry's imports:

```sh
bend main.bend --publish --extra LAWS.bend --extra PROOF.bend
```

`--extra` repeats like `-o`. Paths are CWD-relative and must stay under the entry directory; the existing file and adjacent-license rules still apply. It's the same UTF-8 package format, not a new manifest format.

Added hub-gate coverage for opt-in files, opaque `.blend` source, a carried proof importing its carried law, and the original entry alias. Removed an exact error-wording assertion rather than re-pinning it.

No production package was uploaded. This is a protocol smoke, not a run of the private hub implementation.

Refs #2082.

Keep two-word scalar records on the eager path instead of retaining their boxes through repeated passes. Wider scalar records still use the lazy path from #2036. The existing record tests keep their expected outputs; their comments no longer promise a particular boxing choice.

title: Bounty submission: `--verdict` prints ALL PROOFS CHECK for a file with a definition of type `Empty` (2.0.32)
F32.lerp rounds identical finite endpoints to zero
body:
`F32.lerp(x, x, t)` can lose a finite constant value even when `t` is finite. On main f0cf0a7 (2.0.40), this prints `1`, `0`, `2147483648`:

```bend
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    IO.print(U32.show(F32.bits(1.401298464324817e-45)))
    IO.print(U32.show(F32.bits(F32.lerp(1.401298464324817e-45, 1.401298464324817e-45, 0.5))))
    IO.print(U32.show(F32.bits(F32.lerp(F32.neg(1.401298464324817e-45), F32.neg(1.401298464324817e-45), 0.5))))
```

Expected `1`, `1`, `2147483649`: interpolating the same finite value should leave it unchanged. Both half-products underflow before the weighted sum, turning the smallest positive/negative values into signed zero.

This is different from #1607 and #1749: the coefficient is 0.5, not an endpoint, and neither input is infinite. Observed with `bun bend2/main.ts repro.bend` on Linux x64; no GPU result claimed.

title: Keep same-sign F32.lerp values stable
body:
Fixes #2169.

The weighted sum can round two identical small endpoints to zero. It can also move backwards between nearby positive endpoints as t increases.

Use `a + t * (b - a)` for same-sign finite inputs with a finite coefficient. A zero delta returns the original endpoint, including its signed zero. Opposite signs and nonfinite inputs keep the weighted path, and the existing t=0/1 handling stays unchanged.

`tests/base/f32_lerp_constant.bend` and `tests/base/f32_lerp_boundaries.bend` pass through the Bun CLI and native C. The new case also uses a runtime coefficient from IO.now, so it isn't only checking constant folding. NaN checks test propagation, not payload bits.
The local repo gate passes 56/56.

Still draft: required mini test/perf/ping and Metal/CUDA checks haven't run. AI-assisted; no remote qualification claimed.

title: Run hub entries and inline Bend scripts
body:
Fixes #2083.

`bend name@version/main.bend`, `bend 0x<hash>/main.bend` and `bend --script '…'` now use the regular loader. Package entries keep their module namespace, including a foreign `main`; snippets resolve imports from cwd. Existing local files still win over package-looking paths.

One tradeoff: the public loader takes a disk file, so `--script` needs a writable cwd. The temporary source is removed before execution and on load failure. This is documented; `bend.ts` is untouched, and `--publish`/`--checkup` remain local-file-only.

Locally: 23 CLI scenarios against a real local content-addressed read store, including named/hash inputs, offline cache, foreign JS/C entries, three native builds/runs and failure cleanup. Three more scenarios passed through the actual Lean kernel. Repo gate: 56/56. Added four installed-CLI checks in ping; its bundle builds, but the private hub gate, mini, Metal and CUDA qualification haven't run. Keeping this draft for that reason.

title: Add proof-bound array reads
body:
Fixes #1936 via option 2, not automatic loop versioning.

`Array.get_in(T, a, i, h)` takes an erased proof that `i < Array.capacity(T, a)`. C and JS skip the wrap mask; the logical body is still `Array.get`, with no `@unsafe`. `Array.capacity` is the consuming size projection, usable in the proof's type. Ordinary wrapping reads are unchanged.

Locally checked scalar, boxed-string and multiword elements: three JS runs, three actual Lean-kernel checks, three native builds and six native runs. A proof for index 4 in a four-cell array is rejected. Repo gate: 56/56.

This doesn't make the unchanged tile faster automatically; callers need the bounds proofs. No new performance claim. Mini test/perf, Metal/CUDA and private hub qualification aren't available here, so this stays draft.

title: Nat.div and Nat.mod are one native division each: Base drops the other half as a Nat
body:
`Nat.div` and `Nat.mod` were Base's `Pair.fst` and `Pair.snd` of `Nat.divmod`. A generic def doesn't know the half it drops is a `Nat`, so in C the drop was a `term_sink` test on that half. Every `Nat.div` therefore also computed the remainder, and every `Nat.mod` the quotient.

They now go through two Base helpers, `Nat.div.go` and `Nat.mod.go`, typed `Nat & Nat -> Nat`. Dropping a `Nat` costs nothing, so clang deletes the unused half and leaves one division. The first version of this PR made both names C operations in `comp.ts` (+31 tokens). That no longer fits under the 66k cap, and this version adds 0 tokens to `comp.ts`.

title: Nat.mul divides to test for overflow only when an operand reaches 2^32
body:
**`comp.ts` is 65,980 ttok, under the 66,000 cap (main is 65,966), and `gates/repo.ts` passes.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run. Independent of #2173 and of every other open draft.

## What it does

`nat_mul` tested every product for overflow with a 64-bit division:

```c
return nat_chk(e, b != 0 && a > NAT_IMM / b ? NAT_IMM + 1 : a * b);
```

clang folds the division only when an operand is a constant, so `Nat.mul` of two runtime values cost a `udiv` on top of the `mul`. When both operands are under 2^32 the 64-bit product cannot wrap, and `nat_chk` alone holds it to 2^48-1. The division is now taken only when an operand reaches 2^32:

```c
return nat_chk(e, (a | b) >> 32 != 0 && b != 0 && a > NAT_IMM / b
  ? NAT_IMM + 1 : a * b);
```

The answer is the same for every pair of 64-bit operands: under 2^32 the old test `a > NAT_IMM / b` and `nat_chk` of the exact product agree, and from 2^32 on the old test still runs. One source for the host and the devices, and no builtin.

## Results

One M4, one thread, GPU off, instructions retired and cycles from `/usr/bin/time -l`, the least of 7 to 9 interleaved runs. `bench/runtime` multiplies no `Nat` at run time, so the programs are the 22 kernels of `korulang/koru-benchmarks` (`suites/osprey-compute-kernels/bend`, small integer loops over `Nat`), plus three of them respelled.

| program | instructions, main | this | | cycles, main | this | | cycles over 16 placements, this / main |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `primes` (`d * d > n` each step) | 112.9M | 120.2M | +6.5% | 34.1M | 26.1M | -23.5% | 0.749 to 0.767 |
| `primes` with #2173 too | 112.9M | 84.5M | -25.1% | 34.1M | 23.0M | -32.6% | not swept |
| `primes`, the two tests in the reference's order | 165.4M | 136.5M | -17.5% | 36.4M | 29.0M | -20.4% | not swept |
| `powmod`, product in two 15-bit limbs | 315.4M | 227.2M | -28.0% | 247.0M | 242.4M | -1.8% | not swept |
| `collatz` (`3 * n`) | 289.6M | 278.9M | -3.7% | 97.0M | 95.2M | -1.8% | 0.938 to 1.027 |
| `nestedloop` (`i * j * k`) | 231.5M | 310.6M | +34.1% | 147.4M | 164.3M | +11.5% | 1.113 to 1.115 |

The other 19 kernels are within 0.1% in instructions: they multiply by a constant or not at all. With #2173, `primes` goes from 1.52x of its C reference (`cc -O2`, start-up taken out of both) to 0.96x.

**`nestedloop` gets slower, and it is clang's loop strength reduction, not the test.** Its inner loop is `acc = (acc + i * j * k) % M` over a countdown of `k`. On main the product sits behind the division's select, and the loop-carried chain is `add`, `umulh`, `lsr`, `msub`. With the division gone, LSR rewrites `i * j * k` as two induction variables and reassociates the sum around the remainder, so the chain gains an `add` (9.2 to 10.3 cycles a turn) and the loop five instructions. The same C built with `-mllvm -disable-lsr` runs 231.4M instructions in 145.9M cycles, 1% under main. It still runs under its C reference (176.6M cycles). I did not find a spelling of the test that keeps LSR away for a reason other than luck: merging the overflow flag into the product with an OR (`a * b | flag << 48`) keeps `nestedloop` level (0.99x), but costs instructions on the other programs (+38% on `primes`, +14% on a respelled `factorial`) for a smaller gain on `primes` (0.74x). A 128-bit product and `__builtin_mul_overflow` were slower than this on the limb-multiply `powmod` (1.38x and 1.09x its cycles) and are host-only. Those three were measured on top of #2173.

**Placement.** Cycles on this M4 can move with where code lands, so `primes`, `collatz` and `nestedloop` were built at 16 positions (nops at the head of `work_loop`, 4 bytes a step) with both compilers, 3 interleaved rounds, the minimum per position; the last column is the range of the per-position ratio. `collatz`'s range overlaps main's, so it is no result.

**The bench suite.** The 17 `bench/runtime` programs differ in the runtime's text only: their binaries disassemble identically to main's.

## Checks

All local, against main `f0cf0a7c`:

- **The two formulas compared apart** in C over 200 million operand pairs: every pair of the values 2^k - 1, 2^k and 2^k + 1 for k up to 63 with 0, 2^64-1 and 2^48-1, and 200 million random pairs of every bit width (138 million of them overflow). No difference.
- **Native lane** (every test built and run with the GPU off, compared with its `#|` lines): 883 pass on main and here, no status differs.
- **Memory:** all 904 tests that pass or print to stderr (the runtime's text is in every program, so every C file differs) were built with both compilers with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit: the same output, exit code and count as main on every one.
- **JS lane:** untouched (`nat_mul` is the C runtime's); the JS for seven programs is byte-identical.
- **Metal:** a scratch program that calls `Nat.div`, `Nat.mod` and `Nat.mul` on runtime operands inside a `!` fork tree prints the value computed apart in Python with `--gpu on` and `--gpu off`, on main and here. Its operands are under 2^32; the division path on the device is main's code.
- **New tests:**
  - `tests/run/nat_mul_wide.bend`: products on both sides of 2^32 in either operand and at 2^48-1 exactly, by both paths ((2^24-1) * (2^24+1) and (2^32+2^16+1) * 65535).
  - `tests/run/nat_overflow_wide.bend`: 3 * 2^30 times (2^34+2)/3 is 2^64 + 2^31, which a machine word holds as 2^31, so only the test before the multiply stops it; the first operand is under 2^32 and the second between 2^32 and 2^33.
  - Every operand is scaled by the command line's length, so no lane folds a product. Both print their lines under `bend file.bend`, on the C lane and on the JS lane, on main and here.
  - Five deliberately wrong versions of `nat_mul` (no test before the multiply, the bound inverted, the bound at 2^33, only `a` tested, no `nat_chk` on the product) all fail `nat_overflow_wide`; `nat_overflow` (2^24 * 2^24, the path without a division) fails the last.
- `gates/repo.ts` passes.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates, CUDA, Linux and x86** have not run. On x86 a 64-bit `div` costs more than on this M4, so the gain there should be larger; not measured. `tsc` was not run.
- **An operand of 2^32 or more** still divides.

## Cost

+14 ttok.

title: A def whose tail adds calls to itself carries the sum in a parameter: any spelling of the add, U32, and two or more calls
body:
**`comp.ts` is 67,091 ttok, 1,091 over the 66,000 cap** (main 65,966), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled. Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run. Two commits: the first (`e1b6a3e5`, 66,444 ttok) took one call under `Nat.add`; the second (`2707077e`, first opened as #2184) replaces its mechanism and takes more; a third (`81ca8718`) stops an arm that answers 0 from adding it (its own section below). This description covers the first two.

**2026-11-23, fix (`63cef397`; +113 ttok, 67,204): `d~acc`'s types name its params by their new levels.** The types inside a def's body name its params by level; `acc_def` put `acc` in front without moving them, so `List.length~acc` read its list as `List<acc, a>`, and its eta wrapper named every param `x` at level 0. Either made `facts_hot` add `open`, which makes every bound type hot: `raytracer` sealed every field of its `V3`, `Cam` and `Box` nodes, and many programs on the integration branch did the same (`delaunay` 306 `rfc_seal` sites to 35, main 36). `raytracer` with this PR: equal to main again (16.39G / 4.02G; 16.68G / 4.35G before at its integration step); on the integration branch 15.61G / 4.24G to 15.32G / 3.95G (main 16.40G / 4.02G). `fib` 461M, `pascal` 1,976M, `coins` 489M, `binarytrees` 1,324M, `collatz` 167M, `digitsum` 166M instructions as before.

## What it does

The first commit turned one shape into a loop: a tail `Nat.add` of one call to the def itself, or `1n+f(..)`. This takes the same idea as far as the counts below justify:

- **any spelling of the add**: the call bound by a `let` first, adds inside adds, successors over an add and an add over successors;
- **`U32.add`** as well as `Nat.add`;
- **two or more calls under one add**: every call but the last stays a call, the last becomes the loop. This is what reaches `fib`, `pascal`, `coins` and `binarytrees`;
- **a def that is not flat for another reason** (its operand calls a recursion, or it tail-calls a def that forks): its own recursion still becomes a loop.

```python
def fib(+n: Nat) -> Nat:          def check(t: Tree) -> Nat:
  match n:                          match t:
    case 0n:                          case Leaf{}:
      0n                                0n
    case 1n+p:                        case Node{l, r}:
      match p:                          Nat.add(1n, Nat.add(check(l), check(r)))
        case 0n:
          1n
        case 1n+pp:
          a = fib(p)
          b = fib(pp)
          Nat.add(a, b)
```

Two calls need the sum to live across the call that stays, so the sum can no longer be a local of one C loop (the first commit's `u64 acc`). It is a parameter instead: the def goes on in a second def, `d~acc`, which takes the sum so far first, and a call that stays is handed the sum and answers it grown. `fib` is compiled as if it had been written

```python
def fib~acc(acc: Nat, +n: Nat) -> Nat:      def fib(+n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:                                    fib~acc(0n, n)
    case 0n:
      Nat.add(acc, 0n)
    case 1n+p:
      match p:
        case 0n:
          Nat.add(acc, 1n)
        case 1n+pp:
          fib~acc(fib~acc(acc, p), pp)
```

which is the shape the `hanoi` kernel already has by hand. With one call under the add there is no call left and `d~acc` is a C loop, as in the first commit.

Because the sum is now an ordinary parameter, **the first commit's emitter code is gone** (`acc_of`, `acc_on`, the `u64 acc` local, the wrapped `emit_put` and the branch in `emit_body`): one rewrite on the checked terms in `file_book` (`acc_def`) builds `d~acc`, and the emitter compiles it like any def, so frames, borrows, spares and forks need no case of their own. For the first commit's own shapes the emitted loop is the same statements with `acc` as a parameter.

## The rule

`acc_def(d)`, C lane only:

- d answers a `Nat` or a `U32`, and calls itself somewhere outside a tail position.
- Every such call is an operand of a tail add: directly, under nested `Nat.add` / `U32.add`, under successors, or through a `let` that binds exactly that call and whose name is read once.
- Then, in `d~acc`: the other operands are added to `acc` (bound before the calls), each call takes the sum in turn, the last one as a tail call; a plain tail call to d passes `acc` on; any other answer `v` is `acc + v`. d itself is `d~acc(0, ..)`.
- If any reference to d is left after that (a call in an operand, in an argument, behind `!`, in a closure, in a fork, a bound name read twice), the def is left exactly as it was.
- Never taken: `F32`; a def in a tail cycle with another def (its tail calls would become calls); a def with 247 live parameters (no room for one more).

**Why the reordering is sound, per operator and shape:**

- **`Nat.add`, one call.** The recursion adds from the innermost call out, the loop from the first step on. Add is associative and commutative, and Nats only grow under it, so every value the carried sum takes is at most the answer of the outermost call: it passes 2^48-1 exactly when that answer does, and both stop with the same message. (The first commit's argument.)
- **`Nat.add`, two or more calls.** The same sum is carried through every call of the tree, so the same bound holds: the carried sum is always a sum of some of the terms of the outermost call's answer. Main meets the wall at the last add on the way out at the latest; here it is met as soon as the terms seen so far pass it. Same message, an earlier point in time.
- **`U32.add`.** It wraps, so any order gives the same word and no add can stop the program. Commutativity is used (operands are added before the calls' results) and holds.
- **A call bound by a `let`.** Same sum; the call now runs where its name is read, not at its `let`. Taken only when the name is read once, so no call runs twice.
- **Nested adds and successors.** `1n+x` is `Nat.add(1n, x)`; nesting is associativity.
- **A program that stops or does not return in an operand or a call:** see "Not covered", which lists every case where the point of death can differ. `@unsafe` defs are the only ones that may not return.

## Reach, counted before building

A counting pass over the checked terms (a hook in a scratch copy of the compiler) over every def of Base, the 908 tests that build, 18 demo programs, the 17 `bench/runtime` programs and the 22 koru kernels (`korulang/koru-benchmarks`, `suites/osprey-compute-kernels/bend`). Distinct defs that have the shape and that the first commit does not take; "reached" means the def would actually become a loop (it does not fork, has no other call to itself).

| candidate | defs | reached | on a hot path |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| one call, `Nat.add`, another spelling (let-bound, nested) | 2 | 1 | none (both are in the first commit's own test) |
| one call, `U32.add` | 101 | 97 | none: 96 in tests, `Voices.count` in `app_slash_boss_3d` (at most 24 voices) |
| one call, `U32.xor` / `Bool.and` / `Bool.or` | 1 / 22 / 1 | not taken | none (tests; `Peer.has` in the netcode demo) |
| one call, `U32.mul`, `and`, `or`, `min`, `max`, `Nat.min`, `Nat.max` | 0 | | |
| one call, `Nat.mul` (unsound: a later zero) | 6 | not taken | `Nat.pow`, `Word.to_nat` in Base |
| two or more calls, `Nat.add` | 12 | 6 | **`fib`, `pascal` (`binom`), `coins` (`ways`): the whole kernel; `binarytrees` (`check`): one of its two walks.** Also `Map.size` in Base |
| two or more calls, `U32.add` | 71 | 34 | none: `esize` in `symreg`, once per candidate. 34 fork (the benches' `batch` drivers), 3 mix operators (`symreg`'s `eval`) |
| two or more calls, `U32.mul` / `xor` / `or`, `Bool.and` | 6 | not taken | `symreg`'s `eval` (mixed, below), `ascending` in `pure_par_sort` |
| affine (`d + k * f(rest)`) | 2 | not taken | none (one test; `Word.to_nat`, which is `Nat`) |

So the two-call case is where the hot code is, the other spellings are needed by it (`fib` and `coins` bind their calls with `let`, `check` nests its adds), and `U32.add` is wide but cold: it costs 10 tokens on top, so it is in. `hanoi` is not reached: it already carries its sum in a parameter.

As built: under the first commit, 31 defs outside Base are loops (plus `List.length` and `String.length`); here 93 are loops and 38 more carry the sum across a call that stays or a callee that is not flat (plus `Map.size`). 176 of the 965 programs that build emit different C from the first commit: 161 tests, 7 kernels, 6 demos, 2 benches.

## The third commit: an arm that answers 0 answers the sum as it stands

The rewrite turned an arm that answers `0n` into `Nat.add(acc, 0n)`, which the C lane tests against 2^48-1 although `acc` is a Nat already (for `U32`, an add of 0). Such an arm now answers `acc` itself; in the emitted C, `nat_chk(e, _acc_0 + 0ull)` becomes `_acc_0`. +49 ttok.

No cycles claim (not swept). Of the 17 benches only `histogram`'s C changes (two lines, same output, 44,365.7M and 44,384.4M instructions, within run-to-run spread).

Checks, against the second commit: the native lane (886 pass there, 887 here, no status differs); the memory check (`-DBEND_POISON`, live words at exit) on the 127 tests whose C differs, all the same output, exit code and live count; a new test `tests/run/sum_loop_zero.bend` (one and two calls, an arm that answers another literal, a computed 0, `U32`, and a sum that lands on 2^48-1 before the arm that answers 0), which prints the values computed apart in Python on the interpreter, JS and C, on main, the second commit and this one, and ends with 0 live words; a wrong version that skips every constant fails it.

The tail-cycle check removed is caught only by the 800-million-round scratch file (the stack faults). Taking a fork's call or a call behind `!` prints the same and differs only in the C (the fork is gone, the `!` is lost): no `#|` line can see it. Keeping a def with calls left over is not wrong, only useless.

**Two tests changed.** `tests/io/stack_fault_trap.bend` faults the machine stack with a `U32` recursion whose tail is a sum of one call to itself: that is now a loop, so its result is xored before the adds and the recursion stays one. `tests/run/nat_sum_loop.bend` (from the first commit) asked for fifty thousand steps; on this machine the interpreter and the JS lane (bun 1.3.14, node 26.3.1) fault between thirty and fifty thousand frames, so it asks for twenty thousand.

(2) With the grown sum written as an argument of the tail call, `collatz` ran 6% fewer instructions than the first commit and 14% more cycles at every placement (clang merges the two arms' tails); binding the sum before the calls gives the first commit's code back. ## Not covered

- **Cluster gates, CUDA, Linux and x86** have not run. `tsc` was not run. No timing at 8 threads.
- **The JS lane and the interpreter** are untouched: there the defs still recurse.
- **Only add.** `U32.xor` (1 def), `Bool.and` (23) and `Bool.or` (1) have the shape in tests and two demos and nothing hot; no def has it for `mul`, `and`, `or`, `min`, `max`. `Nat.mul` and `F32` are unsound. Affine sums (`d + k * f(rest)`) have two defs.
- **A def with a call to itself anywhere else** (other arms with other operators, a call in an argument) is left alone: measured a loss on `symreg`'s `eval`.
- **A fork's calls stay a fork** (`a b = f(l) f(r)` then `Nat.add(a, b)`): 42 defs under an add, the benches' drivers among them. Carrying the sum through would make the calls depend on each other.
- **Every way evaluation can differ from main:**
  - The sum is added in another order. A `Nat` sum that passes 2^48-1 stops with the same message at an earlier point: before calls and operands that main would have run first. So a program that passes the limit and also fails, or (in an `@unsafe` def) never returns, in one of those stops with the Nat message here.
  - A recursion whose only failure was its depth no longer fails: the last call under each tail add holds no frame.
  - Inside one tail add, the operands that are not calls now run before the calls (main runs the calls first), and the calls run in the order they stand in the add. A call bound by a `let` runs where its name is read, after any `let` between. If two of them fail, which one stops the program can differ.
  - A bound call whose name one arm adds and another arm never reads does not run in the arm that never reads it (main runs it before the match).
  - A tail call from a taken def to another def is now a call and an add: one frame while that def runs. Where that def calls back without a tail call (only `@unsafe` allows it), a round holds two frames where it held one.
  - Ownership can shift at a call site, as in the first commit: a def that becomes flat is called where its value is needed.

title: A fork-free segment takes its sequential path on the host without testing seq
body:
**`comp.ts` is 66,000 ttok, exactly at the 66,000 cap (main is 65,966): `WL_SEQ`'s `#define` has one space where its neighbours are aligned, which is the token that keeps it there.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run.

## What it does

A non-tail call has two ways to keep its continuation: a frame on the stack (`if (seq)`) or a task node on the heap (the `else`), and a jump into a fork-free def from a forking one makes a task (`!DEVICE && !seq && fid_nofk(F)`). `seq` is set whenever the task at hand is fork-free (`FID_ENTER` and `FID_EXIT` or in `fid_nofk`), so a segment that reaches no fork tested a flag that was always set, and carried a task path it never took.

`WL_SEQ(F)` is `seq`, or on the host true when segment `F` is fork-free. `FID_T` is a constant table, so clang folds it per segment. In a fork-free segment the host build then drops:

- **the test** before each frame and before each jump to another def;
- **the task path**, and with it the calls to `task_node` and `heap_alloc_miss`. Those calls were what made clang give the segment a C frame: `eval` in `symreg` saved `x29`/`x30` and set three constants on every entry, for code it never ran.

A forking segment and every device segment still test `seq`.

**The one case that changes behaviour:** a fork-free closure body entered through a `Clo~apply` that may fork (some other closure forks), from a forking def running with `seq` clear. It used to keep its continuations in task nodes; it now keeps them on the stack above the task's frame, as a fork-free task does. Everything it reaches is fork-free too, so the frames are popped before control returns to the forking code. The new test runs that path.

## Results

One M4, GPU off, one thread unless said. Instructions retired and cycles from `/usr/bin/time -l`, builds run in turn, minimum of 3 to 5 runs.

| bench | instructions, main | this | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

| `queens` | 89.82G | 84.13G | -6.3% |
| `lexer` | 53.41G | 51.92G | -2.8% |
| `tree-matmul` | 62.58G | 62.81G | +0.4% (the worst) |
| the other 13 | | | within 0.02% |

**Cycles move much less than instructions.** Each build was swept over 16 code positions (nops at the head of `work_loop`, 4 bytes a step), cycles on a P-core, minimum of 2 or 3 rounds per position:

| bench | main, min / median / max | this, min / median / max | |

Over twelve variants of the bench (C twins and hand edits of the emitted C, 37.9G to 51.2G instructions) cycles follow taken branches (R² 0.95, about 1.2 cycles each) and not instructions (R² 0.23). The instructions removed here are stores, moves and a never-taken test.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates and CUDA** have not run. x86 and Linux were not measured.
- **`tsc`** was not run.
- **A forking segment** still tests `seq` at run time and keeps both paths.

## Where this came from

`symreg` is 1.37x behind its C twin and no draft had moved it. `eval`'s segment showed a frame set up on every entry for calls that sit on the task path, which a fork-free def never takes. The cycles are a different matter: they follow taken branches, and #2177, which stacks on this one, removes those (`symreg` 12.4G to 8.2G cycles).
