title: A call into a tree recursion runs the callee's returning arms itself and jumps straight to its continuation
body:
**`comp.ts` is 67,709 ttok, 1,709 over the 66,000 cap (main is 65,966; #2176, which this stacks on, is 66,000; the first commit here 66,774, arms under nested tests +205, the frame id's move +212, the continuation run in place +518), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Two commits were added on 2026-11-16 and three on 2026-11-21; each round has its own section below, and the sections before them describe the first commit as it was measured. Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run. Stacks on #2176: the first commit here is that PR.

**2026-11-24, fix (`4a9436ea`; +196 ttok, 68,000): on the device a call's frame is pushed at the call.** The move of a call's frame push (or its id store) below the callee's arguments, made so the host can run the answering arms first, also applied in segments the GPU runs, where those arms are `!DEVICE` and the move only kept the frame's words and the arguments live at once. In a device segment the push now stays at the call under `#if DEVICE` and the moved one is `#if !DEVICE`. Host text unchanged: byte-identical after `unifdef -DDEVICE=0` on all 1,032 tests and 244 bend-benchmarks programs (4 tests and 9 programs change, device-only), native lane statuses equal. GPU (Metal, M4, `--gpu on`, median of 5) on this branch: respelled queens r3 1.993 s to 1.626 s (0.82), r2 2.175 to 2.093 (0.96), runtime `queens` 2.983 to 2.835 (0.95); the other 19 GPU programs level (0.98-1.02; `tree-bitonic` 1.669/1.683 over 10 runs); all 22 and the 46 `!` tests print expected at `--gpu on` and `off`. On `opt/integration` it takes r3 from 1.96 s back to 1.62 s (main 1.60).

**2026-11-23, fix (`7beca704`; +95 ttok, 67,804): an early continuation takes the callee's answer in its own words.** The arms copied above a call wrote their answer to `r0`, which the path where no arm answers still jumps with: clang merged the two into a select before every miss. The answer now goes to `wb_r` words. `pascal` (bend-par) 3.685G / 0.624G to 3.438G / 0.566G (base 3.212G / 0.581G: fewer cycles than the base now, at 7% more instructions, the probes that miss); `pascal` 2,553M / 433M to 2,305M / 418M; `coins` cycles 124M to 104M; `queens` 61.87G / 19.68G to 60.06G / 18.87G; `tak`, `hanoi`, `symreg`, `tree-matmul` as before.

## What it does

A non-tail call pushes a frame that ends in the id of its continuation and jumps to its callee. When the callee is at a leaf of the recursion, it tests its argument, computes a word, pops the id and jumps back through the segment table. In a tree recursion that is at least half of all calls: `eval` in `symreg` walks 63 nodes a tree and 32 of them are `Var` or `Lit`.

The call now runs the callee's returning arms itself. After the frame is pushed and the arguments are in the registers, the caller tests them as the callee would; an arm that returns at once runs in place and jumps straight to the continuation the frame names (`WL_POPN(1); WL_JMP(FID_k)`, where the callee had `WL_RETN`). Any other arm falls through to the call, unchanged.

```c
r0 = _f_0;
r1 = _x_0;
if (!DEVICE && WL_SEQ(FID_eval)) {      // the frame is on the stack
  Term _e_0 = r0;                       // eval's own parameter reads
  u32 _x_0 = r1;
  if (term_aux(_e_0) == CID_Var) {      // eval's own arms
    r0 = _x_0;
    WL_POPN(1); WL_JMP(FID_eval_k1);
  } else if (term_aux(_e_0) == CID_Lit) {
    u32 _v_0 = term_loc(_e_0);
    r0 = _v_0;
    WL_POPN(1); WL_JMP(FID_eval_k1);
  }
}
WL_JMP(FID_eval);
```

- **The arms are the callee's emitted text.** `emit_fork` leaves a `//base callee continuation` line at the call; once every unit is final, `segs_base` replaces it with the callee's parameter reads and the leading chain of its entry segment. The code that runs is the code the callee would have run, on the same registers, so ownership, layouts and frees are the callee's own.
- **Which arms:** one that ends in `WL_RETN` and has no other jump, push, loop exit or return. An arm that calls a spin is left out (clang inlines a spin while it has one call site: with such arms copied, `kmeans` ran 1.9% and `raytrace` 3.1% more instructions). An arm of 8 lines or more is left out. The other arms keep their tests with empty bodies, so the chain reads as in the callee.
- **Which callees:** a def that calls itself twice on one path (`term_calls`), the shape whose calls mostly end at once. Without this rule a recursion down a list got the test too, once per element for one hit at the end, and `lexer` lost 3.1% of its cycles (8.09G to 8.34G, medians of two 16-position sweeps that do not overlap) for no instructions.
- **Where:** the host, and only where the frame is on the stack (`WL_SEQ`, or always after a fork's sequential path). The device compiles the block away.

## Results

One M4, GPU off, one thread unless said. Instructions retired and cycles from `/usr/bin/time -l`, builds run in turn, minimum of 3 to 5 runs. "#2176" is the commit this stacks on.

| | main | #2176 | this | C twin |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `symreg` instructions | 50.77G | 42.75G | 40.81G | 37.96G |
| `symreg` cycles (one placement) | 12.37G | 12.28G | 7.76G | 9.01G |
| `symreg` wall, 8 threads | 0.52 s | 0.52 s | 0.34 s | |
| `symreg` cycles on an E-core | 17.29G | 17.13G | 12.67G | 10.64G |

`symreg` goes from 1.37x behind its twin to ahead of it on a P-core (7.8G to 8.4G cycles across code positions, below, against the twin's 9.01G, which was not swept); on an E-core it is still 1.19x behind.

**Placement:** the gain is mostly cycles, so the three builds were swept over 16 code positions (nops at the head of `work_loop`, 4 bytes a step), 3 interleaved rounds, the minimum per position:

| build | min | median | max |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| main | 12.19G | 12.63G | 13.42G |
| #2176 | 12.15G | 12.43G | 12.72G |
| this | 7.80G | 8.18G | 8.42G |

The ranges do not overlap: the slowest position of this build is 3.8G cycles under the fastest of main. Position by position the ratio runs from 1.47x to 1.67x, median 1.55x. Placement alone moves this build by about 8%.

**Counters** (Instruments' CPU Counters, whole run):

| build | taken branches | returns through the table | mispredicted |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| main | 8.13G | 1.85G | 0.044G |
| #2176 | 8.13G | 1.85G | 0.045G |
| this | 5.95G | 0.92G | 0.044G |
| C twin | 6.29G | 1.62G (`ret`) | 0.021G |

Half of the returns are gone, which is the 32 leaves in 63. `symreg` was never short of prediction (0.02 mispredictions a node) or of cache (no misses): over twelve variants of the bench its cycles follow taken branches (R² 0.95) and not instructions (R² 0.23).

Three small recursive kernels (scaled copies of the `fib`, `hanoi` and `tak` ports in koru-benchmarks' osprey-compute-kernels), instructions / cycles at one placement:

| kernel | main | #2176 | this | C reference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `fib(42)` | 17.89G / 2.86G | 16.65G / 2.74G | 13.64G / 2.03G | 7.38G / 1.74G |
| `hanoi(29)` | 15.85G / 2.88G | 10.76G / 2.32G | 10.22G / 2.08G | 6.45G / 2.20G |
| `tak(38, 19, 9)` | 57.07G / 10.07G | 44.92G / 9.75G | 36.26G / 6.11G | 46.71G / 7.14G |

**The rest of the suite**, against #2176: `merkle` -0.03% instructions, `tree-bitonic` -0.01%, `tree-matmul` -0.17%, `tree-radix` +0.04%, cycles within the noise; the other 12 emit the same C. `queens` is not reached: `solve`'s returning arms are nested under an inner test, not arms of its entry chain.

**Elsewhere:** 52 tests emit different C from #2176. `demos/pure_hvm5_mini`'s C grows 3.2% (72 arms at 42 calls), `demos/proof_typed_eval`'s 7.4% (20 arms at 13 calls), `pure_par_sort`'s 1.3% and `pure_par_sum`'s 0.4%; `app_slash_boss_3d` and the other 10 demos have no such call. Emitting a demo's C took the same time in single runs (0.1 s to 1.4 s each).

## Added 2026-11-16: arms under nested tests, and the frame's id

Two commits on top of the one described above (`9b1dc6ec`, `74a1c357`). Everything in this section is measured against that first commit ("#2177 as it stood", `3394908c`), on the same M4, GPU off, one thread.

### What changed

- **Arms under nested tests.** `seg_base` now walks the callee's entry as nested blocks instead of its leading chain only: a test below the entry chain is copied with its returning arms. The lines between two tests run a second time in the callee when no arm answers, so a nested test is copied only when those lines just name words (a declaration whose value calls nothing but `term_loc`, `term_aux`, `term_peek` or `U32_BIN`); a line that takes a node apart (`ctr_take`), frees, allocates or calls a spin keeps everything below it in the callee.
- **An arm that drops a subterm stays in the callee** (`term_sink`). The drop is a call to `term_drop` out of line, and it gave the segment the arm was copied to a C frame on every entry (`warp_k1` in `tree-bitonic` gained `stp x29, x30`): with such arms copied, `tree-bitonic` ran 10.2% and `tree-radix` 3.7% more instructions. This also takes such arms away from the entry chain, where the first commit copied them; no bench or kernel had one.
- **The frame's id is stored below the arms.** Where a call gets arms, the store of the continuation's id moves after them, so an answered call neither stores nor pops it (`WL_JMP(k)` where the first commit had `WL_POPN(1); WL_JMP(k)`). Not in the callee's own entry segment: there the call closes a loop, and with the store after the test clang vectorises the loop's frame pushes (`st4.2d` in `tak`, which then ran 5.7% more cycles at every placement for 4.8% fewer instructions). A call that gets no arms is emitted exactly as before.

```c
r0 = _f_13;                              // mul_k1 in tree-matmul
r1 = _f_18;
if (!DEVICE && 1) {
  Term _a_0 = r0;
  Term _b_0 = r1;
  if (term_aux(_a_0) == CID_Lf) {
    u32 _x_0 = term_loc(_a_0);
    if (term_aux(_b_0) == CID_Lf) {      // a second test
      u32 _y_0 = term_loc(_b_0);
      r0 = term_pak(CID_Lf, U32_BIN(_x_0, *, _y_0));
      WL_JMP(FID_mul_k2);                // the id was never stored
    } else {
      ...
    }
  } else {
    u64 _sp_1 = term_peek(e.mem, _a_0);  // lines that only name words
    ...
    if (term_aux(_b_0) == CID_Lf) {
      ...
    }
  }
}
if (1) {
  STK(0) = FID_mul_k2;
  WL_PUSHN(1);
}
WL_JMP(FID_mul);
```

### Results against #2177 as it stood

Instructions retired, and cycles over 16 code positions (3 interleaved rounds, the least per position; least / median / most, in G). Another agent was benchmarking on the machine during these sweeps.

| bench | instructions | cycles, #2177 as it stood | cycles, now | per position |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `tree-matmul` | 62.70G to 46.80G (-25.4%) | 7.98 / 8.05 / 8.09 | 5.86 / 5.91 / 5.98 | 0.729x to 0.743x, no overlap |
| `queens` | 84.13G to 71.10G (-15.5%) | 21.82 / 22.05 / 22.27 | 19.84 / 19.89 / 20.08 | 0.892x to 0.916x, no overlap |
| `tree-radix` | -0.3% | 14.92 / 15.22 / 15.97 | 14.58 / 14.75 / 14.81 | 0.924x to 0.988x, no overlap |
| `tree-bitonic` | -0.29% | 20.20 / 20.38 / 20.48 | 20.08 / 20.21 / 20.37 | 0.988x to 0.998x, the ranges overlap |
| `symreg` | -0.08% | 7.69 / 8.13 / 8.47 | 7.71 / 8.00 / 8.39 | 0.956x to 1.048x, the ranges overlap |
| `merkle` | -0.02% | 18.54 / 18.55 / 18.55 | 18.54 / 18.55 / 18.55 | the same range |
| the other 11 | same C | | | |

Counters over the whole run (one run each): `tree-matmul` 4.72G to 4.13G taken branches and 1.889G to 0.247G indirect ones (87% of its returns through the table are gone); `queens` 6.54G to 4.52G taken and 0.857G to 0.551G indirect. Mispredictions barely move (19.7M to 16.9M, 574M to 559M).

`symreg` differs in 9 of its 46 segments (the continuations of `eval` and `esize`, and `floop`): only the frame id's store moved; `eval`'s entry is textually the same.

The koru kernels, scaled as above (`pascal` 30/15, `coins` 1200, `binarytrees` 8000 trees, `ackermann` 3/12, `exprtree` 600 trees):

| kernel | instructions | cycles, #2177 as it stood | cycles, now | per position |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| `tak(38, 19, 9)` | 36.26G to 32.83G (-9.5%) | 6.14 / 6.26 / 6.83 | 6.14 / 6.27 / 6.84 | 0.948x to 1.100x, the same range |
| `fib(42)` | -1.96% | 2.026 / 2.030 / 2.047 | 2.020 / 2.026 / 2.059 | the same range |
| `hanoi(29)` | 0 | 2.073 / 2.082 / 2.109 | 2.072 / 2.082 / 2.107 | the same range |
| `pascal` | 20.57G to 23.56G (**+14.5%**) | 3.99 / 4.09 / 4.33 | 3.77 / 3.89 / 4.18 | 0.927x to 0.987x |
| `coins` | 14.81G to 11.23G (-24.2%) | 4.20 / 4.27 / 4.35 | 4.19 / 4.34 / 4.35 | 0.963x to 1.035x, the same range (main: 3.88 / 3.88 / 3.91) |
| `binarytrees` | -1.0% | 1.513 / 1.535 / 1.666 | 1.472 / 1.501 / 1.537 | 0.894x to 0.994x |
| `ackermann` | 0 | 1.457 / 1.466 / 1.473 | 1.454 / 1.462 / 1.472 | the same range |
| `exprtree` | -0.11% | 1.484 / 1.497 / 1.510 | 1.484 / 1.492 / 1.503 | the same range |

`pascal` is the cost: `binom`'s frequent returning arm (`n == 0`, 42% of its calls) calls two spins and stays in the callee, so the copied tests answer only the rare one (`k == 0`, 8% of calls) and the rest run them twice. It runs 14.5% more instructions for 3% to 7% fewer cycles.

### Per widening

| widening | built | instructions | what it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| arms under nested tests, drops left out (`9b1dc6ec`) | yes | `queens` -15.5%, `tree-matmul` -19.1%, `tree-bitonic` -0.1%, `tree-radix` **+1.0%**; `coins` -21.5%, `pascal` +12.3% | +205 ttok; C of `tree-matmul` +13.9%, `queens` +4.3% |
| the frame's id below the arms (`74a1c357`) | yes | on top: `tree-matmul` -19.1% to -25.4%, `tree-radix` +1.0% to -0.3%, `tak` -9.5%, `coins` -21.5% to -24.2%, `fib` -2.0%, `binarytrees` -1.0% | +212 ttok |
| the same at the callee's own entry | measured, left out | `symreg` -2.8% (cycles 0.915x to 1.016x, overlapping) | `tak` +5.7% cycles at every position: clang vectorises the pushes |
| arms that call a spin, under 12 lines | bounded | `pascal` -8.3% where it is now +14.5%, `exprtree` -6.9%, `tree-bitonic` -2.2% | `raytrace` +3.1%, `kmeans` +2.0%, as first measured |
| arms of 8 to 24 lines | bounded | `kmeans` -0.4% (`szip`), nothing else | none seen |
| arms that drop a subterm | measured, left out | | `tree-bitonic` +10.2%, `tree-radix` +3.7% |
| callees that call themselves once | counted | of `lexer`'s 591M non-tail calls 11% end at once (`gen` 3%, `ident` 22%, `num` 29%); `digitsum` 18%, `collatz` 1% | the measured `lexer` loss stands |
| mutual recursion, a second level, non-recursive callees | counted | under 4% of the calls of any bench (`tree-bitonic` 3.9%, `queens` 0.8%) | |

How the calls of each bench end was counted with a profiling build (every non-tail call tagged with its site, every return with its arm). Of the non-tail calls, those ending at once in an arm under a nested test: `tree-matmul` 86% of 1.91G, `queens` 36% of 857M, `tree-radix` 40% of 238M, `coins` 50%; in an arm that calls a spin: `tree-bitonic` 45% of 2.34G, `pascal` 42%, `raytrace` 50% and `mandelbrot` 49% (where the arm is the whole leaf's work).

**With the current #2175** (`opt/nat-accumulate` at `2707077e`, this branch patched on): `fib`, `pascal` and `binarytrees` are as with #2177 as it stood (same instructions for the first two, -0.4% for the third, cycles in the same ranges). `coins` is slightly worse: 11.62G to 12.00G instructions and 2.33 / 2.42 / 2.65G to 2.50 / 2.59 / 2.87G cycles (overlapping). The additions pay on `queens` and `tree-matmul`, which #2175 does not touch.

### The two known problems

- **`coins`** (#2177 alone 9% slower than main at 13.7% fewer instructions): two things, both seen in the counters. The first commit's block at `ways`' own first call answers almost never (78 of 14.9M calls: that call walks `amount` down like a list), and with it clang lays `ways`' entry out so that every entry takes one more branch: 2.00G to 2.80G taken branches for the same 3.60G branches and 0.80G indirect ones. Under that, the kernel is bound by a store and a reload: each level pushes the first call's result and pops it to add, and the cycles stay between 3.9G and 4.4G from 17.2G down to 11.2G instructions. With the continuation's add run at the answering site by hand, the reload goes and the cycles fall from 4.38G to 2.87G. That is what #2175 removes for sums; nested arms take `coins`' taken branches to 1.60G but not its cycles.
- **`pascal`** (with #2176, #2175's `binom~acc` runs 8% more cycles at 12.8% fewer instructions): once #2176 removes the `seq` test from the loop that descends `n`, clang vectorises its frame pushes (`st3.2d`, eight frames a turn; SIMD instructions 0.0001G to 0.079G, taken branches and mispredictions unchanged). With the pushes kept scalar by hand the build is back inside #2175's range (3.13 / 3.19 / 3.29G against 2.98 / 3.12 / 3.29G; vectorised 3.33 / 3.38 / 3.45G) at 19% fewer instructions. The same barrier makes `hanoi` 2% to 19% and `binarytrees` 4% to 12% slower at every position, so no rule is emitted for it.

### Checks for the additions

All local, against #2177 as it stood (`3394908c`):

- **Native lane:** 885 tests print their `#|` lines on both, 21 differ from them and 1 times out on both; no status differs. The new test is the 886th.
- **C and JS:** of 943 programs that build (tests, demos, benches, the 22 kernels) 64 emit different C (50 tests, 8 demos, 6 benches), +0.14% C in total; `tree-matmul` +14.6%, `pure_hvm5_mini` +5.1%, `queens` +4.4%. The JS of all 943 is byte-identical. Emitting all of them took 214.1 s before and 213.5 s now.
- **Memory:** the 50 tests whose C differs give the same output, exit code and count of live heap words under `-DBEND_POISON`, at the default thread count and at 8.
- **Metal:** the 48 tests that make a `!` call print the same with `--gpu on` and `--gpu off`, before and now (the arms are compiled away on the device; the frame id's move is in the device code of 3 of them, `fork_leaf_handoff`, `gpu_mark` and the new test).
- **New test:** `tests/run/call_returns_nested.bend`: two trees matched together with arms that free and arms that reuse their node, three tests deep, a Bool then two Nats (the shape of `coins`), shared trees read by two walks, a word test under a tag test, one def called by an owner and by a reader, forks, a `!` call, a comb 3000 deep; and the shapes that must stay: a nested arm that drops a subtree, and one behind lines that take a node apart, also on a tree that a reader and a picker share. Its lines are main's on the C lane (1 and 8 threads), under bun and under `bend file.bend`. A counting build takes 9,073 returns under a nested test and 20,271 on the entry chain, at 1 and at 8 threads.
- **Wrong versions:** 20 deliberately wrong copies of the pass, run on the two tests and a scratch file, plain and with poisoned frees, at 1 and 8 threads. 8 are caught (the lines before a test not checked, or any declaration accepted there; the id popped though never stored; the id never stored; the id stored first and again; the arm returning to the callee; the id stored when the frame is in a task; the callee's own entry not popping). 12 print the same: 7 change only which arms are copied (drops, spins, long arms, lists, one arm per test, the id's move at the callee's own entry or nowhere), 3 guard text no program emits, and 2 are gaps: a `!` call given arms, and arms run while the frame is in a task (`seq` clear). No test reaches a copied arm with `seq` clear; that condition is the first commit's.

### Verdicts

- **Nested tests: keep.** It is the part that reaches `queens` and `tree-matmul`. Alone it left `tree-radix` 1.0% up in instructions (its cycles overlap); with the frame id's move no bench of the suite runs more instructions.
- **Drops left out: keep**, as a measured rule like the spin one: the frame it forces is in the disassembly.
- **The frame id's move: keep outside the callee's own entry.** At the own entry it is a gain on `symreg` that I could not separate from placement and a loss on `tak` that I could.
- **Spin arms: not built, worth a follow-up** with a rule on the spin's size: it would turn `pascal`'s +14.5% into about -8%, but as it stands it repeats the `kmeans` and `raytrace` losses.
- **Long arms, linear callees, mutual recursion, a second level: not worth it** on these benches.
- **Running the continuation at the answering site: not built.** By hand it takes `coins` from 4.38G to 2.87G cycles and `fib` from 2.20G to 2.06G (one position each, `fib`'s for 2.4% more instructions); it copies continuation text into every arm.

### Not covered by the additions

- The cluster gates, CUDA, x86, Linux and `tsc`, as above.
- **Clang decides two things here that the compiler does not control:** whether it merges the copied tests with the callee's when the call is in the callee's own entry (it does in `queens`, not in `tree-radix`' `merge`, which is where the +1.0% was), and whether it vectorises a loop of frame pushes (`pascal`, `tak`).
- The sweeps ran on a machine another agent was benchmarking on.

## Added 2026-11-21: an answered call runs its continuation in place

When a call's callee answers at once through the copied arms, the call still stored its frame, jumped to the continuation and read the frame back. Now, when the continuation pops exactly that call's frame, pushes none, and is at most 48 lines, the copied arms run inside a block that an answering arm leaves with a flag set, and a copy of the continuation runs there with its frame reads taken from the caller's words. The sequential frame push moves below the arms, so it runs only when no arm answers. First built as branch `opt/queens-early` (kept), stacked on this PR.

Two restrictions, each from a measurement:
- **The continuation pushes no frame.** Copying `symreg`'s `eval` continuation, which pushes the second call's frame, into `eval` cost 5% instructions.
- **The continuation calls no spin and no drop.** A spin called from a copied continuation gets a second call site and clang stops inlining it: `cfold` put two spins out of line (+5% instructions); `tak` and `deriv` lose their small gains with the rule.

Instructions against this PR's previous head (74a1c357), one thread, GPU off, M4:

| program | change |
|---|---:|
| `queens` | -13.0% (cycles 19.90G to 19.24G, -3.3%, 16 placements, no overlap) |
| `symreg` | -9.3% |
| `hanoi` (koru) | -18.3% |
| `coins` (koru) | -17.5% |
| `fib` (koru) | -8.5% |
| `binarytrees` (koru) | -3.6% |
| `cfold`, `deriv`, `pascal` | within 0.5% |

Every other bench of the suite is within noise.

**Bug found by the checks and fixed** (1dca6d17): a call into another def runs its own task path between its frame push and the arms when not sequential, and that path reads the continuation the push's task branch set. Moving the whole push block below the arms gave such a call the previous continuation at 8 threads (`tests/run/fork_ctor_build` and `mach_scan_sibling` printed wrong numbers and leaked). Only the sequential push moves now; the new test adds calls under parallel lets, which printed 2586831047 for 772016070 on the faulty commit at 8 threads.

**Checks**, against the previous head: all 60 changed tests, benches, demos and kernels give the same output as before on every lane, with the same live-word counts under poisoned frees at 1 and 8 threads; the four Perceus `rbtree` ports checked on C and with the memory check (0 live words). Every deliberately wrong version of the change is caught by the new test, the 8-thread bug included. Not run: the cluster gates, CUDA, Linux, x86; JS and the interpreter on the `rbtree` ports (too heavy here).

## Checks of the first commit

All local, against main `f0cf0a7c` and against #2176:

- **Native lane:** every test built and run with the GPU off at the default thread count: 883 print their `#|` lines on main and here, 21 differ from them and 1 times out on both, no status differs.
- **Memory:** with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit: the 51 of those 52 tests that build give the same output, exit code and count as main. An earlier version of this branch, which answered the calls of every callee and not only of tree-shaped ones (so a superset of these calls), gave the same on all 905 tests that build.
- **The new path runs:** a build that counts the returns taken at a call. The new test takes 12,872 of them; a larger copy 250,000. Both print main's lines at 1, 2 and 8 threads and pass the memory check at 1 and 8.
- **New test:** `tests/run/call_returns.bend`: a returning arm that frees the node it owns, one that allocates, one that drops another owned parameter, a three-word result, a Nat match two levels deep, a returning arm written after the calling one, a shared tree read by two walks, a forking def and forks over fork-free ones; and the shapes that must stay as they were (a recursion down a list, two defs that call each other). Its lines are main's; it prints them on the C lane (1 and 8 threads), under bun and under `bend file.bend`.
- **JS lane:** the JS of all 975 programs that emit it is byte-identical to main's (`compile_book` is the C emitter).
- **Metal:** the 47 tests that make a `!` call print the same with `--gpu on` on main and here; the block is under `!DEVICE`, so the device compiles it away.
- `repo.ts` fails only on the ttok cap.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates and CUDA** have not run. x86 and Linux were not measured.
- **`tsc`** was not run.
- **Arms that call a spin** stay in the callee (bounded above).
- **Mutual recursion** (a tree walked by two defs that call each other) is not recognised as a tree.
- **Tail calls** have no frame to answer and are unchanged.
- **The frame's id is still stored** before an arm answers a call made from the callee's own entry (see above).

## Cost

+774 ttok over #2176 for the first commit, +417 for the two added (+1,225 over main).

## Where this came from

`symreg`'s gap to its twin was put down to branch prediction. The counters say otherwise: 0.044G mispredictions in 12.4G cycles. What the cycles follow is taken branches, about 1.2 cycles each, and a leaf reached by a call costs four or five of them (the jump in, the tag tests, the return through the table). Answering the leaf at the call leaves one or two. Real C calls were bounded earlier at 1.14x for `symreg`; this gives 1.55x inside the segment machinery.

title: perf(io): File.read_line keeps a buffer per handle and answers a buffered line inline
body:
## What

On the C lane, `File.read_line` made one `read(2)` per byte. Now each handle that `read_line` reads keeps a 16 KiB buffer of its own. One `read(2)` fills it with whatever is available, so a pipe or a terminal still answers each line as soon as it arrives. If a whole line is already in the buffer, `read_line` builds the String straight from the buffer and answers right away, instead of sending the work to a helper thread and back. The loop still polls its timers and helper results every 64 answers, as it does for any effect that answers at once, and a refill always goes through the helper. A read that does reach the fd calls `io_sync()` first, as #2155 requires.

The buffered bytes belong to the handle, not the fd:

- `File.read` and `File.read_bytes` answer the buffered bytes first. `File.read_at` and `File.size` are unchanged.
- `File.write` and `File.write_at` first seek back to the end of the last line read, so on an `r+` handle the write lands right after it. This works on any fd that seeks, including block devices. The buffer is dropped only if the seek lands where it was asked. A pipe, a terminal, or a device whose seek doesn't move keeps its buffer, because its reads and writes don't share a position.
- `File.close` does the same seek-back, then frees the buffer. `File.open` drops any stale buffer for an fd number being reused.

Nothing seeks back during reads, so this has none of the failure modes #2157 had: a seek that fails after the bytes are read, a seek that succeeds without moving, or pipes getting slower. Supersedes #2157, and `tests/io/file_read_line_rest.bend` is taken from it.

## Why

A loop that counts the lines and characters of a file with `File.read_line(f, 65536)`, built with `bend rl.bend -o rl`. All builds print the same counts on every run.

Linux (Arch, kernel 7.2), AMD Ryzen 7 5800H. The `main` and #2157 columns are medians of 3 interleaved runs; this PR's column is the median of 5, from a later run on the same machine and inputs:

| input | main | #2157 | this PR | vs main |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| file, 200k lines (9.7 MB) | 8.37 s | 2.45 s | 0.073 s | 115x |
| file, 10k lines of ~4 KB (42 MB) | 26.66 s | 0.51 s | 0.311 s | 86x |
| `./rl /dev/stdin < file`, 200k lines | 7.88 s | 2.49 s | 0.073 s | 108x |
| `cat file \| ./rl /dev/stdin`, 200k lines | 7.14 s | 7.46 s | 0.070 s | 102x |
| `cat file \| ./rl /dev/stdin`, 10k × 4 KB | 22.53 s | 23.44 s | 0.291 s | 77x |

macOS, Apple M4 Pro. Here `main` and #2157 took 4.23 s and 1.05 s for the 200k-line file, and 4.62 s and 4.77 s for 200k lines from a pipe; an earlier commit of this PR (5f050826) took 0.059 s and 0.060 s. The current head beat that commit by 1.2–1.8x in every case in an interleaved run, but the Mac was under load then (load average 6–7), so I'm not quoting its absolute times.

Most of the gain comes from answering buffered lines on the loop. With the buffer alone and every line going through the helper, the 200k-line file took 0.94 s on macOS.

The buffer is 16 KiB. On macOS, comparing 4, 8, 16 and 64 KiB, short lines ran within 0.054–0.070 s at every size. Lines of about 4 KB took 0.25–0.32 s at 4 KiB, 0.18 s at 16 KiB and 0.15 s at 64 KiB. On Linux, 16 KiB was 5–9% slower than 64 KiB. 16 KiB holds a quarter of the memory per handle, which is in line with common runtime defaults (4–16 KiB).

## How to test

- `tests/io/file_read_line_write.bend` (new): on an `r+` handle, it reads lines, writes between them and reads the rest, then checks the whole file through a fresh handle. On the C lane it fails if the seek-back before a write is removed.
- `tests/io/file_read_line_stdout_order.bend` (new): a `read_line` on a handle opened before an `IO.print` must flush the held text, even while another fiber keeps the loop away from its poller. On the C lane it interposes `fflush` and `read()`, and the read fails the program if stdout was not flushed: without the `io_sync()`, it fails every time. The JS twin passes the file through, so every lane prints the same lines.
- `tests/io/file_read_line_rest.bend` (from #2157): `read_line` cut at `max`, lines longer than one chunk, then `File.read` for the rest.
- All `tests/io/file_*`, `read_bytes` and `stdout_file_order` tests pass on the C lane on macOS, and the `read_line` tests also pass on the interpreted and JS lanes. On Linux they pass too, except `stdout_file_order`, which fails the same way on `main` when stdout is redirected to a file: opening `/dev/stdout` with `"w"` truncates it there.

## Risk

- Bytes read ahead now belong to the handle, which is the same trade-off as stdio, Rust's `BufReader` and Python's buffered IO:
  - On a pipe or a terminal, bytes still buffered when the handle is closed are lost. For example, in `printf 'a\nb\n' | (./prog /dev/stdin; cat)`, where `prog` reads one line, `cat` no longer sees `b`.
  - On a regular file, `File.close` puts the shared position back at the end of the last line, but a program that exits without closing leaves it past the buffer.
  - A handle dropped without `File.close` leaks its 16 KiB buffer along with its fd.
- If another handle writes to the same file, this handle's buffer can hold stale bytes, as in any buffered reader.
- A `read_line` loop answers buffered lines without parking. As with any effect that answers at once, the loop polls its timers every 64 answers, and a buffer holds at most 16 KiB of lines.
- Terminals are untested: the session that wrote this had no tty. The JS lane still reads one byte at a time.

title: fix(rt): the thread count reads the cgroup v2 quota on this process's cgroup and its parents (#2163)
body:
## What

`cpu_count` read only `/sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max`, the root's. A quota on a systemd service, or on any nested cgroup, was ignored, so the pool took every CPU. Now it:

- finds the `0::` line of `/proc/self/cgroup`. It isn't always the first line: a cgroup v1 `net_cls` mount, for example, comes before it. The path is read to the end of the line, so a cgroup name with a space works.
- bounds the thread count by each `cpu.max` from that cgroup up to the root, rounding a fractional quota up as before.

Inside a container the cgroup path is `/`, so it reads the container's own `cpu.max`, as today. cgroup v1's root `cpu.cfs_quota_us` and `cpu.cfs_period_us` are still read, once, as before. All of it is under `#ifdef __linux__`, so macOS builds don't change.

Closes #2163.

## Cap

**This puts `bend2/comp.ts` at 66,134 / 66,000 ttok, so the repo gate fails on the cap (55/56). It can't merge as is.** `main` is at 65,981, so only 19 tokens were free, and the fix costs 153. `gates/repo.ts` says the caps are permanent: a file over its cap is made smaller by simplification, and only Taelin can change a cap. So this needs about 135 tokens of simplification elsewhere in `comp.ts` before it can merge. Dropping the cgroup v1 fallback would save about 45 tokens, which isn't enough on its own and would lose the quota inside v1 containers.

## How to test

`thread_count.bend`:

```python
import Base

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    n : U32 <- IO.thread_count()
    IO.print(U32.show(n))
```

On Arch Linux (kernel 7.2, 16 CPUs, cgroup v2 with a v1 `net_cls` mount), built with `bun bend2/main.ts thread_count.bend -o tc.c && clang -std=c11 -O2 tc.c -lpthread -lm -o tc`, run as `systemd-run --user --wait --pipe --collect -p CPUQuota=… ./tc +RTS --gpu off -RTS`:

| where it runs | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| no quota | 16 | 16 |
| `CPUQuota=100%` | 16 | 1 |
| `CPUQuota=200%` | 16 | 2 |
| `CPUQuota=350%` | 16 | 4 |
| child cgroup with no `cpu.max`, under a parent with `CPUQuota=300%` (`-p Delegate=yes`) | 16 | 3 |
| the same, with the child named `my leaf` | 16 | 3 |

The line scan was also run against hand-written `/proc/self/cgroup` files: `net_cls` first, a path with a space, leading empty lines, a bare `0:` line, v1 lines only, `0::/`, an empty file and a missing file. All of them end, and each walks the expected levels.

The first version read only the first line of `/proc/self/cgroup` and still answered 16 on that machine, because of the `net_cls` line. That's why it now scans for `0::`.

## Risk

- The C runtime now opens and reads `/proc/self/cgroup` and one `cpu.max` per cgroup level at startup: a few `open`/`read` calls.
- A cgroup v1 hierarchy's own nesting is still not walked; only the root v1 quota is read, as before. So on a v1 or hybrid host, a systemd service's `CPUQuota` is still ignored.
- A path with `..` (a process outside its cgroup namespace's root) or a container that bind-mounts only its own subtree still falls back to what it can read, as before.

title: A call whose arguments a recursion never changes is computed once, in a copy of the def that carries the value
body:
**`comp.ts` is 68,310 ttok, 2,310 over the 66,000 cap (main is 65,981), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled.** Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run. The branch is on main `b8a88499`, one commit behind `8c329c1b` (#2178), with which `comp.ts` merges without conflict. Independent of every other open draft; it shares `lt_any`, `FL.made` and the `tld_of` line with #2031, word for word, so whichever merges second drops its copy.

**Reach, said first:** this was found on a benchmark built to reward it, and it fires on very little else. Of the 980 programs under `bench/runtime`, `demos`, `tests` and the 39 Bend ports of the koru osprey kernels that build, 6 emit different C (8 sites): the two `binarytrees` ports and four tests. No bench of the suite, no demo and no def of Base changes.

## What it does

A def that calls itself may make, on every turn, a call that reads nothing the turns change:

```python
def go(+i: Nat, acc: Nat) -> Nat:
  match i:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      go(p, Nat.add(acc, check(make(13n))))
```

`check(make(13n))` builds and walks the same tree 1,200 times. The def now computes it once: the arm that holds the call binds it and goes on in `go~fix`, a copy of the def that takes the value as a last parameter and reads it where the call was.

```python
def go(+i: Nat, acc: Nat) -> Nat:          # as compiled
  match i:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      +c = check(make(13n))
      go~fix(p, Nat.add(acc, c), c)

def go~fix(+i: Nat, acc: Nat, +c: Nat) -> Nat:
  match i:
    case 0n:
      acc
    case 1n+p:
      go~fix(p, Nat.add(acc, c), c)
```

The rule (`def_fix`, run at the end of `file_book` on each def that calls itself, on the checked terms, so both the C and the JS lane take it):

- **A loop** is a def with a direct call to itself, in tail position or not (a tree walk that passes a context down is covered; the value rides down every call below the first).
- **Fixed** is a call whose every variable is a parameter that each live self call of the def, in every arm, passes back as the same variable. A parameter that one self call passes back and another changes, one that is matched and rebuilt, and a name bound again by a `let` are not fixed.
- **Worth it** is a call that runs a def that loops or is not flat, directly or through flat callees. The largest such term is taken (`check(make(13n))`, not `make(13n)`). A call to a flat def without a loop (`Bool.not(s)`, `half(n)`, a constant def) is left: 57 such sites in the corpus, 44 of them a float-literal helper or a constant def.
- **Words only.** The call's result is a word, or a record laid out as words (a `Bool`, a pair of numbers). A result that is a box is left where it is; see Not covered for the measurement.
- **Evaluated where it was.** `go` keeps its body. Only an arm that holds the call binds it, at the head of the statement that holds it, and only self calls of that statement and later ones go to the copy. So a loop that turns zero times, or never reaches that arm, never makes the call; a call that stops the program or does not return does so in the arm that reached it.
- **Never a call the def may not evaluate:** one under a lambda, in a partial application (its arguments run when it is applied), in an unused `let`, in an erased argument, or inside a call the emitter unfolds at compile time (`emit_fold`: the unfolded body may drop the argument).
- **Not across a write.** In an `@unsafe` def a `+` parameter may hold an Array, and a write through one handle shows through the others; so there a parameter whose type holds an Array, or anything but datatypes (a closure, a type variable), is never fixed. In a checked def a `+` parameter is `Data`, which holds neither.
- **Not a call with a `!`, a foreign def, a lambda or a `let` inside it, or a call to the def itself.**
- **One call per def**, the first found in an arm that also calls the def; the same call written in other arms reads the same value in the copy.

Where the line with compile-time folding is: a call the emitter can unfold within `FOLD_FUEL` (a flat def on constants, `tri(3n, 0n)`) is unfolded as before and never taken; one it cannot (`check(make(13n))`: `make` is not flat) is computed once at run time.

## Results

One M4, one thread, GPU off; instructions retired and cycles from `/usr/bin/time -l`, the least of 9 interleaved runs; wall time from `hyperfine -N`, 30 runs. `binarytrees` is the kernel of `korulang/koru-benchmarks` (`suites/osprey-compute-kernels/bend`), not added to this repo.

| `binarytrees` | instructions | cycles | wall |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| C reference (`cc -O2`) | 6,946.0M | 1,053.8M | 276.3 ms |
| main | 1,639.2M | 275.1M | 71.9 ms |
| #2031 (fuses `check(make(d))`) | 955.9M | 171.5M | 46.0 ms |
| this | 13.6M | 4.2M | 1.2 ms |
| this on #2031 (it takes the fused `check<make(13n)`) | 12.9M | 4.2M | 1.2 ms |
| the call passed into the loop by hand | 13.6M | 4.2M | 1.2 ms |

A Bend program that prints a constant runs 12.2M instructions, so what is left is start-up. The forked port (`bend-par`) goes from 165.5 ms to 1.6 ms at the default thread count and from 70.7 ms to 1.3 ms at one thread.

A recursion that is no tail call, as a scratch program: a walk of 2^18 nodes that passes `k` down and adds `tri(k, 0n)` at every node runs 286.3M instructions on main and 24.2M here with `k` = 200; with `k` = 0, where the call costs nothing, 24.2M on both, so carrying the word is free there.

Every other program whose C changes, same method (7 runs):

| program | instructions, main | this | |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `tests/rfc/share_loop` | 17.42M | 12.21M | -29.9% |
| `tests/reg/array_half_loop` | 14.79M | 12.34M | -16.6% |
| `tests/reg/array_node_loop` | 13.31M | 12.27M | -7.8% |
| `tests/compile/literal_reads` (a loop of two turns) | 12.20M | 12.22M | +0.2% |

Those four tests are loops written around exactly this shape as regression witnesses (a tree shared per turn, an Array built and dropped per turn). They print their lines, but they now make the call once, so what they were written to exercise on every turn runs on the first turn only. They are left as they are here; keeping their point needs the call to read something the turn changes.

**The bench suite:** all 17 `bench/runtime` programs emit byte-identical C, so nothing was measured there. **Demos:** the 18 that build emit identical C. **Base:** rooting all 299 defs of a file that only imports Base (65 call themselves; templates come in through the tests that instantiate them) finds no site.

**Compile time:** no difference above the noise. Timed inside the compiler, the pass takes 0.8 to 1.4 ms of `compile_book`'s 26 to 54 ms on `lexer`, `terrain`, `merkle` and `symreg`, 4.7 ms of 260 ms on `pure_hvm5_mini` and 6.2 ms of 576 ms on `app_slash_boss_3d` (about 1% of a whole `bend file.bend -o file.c`, checker included). `hyperfine` on that command, 7 runs each: the median over the 17 benches moves by +0.7% (from -7.3% to +4.8%, which is the spread of the runs), `app_slash_boss_3d` 677.6 ms to 680.4 ms, `pure_hvm5_mini` 337.0 ms to 343.6 ms; emitting C for all 904 tests with `#|` lines, one after the other, took 130.8 s on main and 131.0 s and 132.8 s here.

**Emitted C** grows by 0.4% to 1.2% in the six programs (the def's body is emitted twice).

## Checks

All local, against main `b8a88499`:

- **Native lane** (every test built and run with the GPU off, compared with its `#|` lines): 883 pass on main and 884 here (the new test); no status of an existing test differs. It ran before two edits to the pass that change no emitted C (all 980 programs emit byte-identical C before and after them); the two new tests were run again afterwards, on both lanes.
- **Emitted C** of the 980 programs that build: 974 byte-identical, 6 differ (above). **Emitted JS** of the 1,033 that build: 1,027 byte-identical, the same 6 differ; those 6 print the same as main under `bend file.bend` and as a built `.js`.
- **Memory:** the 4 tests whose C differs, the 2 new tests and both `binarytrees` ports, built with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit: the same output, exit code and count as main.
- **Adversarial programs** (35, kept outside the repo), each on main and here: C with poisoned frees and the live count at one thread, C at the default thread count, and the JS lane; output, exit code, first line of stderr and live words all equal, and the defs the pass fired on are the ones each program names. They cover: zero turns around a call that stops the program, and around one that never returns; one turn around a call that stops it (it stops); the call in one arm of two, reached late, and never; a parameter passed back by one self call and changed by another; swapped parameters; a rebuilt parameter; a rebound name; nested loops; two fixed parameters under one def; forks (the loop under a fork, the call in a fork's branch, a forking tree walk); `!` calls; a second entry through another def with another value; closures (a call under a lambda never applied, a self call under a lambda); a partial application; an unused `let` and an unfolded call that drops its argument; boxed and Array parameters; an Array an `@unsafe` loop writes through one handle and reads through the one it passes back; results of two words and of a `Bool`; a `U32` loop with a default arm; a def that opens a lambda past its parameters; erased type parameters with function types as type arguments; an IO loop; a `!` fork tree.
- **Wrong versions:** ten deliberately wrong versions of the pass were built as compilers and run on those programs; each is caught by at least one. Taking every parameter for fixed; reading only the first self call; binding the call in arms that do not hold it; looking under lambdas; into partial applications; into unused lets; dropping the unfold test; a key that ignores which variable a call reads; allowing Arrays in `@unsafe` defs (prints 370 where main prints 750); binding at the head of the arm instead of the statement.
- **Metal:** none of the six changed programs makes a `!` call. Two scratch programs do (a loop that calls itself with a `!`, and a `!` fork tree whose leaves run a loop the pass fires on): both print the same with `--gpu on` and `--gpu off`, on main and here; the tree's value was computed apart in Python.
- **New tests:** `tests/run/loop_fixed_call.bend`, 14 shapes whose numbers were computed apart in Python, every count scaled by the command line's length so nothing folds; the pass fires on 10 of its defs and must leave 5 alone. `tests/run/loop_fixed_call_stop.bend`: one turn whose arm first binds a call past the Nat wall and then holds a fixed call that never returns stops with the Nat message. Both print their lines on the C lane and under `bend file.bend`, on main and here. Of the ten wrong versions, the first test fails eight and the second the one that binds at the head of the arm; the tenth (no unfold test) cannot be pinned by a repo test, because main's own lanes disagree on its case: the C lane unfolds `pick(boom(k), 0n, acc)` and drops the argument, the JS lane evaluates it and stops.
- `tsc` reports the same 3 errors in `comp.ts` as on main.

## Not covered

Every way the order of evaluation or the sharing can differ from main:

- **Within one statement** the fixed call is bound first, so it runs before calls written to its left in that statement (main runs a statement's calls that are not flat first, left to right, then the flat ones in place). A program differs only if two calls of one statement both go wrong: `Nat.add(boom(i), hang(k))` stops with the Nat message on main and never returns here. Statements before it (earlier lets) still run first.
- **A call in a fork's branch** is bound before the fork, so on the first turn it runs before the other branch starts, not beside it.
- **Later turns no longer make the call.** A program that would have died in a later turn's call (out of memory or stack) no longer does.
- **A def tail-called from exactly one place in the loop** has two callers after the copy and is no longer emitted in place at that tail.
- **No sharing changes:** the value is a word. A boxed parameter the call read is kept and dropped as before, on the first turn only.

Left out:

- **Boxed results.** Measured with a variant of the pass that takes them (20,000 turns, a 1,000-node list, instructions / cycles against main): a consumer that only reads the list 2.12x / 1.49x; one that rebuilds it 1.34x / 1.47x; a small record after a costly call 7.4x / 5.9x. But the cost is not local: with a second, unrelated loop over the same list type in the file, 20 turns of a shared list make that loop run 2.7x the instructions and 1.74x the cycles (1,796M / 368M to 4,898M / 638M). The mechanism is inferred from `facts_hot`, not traced: a shared value forces its type hot for the whole program. Not clearly a gain, so left out; taking them only where the type is already shared would need the emitter's facts.
- **A second fixed call in the same def**, and the same call when no arm that holds it also calls the def (a call only in the exit arm).
- **A self call bound by a `let` before the statement that holds the call** keeps calling the def itself: only later calls can take the value.
- **Loops through another def** (a helper that matches a computed value and calls back): only a def's direct calls to itself are read.
- **IO loops:** an action is a function of its continuation, so its calls sit under a lambda.
- **`@unsafe` defs:** parameters whose type holds an Array, a closure or a type variable.
- **Cluster gates, CUDA, Linux and x86** have not run.

## Cost

+2,329 ttok. Each def the pass fires on is emitted twice.

title: The native lane skips an argument that `bend file.bend` and the JS lane evaluate, when the call's selector is a literal: one prints 100, the others stop with the Nat message
body:
### What you did

`bend drop.bend`, `bend drop.bend -o drop.js && node drop.js`, and `bend drop.bend -o drop && ./drop`, built from main `8c329c1b`.

### What happened

The file checks (`ALL PROOFS CHECK`). `bend file.bend` and the JS lane stop the program; the native executable prints a result.

```text
$ bend drop.bend
bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1

$ bend drop.bend -o drop.js && node drop.js
bend: a Nat past the largest immediate 2^48-1

$ bend drop.bend -o drop && ./drop
100
```

`pick(boom(k), 0n, 100n)` never reads its first argument, and `boom(k)` goes past the Nat limit. The C lane never runs `boom`; the JS lane does.

It depends on the selector being a literal:

| call | `bend file.bend` | JS | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pick(boom(k), 0n, 100n)` | stops | stops | `100` |
| `pick(boom(k), Nat.sub(k, k), 100n)` (a run-time zero) | stops | stops | stops |
| the same call, with `pick` rewritten to return `z` without a match | stops | stops | stops |
| `x : Nat = boom(k)` as an unused `let`, then print `100n` | `100` | `100` | `100` |

So the C lane skips the argument only where it can unfold `pick` at compile time. That is my reading of the table; I did not trace it in `comp.ts`.

I am not saying which answer is the right one, only that the lanes differ on a checked program. #775 was the same shape with a difference in cost only, and #1726 to #1729 went the other way (the native lane evaluated an overflowing call the result did not need).

### The file

```python
import Base

# stops the program: a Nat past 2^48 - 1
def boom(+k: Nat) -> Nat:
  Nat.mul(Nat.mul(k, k), Nat.mul(k, k))

def pick(x: Nat, y: Nat, z: Nat) -> Nat:
  match y:
    case 0n:
      z
    case 1n+p:
      x

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    +k : Nat = Nat.add(100000n, List.length(&1, String, args))
    IO.print(Nat.show(pick(boom(k), 0n, 100n)))
```

### bend version

bend 2.0.40 (main `8c329c1b`)

### uname -sm

Darwin arm64

### clang --version (the first line)

Apple clang version 17.0.0 (clang-1700.6.4.2)

Found while testing #2180.

title: `@unsafe` lets a function be a `+` parameter, and the native lane fail-stops when a closure with a run-time capture is applied twice (`bend file.bend` and JS print the result)
body:
### What you did

`bend twice.bend`, `bend twice.bend -o twice.js && node twice.js`, and `bend twice.bend -o twice && ./twice`, built from main `8c329c1b`.

### What happened

`bend file.bend` and the JS lane print the result; the native executable fail-stops, at one thread and at the default count.

```text
$ bend twice.bend
5

$ bend twice.bend -o twice.js && node twice.js
5

$ bend twice.bend -o twice && ./twice
bend: runtime fail-stop
$ echo $?
1
```

`twice` takes a function as a `+` parameter and applies it twice. Without `@unsafe` the checker refuses the def:

```text
- expected : Data
- observed : Type
Note: +f can be used many times, so its type must be Data.
```

With `@unsafe` the file is accepted (`--check-only` reports only that `twice` and `main` rely on unsafe code), and the C lane then fail-stops on the second application.

What I found about when it happens:

- The closure has to capture a run-time value. `x => Nat.add(x, 0n)`, which captures nothing, prints the result on all three lanes.
- A loop that applies `f` once a turn (`loop(p, f, Nat.add(acc, f(7n)))`) behaves the same way: 147 on `bend file.bend` and JS, fail-stop natively.
- A closure built by another def (`mk(c)` returning `x => Nat.add(x, c)`) behaves the same way.

The guide says `@unsafe` "skips the termination check" and that "reusable variables require `Data`". So either `@unsafe` should not lift the `Data` requirement on a `+` parameter, or the C lane should run what the other two lanes run. I do not know which is intended.

### The file

```python
import Base

@unsafe def twice(+f: Nat -> Nat) -> Nat:
  Nat.add(f(1n), f(2n))

def main() -> IO(Unit):
  do IO<Unit>:
    args : List<String> <- IO.args()
    +k : Nat = List.length(&1, String, args)
    IO.print(Nat.show(twice(x => Nat.add(x, k))))
```

title: fix(comp): a full ring refuses a push, and its task goes to the next ring (#2103)
body:
`ring_push` reserved its slot with a fetch-add on `put` and then read `get` once. A stale `get` (#2103), or a ring that was really full, posted `ERR_RING` and killed the run. The slot it had already reserved was never written, which is the hole #2102 describes.

A full ring now refuses a push instead:

- **`ring_push`** moves `put` with a relaxed CAS, and only onto a slot that is free. A refused push reserves nothing. It returns whether it took the task.
- **The two callers** (`task_deal`, `monk_step`) keep their shape. A refused task goes to `task_miss`.
- **`task_miss`** is out of line (`FAR`). It deals the task to the next ring the caller's own rule picks: `ring_pick` on a grow, or a fresh `H_CURSOR` value on a drain. So a turn still visits every ring that holds a task. It posts `ERR_RING` only after `CUBE_T` refusals in a row.

Blocking until `get` moves is not safe here. On a drain turn, a ring's owner stops at its `put0` snapshot, so a ring full of next-turn tasks never drains. On the GPU, a lane can't wait on another lane in its own SIMD group. That is why a refused task goes to another ring instead.

Supersedes #2159, which retries the room check 64 times. That makes the false error rarer but doesn't remove it, and it leaves the reserved-but-unwritten slot.

Closes #2103.

## Cap

`bend2/comp.ts` is **66,202 / 66,000 ttok** (main is 65,981). `bun gates/repo.ts`: **55/56**, failing only on that cap. This needs about 200 tokens trimmed elsewhere, or a cap decision.

## Tests

`bun gates/test.ts`: **1861/1861**.

## Full rings

A real ring never fills in the benches. To make rings fill, I built every runtime bench with `RING_LEN` forced to 4, 2 and 1 and ran it on CPU (16 threads) and Metal, against main:

- Everything that passes on main passes here, with the same output.
- main dies with `runtime fail-stop` (`ERR_RING`) on `tree-bitonic` at 4 slots (CPU), on `tree-bitonic` (CPU and GPU) and `kmeans` (CPU) at 2, and on `kmeans` (GPU) at 1. This branch prints the right result in each of those.
- What still fails at 1–2 slots fails on main too, and here it only fails after 128 refused rings in a row, which is real exhaustion.
- There were no hangs and no wrong outputs. main's GPU results at these sizes change from run to run.

## Perf

`gates/perf.ts --pin` on the cluster: 4 runs of this branch alternated with 11 runs of main, 5 rounds each. Ratios are medians against main; every run passed 124/124.

| | SEQ-CPU | PAR-CPU | PAR-GPU |
|---|---|---|---|
| this PR | 0.996 | 0.992 | 1.000 |
| #2159 (3 runs) | 1.018 | 1.036 | 0.999 |

The GPU cells that a first version slowed down are back at baseline: `raytrace` 1.000, `histogram` 1.001, `tree-bitonic` 0.992 and `bfs` 1.002. The CAS itself measured free. What had cost 2–4% was retry code inlined into the kernel, which is why the retry lives in `task_miss`.

The remaining shifts are about +1.5% at most: `kmeans` GPU, `queens` and `symreg` SEQ, and `queens` PAR. That is code-layout size, and #2159 shows similar shifts in other cells.

title: A def whose tail adds calls to itself carries the sum in a parameter: any spelling of the add, U32, and two or more calls
body:
**Stacks on #2175** (the first commit here is #2175's; review the second). **`comp.ts` is 67,042 ttok, 1,042 over the 66,000 cap** (main 65,966; #2175 66,444; this adds 598 to #2175), so `repo-gate` fails until that is settled. Measured on one Mac (M4), not on the cluster: the `test` and `perf` gates have not been run.

## What it does

#2175 turned one shape into a loop: a tail `Nat.add` of one call to the def itself, or `1n+f(..)`. This takes the same idea as far as the counts below justify:

- **any spelling of the add**: the call bound by a `let` first, adds inside adds, successors over an add and an add over successors;
- **`U32.add`** as well as `Nat.add`;
- **two or more calls under one add**: every call but the last stays a call, the last becomes the loop. This is what reaches `fib`, `pascal`, `coins` and `binarytrees`;
- **a def that is not flat for another reason** (its operand calls a recursion, or it tail-calls a def that forks): its own recursion still becomes a loop.

```python
def fib(+n: Nat) -> Nat:          def check(t: Tree) -> Nat:
  match n:                          match t:
    case 0n:                          case Leaf{}:
      0n                                0n
    case 1n+p:                        case Node{l, r}:
      match p:                          Nat.add(1n, Nat.add(check(l), check(r)))
        case 0n:
          1n
        case 1n+pp:
          a = fib(p)
          b = fib(pp)
          Nat.add(a, b)
```

Two calls need the sum to live across the call that stays, so the sum can no longer be a local of one C loop (#2175's `u64 acc`). It is a parameter instead: the def goes on in a second def, `d~acc`, which takes the sum so far first, and a call that stays is handed the sum and answers it grown. `fib` is compiled as if it had been written

```python
def fib~acc(acc: Nat, +n: Nat) -> Nat:      def fib(+n: Nat) -> Nat:
  match n:                                    fib~acc(0n, n)
    case 0n:
      Nat.add(acc, 0n)
    case 1n+p:
      match p:
        case 0n:
          Nat.add(acc, 1n)
        case 1n+pp:
          fib~acc(fib~acc(acc, p), pp)
```

which is the shape the `hanoi` kernel already has by hand. With one call under the add there is no call left and `d~acc` is a C loop, as in #2175.

Because the sum is now an ordinary parameter, **#2175's emitter code is gone** (`acc_of`, `acc_on`, the `u64 acc` local, the wrapped `emit_put` and the branch in `emit_body`): one rewrite on the checked terms in `file_book` (`acc_def`) builds `d~acc`, and the emitter compiles it like any def, so frames, borrows, spares and forks need no case of their own. For #2175's own shapes the emitted loop is the same statements with `acc` as a parameter.

## The rule

`acc_def(d)`, C lane only:

- d answers a `Nat` or a `U32`, and calls itself somewhere outside a tail position.
- Every such call is an operand of a tail add: directly, under nested `Nat.add` / `U32.add`, under successors, or through a `let` that binds exactly that call and whose name is read once.
- Then, in `d~acc`: the other operands are added to `acc` (bound before the calls), each call takes the sum in turn, the last one as a tail call; a plain tail call to d passes `acc` on; any other answer `v` is `acc + v`. d itself is `d~acc(0, ..)`.
- If any reference to d is left after that (a call in an operand, in an argument, behind `!`, in a closure, in a fork, a bound name read twice), the def is left exactly as it was.
- Never taken: `F32`; a def in a tail cycle with another def (its tail calls would become calls); a def with 247 live parameters (no room for one more).

**Why the reordering is sound, per operator and shape:**

- **`Nat.add`, one call.** The recursion adds from the innermost call out, the loop from the first step on. Add is associative and commutative, and Nats only grow under it, so every value the carried sum takes is at most the answer of the outermost call: it passes 2^48-1 exactly when that answer does, and both stop with the same message. (#2175's argument.)
- **`Nat.add`, two or more calls.** The same sum is carried through every call of the tree, so the same bound holds: the carried sum is always a sum of some of the terms of the outermost call's answer. Main meets the wall at the last add on the way out at the latest; here it is met as soon as the terms seen so far pass it. Same message, an earlier point in time.
- **`U32.add`.** It wraps, so any order gives the same word and no add can stop the program. Commutativity is used (operands are added before the calls' results) and holds.
- **A call bound by a `let`.** Same sum; the call now runs where its name is read, not at its `let`. Taken only when the name is read once, so no call runs twice.
- **Nested adds and successors.** `1n+x` is `Nat.add(1n, x)`; nesting is associativity.
- **A program that stops or does not return in an operand or a call:** see "Not covered", which lists every case where the point of death can differ. `@unsafe` defs are the only ones that may not return.

## Reach, counted before building

A counting pass over the checked terms (a hook in a scratch copy of the compiler) over every def of Base, the 908 tests that build, 18 demo programs, the 17 `bench/runtime` programs and the 22 koru kernels (`korulang/koru-benchmarks`, `suites/osprey-compute-kernels/bend`). Distinct defs that have the shape and that #2175 does not take; "reached" means the def would actually become a loop (it does not fork, has no other call to itself).

| candidate | defs | reached | on a hot path |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| one call, `Nat.add`, another spelling (let-bound, nested) | 2 | 1 | none (both are in #2175's own test) |
| one call, `U32.add` | 101 | 97 | none: 96 in tests, `Voices.count` in `app_slash_boss_3d` (at most 24 voices) |
| one call, `U32.xor` / `Bool.and` / `Bool.or` | 1 / 22 / 1 | not taken | none (tests; `Peer.has` in the netcode demo) |
| one call, `U32.mul`, `and`, `or`, `min`, `max`, `Nat.min`, `Nat.max` | 0 | | |
| one call, `Nat.mul` (unsound: a later zero) | 6 | not taken | `Nat.pow`, `Word.to_nat` in Base |
| two or more calls, `Nat.add` | 12 | 6 | **`fib`, `pascal` (`binom`), `coins` (`ways`): the whole kernel; `binarytrees` (`check`): one of its two walks.** Also `Map.size` in Base |
| two or more calls, `U32.add` | 71 | 34 | none: `esize` in `symreg`, once per candidate. 34 fork (the benches' `batch` drivers), 3 mix operators (`symreg`'s `eval`) |
| two or more calls, `U32.mul` / `xor` / `or`, `Bool.and` | 6 | not taken | `symreg`'s `eval` (mixed, below), `ascending` in `pure_par_sort` |
| affine (`d + k * f(rest)`) | 2 | not taken | none (one test; `Word.to_nat`, which is `Nat`) |

So the two-call case is where the hot code is, the other spellings are needed by it (`fib` and `coins` bind their calls with `let`, `check` nests its adds), and `U32.add` is wide but cold: it costs 10 tokens on top, so it is in. `hanoi` is not reached: it already carries its sum in a parameter.

As built: under #2175, 31 defs outside Base are loops (plus `List.length` and `String.length`); here 93 are loops and 38 more carry the sum across a call that stays or a callee that is not flat (plus `Map.size`). 176 of the 965 programs that build emit different C from #2175: 161 tests, 7 kernels, 6 demos, 2 benches.

## Bounds by hand, before the compiler work

The four kernels rewritten in the source with the sum passed through the calls (`fib(pp, fib(p, acc))`), built with main. Instructions retired, one thread:

| kernel | main | by hand | | this PR |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `fib` | 627.9M | 482.1M | -23.2% | 472.7M |
| `binarytrees` | 1,639.2M | 1,364.0M | -16.8% | 1,344.1M |
| `pascal` | 2,570.0M | 2,043.5M | -20.5% | 1,976.2M |
| `coins` | 653.6M | 519.7M | -20.5% | 519.4M |

Keeping the sum in the frame instead (`fib(pp, Nat.add(acc, fib(p, 0n)))`) gives -2.9% on `fib`, which is why the calls take the sum. `symreg`'s `eval` adds in one arm and subtracts, multiplies and xors in three others: with only the add arm carried, by hand, it runs **+1.3%** instructions on main and +5.3% on #2177, so a def with a call to itself outside the add is left alone.

## Results

One M4, one thread, GPU off, `cc -O3`, `/usr/bin/time -l`. Each build is swept over 16 placements (0 to 15 `nop`s at the head of the text, 4 bytes each), 3 rounds, the least per placement; cycles are least / median / most over the placements, and the last column is the range of this / main over the same placement.

| kernel | instructions, main and #2175 | this | | cycles, main | this | this / main |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---:|
| `fib` | 627.7M | 472.7M | -24.7% | 102.1M / 103.2M / 110.3M | 79.5M / 81.6M / 87.2M | 0.721 to 0.848 |
| `pascal` | 2,569.8M | 1,976.2M | -23.1% | 439.2M / 453.3M / 466.9M | 339.1M / 350.9M / 369.5M | 0.728 to 0.841 |
| `coins` | 653.4M | 519.4M | -20.5% | 146.8M / 147.0M / 147.2M | 91.7M / 101.2M / 103.5M | 0.624 to 0.705 |
| `binarytrees` | 1,639.0M | 1,344.1M | -18.0% | 268.8M / 279.1M / 298.5M | 235.1M / 236.9M / 248.3M | 0.790 to 0.914 |

The three kernels #2175 already reached keep its numbers (against #2175, same sweep): `collatz` 167.2M and 167.2M instructions, cycles 0.985 to 1.004; `digitsum` 166.7M and 166.7M, 0.956 to 1.038; `textstats` 201.4M and 201.4M, 0.991 to 1.020. The other 15 kernels emit identical C.

**With #2176 and #2177** (which attack the same recursions from the call and return side). Instructions, and the median cycles over 16 placements:

| kernel | main | #2176 | #2176 + this | #2177 | #2177 + this | this alone |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `fib` | 627.7M / 103.3M | 585.1M / 99.6M | 415.1M / 73.8M | 481.4M / 74.1M | 399.4M / 68.4M | 472.7M / 81.6M |
| `binarytrees` | 1,639.0M / 278.9M | 1,634.4M / 283.6M | 1,270.7M / 226.7M | 1,477.0M / 234.9M | 1,191.9M / 214.1M | 1,344.1M / 236.9M |
| `pascal` | 2,569.8M / 455.1M | 2,249.8M / 455.5M | 1,723.3M / 379.5M | 2,249.8M / 456.0M | 1,723.3M / 380.7M | 1,976.2M / 350.9M |
| `coins` | 653.5M / 147.1M | 593.7M / 146.9M | 474.6M / 102.2M | 564.1M / 161.0M | 445.0M / 103.2M | 519.4M / 101.2M |

In instructions the gains add on all four (within 1.5 points of the product on three; `fib` overlaps: -23.3% and -24.7% give -36.4%). In cycles they add on `fib` and `binarytrees`. On `pascal` they conflict: #2176 removes 12.5% of the instructions at no cycle gain on main, and on top of this PR the build runs 8% more cycles than this PR alone (375.2M to 385.2M over the placements against 339.1M to 369.5M; not traced). On `coins` #2177 alone is 9% slower than main in cycles (1.036 to 1.115 per placement) and level with this PR once both are in. `hanoi` and `tak` are not reached and emit identical C.

**Bend's suite.** 15 of the 17 `bench/runtime` programs emit byte-identical C to #2175. `histogram` (`half`, taken by #2175, now through `half~acc`): 44,362.6M and 44,363.6M instructions (+0.002%), cycles 6,271.4M / 6,349.9M / 6,629.4M and 6,270.1M / 6,348.5M / 6,618.4M. `symreg` (`esize`, two calls under `U32.add`, once per candidate): 50,766.6M and 50,760.4M instructions (-0.01%). Its cycles move from 12,201M / 12,639M / 13,423M to 10,733M / 10,922M / 11,131M at every placement, with every segment of `eval` textually identical in the two builds: that is the segment order shifting (nine `esize` segments become six, placed before `eval`), the layout sensitivity of this bench, not a gain of the rule.

Compile time: `app_slash_boss_3d` 680 ms and 669 ms; the 161 tests whose C changes, 14.23 s and 14.43 s in total (+1.4%).

## Cost

Measured by removing each part from the final file (ttok):

| part | ttok |
|---|---:|
| the rewrite: one or many calls under one `Nat.add`, nested adds, `d~acc` and its caller (#2175's one-call version was 478) | 786 |
| a call bound by a `let` | 163 |
| successors over and under the add (#2175 had them) | 60 |
| the sum bound before the calls (`collatz`, below) | 37 |
| the tail-cycle check, the arity guard | 11, 9 |
| `U32.add` | 10 |
| two or more calls | 0 |

166 of the total are the comment.

## Checks

All local, against #2175 (`e1b6a3e5`) unless said:

- **Native lane** (every test built and run with the GPU off, compared with its `#|` lines): 884 pass on #2175, 886 here (the two new stdout tests); no existing test's status differs.
- **Memory:** every test was emitted by both compilers: 747 emit byte-identical C; the 161 that differ were built with `-DBEND_POISON` and a count of live heap words at exit, and give the same output, exit code and count, at the default thread count and at one thread (`nat_sum_loop`, edited here, was compared on its new source). So do the new tests and the adversarial files, against #2175 and against main.
- **JS lane:** byte-identical on all 959 tests that emit JS (alone, and emitted after the C in one process), apart from `stack_fault_trap`, whose source changed.
- **Metal:** the 8 tests with a `!` whose C changes, an adversarial file with the def behind `!`, and the new tests print the same with `--gpu on` and `--gpu off`, under both compilers.
- **Demos:** the 6 whose C changes build; `proof_numerics` prints the same.
- **New tests**, each printing its lines under `bend file.bend`, as JS under bun, and on the C lane of main, #2175 and this branch; the numbers were computed apart in Python:
  - `tests/run/sum_loop_shapes.bend`: one call in every spelling, `U32` past 2^32, a tail call to a def that forks, an operand that recurses, an operand that reads a list the call also gets, an absurd arm; and what must stay a recursion: a bound call used twice, `U32.sub`, `F32.add` (64 ones under 1e8, where the order changes the answer), a call behind `!`, a call in a closure.
  - `tests/run/sum_loop_calls.bend`: two calls bound by lets in either order, nested, under successors, three calls, `U32`, erased parameters, an operand that consumes a list beside the calls, a tree lent twice and then given, a sum that lands on 2^48-1, the def under a fork with another def beside the sum, a tree twenty thousand deep on either side, an Array of closures called at its leaves; a bound call used twice stays.
  - `tests/run/sum_loop_overflow.bend`: one past 2^48-1 over a tree stops with the Nat message.
- **Adversarial files** (scratch): the same shapes at larger sizes (three million steps, a tree a million deep on each side), the overflow with the extra one at the root and at the last leaf, the def under `!`, as a function value and as a template, and a pair of `@unsafe` defs in a tail cycle run for 800 million rounds.
- **Wrong versions:** 15 deliberately wrong versions of the rule were built as compilers. The new tests fail 11: `sub` taken for `add`, `F32` taken, the sum dropped where the def answers, operands dropped, a name bound once but read twice taken (times out: `2^40` calls), successors counted as one, the sum started at 1, only the live arguments rebuilt, an operand left untyped (the compiler refuses), the absurd arm summed (the compiler refuses), only the first call threaded. The tail-cycle check removed is caught only by the 800-million-round scratch file (the stack faults). Taking a fork's call or a call behind `!` prints the same and differs only in the C (the fork is gone, the `!` is lost): no `#|` line can see it. Keeping a def with calls left over is not wrong, only useless.

**Two tests changed.** `tests/io/stack_fault_trap.bend` faults the machine stack with a `U32` recursion whose tail is a sum of one call to itself: that is now a loop, so its result is xored before the adds and the recursion stays one. `tests/run/nat_sum_loop.bend` (from #2175) asked for fifty thousand steps; on this machine the interpreter and the JS lane (bun 1.3.14, node 26.3.1) fault between thirty and fifty thousand frames, so it asks for twenty thousand.

**Found on the way.** (1) An operand moved under the new add without its type made the compiler stop with "a type the C facts cannot read" whenever it was a call that is not flat (found by an adversarial file and by `tests/reg/array_function_element`); every term the rewrite builds is now typed, and a wrong version without it fails the new tests. (2) With the grown sum written as an argument of the tail call, `collatz` ran 6% fewer instructions than #2175 and 14% more cycles at every placement (clang merges the two arms' tails); binding the sum before the calls gives #2175's code back. (3) Behind `!`, a recursion deeper than the device's 1,023 frames faults on Metal on main and on #2175 (`bound!(5000n)`, the let-bound sum of the tests); a def taken here loops, so it prints its answer.

## Not covered

- **Cluster gates, CUDA, Linux and x86** have not run. `tsc` was not run. No timing at 8 threads.
- **The JS lane and the interpreter** are untouched: there the defs still recurse.
- **Only add.** `U32.xor` (1 def), `Bool.and` (23) and `Bool.or` (1) have the shape in tests and two demos and nothing hot; no def has it for `mul`, `and`, `or`, `min`, `max`. `Nat.mul` and `F32` are unsound. Affine sums (`d + k * f(rest)`) have two defs.
- **A def with a call to itself anywhere else** (other arms with other operators, a call in an argument) is left alone: measured a loss on `symreg`'s `eval`.
- **A fork's calls stay a fork** (`a b = f(l) f(r)` then `Nat.add(a, b)`): 42 defs under an add, the benches' drivers among them. Carrying the sum through would make the calls depend on each other.
- **Every way evaluation can differ from main:**
  - The sum is added in another order. A `Nat` sum that passes 2^48-1 stops with the same message at an earlier point: before calls and operands that main would have run first. So a program that passes the limit and also fails, or (in an `@unsafe` def) never returns, in one of those stops with the Nat message here.
  - A recursion whose only failure was its depth no longer fails: the last call under each tail add holds no frame.
  - Inside one tail add, the operands that are not calls now run before the calls (main runs the calls first), and the calls run in the order they stand in the add. A call bound by a `let` runs where its name is read, after any `let` between. If two of them fail, which one stops the program can differ.
  - A bound call whose name one arm adds and another arm never reads does not run in the arm that never reads it (main runs it before the match).
  - A tail call from a taken def to another def is now a call and an add: one frame while that def runs. Where that def calls back without a tail call (only `@unsafe` allows it), a round holds two frames where it held one.
  - Ownership can shift at a call site, as in #2175: a def that becomes flat is called where its value is needed.

title: perf(parse): column and newline queries read a line table instead of scanning back
body:
> **This PR edits `bend2/bend.ts`, which AGENTS.md marks as human-written.** It was opened at Nicolas's request, as a proposal for the file's owner to review, rewrite or close.

Closes #2003.

**What.** `parse_col` searched back to the previous newline at every query, and `parse_nl` rescanned the whitespace before the same position at every query. With n nested lambdas on one line, or n spaces before their closing `)`, both add up to O(n²).

`parse_book` now builds a table once per file (`parse_lines`): the line of each position, and each line's start and first non-blank position. Both queries read it in O(1). Their answers depend only on the position, so backtracking needs nothing restored. `parse_col` now takes the `Parse` instead of the source string; its 8 callers all passed `p.str`.

**Parse time** (in-process `parse_book`, best of 9; the issue's family: n lambdas and n spaces before `)`)

| n | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 3.4 ms | 0.8 ms |
| 2000 | 19.8 ms | 1.4 ms |
| 4000 | 64.7 ms | 2.9 ms |

`base.bend` (best of 60, alternating runs): main 4.9–6.4 ms, this PR 5.0–5.3 ms. Building the table takes 0.33 ms for its 90k characters.

**Checks**
- Every `.bend` file under `tests/` (1874 files) prints the same output and exit code with `--check-only` as on main, error messages included.
- A fuzz test of the old and new functions over 310k positions in random strings of spaces, tabs, `\r`, `\n` and text found no difference except one. At position 0 of a source that starts with `\n`, the old `parse_col` returned 0 (`lastIndexOf` with index -1), and the new one returns 1. The parser always skips whitespace before asking for a column, so that position is never queried.
- `bend.ts` 45949 → 46089 ttok (cap 48000).
- The cluster gates (`gates/test.ts`, `gates/perf.ts`) were not run.

title: perf(parse): a group's operator names are resolved once, not again by each outer group
body:
> **This PR edits `bend2/bend.ts`, which AGENTS.md marks as human-written.** It was opened at Nicolas's request, as a proposal for the file's owner to review, rewrite or close.

Closes #2011.

**What.** Each `(.. : T)` group calls `parse_term_ns` to give its operators `T`'s namespace. The walk goes through `Bool.and`, `Bool.or` and `String.append`, so with n nested groups each outer group walks every inner chain again: O(n²).

A walk renames every `.op` it reaches. Walking the result again reaches no node the first walk did not: a renamed op is either one of those three names, which the walk goes through as before, or a name that stops it. A second walk therefore changes nothing. The parser now marks a term in a `WeakSet` on `Parse` (`nsd`) when its walk returns, and an outer walk stops at a marked term. As the issue notes, a fixed name alone is not enough, since its arguments can still hold unresolved operators. An unmarked `Bool.and` is still walked.

- The mark is set only after the walk returns. A walk that throws during a backtracked parse leaves nothing marked.
- After a walk, the parser changes a term in place only by this rename and the `!` flag on a `Ref`. `body_sub` wraps terms in new `Sub` nodes and does not mutate them, so a marked term cannot gain a new `.op`.

**Parse time** (in-process `parse_book`, best of 15; n nested `(.. && True{} : Bool)` groups on one line)

| n | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 500 | 7.6 ms | 0.7 ms |
| 1000 | 32.3 ms | 1.1 ms |
| 2000 | 136.7 ms | 1.8 ms |

#2185 (the #2003 column fix) makes no difference on this family on its own. `base.bend` (best of 60, alternating runs): main 4.2–4.7 ms, this PR 4.4–4.8 ms.

**Checks**
- Every `.bend` file under `tests/` (1874 files) prints the same output and exit code with `--check-only` as on main, error messages included. About 430 of them use operators inside `: T` groups.
- `bend.ts` 45949 → 46041 ttok (cap 48000).
- The cluster gates (`gates/test.ts`, `gates/perf.ts`) were not run.
- This PR and #2185 both change the `Parse` type line, so whichever merges second needs a one-line rebase.

title: fix(io): preserve errors in zero-cap line reads

Native `File.read_line(file, 0)` now uses the existing zero-byte read path. It returns `EBADF` on a write-only handle and leaves unread buffered data available on a readable handle.
